Slumdog opens up with a bang and leads to a question appearing on screen, a la Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. We're asked whether Jamal has won the show by either cheating, being lucky, or if it was written. Yet ironically, the show Jamal is on, the centerpiece of the film, is not the best part of it, though it probably has some of the most humor. No, it is in fact the flashbacks where we are told of Jamal's life and the simple, yet beautiful love between him and Lakita. Boyle manages to take a stale idea about love and makes it fresh again in one of his best films.

Jamal (Dev Patel) is a slumdog living in the poverty stricken areas of Mumbai, India. He is a sincere boy, much like the main protagonist from City of God with which this film holds several comparisons towards, and is easily sympathized with from the beginning. He is the Oliver Twist of our generation. His life story is told through intricate weaving of flashbacks through the game show he is on and in his interegation, where somehow the men that electrocute him do not understand how a slumdog could be so intelligent and sincere. Despite this and all the dangers and perils Jamal encountered in his life, he survives. His energy is infectious like the rest of the film.

Through the flashbacks, we meet characters like Lakita (Freida Pinto), the love interest of Jamal who endures as much trauma and pain, if not more, as him, who has a strong vitality of life and endures on. Both her and Jamal represent something all of us could use a little more of in these hard stricken times: hope. Jamal's brother Salim (Madhur Mittal), shows what happens to the other poverty children, where corruption and desperation seeps in and anything will be done in order to be on top and away from the bottom in which they had been stuck at. He joins mobs, does horrendous acts to people, yet he's not totally nonredeemable by the end. There's always hope.

The mainstream audience is hardly exposed to the degregation and poverty of India, and trust me, its there. Some have complained that Boyle glamorizes poverty, but its obvious they are watching a different movie. His highly stylized and frenetic camera movement does not make the poverty seem any less gritty, rather its just a technical move which is highly effective and captivating film making. If the favelas seem like the type of place you want to live in, well then all the power to you. But Boyle's use of authentic locations bring out the dirty, grimy world many inhabitants of India have to endure on a daily basis, in a country far too over populated. One shot shows Jamal running through the streets of the favelas and Boyle pulls back the camera three times, finally coming back far enough to reveal the long stretches these poorly made homes and stalls extend out to. It is a breathtaking moment.

The rest of the relatively unknown cast, such as Prem (Anil Kapoor) and Inspector (Irfan Khan) round out the movie with memorable and outstanding performances. The amount of heart present throughout is tremendous and makes for one of the most uplifting movies of the year, even if some horrible things do happen. And those horrible scenes are really that terrifying - one scene involving spoons and eyes will certainly stick with you long after the movie ends. Yet the humor is here too and a few red chilies are guaranteed to put a smile on your face. The whole experience is one long, speeding bullet of energy and magic, fable like qualities.

Danny Boyle has proven to be a master of genres, whether it be horror, drug related, comedy, sci-fi, family, and now Bollywood/romance films. I don't know how much longer he can keep this up, but hopefully forever. I obviously loved this film and it will go down as something that people, and myself, will remember for years.

Slumdog Millionaire is the film garnering the most acclaim for the 2008 awards season. It is the critical darling in an even bigger way than Little Miss Sunshine and Juno have been in recent years. It started off with a bang when it came out of nowhere to win the People's Choice award at it's Toronto Film Festival debut, before it even had a commercial distribution deal. Then it found its place onto so many top ten lists of professional and amateur critics alike, that it's 86 percent approval rating helped it land in the #6 spot on Metacritic.com's best-reviewed films of the year list. Most recently, it took home four Golden Globes, including the "big three" (best screenplay, best director, best picture). With a whopping eleven British Film and Television nominations and a big chance to take home lots of gold on Oscar night, things are just beginning for this Little Film That Could, and naturally, I went in with high expectations.

To say I was disappointed is a major understatement. This is easily the worst film of the 2008, a year that I didn't think could stoop any lower after the eye- and ear-sore that was Mamma Mia.

The so-called plot, based on the novel "Q&A" by Vikas Swarup, follows a street kid as he answers every question correctly on the Indian version of the once-popular game show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." The opening scene reveals that the story is told in flashback, as the iconic game show footage is inter-cut with the boy being interrogated after the fact, as he has been accused of cheating. How could a "slumdog" know more than other distinguished guests who have never passed a certain milestone on the show? Why of course, every single question he's given is related to a significant and horrifying event from his childhood surviving the Mumbai slums. In chronological order, no less. What a convenient story-telling device!

Try contrived. And just as gimmicky and manipulative as the brainless former hit of a game show we all used to love.

The acting here is downright insulting, to the point that I wonder how so many people have fallen for the movie so hard. The hero, Jamal, played by Dev Patel in his adult years and in all the game show and interrogation scenes, perpetually looks like a deer caught in the headlights. It's as one-note a performance as I've ever seen in such an acclaimed film. Freida Pinto, the object of Jamal's affection, is given nothing to do but look pretty and sad for the whole film. The interrogator and his buffoons, the children playing the two leads in younger years, and the trio of actors playing Jamal's brother at different ages, are all completely forgettable. And the "Millionaire" host, dressed in a glittery suit with perfect hair and diamond-stud earrings, comes off as an even smarmier version of Regis Philbin, with a creepy dash of George Michael thrown in.

Director Danny Boyle, one of the biggest hit-and-miss (but mostly miss) directors in recent history, uses splashes of vibrant colour and dizzying hand-held cameras to glamourize Indian life in the slums. Such techniques are used to great effect in other films I have loved, such as Moulin Rouge, Once, and Rachel Getting Married. But here, it is simply a nauseating assault of the senses. Boyle could take a page from Alfonso Cuarón's book, who recently gave us Children of Men, a beautifully-shot, but not at all glamourous film set in apoplectic England. That film managed to put together some breathtaking hand-held shots of a depressing world, without making it look like a music video or a tourism ad. Slumdog on the other hand, is so falsely pretty, it made me feel sleazy just watching it. 

It doesn't help that the flick doesn't know what genre it wants to be. Count me as one of the shocked few in the audience when this "crowd-pleaser" opened with scenes of graphic torture. The comedy works on the level of an eight-year-old. Newsflash: human excrement is still not funny. The romance, if you can call it that, has zero energy, heart, or heat, and the big payoff dramatic moment falls completely flat. We know from the start what is going to happen, because "it is written." And the Golden Globes also featured a major spoiler in its telecast. Way to go Foreign Press. If that's not enough, the closing credits are staged as a Bollywood musical.

It really shouldn't come as a big surprise that this film has become such a hit. It panders to the audience, and is as witless and empty as the junk food television it is based on. If you're looking for something just as intelligent, save yourself some trouble, stay home, and watch Deal or No Deal instead.

Slumdog Millionaire is one of those uplifting feel-good films that will eventually catch up with the general movie-going audience once the strong word-of-mouth lets loose (and a few Oscar nominations including Best Picture and Director); and unlike the overpraises of overrated and forgettable Juno and Little Miss Sunshine, this one deserves the praises it's getting- from the critics and the audiences alike. 

The film tells a tale of Jamal Malik, an orphaned boy living in a slum of Mumbai, India, and his triumph to overcome the odds of being; and his destined journey to find the love of his life; Latika played gorgeously by Freida Pinto. Even the plot sounds corny and a paint-by-numbers film, it's not. Don't let my amazingly simple synopsis fool you. 

The movie is many things exploring many issues and themes: it's about poverty; survival; brotherhood; redemption; growing-up; etc and above all those things, destiny. Slumddog Millionaire is a carefully structured film; featuring a distinctive original soundtrack by A. R. Rahman; and a great romance story to back it up. 

To put it simply, Slumdog Millionaire is a modern fairy-tale where you want to cherish almost every moment. You can call the romance between Jamal and Latika as cliches, but I see it more like a string of coincidences. Besides, this is a fairy-tale bound to end with a happy ending. I don't know if it has the legs to stand a test of time as a classic, but this made me smile for a whole week; and before I knew it, I went to see it again-this time with my family.

"D: It is written." Accused of cheating and desperate to prove his innocence, an eighteen-year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai reflects back on his tumultuous life while competing to win 20 million rupees on India's Who Wants to Be a Millionaire in Danny Boyle's inspirational drama. Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) may not have a penny to his name, but that could all change in a matter of hours. He's one question away from taking the top prize on India's most popular television game show, but as with everything else in Jamal's life, it isn't going to be easy. Arrested by police under suspicion of cheating, Jamal is interrogated by the authorities. The police simply can't believe that a common "slumdog" could possibly possess the knowledge to get this far in the game, and in order to convince them of how he gained such knowledge, Jamal begins reflecting back on his childhood. As young boys, Jamal and his older brother, Salim, lived in squalor, and lost their mother in a mob attack on Muslims. Subsequently forced to rely on their own wits to survive, the desperate siblings fell back on petty crime, eventually befriending adorable yet feisty young Latika as they sought out food and shelter on the unforgiving streets of Mumbai. Though life on the streets was never easy, Jamal's experiences ultimately instilled in him the knowledge he needed to answer the tough questions posed to him on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. And though Jamal makes a convincing case for himself, one question still remains: why would a young man with no apparent desire for wealth or fame be so determined to win big on a national game show? Of course, it won't be long until everyone finds out the answer to this burning question, because as Jamal sits down to find out whether he will be rich beyond his wildest dreams, 60 million viewers remain transfixed to their televisions eager to see if he'll correctly answer the final question. Review Slumdog Millionaire deserves its Golden Globe sweep (Best Motion Picture - Drama, Best Director, Best Original Score, Best Screenplay). The surprise hit will jolt you out of your ennui from all sides. Simon Beaufoy based the screenplay on Vikas Swarup's bestselling novel 'Q and A', about Jamal Malik, a poor orphan from the slums who wins the US$410,000 jackpot on "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?" to attract the attention of the woman he loves. He is accused of cheating, however, and to explain how he managed to answer each question, he recounts the fascinating tale that is his life. Director Danny Boyle (Sunshine, 28 Days Later, The Beach) and director for India Loveleen Tandan produced a frenetic film that still manages to be riveting enough to focus on equal parts colorful Indian landscape and gritty human reality, allowing you to experience a wide range of emotions. The original score by A.R. Rahman complements the visual assault with a fluid infusion of Indian-flavored electronic beats. The film is brilliantly cast, with Dev Patel as the older Jamal, Madhur Mittal as Jamal's older brother Salim, and Freida Pinto as the older Latika, Jamal's childhood friend and ultimate love interest. The three main characters' stories unravel from their past lives, and the actors who play them in their early teens and childhood all contributed marvelously (Boyle was reportedly crushed to learn of some of child actors' real poverty-stricken lives, and ensured them of their education and trust funds). Slumdog Millionaire is a socially-relevant drama that's also funny and heartwarming, modern without being cold. Consistent with Boyle's style, despite tackling dark themes, it still has room for positive vibes, daring you to see the beauty in despair. It may not be a Bollywood flick but it ends in traditional Bollywood style: a grand production number!

Danny Boyle's best film and 2008's Best Picture winner (it was written) bursts off the screen in a flurry of color and sound to immerse the viewer in the slums of Mumbai before lifting him to the sky with an invigorating tale of tenacity and young love. The film packs more exuberant energy and beautiful images per minute than any film in recent memory, and thanks to Danny Boyle's remarkably creative direction and the best efforts of his talented cast, the effect is exhilarating rather than exhausting, uplifting rather than oppressive. The eclectic story and international cast and crew have made a film that is both escapist and poignant, one that sweeps the viewer off his feet but stays with him after he lands. I find it heartening just to know that a movie so new, inventive and full of life can still find its way to the screen.

A teen wins 10,000,000 rupies on the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?", is accused of cheating, and tortured. It is then he begins to tell the story of his childhood in the Mumbai slums, and how he was able to answer all those questions. Moviemaking and storytelling at its finest, blending seemingly incompatible stories while incorporating all of the elements that make a great film. With the obvious preface that I have not seen every movie this year, this is the best film of 2008.

It is hard to believe that a film set in the slums of Mumbai (formerly Bombay) can be so gorgeous, but Slumdog Millionaire absolutely is.  I had the privilege of seeing this film during the Austin Film Festival, where a crowd of 1200 at the historic Paramount Theater gave director Danny Boyle a standing ovation.  And I patiently waited my turn to ask my own burning question.  He is delightful.

But the film: the story is based on a novel called Q&A by Vikas Swarup, about a kid from the slums who ends up on India's version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire.  The producers are convinced he is cheating, because how could a kid with no education possibly be able to answer such obscure questions, but Jamal tells the story of his life that by fate happens to cross paths with each of the questions. 

I had tried to listen to the audiobook version years ago on a roadtrip to Nebraska, but it just wasn't the right fit for the trip.  This film though, which takes liberties with the original (including a scene reminiscent of Trainspotting's worst toilet in Scotland -- which, btw, is what I talked to Boyle about), is completely engaging from the first scene to the last.

I have a weird relationship with Indian cinema, having cataloged hundreds of Bollywood films for the Ole Miss library without ever watching one from start to finish -- so I recognized several familiar faces, including Anil Kapoor (as the Indian Regis), and Irfan Khan (who was AWESOME last year in Mira Nair's the Namesake).  But there are certainly stars-to-watch in this film, especially Dev Patel (Jamal the adult).

In the post-film Q&A, Boyle discussed how though the saying goes never to work with children or animals in a film, he actually enjoys working with children because they work without pretension; their performances are genuine, but they don't understand why they have to do 25 takes.  The children in this film (Jamal, his brother Salim, and soul mate Latika) are phenomenal.

This film is not to be missed, and if there is any justice in the film world, we will hear Boyle's melodious Scottish brogue on Oscar night.

"Slumdog" Jamal who grew up on the streets of Bombay is at the brink of winning the grand prize of India's version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire when is is "questioned" by the police suspecting fraud. Danny Boyle's latest and highly acclaimed project has a lot of the energy that marked his debut. The clever structure of the film uses his explanations on how he knew the answers to fill in the background of what life is like for the most impoverished members of Indian society, brutalized in religious riots, either ignored or harassed by the authorities and exploited by criminals. In this way it's like a more light-hearted and less violent version of City Of God and has a modicum of the power and grittiness of that film. Some of the more disturbing aspects of what these kids go through was made more so by the fact that I watched this film in the company of an Indian person who assured me that these practices actually do go on (and in fact were even toned down for the film version). The entire cast are excellent, even the youngest of the children playing younger versions of the protagonists and the mix of comedy, action and drama is balanced perfectly. Unfortunately the film's strength and depth of character falters during the last reel. Blaming walloping great plot contrivances on "fate" just seemed lazy and the crowd pleasing ending felt a little hollow to me, marring what otherwise was an excellent film. The rest of it is definitely strong enough to warrant a viewing though and for me this is easily Boyle's best work since Trainspotting.

"A. He cheated" 
"B. He's lucky" 
"C. He's genius" 
"D. It is written" 




Eighteen year old Jamal Malik is having an amazing answering streak on the Indian version of the television game show, "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire". He's only one correct question away from the big prize. However, some, including those associated with the game show, question how someone like Jamal, a self confessed non-genius who grew up in the slums of Mumbai, can be doing so well on the show when others who are brighter, more educated and wealthier than him have failed. Is Jamal cheating? Is it purely luck that they have asked him the questions to which he knows the answers? Seeing Jamal's life journey to this point ultimately answers these questions. His life journey includes being orphaned at an early age; growing up with an older brother, Salim, who was both his guardian/protector and antagonist; and having a relationship since childhood with another orphaned child, a girl named Latika. His motivation for being on the show also may provide some answers to his success. Perhaps it was all just meant to be. Boyle's cinematography so enlivened by the sights and sounds of India's crowded shantytowns and bustling metropolis, as well as the careening emotional fluctuations of his protagonists. Employing his trademarked visual frenzy, Boyle wraps the viewer up in the chaotic motion of Indian street life, where life is cheap, the ramshackle communities are built on towers of rubbish, and the citizens make do the best they can. To track his impending "Millionaire" question showdown, Jamal is forced to relive his life for the local authorities, plunging back to horrors buried and childhood lost. Boyle plays with time and location to a dazzling degree, keeping the audience unsettled as the camera shadows Jamal's extreme boyhood trauma, facing shocking parental loss, "Oliver Twist" style exploitation from a kingpin of child street beggars, and the continual elusiveness of Latika, whose liberation from the clutches of sexual and physical abuse becomes a personal quest for Jamal. Slumdog Millionaire argues that the most valuable knowledge is that learned first-hand, though no intimate familiarity with the Bollywood cinema Boyle is paying respect to is necessary to be swept up in the director's rollicking, heartfelt saga.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is Danny Boyle's most accomplished film to date. It is terrifically, sometimes breathtakingly shot, and completely absorbing. The screenplay smartly structures the film about a boy in India who gets a chance to be on the Hindi version of WHO WANTS TO BE A MILLIONAIRE. I loved how every time a question came up, it made him think of something from his past. It's definitely one of the year's finest pictures, and it has many Oscar nominations in its near future.

Boyle takes a trip to slums in his latest pic; originally titled Scenes of Kids Running From Men With Sticks; a scantily-clad love story that includes no less than ten hyperactive chase scenes set to bass-heavy world music; a frenetic movie marred by stock dialogue and a romantic heroine with all of seven minutes of screentime; Boyle might look flashy to the M.I.A. fans in the house, but to everyone else he's a Meirelles and Innaritu knockoff who should keep to his own kind and make those zombie pictures. 
The crucial problem with liking this film is its absolutely grotesque undertones. Here we have Jamal, a poor chai-wallah, appearing on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, and the first thing we are asked is the same thing he will be asked to provide the movie's narrative pull: How did he know the answers? On cue, your choices arrive: A) He Cheated B) He's Lucky C) He's a Genius D) It is Written.
At the end of the film, we will receive our answer: D, It is Written.
This may seem like a rags-to-riches fairy tale, but let's examine this curious 'destiny' of his. It's a gigantic difference to simply let the coincidental anomalies play out and let Jamal take home the prize and to say it is his very fate to do so--after all, one implies at least a shred of shrewdness, while the other is fatalist (and almost works against the struggle-to-overcome storyline). Just look at what Jamal's savior is--an American television show; it's hand-me-down capitalism from The Developed World; this movie, in no uncertain terms, actually tells you that it is impoverished young men's destiny to be saved and rescued from certain ruin by American television. Is there really not another story of overcoming to be told? In a movie ostensibly about India, it seems remarkably Western; down to the British director helming it--it provides ignorant Americans a chance to see themselves not as invaders or enemies (see, it's the Indians who torture! not us!) but as true messiahs--and you didn't have to do anything! Nothing at all! Just syndicate television shows. Just imagine how much better India will be when we give them Deal or No Deal.

This is a Dickensian tale brought to life, not in the gutters of England, but the slums of India. It is a blend of hard, ugly reality and magical, romantic fantasy. We see a hard life, hard lived growing up in the toughest of situations - but the character and the narrative is driven by pure, powerful love and destiny; the stuff of fairy tales. What happens here happens because it was meant to happen. Jamal Malik is a contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? and he has made history by reaching the final question, but that can't possibly happen, what could a poor uneducated kid from the slums know about the world? His life brought him the answers and throughout this film we follow his key life changing events and how they were connected to every question asked, particularly when they pertain to his life with his one true love, Latika. His entire quest throughout the show is an attempt to find her, who was tore from him countless times through terrible circumstances. That sound you can hear is every die hard romantic in the audience's hearts swooning. It reads as fairly standard on page, but thanks to Danny Boyle's energetic visual style and no-nonsense approach to sentiment and the rich, beautiful scenary of India it becomes something altogether unique and unforgettable. It earns every moment of triumph and joy because it refuses to pull it's punches when depicting the kids troubled lives.

The film puts storytelling at the forefront, the main characters work as archetypes (while the supporting cast are more rounded and ambiguous) and it is the journey that takes precedence and it is delivered at a blinding pace and never sags once. I was enthralled from minute one right to the exhilirating end credits sequence.

one of the most original forms of storytelling i have seen in years, this brilliant film is nothing short of a masterpiece. it blends multiple genres, never focusing too much on one nor the other, allowing itself to be an appealing picture to a wide audience. you are taken far away from the touristic side of india, travelling deep into the heart of the mumbai slums. danny boyle's directing is precise with heart and passion, incorporating technical camera work which allows you to feel as if you are right there with the film's underdog protagonist, experiencing his every obstacle with him. simon beaufort's screenplay is a touch of genius, giving the audience equal parts crime story, drama, comedy, romance and a view of the third world. at times you will feel like crying, others you will laugh, and most moments, you will smile, realizing that among every dramatic aspect of this deep experience, is a feel good film that allows you to root for the underdog, and most of all, its a simple love story that works on a truly epic level, chronicling the life of a young man who came from nothing, but managed to find a gem amongst the slums he calls his home. phenomenal acting, and a true sense of its setting carry this to be the best film i have seen this year, and i have a feeling it will not be topped. it is the best work danny boyle has ever done, one that deserves to be rewarded. the oscar race has begun, and this is one hundred percent deserving of a place among the five best picture nominees of the year.

Jamal Malik is competing on India's version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? You don't just watch Danny Boyle's magnificent Slumdog Millionaire, you get swept up in its magic. Irish-born Boyle (he behind the dark magic of Shallow Grave, Trainspotting and 28 Days Later) sets his camera in the Indian capital of Mumbai and tells the story of Jamal (Dev Patel, outstanding) who is one question away from winning 20 million rupees on the Indian television version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?

But first, there's a torture scene. The police believe that 18-year old Jamal is a fraud, since he's managed to answer every question correctly. The show's host (Anil Kapoor, wonderful) the police inspector is determined to find out how this illiterate slumdog knows so much one night before he goes back onto the show.

Slumdog Millionaire, adapted from Vikus Swarup's episodic novel Q & A by Simon Beaufoy, brims with heartbreak and even welcome bits of humor. The colors of Mumbai pop off screen with a bristling sense of urgency. It's flashy, but never in a superficial way. That it looks at Mumbai through so many angles make it all the more vital (especially given the fact that Mumbai was the site of horrific terror attacks within days of the film's release).

We learn Jamal's brutal history through flashbacks. The question he's asked on the show happens to have answers found in Jamal's sordid back story. We see him growing up in poverty with his wild older brother Malik (later played by a forceful Madhur Mittal) and their mother. Every major incident of Jamal's life, including witnessing his mother's murder in an anti-Muslim riot, informs Jamal's answers. From there he goes into child exploitation to working a meager job. When he's eighteen he manages to track down his brother and his childhood sweetheart, Latika (the beautiful Frieda Pinto), now a plaything for the gangster Malik works for. Jamal gets on the show in the hopes Latika will see him.

Boyle doesn't sentimentalize at all. Instead he uses magical realism to allow some sense of hope to get in, and allow us to gleefully cheer on Jamal.

With help from cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle, using digital cameras to capture the vitality of Mumbai, Chris Dickens' amazing editing and a pulsing score from composer A.R. Rahman (with help from M.I.A.) Slumdog Millionaire grabs you on waves of heartbreak, romance and even suspense. It's a whoosh you won't soon forget, so that by the time the Bollywood dance number that ends the film occurs, you feel as if you've just been through a life-changing experience.

Is that enough to call Slumdog Millionaire one of the past decades very best? Final answer: Yes.

"Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million rupees. How did he do it? A. He cheated B. He's lucky C. He's a genius D. It is written" Danny Boyle's Slumdog Millionaire is the film world's first globalized masterpiece. This extravagantly eager romantic fable is set in contemporary Mumbai, the former Bombay, but it draws freely, often rapturously, from Dickens, Dumas, Hollywood, Bollywood, the giddiness of Americanized TV, the cross-cultural craziness of outsourced call centres and the zoominess of Google Earth. It's mostly in English, partly in Hindi and is directed by a Brit, with the help of an Indian co-director, Loveleen Tandan. The young hero, Jamal Malik, is a dirt-poor orphan from the Mumbai slums. "Is this heaven?," Jamal asks after tumbling from a train and looking up to see the Taj Mahal. I had the same feeling after watching the first few astonishing scenes: Was this film heaven? The answer, as I watched it again and again, turned out to be yes. Yes because of what Slumdog Millionaire does - gives the film medium a jolt of cyclonic power - and yes because of what it is: a timeless story of unswerving love that's been married to a madly extravagant Hindi version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" Simon Beaufoy's screenplay was inspired by "Q & A," a modest though ingenious first novel by an Indian diplomat named Vikas Swarup, and inspiration is the right word. Nothing else could explain the daring and sweep of Beaufoy's writing, which takes off from the book's premise, leaps from genre to genre with a Parkour athlete's agility, and evokes the rags, riches, horror, hope and irrepressible energy of "Third World" life with a zest that honours "Oliver Twist." The premise is simple. As a plucky quiz-show contestant - a slumdog underdog - Jamal keeps giving correct answers to obscure questions and winning more and more rupees. This raises the question of how he could know what he seems to know, since the 18-year-old kid has grown up in grinding poverty. For the show's producers, and the police, the answer is he must be cheating. That's the wrong answer, and the wrong question. The right question is whether poverty and knowledge are mutually exclusive, and the answer given by Jamal's example is no, they are not, provided the knowledge is based on experience. This quiet, passionate, whipsmart kid has lived almost every answer he gives; the questions he needs are provided by destiny. In another filmmaker's hands, this could have been the stuff of turgid melodrama, the story's contrivances laid bare. But Boyle directs with such enthusiasm and exuberance that his energy lifts the film to the clouds. Slumdog Millionaire is incredibly colourful, fast-paced and thrilling to watch as cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle (Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg's frequent DP) uses film cameras, digital cameras, even the video function of a small, unobtrusive still camera, and his images come at you like light itself, in waves and pulsing clusters captures. He captures India's vibrancy with a lens that constantly roves Mumbai's teeming streets or hovers overhead, capturing the country's eye-popping colours. Boyle's storytelling is economical; a tale with the sweep of an epic comes in at exactly two hours, set to the evocative rhythms of A.R. Rahman's phenomenal score and the propulsive beat of the hip-hop-infused soundtrack. It's funny, when you look at the role destiny plays in Slumdog Millionaire, and then at its director's career. Danny Boyle seems to have enjoyed an equally happy fate as the one of Jamal. Many of his previous films, from Shallow Grave through Trainspotting to the beguiling and under-appreciated Millions, are infused with the sheer joy of filmmaking, and all aswirl with ecstatic techniques. A now-infamous scene in Trainspotting is all aswirl with the same stuff that makes for a hideously funny sequence in Slumdog. Still, Boyle had been having his ups and downs - The Beach was a classic downer - and he'd done his most distinctive work on a relatively small scale. Then destiny, in the form of smart and non-greedy producers (people who still understand that cinema isn't a fucking business, that it shouldn't be made inside fake studios), put him together with Simon Beaufoy's screenplay - the writer's best-known script to that point had been The Full Monty - and the result will make film history. The scale of Slumdog Millionaire is close to cosmic. Jamal's fate transcends the slums; it transcends India. He really is an Oliver Twist for the 21st century, just as his beloved Latika is a multinational mingling of Juliet, Lara and the Vivien Leigh of Waterloo Bridge. In fact, their shared fate plays out in the midst of such crowds as to suggest that every citizen of Mumbai found work as an extra. Jamal and Latika are also two of three Third World musketeers who banded together for self-protection in childhood. The third is Salim, Jamal's brother and the source of a harrowing sibling rivalry. The children in the film come from Mumbai's slums, and their performances would put Hollywood moppets to shame. Jamal is played as an adult by Dev Patel, a second-generation Indian born in London, still most famous (until now) for his role as Anwar Kharral in E4's fabulous series "Skins." Those who were addicted to that show know that he's a hugely appealing young star, not conventionally handsome, who has mastered the art of suggesting by withholding - you can almost see Jamal's thoughts in process - along with the risky business of putting his character heedlessly out there when love or danger demand it. Great, great things are coming for him. Then there's Freida Pinto, an Indian model in her first prominent feature role, who's exquisite as Latika, an apparently tragic heroine whose destiny is brighter than she can know. Anil Kapoor, a Bollywood veteran, plays the quiz-show host, Prem, as a supremely smarmy snake. And another legend, Irrfan Khan, adds a lot as a police inspector with a heavy hand but a quick, mercurial mind. A very special mention, too, to all the children who play the three characters at various ages. Particularly touching is Ayush Mahesh Kedekar, who plays Jamal at 7, a little boy who retains his sweetness and innocence amidst the squalor of his existence. After the marvel that was the performance of the young Alex Etel in Millions, Boyle proves once again just how adept he is in working with children. There's sadness and tragedy within Slumdog Millionaire - starvation, genocide, child prostitution and overwhelming oppression - but there's humour, humanity and dignity as well. Boyle, 12 years after Trainspotting, a film that could be described as the polar opposite of this one, seems to have freed himself here to bring his brilliance as a director to its fullest fruition. This is Boyle's best film to date, which is saying quite a lot; He's made a joyous, fun, and wonderfully accessible film that should be able to be witnessed by everyone at least once. I can honestly say I've never seen anything like Slumdog Millionaire, and I welcomed it with open arms and eyes. In these worsening times for feature films, timidity and mediocrity bickering for bottom honours at the multiplex, Slumdog Millionaire breaks through to the top. It's the best film of 2008. It's a masterpiece. "D. It is written."

A film from Danny Boyle means at least a few things, including a distinctive visual style featuring a lot of camera movement and a good soundtrack consisting of a lot of electronic music. It is certainly even more wonderful when you have a great story, presented in a series of effective reveals, great performances, and pretty much everything else coming together wonderfully.

As my opening lines suggest, the story is about a boy from the slums, Jamal, who has traveled a long way to arrive at the Indian version of the game show, "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." Having arrived at the final question, Jamal is forced into questioning, concerning how he knew the answers to the previous questions.

Prem Kumar: Its getting hot in here.
Jamal Malik: Are you nervous?
Prem Kumar: [audience laughs] What? Am I nervous ? Its you who's in the hot seat, my friend!
Jamal Malik: Yes, sorry. 

The result is a reveal of many events that occurred in Jamal's life, taking him back to his early youth, when he was forced to stay on the move with his brother, Salim, after his mother was killed. During this time, Jamal also formed a great bond with another girl from the slums, Latika. Latika becomes a large drive in what Jamal wishes to do, and much of the story is wrapped in the suspended romance between the two.

What may seem cliched comes off so much better, being elevated beyond a coming of age drama mixed with romance, into a very well made story that keeps one engrossed throughout.

Prem Kumar: Final question for twenty million rupees, and he's smiling. I guess you know the answer.
Jamal Malik: Do you believe it, I don't!
Prem Kumar: You don't? So you take the ten million and walk?
Jamal Malik: No. I'll play.

While given an R rating, this film is certainly wonderful enough for many to enjoy. It has all many elements of comedy, drama, adventure, romance, and suspense. It is a film about friendship, gratitude, love, betrayal, poverty, hope, and chance. It is well made, well casted, and easily some of Boyle's best work as a director.

To American eyes, the children in Slumdog Millionaire might as well be from another universe.  The slums of Mumbai differ very little from the slums of some two thousand years ago: they're packed with people, animals and garbage.  It seems there's not a vacant street or quiet spot in the whole town.  But such is the life of Jamal (Dev Patel), an 18-year old boy from the slums who impossibly wins 10 million rupees on the Indian version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire".  He is held by police on the assumption that he is somehow cheating, and only by explaining the coincidences in his life that lead to his knowing the answers can he hope to escape.  Despite the sad nature of this boy's life, the movie plays out as a fairytale, so much so in fact, the subtitles appear onscreen as if they were written on the pages of a children's book.  The first half of the movie focuses on Jamal's flashbacks to his childhood, and his life with his brother, Salim.  The last half of the movie isn't quite as gripping as the first and seems a bit more cliched, but then, as I said, this IS a fairytale (so of course the three street children grow up to look like models).  Jamal is the Knight in Shining Armor, his older brother is the wayward son, and the female lead, Latika, is the damsel in distress (she's almost a literal fairytale princess held captive by a wicked king whom she's been forced to marry).  It's the wayward older brother whose story is least compelling, as he moves from street-smart urchin to wanna-be hiphop gangsta, his character enters very wornout/cliched territory (if ever a movie injected unwanted cool "style" points into it's character, this would be it).  But it's a minor quibble.  It's the pre-teen kids who steal the movie.  Flashbacks show a childhood that is simultaneously horrifying and exhilarating: death and danger lurk around every corner, but the vibrant city street life leaps forth in a celebration of life.  It's a story of the lowest rung on the bottom of society's ladder.  A story of children who must literally steal or die, children with no future and no place to turn for help.  That it's both heart-breaking and uplifting is a testament to the filmmaker.  Even if the 3rd act pushes a little too forcibly towards that fairytale ending, it's still an unforgettable journey.

Good luck pinning Danny Boyle down. The director of such wildly divergent films as Trainspotting, 28 Days Later, Millions and Sunshine chews through genres the way some actors chew through scenery. Yet in each, Boyle leaves his utterly distinctive signature â a hybridization containing equal measures darkness and light. His are fables of often relentless despair that always give way to something beautiful and transcendent just when the viewer cannot take a momentâs more gloom. No matter how wretched Boyleâs situations, hope is, at all times, just a frame away. Slumdog Millionaire opens with a pair of policemen brutally interrogating a young man, using torture to coax him to talk. So far itâs not working. Convinced the boy in their custody is a criminal, one of the men asks the other how a kid from the slums can make 20 million rupees on a game show without cheating. âI knew the answers,â the young man responds wearily. With those words, Slumdog Millionaire bounces back in time, cleverly showing us exactly how Jamal Malik, an 18-year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, came to find himself on the cusp of an unimaginable fortune. Slumdog Millionaire flies on the wings of an effervescent energy, bursts with dazzling color, and is set to the pulse-pounding music of Indian superstar, A.R. Rahman. Danny Boyle has always been at the forefront of the digital medium, and with Slumdog Millionaire, he shows why he deserves to be at the pinnacle of those courageous artists who dare greatly and succeed beyond even their wildest dreams. Slumdog Millionaire sets groundbreaking, hyper-stylized, breathtakingly beautiful images amidst heartbreaking squalor. As usual, it is a fable, and if you try to apply the strict rules of reality, you will come away disappointed. Instead, surrender to the contrived magic. This is an unabashed, unrepentant, irrepressibly idealistic film. Slumdog Millionaire pulsates with life and should be celebrated loudly and lustfully. Although there is sadness and tragedy in a film that examines poverty with a Dickensian forensic lens, there is also something greater â a humanity and humor, a dignity and majesty that never ceases to shine through. Time and again, Jamal combines an inherent determination to succeed with a fierce devotion to the transforming, surmounting, mountain leveling power of love. Slumdog Millionaire is, quite simply, one of the best films of 2008. You wonât find a better romantic crowd-pleaser all year.

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i], the latest film from filmmaker Danny Boyle ([i]Sunshine[/i], [i]Millions[/i], [i]28 Days Later[/i], [i]A Life Less Ordinary[/i], [i]Trainspotting[/i], [i]Shallow Grave[/i]), is a romantic fable and coming-of-age tale set in modern-day Mumbai (formerly known to Westerners as Bombay). Its also a clear-eyed exploration of the effects of globalization on India through the experiences of a young man and his improbable rise as a game show contestant on the verge of winning 25 million rupees. Filmed with Boyles trademark hyper-style (e.g., lots of quick cuts, handheld camerawork, filters, film lab, processing, and canted angles), [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is the rarest of films: easily accessible to English-language audiences while retaining its Bollywood influences (and flavor). 

Adapting Vikas Swarup's bestselling novel [i]Q and A[/i], Boyle and his screenwriter, Simon Beaufoy, center [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] on Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), a young Indian, Muslim by tradition, whos on the verge of winning 25 million rupees on the Indian version of [i]Who Wants to be a Millionaire?[/i] hosted by Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor). With only one question remaining, the show runs out of time. With millions of Indians from every social class waiting for the final question and Jamals answer, Jamal leaves the television studio, only to be arrested and tortured by a police inspector (Irfan Khan), who suspects Jamal of cheating. Jamal, the slumdog of the title, has no formal education and works as a lowly tea server for an Indian call center. 

As the police inspector questions Jamal, Jamal circles back to the formative experiences that make him who he is, flaws and all, from: his early life in a Mumbai slum, the wrenching loss of his mother during an attack by Hindus on Muslims, his conflicted relationship with his older brother, Salim (played by Madhur Mittal as an adult), through the exploitative, Dickensonian orphanage that takes in Jamal and Salim, the friendship with a young girl, Latika (played by Freida Pinto as an adult), who becomes Jamals great unrequited love, a lucrative interlude as a faux Taj Mahal tour guide, Salim's disturbing willingness to use violence to survive and advance in the criminal underworld, and ultimately, back to the game show and the questions Jamal semi-miraculously answers to the growing excitement of millions of television watchers, due to more to chance than anything else. 

Stylistically, [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is often a wonder to behold. Boyle uses every quiver in his stylistic arsenal, from quick cuts, colored filters, canted (or dutch) camera angles, handheld camerawork (especially during the frequent foot chases), and visual compositions that emphasize natural and man-made beauty. Boyle finds visual beauty even in the slums, using color (mostly from fabrics or piles of debris) to create striking, almost abstract compositions. At no time, however, does Boyles style undermine or interfere with the central purpose of narrative film: joining in and participating in the central characters emotional and dramatic journey.

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is, at its core, a conventional romantic fable involving star-crossed lovers, seemingly impossible obstacles (e.g., social class, social mobility, etc.), and overcoming them, often with help from luck or beneficent strangers. If anything, that makes [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] predictable, even formulaic, but, as Boyle and Beaufoy prove, its often not the formula that counts, but what you do with it, how you breathe life into moribund conventions. It helps, of course, that [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is set in an exotic location, modern-day India (exotic to English-speaking, Western audiences, of course) that help mask how closely [i]Slumdog Millionaires[/i] follows genre conventions all the way through to the tear-inducing, crowd-pleasing ending.

Style and story aside, its hard to argue that [i]Slumdog Millionaires[/i] feel-good ending isnt well earned. Like Boyles earlier film, [i]Millions[/i], [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] runs the gamut from life affirming, to uplifting, and (here comes the dreaded i word) inspirational. [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is certainly all those things. But why would anyone expect anything different from a film thats part romantic fable (destiny rears its read, multiple times) and part wish-fulfillment fantasy (e.g., what winning the lottery is for millions here and elsewhere).

Anyway, I've always been a fan of Danny Boyle and when I first heard about this film I was a little skeptical. Danny Boyle's style of german expressionist camera angles and use of color drew me to the conclusion that this film was going to be a toss up. Maybe I wouldn't like it. Then I remembered 28 days later and how he really shed his style in that film. Sure the expressionist camera angles were there, but he layed low on the color. An apocalyptic setting shouldn't be pretty unless you're trying to endorse the apocaplyse.
However, I was wrong. Since, Boyle has been spending a lot of time in India he's seem to fallen in love with the place and it really shows in his directing. Instead of trying to make the place look like the slum the script wants it to be, he shurgs that responisbility and makes it look like it's the setting of the Darjeeling Limitied. Everything is brightly colored. Even the shit looks nicer than normal shit.

While that conflicted with the idea of the main character came from a slum that's closered to the slum in City of God. The actions in the script conflicted with his likability as a person. Why would a character, you're trying to paint as good, steal from tourists? I mean, I understand liking theives movies, but it just wasn't likeable. Maybe it was because of M.I.A. song in the background making it sound a little more malevent than it should, or maybe I'm looking too much into it but I just didn't see what was so cute/nice about him stealing from people on vaction. Now that family is carless and probably can't get the money. So now they are stuck in this place. Huh? How about that?

However, Boyle's style choices have taken an interesting change. Maybe it was India, maybe it's something all directors are gonna start doing now or maybe it's cause he saw 28 Weeks Later, but the meshing of different camera settings and styles was a nice choice. In a world so crowded and magical as India I really thought it was something nice in this sea of normal and bland. This decision really drew the audience into the piece and made the film a little more magical than any color pallet choice would have.

India is fast emerging as one of the world?s fastest growing economies, a fact that seems to be in conflict with their poor infrastructure and the slums that fill their cities. The cinema of India is not particularly well known for depicting any of this, it?s mainly known for large budget audience pandering musicals, a cinema that most in the west are aware exists but which few have bothered to see. Oddly it is mostly outside filmmakers who have been more interested in depicting the social hardships in India with movies like Water, which was made by the Indian-Canadian filmmaker Deepa Mehta. The new Danny Boyle film, Slumdog Millionaire, would seem to be a much more realistic depiction of the streets of India; but it?s quickly apparent that it is just as interested in pleasing audiences as the Bollywood musicals, except that it?s western audiences it seeks to please. 

The film follows a young man from the streets of Mumbai India named Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) who finds his way onto the Indian version of ?Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? (which looks and sounds identical to the American version), where he?s reached the level of ten million Rupees despite a lack of any formal education. The local authorities are highly suspicious of his advance through the ranks, so they arrest him and subject him to extreme interrogation. A more disciplined inspector (Irfan Khan) eventually shows up and decides to ask him, question by question, how he managed to attain all this knowledge. At this point the film begins a series of flashbacks in which it is revealed where he learned each question and which together tell the whole arc of Jamal?s life and how he came to find himself on a game show. 

It would be reductive to call this an Indian version of Forrest Gump, but the similarities between the two films are striking. Both films tell the recent history of a country through the life story of a seemingly unimportant and lowly citizen who stumbles through larger events. Both are told through framing stories, though this game show story is significantly more interesting than Gump?s bus stop talk, in fact as far as framing stories go this game show scheme is really top-notch. Unlike Gump, though, Jamal is less likely to actually stubble through historical events so much as social touchstones of changing times. This is one of the film?s weakness, it occasionally feels like a white tourists guided tour through India?s stereotypes, almost like the writers brainstormed everything that comes immediately to mind while thinking about the country and through them all in. Bollywood films: check, Hindi Muslim conflict: check, Taj Mahal: check, telemarketing: check, they leave almost no stone unturned, and this is a problem when it would have felt much more natural for them to stick to one region. It?s almost like if an Indian decided to make a movie about America and made absolutely certain that he included refereces to the Western movie genre, a rally about the abortion issue, a trip to the Lincoln Memorial, and someone working at the Coca-Cola factory. 

Another major work I?d compare the film to is Dickens? ?Oliver Twist,? especially during the flashbacks to Jamal?s young days as an orphan on the streets. These scenes are particularly effective at capturing the chaos of the Mumbai streets. The depictions of the Mumbai ghettos feel somewhat influenced by Fernando Meirelles? excellent City of God. While the life lived by the young Jamal is quite grim but there is a sense he doesn?t really see it that way, there is a sense of Dickensian joviality to his exploits. He?s a precocious little slumdog and in the tradition of these sorts of stories he finds all kinds of creative and somewhat amusing ways to get by. 

The camera work here is often handheld and the cinematography is relatively grainy compared to most movies, and the editing is fairly aggressive. This camera work is not done to make the audience even subconsciously think they?re watching a documentary, it?s closer to what Paul Greengrass has achieved with movies like The Bourne Ultimatum, except here it?s applied to a drama instead of a thriller. The catch is, that Boyle rarely ever goes too far with any of these techniques, the handheld camera isn?t anywhere near as obvious as in Greengrass? work, the grainy film stock is still clearly 35 millimeter and still quite slick, and the editing shouldn?t be disorienting even to the most sensitive of viewers, but each technique is used just enough to give the movie a certain degree of grit and keep the pace very fast. 

The film?s music mostly excellent. The original music was composed by a legendary Bollywood composer A. R. Rahman who has clearly mastered the art of using Indian instruments and musical styles to score films. Rahman?s score is very effective and is probably part of why the film moves so quickly while telling a story with a pretty large scope. However, I do take issue with the film?s use of the M.I.A. song ?Paper Planes,? a song that is closely associated with the summer of 2008 and feels completely out of place in a flashback scene set before the song was even written. 

The film?s spoken language is divided between English and Hindi, which can be a jarring mix. The entire section featuring an Adult Jamal including the game show segments are in plain English, while most of the flashbacks to him as a child are in subtitled Hindi. I really wish that Boyle had just stuck with one language or the other, he should have either made the whole film in Hindi to reflect the actual language of the Indian people, or if he wanted to avoid the whole subtitle thing he should have done it consistently. As it is, the film seems to depict Jamal mysteriously switching languages somewhere around puberty, and the rest of the country following suit. This is made all the more confusing when instances pop up of his character actually speaking English to American, British, and German tourists, making it rather unclear when the spoken English is supposed to simply be a translation for the audience or an actual instance of the character speaking English. 

This language problem is made all the more annoying because of the filmmakers decision to use stylized subtitles. These are subtitles that appear in a number of different areas of the screen rather than staying on the bottom like most film subtitles. I didn?t like this technique in Man on Fire, I didn?t like it in Night Watch, and I don?t like it here. When subtitles consistently appear in the same place at the bottom of the screen it?s a lot easier for them to blend in with the language of the film and cease to be noticed then when they?re bouncing all over the place. 

This language material is distracting, but certainly forgivable, what?s not so forgivable is that the film can be a little predictable at times. Particularly in a pair of scenes that are meant to be suspenseful Who Wants to Be a Millionaire questions, like situation about 2/3 of the way through the movie where he?s given an opportunity to cheat, but anyone whose caught on to the film?s intended message about fate know exactly how Jamal will handle this. More egregious then this is a case of incredibly obvious foreshadowing where Jamal runs across a piece of useless trivia early on in his life, and it doesn?t take a rocket scientist to know this is going to come up again in the final question. Did I only pick up on these because I?m jaded by seeing so many other movies? Possibly, but if Boyle had been a little less blatant in his foreshadowing on that second point it would have been a little more suspenseful. 

A lot of the negative things I?m bringing up aren?t really huge problems; in fact they?re flaws bordering on nitpicking. The reason I find this so interesting is that Danny Boyle?s last film, Sunshine, had a flaw toward the end that was much more egregious then anything I mentioned; and yet I found myself much more willing to forgive Sunshine for its flaw then I am Slumdog Millionaire. I think this is because all of that film?s problems were confined to the last fifteen minutes and leave the preceding ninety minutes completely flawless, whereas Slumdog Millionaire?s flaws are littered throughout the movie and pervade the entire project. 

I have problems with the movie, but that doesn?t mean Slumdog Millionaire isn?t a movie I can happily recommend for anyone to see. At the end of the day this is a feel good story about a character triumphing over adversity, and one that knows when to pander and when not to pander and never feels saccharin. Basically, it?s a crowd pleaser for people who know how to detect cheese; I?m not surprised that it was able to get enthusiasm from festival audiences. It should not however be mistaken for a wildly creative film. In one key way, it actually reminds me of Mel Gibson?s Apocalypto in that both films take stories that might seem cliché, but tell them in areas we?re not so used to seeing on screen in order to seem more fresh then it probably is. For the most part, Slumdog Millionaire probably is strong enough to get away with this.

Slumdog  Millionaire comes pretty close to being a perfect narrative film. With only a few missteps that I assume we're due to cutting it down in length. Besides that Danny Boyle has officially proved that he can work any genre, without any problem. This isn't an average love story, but it feels like a new classic already. Usually when I gripe about films not being entirely in there native language I take it down in points. Here it feels like a fairly and therefore works on its behalf.

I also really enjoyed this movie even though you can see a lot of the plot coming.  The colors are vibrant and even though much of the movie is set in the dusty corrupt slums, where in American gritty urban pics the images are often extremely dark and without color, this movie is always visually interesting.  The action is often so fast that colors appear smeared or streaked across the screen and that's not a bad thing.  I thought the editing and camera work was done very well especially with the constant flashbacks to different points in Jamal, Salim and Latika's lives.  The few adult characters, in particular the game show host, the police interrogators, the gangsters, and the brothers' mother listed here on Flixster, gave solid supporting performances.  Dev, Madhur and Freida as the oldest teenage versions of Jamal, Salim and Latika give good performances, but I actually liked the younger actors who played the three main characters better.  

The early parts of the movie are filled with both really funny moments that people of any culture could appreciate and troubling tragic moments that are also universal.  Jamal, the always good hearted romantic, Salim, the older and opportunistic brother, and Latika, the beautiful girl who Jamal spends his life pursuing are orphaned around the ages of 6-8.  They are the Three Musketeers!  They have lots of adventures together, but at times the brothers are separated from Latika.  Eventually they grow up to be pre/early-teens and the adventures continue.  Life on the streets is tough, filled with scams, fleeing from the authorities, and revenge, but Jamal always has the hope that he will find Latika.  I recently learned a bit about Charles Dickens and so his famous stories with strong elements of social justice were fresh in my mind when I saw this.  All the scenes with the children or pre-teens living on the streets and doing what they can to get by as controlled by a couple local gangsters definitely invoked Dickens, especially Oliver Twist.

It's no spoiler to anyone who has read a little about this movie that Jamal is interrogated on suspicion of cheating to win money on India's Who Wants to Be a Millionaire.  This is where the story begins to unfold.  However, all of Jamal's life experiences connected in his mind to his brother or his love help him legitimately pick the right answers.  And through the way the script was written and the film was edited it is shown that all three orphans are always linked together to the end.  And there are little things you'll notice on repeated viewings.  I must say, the movie didn't make me feel a rush of emotions when Jamal and Latika are reunited like I expected it might, but still it is a little movie that has had a long road to the recognition and kudos it has been receiving.

It's Danny Boyle's culmination-film, combining elements of "Trainspotting," "28 Days Later," "Millions," and "Sunshine" together in one gigantic sweep-of-a-movie.  Like in all of these films, Boyle explores the theme of destiny and how this relates to the world the characters find themselves in.  In "Trainspotting," it was the world of heroine.  In "28 Days Later," it was the world coming to an end.  In "Millions," it was the world just before England converted from pounds to the Euro.  In "Sunshine," it was the world beyond our own.  And in "Slumdog Millionaire," it is the world of Mumbai, 2006.  Although far from perfect, it's still a powerful film pulsating to the rhythm of life, the loss of innocence and the return (for one man) to it.

Danny Boyle may very well be one of the most versatile filmmakers working today.  From dark comedy (Shallow Grave) to horror (28 Days Later) to family friendly (Millions) to science-fiction (Sunshine), Boyle has shown a remarkable and rare versatility that allows him to transition from one genre to the next, executing the rules and conventions to perfection while simultaneously infusing and enhancing each film with a trademark style that perfectly toes that line between indie sensibilities and mainstream appeal.  Slumdog Millionaire is another notch on the British filmmaker's belt and yet another sensational display of his ability to work within any context; an accomplishment even more impressive considering the film was shot entirely in India and is infused with perfectly executed conventions of a genre that has been vastly unexplored by both American audiences as well as Boyle: the Bollywood film.  A celebration of human vitality and resilience, Slumdog Millionaire is already being included on many critics' lists, Yours Truly being one of them, as one of the best films of the year. 

The film begins with this question: 

Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million rupees.  How did he do it?

A. He cheated
B. He's lucky
C. He's a genius
D. It is written

Indeed, that is the question a Police Inspector (Irfan Khan) is trying to answer when we first meet him brutally interrogating the incarcerated Jamal (Dev Patel).  Only one question away from the grand prize on India's version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" just a day before, Jamal was arrested on order's of Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor), the show's selfish host, who is mystified at how a penniless, 18-year old orphan from the slums of Mumbai can know so much.  Accused of cheating, Jamal must explain to the Inspector how it is he knew all the answers.

As Jamal's story unfolds, it becomes clear that the boy has never dabbled in deceipt or deception.  He recounts to the Inspector a tale of amazing coincidences that spans his entire childhood and includes landmark events - the murder of his mother at the hands of religious zealots, his meeting of a Bollywood celebrity, his annexation into a group of child laborers - that have been burned into his mind and happen to include clues to the answers of every question he has faced on the show.  Jamal is not concerned with the money though, instead trying to use his exposure on the show, which is watched by millions, to reach out to Latika (Freida Pinto), a girl for whom he has pined since their slumdog childhood and who he hopes he can rescue from her position as a servant for a Mumbai crime boss.  However, to get to her, he must attempt to reconcile with his brother Salim (Madhur Mittal), who abandoned Jamal as a teenager for a life of organized crime under the headship of Latika's master. 

Slumdog Millionaire succeeds beautifully because it has something for everyone.  At its core it's an exhilarating love story; the kind that's not overly sappy or melodramatic, but touching and dramatic enough in its scope to leave you feeling hopeful and vibrant upon leaving the theater.  Additionally, the film is the quintessential underdog story; an uplifting tale of an Everyman's triumph over the suffocating poverity into which he was born.  Part of what enables the film to succeed on both levels is the cinematography of Boyle regular Anthony Dod Mantle, who can bend fast-paced action and breath-taking landscapes to his visually emotive will.  Rarely has a city been captured with such simultaneous beauty and sprawl, yet Boyle and Mantle capture the so-called "maximum city" of Mumbai spread out with all its dirty secrets on display.

But the film, probably moreso than any he's done before, ultimately excels due to Boyle's talent for fusing the indie with the mainstream.  He can still dedicate the care and precision necessary to delve into the Dickensian story of Jamal, yet he makes the intimacy easy to swallow with a pop sensibility displayed in his eye-popping visuals and his ecclectic, hip-hop score.  His skill with pastiche ensures a roller coaster feel for the film - exploring the highs and lows of every sequence of events without any emotional overload.  Time and time again Slumdog Millionaire testifies to Boyle's prowess as a filmmaker, finding humor in the dark and planting reason within the melodramatic, never once coming across as awkward or out of place. 

The story, relying on its almost providence-like coincidences, may very well come off as gimmicky to some, especially those purposely looking for flaws to exploit.  I don't see it as a gimmick as much as a thesis questioning how anyone comes to know the things they know about life and love.  Often the life lessons best learned are learned on accident, through uncontrollable situations in life we don't understand at the time.  Slumdog Millionaire stands as an embodiment of the idea that hindsight is 20/20 and that through resilience and the pursuit of our dreams, we can understand all things happen for a reason.

Few movies have tugged at this writer's heartstrings like Slumdog Millionaire.  It's hard to put a finger on exactly what makes this movie so heart-melting.  Perhaps the depravity in which two orphan boys spend their young lives.  Perhaps the chorus of a nation starved for something to cheer.  Perhaps the shimmer of light giving hope in a desperate situation. Perhaps it is love.  Slumdog Millionaire is able to paint a portrait so vivid and so intense that it comes to life.  Without being gimmicky we are given a glimpse into an almost unimaginable life fraught with endless devices to break the hearts and minds of little boys and girls growing up in such brutal conditions.  Slumdog Millionaire combines an awesome story, with an excellent cast who shine at every possible opportunity.  The script is well crafted and departs from the usual well of cliches that most love stories drop their buckets into leaving us parched.  Slumdog quenches that thirst for a love story that can take us beyond the basic element of boy meets girl and into elements of despair, hope, taking a risk and gambling everything to be with the one. Cinematography and soundtrack accentuate and highlight the key moments without overstimulating our senses.  I thought that the Dark Knight would run away with Best Picture this year, but little did I know that a diamond in the rough like Slumdog Millionaire would appear from nowhere and steal my heart.  And so we take a ride with the main character, Jamal, on a train built on hope and run on love to escape from brutality, poverty, and cruelty - the mental slums to a singular place where something good awaits, where destiny awaits, where love awaits.

This year Boyle has given us, together with Aravind Adiga's "The White Tiger", another disturbing portrait of late capitalist India, a place where the old world of class animosity and contemporary Third World internationalism has birthed a new individualist mentality of venal ruthlessness and spiritual resilience. If this vision is cynical, it also appears to be buoyant.

A brilliant and moving tale, Slumdog Millionaire seems more like a classic fable told in a modern way. It's a fairy tale, but moves with a force rarely seen in modern film.
Jamal is one question away from winning the top prize in India's version of Who Wants to Be A Millionaire. Then we cut to him being interrogated on how he supposedly cheated. It's not graphic (nothing is in the film) but it is tough to watch. He explains that he knew all the answers. So, the film proceeds to skip around in time from the interrogation to the game show, to the various periods in his life that explain how he knew each answer. We've seen this narrative style before, from old Japanese cinema to the Nolan brothers' The Prestige and Memento. Slumdog, however, is so seamless in the way that all three paths converge that you won't realize they had until you leave the theater.
Also of note is Danny Boyle's masterful imagery. I was filled with such elation as the two boys (Jamal and Salim, his brother) jumped from rooftop to rooftop and through the labyrinthine chaos that was Mumbai, and their misadventures on a train, and their hustling in the Taj Mahal. Particularly moving was a certain episode involving an outhouse (but to say any more about it would ruin it). I was genuinely saddened and worried as the boys went to an orphanage that has a despicable purpose. Having lived in Eastern Europe, much of the imagery and culture was very familiar. It was all the more poignant watching these kids struggle through what should be happy years for any child.
But, nevertheless, the sadness only makes the achievements of Jamal more engaging and moving.
The term "tear-jerking" to me denotes some kind of emotional theft; it implies shameful manipulation. To jerk a tear is criminal, but to evoke tears is human. That is the central reason why I love this movie. One particular image (that won't ruin) did so evoke me. That is rare, considering the hardened film watcher that I am. This film connects on a global level, with the main themes of loss and gain. Do yourself a favor as a human and see this movie. It is an important movie. Perhaps, even inspiring.

Slumdog Millionaire, at first glance, sounds like the kind of magically sweet film that would be sure to woo even the most hard-hearted of audiences. An Indian youth, Jamal, goes on India's version of the "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" game show and astounds everybody by winning big. How could a street rat such as this know the answers to so many difficult questions? The answer is simple: each question's answer has factored improbably into his life at one point or another. So the movie glides through both the game show itself (plus the police brutality afterward), and Jamal's life before the show -- mostly involving the love of his life, Latika. Unfortunately, the magic that the plot synopsis promises isn't in quite as much abundance as you might be expecting. The questions are mostly things like, "What statesman is on the United States $100 bill?" The story shows Jamal becoming a con artist at the Taj Mahal, taking people's money and feeding them made up histories of the structure. The film takes some time to get a good rhythm going, being at first a bunch of disparate moments. One question regards the star of a certain Bollywood film, which Jamal remembers in a brief sequence involving an outhouse. How this functions with the rest of the movie is unclear, unless it's simply meant to show how much he will persevere to reach his goals... or merely to highlight the rough and tumble world that is the slums of India. When the movie finds its footing, realizing that its main story is the on again off again love affair between Jamal and Latika, Slumdog Millionaire makes up somewhat for its earlier sputtering. Of course, there is the new problem that the two stars -- Dev Patel and Freida Pinto -- have little chemistry together. The movie doesn't give them a chance to develop any sparks, either, so when they meet up briefly in an allegedly tense moment in a kitchen... it's easy to look at the screen and realize what sort of emotions are supposed to be elicited. But there's not much to make it as strongly emotional as it would like us to believe. Director Danny Boyle (28 Days Later) is always present. His quick moving style mostly works here. Like a subdued Baz Luhrmann, Boyle allows the action to thrive by way of the mesmerizing scenery of India. The colors are bold, the characters are broad, and that mostly works. So maybe Jamal's obsession with Latika feels more like a product of a screenwriter than a natural extension of the character. But on an intellectual level, you the viewer know what is at stake and if you're willing to go along with it then the film can often be quite tense. The scenes of the "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" game in progress are among the best, with the heartbeat sound effects adding to the feeling that Jamal could lose it all at any instant. I'm not sure how strong that feeling will be on a second viewing. And I'm not sure how much slack I would be willing to cut the film if it were not being hailed as one of the year-end award contenders. And I'm not sure how to feel about the final question -- alluded to throughout the film in painfully obvious ways. I think I like Slumdog Millionaire. I'm disappointed to say that it is not among my favorites for the year 2008. I'm disappointed to say that I'm disappointed at all. The conceit is brilliant, but the execution leaves much to be desired. P.S. Anil Kapoor (who played the game show host) absolutely rocked. Also, I wish that Irrfan Khan had gotten a meatier role, as I was much impressed by him in 2006's The Namesake. Oh well.

Danny Boyle's "Slumdog Millionaire" is a perfect example of filmmaking at its absolute best, as well as Boyle at his highest peak as a filmmaker.  The film starts off hitting the ground running and never lets up and it completely immerses the audience into the Indian slum world of Jamal Malik, his brother Salim, and his true love Latika.  The film revolves around Jamal being a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" while he surprisingly gets every question right up until the final one.  I don't want to reveal very much about the film and how it unfolds because discovering it for yourself is part of the joy of the experience, but the basic premise is that the reason he knows most of the answers is because of certain moments in his life, and therefore the history of Jamal, Salim and Latika is shown through flashbacks almost every time a question is proposed.  It may not sound like much but it is brilliantly and flawlessly executed and never becomes a gimmick but works beautifully to tell the riveting and heartbreaking journey of these three characters.  It is very rare that I see a film that never makes one false or unnecessary step, but this is one of them as the craftsmanship is superb and not a single shot is wasted, everything pushes the story, themes and the characters forward.  Boyle takes us on a journey of loss, love and survival unlike anything I've ever seen before and I was totally riveted and compelled the entire time (never once did I glance at my watch).  Everything about the film was right and just fit together like a glove, and it really has to do with how Boyle uses every aspect of film to its fullest extent while still keeping to his unique style.  The cinematography is gorgeously gritty and the editing is razor sharp while the encompassing sound design is backed up by one of the best soundtracks I've heard in a film.  The actors all do a great job, especially the exceptional younger ones, and it really is a testament to the use of practical unknowns because never once did I think I was watching an actor, but a real human being I grew to really care about and invest in.  This is not an easy film to take in at times but it is never done in an exploitative way, and Boyle never goes for the obvious or easy way out in order to play with our emotions.  This is a masterful work from an experienced filmmaker who knows how to respect the audience and receive ours in return.  At its core this electrifying film is a love story, but to classify it as such is too restricting, it really is a story about life, chance and destiny that will stay with you for a very very longtime.  Without a doubt, Danny Boyle deserves an Oscar nomination for best director, and the film itself is worthy of every accolade it receives because it is one of the best, if not THE best film of 2008, a true modern masterpiece.
