In this media-saturated age, it really has become somewhat of a rarity that a film (no matter the country of origin) affords its audience with the opportunity to look into a world that is as honest (as possible) as it is poignant. On one hand, I did feel that this story was a particularly ingenious spin on Dickensian and Greek narratives that are fit for today's audiences. On the other hand-however-I do have this leeching sense of cynicism that whispers to me that this was a tad too schmaltzy for my taste; but then again, one really cannot question on whether the events that unfold in this love story could actually happen. It is a movie, after all. 

	Directed by Danny Boyle (Sunshine/ Trainspotting) and the Simon Beaufoy adaptation from the best-selling book 'Q&A'  authored by Vikas Swarup, the story is centered around 18 year-old Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), an uneducated kid from the desolate and dank slums of Mumbai is one question away from winning the top prize of 20 MILLION Rupees (roughly the equivalent of $322,980 US dollars) in India's version of 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire." With that built-up excitement, there's just one roadblock in Jamal's path to fame and riches: the powers the be (the host of said game show) had Jamal arrested under the suspicion of cheating. From there, the Mumbai police had the poor kid brutally interrogated for the next few hours only to accidentally rendering him unconscious. 

	The following morning, his interrogation continues in an albeit more passive fashion through an interview conducted personally by the police commissioner of Mumbai (Ifran Khan). Whilst Jamal's criminal inquiry is going on, the commissioner plays a tape from last night's "Millionaire" and asks him to reveal his knowledge on where he got each answer from. In a form of desperation to prove his innocence, Jamal spills his guts and tells his life story leading up to events of his appearance on the game show. From there, he tells of his strange adventures that he had while growing up in the slums with his brother Salim (Madhur Mittal). Jamal and Salim's adventures that they went through ranged from surviving ultra-right winged extremist gangs, train hopping across India, to Jamal loving and loosing of Latika, a childhood friend that he loved since loosing his mother. 

	As this interview unfolds-and to the bemusement of the police commissioner-his true motive for being on the game show goes well beyond the seemingly petty pursuit of fame and fortune. Their final question to him was this: why? Its not that Jamal cheated because he really didn't. He's definitely had a rough life, indeed. He knows the answers not because he randomly acquired them through his current profession as an assistant phone basher at an English outsourcing facility for mobile phones. The plain and simple answer is that he's lived each answer. 

	Aside from my aforementioned reservations about the conventionality of the love story-a schmalzy puff piece that was perfectly tailored for Academy voters. From some certain recollections, I described the movie as a 'flavor of the month' movie that will push the status over onto an ironic sense of over-saturation. I recently saw the movie again for the first time in a couple of years, and I have to admit that this movie-despite what I felt-still holds up pretty well. I think that the tried and true rags to riches love story actually elevated this Bollywood tale in almost every way-from the visuals, the music, to even the flawless direction. What's more to rave is that there's no eyre of pretentiousness that typically comes with movies of this ilk.

How to make a sure-fire hit:

1.  Start by choosing a third-world setting, preferably one with a marked contrast between the wealthy and non-wealthy residents of that setting.

2.  Develop a thinly-sketched story; character development should be sacrificed in lieu of depictions of squalor and suffering.  Include certain key plot points: death in the family, children running around in packs on their own, and an ill-fated love interest.

(2 1/2.  Even better if you can wrap up the plot with a gimmick of some sort that ties everything together.  Oh, like having all of the questions on a game show coincide chronologically with the major life events of the contestant.)

3.  Add lots of camera tricks and filters, both to cover up the essential flimsiness of your story and to bludgeon your viewers into submission.  Adding this stuff gives your film a sense of "energy" and makes critics call it "visually stunning." 

4.  When writing the dialogue, be sure to include as many trite phrases as possible.  Stuff along the lines of "love conquers all."  If this stuff were said in a drama set in the Western world, we'd laugh at the screen.  But when uttered by a slumdog, it is wildly successful.

5.  Pay attention to the world zeitgeist.  Make a film with a sappy, upbeat ending if most people are feeling depressed. 

6.  Market it to intelligent, liberal audiences.

(See also: Babel, Hotel Rwanda, The Kite Runner, and to some extent, City of God)

And... voila.  Slumdog Millionaire isn't a terrible film -- it is merely a very average film dressed up with camera tricks and emotionally manipulative scenes.  If you watch films to "feel good," then by all means, check this one out.  It's certainly never boring, and the ending does pack quite the emotional wallop.  But if you watch films to learn something about yourself or others, to think about important issues, to really empathize with characters onscreen -- look elsewhere.

A real tour-de-force from Danny Boyle.  It's a Dickensian tale in contemporary India, with action and romance.  As such, it is an entertainment but with something extra, in its portrayal of Jamal, a lower caste orphan, his older brother, Salim, and his true love, Latika.  

As the movie begins, Jamal is one question away from winning the big prize in Who Wants To Be A Millionaire.  And he's being tortured.  You see, the host of the show asked the police to investigate Jamal, since he couldn't believe a person from a lower class could get all of the questions right.

Jamal is played a videotape of the questions and answers, and he proceeds to tell the police his life story, which explains how he came up with the right answers.

This has been deservedly praised, though some critics feel there are too many coincidences and the movie is manipulative in parts.  I didn't find this movie was excessive in that regard.  It was just excessive enough.

When, through great casting, you establish a protagonist who is easy to root for, it's manipulative, but the right type of manipulative, if that makes any sense.

Once again, the most satisfying conventional moviegoing experience on offer is a Danny Boyle film consigned to a handful of arthouse screens.  What the fuck?  By rights this is a blockbuster: gripping narrative, thundering pace, sharp script, epic locations, kickass visuals, big ol' love story... but what really makes it special is its setting, and its fearlessness in turning the everyday horrors of India into an utterly recognizable story while diluting none of their awfulness.  The young childhood scenes in particular are truly potent in their mix of nostalgia and trauma.  I became less interested when the source of adversity shifted from real-world social imbalance to a series of underdeveloped, money-hungry thugs, but the love story's barreling full steam ahead by that point, and while we all know where it's headed, there are at least a couple of complications in the quiz-show thread that throw your expectations and keep the tension high.  The visual design is worthy of its own paragraph, but I'll just say, see the damn movie.

This is a film which blends hollywood and bollywood conventions, and brings the tragic stories of many of the destitute in mumbai to life. It is a brief glimpse of the role money plays, the role of corruption, and the role of the beggers heart in such a turbulent country. With amazing editing, a wonderful score by AR Rahman, and solid acting frome everyone to the littlest child, to the protagonist Jamal, we really get a sense of the Indian spirit. They are obesessed by media and bollywood, willing to cut each other down, until they prove themselves to be the real deal, and then rejoice in their triumphs. It is a harrowing tale which really goes to dark places , like the childrens begger camp, the brothels, and enormous slums. It is romantic in it's direction as Danny Boyle shoots dramatic vistas of the Indian countryside, large high rises, and moments of true tension, all against the backdrop of who wants to be a millionaire.  [/color]    [size=5][color=DarkRed][b]"S[/b][/color][/size][color=Wheat]lumdog Millionaire" is a rousing and beautiful masterpiece, a heartfelt story of survival and endurance, brotherhood and love. It overflows with so many ideas and possibilities you'll immediately want to start talking about it. It's been a while since a film has been so striking and indelible with its storytelling and contained characters and situations we care about so deeply. The director is Danny Boyle, who proved long ago he was a unique asset to filmmaking with "Trainspotting" and "Millions." Even after those achievements, he has outdone himself.
 
 It helps I went into "Slumdog Millionaire" almost completely unaware of what its plot. I encourage you to do the same. Do NOT research this film or read any critics' opinions that give away crucial plot points. I'll be careful what I write, but I still propose you see the film first and then come back to this review.
 
 ...OK, you have seen the film. That, or you have enough faith in me to not spoil things for you. "Slumdog Millionaire," as you may already know, tells of a poor kid from Mumbai, India who becomes a contestant on India's version of [i]Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?[/i] The young man's name is Jamal (Dev Patel), who, at the beginning of the film, is one question away from winning the jackpot: 20 million rupees. He's gotten further in the game than any other 18-year-old in history, and he has a choice to either take 10 million rupees and go home or risk losing everything by answering the final question incorrectly.
 
 Jamal's uncommon knowledge and success rate leads the host of the show, Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor), to suspect him of being a cheat. At the end of the show's first day of taping, with only one question left, Kumar hands Jamal over to the police. The chief inspector (Irfan Khan) inflicts torture on the young man to try and make him confess to cheating. His suspicion comes with good reason, I suppose. How would an uneducated "slumdog" from Mumbai be able to get so far in the game? Jamal's simple rational: "I knew the answers." 
 
  From here, the film goes back through all the different questions Kumar asked and flashes back to the moments in Jamal's life when he learned the answers. The flashbacks are than a gimmick; they're essential to the development of the characters. 
 
  Jamal grew up under the protective wing of his older brother, Salim. As little kids, they played cricket in a restricted military zone and were chased by the police around the garbage-filled streets of Mumbai. These stark and raw images, shot up close and from far away, are disheartening and unforgettable. But Boyle doesn't necessarily denounce the conditions of the ghetto neighborhoods. He does a smart thing: he photographs Mumbai tactfully and never passes judgment. He realizes there are people living here and by showing their ways of life, suggests the area possesses its own beauty. While we are prone to shudder and feel pity, we're also fascinated and respect the backbone of Mumbai's citizens. 
 
  After a tragic incident leaves Jamal and Salim orphaned, they forge their way through life as street urchins, earning money and food wherever they can, whether it's begging citizens on the streets, standing atop moving trains to steal from the cars below, or posing as tour guides at the Taj Mahal. Along the way, they meet an orphaned girl named Latika, whom Jamal falls in love with and vows to always protect, even at his young age. Throughout his life, he will lose Latika at least three times, but she's permanently implanted in his heart and mind.
 
  I've left out a crucial and disturbing plot development when Jamal and Salim are young, but I will not reveal it here. You'll know it when you see it and I believe such acts of cruelty really occur in a place as devastating and poor as Mumbai. I have not read Vikas Swarup's novel, [i]Q and A[/i], on which this film is based, but I believe it contains the same hard truth as the film, that it served as inspiration.
 
  It's important to note the hardships Jamal, Salim and Latika experience are hardly pleasant. This isn't a kiddie adventure film, but a serious coming of age story with grave implications. We must remember these kids do what they do to survive. 
 
 Jamal is at the center of it all. Through his strength of will, good faith and humility, we grow to care for him. Against all odds, he chases after anything he needs, with his own spirit and love for Latika driving him. He eventually ends up on his own after Salim and Latika make friends with Mumbai's head gangster. They come into a life of wealth but also servitude. Years later, Jamal finds them and tries to reach Latika the only way he knows how...
 
 In regards to the storytelling, "Slumdog Millionaire" is brilliant. The flashback technique completely engages us while the technical aspects--photography, editing, music, special effects--aid and enhance the viewing experience to one of supreme greatness. Boyle and his director of photography, Anthony Dod Mantle, go to extreme lengths to get their shots, which, coupled with Chris Dickens' flashy editing style, place us in the middle of a chaotic, modern India, and it's thrilling and absorbing.
 
  Above all, "Slumdog" never stops believing in the power of the human spirit to overcome adversity. The most important thing Boyle does is continually bring us back to Jamal's love for life and Latika. He builds a lot of tension in the way he suspends and gradually reveals how Jamal came to know the answers to the [i]Millionaire[/i] questions. We're completely immersed at all times and from all sides.
 
  "Slumdog Millionaire" is the kind of film that excites me about going to the movies. It's enormously entertaining and, by the end, projects a feeling of elation. Though it's not always pleasant viewing, it contains a positive and hopeful energy. If you followed my advice, you already saw the film before finishing this review. And if you're like me, you've already told your friends about it. Now stop and consider how happy and exhilarated you are. What a wonderful and glorious thing it would be if everyone saw "Slumdog Millionaire."[/color]

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] opens in a police station with 18-year-old Jamal being tortured to try to get him to talk. His head is held down in a bucket of water. He's hung from the ceiling by his hands. He's shocked with electrical currents. His body convulses. He spits out blood. What sort of information can this kid possibly be withholding to elicit such barbaric treatment? Surely lives must hang in the balance.
 
Well, not quite. As it turns out, Jamal is a guest on India's version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire". He was one question away from winning the big 20 million rupee prize when filming ended for the day. The show's host thinks Jamal must be cheating --after all he's an uneducated orphan "slumdog" who couldn't possibly know the answers -- so the cops are called to try to get him to fess up.
 
Eventually Jamal is untied and shown a video of his performance on the show thus far. First we flash back to Jamal being asked a question on the show, then further back to the particular childhood experience which explains how he came to know the answer, then back to the show where he answers the question correctly, then back to present at the police station. One question at a time. Lather, rinse, repeat.
 
Bit by bit we learn Jamal's life story. He and his older brother Salim lived with their mother in a huge makeshift shantytown on the outskirts of Mumbai. After she's brutally murdered when they're about 8 or 9, they live in a junkyard with a fellow orphan named Latika. Eventually they're all lured away to an "orphanage" and are forced to spend their days begging in the streets. 
 
The kids often find themselves being chased thru the crowded streets by would-be oppressors. The street scenes are filled with vibrant colors and accompanied by loud high-energy music. Abject poverty has never looked so hip and modern.
 
Eventually Jamal and Salim hop on a train to escape from Mumbai. Latika gets left behind. Jamal is heartbroken and vows to go back to save her as soon as he can. He spends the rest of the film trying to do so. 
 
After riding the rails for days and covering many hundreds of miles, wouldn't you know it, the boys end up falling off the top of the train right outside of the Taj Mahal. How's that for convenient? Not only does it allow the director to set several scenes in and around one of the world's most beautiful buildings, but it also gives Jamal an opportunity to earn some money by posing as a tour guide.
 
After this little diversion, it's back to Mumbai to rescue Latika who's fallen under the control of brutal gangsters. Though a teenager now, Jamal is still as sweet and earnest as he was when he was little boy. Not so, his brother Salim, who's developed into a full-fledged thug.
 
[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is nothing if not a crowd-pleaser. The good guy (Jamal) is very, very good and the bad guys (just about everyone else) are cartoonishly bad. Even the game show host is a condescending prick. There are no messy moral dilemmas to contend with. We want Jamal to win the money and we want him to get the girl. It's as simple as that.
 
There's no denying that this is a very entertaining film. Action, violence, romance, suspense, thumping soundtrack, exotic location, stunning visuals...what more can one ask for? 
 
Oh, I don't know. A less predictable plot maybe. Fewer contrivances. 
 
When it comes right down to it, [i]Slumdog'[/i]s real appeal is not in its story, which is really quite conventional. It's all about its style. 
 
I did like it. I really did. But I didn't love it.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is a rare film that has nearly all its elements in place to be an engaging and uplifting. What starts as an eye-opening, disturbing culture study turns into an endearing love story that captures the audience by its sentimental hands and puts them on a cinematic roller coaster ride. 

All the performances are great, in addition to brilliant editing and cinematography that matches the film's whirlwind pace. What could have been a maudlin story is elevated into pure emotional vibrancy by Danny Boyle, who truly understands that each characters is facing opportunity and some people take it differently than others. 

Though there are some undeveloped characters whose opinions would have made the film even more interesting, including the Detective interviewing the protagonist and a local crime lord, yet the main characters take all the focus that is rightfully there's. Slumdog Millionaire is a rags to riches story that seems like something straight out of Charles Dickens. It's also one of the best love stories ever put on film. Danny Boyle has been a director on the rise ever since his big debut film "Trainspotting", as well as works like the amazing "28 Days Later" and the criminally underrated "Sunshine". With each new film, Boyle has made the most ballsy of choices. In fact, he stands out now as one of modern cinema's most daring directors who simply makes the films he wants to make. Be it a film about drugs, zombies, science fiction, or whatever, Boyle has always been a director to watch for. Here, Boyle decides to journey into the heart of Bollywood filmmaking by shooting all on location in Mumbai, India. The film itself makes the slums of Mumbai almost a living, breathing character as much as the protagonist Jamal Malik is. The dazzling cinematography is breathtaking and portrays the frenzied, dizzying life of someone living in the slums of Mumbai. It also gives life to the way Indian as a whole is a very spontaneous country and trying to control your time their is simply impossible. This plays into the large theme of destiny that is oft mentioned in the film. 

The screenplay is wonderful, the all the actors bring the vibrant characters to life with energy and chemistry. What also stands out is the music, which is simply put, amazing. In fact, one could say that A.R. Rahman's score becomes a character all of its own. This plays out well in the film because Boyle is a director that truly understands the importance of scores and also has a great way of perfecting the use of music in film. The ending of the film is brilliant and beautiful, so I won't spoil it for you. You need to see this film. It's beautiful, heartwarming, intense, and all around a wild, joyous ride.

Some of the music and filming techniques (like the shots with a lowered framerate) made the film feel a little dated to me -- it had a 90's feel that a lot of Danny Boyle films have -- but it adds to the film's charm.

Vibrant cinema = Slumdog Millionaire! Based on the novel "Q & A" by Vikas Swarup, Slumdog Millionaire is a fast-paced, artistic, electrifying, and poignant film. This is the premise: Jamal Malik is an orphan kid from the slums of Mumbai who is one question away from winning 20 million rupees on the Indian version of "Who wants to be a Millionaire?" When the show breaks for the night, Jamal is arrested and tortured by the police to find out how he could come so close to winning (is he cheating?). Jamal then starts telling the amazing story of his 18 years of life that will reveal the key to the answers of the show.

The movie transitions so smoothly from focusing on "How does he know the answers?" to "What is Jamal's story?" that very early in the film you start seeing and feeling the story through Jamal's eyes. The original narrative and the detailed story are not the only compelling factors in this art flick â the film is also a richly creative visual experience. Mainly shot in Mumbai, it shows the real and tough parts of the city; instead of the palatial, waterfall-washed sets usually employed in Bollywood films.

India is a world of contradictions and extremes. At the same time, it is literally a jumping, overflowing center of human energy. This film captures all this energy visually, but above all, it is represented through the development of its outstanding characters. It is not an easy task to combine tragedy, humor, and love in the same plate -- but this movie does it and does it very well. Slumdog Millionaire is Danny Boyle's magnificent, elating cinematic adaptation of Vikas Swarup's prize-winning 2005 novel Q and A. Boyle's masterwork is simply the essential motion picture of 2008; an exquisite and engrossing filmic experience, infused with a searing portrait of the resilience of human spirit. It's a timeless, Capra-esque tale of adversity and rags-to-riches, told with dazzling passion and stunning visual agility. While housed in a bleak setting inhabited by a congregation of truly vile characters, Boyle's film is almost guaranteed to appease any viewer with a soft spot for beautifully sculpted contrivances. Slumdog Millionaire is a charming, uplifting tale about hope, destiny and love, and it will enrapture those who are willing to venture into its expressively-crafted world. For the record, a majority of the dialogue is articulated in English; however, some large segments are delivered in Hindi. But Boyle - in an utter masterstroke - has handled the subtitles colourfully and playfully, unlike the drab subtitles we're accustomed to reading. Slumdog Millionaire is a feverishly-paced, subtitled picture created with subtitle-phobes in mind. This is a visual and emotional journey that's brash, lively and compulsively enjoyable.

Uneducated 18-year-old Jamal Malik (Patel), a poor orphan from the slums of Mumbai, is poised to win a fortune (a staggering 20 million rupees) on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?. Defying all odds and expectations, Jamal has managed to answer every question so far correctly, rapidly approaching the top prize (an unprecedented feat in Indian television history). However, some grow suspicious of how a slumdog could be so knowledgeable, and capable of answering the extremely tough questions. Accused of cheating, Jamal is arrested and brutally interrogated by the police. Proving that life experience is far more valuable than education, Jamal is forced to relive his tumultuous early years for the authorities. The result is a flashback-rich tour into the horrors of Jamal's childhood; his episodic memories relating to each seemingly impossible question put to him on the show. A recurring individual in his memories is a certain Latika (Pinto), whom Jamal is in love with but frequently torn apart from.

"A few hours ago, you were giving chai for the phone walahs. And now you're richer than they will ever be. What a player!"

The structure of Slumdog Millionaire - as scripted by Simon Beaufoy (who also wrote The Full Monty) - may be borderline contrived, but the frenetically-told story amazingly submerges a viewer into its universe and produces suspense despite the outcome being quite obvious from the onset. The point of the story isn't whether Jamal will win the money...it's if he'll get his girl. Make no mistake, there's nothing special about the fairly conventional plot, nor the way it's played out. In this sense, Slumdog Millionaire shouldn't be a great film... But it is a great film. Boyle's direction oozes passion at every turn, offering an energy which keeps the film constantly in motion. The setting in Mumbai is another stroke of genius. To the untrained eye, the location is merely window dressing. But with this dressing comes a unique exotic flavour and an open window into a fascinating culture. The story works on multiple levels - it can be perceived as a romance, a thriller, and a glimpse at the ways in which a fast-developing economy is convulsing the fabric of Indian society.

Fresh from a picture which spent almost a year in post-production in order to get the special effects right, the post-Sunshine Danny Boyle was eager to race onto a project which could be shot fast and furiously. Employing his trademark visual frenzy, Boyle ensnares the viewer in the chaotic motion of Indian street life. Filmed predominantly on bustling locations, Slumdog Millionaire whips along with unguarded authenticity and an understanding of those struggling to survive at the impoverished base of a restrictive caste system. The engaging, agile camera turns the narrow corners of the slums and flies at the high speed of a train on which Jamal and his brother hitchhike. Boyle's collaboration with director of photography Anthony Dod Mantle thrusts a viewer headfirst into the chaotic and despairing world of its three youthful protagonists, wonderfully encapsulating both the excitement of children running amok and the relentless terror they experience on the street that's triggered by authority figures on both sides of the law. Production design is absolutely top-notch, emanating authenticity at every turn. On top of the terrific location work, the set for Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? could be easily mistaken for the real deal. Not just the set design and cinematography, but the sound effects as well as the traits of the host are also spot on. Slumdog Millionaire simply looks and sounds flawless.

Movies that tend to get the Oscar community talking are usually thoughtful, introspective films with a heavy dosage of tragedy. Million Dollar Baby, Brokeback Mountain, Crash, Babel, Munich, and Mystic River are examples of Oscar contenders that refuse to leave you smiling once the credits begin to roll. Slumdog Millionaire stands out due to this. It is a movie that draws you in, makes you smile, and ends on an uplifting note. In a way, it's tough to believe a film that commences with such a brutal edge would eventually become so enriching and deliriously joyful. The opening sequence is pervaded with an ominous undertone, featuring scenes of torture taking place in the bowels of a drab police station. But Boyle's continuing sense of humour and decency buoys the moments of darkness and the eventual fairy-tale ending. Scotsman Boyle hasn't travelled to India with the intention of exposing the horrors of the slums at all... He headed to India to shoot an interesting story; one that could only take place in the ever-changing, ever-alive India. The conventional plot may not have succeeded in a more familiar setting. With Boyle's kinetic cinematic energy generating breakneck pace, and the true wonders of an exciting new culture, not to mention the stimulating and vivacious soundtrack, Slumdog Millionaire suddenly becomes sparky and vibrant. It ends predictably, but the journey to its conclusion is consistently extraordinary.

The entire cast shines. From the inexperienced Dev Patel to the veteran Bollywood star Anil Kapoor, talent is omnipresent. Patel is extremely appealing and likable as the protagonist. He's shy and soft-spoken, and we root for the poor little guy from the outset. Ayush Mahesh Khedekar and Tanay Hemant Chheda also excel as Jamal at different stages in his life. Freida Pinto is simply beguiling as Latika. Her chemistry with Dev Patel is extraordinary. Their emotionally-charged performances allow a viewer to become completely invested in their relationship...longing for them to be reunited, and becoming heartbroken when they're torn apart.
Anil Kapoor is remarkable as the smarmy, cunning game show host who patronises Jamal every chance he gets, and whose motives are ruled by his desire for ratings.
Madhur Mittal, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail and Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala are uniformly excellent as Salim at different points in his life.

Slumdog Millionaire contains all the necessary elements to ensure it's a winner in general release (although one of the studios set to distribute the film was unsure of its commercial worth and was considering a DTD release) as well as a major Oscar contender. It's superbly acted by an able cast, it's wonderfully photographed, and it's overflowing with rich, unconventional location work. This groundbreaking tour de force has as much heart as it does energy, and it ultimately avoids becoming as formulaic as its premise might have allowed in the hands of a lesser filmmaker. The actors' enthusiasm, coupled with Boyle's passionate exertions behind the scenes, generates pure magic out of Slumdog Millionaire. A story of coincidences, luck and eventually destiny, this is a classic, if slightly clichéd tale, and one that has rarely felt or looked so alive with such astonishing visual flair. Laden with satisfying doses of humour, romance and suspense, Slumdog Millionaire is one of the best and most crowd-pleasing films of 2008, and it thoroughly deserved the honour of receiving the Best Picture Oscar.

SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE
Written by Simon Beaufoy
Directed by Danny Boyle
Starring Dev Patel, Freida Pinto, Madhur Mittal and Irrfan Khan

They say that every moment in our lives has led up to the one that we are experiencing right now; that it is written, predetermined or fated.  I suppose this is true for me.  I certainly wouldnt be writing this review of Danny Boyles SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE had I not seen the film to begin with.  And, according to Boyle, he would not have made the film if he didnt need to dive into a project that was thoroughly grounded and connected to the earth after making his last sci-fi flick, SUNSHINE.  So with fate appropriately in place and gently leading the way, Boyle has made a film that honours the concept itself and has a great time getting caught up in it instead of fighting against it.  The trouble though is that by acknowledging every move in fates game plan, SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE kills the mystery and makes fate into a trap instead of the comfort it could be.  

The title, SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE, refers to a particular person, Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), as he grew up in the slums of Mumbai and is now the unexpected position of being a finalist on Indias version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire?  Doctors and lawyers, they havent made it this far in the game and yet here is this young kid who works in a call centre on the verge of taking the big prize.  The kid doesnt even answer the phones; he gets the coffee for the people who answer the phones.  How could he know the answers to all these questions?  He has no formal education; he doesnt come from a well-respected background. The answer is simple.  He must be cheating.  And so when the show breaks for the day, Malik is secretly taken into custody and tortured by the police so that he can explain to them just how hes done it.  Not surprisingly, he doesnt take too kindly to the torture and he also doesnt believe that he has anything to hide.  Malik simply sits down with the detective (an underused Irrfan Khan) and explains, question by question, how his life experiences taught him everything he needed to know.

Boyle likes to play with style in his movies and SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE is certainly no different than SUNSHINE or TRAINSPOTTING on this level.  Thankfully, his style is never solely used to make up for a lack of substance but there is still something to be said about overdoing it.  It is beautifully shot, full of life and colour, but it is often excessive and distracting.  I mean, even the sub-titles are over-stylized, appearing anywhere on the screen and boxed by another bright colour to separate them from the image.  I wish Boyle would learn to trust his natural instincts more and not feel he needs these embellishes to keep our attention.  He just doesnt do simple and all the while that hes putting these flourishes on the image, he misses how the rigidity of Simon Beaufoys story is stifling the plausibility of Maliks plight.  Essentially, Malik must give us his entire life story as it relates to the game questions.  The structure becomes deliberate and expected very quickly  question, explanation, question, explanation.  There is no room for surprise and how boring is fate without that particular element?

SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE is still a crowd pleaser.  Its just of the contrived and conventional variety but cleverly disguised as topical and concerned.  Boyle does expose us to an original love story between Malik and his childhood love, Latika (played as an adult by Freida Pinto), told in the unlikely setting of the dangerous Mumbai streets.  Poverty and corruption frame what is a genuinely believable and moving love between these two young actors.  They are not only both beautiful but they are both innocent and sincere.  You will root for them and you will delight in their ultimate outcomes that culminate in a jubilant closing credit sequence (stay in your seat, trust me).  But if whatever events in your life led you to seeing this movie and made you into the kind of person that can see past the flare to the formal, then you know that fate is not as specific nor as simple to spot as Boyle seems to believe.

Danny Boyle has directed so many genres and has done so well with all of them that I can confidently say that he just flat out knows how to direct movies. His style doesn't change, but his ability to tell a story doesn't either. It all comes together very well for "Slumdog Millionaire" which is probably one of the toughest positive films in years. It's absolutely incredible the struggles the characters face in the film, and Boyle transfers all of these real life events and cultural factors onto the screen quite poetically and beautifully. It doesn't end up being a cheesy story at all, it's actually rather realistic, and at times it's hard to take. The Indian culture is illustrated beautifully with all the grit and rich colors, and vibrant characters, this film is truly brought to life. I don't think there's another director out there who could've done it better. He also does a great job with pacing. His quick cutting and stylized shooting and editing styles help to speed up the film in some of it's slower moments. Not to mention the fantastic choice of music, mixing mostly Indian music, always with a great beat and some American music as well, when appropriate. It all comes together and tells a great and compelling story in an entertaining way.

The acting in the film is very good from the entire cast. Three separate actors have to play the main character, Jamal, as well as his brother Salim. All three actors who play both characters do a great job. Even the younger actors show a great range, while none of the 6 actors have one particularly weak link of any kind. Much of the supporting cast must've been famous in India because many of the older men in the film just did a magnificent job. The love interest, Latika, was believably gourgeous when the final actress began to play the more mature version of the girl. There is no specific actor in the film that I can look at and say was miscast.

The writing is all very well done. The movement in time is something that could've easily been screwed up but it's handled quite well. It also would've never ever worked as a narrative and the movement in time seemed very logical and necessary to effectively tell the story. The character arch's throughout the film are done to perfection and I can't say there were many moments were I thought something could've been more fleshed out. I suppose the romance plot line was a little simplistic and could've been delved into more, but it was believable enough that it didn't really effect the overall quality of the movie. Another big strength is the fact that it has a very wide appeal. The story is a very universal struggle that any culture can understand. It also should appeal to both sexes as it seems to cross into enough genres that it can interest both men and women. I don't know who truly would not enjoy or get something out of this film. As a whole it could be most easily compared to "City of God" but a little more positive, and I mean that as the highest of compliments. I had very few problems with any part of the film and the writing is no exception.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is a totally welcome and very pleasant surprise. It seems there is one of these type of films a year, a small film festival darling that becomes a buzzed Oscar contender.  Usually I find these films to be little more than hype and myself offended by their paint by the numbers attempts for adoration, I find myself underwhelmed at best.  So this year's Juno or Little Miss Sunshine would seem to have been Slumdog Millionaire.  However if those films left me shaking my head at their reveling in mediocrity, Slumdog Millionaire is a complete surprise.  This is not only the little film that could win the Oscar for best picture, it is legitimately deserving of such an accolade.

Our hero is Jamal, a young man, who dominates India's Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, much to the chagrin of it's cruel host (the performance of the film delivered by Anil Kapoor).  Soon the police, thanks to the host, are wondering how Jamal, an uneducated kid, know the answers and after some despicable approaches they try another approach to get the truth.  Jamal has to tell them how he came to get each answer. As he does we flashback to his circumstances which include being orphaned, surviving on the streets with his brother Salim (a compelling figure), and meeting his true love, an orphan named Latika. 

There is rough stuff here.  Torture, a Fagin like monster (you will hate this guy with an absolute passion), horrible betrayal, forced prostitution, and the Mob figure in.  However, there is also resilience and humor (the scene with the brothers pretend to be guides is hilarious).  Running throughout are the two important relationships in Jamal's life, a troubled one with the complex Salim and the soul mate love he has for Latika, the woman imprisoned by fate to a soul deadening life.  Three actors play Jamal (and the same goes for Salim and Latika) and they are indelible.  Dev Patel plays Jamal as a man and he is a winning hero, resolute and likeable.  Older Latika must be a powerful and wonderful presence to support Jamal's refusal to give up against all odds and Freida Pinto absolutely is.  She also has to go to the top of most beautiful actress lists.  Madhur Mittal, as older Salim, and Irfan Khan, as the lead police inspector, deliver nuanced work in support.  

The cinematography is gorgeous, the soundtrack is the best of the year, and the pace is crisp (there is never a moment of boredom).  To go along with commentary on India's growth as a Business giant, there are sharp critiques on sexism and class bias.  I also have to state that this is not a Bollywood film.  There are not countless music numbers and Latika is a far more fascinating female figure than I typically find in Bollywood films.  However that said stick around for the credits.  The film is codirected by Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tanden (whose contributions should not be overlooked).

Slumdog Millionaire is that rare movie you go out to see that just seems different--in a good way.

We follow Jamal Malik, an impoverished young Indian boy who grows up in the slums outside of Mumbai. He is a witness to unscrupulous human torture, filthy living conditions, and environmental degradation to the otherwise beautiful land around him. But what sets Jamal apart from the rest of his friends and schoolmates is his most admirable character, his unending respect and care for the good people in his life.

At around six years of age, Jamal and his brother, Salim, see their mother killed--essentially decapitated with a long board of wood--by a grassroots Hindu terrorist group after the Muslim denizens of the city.

So, the two boys, realizing that they must make lives for themselves, embark on a journey away from their homeland, not knowing at all what's in store for them. Along with them goes a young orphan girl, Latika, about whom Salim seems not to care but with whom Jamal--in the young, ripe, developing stage of his life that he's in--begins immediately to feel a personal connection. From this point on, Latika is Jamal's perceived reason for existence in the world.

Soon after, a man in his 30s and his friends offer the three transient children bottles of Coca-Cola. The man convinces Jamal, Latika, and Salim that with him lies a better life, one with good food to eat and other children to play with.

The man, however, turns out to be far less a friend than the children had thought. And when the children manage to run away--fear-ridden but nevertheless once again free--Jamal and Salim become separated from Latika, a situation Jamal does not handle well.

Throughout his young life, Jamal longs for his only true romantic partner--and, on the way to finding her again, he gains valuable knowledge that will soon help him become a champion of the Indian version of the game show "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" It is Latika's favorite TV program, and Jamal believes that by being a contestant, he will be able to reach her once again. He's right.

What's most fascinating about Slumdog Millionaire is not at all the frame of the story but rather the unique, emotionally moving side-notes that Jamal encounters from beginning to end.

The movie is shot beautifully through the direction of Danny Boyle (Trainspotting), who mixes trademark Bollywood style with the astounding audio-visual connection between hit modern music and his picturesque filmmaking. Never has M.I.A.'s "Paper Planes" seemed more appropriate to be played--or as meaningful as a song itself--than in the scene in which it is used here.

Ambitious but eventually imploding in a crescendo of cliches, "Slumdog Millionaire" will likely win this year's Overhyped Film of the Year Award. The first forty minutes of this film are impressive and very natural; the best scene involves the extreme lengths protagonist Jamal will go through to get a movie idol's autograph. The exposition is also a damning expose of the cruelty visited upon India's orphans. One particularly harrowing scene involves Jamal and his best friend Salim running for their lives from a mob intent on killing every Muslim in sight, with the two boys running into an Apocalypse Now level hallucination (or was it real?) of Rama. Weird, good stuff there.

But unfortunately, the film begins to collapse upon its own weight and pretensions with its clumsy, implausible character development, particularly in the case of Salim. After Salim, for all intensive purposes, severs his brotherhood with Jamal with a gun and rape, we fast forward to the men now as young adults, renewing their relationship. (One punch to the face makes amends). This contrivance allows Jamal to attempt to rescue his lady love Latika, and he hatches a frankly retarded scheme of whisking her away at an train station. Salim lurches back and forth between good and evil like Long John Silver on meth. All of these episodes is done in the context of answering questions to "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire", which only adds another layer of contrivance.  

"Slumdog" eventually degenerates into Ye Olde Underdog Triumphs With Everyone Feeling the Tension flick, complete with a hackneyed cross section of demographic India cheering on the plucky chai-walla on an inexplicably popular TV game show. The closing scenes are so cliche that it fails the Mute Button Test. That is, you could hit the mute button, and say aloud what you think the dialog will be, and you'll probably be right.
 
The fatal flaw of "Slumdog", beyond the clumsy editing and ridiculous contrivances, is that Boyle utterly fails to capture an appropriate tone for the film. I guess Boyle was attempting to capture a gritty portrait of the hardknock life of India's poor, (which he brilliantly succeeds in doing in the first half of the film), but he makes the woeful misjudgment of directing the film towards a romantic adventure, complete with dastardly cardboard villains and a useless damsel in distress. The love story of Jamal and Latika is essentially shoehorned into the story, and the zero chemistry between Dev Patel and Frieda Pinto doesn't help matters. 

With its stilted dialog and three dozen plot conveniences, "Slumdog Millionaire" is a very frustrating film, particularly after the promising first half. "Slumdog" is a superbly-photographed, well-scored but ultimately mediocre film that veers away from its dark first half in favor of a crowd pleasing rags to riches story. So, if you're in a crowd and only want to be pleased, this film is for you. Otherwise, give this sugar coated exercise in poverty voyeurism a pass.

Ah India! A country so beautiful and at the same time decayed by religious and political strife. It would be hard to take a bad photo of Mumbai. Danny Boyle does not disappoint, on the contrary, he has created a film which so completely captures the beauty and chaos that is India -- the juxtaposition of the breath takingly peaceful, serene and romantic Taj Mahal surrounded by the slums of the lowest caste eagerly peddling their wares, and watching Indian 'Millionaire' on beat up television sets. Via the Indian train, the film captures both Bombay and it's surroundings as well as Agra and the Taj Mahal. The gist of the story is so inherently Hindu that at times I wanted to cry out of plain adoration and respect for Jamal, the protagonist. As is the Hindu belief in karma, if you do good and true things, then good things will come your way. Danny Boyle took a script that could so easily have been turned into an average film and enhanced it so ingeniously by shooting entirely on location in Mumbai (even using some actual Bollywood sets -- not to mention the ingenious Bollywood dance sequence during the credits). The child actors he used are Mumbai natives, whose performances were heart breaking, honest, and completely accurate due to the fact that A) they have lived and experienced the material and B) they adore Bollywood. EVERYONE in India adores Bollywood. Side note, when I was in India the Indian version of 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire' (aka "Kaun Banega Crorepati?") is a show that appeals to the entire caste system -- I conversed about the show with taxi drivers, waiters, children in the streets, and business men. And Boyle captured this in the film -- television and technology in some ways as a tool bringing together a nation. It was clever how Amitabh Bachchan made an appearance in the Slums (in reality he is the host of Indian Millionaire, not to mention a legend of Bollywood film). When I was in Bombay, our Bollywood host took us to Mr. Bachchan's favorite restaurant guaranteeing that we would see him there and we did!) I highly recommend seeing this film. It made me want to go back to India and spend more quality time with the children.

I thought that this movie was good, but it fell short of all the "best picture of the year" hype that's it's been getting.  What struck me most about it was how there isn't really anything truly new or unique about it.  (Of course, I blame this on the fact that we had watched Paranoid Park the night before.)  There isn't a whole lot here that you haven't seen before in City of God or any other movie about poverty, hardship, troubled childhood, gangsters, and lost love.  Snobbish criticisms aside, it's still a well-made film.  Boyle manages to make the whole thing pretty visually impressive.  It gets a little too flashy at times, but it holds your attention.  And it's hard to find fault with the story because it's compelling enough to make you care about the main character and what happens to him in the various stages of his life.  Ultimately, it's a crowd-pleasing rags-to-riches tale, and there ain't nothin' wrong with that.  It's full of dark, rough-edged subject matter, but it's all framed in a relatively conventional, accessible way.  This means that it's not revolutionary filmmaking or a life-changing viewing experience, but it's an interesting and entertaining movie well worth two hours of your time.

RATING (0 to ****): ****
 
 Danny Boyle, director of such films as "28 Days Later", "Sunshine" and "Trainspotting", is a man who has stated that he does not work well with Hollywood movies. His response was to shoot "Slumdog Millionaire", a screenplay concerning the Indian version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" and its latest hot contestant, Jamal (Dev Patel), with no actors known to mainstream American audiences, and with compact digital cameras.
 
 "Slumdog Millionaire" turns out to be a very Hollywood story, chronicling Jamal's rags-to-riches story in two different segments: his childhood as an orphan running around the slums with his ill-intentioned older brother Salim, and an investigation concerning whether or not his success on the show was due to cheating.
 
 The film opens with some very difficult-to-watch torture scenes, all because of a belief that no "slumdog" could answer those questions properly. You may have heard it being compared to "Forrest Gump", and it's not hard to see why. As Jamal works to convince his interrogators that he was not cheating, his answers have instead coincide with his numerous painful memories.
 
 But like any great film whose hero is stuck firmly in the muck, Jamal never asks for your sympathy. He knows what he wants: the girl, of course. Latika (Freida Pinto), who Salim shut out from the beginning, gets frequently separated from our hero. But Jamal will stop at nothing; in an early scene where he's locked in an outhouse as a famous movie star appears, you get a great sense of his willpower and undying spirit.
 
 Though running at a mere two hours, "Slumdog Millionaire" has a very epic feel to it. Although I have not seen it yet, I'm not holding my breath for Baz Luhrmann's "Australia" to have the same breadth, or the same power. Much like "28 Days Later", Boyle provides for audiences another long, difficult journey, even if this one serves to be far less bleak.
 
 A testament to the power of cinema is when even a Y2K fad like "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" can evoke the same suspense eight years later, even though you have an even greater sense of what's going to happen. Whether or not you want Jamal to have a better life, or to finally be with Latika, you're with him.
 
 In the event that AMPAS does something stupid like not nominate "WALL-E" for Best Picture, "Slumdog Millionaire" is the one. We still have a couple months for other movies to potentially prove me wrong, but if they top this, color me surprised. Absolutely, positively do not miss!

This is the new film from Danny Boyle, and rather odd it is too; quite unlike anything I've seen from him before.

The film opens with the police trying to beat a confession of cheating out of a contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, one question away from winning 20m Rupees.

It becomes clear in the course of this interrogation that our hero is not the brightest of chaps, yet here he is, on the verge of winning a fortune in a general knowledge quiz. How then, does he know the answers? 

It transpires that each of the questions he's been asked trigger a memory of a significant event in his life. Essentially, the Who Wants to be a Millionaire thing is a plot device to allow us to watch a coming of age story of two brothers growing up in the slums of Bombay (later Mumbai) in a series of flashbacks.

For what seems a rather silly idea, it's fitting that the first story is quite light-hearted, but later ones get quite dark, as the brothers' lives gets harder and harder - which isn't to say that there aren't still light moments, just that they're punctuated with much nastier ones.

It's all a bit implausible, but it rattles along at a good pace and it's good fun. 

To be honest, the silliest thing is that the first two questions are bloody impossible, and the ones for 10m and 20m Rupees (especially the 20m Rupees) are utterly facile, even allowing for the film being set in India - one of them's a noddy question about cricket with 3 obviously wrong answers...

It's different, but enjoyable. Anil Kapoor is particularly good in the Chris Tarrant role, but everyone's good, even the kids at the start.

There's a funny riff on Bollywood post-credits too.

 [left]'Slumdog Millionaire' is something of a miracle. In an industry where heartbreak and tragedy often rule out, here is a movie you can genuinely root for. One that hits all the right notes. Whatever you may take away from Danny Boyle's aesthetic journey through India, it will almost certainly leave you with a smile and sense of wonderment.
 
 Oddly enough, there isn't anything particularly groundbreaking about 'Slumdog Millionaire'. It is in many ways a traditional rags to riches story, but told with such freshness and endearment that everything you see on-screen is exciting and unpredictable. A bizarre story, told through the eyes of a young man competing on India's version of 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire'. One question away from the million dollar question, our main character Jamal is arrested and accused of cheating. He has, as time will soon show, become a national hero. Because Jamal does not come from a privileged background. He is, in fact, an orphan who has not had a proper education since he was a young boy. But there is an amazing story intertwined, and it's as dazzling as it is unforgettable.
 
 To prove his honesty, Jamal traces his steps back to the very beginning. He tells the story of his life, weaving in every question asked on the show and applying it to a life lived without any shortcuts. From innocence to maturity, and a never ending search for one girl's affection. We're given access to a side of India rarely seen by outsiders, as beautiful as it is impoverished. There is such passion behind Boyle's direction, an English filmmaker who has given us a very diverse collection of films throughout the years, and he presents us with a picture that desperately seeks for truth and greatness. A vision that affirms life around every corner even when encountering the lowest of lows.
 
 'Slumdog Millionaire' is the right film at the right time. It's an underdog story we can all cheer for, and one that has the awesome potential to move an entire audience. The film's cast, many characters are played by multiple actors as the years pass, all come together to form something very special. Dev Patel in particular, who plays our present day Jamal, is a great young talent who delivers a fine performance. And from its dizzying but fantastic editing to breathtaking cinematography, 'Slumdog Millionaire' is everything you could ask for in a film and then some. Nothing I say could possibly give a film like this justice, you simply have to experience it for yourself and witness the power. 'Slumdog Millionaire' is about as good as they come. A fairytale story you will never forget.

As it stands, SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE is the ultimate amalgamation of artistic vision and the creative process.  The visual medium has found its ideal story and director Danny Boyle has both the material and the medium to show off his niche as both artist and entertainer.  And looking by the results, Boyle is more than entitled to show off, since much like a peacock, he does it so very well, one figurative feather at a time.   

With such sharp source material, the book Q&A by Vikas Swarup, as envisioned by Danny Boyle, long with a cinematic eye, SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE is a simple but epic story that manages to grab our attention, break our heart and make us want to stand up and cheer.  I was unbelievably impressed at how an idea based around WHO WANTS TO BE A MILLIONAIRE, set in Mumbai, can make for a fascinating watch.  
A young boyâs journey through the slums of India and his relentless effort to survive anchors this incredibly moving film.  At its start, we are watching the famed game show on television.  Now perhaps twenty, the contestant, Jamal, is in the studio, in the hot seat, and as he responds to each question, one at a time, he looks back and we begin to see and understand how each of his answers has shaped and been impacted by Jamalâs short but triumphant existence. 

Boyleâs efforts pay off.  It is hard to find a more commanding and dramatic movie.  With such a force, it is clear that Boyle really understands how to use film visually to maximize the power of each image and how to use editing to build on tension and emotions to the highest possible effect.  

Boyle has also aced in casting his actors.  His three leads are each portrayed by three formidable young actors.   Despite the decision to have three unknowns playing characters at different stages of their young lives, he is able to garner much empathy and, when need be, anger for each of his characters throughout.  

By the end, teary eyed and all, and I am not giving away more than I need to, it is a winning story of both love and pride, a foreign ride that seems far and exotic yet so easy to understand.  Boyleâs technique is spot-on, through refined imagery and the simplicity of a story, he shows us one boyâs will power to live and, by doing so, how lucky we are to be living.

[size=3]Boyle is not just unique because he uses his childhood nickname in film credits. He's also one of the world's most protean filmmakers. His goal seems to be to try his hand at every genre that exists. His broad resume includes "Trainspotting," "The Beach," "28 Days Later," "Millions," and "Sunshine." ("Sunshine," incidentally, was a gripping piece of science fiction starring Cillian Murphy that was one of the most criminally overlooked films of 2007.) [/size]
 
[size=3]This time Boyle operates within the genre of the feel-good melodrama. [/size][size=3]This isn't entirely new for him. So to make it more of a stretch, Boyle left[/size][size=3] the Western world and explored a new continent, a new country, new music, new religions and several new languages. "Slumdog Millionaire," his brand-new work, was filmed in and around Mumbai, much of it in the vast slums there, with an all-Indian cast speaking their native languages in addition to English. (Mumbai was known in the 20th century as Bombay.)[/size]
 
[size=3]How did a fiftysomething Irish Catholic born and raised in England have the gumption to take on this project? More astounding: how did he pull it off with such commanding aplomb? [/size]
 
[size=3]"Slumdog Millionaire" is not deep or complex. It is a melodrama through and through. But it's one of the best you'll ever see, and it takes on social issues with a force you rarely see in mainstream moviemaking. But I must admit the social commentary was a bit predictable. The story focuses on two boys from what Americans would call the 'under-class.' Caste language is never mentioned in the screenplay, but these boys appear to be from the group that was once called the 'untouchables.' In one early sequence, they are shown attending to outhouses.[/size]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3][img]http://images.nymag.com/images/2/daily/2008/11/20081112_slumdog_560x375.jpg[/img][/size]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3]These "slumdog" brothers (the word 'slumdog' appears to be common in India) are orphaned at a young age when their mother is killed in an anti-Muslim riot. The riot is one of the most horrific scenes in the film. Equally harrowing are sequences in an orphanage where the boys temporarily reside.[/size]
 
[size=3]Breaking out on their own, the boys scrape by as petty thieves and scam artists. There are several great scenes involving cons perpetrated against white tourists who are looking for "the real India." They certainly find it when they encounter these fast-hustling but good-natured boys. The child actors playing the boys are magnificent.[/size]
 
[size=3]The middle segment of the film focuses on the boys in their teenage years, when their life paths suddenly diverge. I won't give away the details, but it involves the limited options uneducated boys have for getting out of poverty. The last part of the movie depicts them as twentysomethings, when one of them becomes something of a national hero as the only lower-class person ever to do well on the TV show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire," which apparently was as big a hit in India as it was in Britain and America.[/size]

[size=3]It is absolutely amazing to hear the class background of the young man discussed over and over on the TV show. Imagine a contestant on an American game show being repeatedly referred to by the host as a "lowly maid" or an "uneducated car mechanic." That's what this young man has to endure. I have no firsthand experience of Indian society, so I cannot judge whether this characterization is accurate. But I suspect that it's not far off.[/size]

[size=3][In personal conversations with Indians in New York, I've heard it said numerous times that caste stratification in India still lingers even though it was formally outlawed. My closest Indian acquaintance has several times said that corruption in the country is so deep and ubiquitous that it would not be hard to have someone killed there, as long as one had enough money to pay off the officials.] [/size]
 
[size=3]The young man's success on the TV show is so hard to accept that he is arrested and subjected to brutal interrogation by police determined to uncover his method of cheating![/size]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3]Woven like a thread through this storyline is the theme of lost love. The young man who is on the game show met a girl when he was at the squalid orphanage. I won't reveal how they got separated (it's one of several heart-pounding action sequences in the film involving mortal danger). When the boy becomes a teenager, he struggles mightily to find the girl again. To some degree like Romeo and Juliet, these two young people find social circumstances continually tearing them apart.[/size]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3]Despite being corny, melodramatic, and rather simple, "Slumdog Millionaire" is one of the most rousing and inspiring films of the year, and it comes highly recommended.[/size]
[size=3][/size] 
[size=3]One final note -- At the tail end of the film, there's a sequence indicating which genre Boyle wants to try next: the movie musical! That's all I'll say. You have to see it for yourself.[/size]

First off, I went into this movie with sky-high expectations. That is most always a bad thing. So, of course, naturally I was disappointed. The movie is based on a book, "Q&A", and this is made evidently clear by jarring shifts in character progression. For example, one of the character takes on a dark side, but there was no lead-up to the change. Suddenly, he was bad. On top of that, there are shifts in age, which confuses matters even more. That would seem natural, since this is a movie of flashbacks, but it makes for a non-cohesive narrative structure. And, sadly, the movie uses a "cheap" technique of having a game show, and results of the game show, as a plot device (the major backbone of the film). In my opinion, the results of a game show are too random. Does a player of a game show deserve the audience's sympathy just for being a player of a game show? Not by the standards of a movie, in my opinion. How can the winning of large of sums of money via a game show be congruent with other scenes in the movie where money leads to evil actions (such as the maiming of children in order to produce more effective street beggars). And, like many movies, there is a cookie-cutter aspect to the ending. Granted, many movies are like this, and it's part of many successful movies basic structure. But, I didn't buy it, because there wasn't sufficient character build-up for it to be a deserved payoff.
I appreciate that different aspects of Indian society were revealed, and it's important for Americans to learn about other cultures. It's just too bad that the movie is too scattershot to be worthy of the society that is presented.

In the middle of the film Jamal and Latika are standing in a kitchen with Who Wants to be a Millionaire playing on the television set in the background.  Jamal asks Latika why everyone finds the show so appealing to which she responds that it is an escape from reality -- a way to imagine yourself being given the opportunity of a better life.
The theme of escaping from reality is constant throughout Danny Boyle's rags to riches story which is similar in style to Fernando Meirelles and KÃ¡tia Lundâs City of God, albeit with clear East Indian undertones.  Jamal is a Muslim orphan from the slums of what was then Bombay.  Boyle displayed an admirable attempt at depicting Mumbai's deeply disturbing poverty and the conflict between Muslims and Hindus, as well as the irony ridden in the process of Bombayâs growth and development during its transition to becoming Mumbai.  That being said, the film loses steam as it shifts its focus to the love story element between Jamal and Latika while still continuing to display the misery and the suffering of the poor and the disadvantaged people of the city.  Boyle was no doubt incorporating a modern take on Bollywood, but Bollywood is all about glitz, glam and romance.  Its emphasis on fantasy as opposed to the hard to accept realities of life is precisely what draws hundreds of millions of viewers to its productions each year.  Boyle could have made a really powerful critical statement about Bollywood if he properly juxtaposed poverty and suffering alongside Bollywood themes but instead he allowed the misery of poverty to be overshadowed by the romantic aspect of the film.  
The film ends with Jamal winning the show, finally kissing his one true love Latika and everyone bursting into song and dance for the credits.  This happy ending allows the majority of the audience to leave with a warm feeling in their stomach because Jamal -- the Muslim orphan from the slums, the Chai boy assistant from the telemarketing company -- did get a better life in the end.  But what about the other orphan boy who had his eyes plucked out with a spoon so he could make more money begging, or the Muslims that died during the Hindu pillage of their slum?  What about those people?  Who does the audience end up remembering and perhaps more importantly, what exactly was it that Boyle wanted us to remember, or forget?

Being both immensely moving and beautifully formulated, Slumdog Millionaire will never release you out of its massive grip of charm and it certainly places itself into this year's best movies shelf. This is not a story that has been told and retold, hashed and rehashed. It is fresh and engaging - all at once upbeat, romantic, violent, culturally insightful, desperate and more than fantastic.

The story involves Jamal, an 18 year old orphan who is accused of cheating in the Indian version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." With one question away from the grand prize, the show finished and Jamal was taken to the police station for questioning. The film opens up with Jamal being interrogated and tortured by the police in attempt to make him explain how he cheated. Jamal insists to the police inspector (Irfan Khan) that he knew all the answers. The movie then constantly moves by Jamal talking through each question that he got right to the later turned sympathetic inspector, and in explaining how he got all the answers. Jamal tells his life story of growing up in the unsafe slums of Bombay with his quarrelsome brother Salim, of how he managed to get on the famous TV show and of Latika, the girl he's loved all his life.

Danny Boyle seems to never make the same movies twice. From a Zombie inhabited genre to general science fiction, and until now, an adventure love story untold like any other which will surely lend some joyful tears to the audience. What he always kept among all his movies is the clean and direct manner he tells his story while still managing to infuse it with an elaborate and eye-catching visual style. But Slumdog is an exemption in a way which Boyle himself has never been able to achieve, or any other filmmakers in fact. Right from the start, Slumdog captures and contrasts the goofy garishness of the TV show and the vision of the slums of Jamal's childhood that is both desperately sad in its poverty and yet somehow thrilling in the way that they are packed with life in virtually every corner. It's a rare movie that can freeze your breathing in one moment and only a few seconds later you'll discover that you're feeling so optimized and regenerated from the darkness that our main character managed to prevail. I know being reborn can be a cliche, but I think that's actually what happened during the moment I finished watching the movie. And believe me, that feeling awfully seldom comes to me.

You've probably heard of this a lot of times before, but I'll just lay it out here again: if there's one movie that could surely make you happy this year, make this your ticket to life celebration and marriage to a rather engaging smile. Slumdog Millionaire is palpably this year's audience winner. Every countable aspect of this movie warrants all the praises it has received, above all is director Danny Boyle. I seriously can't make up the likelihood of a viewer sitting through the movie without feeling outright euphoric after the credits roll (even the Bollywood-dancing credits gave me a great deal of extra pleasure).

An enchanting and engaging romp through the slums of India as a young man lives out a modern rags to riches tale and picks up a romantic interest along that way that, unsurprisingly, is very much off limits later on in life. Slumdog Millionaire follows damn near every cliche in the book, but Boyle embraces this idea and has crafted a stylized and compelling story that is considerably more than the sum of its parts. The cinematography is incredible and the early chase through the streets of Mumbai was one of the most enjoyable and riveting scenes in all of cinema this year, beautifully paralleled not much later by another similar chase through the streets. My score would likely be lower, but Slumdog Millionaire reminded me why the cinema is so great and this film has a special place in my heart for that very reason.

Now this is an interesting concept: a rags-to-riches tea server in India climbs the "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" ladder, with every answer to the questions linking back to a pivotal moment in his life.  Clever concept that works for the first two thirds meets predictable ending and a lead actor who gets by most of the movie looking confused with his mouth hanging open.  But barring the largely Capra-esque ending, this movie delivers some incredibly powerful images when it isn't busy moving from one chase scene to the next (kids are chased through the tight, inner workings of India's slums for what seems like every other scene in the beginning, though that is largely to set up our protagonist's "slumdog" moniker).  No one will be surprised at all by the ending but more than a few may be surprised by how fast the film's running time goes by.  This is a relentless film of love, hope and the need to shut up a stuffy game show host who accuses you of cheating (the key event that sets up the entire action of the movie).  It's not a happy ending for all (indeed, children have their eyes burned out, although one character goes out in a blaze of glory while sitting in a bathtub full of money... which is just awesome) but the end result is one of composure and opportunity for the majority of the players.

Oh well, in this multi-cultural age, it should not wonder anyone that the latest British film from Danny Boyle [yeap...remember Trainspotting!you cannot get more brit than that!] is actually...Indian!!!! That is not bad a bad remark at all, however, while to most viewers, the miseries, drawbacks, hardships and lack of justice our hero Jamal goes thru in the film, might appeal or be something new, like a lighting striking in their heads, a wake up call and realisation that after all we are not that bad on this side of the world, I cannot shake the feeling that I've seen it all first hand coming myself from a far away country with similar problems. 
While I did not have a childhood anywhere near that of Jamal, Salim and Latika, I had the "wake up call" earlier than loads of people here or anywhere else but those less fortunate countries in the world.
But I won't go into that and appreciate the film for what it is. It is still amazing to see the slums in Mumbai and how the, not only racial but religious division might still be at work in such a vast country and how the social classes still are a problem. 
Despite all these, Slumdog Millionaire is a very upbeat film, it made me laugh quite a lot, familiarity I would say, and the knowing that , all the situations were very real indeed and not scripted just to make the film more appealing or exaggerated. People laughing at Jamal pretending to be a tourist guide at the Taj Mahal was not just because it was funny to listen what he was saying, but because they knew that is very real, it's a fact. And it is precisely there that I think the beauty of the film resides!all those familiar situations are told in a nice way, hey! It is still reality, probably not all those kids are bound to be half as lucky as Jamal but the point of the story come across just fine without the need to be cruel ,I must admit many times I thought tragedy will finally struck and kill Jamal or Latika as probably would happen in reality and found myself cheering for them when triumphing against all odds.
Dev Patel is amazing in his Jamal suit. But I think personally the youngest Jamal boy deserves loads of credit for paving the way for us viewers to like Jamal so much!that kid really is so cute!!! The same goes for Salim's youngest self, which in turn with years turn into the kind of conflicted brother he is. The performances by these 2, when they are young or older are just fantastic!!! But hands down to Patel. The film holds together because of him and all his younger representations.
The Music is also amazing, just to remind you how make or break or add can be a soundtrack! I will be buying this one for sure! I even didn't mind that Bollywood dance and the end credits! I even thought it was cute despite Dev Patel inability to dance! 
Overall, I think Danny Boyle has made a beautiful film [it was about time] and his work is just great! Go and see it because you will not regret it !!!!
