With recent Academy Award heavyweights like "No Country for Old Men" and "There Will Be Blood", it seems as though we're outgrowing traditional pieces with happy endings. Then, "Slumdog Millionaire" comes along - a film that wrenches at your heart in the developing moments until it begs you to rise and cheer with glee at it's ending (all capping off with a Bollywood dance number). It's manipulative, overly melodramatic, and has elements of many stories we've seen before - but we've never seen it told quite like this. This is fascinating, innovative, and a completely stylized take on what is fairly familiar material.

The film opens with Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) undergoing interrogation by a detective played by Irrfhan Khan (from "The Namesake"). The night before, Jamal was highly successful on the Hindi equivalent of gameshow sensation "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?", earning a total of 10 million rupees before the time ran out. Now, Jamal is one question away from the grand prize and he will return to answer the question the following evening - that is, if he can convince the police that there was no foul play involved. Suspicious, slimey host Prem (Anil Kapoor) turned in Jamal to authorities under the belief that Jamal had been cheating. How could an uneducated slumdog, he thought, be able to answer questions such as "Who is on the American $100 bill?"

Jamal reveals how he knew the answers - all intricately weaved into his life experiences and miraculously appearing on the show, as if by fate. Through a series of flashbacks, we're introduced to "The Three Musketeers", the name Jamal (Ayush Mahesh Khedekar (youngest) and Tanay Hemant Chheda (middle)), Salim (Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail (youngest), Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala (middle), and Madhur Mittal (older)), and future lover Latika (Rubina Ali (youngest), Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar (middle), and Freida Pinto (older)) have playfully named themselves. After Jamal and Salim's mother is killed in a riot, they find themselves working for men who own a house full of child beggers - going as far as blinding them as "blind singers make double". Later, they find themselves as tour guides at the Taj Mahal, and finally we see where they are in present day. It's no surprise that Salim ends up being the "bad" brother, and Latika ends up being the woman Jamal pursuits throughout his entire life. Due to the setting and the style, these flashback sequences reminded me very much of "City of God".

The best thing about "Slumdog Millionaire" is how rich it is - you can come out of it thinking it's nothing more than an epic romance, and others may see it as a showcase of the economic progression of India (with "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" representing complete modernization). Anyway you want to perceive it, the film has an undeniable charm due to the unlikely hero played by Dev Patel. Patel doesn't look like any conventional lead, nor does he exude the confidence and spunk you'd expect from a heroic lover - rather, he's a perfectly cast underdog. The final moments of the film descend into a completely traditional romantic drama, however at that point we're able to overlook all cliches as we've come to love these characters, especially Jamal, so much.

Danny Boyle is known as the kind of guy who never makes the same film twice, and I think this is unquestionably his best. It's appeal is universal and i'd imagine that it's as much of a heavyweight powerhouse at the Oscars this year as anything else out there. This is perfectly stylized, and not in the masturbatory way "300" is - here, even the subtitles pop up like colorful speech bubbles, yet it's never distracting. I read a review that claimed it's the perfect counter to anyone who fears subtitles (about 1/3rd of the film is Hindi), and that's absolutely true.

I had my reservations about the film, but for what it is I think it's certainly up in the Top 10 of the year. It's a feel-good melodrama that is as absorbing as anything else that's come out over the last 12 months.
Excellent acting, cinematography, direction and last but not least, music. A story that stays with you for quite sometime; this is going to be a nominated film.

He and Salim eventually team up with a fellow waif, Latika, but Jamal loses track of her and then spends the rest of his life (admittedly, he's pretty young) Searching to Regain his One True Love.  He can't get very far without Salim, but is Salim's competence outweighed by his selfishness?  If Jamal ever does find Latika, will she be able to live up to his now epic expectations of her?  Does she even want to?

A heartbreaking, sublime story is only turned into a bit of a cliché by the overwhelming emphasis on the lost (and found...repeatedly) love story between Jamal and Latika. While the heart of the movie should by rights be the divergent paths that the lives of Jamal and Salim take after the death of their mother, instead we're hand fed essentially the same tale that movies like Forrest Gump did so much better.

I hate to sound so negative. Slumdog Millionaire is a great movie that simply focuses on the least interesting of its parts. Urban India, the hopes of millions of poor people hanging on the answers of one of their own, the way that lives can be sent off on wildly divergent paths by tragedy, the way our experiences can become all of what we are - all these themes are captivating in the few moments that they're addressed. 
Banal, Hollywood-style drama simply doesn't take Slumdog Millionaire as far as a focus on those real world, substantive topics would have. Instead, we get a lite version of what this story could have been. We're left with entertainment instead of art.

The strongest aspect of this film is its location. Boyle captured some amazing shots of Jamal's slum. Gorgeous and devastating all at the same time. How he managed to make me say wow at what I thought was a beautiful lake, when it really is a floating sewer, I will never understand. Seriously, it was beautiful.

Also, I really do appreciate the, er, "message" of the film. The idea that life experiences, however they may seem at the time, are always valuable in the future.

Finally, this film continues the run of amazing child performances this year. THAT is what kept me in this movie more than anything.

One of the most unique movie going experiences you can have, Slumdog Millionaire takes the feel-good movie cake and will leave you more that satisfied.
Slumdog is the story of Jamal, a slum kid in the center of India, Mumbai. Once the officers let him take a breath we are handed the story of this young Indian man, and his quest. Not a quest for fame and fortune, but a quest for love. A quest for Latika (the extremely HOT Freida Pinto).
To give away the quest is to rob anybody who hasn't seen the movie yet. Slumdog is too much fun. You cannot help watching the seemingly authentic life of India reveal itself right before your eyes. Ladies and gentleman, this movie is the real deal. From the flawless editing to the poppy soundtrack, this movie shines in so many ways it could have easily screwed up on. Boyle doesn't just make a movie, he creates a unique experience that will have terrible copy-cats scratching their heads for years to come. Slumdog Millionaire uses real slum kids to fit younger versions of Jamal, Latika, and brother Salim (Madhur Mittal plays the oldest version). These kids are not only cute beyond belief, but also fine actors.
Slumdog has no dull moment, and will keep you curious the whole way through. In Slumdog it's not the ending that keeps you guessing, but the journey it takes to get there. After seeing the Oscar telecast it seems like the movie's destiny, like it's hero's, was written.

When [i]Sunshine [/i]came out last year, I called it the "2001 for the punk rock generation."  With [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i], I'm further convinced that Danny Boyle is a director of ambitious style and little substance.  I came out of [i]Slumdog [/i] feeling like I had just attended a rock concert, the queasy motion, mahine-gun style editing, and almost unbearably loud soundtrack having all but deadened my senses.  And while rock concerts are fun, they're very rarely interesting works of art.  Using what I mght call Xtreme filmmaking, Boyle tells the story of a boy growing up in the slums of India with his friends, thieving and cavorting, and falls for a local girl who is seperated from him.  He spends about half of the movie trying to get her back, though one could hardly care, their relationship never being fully realized or established.  Creating a thread for the movie is Jamal's appearance on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be A Millionaire? where he inexplicably knows every answer, despite much of the highbrow Indian audience viewing him as just a lower caste uneducated oaf.  Of course, the questions all seem to form a quite linear chronological path for him to reflect on events of his life.  How convenient.  But this film is not about the plot or the characters, really.  It's about "How cool can I make this look?"  Descending into straight music videos for many sequences in the film, Boyle never seems to go against his impulses, infusing the film with every possible stylistic instinct he could muster.  Even the subtitles are rendered in differet colors and displayed in different areas of the screen like a VH1 pop-up video.  The ending credit sequence, a musical send-up of the greatest genre mankind has ever thought of, Bollywood, is so obnoxious that my friends and I had to run out before we could all declare this one an unmitigated disaster.  And though I did find myself having a lot of fun, and the actors were all magnificent, this film really was a waste of time and belongs not n a movie theatre, but instead on MTV.

Personally, i can't stand the game show 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire'.  I hate how they drag out everything, ask really inane random questions, try to create tension and drama like it was a work of fiction instead of a game show, give me Jeopardy anytime, a time buzzer, if you can't answer the question, move on.

Despite my dislike for the show and its silly format, director Danny Boyle and the screenwriter have turned it into the backbone of a beautifully crafted story of two brothers growing up and struggling in the slums of Mumbai, India.  Credit is given to Boyle who made the british film 1/3 in Hindi with the rest in English despite pressure from the producers to make it entirely english language (and considering there are nearly NO native english speaking characters, this would have been asinine) and recruiting many of the local children to play the street urchins in this curry-accented take on Oliver Twist.

The remixed pulse pounding soundtrack of traditional banghra music with modern drum n bass beats as well as a smartly potrayed look at India and all its modern changes into the 21st century, are done with a vibrant sincerity and honest attempt at capture the exotic beauty of life among the most poverty stricken.

My only real criticism (if you can call it that) is the Hollywood-esque conclusion off the movie which takes away from the edginess of the rest of the film, but seeing all the crap and struggles the main characters go thru, this kind of ending was actually welcomed.  Also the Bollywood-esque closing credits sequence seem tacked on as well.

Still a great film and fantastic example of how new and original ways of storytelling isn't dead yet.  Hollywood filmmakers, please take notes.

I was somewhat perturbed at the use of the term "crowd-pleasing" in ads for Danny Boyle's "Slumdog Millionaire," because before the Fox Searchlight logo even rolled, I knew the outcome of the film. The ending can be easily surmised by anyone even peripherally familiar with the language of film, and while I'm not suggesting that the plotting was poor, the tenser moments were stifled by precognition.

The style of "Slumdog" is at once odd and familiar, as the Indian techno-pop flavored chase sequences bear close cinematic resemblance to those from Boyle's own "28 Day's Later," while speaking, I can only assume, to the musical inclinations of the Indian youth. There's a heavy use of dutch angles in the flashback sequences, which seem to delineate the two worlds of the protagonist, Jamal.

The character's back-story is revealed through "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" questions, which fate has contrived to deliver him each of the answers to. Jamal is accused of cheating, and carefully unravels his history to his captors. The structure is interesting, but occasionally services the questions more than the character.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is an overhyped but fine film about the underdog getting his big break, but when you dabble in fate, you dabble in murky screenwriting territory. Boyle is a talented director, and the dramatic and emotional impact of his scenes only occasionally miss their mark. It's an uneven victory, but consider me pleased.

[font=Verdana][size=2]Tagged as the ultimate underdog story, Slumdog Millionaire worked off it's own morals in order to get to where it is right now.  Boyle's film originally was in danger of missing a theatrical release in the States altogether before an exec from another studio loved it so much, he decided to front the money necessary for its release.  As it continues to sweep audiences off their feet across the country (now in a wider release), Slumdog Millionaire has set its sights on a possible Oscar nom.[/size][/font]
 
  [font=Verdana][size=2]And I must say it deserves one.  Boyle picked a terrific novel to adapt, and really went the extra mile to immerse his audience in a realistic, yet wondrous side of India.  Resorting to digital cameras in many areas in order to give the film a free-flowing environment, Boyle embraces the streets and sights of India, from the slums of Mumbai to the steps of the Taj Mahal.  Working mainly with child actors, Boyle crafts a film rich in emotional impact.  In typical Boyle fashion, Slumdog Millionaire[/size][/font] [font=Verdana][size=2]benefits from some choice editing at certain moments that amplify the intended impact.[/size][/font]

[img]http://www.rowthree.com/wp-content/uploads/2008/08/slumdog3.jpg[/img]

 [font=Verdana][size=2]Relative newcomers Dev Patel and Freida Pinto execute their roles well.  Since their faces aren't known to most audiences, the young actors really become Jamal and Latika, despite suffering from limited screen time.  The plot itself begs its audience some leniency on carry-over effect of the connection between Jamal and Latika.  The characters suffer long periods of time apart amidst growth out of adolescence; yet maintain an undying affection for each other.  Furthermore, Salim factors largely into the film, but his ambitions are never clear.  It's a little suspect and convenient considering the forces that keep them apart and pull them back together, but the logistics of the love story fail to entirely bog the film down.[/size][/font]
 
  [font=Verdana][size=2]Slumdog Millionaire is another success by Boyle, who's body of work is about as eclectic as any director's.  There is some similarity to Boyle's 2004 film, Millions, but rest assured Slumdog Millionaire stands on its own.  The film reckons to be a surefire Oscar contender, and will possibly ride its own morals all the way to the top of 2008's films.[/size][/font]

The new Danny Boyle film Slumdog Millionaire opens with torture and ends with dancing, and the journey that takes place between these bookends is one of the best times I?ve had at the movies all year long.  Boyle (28 Days Later, Millions, Trainspotting) is gutsy, a filmmaker who seems to enjoy taking big artistic risks on the road to creating broadly appealing movies.  He has mastered the artsy crowd-pleaser, films infused with individuality and the independent spirit, while telling stories that seem to find an audience beyond the art-house theatre crowd.  Slumdog Millionaire is no different.

Despite its exotic Indian locale, the immediate Western connection to Slumdog Millionaire comes in the form of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, the trivia game show that once bogged down our airwaves five nights a week at the peak of its national craze.  As the film opens, Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) is being roughly interrogated by Mumbai police for getting so far along on India?s version of the game show that he stands to take home the top prize, despite not just a lack of formal education, but that the fact that he is quite literally a street kid, a slumdog.  Providence has seen to it that each one of the questions that Jamal has been asked on the TV show are somehow intrinsically related to his own life story.  He relates this harrowing biography to the police, and to us, the audience, a story that is at times a tale of coming-of-age horror, a bitter crime drama involving his morally questionable brother Salim, and a grand love story between himself and his childhood friend Latika.

The story is suspenseful and emotionally moving, and the minute I knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that it worked exactly the way Danny Boyle wanted it work was when he successfully displays a brief montage at the end of the film of memorable moments from within the very film we just saw.  That?s really bold, but it worked.  As I revisited those little moments, moments that I had witnessed not even two hours before, I grinned like they were scenes from one of my favorite movies.  Boyle got me.  He was so confident that people would love this movie, he knew a second or two from the ?good parts? edited together would deliver the cinematic equivalent of a joyous hug.  I may have admired this one achievement in Slumdog Millionaire more than any other.

There?s a lot to admire in this energetic film.  Beyond the familiar suspense of the game show itself, there?s the dangerous and beautiful locale, fairly alien to my American eyes, where hideous mountains of garbage take on a strange otherworldly quality.  There?s a killer musical selection, including an early stand-out chase sequence in a shanty town set so perfectly to the jangly beat of an M.I.A song, that I don?t think either the scene or the song can exist without the other.  Dev Patel?s performance is earnest and real, and the child actors playing young Jamal, Salim, and Latika are simply amazing.  Frieda Pinto as the modern day Latika is profoundly beautiful.  I found it difficult to keep myself from running up to the movie screen and attempting a prolonged make-out session.

Before the movie started, I overheard a conversation between two strangers sitting to my right, jokingly worried they were about to see something pretentious and dry because of the reputation of the art-house venue where the screening was taking place.  Slumdog Millionaire may look different than what?s usually playing at the megaplex (there?s not a white person in sight for one thing, and I didn?t miss ?em), but the journey is far more rewarding than the latest Hollywood blockbuster, and, honestly, just as widely appealing.  It?s tragic, exciting, romantic, funny, and uplifting, running the gamut of human emotion while telling an unpredictable story that never fails to entertain and move me.  If you can tell me a better reason to watch movies, I?d like to hear it.

This movie is by far one of the best and most surprising films that I saw this year.  I expected a fairly straightforward romance but what I got was a much deeper, darker and very culturally masterpiece of film; a history about destiny, love versus money, the bond between brothers, friends and family.   Look for a multiple Oscar nominations easily may get a Best Picture of the year.  The story of an Indian orphan teen who transfixes a nation with hope in the Hindi version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire game.  The movie is structured based on this game and shows in every Q&A a touch off an event of the main character, a troubled indian orphan history with flashbacks that fills in like pieces of a puzzle, which I consider a very creative way to develop this movie a BRILLANT move from the director.   During the game each question increases in difficulty and Jamal the main character ponder his answers revealed more of his brothers life, their childhood, their orphaning and the moment they parted ways, in each answer we discovered how he learned his responses, taking the audience through a Charles Dickens crash course of Indian history about religious persecution, child slavery, gang warfare and finally a country that emergence as the customer service call center of the world with great prosperity.   A life lesson of how lucky was the main character to be alive, sane and a decent person after the horrors he is seen through his short life.  If you ask me the question should I go to see this movie?.. my final answer should be: do not miss this movie, you will capture the feel of a great city of Mumbai, India A MUST SEE GO!!!
Haunting yet beautiful depiction of the not so perfect lives and places of Mumbai and India. Just brilliant.

 b) He is lucky

Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million rupees. How did he do it? A: He cheated B: He's lucky C: He's a genius D: It was written

Director: Danny Boyle Starring: Dev Patel, Anil Kapoor, Saurabh Shukla, Rejendranath Zutshi Running time: 120 minutes Country: UK

Awww...what a beautiful, magical, inspiring and very thoughtful film this is that I really do appreciate for being what it is. Slumdog Millionaire is so magical because of the beautiful technical design of the film especially the breathtaking cinematography and music score. When I first saw Slumdog Millionaire, I liked it but I thought there was something genuinly missing from it but I was unsure what it was but after seeing this masterpiece again, I truly do think it is a breakthrough in not only Danny Boyle's career but also reveals a whole new kind of way of filmmaking for the future. I am going to start loving films that have been made by British filmmakers but starring Asian actors/actresses which is where this is like Bend It Like Beckham because that was rather similar. Slumdog Millionaire is a film that goes beyond words. It is really original when it comes to the "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" show but is seems like a very well adapted story when it comes to seeing Jamal grow up from living in the Slums to becoming a famous millionaire. Slumdog Millionaire is one of the 2008 films that have earned a lot of glory and powerful critical reactions to its inspiring and glorious feeling.

Dev Patel's performance as Jamal is absolutely fantastic. This film follows the story from his childhood all the way to his outstanding breakthrough in his life. Because of his success in the show by winning it all it is a big question of whether he cheated, whether he's a genius, whether it was luck or whether it was his destiny. This film tells us the answer of that question as it is goes on. Jamal's character is a deeply interesting one because it felt like he wanted us to know what he was going through in his life. I think the message the character tries to send is that he not only wants us to see what life was for him as a young child but also for people in richer countries to understand what it is like for those people who lives in those kinds of places or who are poor anyway. I became really interested, motivated and inspired my Jamal's personality and the way he was with people throughout his teenage years. He was a very friendly and beautiful boy and he was still like that as an adult during "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?"

Boyle's work in Slumdog Millionaire was absolutely superb with a new kind of way of creating films especially ordinary dramas. Boyle's direction of Slumdog Millionaire was so brilliant, it combined two races of human beings into one. Danny Boyle is one of the best filmmakers ever and it's as simple as that. In my opinion, Danny Boyle is the Stanley Kubrick of this generation because he is one of those directors who can create anything in almost every genre. Boyle's done drama, crime, family, horror, science fiction and romance. I'd like to see him do comedy, animation, action, war or western because I seriously think he can pull it off. The script is fantastic! It deserved the script Oscar win despite that I prefer The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button.

This is an absolute masterpiece but despite how good this film really is, I still think that the Best Picture glory should have gone to The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button. Danny Boyle probably deserved his Best Director Oscar because he was long overdue for one anyway and I am so glad that Slumdog Millionaire was the film that he earned one for. It is one of the best films of 2008. It is my third favourite Danny Boyle film after Trainspotting and 28 Days Later. Slumdog Millionaire is a fascinating masterpiece that I really love and appreciate for what it is like most people hopefully do.

Awesome ! This is definitely best movie of 2008. I may prefer The Dark Knight, but Slumdog Millionaire is something very different from other movies this year that I can't describe with my words. Watch it and you can't lose any second. Danny did a brilliant work again !

A celebration of all this is possible in life. Danny Boyle's masterpiece is a fascinating mix of friendship, betrayal, loyalty, yearning, hope, luck, and, ultimately and most importantly, love. The film follows Jamal, as he participates in "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" and subsequently is taken to a police station for questioning. Why? Because he is a nobody who is about to answer the final question and win 20 million rupees. Just how he did it is the questions posed at the beginning of the film, and the show provides the narrative framework for this wonderful film. With each questions we learn about his past life. We see him growing up in the slums with his brother Salim after his mother is killed. We see him meet Latika, the girl he falls in love with. We see his suffer atrocities, which at times are utterly devastating. And as you see all of this, it reminds of the awe that film can inspire. This film is supremely beautiful and wholly creative in its framing, pacing, and editing. And then there is the acting, which is lovely. Dev Patel and Freida Pinto are the best couple put on screen this yea (along with Wall-E and EVE of course)  and it is beyond easy to root for this couple to find one another and fall in love. It's easy to root for this film to succeed as well, because it is easy to believe that it will not be seen by as many people as it should be, but it will certainly be shown its proper respect come awards season.

Combine that with the CUTEST FREAKING child actors in all of India, a rollicking score, and a full-out Bollywood tribute at the very end (at which my male companion groaned and groaned but still couldn't stop smiling) and it is a darn good time. The first 2/3rds of "Slumdog Millionaire" were intoxicating, raw, exquisitely filmed, unique, emotional and on its way to being one of my favorite movies of the year. Unfortunately, the films final act felt incredibly disingenuous. Danny Boyle can't be faulted for his ambition, nor his willingness to confront some pretty dark issues in this movie, but after an amazing journey undertaken with the stories main characters, who are all wonderfully played by various child actors, Boyle tries to wrap everything into a very neat little package, one which I simply could not swallow. So manufactured is this conclusion that if this were an American film about American characters, it would be heaped in scorn for its wish-fulfillment fantasizing. I don't want to be too hard on this movie, its definitely worth watching, and despite some of its bleak and disturbing content, something that I can see a family enjoying together, it's just not 'best of the year' material.

shooting style aside, the story is perfect, and all of the no-name actors are great... 

danny boyle has made a great film about human suffering, the corrupting effects of money, and true hope and love which conquers all.  the film feels real and true while still maintaining a fascinating sense of romantic adventure.  

no matter who you are, romantic or skeptical, hopeful or cynical, i think this film could intrigue you.  it's tragedies, it's triumphs, it's suspense, it's themes, it's real life power... everything is totally engrossing.  simply a great and powerful film.

'Slumdog Millionaire' is a typical rags-to-riches story, using the slums of Bombay/Mumbai as the backdrop, as well as 'Who Wants to Be A Millionaire'.

Even though it is an Indian movie, the director is actually Danny Boyle, the guy behind 28 Days and Trainspotting. The movie is gritty and attempts to portray India as it is - with its smells, mess, religious tension, poverty as well as the excitement, the smiles, and the dreams of the people.

Slumdog Millionaire traces the story of Jamal Malik who enters 'Who Wants to Be A Millionaire' and can answer every question that is asked. Is he a cheat? How could be a 'chai-walla' (tea maker), be that smart?

Highly recommended.

I've realized that I need to see films twice before passing full judgement, but here it goes anyway:

This film may very well be the best on the year (pending on the quality of "Curious Case of Benjamin Button", which is due out this week)...so why do I take off half a star? The screenplay is heart-warming, the editing is sensational, and the direction is captivating. Sure much of it is predictable, but how the story is told outweighs what is told and the way that this one is told lacks a certain gentleness to its narrative flow. Had it been released in in 2006 or 2007, it wouldn't be winning awards against the likes of "The Departed" or "No Country for Old Men."

Nevertheless, I enjoyed it tremendously and think it's a great experience that everyone will walk away feeling good about.

Predicted Oscar nominations for Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay, Editing, Cinematography, Score (maybe), and Sound Mixing.

The cast is amazing, the earthy, gritty feel of third and first world Mumbai is incredible, the emotions of the third act will knock you flat and the rather clever script which uses the gameshow as a structure to tell the entire story is exceedingly clever.  There's a few quibbles - the first ten minutes is a bit clunky, the pace lags a little in the middle, Anil Kapoor is terrible and there's some character turns that go unexplained,  but who really cares when there's so much to love in this dark and yet vibrant (and culturally accurate) and hopeful film of winning against the most impossible odds imaginable! A recipe for a perfect Hollywood film could not have been better written than Slumdog Millionaire. But for the absence of Julia Roberts and her ilk, the film has the perfect ingredients for a terrific dizzying flight-of-fancy crowdpleaser complete with a little something for everyone. There is the quintessential story of the underdog done good, the 'exotic' locales, the intoxicating soundtrack, beautiful young endearing leads, lovable child actors, unrequited love, cardboard villains, a dash of violence, colorful cinematography, robust editing and a truly compelling storyline well-told through the framing device of a widely popular game show.  What's there not to love? The only thing the film demands of you is to leave logic behind. Suspend your cynical disbelief.  Flatline that brain and enjoy the ride while they show you a picturesque shanty town, improbable reunions or a million dollar question that revolves around one of the most famous widely acclaimed stories of the past century.

It seems more or less that he would just throw the camera anywhere, tell his  actors to do the scene while they follow them handheld. I'd probably give more praise to the editor for being able to assemble the story from what I'm sure are countless hours of shaky handheld footage.

It won me back over slightly going into the end, even though it is cliche and has been seen before. But then, the ending credits give us a musical dance number that really threw me off and was incredibly out of place. For me, it ruined the feeling that the ending presented to the audience. I guess it was their way of giving a nod to "Bollywood". Despite being named by some critic circles "Best Picture", it will probably get an oscar nod for Pictures just as a thank you for being here, like with Little Miss Sunshine and Juno.

Like 2007's Juno, Slumdog Millionaire is essentially a feel-good film by a good director that is given much more credit than is due. Juno was cute like an emasculated Wes Anderson film. Slumdog is like modern live-action Disney film in spite of its violence, which hardly rivals what Disney films have been doing recently. This fictional biography is based entirely upon deus ex machina. It is concerned with building a harmonious world founded on the marble floors of dreamy ideologies and sated with a pleasant, immediately gratifying style.

Danny Boyle's $15 million Hindi fairy tale radiates with the feeling of a call to action. This is a breathlessly paced film, moving all around the emotional map, about a Mumbai orphan who emerges from the slums on the might of his sparkling ability to retain minutiae. The story's shy, pure and heroic protagonist reaches remarkable, vindicating heights merely with the mental and social experience of being a slumdog. He is a beacon of idealism for the hopeful masses. What I admire objectively is that this hyperkinetic melodrama's general allure will acquaint millions of moviegoers with the real India for the first time.

We react to the tragedy of the India of social classes that appear as if to be estranged by dimensions. A woman crawls from a cardboard box. Men bathe at a fire hydrant. People excrete waste on the sidewalk. On the other hand, the world's largest middle class, mostly lower-middle, but all the more highly regarded. Millionaires. Mercedes-Benzes and Audis. Luxury condos. Education is bursting at the seams. A thriving computer section. A cascade of doctors and neurosurgeons.

Complete with a musical sequence at the end, but also an early scene of electric shock torture, Boyle's rags-to-riches tale balances these two Indias by cutting between a hell of destitution and predation and the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire. It tells the story of an orphan from the slums of Mumbai who is born into a brutal existence. A petty thief, impostor and survivor, mired in dire poverty, he improvises his way up through the world and remembers everything he has learned. He finds a small place in the Mumbai gangland, and even falls in idealized love with a girl who keeps eluding him.

Sort of an Indian City of God, the film's flashback storytelling follows his life until his appearance as the show contestant. At the point in his life where he is a contestant on the show, the film takes on a Bollywood-laced magical prestige. Proposed as a "slumdog," he gives the correct answer to question after question and becomes a nationalized idol to audiences who are watching the show live. The flashbacks show the experiences through which he happened to pick up the observations that are now winning him millions of dollars. He doesn't volunteer this astonishing information. The film opens as it's beaten out of him by the show's sweaty, violent security staff. They are convinced he must have stolen the answers.

This crowd-pleaser, scripted with a brisk pace by Simon Beaufoy, uses attention-grabbing cinematography by Boyle's regular DP Anthony Dod Mantle, Chris Dickens's machine-gun- speed editing, and Boyle's trademark energized, driving, uber-modern soundtrack. One could expect from that description a gimmicky film directed by an insecure show-off. But Danny Boyle is one director whose films are made in that style and yet, like a more diplomatic Spike Lee, our abstract familiarity with delight and social ecstasy are stimulated by his work, even by his lesser films such as The Beach and A Life Less Ordinary. Slumdog Millionaire has no underpinnings beneath the marble floors of dreamy ideologies and immediately gratifying style, but I can't deny that it does have that Danny Boyle touch.

I've always been a fan of Danny Boyle's films and I'm in the camp that thinks he isn't quite getting the credit he deserves for his vast array of well made films. I admire the diversity of his career with his directing grace in such films as "Shallow Grave", "The Beach", "A Life Less Ordinary", "28 Days Later" and "Millions". He masterfully went from the dark and raunchy world of drug addiction (Trainspotting) to the horror genre of flesh eating zombies possessed by rage and fueled by killing (28 Days Later) to the ever touching and heartfelt joy ride of two little boys adventures after finding tons of money in "Millions", one of that years best films. "Slumdog Millionaire" is a thrilling rags to riches story set in India centered around Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) as a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?" Jamal, a driven and resilient young man that grows up far to fast has become a solo traveler having parted from his brother and the other street pals that once accompanied him. He originally uses the show as not a means for fame or fortune but rather as a platform to find, Latika (Freida Pinto), the girl he loves that has also been pulled from him. Due to the shows popularity and her interest in it, Jamal knows that it would be the perfect opportunity for her to see he is, in fact, alive and to find him, as he has no idea where she is or if she is even alive. It just so happens that along the way he keeps answering the questions correctly, thus thrusting him into not only the countries spotlight but an unforeseen and dangerous life threatening position of being accused of cheating by the shows Security and scandalous Host. This leads to his being tortured for his in depth explanations of how he could have possibly known all of the correct answers. In his explanations there in lies the fast paced exhilarating pace of this incredible journey of survival that takes Jamal form the slums of Mumbai as an orphan to the grand stage and only one question away from wealth and ultimately freedom from the extremely cruel and poverty laden streets. As each question is answered the live action flashbacks of his explanations to his captors illustrate how it was a part of his tumultuous journey and a key moment in the telling of the story by the scarring effects it had on his life, the answers were not merely remembered but rather burnt into memory based on the terribly brutal circumstances and horrible things he has already endured in his young life.

The film felt very much along the lines of the great Brazilian film "City of God" in it's tragic survival tale of youth violence on the poverty stricken streets. Patel gave a strong performance as the film's protagonist, Jamal and his love interest is equally well crafted by newcomer Pinto. "Slumdog Millionaire" is an excellent film that is sure to get serious consideration for Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay and the music is as thrilling as the action sequence keeping your eyes glued to the screen and your butt on the edge of your seat. Will Danny Boyle finally become a household name? If so it will be because he deserves it.

Damn, this was good. I mean, no, really: damn, this was good. It's such a rare experience to walk out of a so-called "feel-good movie" feeling good not only because the story itself was legitimately uplifting, but also because everything just WORKED. Calling this a game-show version of City of God may sound inadvertently deprecatory, it's actually a very apt comparison; the good news is, while not nearly as dark or violent, Slumdog Millionaire is very nearly as good as Meirelles' 2002 masterpiece. Stylishly directed by Danny Boyle (of Trainspotting and 28 Days Later fame) in a way that's flashy but adds to the goings-on, this is a simple story amazingly well-told with great performances and visuals to accompany it. The main character is so damn likable that you're really on the edge of your seat the whole time just hoping he'll pull through. In a year distressingly absent of great movies, here's one that's crept in just under the finish line. I can't even begin to tell you how welcome it is.

Danny Boyle's absolute worst (and that's saying a lot). Complete and utter bullshit from start to finish, with an as-conflicting-as-possible message to boot. Money is, once again, the root of all evil? Okay, then why are the characters able to walk away with so much of it at the end? Why not let Love stand alone in victory, triumphant over the Greed that overtook the protagonist's brother? Sure, it didn't matter for Jamal at the end whether or not he got the money... I just wish the film had the same conviction and honesty. Tonally, this thing's a mess; there are gruelling scenes of torture, violence, and mayhem oddly contrasted with strange moments of juvenile humour (Jamal falling into a well of poop? HILARIOUS!!!!!). Boyle, it seems, can't allow a single scene to play without some kind of wacky visual trickery; not a moment goes by without ugly and murky cinematography, canted camera angles, blurry motion, and pointlessly LOUD and OVERBEARING sound design! Also, like most of Boyle's films, the director seems to assume that his audience is made up of complete and utter idiots. For example: Boyle constantly reminds us of scenes we've JUST SEEN by flashing back to them... this is usually after no more than two minutes of screentime has ellapsed! And finally... destiny? Really? That's what it all comes down to? Are you serious? I wasted two hours of my life watching this piece of shit to learn that certain events in my life were destined to happen? In a film that features child torture, implied pedophilia, murder, and kids pulling guns on each other, I think it should have come to a slightly more mature conclusion than "Guy Gets Girl," complete with idiotic freezeframe and... a dance number? Seriously?! After all that, a DANCE NUMBER???!!!! Boyle's clearly lost it completely; whatever shred of talent he once had has been devoured, and the audience are the ones left to suffer for it.

How does a movie about a TV game show with a cheesy dance number during the credits end up being so good? The directing (especially in the slum scenes), cinematography, chemistry of the characters (especially as children), and Jamal's passion for survival and for Latika make it work. Indian culture with its beauty and flaws is itself a character that lends reality and impact. A happy ending makes you want to see it again!

[b]Slumdog Millionaire[/b] is British director Danny Boyle's film about life and suffering in a modernizing India, a tale that is both unrealistically (but effectively) uplifting and classically appealing. It is a very good film - the cinematography is top of the line and the acting is excellent - and it is surely a crowd-pleaser, but it is difficult to see how Boyle shot amidst those endless mazes that are Indian slums and still came out with a happy, positive tone. In the film, the slums are not a metaphor for the endless maze of poverty but a sort-of launching pad for Jamal, the ambiguous and charming main character. 

Perhaps Boyle saw hope in the slums - perhaps there is a humanity there that one can't see from a wide angle shot. When Salim is sitting on an in-construction building looking at the new development where the slums used to be, it is implied that the ghetto has been moved. [i]It doesn't just go away.[/i] And yet it seems that Boyle forgot this, but there must have been one for him to shoot in. Slumdog is cock-eyed in its optimism, but that doesn't make it any less of a visual and aesthetic accomplishment. Great performance from newcomer Dev Patel and from seasoned actors like Anil Kapoor.

Slumdog Millionaire has one of the most original narrative structures I've ever seen. It's one of those films that, on paper, doesn't sound like it should work, but the marriage of styles and talents come together perfectly to create something remarkably novel and unique. Between Trainspotting, 28 Days Later, last year's Sunshine, and this film, Danny Boyle has reinvented himself more than any other mainstream director that I can think of, and is quickly becoming one of my favorite filmmakers.

His frenetic direction along with the dazzling cinematography naturally compliment the setting in the slums and busy streets of Mumbai. Half spoken in Hindi, the film--based on Vikas Swarup's novel "Q&A" but liberally adapted by screenwriter Simon Beaufoy--is about a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?" He is one question away from winning the grand prize of 20 million rupees. But this is not ABC, and the host is no Regis Philbin.

They think he's cheating, and the film opens in between shows as he is being tortured and questioned. How does a boy who survived the slums and homelessness in modern India know the answers to all these questions? We can only conclude as we find out through a series of flashbacks: it must be destiny. After all, he did it all for a girl.

Boyle takes classic Hollywood storytelling, wraps it in stylish, Bollywood packaging with a cast of mostly unknowns, and Slumdog ends up resembling City of God, but combined with the tension of a gameshow to create a film unlike any other. It is a mesmerizing, unusually satisfying tale of life and luck, Boyle's best film, and one of the best of the year.

Slumdog Millionaire will go down as the crowd pleaser of 2008. A film that is full of so much heart and belief, its hard not to get swept up in the spectacle. The story has so many layers to it as it is able to balance a redemption (or rags to riches) story along with a stirring love story that is unrelenting. At its core, Slumdog Millionaire is a fantasy story wrapped up in the seedy underbelly of India's streets, and director Danny Boyle doesn't forget this. Instead of putting emphasis on either one, Boyle perfectly mixes both threads and weaves them seamlessly. Not one aspect over powers one another, instead they feed off each other allowing us to not only feel for our main characters and their plights, but to fly briskly along with this fantasy yarn. It hooks us in during the first act as Jamal Malik recalls his life and how each part of his life has led him to answers and possibly the one thing he has been searching for and needing for all of his life. Much credit must be given to Danny Boyle, who is able to capture the beauty of Jamal's relationship with his love Latika, while being able to place it in the backdrop of the impoverish slums where our main characters grew up. Boyle is able to use many camera techniques to heighten our senses and to push us into a scene. At night, when there is something morally questionable occuring or a shot of the slums, Boyle uses a digital camera to create a stark and grainy scene, almost as if we're there and taking part. On the other end, when there are shots of Latika from Jamal's point of view, Boyle puts emphasis on an angelic glow surrounding Latika and creates this dreamlike sensibility to the shot, almost showing us the sheer beauty and wonder Jamal sees (and feels) everytime his eyes gaze upon Latika. And ultimately this is where the beauty lies in Slumdog Millionaire. Its not anymore about rising from the ashes than it is about a love story. Instead, its a kinetic and stirring story thats about finding the beauty and the grandness to life. Sure, the story may come off being serendiptious or a film brimming with coincedences at times, but ultimately it begs us to look at the moments in our lives and how every moment is a building block to not only our lives, but our souls. Life's not about winning 20 million rupees or finding our mugs on tv sets and gaining popularity. It's about those moments that live in the back of our minds or that feeling we get when we simply see the people we love. Its full of heart, full of love, full of soul and most importantly, its full of life.

The power of education, money, and technology pales in comparison to the strength that an individual can attain through the force of love. An eye-opening, heart-wrenching, pulse-pounding film on so many levels, Danny Boyles Slumdog Millionaire is a brave and novel attempt that both entertains and informs. The film is very novel in the fact that its main story centers around a poverty-stricken boy who ends up on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire. As he escalates closer and closer to the top prize of Rs. 20,000,000, the producers think hes a cheat and he cant believe whats happening either as every question somehow relates to an incident in his life. Though the plot initially sounded far-fetched, it unraveled in such a fast-paced and carefully crafted manner that by the end I was on the edge of my seat rooting for Jamal to win that prize, and realize his dreams. Presented in a series of flashbacks, most of the narrative is spend chasing our protagonist throughout India, from the slums of Mumbai to the steps of the Taj Mahal, as he struggles to live in a world that is seemingly against him at every turn. The only shimmering light in this boys life, and the reason he is on the show, is to find the love of his life, a girl named Latika. Though how he manages to find and lose her throughout his life was absolutely heartbreaking, it also helped shape the subsequent events that help him answer the questions on the show. Therefore the film informs through the exploration of three subjects: Depicting the harsh reality of poverty in modern-day India, the ethereal force of love that rings with total purity and absolute selflessness, and the role destiny plays in ones life. Its a very harsh, realistic film while also having elements of a fairytale, ala having an underdog rise to the top. Its very well acted, with the child actors who play the young versions of Jamal, Salim, and Latika leaving the largest impression. Even their adult counterparts and the supporting players including Bollywood stars Anil Kapoor and Irrfan Khan lend natural, engaging performances. Moreover, its gorgeously shot, edited with aplomb, and has a score thats both haunting and irresistibly catchy. In summary, walking out of this one, I felt absolutely floored at the power and beauty of Slumdog Millionare. This is definitely one that cannot be missed.

[font=Arial][color=DarkRed]If there is one independent movie that seems to be picking up momentum this awards season, it's [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i]. The film seems destined to break out into the mainstream, especially in a time where audiences could use a happy story given the ongoing news of economic downturns. [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is a highly spirited rags-to-riches tale that marries Hollywood and Bollywood into one fantastic product. 
 
 Jamal (Dev Patel) is an 18-year-old kid who grew up impoverished in India's favellas. He's also on the verge of winning 20 million rupees on the Indian version of the Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? Game show. The TV host reminds Jamal that lawyers and doctors have never gotten as far as he, a lowly "slumdog" from such humble origins. As each question emerges we discover more about Jamal's life, from escaping a riot, touring India as a stowaway on a train, conning American tourists at the Taj Mahal, to his assistant work at a call center. Throughout Jamal's life are two constants: Salim (Madhur Mittal) and Latika (Frieda Pinto). Salim is Jamal's scheming older brother who has a loose sense of morals. He finds a life of crime as a suitable escape from poverty. Latika is a young orphan girl that Jamal befriended as a child. He declared that she was the "third Musketeer" in their group and has always sworn to love her. This is complicated because Salim's crime boss wants Latika for a prize, and Salim keeps his younger brother away from Latika. Ultimately, as an entire nation watches with baited breath, Jamal explains that he is appearing on TV because he knew that Latika, his love, would be watching somewhere. 
 
 It's like [i]City of God[/i] and [i]Forrest Gump[/i] had a baby that was raised by Oliver Twist. The film is given a dynamic energy thanks to director Danny Boyle's exuberant camerawork and skillful style. Boyle is a director that knows how to make images jump and [i]Slumdog[/i] feels like it is coursing with life. The feel-good fantasy nature of the rags-to-riches plot is offset by some pretty harrowing violence, and Boyle makes great pains to show the realities of living in squalor. At one point a very Fagin-esque local crime lord collects young orphans to be beggars and he has a foolproof scenario to make these kids sympathetic ad thus big earners: he blinds them with hot liquid. Despite the fantastical elements, [i]Slumdog[/i] is rated R for a reason and that's because it does show the cruel reality of a life in the slums, granted it's nowhere near as bleak and formidable as something like [i]City of God[/i]. After all, the kid gets to win on a game show, though the movie does open with Jamal being tortured by the police. Boyle has a tremendously natural eye for crafting visuals that delight the senses; he can make his shot compositions feel interesting without ever truly calling attention to being flashy. The views of India are beautiful and fascinating. Plus, having a majority of the movie in a foreign dialect was appreciated (Boyle provides different color background for different character's subtitles, a nice touch). There's a magic feeling to the film that definitely takes hold of the audience, an uplift that channels smiles and gasps of joy. While I'll still credit [i]Millions[/i] as Boyle's best film since [i]Trainspotting[/i], his work on [i]Slumdog[/i] is deserving of praise. I don't know if another director could have made a film with so many contradictory elements (feel-good flick with child prostitutes?) run so smoothly. 
 
 The movie is also given a brilliant story structure by screenwriter Simon Beaufoy ([i]The Full Monty[/i], [i]Miss Pettigrew Lives for a Day[/i]). The movie is built around a steady stream of flashbacks linked to the questions Jamal tackles on the game show. So the host will pose a question and then we'll be treated to a 10-15-minute flashback to Jamal's life to discover how he knows the answer. The approach is fresh and it reinforces the magical notion that Jamal's life has all been leading up to this moment of glory. Beaufoy's script smartly weaves many storylines together to give us an emerging sense of who Jamal truly is. He manages to write an uplifting and hopeful tale that stays clear from easy sentiment. Indeed, [i]Slumdog[/i] is an accomplished feat of writing as well as direction. Working from the Indian novel Q&A, Beaufoy has written a modern-day fairy tale in the same fashion as the Brothers Grimm, which means he didn't skimp on the unpleasantness and hardship. Yet [i]Slumdog[/i] is able to find great human spirit amidst the squalor. I doubt I'll see a climax more rousing and crowd-pleasing all year. Seriously, you'd have to have a pretty hard heart not to feel some excitement and jubilation in the closing moments. 
 
 This unlikely fantasy is aided by sharp performances by a collection of actors. Jamal is an unassuming yet plucky underdog, and Patel nicely handles these elements. He's a stringy kid but he carries himself with charm and fortitude. As he grows confident he spars with the combative TV host, and it's fun to watch. Pinto is a swell looking beauty with a great smile but I wish the story had given her more to do as an actress. The young actors who play Jamal, Salim, and Latika as young children actually give the best performances. 
 
 And now after all my effusive talk comes the time where I must voice my minor reservations with [i]Slumdog[/i]. First off, the structure is ingenious but having Jamal interrogated by the police after the fact seems unnecessary, plus it also tips off the audience from the beginning that this kid has already won it all, which sucks some of the tension out of the game show format. I really think the movie would have been better served just playing out the game show in real time instead. Also, it's a bit too convenient that every one of the quiz questions triggers a memory in a linear fashion. Jamal can tell his life's story from beginning to end, but the movie would have been more challenging and interesting if the quiz questions forced Jamal to bounce around in his own memory. That way the script would provide more mysteries that could lead to even more satisfying answers. The Millionaire game show also goes on a commercial break and Jamal is astoundingly allowed to leave and go to the bathroom after he knows one of the high-money questions. In the age of wireless Internet, no game show would ever allow the contestant to leave its sight. Finally, the movie is presented like a Dickensian fable told in chunks, which means I found it hard to fully embrace the central romance that drives Jamal. I will readily follow the romantic notion of locating your true love, however, I will feel more involved in that search if the combined time Jamal and Latika spent together was longer then like a week. Seriously, they see each other every few years for a moment and then are broken apart, only to find each other again for a few moments to be broken apart. She's more a symbol than a fully translated character, though this did not stop me from rooting for a happy ending.
 [i]
 Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is a thrilling, funny, and triumphant story that courses with lively electricity, thanks to the deft direction of Danny Boyle. This movie is enormously entertaining while still baring a social conscious about the plight of those impoverished, though I hope people don't get the mistaken idea that all that character-building impoverished life styles will lead to future fortunes like Jamal. The movie is hopeful and uplifting while also balancing tense violence and improbable circumstances. While I'm not onboard with the critics calling this the best film of 2008, it has some minor flaws in approach to storytelling and character, [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]has all the right markings to be a crowd-pleasing sensation. After all, it is destiny. And that's my final answer.

British director Danny Boyle takes another intriguing career turn with this heartfelt underdog tale. Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) is a street kid (or "slumdog") who has landed an appearance on India's version of the hit TV game show WHO WANTS TO BE A MILLIONAIRE? Jamal exceeds expectations on the show, and the producers alert the police after they become suspicious of his methods. The young contestant is subsequently arrested and is interrogated at the hands of a nameless police inspector (played by Bollywood star Irfan Khan). As the interrogation proceeds, Boyle tells Jamal's story through harrowing flashbacks that both show the terrible poverty of Mumbai and help explain how he knew the answers to the MILLIONAIRE questions. SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE is a tightly woven story that has been expertly edited into shape. The contrast between Jamal's upbringing and his chance of escaping it on the show are adeptly juxtaposed. Mumbai is portrayed as a place of terrifying poverty and unforgettable brutality, and Jamal and his brother get into a never-ending succession of challenging situations. But the way Boyle ties together Jamal's life experiences with his answers on the show is quite brilliant, and the film really does run the full gamut of emotions as we see him growing up, falling in love, coming close to death, and teetering on the brink of escaping from his terrible predicament. The film belongs to Boyle's cast, who are mostly unknown outside of India. Patel, in particular, gives a startlingly mature performance that audiences are likely to remember long after the credits role on this affecting feature.

The setting includes a lot of people in unfortunate circumstances putting so much interest in a game show when they are living in poverty and the world around them is crumbling. ''It is written.'' The story of the life of an impoverished Indian teen Jamal Malik, who becomes a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?", wins, and is then suspected of cheating. Dev Patel: Jamal Malik Winner of the Audience Award at the Toronto Film Festival, Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tandan's radical Slumdog Millionaire is the feel-good story of an orphaned, street-wise young man trying to strike gold on India's version of the TV show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" while hoping that the girl he has loved since childhood is watching. Based on the novel Q&A by Vikas Swarup and supported by the stunning cinematography of Anthony Dod Mantle and the music of A.R. Rahman, Slumdog shows us the chaos of Mumbai (formerly Bombay) India where it was filmed. Submerging the viewer in a cacophony of colour and sound, the camera swoops and swirls in an often dizzying pace, taking us from the desolation of back alleys and garbage dumps to modern high rises and the fantastic beauty of the Taj Mahal.
Boyle has nine different non-professional actors in three different time frames, each faithfully representing their character as they grow and develop. In the opening scene, the hero Jamal Malik, brilliantly performed by Dev Patel, is being questioned by Police Inspector (Irrfan Khan) who simply cannot understand how a mere slumdog like Jamal, without any education, can answer question after question on the game show without resorting to lying or cheating. In a city of 13 million people where the police know they can get away with almost anything, the methods of torture used to extract a confession are graphically displayed. With Jamal, however, they only succeed in uncovering the deeper layers of his character as the film flashes back to specific incidents in his life that reveal how his knowledge was gained by personal experience. He knows, for example, that the star of the 1973 film Zanjeer was Amitabh Bachchan because he was his favourite actor/idol as a little boy and was willing to cover himself with filth just to get his autograph. Built on memory, the film relives Jamal's life from the death of his mother, to his entry into service to a cynical gangster who turns street children into blind beggars, reminding us of the millions of third-world children, not as lucky as Jamal, who fight against unending poverty each day. Jamal is fortunate to have allies, however: his brother Salim(Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail) and Latika (Rubina Ali), another orphan that Jamal becomes attached to form the "Three Musketeers", ready to do battle with the world. Salim reminding me of a City Of God result for his character, whom inevitably also redeems himself, while showing God as a salvation for greed and killing. Though circumstances lead the three into different areas when they become adults, Salim (Madhur Mittai) into the criminal underworld, Latika (Freida Pinto) to be kept by a rich man, and Jamal to become a chai wallah, a server of tea to telemarketers. However Jamal does not give up, knowing that his life is governed by destiny, fate and ruled by unending love. Using their wits to survive, the funniest scenes include Jamal and Salim finding themselves as tour guides at the Taj Mahal, inventing stories or the part where Jamal is locked inside an outhouse while his childhood hero star Amitabh is outside signing autographs; escape involves having to go through smelly excrement. Highly amusing and the child actors maintain the harshness and innocence realistically similarly to City of God. The center of the film, however, revolves around Jamal's contesting for millions of rupees on the game show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire"; not necessarily to become rich but to woo his soulmate Latika whom he knows is a fan of the show. We cheer for Jamal to win his fortune and most importantly, to get his love back. While we are aware that the story is an unlikely fantasy, we also know that as barriers between individuals and nations break down and the world moves toward a greater sense of unity, the distinction between what is possible is broken down into a singularity. Slumdog Millionaire may be the best film of the year, while in real life headlines telling us daily that the economy is dying, and that climate change threatens our very existence; a film that is a pure celebration of life is welcomed with open arms. Danny Boyle gives us his best film yet.

Slumdog Millionaire starts promising enough. We are introduced to Jamal Malik, an unlikely contestant on a popular television trivia quiz show just a question away from winning the much coveted price. Suspected of cheating, he is detained by the authorities prior to his big night. After all, how could a bottom-wrung lowlife possibly answer each question he is posed on the show? As he is interrogated, the story flashes back to reveal his troubled yet fateful childhood. How does he remember the name of the lead in a bollywood film, the inventor of the revolver, or the winner of a football match long gone and forgotten? Well, the flashbacks will explain. Slumdog begins with a jolt of energy and is photographed beautifully on location in Mumbai. The performances especially from the child actors are great. However there were a number of problems that prevented me from fully embracing Jamal's world. It begins with the inherently flawed fragmented timeline. The movie begins after Jamal has answered 90 percent of the questions. That strips away any suspense during the game show flashbacks. I spent a good deal of the movie in denial, hoping the ending wouldn't be as predictable. The big disappointment happens about two-thirds of the way through when the film started questioning its own integrity by shedding its hard-edged dicken-esque tale about troubled youth only to cop-out as a conventional romantic story. The theme of luck and destiny only add bile to this bag of vomit (had the film been treated with less realism it might've been a little easier to digest). Towards the conclusion I kept hoping for a twist ending, a tragedy, a deus ex machina... anything that would redeem the promising bit of the film. The twist is that there is no twist. Slumdog has an air of fairytaleness but lacks any challenging qualities its subject matter demands (think City of Gold). It is better than most holiday movie out there but then again like the film, that doesn't really say much.

Mumbai, the present day (and the recent past). Jamal Malik is one question away from winning Indiaâs version of the quiz show âWho Wants To Be A Millionaireâ. During a break in filming, Jamal is arrested on grounds of fraud and is interrogated. Jamal claims he has not cheated and that he knew the answer to every question. Jamal explains how he knew these answers by recalling moments of his life. Jamal remembers trawling through a pool of faeces to meet the actor, Amitabh Bachchan, his idol (the first question relates to a film featuring the actor) and the death of his mother in a religious conflict. After this, Jamal, his brother Salim, and their friend Latika are taken in by an orphanage run by Maman, which is a shield for organised child labour and begging. Salim is expected to assist the blinding of Jamal to increase his value, but the three children escape although Latika is left behind, apparently deliberately at Salimâs hands.

The brothers work as unofficial tour guides at the Taj Mahal, but they return to Mumbai to search for Latika, where she works as a dancer in the red-light district. They are discovered by Maman, who is shot by Salim. Salim then falls in with local gangsters; after which the boys drift apart. Working in a call centre, he discovers where Salim now lives and contacts him. Latika is now married to the gangster Salim works for. Salim tries to convince Latika to leave with him, but she resists. When she finally agrees, she is followed by Salim and other thugs, who slash her cheek. Jamal enters the quiz show because he knows she will be watching. Back to the present, the police find Jamalâs story âbizarrely plausibleâ and allow him to return to the show, where he successfully answers the final question. Salim kills Latikaâs husband before being shot himself, allowing Jamal and Latika to be reunited.

âSlumdog Millionaireâ has become one of the most anticipated and acclaimed films of the year. Nominated for four Golden Globes and countless other criticsâ prizes already, it is being talked of as one of the main serious contenders for Oscar recognition in 2009. Much like Jamal himself, âSlumdog Millionaireâ has arrived seemingly from nowhere; a small British film that looks set to take the international box office by storm. The film also confirms the prodigious talents and appeal of its director Danny Boyle, who of course has a number of previous successes under his belt, for instance âTrainspottingâ and â28 Days Laterâ. This project is a change of pace after his recent excursions into the sci-fi and horror genres but âSlumdog Millionaireâ might actually be Boyleâs most satisfying film to date.

The film has been described accordingly as âheartwarmingâ, âcheeryâ, âa modern fairy-taleâ and various other clichÃ©s that immediately mark âSlumdog Millionaireâ down as emotionally manipulative Oscar-bait.  The denouÃ©ment, of the filmâs destined lovers reuniting at a Mumbai train station and then breaking out into a Bollywood style dance routine might be considered sentimental and formulaic but within the context of the film it seems right and never exploitative. Such a negative conclusion would be doing the film a great disservice. Despite the uplifting climax, Boyle never shies away from showing the numerous disappointments and tragedies Jamal experiences. The death of Jamalâs mother and the entire slaughter of a small Muslim community at the hands of a Hindu mob is shown in vivid detail and the cruel and exploitative child labour operations run by Maman are also depicted with intense honesty, which includes the deliberate blinding of a child, which Boyle refuses to conceal. Jamal is also brutally interrogated by police, suffering attempting drowning and electric shocks in an attempt to force a confession for fraud.

Therefore do not be fooled by the marketing and publicity that is trying to depict âSlumdog Millionaireâ as a feel-good underdog story - there is more depth to the film than this, and Boyle also shows the two sides of modern India. As years pass, Mumbai has the impression of growing prosperity; an increase in the number of plush apartments and office blocks, but much poverty remains. This poverty is difficult to escape, and even when one does, one is still tainted by it. Just witness the degree to which the quiz show patronises and the police brutalises Jamal because of his background. What could this âslumdogâ possibly know? He must be cheating! Boyle reiterates the socio-economic divide that India retains and is potentially increasing as the country becomes more prosperous, but with this prosperity achieved by a narrow percentage of the population.

Boyle uses his trademark kinetic camera to great effect in the Mumbai slums, capturing its urgency and energy. Salim and Jamalâs escape from airport security through these slums reminds one of Renton and Spudâs frantic fleeing after robbing a shop in the opening scene of âTrainspottingâ. This is further proof of Boyleâs versatility as a director, able to utilise his talents and natural instincts across a series of genres. Much like another Oscar contender, âFrost/Nixonâ, âSlumdog Millionaireâ shows an interest in the artificial nature of television. Boyle regularly alternates between the filming of âWho Wants To Be A Millionaireâ as the audience at home would see it and breaks in the filming/behind the scenes details. As in âFrost/Nixonâ, television reveals not âthe truthâ but a version of the truth which is staged and manipulated, and in one interesting scene, interfered with by the quiz show host himself.

The creative input of Simon Beaufoy, sceenwriter of âThe Full Montyâ and A.R. Rahman, who provides a pulsating score that merges both traditional and modern India (assisted by British/Sri Lankan rapper M.I.A) is vital to the success of âSlumdog Millionaireâ, showing the film is not just a directorial tour-de-force. The young cast equip themselves well, from the youngest actors in the three main roles and Dev Patel (the adult Jamal), known thus far for his role in the Channel Four teenage drama series âSkinsâ. A film that unites both critics and audiences, âSlumdog Millionaireâ is gaining critical momentum prior to the major awards ceremonies of the season and is one of the finest films of 2008, offering insight, wit, romance and drama; the full package.

How spectacular!  After reading the descriptions of the film online, I thought it would be a feel-good male-version of what Amelie did for me as a woman.  While I am much endeared to Amelie, Slumdog Millionaire is not to be compared.   It is not a "feel-good."  It is full of sadness with a message of prevailing hope that only shines through in one part (will not spoil).  

When the film first got underway and I noticed the trend of matching a game show question plus a tragic poverty scenario that spells an answer, I began to make assumptions that it might be too contrived. Tisk-tisk.  Somewhere along the way, and relatively early-on,  I got lost in the story and was able to suspend my notions of a constrained story.  Perhaps it was the shock of it all.  How much footage of dirty kids picking through dumps in India have we seen but never known their stories?  Ever had a gypsy child tried to rob you while you were traveling abroad and felt so shocked, unable to excuse the crime?  This film takes you into the mindset, in a way that while seemingly obvious, introduces the nuances.  Slumdog Millionaire also addresses the sex trade but doesn't show us head-on.

We know from the title that a poor street boy wins the lottery, so clearly this is not the reason for seeing it.  At the heart of the story, is hope and enduring love.  

Why do films like this not get widespread distribution?  Unbelievable, America!  

Finally, I have to agree with my friend Leslie Kendall Dye's comments that "you can't gleefully juxtapose brutal violence and rape with a (badly danced) Bollywood number at the end. It doesn't make it all ok. It would have been nice if the lead actress had been more than a Barbie Doll."  I agree, here, Leslie.  Although this is probably a nod to the Bollywood genre, there was something much-lacking about the ending.  For me, maybe the casual clothing - vs. the traditional flowing garments - tipped it over the edge.  Maybe they could have done more with the ending and tacky special effects, putting them out in a surreal nature scene.  Or something. ;)

There I said it.Slumdog Millionaire shines like a million dollar.Definitely one of the year's best.Danny Boyle showed us he is more than a just above-average director.Boyle handles it all with steady hand, creating stunning visuals with composition, editing, and tempo changes; adding mood with a stellar soundtracks, and allowing his actors to breathe free and give some powerfully natural performances.Sometimes you get a small glimpse at a pattern of humanity the interweaves us all. This film taps on such a painfully gorgeous cruelty in life's circumstances the culminates into hope from tragedy that we all can take note from. There is nothing polished or censored. It is gritty, in your face and at time tough to watch. It defies normal Hollywood visuals as it does bother dressing to make the image favorable. Boyle treats us to a touching love story, backdropped into a world of crime and poverty in Mumbai, India. It is such a simple tale, yet told in gorgeous flashback, peeling back layers when necessary and enhancing the relationships between our lead Jamal and those around him; those on his "friends and family" plan. Here is a young man from the streets, a boy who witnessed his own mother's murder, living only to be reunited with the one person he truly loves, Latika. His bond to her leads him on an adventurous life full of violence and cruelty, events so harrowing that one would be hard-pressed to forget even the smallest detail about them. This is a great fact for Jamal as it will soon be shown how his life was lived with a destiny to be achieved. When he becomes a contestant on "Who Wants to be a Millionaire", it's as though the questions were written especially for him.Accused of cheating and arrested by the police, he is tortured to discover how he was able to trick the system. Only when nothing yields results does the Inspector, decide to hear Jamal out and find the truth. What transpires is the film we have come to watch a story told from a police chair, one of how the rough and tumble life of a slumdog gave him the exact right experiences to keep going towards a purse of twenty million rupees. Boyle, never one to go conventional, cuts between flashbacks of childhood, with Jamal in the hotseat on television, thinking of his past tragedies to continue the game as long as he can, in hopes that his love is watching, wherever she may be. With gorgeous cuts at the start flashes of memories jumbled together as he is submerged in water or electrocuted the structured chaos soon calms down to a normal pathway of three converging timelines: childhood, the previous night's game show, and the present incarceration. We are shown exactly what we need at exactly the right time. The film couldn't have been shot any other way and be nearly as successful as it is. This is a film that not only should be taken seriously, but also very intriguing to watch. There are tense moments, disturbing moments, comedic moments, and overall, moments who can't walk away from. This movie has everything. It is action, suspense, drama, comedy, political commentary, a love story and so much more; a timeless story with a refreshing twist. The cinematography is breathtakingly beautiful, the acting superb, the writing fantastic, and the music perfect. I can't say enough good about this movie. It is truly a joy to watch, as we are carried through the life of it's main character.A tale of destiny and striving to be good, Slumdog Millionaire is an uplifting parable showing how karma works. Everything happens for a reason, nothing is left to chance. Perhaps it is all written, but that doesn't make the journey any tougher to endure. Jamal could have, understandably, given up at many times in his life, but his drive would not allow him that convenience. Conquering all odds, coming from the streets, to the point he didn't even know Ghandi's face was on his own country's currency, Jamal gets the chance at a fortune and an opportunity to finally be free.
