Nearly Perfect. A joyous and intriguing film that is completely, individually unique and aggressive in storytelling and narrative. This is a lock for Best Picture nomination, and may even win. This is a film, like Wall*E, that is for everyone. I can't imagine anyone not liking this film. It's fast paced and well edited, it's narrative is completely engrossing and it's characters are well developed and stimulating. One of the best opening sequences this year begins by asking us a question: "How did Jamal Malik win 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire'? A - He cheated B - He knew the answers C - Some one told him D - It is written." The answer is given to us by the end. I won't give it away.

The story starts with Jamal(Dev Patel) in prison, being questioned about his appearance on the television program. He precedes to tell them how he knew the answers. Conveniently, he learned the answers in perfect sequence in comparison to his childhood and life story. As each question is asked, we see a glimpse of his past and the reason that he knows the answer. This kid has been through a lot. The movie is simultaneously exciting, disturbing, fun, action oriented, and light spirited. There are moments of pure joy at the prospect of Jamal finding happiness in simple things, and then there are moments of utter disgust, such as an "orphanage" Jamal is taken to.

Jamal's greatest necessity, however, is Latika(Freido Pinto), a girl that Jamal befriends as a child. They lose each other and Jamal spends the rest of his life trying to find her. Many times, their paths cross and Latika ensures him that they can never be together, but that doesn't stop Jamal from trying. The film revolves around trying to decipher what true wealth and riches are. A character like Salim(Madhur Mittal) finds nice cars and lots of money to be the only thing in the world that could provide happiness. He'd even go so far as to kill someone in order to get it. Latika believes that happiness is what you make of it. She sees things as black and white: There's no way that Jamal and she could be together, therefore they must try to find happiness apart. Jamal, of course, believes that true wealth and happiness is simplistic love, and he will do anything that it takes to make sure that Latika realizes that.

The movie was touching, but didn't shove sentimentality down the audience's throat. The emotion was real and motivational. The funny moments in Jamal's life, and the horrible moments in Jamal's life(and he has some really awful moments) lead up to a finale that could never state its meaning clearer: Never give up. It's a theme we've been missing in the movies lately. A lot of films get so drab and depressing, that it's great to see that this year, so many films have taken the opposite route. 'Milk' was always funny and inspirational, and this film as well. As much as I thought last year was one of the best years for movies that we've ever seen, it seems as though the filmmaking world decided that serial killer movies needed to be replaced with joyful films this year. I'm glad.

What makes this film great, more than anything else, is the utter likableness of the characters. Jamal goes through shit, yet is always bright and cheerful(though quite nervous; he reminds me a bit of David Archuletta). A great sequence to exemplify this: Jamal and his brother arrive at the Taj Mahal, not knowing what it is("Is this heaven"), and in an effort to make a quick buck, they take idiotic Americans on tours, improvising their own versions of how the palace was built and what happened there. They offer to take people's shoes as they enter the temple and steal them.

The movie also makes statements about "The real India." Every aspect of India we've known or heard about, and those we haven't, are shown to us here. Anthony Dod Mantle, our DP extraordinaire, carefully chose fantastic angles to enhance the feeling of each part of India we see. The shots of the poor India, where men pay a couple cents to shit into a hole, are filmed very classically, whereas the action oriented India, full of gangsters and thugs, becomes a flurry of diagonal shots. The love story is told through sweeping camera shots and bright, vibrant colors. We even get a musical number ala Bollywood. This part may be out of place, but it plays during the credits, so it's all good.

The writing is also magnificent. Simon Beaufoy taps into Vikas Swarup's novel and makes the story even better. Each piece of dialogue is driven and straight forward, particularly the dialogue between the brothers, and the dialogue between Jamal and the Host of the television show. Both these instances supply dialogue sufficiently foreboding of their dynamic relationships and the mess they get each other into.

But, let's not forget what makes a film: Direction! Direction! Direction! Danny Boyle(director of cult classic, 'Trainspotting' and recent masterpiece, 'Millions') will more than likely go home with the Oscar on his mantel. This man is brilliant. This film could have gone down the tubes instantly with the wrong person to piece it together, but Boyle is more than up to the job. His creative and artistic choices add to the dexterity of the film and of its integrity. What a man. What a film.

To conclude, 'Slumdog Millionaire' will most likely turn out to be one of the most talked about films of the year. It won the audience award at Toronto, I believe it was, and is the leading contender for Oscar Gold. It deserves it. I'd go see this movie again in a heartbeat. See it in the theater, there is no other way to see it. It is meticulously well put together and emotionally satisfying, as well as God-damned entertaining and beautifully shot. See it to look at it. See it to bask in it. See it to feel happy/sad/confused/shocked/humorous/joyful/inspired. See it, because if you don't, you'll be missing one of the best films in recent years.

This is an extrodinary film. On the one hand, it illuminates an area of life which should make for a harrowing movie (see "City of God" for example) but, on the other, it's as exhilirating and colourful as a mid-90s Baz Luhrman movie. And it works; fusing disperate styles to create an intoxicating story.

When Danny Boyle is at the height of his powers, as he is here, he understands that his audience's passage to his characters is be experiencing the pleasures and pitfalls of their lives as they do. His presentation of life in Indian slums is neither condescending or depressing because it's being introduced to us as the playground of children. But neither does the colour blot out the darkness (although marks deducted for using the same metaphor here as when Ewan McGregor made a dive into a toilet in Trainspotting)

Every beat of the film is designed to be viseral and affecting; chases and loving reunions alike are played fast and furiously. But, even as time passes and the city of Mumbai becomes glitzier and the skyskrapers ascend higher, Boyle keeps reminding us that those in the slums have been left behind. Whether literally or spiritually. There is obviously a slant of social activism here; and Boyle cheekily plays with the idea that the whereas the India of his characters' youth is united by shared experiences, the only thing that unites Indians in his 21st Century is the shamlessly western guilty pleasure which is "Who Wants to be a Millionare?"

A complicated film posing as a simple love story; I found myself constantly comparing notes with Luhrman's cinema. He too understands the power of a simple love story played with a lot of noise and colour; but spent much of his career ignoring the wider social story. And when he did try that, in Australia, he fell on his face because his wandering epic couldn't decide how much it wanted to be a love story and how much a commetary. Boyle's film achieves both and I think it's because he's made a braver decision to get away from his familliar, safe ground. He challenged himself to understand Indian culture, and then challenges us to not become as intoxicated as he has. He doesn't just absrob a few bits of the culture and then force his own movie making aesthetic upon it; he has dived in feet first.

That means eliciting strong performances from a clearly inexperienced group of young actors. They're raw, but they work, especially in the fact that all the different groups of actors playing the same characters at different ages clearly have a strong rapport with one another. The music is also fantastic. A fabulous combination of sitars and electronica which feel like they belong perfectly to *this* version of India.

Not quite Bollywood, not quite Hollywood, just look at "Slumdog Millionare" as the movie which illustrates the worst aspects of globalisation... but in the very best way possible.

Slumdog is a good movie regardless, it shows the contrast of relationship (Salim and Jamal), love story (Jamal and Latika), and of course the haunting Mumbai city!

Danny Boyle love to mock certain culture and country, like what he did in Trainspotting (1996). He mocks the lifestyle of Scottish people yet at the end we still experience the 'feel - good' aura! (Love this guy!). In 2008 he did it again and now we see the exploitation of Indian people, mostly the central city, Mumbai.

The movie direction between the game show and Jamal's childhood flashback is quite enchanting. But it still left a silly plot hole.
You will feel the excitement and passion of Jamal's life story, the adventure he undergoes, the violent he witness and the love he finds is exhilarating.

The movie arouse many eye-brows between Indian people and i tell you why;

1. Mumbai looks scary! I've been there certain times and no it's not like what they show. Yes, I get it they are Slums children, and I gotta agree by certain scenes (Like, Stealing foods, Beggars, etc). But I still hope that they would show how Mumbai is like in the present days!

2. The language, yes I know that this is an English movie but the transformation between the younger Jamal to the elder one is hard to believe. His English accent sound westernize, and that makes certain people criticize! I'm not saying that Indian people isn't fluent in English, Heck I think that we are more fluent then certain countries (Again, No pun intended!), but they are Slums. But, my perception is different, Have you seen Memoirs of Geisha? Japanese people talk fluent English, so why not Indians?!

3. The questions. I was laughing very hard when Jamal was asked who the heroic figure in the 1000 Rupees note is? And he said 'I don't know'. Stop! when you spend your childhood stealing people's money, you would know it, I'm certain.

Once you passed this debate you would see that Danny Boyle's Slumdog version is only meant to be a feel-good movie and fiction, and he did an awesome job!
Though some scenes makes me cringe (specially the last line), And the scene where the younger Jamal jump into the crap pile is exaggerated! I was offended somehow.

Dev Patel is a great young actor, he balances his thick-British accent to the max, and his emotional expression is surely believable. Freida Pinto, though not as stunning as Aishwarya Rai, she is cute and act well for a supporting role. Other cast did good, specially Irfan Khan (The Namesake, A Mighty Heart) was a treat!

Background music is superb, it's about time that people recognize how talented Mr. A.R Rahman is (Check out his other score in Bollywood movies; Lagaan, Dil - Se, etc)

Still it's a hit and miss movie, some people will love it and some not. This is not the best Bollywood / English movie in my opinion (i still prefer Moonsoon Wedding) but it is one of the best movie of 2008.

In what has been a weak year for movies in my opinion, Slumdog Millionaire separates itself from most of the pack.  It will likely find a place somewhere in my top 10 list for 2008, but don't fall get too excited.  While this movie deserves a wider audience and lives up to the hype in many regards, it is by no means the best picture of the year.  The structure of the scenes could have used more careful editing and organization to maximize the suspense of the game show scenes.  I was never on the edge of my seat, and even the best scene in the movie, one involving a battle of wits between the host, played with perfection by Anil Kapoor, and the contestant, Dev Patel was made too predictable to serve as high drama.  That said, there are some interesting messages about love and fate sprinkled throughout, and its an ambitious movie, in that it tries to deal with a variety of topics in its two hour window, meaning it was never boring.  The performances of the adult actors, apart from Kapoor's, are mediocre at best.  I think its the kids who steal the show in that regard.  See this movie, it is terrific on its own merits.  Just don't go in overly influenced by the critics.

The movie started off really well, and just got better and better as it went on. I was quite literally on the edge of my seat for the last 20 minutes of the movie - it was just incredible! I can't even describe how perfect it was. The script was captivating, capturing humor, emotion, sorrow, hardship, love, and shock in one boy's story. The story was complicated enough to keep you enthralled and guessing but simple enough to follow. The cinematography was also wonderful, set in the diverse Indian background. And the MUSIC!! It was so random and so PERFECT!! It added SO MUCH to this movie, I seriously need to get the soundtrack immediately! What a GREAT movie! Ahh, Slumdog Millionaire. This year's surprise critical darling was a fun time that kept me hooked and smiling most of the time.

In a way, this could be seen as a bunch of vignettes, but the underlying story keeps things moving and makes us connect with Jamal. 

While some things were very convenient and slightly contrived, I had very few issues with the story. It was easy for me to get engaged and remain that way for 2 hours.

My biggest issues are twofold. One would be in that the characters are fairly flat, though despite that they certainly serve the movie well. The other would be the movie's overly stylized... For someone who loves foreign films, I was very aware that this movie catered to a western audience.  The symbolism in one of the last scenes was memorable: the back-to-back scene of the trash in the gully & the money in the bathtub...money obtained through dishonest ways will always have blood associated (whether literal or symbolic).

Danny Boyle promised me a great deal with Trainspotting.  I waited very patiently for the film to come near my college town of Hattiesburg MS...and finally got to see it in New Orleans....  I couldn't wait.  It was unlike anything I had ever seen.  Then came 28 Days Later.  Horror unlike anything I have seen.  And then Millions.  How could this same director get into the heart of two children when he had just ripped out hearts?

None of these films compare to Slumdog Millionare.  Please trust me when I say that you cannot wait to see this film, just as I couldn't wait to see Trainspotting.

This is the best film of the year (at least of the many I have already seen).  It will be very difficult to beat for the Academy Award, at least in my opinion.

The concept, is genius in itself.  A boy from the slums of India finds himself a contestant on Who Wants To Be a Millionaire.  We find out rather quickly that most people don't do very well on this show.  Jamal, our lead does very well, which leads to suspision of cheating.

Not knowing whether he is defending himself or not we follow Jamal's story from his slumdog youth with his brother Salim to present day.  

Very little should be said about the plot of this film, but not only is the concept wonderful, but the way Boyle uses it throught the unweaving Jamal's life is expected, yet oddly suprising.  You have to see it for yourself.

Music has a major role in the film, as did Trainspotting, and I'm desperate to get the soundtrack as well.  

All of the acting is wonderful, but the standouts are the two boys who play Salim and Jamal at their youngest.   Speaking their native language, these kids seem to be showing us their actual lives.  Adult Jamal, played by Dev Patel is also incredible.  If the Oscars awarded promising performers, the award would be his.

It has been a long time since a film enraptured me this much and led me to tears at the end.  As much as I loved MILK, Slumdog took my emotions to an even more raw level.

Great insight into the extremes that make up India in terms of culture, class struggle, corruption, love and ambition.  The portrayal of life in Mumbai is bluntly accurate. However, the shock factor of poverty is a relied on quite heavily and becomes rather cliche.

This was a random movie expedition and I am glad that in keeping with my self imposed moratorium on not watching films, unless of extremely high quality, seems I was in luck. Two thumbs up. 
The plot had three sub areas and each area had a story and precise amount of justice was done to all three. Not a mean task by any standards. 
I am always concerned of entropy when I see a film of  Indian setting for foreign audience. I guess the director allayed my fears and did so with aplomb. Yes you can go and watch this film with your American boy friend without having to explain it on your trip back. You could actually be critiquing the film together within the same coordinate system.
The last point I would like to make is that its a film with several melancholic moments, something I generally despise...but those melancholic moments are sugar coated, something which I generally despise more, but the grace with which the melancholy is made palatable without compromising with its intensity neither using crass humor, is wonderful and I love it. The curve of unhappiness becomes the curve of happiness without any discontinuities. I would actually say it is a c-3 or c-4 continuous curve. 

I know I am a  nerd....and am not aplogetic about it !
Story: 5* Cinematography: 5* Direction: 5* Screenplay: 4.5* Acting: 4.5* Editing: 5.0* Music: 5.0*

Danny Boyle's films are always superior.  This modern day fable about enduring love, destiny, the hard knocks of life and game shows set in India is no exception.  However, i was expecting just a bit more...i mean reviews and work of mouth on this movie have been off the charts good...so i guess i was thinking this would be IT for Danny Boyle, but not so....  IMHO it is a very solid film, but will not be one of the ones that Boyle (or perhaps anyone) will be remembered for.   Still, if you get a chance to see this on a big screen, i would encourage you to go.
Excellent, non-linear storytelling. And a very candid representation of modern south asian culture, none of that "romanticising ethnicity" bullshit.
I hope I can make movies this good when I grow up.
incredible to watch how the most distressing events of a life could assemble themselves into a luminous moment for all who are downtrodden
Beautiful film. Danny Boyle continues to amaze me. Will definitely be one of my top three films of this year.

I thought that it was really well made. My only complaint is the fact that the movie centered around an episode of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire. I just couldn't get past how cheesy that was. It was creatively incorporated throughout the plot, but it was still cheesy.
G-R-E-A-T movie, all-around! The life of this young man is incredible and the way it is told is uniquely portrayed!

I drove a long way in subzero temperature to see this movie. Not only that, I paid. I can't even remember the last I paid for a movie (okay, that's a lie, it was the new Superman at the drive-in). I didn't get home until almost 1 a.m. and had to work all day the next day. And I would do it again tomorrow if I could. This is easily the best movie of the year, along with The Dark Knight. It exceeded my expectations by achieving almost City of God proportions (which is one of my top 5 favorite movies). This is one of those rare movies (like City of God) that grabs you and doesn't let go.

I don't know what to say. This film just adds to my love of films. I love films! And Slumdog Millionaire is one of the best of the decade! Yes, skip just this year, this is one of the best movies of the past decade. Yes the film has a strange premise, but rarely is there a movie that has characters so real that in the short span of two-hours there is a connection between the audience and screen that is nothing short of magical.

Well written, compelling story. Well executed, shot, acted, etc. Then at the very end they just had to ruin it with this utterly ridiculous and completely incongruous Ballywood-esque dance number during the end titles. Like, WTF did that have to do with anything in the movie?

Great and captivating movie. There is a great blend of romance, crime, drama and humor but it all molds together and it doesnt feel like the movie is at all lagging. There is not one scene where it begins to feel as though it is milking every bit of emotion to completely making the scene or dialogue theatrical. It is subtle and then WHAM, you are struck by moving horrors of the slums of Mumbai. The non-linear story-telling works and is the second best movie I've seen this year.

More then anything else, Slumdog Millionaire (which is based on a book called Q&A) is a story not only about a boy from the slums of Bombay but a story of a country that has risen to be at the center of the world, because it "knows the answers". A country which was once considered a third-world democracy.  This is not your typical rags to riches story of Bombay Dreams, Slumdog gives you a real, honest, filthy, dirty look at the City of Dreams and yet it comes out with a beautiful view of hope filled with the colors, love and music of India.  It is a story of 21st century urban modernism.  The film reminded me of a line from one of my all time favourite books 'Maximum City - Bombay Lost and Found', "Bombay is the future of urban civilization on the planet, God help us."

Slumdom Millionaire est sans aucun doute un des meilleurs films de l'annee.  Danny Boyle (Transpotting) nous offres un film d'une grande beaute.  Les paysages de l'Inde sont magnifiques.  L'excellente trame musicale du film, accompagne tres bien ce film filme nerveusement.  Des bon acteurs, un scenario sans longueur, une realisation originale... finalement tout pour faire un divertissement de grande qualite!!!!
This movie was really amazing.  The acting was excellent and the storyline was very clear and well written.  Excellent movie!
A very touching story but the story can be more original.

A beautiful film, on the eyes, ears and mind. the performances throughout are really special, as they are, for my knowledge primarily from untested talent, but they all really deliver some standout performances. The story is a great one, and the cross cutting throughout makes for a really brisk two hours. One of the highlights of the film for me was the choices of music throughout the film, its a really diffrent blend of music that adds a lot to the images. As much as i loved the first hour and fifty minutes of this, I was rather downright dissapointed with the last ten, maybe even to the degree that it would deter me away from rewatching the entire film a second time. Not to give anything away about the ending but it goes from borderline corny, to fullblown corny in the span of ten minutes, whereas everything prior the end felt so fresh and unexplored.In the end i guess i would say its a great movie but that the end was   real letdown for me.

A conventional crowd-pleaser that benefits from a deeper story, a cultural twist, and more artistic intentions. It also suffers from a few of the same faults, including a few less compelling character choices in the last portion of the film.

It's a beautifully shot film. Occasionally, the editor gets a little out of control, but the film itself is meant to be vivid and bombastic, so it ultimately serves that well.

One of my favorites this year, easily (one of maybe 5 films I saw that were at all special). Stay for the credits, it's a huge treat! And I disagree with some of my friends on this, the homage fits the movie's tone beautifully (especially considering the film is as much about the culture as it is this single romance).

A lot of amazing stuff in this film, but I have to say the depressing garbage dump that is the slums of Mumbai, India, are beautifully realized.

Absolutely loved it -- the acting, the colors, the editing, the soundtrack, everything.
Just a great story, well-acted.

A beautiful love story running beneath the storyline of a mean and harsh life. I liked the contrast between the characters, and felt the movie struck an excellent balance between the love story and the meaner aspects of life. Interesting, thoughtful, and entertaining.
unique and captivating. the ending was a cheesy though
I had heard good things and the film exceeded my expectations- it was funnier than expected, and was more of a "thriller" than I thought it would be.

I walked out of the theatre after watching this thinking, "Well, I know who's going to win the Oscar for Best Director." I wasn't wrong either.

It's difficult to summarise the movie because there's just so much going on. I think it almost requires a second viewing. Did it deserve to win the Best Picture Oscar? I guess, but only because the other nominees just weren't up to snuff. It was more a case of it being the better movie rather than being a fantastical movie. (Spoiler alert) 
Really well directed and the first part of the film with the kids was especially well done but if you think about it then the girl turns out to be a gold digger (she lives with an rich old man and will only go with the boy when he has money) - so is that really a happy ending? It's true that it's Dickensian and it's like a fairytale - it has one-dimensional characters (the hero is flawless, baddies very bad and the dream girl just a non-character) and a main character with no other aspirations in life than just to find the girl he last saw when he was five. This is a fantastic story.  Boyle did a great job in showing how life is in Mumbai for a young person without education or money.  This is a good film for anyone to watch.
Incredible.  Simply Fabulous!  Great cinematography, storytelling, acting!  It's all here!
One of the best movies I've seen this year.  Totally recommend it!!!

A true modern love story.  Very unlike anything else I've ever seen.  I can clearly see what it's a contender for the title of "best film of the year."  Personally, I cannot judge because I have not seen the other contenders.  Winning performances.  Danny Boyle is now, officially, among the ranks of Aronofsky and Kubrick as one of my favorite directors.

EDIT:  The more I think back on this film since I saw it, the more excellent I think it is.  I want to see it again.

I very rarely give any movie 5 stars, especially a serious movie.  I laughed, I cried, overall I was left with a fuzzy warm feeling inside and I don't care who makes fun of me.  I think this is a must see and one of the best movies I have seen in a long time.  The acting was great, especially the little kids.  The story was believable and the movie was shot beautifully and I think portrayed the slums of India very accurately (but I have no clue).  I think the young Jamal should win actor of the year.

And even the somewhat unrealistic ending doesn't spoil it, it just reinforces the story. It definitely stays with you...
Just like fusion cuisine. Lots of ingredients (slum drama, love story, social document and Bollywood) that can ruin or amaze the senses. This one makes one's day.
Danny Boyle's best film since Trainspotting... definitely one of the years best and most uplifting
takes you on quite a journey.

Best movie of the year so far. It once again proved that a great movie does not need famous actors or big budget to back it up. All it needs just a good story that reaches to people's heart, sincere acting and focused directing. Highly recommended, just do it!

On the outside Slumdog Millionaire is a gritty, dirty and smelly film displaying the nasty cruel and very sad world of India. But like most misunderstood things, at heart this is a beautiful, poetic and moving film about love against all odds.

The cinematography is at times, superb. The performance of Dev Patel is quite understatedly perfect. 

The screenplay for me is the real winner. The general structure of the story and the characters is quite fantastic and original. It's really just a simple little story that is in many ways so complex.

There are also fantastic little symbolic concepts all over the place if you look for them. And not to forget the soundtrack can be at times truly inspiring.

Overall this is one of the best films of 2008 and has a VERY good chance of taking out that Oscar for Best Film.
a masterpiece... Pinocchio, Odissey and much more ( f.e. Rossellini and neo realism...)

I just got home from seeing Slumdog Millionare and my heart is still aching. I was so into this movie from start to finish  - never knowing what would happen next  - and deeply attached to the main character. I really, really recommend it.

By far one of the best movies of 2008. Inspirational, uplifting, emotional! This is a great character driven piece of cinematography with a unique kind of story pattern... I loved the photography and the angled shots in which Boyle is a true master! The music seemed always matching perfectly the mood of the scene. I was stunned by the last editing effort in the final scene at the train station when Jamal is crossing the train platforms... look at it carefully: it is one of the most wonderful montages I have ever witnessed!

The acting was great. But Boyle seemlessly tells this Pauper story in a very compelling and powerful way. I'm excited for this movie and Boyle has once again proven that he is THE filmmaker to watch. Danny Boyle has made his mark on cinema by applying his talents to a wide multitude of genres. Boyleâs latest effort, Slumdog Millionaire, pushes his eclectic collection of films that much further.

Slumdog tells the life story of a young Mumbai boy from the slums, Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), and uses the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? to detail the events of his life, in particular his search for Latika, his destined love.

Slumdog Millionaire is a modern day fairy tale. The filmâs story is told through a carefully crafted nonlinear narrative structure using a plethora of flashbacks. The game show portion of the film acts as present day and as the filmâs plot device by using carefully crafted questions to tell a new part of Jamalâs past life. Simply put, the film is more about the way Jamal reaches his destination rather than the actual destination itself or the game show. And boy is it well done.

Thereâs so much to love about Slumdog that itâs hard to simply summarize it all. This is a special film. For me, itâs one of those very unique masterpieces that come along once or twice a year rendering the critiquing of the film to be difficult. I know, it sounds funny. It should be rather easy to spew words out to detail what you love about a film. In this case, it hasnât come easy. This film is just good.

Boyleâs years behind the camera comes to fruition with this film. The high paced frantic cinematography Boyle offered up in 28 Weeks Later is combined with the beautiful cinematography he developed with 2007âs Sunshine. The film is expertly handled and it is a noticeable quality. Boyle absolutely knew what he was doing and it shows through his visionary work.

Story wise there is lots to love. True vision of slum life in India or not, the film is still very captivating and oozing with emotion as the boys fend for themselves, survive on their own and grow into being young adults. Certain Indian journalists have attacked the film for not being exactly precise (one writer complained about how these boys would never know the name of Samuel Colt as they would never refer to the gun as a Colt).

Other Indian journalists have opened their eyes and realized that Slumdog is not supposed to be a documentary piece on life in Indian. I, for one, would rather not make comment on what I havenât experienced. All I know is that loads of inaccurate films are made about all types of locations, from Boston to countries in Asia. Whether this film is one of them or not is besides the point when judging how technically sound and enjoyable the film is.

For as much charm this fairy tale holds there is an equal amount of gritty crime thriller to be savored. Part of the success of everything staying rather balanced is the ensemble performance. The three children in the film are played by three different young actors. All three versions stand out remarkably. The youngest versions of Jamal and his brother Salim have an uncanny ability to perform their scenes naturally.

As the story progresses and the boys grow, new actors are introduced and they each uphold the quality of acting. The film culminates with Dev Patel (Jamal), Freida Pinto (Latika) and Madhur Mittal (Salim) rounding out the tremendous youth performances. Not to be forgotten are Ankur Vikal, who plays crime boss Maman, the filmâs most evil character, and Anil Kapoor, as the game show host Prem Kumar. The film wouldnât be what it was without each and every one of these names and more.

Slumdog is one of the freshest films youâll find in cinemas right now. Aiding this is the absolutely scorching and energizing score by Indian composer A.R. Rahman. The score, which also features musician M.I.A. and her hit song Paper Planes, is unlike most things heard in films. At times itâs intense and at other times itâs joyful. Rahman uniquely covers all grounds with his own brand of music.

Slumdog Millionaire is simply the incredible culmination of lots of talent. As much as the film is to be credited to Boyle for his directing prowess, it would have been impossible without the actors the film had, Rahmanâs engaging score or Simon Beaufoyâs carefully structured screenplay of the Vikas Swarup novel Q and A. Nominated for 10 Academy Awards, I can only hope the charming Slumdog Millionaire walks away with a great deal of Oscars. Boyle may finally be getting the credit heâs always deserved.
Systematically engineering together all that makes a 'Bollywood film' sparkle, Danny Boyle's 'Slumdog Millionaire' is a lazy but fun ride.
The story is compelling and Danny Boyle's direction is exemplary.
so good, danny boyle really hasn't done wrong in my book. This also qualifies my theory that all movies become 20% better when you end with a dance number. 40% for a bollywood dance number.
Easily one of the top 3 films of the year.  If you don't see it, then don't complain that there aren't any good movies out there...you're just not willing to see them.
Yeah, it's good. I kindof don't really see the huge deal, though. But then again, it's a happy movie. I like sad movies.

Part Dickens, part CIty of God, this film begins as a gritty matter-of-fact look that the lives of two boys living in abject poverty, but ends in a sugar-coated romantic melodrama--with a little bit of Scarface thrown in for good measure.  I wish Irrfan Khan was given more to do.
worth the hype.  Not for kids though.  Will remind you of the real world we live in and how very blessed we are.  Take nothing for granted.

I wouldn't be surprised if the year ended and this ended up being the year's best live-action picture. Danny Boyle's "Slumdog Millionaire" returns to his guerrilla digital video aesthetic from one of my favorites, "28 Days Later", to tell what turns out to be a very Hollywood story. Just that it's in India.
Although it spans a mere two hours, this story-- which is easily compared to "Forrest Gump" as every one of the hero's answers to a question links to something in his childhood-- is a true epic. And time and time again, you'll be cheering for our protagonist (I guarantee you'll love him by the time he escapes the town's outhouse just to get an autograph from a visiting action star) and the love of his life who just keeps slipping away. The story manages to be as dark in tone as "28 Days Later", but the perspective is incredibly optimistic and it makes "Slumdog Millionaire" a much more feel-good film than this year's "Happy-Go-Lucky".
A testament to the film's power is that in spite of its inherent predictability, it will have you on the edge of your seat and hyperventilating towards the end. The person sitting next to me caught me covering my mouth during one crucial scene, but a couple minutes later I could tell she, too, was into it.
Such a great movie...A Must See...makes you laugh and cry and even wanna do a little dance!...
Without a doubt, my favorite movie of the year.
One of the Best Movie, I've ever seen.  highly recommended!!
This is one of the best movies I have seen this year.  Visually beautiful, great soundtrack, a great story, and a look into an unfamiliar culture.

The best film of 2008. An original intense thrilling heartwarming heartwrenching film. Apparently when a film like this come out you either love it or hate it; I love it. The movie takes a lot of risks, and I believe that all of them pay off. It's a brilliant work from Mr. Boyle. Cinematography is cool, direction is dazzling, and the acting is great. Worth spending $11-14 at the theater. You will not be disappointed.

In a movie with such a crafty cinderella tale, and completely unique structure, it awes me that Danny Boyle so completely stole the show with his arresting visuals and hypnotic rhythm. Three time-lines are seamlessly weaved, there is never a moment of "Hum... What?" The camera work is quite simply astonishing, young Jamal is on the run from the cop (five minutes in) and by the end of the chase the audience is out of breath. The soundtrack (lots of M.I.A) fits like a glove and even the subtitles are easier to read and come off as originally done. This is the underdog story to top all underdogs, I mean at least Rocky could physically knock a few guys out here and there. The cast feels real and the young actors here (the main characters where portrayed at three different ages) are superb, specially the three youngest ones (you'll know what I mean). At times you'll fringe, you'll look away, you might even shed a tear but I promise that by the end you'll leave the theaters with a sense of satisfaction, this is one movie that won't cheat you out and chances are you'll love it for that.

If you are going to see one movie this year, make it "Slumdog Millionaire."  It deserves to be this year's Oscar winner, and it certainly deserves much acclaim.  The way in which this film is put together, the acting, the directing, the editing, the casting, costumes, etc. all come together to make this film amazing - simply amazing.  

It's an uplifting film in a time when we need such a film to come to the fore.

A young Mumbaiite is forced to flash back on his crap-filled childhood while competing for the grand prize on the Indian version of "Who wants to be a Millionaire?"  A beautifully filmed epic of inner-city youth, reminiscent of the legendary "City of God".  Not for the faint-of-heart.  Not for the stupid.  A very good film.

I JUST got home from the screening tonight of Slumdog Millionaire. Oh MAN it was SO GOOD. The story, the editing, the MUSIC (that was amazing!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!), just unbelievable.
I've hardly ever felt tension in a movie quite like when Jamal sees Latika the first time at the train station... (I won't give away what happens for those who haven't seen it)

His passion rivals that of Romeo talking about how the walls of the Capulets cannot keep love out, and the kinsmen are no stop to him. :)

I LOVED IT.

This is not just a movie - it's a cinematic feat. Even being able to film such a movie at all is remarkable in it's own right, but to make a film this powerful and with this much passion... oh man it was amazing.

Strangely enough Slumdog Millionaire is the only one of the 5 Oscar Best Picture Nominated films that I've seen so far! Crazy. I am going to try to see Milk this week and hopefully get to see Benjamin Button soon too. But even though I haven't seen those other ones yet, I think it's gonna be pretty hard for anything to beat Slumdog Millionaire. SO AWESOME. This soundtrack/musical score has got to win the Oscar, too. I think this one's in the bag for Best Director, Best Film... probably one of the Sound awards too. Amazing!

We see the film through the eyes of Jamal, as we journey through his impoverished childhood with corrupt conditions he faced everyday and what eventually led him to the game show.  The reality of some of the events is chilling & at times disturbing, but I can't deny the film's profound story to be a compelling tale to the end.  It may get some recognition at award time.

In typical Boyle fashion, there are just some things about this movie that are sloppy and don't work- but thanks to Dev Patel and some other crafty moments, the film is a pleasing, if not sappy and obvious, tale of one pauper getting to feel like a prince.

Really great.  Though there is some brutality and at least one gross-out scene, I question the R rating.  Certainly mature young teens should do fine with it.  Mr. Boyle should be proud of this work and all it took to film it.

I heard a man comment as we left the theatre... "You know, it was okay, but I really would have liked it better without the whole game show. I mean, that he knows all the answers to these questions because of life experiences and that he gets selected and that he is doing it for these reasons... it took away from the realism of the movie. I understand there's a certain amount of suspension of disbelief, but this was almost too much."

I had to bite my tongue. The game show is the conceit of the film, the vehicle that allows everything you've seen to happen. Without the game show, you are watching a morality tale in India in a boring linear fashion, without any of the intrigue or suspense created by the interrogation sequences of the present. Without the game show, you lose the rags to riches tale, leaving you without the moral complexity of "it's not about the money, it's about the love - love is the riches." Without the game show, you wouldn't have as big of an audience. The game show is meant to contextualize, to highlight the glitzy showiness of American culture, and how the dream of prosperity transcends abject poverty to make happiness possible for any person, even if it isn't through money and fame.

It's not about the game show. It's about you. It's about me. It's about them, and their hardships, and the hardships of everyone who hasn't had an easy life. It's about India and culture and pride and memories and the small moments in life that can culminate into something important, be it a game show or true love.

This exhilarating British and Indian co-production, based on Vikas Swarup's novel Q&A, is quite simply a breath of cinematic fresh air. It follows hapless Jamal, an orphan from the slums of Mumbai as he escapes from the streets, eludes gangsters, cons tourists and becomes an unlikely contestant on "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?"---all for the sake of love, no less. Danny Boyle pulls all the punches in evoking an India we in the west have not yet seen. It has that feel of gritty urbanization and dog eat dog survival seen in films like Salaam Bombay, Pixote and City of God, but filled with enough good spirit to not shame us from enjoying it too much. With buoyant energy and sincere melodrama, Slumdog gives you a story you won't forget long after you've seen it.

This was a great movie. From trainspotting, to 28 days later, to sunshine, to millions, danny boyle does alot of varied and interesting work. None of his movies look the same, but they give you interesting perspectives on the world.
Now onto the plot- boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl. The premise is simple enough but what seperates this movie from other movies is the atmosphere this movie creates. The movie transplants you to a place uncommonly seen in movies, india, from a perspective that's not commonly seen in movies- from the poor citizens. This isn't the india you see as an outside tourist. It isn't pretty, it isn't inspiring. the locals are poor and they are doing the best they can to surivive. 
From this area we follow the story of two brothers, and the different paths they take. One of the brothers adapts the dog eat dog mentaility that is engrained in this area. He steals, he cheats, he kills in order to survive. The other brother, the one we grow to root for, takes the opposite path, he's truthful and hopelessly romantic seemingly oblivious to the hurtful things that happenin his life. Living in the sums is rough. Several bad things happen to him over the course of many years, and yet he still keeps his optimism- the belief that he will be with his soulmate in the end. The undying devotion is admirable, even if it isn't realistic. You root for him because you want the underdog good guy to win, he deserves to win
 *spoiler alert*
In the end the optimistic brother wins because as the movie says ,"it is written". which is ironic because afterall, this movie was a story, written by a screenwriter(simon beaufoy). I think it was the screenwriters intent was to emphasize the role of fate has in our lives. But i took it differently, i though it was a tongue and cheek commentary of the society placed in india. That there is no way to socially climb out of the slums of india. the upper class look down at the poor as unworthy. The only way to leave is some miracle gameshow in which by miraculous chance has questions based off your life. You win only because the screenwriter of the story wanted you to win. In real life Jamal doesn't get the girl because he would have been shot or blinded or some other horrible thing. He would have never got on "who wants to be a millionaire", he would definately wouldn't win millionaire. But this movie isn't the real world. It's a fairy tale.

Slumdog Millionaire
Expected: 9 January
Danny Boyle, never a man to be tied down to one genre, is back with yet another graceful, oddball tale. Skins? Dev Patel stars as an Indian kid appearing on the sub-continent?s version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire. When he?s arrested on suspicion of cheating, the lad tells his life story and explains why he?s so seemingly knowledgeable about so many subjects. 

"Slumdog Millionaire" is, by all means, a visually superior film. Although the two films could not be more different, "Slumdog Millionaire" is this year's aesthetic achievement to rival last year's "The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford" in quality. From start to finish this is, pardon the use of a rather silly and frequently used expression, a 'visual feast'. The editing, digital cinematography, and Danny Boyle's direction (with co-director Loveleen Tandan) create a fascinating aesthetic which is perfect for the material. Barely anyone (among the vast minority of people and critics who didn't care for this massively acclaimed film) is complaining about the film's technical virtues however, so how about all that contrived, sappy melodrama? 

To my surprise, "Slumdog Millionaire" is very tasteful in almost every respect. The romance scenes are either beautifully understated (most of the scenes with them as children/young teenagers, and a couple after that) or fantasy melodrama like much of the stuff near the end of the film (although the actual final pre-credit shot itself is again, a tender and beautiful moment). I have no issues with the fantasy melodrama however, because most of the film is done in that tone. Even the very realistic and brutally true-to-life scenes involving the raids of Muslim sections of the slums by Hindus, and the luring of children to a life of begging on the streets (for gangsters and criminals) in exchange for accommodation and food are done in a manner that is both tastefully evocative of reality while fitting in tone with much of the rest of the film, which has a more hopeful tone. It sounds improbable, but that's what the screenwriter and director(s) achieve here. The film doesn't strive for 'gritty realism', but everything in the film (yes, everything) is perfectly evocative of reality. The trouble with 'gritty realism' is that it often is gritty and hopeless in a way life rarely is to most of us, and is actually laughable if done wrong. Jamal's flashbacks to the begging end in misery, but before that we get the happiness and relief of slum life that these children felt. The raid is unrelentingly horrifying, but it is a haunting memory rather than something the film dwells on without stopping. The film also gives us scenes of comedic escapism which are still within the realm of plausibility as well. 

If you don't know the general plot by now, here it is: Jamal is a boy from the slums of Mumbai who has reached the final question on "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" against all odds. The film, through a plot device I won't reveal even though it's only a mild spoiler, reveals the sources of Jamal's knowledge of the answers to each question (except for the ones he doesn't know and guesses at/uses the lifelines for) through flashbacks to him throughout his childhood and teenage years. Here enter the accusations of the film's supposedly 'hilarious', 'impossible', and 'dumb' contrivances. There's no way a chai wala knows the answers to those questions, and it's too convenient that he happens to have experienced something suitable for all those answers. I beg to differ. With a life like Jamal's (which is, believe it or not, being led right now by many children in India) I should hope that he gained at least that much knowledge. He didn't actually know the answers to every question, and on a game of both luck and knowledge it's entirely plausible to me that Jamal's game could actually happen. The only huge contrivance is the nature of the very last question and what happens when it's asked, but by then the movie had me in its grasp and the ploy worked. The fact that every member of the cast is absolutely excellent, including the child actors, doesn't hurt either. 

It sounds odd, but "Slumdog Millionaire" seemed to me like it found a way to combine a realist look at India (and, according to the Indian person with whom I attended the film, it is absolutely spot-on in almost every regard, and certainly doesn't contradict anything I saw during my short visit to India) and a romantic melodrama. The end result, with the screenplay that combines the drama, comedy, and thriller genres to great effect, is both an aesthetic triumph, and unlikely as it sounds, a crowd-pleasing masterpiece. Also, the music is brilliant, both the original score by the legendary A.R. Rahman and the excellent choices made when it comes to the pop music included in the film (though that is to be expected from a Danny Boyle film). As for those moaning about the love story, perhaps you have not found that person yet, get back to me when you do.

I am utterly confused by Slumdog Millionaire. A part of me wants to rejoice in the feeling of the triumph of the small man and in the spirit of hope that this movie appears to engender; you know, that "if the office Tea boy can surmount such incredible odds, so can I" kind of feeling. The movie is slickly made; the story is told through seamless exploration of flashback of flashbacks. The casting, particularly of the small children in their respective roles, is fabulous. The score by AR Rahman is unremarkable, but not bad.

On the other hand, a large part of me is repulsed by the crass, tasteless portrayal of the indigent underbelly of the city - a sure-fire formula for some foreign movie awards, as well as for captivating the Western audience, which has always been drawn towards displays of poverty and squalor in third world countries. That sentiment is amply echoed in the dialog when the American couple, being shocked at seeing the young boy beaten, hurriedly hands him a hundred dollar bill - the panacea to all the travails of his young life - indicating that this is what real America is. Ironic, that the director did not quite realize how accurate this portrayal was - the typical American response of solving 'issues' by throwing money at them! 

There are some inexplicable time-leaps in the movie, that leave the audience nonplussed as to how the slum-dwelling brothers suddenly learnt to communicate in English so well and how Salim managed to get hold of a gun (particularly since Mumbai is no Texas!).

And I wonder how Mr. Bachchan and Mr. Khan have taken this portrayal of the show host as a sleazy, reprehensible douchebag.

Slumdog opens up with a bang and leads to a question appearing on screen, a la Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. We're asked whether Jamal has won the show by either cheating, being lucky, or if it was written. Yet ironically, the show Jamal is on, the centerpiece of the film, is not the best part of it, though it probably has some of the most humor. No, it is in fact the flashbacks where we are told of Jamal's life and the simple, yet beautiful love between him and Lakita. Boyle manages to take a stale idea about love and makes it fresh again in one of his best films.

Jamal (Dev Patel) is a slumdog living in the poverty stricken areas of Mumbai, India. He is a sincere boy, much like the main protagonist from City of God with which this film holds several comparisons towards, and is easily sympathized with from the beginning. He is the Oliver Twist of our generation. His life story is told through intricate weaving of flashbacks through the game show he is on and in his interegation, where somehow the men that electrocute him do not understand how a slumdog could be so intelligent and sincere. Despite this and all the dangers and perils Jamal encountered in his life, he survives. His energy is infectious like the rest of the film.

Through the flashbacks, we meet characters like Lakita (Freida Pinto), the love interest of Jamal who endures as much trauma and pain, if not more, as him, who has a strong vitality of life and endures on. Both her and Jamal represent something all of us could use a little more of in these hard stricken times: hope. Jamal's brother Salim (Madhur Mittal), shows what happens to the other poverty children, where corruption and desperation seeps in and anything will be done in order to be on top and away from the bottom in which they had been stuck at. He joins mobs, does horrendous acts to people, yet he's not totally nonredeemable by the end. There's always hope.

The mainstream audience is hardly exposed to the degregation and poverty of India, and trust me, its there. Some have complained that Boyle glamorizes poverty, but its obvious they are watching a different movie. His highly stylized and frenetic camera movement does not make the poverty seem any less gritty, rather its just a technical move which is highly effective and captivating film making. If the favelas seem like the type of place you want to live in, well then all the power to you. But Boyle's use of authentic locations bring out the dirty, grimy world many inhabitants of India have to endure on a daily basis, in a country far too over populated. One shot shows Jamal running through the streets of the favelas and Boyle pulls back the camera three times, finally coming back far enough to reveal the long stretches these poorly made homes and stalls extend out to. It is a breathtaking moment.

The rest of the relatively unknown cast, such as Prem (Anil Kapoor) and Inspector (Irfan Khan) round out the movie with memorable and outstanding performances. The amount of heart present throughout is tremendous and makes for one of the most uplifting movies of the year, even if some horrible things do happen. And those horrible scenes are really that terrifying - one scene involving spoons and eyes will certainly stick with you long after the movie ends. Yet the humor is here too and a few red chilies are guaranteed to put a smile on your face. The whole experience is one long, speeding bullet of energy and magic, fable like qualities.

Danny Boyle has proven to be a master of genres, whether it be horror, drug related, comedy, sci-fi, family, and now Bollywood/romance films. I don't know how much longer he can keep this up, but hopefully forever. I obviously loved this film and it will go down as something that people, and myself, will remember for years.

A visually stunning movie, but not entirely in control of its narrative. Danny Boyle, of Trainspotting fame, is in love with the color, the pattern, the energy, and the squalor of India, and with the determined optimism of its people. He tells the Dickensian story of the rise of a desperately poor boy and his brother. They emerge from truly horrific circumstances to varied forms of success. Unlike Dickens, though, Boyle doesn't leaven the horror (and they are the sorts of scenes that made me close my eyes) with any sympathetic characters. These boys don't meet any kindness or compassion along the way. The cruelty they encounter is total. The end result is to make the story more melodramatic than the director may have intended. Or not. It is without a doubt a melodrama, but it might have been more. Still, it's loads of fun to look at, and there's the expected happy ending. And a hilarious dance video at the end.

The short synopsizes of this film out there don't do it justice. Yes it has to do with an Indian version of Who Want's to Be a Millionaire, but the three central characters are Dalits or of the untouchable caste from the oppressively downtrodden slums of Mumbai. And worse they are Muslims. But the movie isn't pro-Muslim as soon becomes apparent. 
  
 The central question is how a young man from that background had the knowledge, [i]or intelligence[/i], to answer the questions on the show. The story uses the format of showing the questions one at a time and then him telling the police (whom the quiz show host had had arrested for fraud, and tortured in order to force him to tell them how he'd cheated) how he'd come by the answers. There was a thematic slant favoring destiny, which I didn't like, and an emphasis on truth, which I did. 
  
The inventiveness in every aspect of filmmaking, even down to the Hindi subtitles (about 50% of the dialogue) which was the best way of presenting them I'd every seen (you could watch and read at the same time), was spectacular. My only objections were to the ending which was straightforward but not up to the quality of the rest of the film; and to the title, which blunted the force of introducing the derisive term, slumdog. It should have been titled [i]Rough[/i].

Truly one of 2008's best, as well as this year's most engaging film.  This is my favorite Danny Boyle movie, which is saying something, as he has done Trainspotting and 28 Days Later.  It's about this Indian kid who is on the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire.  Right off the bat, you know that he has gotten far on the show because he is being aggressively questioned by the police about cheating, their logic being 'how can an uneducated boy from the slums know all these answers?"  You, the audience, find out through a series of flashbacks.  You really connect with these characters and you end up rooting for Jamal to win with the rest of India.  It's Danny Boyle's best work; there's lots of dazzling colors and camera angles, but also the unknown Indian cast do equally well with their parts.  I lost myself in this one, and it was one of the fastest two hours I have spent in a theater this year.

Definitely make an effort to see this unique tale of growing up in the poorest of places which is used to tell how a young Indian teen makes a bid for a million dollars and his lost love.  It even has a crazy dance number for the credits!

Maybe this simplicity is what audiences are warming to. Yet the young heroes of Boyle's earlier "Millions", faced with an equal fortune, had a complex moral dilemma to resolve amongst themselves. Jamal just has to survive whatever Beaufoy chooses to throw at him next - and he has at least three lifelines to help him out. Patel, late of TV's "Skins" is too blankly ingenuous: you can see why the authorities might doubt this rather opaque young man's ability to come up with the right answers by himself, but nothing on or about the actor's face suggests hard-won worldly wisdom, while Pinto, as his childhood sweetheart, sports the kind of glowing skin more common to the Laboratoires Garnier than the Mumbai slums. If it's a fairytale we're being sold here, it's a fairytale with at least one eye on the international marketplace; you can equally see it in the way the quiz show's questions gradually move from specifically Indian subjects to a more American line of inquiry. Whose face adorns the one hundred dollar bill? Who invented the revolver? Guns and money, money and guns: I know I'm in the minority on this, but I can't help but feel this bling fantasy is far less innocent, charming, or even convincing, than is being claimed.

We learn of a devastatingly tough lifestyle as Jamal, along with his brother Salim and lost love Latika, braves the dangers of the cruel slumdog environment.
That's merely the movie in a nutshell and I won't elaborate because I can't give away anymore. All I want to say this that I'm not one to give away five stars willy-nilly but I really believe that director Danny Boyle has created a masterpiece here. It's a story of heartache and follows the harsh reality's of an impovished life in the slum's of Mumbai. How can one even begin to describe what an incredible experience this film is?  It is "inspiring", "well-acted", yadda yadda [insert usual strong generalized phrases about the movie here].

But just consider this: how beaufitul this is shot and scored.  Slumdog doesn't really seem to focus on the idea of "rags to riches" inspiration but rather on presenting this story in a way that is interesting and entertaining.  Though I saw poverty all over the place, I never really pitied the main character.  The movie ends up having its audience in a wide-eyed cheer for him, rather than an empathetic depressed state.  The sadness of this story is masked by the complete brilliance of the production.  There is just one beautiful shot after another in this.  The staging of the characters in the setting, and the centering of all this in the frame is done so well in one shot after another.  

Moments the production really shines is when characters are on the run and there are these strange and mesmerizing instumental compositions pulsating through the screen.  

Also consider the way in which Patel plays Jamal.  He is subdued; this is great because with the life he has had up until this point, he should be.  His life as a "Slumdog" has trained him to be passive and quiet.  When he is being confronted by the workers from the game show, there are never shots of him acting enraged, yelling, lashing out, etc. (except one time); only passively speaking the truth.  This is great stuff.

The hybrid emotions that come from the way question answers are juxtaposed to past events that lead to them is innovative and one of 2008's freshest ideas.  When the final answer comes, the event that it is cross-cut with drives home this theme and is incredibly symbolic in nature.

But the purpose of this film is to celebrate the triumph of the human spirit.  These production techniques serve to intensify the accomplishment and survival of its main charcter.  They could have gone with slow camera movements and melancholy orchestral compositions, and the film would have struck in a completely different mannor.  Like I said, the production results in us standing up and cheering for its characters, rathen than feeling sorry for them.  This makes for a great experience.

You've never heard of it, yet. It doesn't matter. A third of it is in Hindu. That doesn't matter. Until the minutes  before the end credits, it's mostly  unbearably depressing. Doesn't matter, either. The pure LIFE in this movie does, though. "Slumdog" follows Jamal Malick as a child orphan in Mumbai, India living an existence only matched by Oliver Twist. He has nothing. He has instincts and experiences, mostly borderline fatal. As a teenager he finds his way on an Indian version of "Who Wants To Be A Millioniare," and comes off as a natural born genius. He isn't. The movie flashes back and forth between the past and present and explains to us how Jamal could possibly know the answers to these questions. Throughout his life they are given to him by chance. He uses them well. This is the type of movie that climbs for the high summit on fairy dust that makes you feel cozy inside. It's also for everyone. The years-long  love story between Jamal and a childhood friend will swoon the girls, the rag to riches grittiness of it will pump up the guys. You wouldn't think this to be a Danny Boyle film, a Brit who did the uber-dark "28 Days Later," and "Trainspotting" but his new film explodes with color. The cinematography opens up gashes inside Indias underbelly, and you can smell the rotted out slums. Sogginess never looked so potent.  Here's an interesting moment in cinema this year: Jamal and his brother Salim as children on top of a moving train, stealing food from passengers over a soundtrack playing M.I.A's "Paper Planes." Classic. It's paced beautifully and lead Dev Patel (as 19-year-old Jamal) has potential as an actor. The camera loves him. Do me a favor and ignore the Discovery Channel moments showcasing the bowels of poverty stricken India. It's all for the story, not for sobs. Backlashers will say its predicable and too heavy in the pay-attention-to-the-rest-of-the-world kind of thing, but don't listen. They know not what they say. For a nice night out to the movies, and a much needed lift, I present "Slumdog Millionaire," one of the best pictures of the year.

Slumdog Millionaire is an energetic feat of storytelling bravado that lacks a believable center.  I wanted so much to love this film, and parts of it I did, but overall I can only say it achieves a "like" from me.  Jamal and Latika's romance, which is the core of the film, needs to be developed further.  For the rest of the film to be so steeped in realism, even exuberant and vibrant realism, their relationship is pure Hollywood contrivance of the most predictable and, ultimately, boring sort.  However, Slumdog Millionaire is gorgeous to look and Boyle and the child actors bring such a fresh energy to the first half of the film that I was able to overlook the more flat second half.

The thing that saves Danny Boyle's latest from routine is certainly his collaboration with cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle, who has worked with Boyle on two of his previous films. Mantle and Boyle are a match made in heaven when it comes to a DP and director joining forces. The visual panache of Slumdog is at the top of the cake, a pure marvel of art and technical skill fusing together to paint some enticing pictures that are cut away from way too quickly. Its storytelling efforts fall somewhat lower. 
Part 21st century fairy tale and "City of God in India", there really is no guessing where this tale is gonna go because after all, like the film says "it is written." 
For me it didn't work, and I was not really drawn in. I wasn't won over to root for our hero Jamal, it was just assumed that I would. Same goes with the love story. While cute, and providing what should be the base for the entire film, it never felt more than a prerequisite. The infusion of environment and character through sight and sound was spun at such a frenetic pace that I never felt I could get a clear handle on things. Boyle does like his films at a clip and I had no issues in prior works... Do I just need a more static film? This also happened in the before mentioned City of God.   

Boyle proves yet again that he is a chameleon when it comes to the projects he chooses, yet his thematic and philosophical fascinations regarding the goodness of human kind vs. the folly of humankind kind are all in tack for Slumdog.
The performances from the kids (at all ages) are fine, Boyle knows how to work with them.
Though Slumdog is a bit drawn out and gets winded - and they really try to pace the thing fast - there were plenty of moments that made me smile and its merits on the technical side alone is worth the price of admission. It does seem that it is a film that is getting people out to the theater who might not always be exposed to other cultures and languages (half the film is in Hindi), so that is always a plus.

[u][b]Slumdog Millionaire (2008)[/b][/u]
Starring: Dev Patel, Ani Kapoor, Saurbah Shukla
Directed By: Danny Boyle
Grade: A-

Destiny! Slumdog Millionaire definitely lives up to the hype, providing an entertaining and passionate story. One of the reasons I couldn't wait to see Slumdog was because I didn't know what to expect. The plot synopsis seems a bit cheesy and boring, but SD is far from that. The film begins as Jamal, Dev Patel, is under interrogation by Mumbai police for cheating on India's version of Who Wants To Be a Millionaire, being only one question away from winning it all. As Jamal tries to avoid further torture, he begins to explain to the police how he knew each of the answers. Flashbacks present Jamal's boyhood and explain how he got to the show.

As we go through the life story of Jamal, it's a very unfortunate one, and we see why he doesn't value that prize money much in the end. He continues to lose the love of his life in his wild journey, and finally receives the prize he most desires by the end. Boyle captures this story beautifully and the emotion attached to the characters are very strong, which help to make the story better and better. 

Danny Boyle deserves, at least, a best director nomination. He's done the best job of any that I've seen this year, and is the main reason why this film thrives so much. The film flows beautifully, and the cinematography and camerawork were fantastic. Boyle captures plenty of remarkable and beautiful images throughout the film. We also get some great performances from some unknown young actors. Katel, Kapoor, and Shukla all do their part and as a group do a fantastic job for such an inexperienced and young ensemble. The score is fantastic and captures the mood and setting of SM. Not only that, but the score is definitely one of the more enjoyable ones of the past few years. Overall the film is a great story and one of the best I've seen this year.

Very solid movie and well worth a watch. Superbly directed, casted, costumed, and acted, the film develops along a subtle non-linear plotline. I think that most audiences will miss some of the subtle humor that makes the film both endearing and poignant. 

A couple of criticisms are important, however. First, the film's elements are bit too on the nose and crossing the line into the unbelieveable abruptly removes the viewer from the story and reminds them that they are watching a scene designed to construct the plot elements. Fortunately, these jarring moments are few. A nice backdrop for a simple love story, the adherence to Indian cultural elements should be commended. Finally, I was audibly disappointed at the decision to include the stereotypical dance party/music video at the end of the movie during the credits. I don't understand why Bollywood/Hollywood movies feel it necessary to do this but it strikes me as pandering. 

Nonetheless, certainly a movie to see and experience if only to capture a small glimpse of what life is like on the streets in absolute poverty and witness the absurd religious and economic calamity that is the motherland.

Boyle's cinematography is just as fantastic in this as it was in 28 Days Later and this is every bit as engaging as well. The story telling in this is very unique and gripping from the start. Usually when Oscar season comes about finding a movie with a glimmer of hope tends to be difficult to say the least but this does not disappoint in that department. Great movie, worth seeing for sure.

There are two ways you could look at "Slumdog Millionaire."  One way would be to say (as I have read) that the film is a complete fairy tale and its story is impossible to believe, and that it is a Disney-ized version of a Bollywood film with a cheesy happy ending.  I think that whoever feels this way about "Slumdog..." has a valuable point.  
But there's another way to look at the film, and if you haven't already figured out by my high ranking, it's the way I look at it.  This is to say that "Slumdog Millionaire" can be a fantasy if it wants to be, but whatever it is -- it is an uplifting story at a time in the world when we need it, and it is stunning sensory cinema at a time when everyone is running off at the mouth about the merits of movies far less artistic and adventuresome.
I take issue with those who would call this "sappy" or "Disney-like."  Um...did you not pay attention to what the main character, Jamal, went through as a boy?  What, are those the lost scenes from "Aladdin"?  Because that's about as close to Disney as this gets.  
On the contrary, the film is energetically edited in a simple way, with the street punk Jamal (played fantastically by Dev Patel) contemplating questions on the Indian version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" while we are exposed to flashbacks of his treacherous life, which often provides seemingly fate-driven connections to the answers to his questions on the show.  I will grant you, the structure is simple.  But it works.  Damn...it works really well!
Danny Boyle gives "Slumdog Millionaire" the kind of energy that I found missing from a few of the other excellent films (and touted potential Best Picture co-nominees) like "Milk" and "Frost/Nixon."  There is artistry in the camera work and stunning visuals that are paramount to the storytelling.  There is also a funky, contemporary, kinetic, memorable score...one of the first this year that has really just grabbed me by the neck.  (I read somewhere that Boyle told his composer that he didn't want "any damned cellos," and I think this is exactly why the film is not as cheesy as it could have been...it got the right director to give it the street edge the story called for.
Heartbreaking, heartwarming, exciting, stunning...all of the adjectives work.  And if this bunch of no-names ends up hitting the Oscar podium in a few months, it might just be because the film so deftly straddles multiple time-honored film genres.  It's a coming of age story, it's Dickensian, it's a drama, it has comedic moments, it's a gangster film.  And, to top it off, it's probably mainstream America's first true taste of India -- and the films from that region are a whole other can of worms with many delights to be had.

It might seem strange for a review with this high a score to seem negative, so understand that I did really enjoy the film--it was beautifully edited and very engaging. I also thought the structure was a testimony to Danny Boyle's vision and creativity. Who else would have thought to use "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" questions as a device to propell the story? 

I found the best aspect of the film to be the early flashback scenes of Jamel, his brother and Latika. I liked their story, and all the innovative ways they managed to survive. I also thought the rebellious character development of Jamel's brother was really well-done. He makes a lot of mistakes, and seems in many circumstances to be bordering on sociopathy. But every so often he comes around and makes a sacrifice for his brother. This was probably the best element of the film.

Now, I wasn't quite so impressed with the performances of Dev Patel and Freida Pinto. I thought they did fine--nothing to spoil the film. But whenever we saw these latter moments of interaction between them, the plot began to drift away from its roots as a "City of God"esque reality piece, and into a sappy love story. This made the third act suffer. It also distracted me from some of the suspense, and other aspects of the story (such as the final redemption of Jamel's brother).

Also, I was a bit bothered by the theme of "destiny" in the film. For something this socially conscientious, it was a little off-putting to use simple destiny as an explanation for the lead character's success. To me, he didn't seem to be an especially upright or morally-correct young man, and to see all these other people around him fall led me more to the conclusion that he was just lucky. Maybe filmmakers like Danny Boyle like the concept of "destiny" to justify their own success. Or maybe he just used it as a plot device. 

I'd say that I highly enjoyed the film, and that it was a close-call between giving the film my top rating or holding back. In the end, I thought the third act suffered, that a few of the plot developments were kind of cheesy or unbelievable, and that the themes were problematic for the subject matter. But I will make a guess right now that this will be one of the oscar contendors for the big prize, and I wouldn't be disappointed if it won.

The indomitably overhyped "Slumdog Millionaire" makes for a perfectly enjoyable crowd-pleaser with occasional intimations of thematic depth and sociological/political interest, but I can't help but find the whole enterprise a little dubious: another entry into the condescending-to-real-world-suffering sweepstakes that includes other overrated pieces of decadence like "City of God" and "The Last King of Scotland." By concocting a blatantly fantastical Hollywood- (or, more appropriately, Bollywood-)style story and wedding it to a sometimes recklessly hyperkinetic aesthetic style---smash-cut-heavy, lit and shot for maximum visceral impact, etc.---director Danny Boyle puts on one undeniable hell of a show but makes one wonder whether he actually has something substantive to say about the Indian society he purports to expose, or whether he's more interested in exploiting real-world suffering and class division for pumped-up, tasteless sensationalism. There are glimmers of deeper themes peppered in here and there, but most of it is crushed by the inexorable tread toward sentimental uplift. I was certainly not bored, but I found the whole thing pretty shallow overall. But people left and right seem to love this movie, as the ratings below demonstrate. Guess I must be missing something.
