I had never heard of this movie until it started getting Oscar/award buzz. And for a foreign film, I was shocked it actually got American award buzz. Nonetheless, I had to see it. I knew that the basic center of the movie is basically a love story, so it's a matter of how effective the film is at telling it. In this case, extremely. At first thought, the premise that it all revolves around the WWTBA Millionaire show seems comical, but really, it made what would normally be a common tale of growing up and love, into a much more unique way of telling the classic story. At one point I thought of it as a Indian Forrest Gump. Nonetheless, director Danny Boyle did an exceptional job with this one. Now, much like Seven Pounds, the way the plot works seems a little too improbable (each question he's asked just so happens to involve a specific dramatic event in his life), but if viewers can accept that that's just the way the story is told, then it's pretty cool. It's funny because you know as each question is asked, you'll learn more about Jamal growing up, and while your watching it, you'll forget what the question even was, that's because viewers will lose themselves in the plot and learn to care for Jamal more than the damn answers. That's the most significant and amazing thing about the film, that the game show really isn't that important, in some ways yes, and in some ways no. The guy who play the oldest Jamal did a pretty damn good job. Even though most of the time he has to act nervous or scared, he still was very good at it. One little thing that annoyed me is that they played that one hip hop song from Pineapple Express that I'm sick of, I wonder why they chose that. That's just a little side note. Overall, the film is well done, pure and simple, but why it isn't 5 stars for me or even 4 1/2, is because it really doesn't pull too many NEW punches, there's nothing absolutely mind blowing about it and, to me, love stories can only get so good. Don't get me wrong, it is very original for the most part, but I just can't slap on a 5 star rating for this because, well I'll just say it, it's no Departed or No Country for Old Men.

One of the more difficult things (at least for me) is reviewing movies based on actual events or adapted from a previous story (be it movie, book, short story, etc.). This is mainly because I'm unsure if I should consider the original story when determining whether or not I like a movie. As a general rule I do not. They are two completely separate entities that should only be judged on their own merits. I say this, but if I've read/seen/heard the original story, it's tough not to.

That being said, I remember hearing this story as a blurb when it happened, but really didn't take the time to research it further. To be perfectly honest, I still haven't. This is for a good reason: this is an incredibly told story and I want to believe this is how it happened (although, I'm pretty sure that some liberties have been taken).

I'm a little unsure why Slumdog Millionaire hasn't had a wide release. It's an indie movie like Juno was an indie movie last year: one that everyone will like. It's got the classic trappings of a complete underdog overcoming incredible odds to accomplish something unbelievable. It's got something for everyone: romance, tragedy, social commentary, comedy, action, adventure, drama...it's literally every great genre of film rolled into one movie that 100% works on every level.

That being said, I walked out having thoroughly enjoyed the movie, but there wasn't that extra 'oomph' that five-star films have. I don't know why, it was incredible in every aspect, but I didn't walk out of the theater immediately wanting to see it again. Because of this, I knocked off half a star for purely personal reasons. This could very well win the Academy Award for Best Picture this year--and it totally deserves it-- but to me, there was just something lacking that I can't quite put my finger on.

So this is wonderful in terms of 'structure'. I dont know how the plot was developed in Vikas Swarups's original novel, but the adaptation works extremely well. Most of the story is in flashback, because we meet Jamal when he is at the police station. We realize its is the second last question that has landed him here. Then we take off with him from here straight into the last climactic scene where he answers the 3 musketeers question and wins the money and the girl.The movie though is much more than the story. Its Rahman's music, its the camera that captures mumbai's underbelly with such vivid colors and textures that it as gritty as it is glamorous. Its glamorous because of its fairy-tale optimism, and humanism, and romance of the underdog. What is truly remarkable is the POV of Danny Boyle, its a sympathetic perspective, its an outsider than is telling you the story as an insider. That saves the day for the modern fairy tale. Its good cinema- its middle of the road cinema, part truth-part fantasy, but ultimately brilliant storytelling, stunning images, and enough drama to make the skin crawl one moment, and to hold back tears in the next. Now that's really good cinema and really good storytelling.

Danny Boyle is back behind the camera with a change of scenery and a story of one slumdog's rise from nothing to something in the blink of an eye on the Hindi version of 'Who Wants To Be Millionaire'. Nobody believes what is happening, not the presenter, nor the police, however as Jamal Malik continues to defy convention by getting question after question right, we are not only watching a potential millionaire in the works, but are also thrown into the distant journey of his past. With one question separating Jamal from an astounding 20 million rupees, one question remains; why is Jamal really on the show?

Slumdog Millionaire is a story of love, life, family, poverty and ultimately one mans rise from the foundations of dirt to the creation of gold through life itself. In a world where wealth can be won in an instant, it is only those who strive for the inspiration and delve into their own determined mind that can achieve this, which Jamal is, an underdog. And we all know how much we love to connect-to and adopt an underdog no matter whom, why or where he or she is.

From the first scenes where we see Jamal being tortured in the Police Station as he is held in the same contempt as a common thief to the final suspense fuelled moment, Danny Boyle manages to tug on every heart string available to viewer all at a swift pace. From heart-warming entertaining scenes, such as when Jamal and his brother Salim pretend to be Taj Mahal tour guides to the foreign tourists, we are juggernauted and catapulted into the emotional opposite with Jamal constantly fighting the demons keeping him apart from the only girl that brings to a smile away. It is this constant emotional battle that keeps our eyes open and our mind ticking. Why? Because we simply want to know how Jamal got there and where he is now headed.

Danny Boyle is almost flawless in his melodramatic direction of Slumdog; he allows the film to build without ever dragging out a section of the film to the point where you wish Jamal would stop reminiscing. However I mustnt overlook the other technical and stylistic aspects which allowed this film to flourish, most importantly Anthony Mandles beautiful cinematography of the various contrasting lands of India and Chris Dickens smoothly worked editing guarantee that the brilliantly written script from Simon Beaufoy flows effortlessly into creating a wonderful modern fairytale that will by the end make you laugh, smile or cry, or all three.

When I first heard Danny Boyle, the director of Trainspotting, 28 Days Later and Sunshine among others, was attached to direct a Romantic Drama set within the deep confines of Indian culture and society, I laughed. However its Boyle who is having the last laugh, as he has created a chilling, yet warm, frightening, yet uplifting film that touches upon pretty much every human emotional response available, but will definitely leave you exiting the cinema with one feeling fresh in your mind and your gut; that you have seen something special.

[left][font=Microsoft Sans Serif]The outcome of [i]Slumdog Millionare [/i]is fairly predictable - but Danny Boyle's latest is anything but bland and overdone, in fact, it's an exciting discovery. [i]Slumdog Millionare [/i]is bursting with energy and life, and carries an affirming message - even in the toughest of circumstances, life is full of joy and love. While it carries such a positive message, [i]Slumdog [/i]never feels artificially joyful or sugarcoated. Actually it's the opposite of sugarcoated, with some horrifically brutal scenes that show how dangerous life can be for lower-class people in India.[/font][/left]
[left] [/left]

[left][font=Microsoft Sans Serif]Part of [i]Slumdog[/i]'s major success lies with the mostly young cast - all the actors who played Jamal and Salim at the different points in their lives were fantastic. Often when different actors play the same character, it feels odd and takes you out of the film - but that's not the case here, all the young actors gave a sense of consistency to the character, and I never doubted that I was watching the same person as before. And, obviously, [i]Slumdog [/i]works so well because of Danny Boyle. While [i]Sunshine [/i]and [i]28 Days Later [/i]were very good, this is the best work that I've seen from him yet (have yet to watch [i]Trainspotting [/i]and[i] Millions[/i]). Boyle's beautiful cinematography and knack for picking perfect music is possibly at its best here, and the emotion he brings to certain scenes is almost overwhelming. Overall, [i]Slumdog Millionare [/i]is one of the most refreshing, engrossing, and all-around best films of 2008.[/font][/left]

A wonderful movie. Boyle's direction here is stands out above all else this year and he deserves an Oscar. This is MTV meets Classic American Cinema. It's The Fast and Furious meets It's a Wonderful Life. To me, it seems that film has been headed in to this cathartic spot for years. And sure, Boyle has turned in similar work in the past...but never has he so perfectly melded the modern with the classic. This is Forrest Gump on crack.

The script is perfect here. It's a believable fairy tale set on the tough streets of India, of all places. Every note is perfect...it's fun, it's funny, it's rough, it's moving, it's romantic. The set-up of the story is just fantastic. I was just as engaged in Jamal's life growing up as I was in his "present" circumstances where police officers are questioning him for supposedly cheating on "Who Wants to be a Millionare?"

The performances are great and so are all the technical aspects of the movie. But...really...this is Boyle's film and seemingly the start of a new style in film that will be ripped off for years to come. A great cross-cultural experience.
Definitely worth a watch....well written, great performances, excellent story telling.

[left][font=Courier New][size=2]Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) is one question away from winning on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire" as the night's taping comes to an end. On his way out he is abducted by local authorities after it is believed he is somehow cheating at the game. Being questioned, he unravels a tale of lost love and a man's journey to reclaim the woman he loves. Without a doubt, Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tandan's [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is one of the most beautiful and moving pictures you are going to see this year.

Danny Boyle has had a rather interesting career. He seemed to come out of nowhere with films like [i]Shallow Grave[/i] and [i]Trainspotting[/i], and became an overnight sensation. His films after those two were a series of hit and misses with audiences (at least stateside). [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is Boyle's best work since the brilliant horror film [i]28 Days Later[/i]. The usage of colors and the landscapes (both beautiful and otherwise) paint an amazing canvas for these characters to exist on. And Simon Beaufoy's wonderful screenplay, based on the novel by Vikas Swarup, is one of the year's best.

The three actors who play Jamal (Ayush Mahesh Khedekar during the childhood scenes, Tanay Chheda during the early teen scenes and Dev Patel during the late teen scenes) were all fantastic in the film. I know Patel from the BBC series "Skins," which is a rather trashy series but I like it anyway. Here he shows that he is a gifted actor. There are few films this year where I've felt a deep connection with the characters, but [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] managed to create a connection unlike any other film this year. And Patel gives one of the best performances of the year, and crafted one of the year's most endearing characters.

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] could possibly be the most romantic film you could see in 2008. Jamal's never-ending quest to find the girl he loves, Latika (Rubiana Ali during the childhood scenes, Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar during the early teen scenes and Freida Pinto during the late teen scenes), is one of the best love stories to come along in years. Their love story isn't an easy one, and the two face a lot of difficulties along the way. But Jamal's unyielding struggle to find her no matter what stands in his way is one of the most beautiful love stories ever put to film. 

I guess this might make me sound like a big softy, but I'm cool with that. By the end of the film, I was so moved at what I had just seen that I was almost in tears. The end credits have a nice dance number that was somewhat uplifting, but the feeling still remained the same. [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is just an absolutely stunning film that finds beauty and humor even in some of the worst of places and situations. The film joins the ranks of similar films like [i]Modern Times[/i] and [i]Life is Beautiful[/i].[/size][/font]

After the absolute worst summer in my movie watching history, I have hit a winning streak this winter/holiday season. I can only hope it continues. Wow, what a neat movie [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is! I thought the way in which it was put together and told was very fresh and new. Actually unique is what I want to call it, which is a word in description I don't use lightly. The actors, at least for me, were all unknowns which is always nice. And they all, from kids to adults, did a fantastic job acting. Now, often I have a very difficult time believing movies set in the middle east that are for the most part all English and without subtitles. I get caught up thinking about how there's no way there can be [i]that[/i] much English speaking. This in turn is a constant reminder that I'm watching a movie. I know it's weird, but it's a personal hang up of mine. Well, this movie kept me plenty engaged enough to overlook it completely. Oh Slumdog had [i]some[/i] subtitles, but not nearly as much as you'd think it should for the area it was set in.
Something I found the movie depicted well was the way in which the orphaned brothers had to live. I imagine it's not unlike a great many children growing up in the middle east. It's very easy to see how they end up victimized by the only thing they see as welcoming them...Muslims. 
One thing that surprised me was the R rating by the MPAA. I can only guess it's because of the violence, but unless I am just a completely desensitized American, I didn't find it to be all [i]that[/i] violent. There was one or two brief sexual situations, but no nudity. I would have no problem watching this with my 15 yr old daughter. 
To sum up [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] had the perfect balance of drama, romance and action and can be correctly placed in any of those categories. The only thing keeping this movie from a 10 is, well, because 10 is perfect and I will rarely if ever give a movie such a rating.

This film works on so many levels, from acting to story design to cinematography.  In the end, everything is working in unison to lift up the story and, in so doing, to lift us up.  I dare say people were floating out of the theater.  The film, thankfully, does not sugarcoat the world, but it does show that even in a very difficult situation love can be found and should desperately be sought.  Congratulations to everyone involved in this fine film.  This is the type of movie that honors me as the viewer.  Thanks!

A stunning study on the haves and the have-nots set in Mumbai, India and featuring some incredible performances from the mostly young cast: the kids are amazing, particularly in presenting the brutality that is an everyday event in their lives. Slumdog Millionaire 
directed by Danny Boyle
written by Simon Beaufoy
based on the novel by Vikas Swarup
starring Dev Patel, Anil Kapoor, Madhur Mittal, Freido Pinto, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail, Ayush Mahesh, Khedekar, Mahesh Manjrekar, Ankur Vikal, Irrfan Khan, Rubiana Ali

Slumdog Millionaire is  a deceptively simple story  told intricately and with great subtlety  about the vagaries of love and the complications that often arise when one makes a concerted effort to gain  it.

Jamal Melik (Patel) as the film opens is being detained by police and tortured because they as well as the officials at the Indian import of the American game show Who Wants to be a Millionaire? think that he cheated.  He has risen from the slums of Mumbai to being one question away from winning 20 million rupees and the host, Prem Kumar (Kapoor) believes it is impossible for such a lowly person to know all the answers.  One by one Jamal goes through the questions and the film reveals the moments in his life where he learned them.  We are provided with instances  that go back to just before Jamal and his brother Salims (Mittal) mother is murdered by Anti-Muslim zealots.  The boys become orphans and get by doing anything and everything to survive.  Mostly they live amidst the trash heaps and ingeniously devise methods of stealing whatever isnt nailed down from tourists who are necessarily charmed by dirty Indian children who play up their impoverished state for their rubes.

The film is a thrilling portrait of a most degenerate area in a vast and grand country that is slowly pulling itself into the 21st century.  This is not the travel book version of India.  Its a filthy and crumbling place consumed with wretchedly attired beggar children who are maltreated and groomed in various illicit ways in order to make as much money as possible singing for passerby.  

One day during a rainstorm the boys have found cover.  A young girl their age is being pelted by the rain and Jamal invites her up.  She is also an orphan girl and the three become inseparablethe three muskateers.  Her name is Latika and Jamal quickly forms an attachment to her.  When a man named Maman (Vikal)  takes the children to an orphanage they imagine they have landed in a place where they will be cared for and fed well.  Unfortunately they are unaware of Mamans vicious techniques for making the children into the most effective beggars on the streets.  After a terrifying incident the boys escape but Latika is left behind.  Jamal pledges to go back for her and several years later he makes good on his word.

The agonies of poverty and deprivation are exploited to full effect in this film.  There are scenes where swarms of children fan out in order to bleed money from as many sympathetic persons as possible.  Its grimy, horrific and a necessary portrait of the underbelly of India and draws attention to its problems with keeping abreast of the terrible conditions which many of its citizens reside.  The film suggests that this problem will have to be effectively addressed if India is going to continue to ascend onto the Worlds stage. 

Throughout this film there is a tremendous energy that coupled with bright, intoxicating colors create a portrait of a country on the move.  The slums are vibrant places consumed with life and viability.  They are not demonized nor are their inhabitants treated as victims.  Rather, the situation is merely presented without any commentary and the viewer can make up their own mind about how they perceive the conditions under which life is brought forth.  This is an exceedingly open film replete with joy, passion, and a forthright urgency that is dynamic and explosive. Yet it doesnt shy away from disclosing a much darker world that has arisen as a necessary side effect of the progress that is pushing forward relentlessly.

The narrative demonstrates how Jamal climbs up the ranks on his way to the potential big payoff.  Each question brings him closer to what is presented as his destiny and this is directly tied into Latika (Pinto) and everything she means to him.  The film is a series of gains and losses as Latika repeatedly slips from Jamals  grasp as he struggles on in the hope of bringing her near to him once again. 

Salim takes a decidedly different path from his brother that is set from the moment he first picks up a gun.  He develops into a key member of crime boss Javeds (Manjrekar) syndicate.  His presence is felt throughout the film as a grim counterpart to all the riotous thrills that Jamal has realized with his successful run on the game show.  The very end of the film shows two very different outcomes for each brother that work exceedingly well within the context of the story.  Salim becomes a hard man embroiled in a life beset with terror, fear, and ruthlessness.  Salim is lost at some point in the story.  He falls into a lifestyle that is broken and degrading.  There is not one instance where Salim and his ilk are glamorized.  Its a brutal life and Salim has chosen it for himself and seems unable or unwilling to walk away. 

The tension surrounding the execution of the final answer in the contest is decisive and pronounced.  The film builds it expertly throughout and the result is entirely in doubt to the very end.  It could have gone either way and essentially it doesnt much matter how it turns out.  Immediately after Jamal is crouched low and leaning up against a building.  He doesnt appear to be particularly charmed by his enormous victory.  He is looking for Latika because ultimately it was for her that he even attempted to go after the money.  He says that he participated only because he hoped she was watching.  Much of his  life he has burned for this one person and nothing can  divest him of the drive to find her at last.  Their tormented relationship is as profoundly moving as anything that has been seen this year.  The agony is pervasive and the earnestness with which Jamal seeks Latika is immersed in a poetry that all great love stories must contain if they are going to move the audience into that place that all such stories reside.  This film masterfully sets up this dynamic and makes it matter to an audience that is looking to be so moved.

The film reveals a tremendous hunger throughout India as 90 million people tune in to see if Jamal has what it takes to win the game.  Thats the equivalent of the American Super Bowl which is easily the highest rated show in any year.    

Latika is a character who is lifted out of the slums only to find herself subjected to type of bondage that makes her into a deeply sympathetic character that the audience roots for.  Freido Pinto, in her first film, captures the innocence and world weary aspect of her character with a sturdy ease that is vital to Jamals arc.  She must be presented as someone worth pining for and Pinto does this through her gentle portrayal of Latika and her genuine approach to the characters inherent longing.  Latika grows up over the course of the film into a woman who has experienced great pain and suffering.  There is a sense that both Jamal and Latika are two people who have been driven to one another to realize a grace that they have heretofore been deprived of.  They truly need each other and the film makes this fact a driving force of its narrative.

The performances in this film are convincing and thoroughly natural.  Dev Patel has a haunted countenance throughout the film which conveys his characters bewilderment and mounting sorrow over the possibility of losing his one true love.  Patel captures Jamals intensity and focus.  He is so good and generating a lasting hope that is carried through the duration of the film.  His is a story that has a necessity about it that Patel brings enthusiastically to his role.  Madhur Mittels character carries a tremendous weight on his shoulders that is made manifest in the final moments of the film.  Salim is presented throughout the film as the more adventurous of the two who exploits his position as the eldest in his relationship with Jamal.  Salim disappears into the fabric of the film only to arrive at a strange destination that is in direct opposition to how Jamal has come to live his life.  As mentioned Freida Pinto carries herself with a decisive purpose as Latika maneuvers her way through her conflicting and occasionally stifled life.  Anil Kapoor has all the charisma and affability one could possibly expect of a successful game show host.  His character carries much of the film with his contagious charm coupled with abrasiveness that gives him bite and sets him up as an example of what a corrosive and slightly inhospitable host can bring to such a circus.  Much of the films power comes from the two young actors playing Jamal and Salim as children.  They are convincing in their roles as impoverished dreamers who pounce on any opportunity to improve the quality of their lives.

Overall, this is a masterful telling of a story that has a lasting, eternal quality.  The characters are realistically drawn and the film never falls into the quagmire of sentimentality.  It is never simplistic although the main thrust to the story is perhaps one of the simplest driving factors in any film that wants to present a credible romantic entanglement.  These are would be lovers torn apart over the course of a dozen or so years struggling to finally reach a place where their love can be actualized.  This is a film about brotherhood and respect.  Jamal finds himself one question away from national celebrity.  Already there is a sense of how his accomplishments have garnered him tremendous media coverage.  But Jamal is not unduly affected by this attention and proceeds to approach the game with the same calm temerity with which he approaches the rest of his life.

Boyle shoots Mumbai like the landscape of an alien planet, or some kind of lucid dream, making unimaginable conditions for human life seem vibrant and beautiful, which enhances the film's wholly absorbing sense of escapism. This film is about stepping into another person's life rather than passively observing it, and that kind of empathy has more than a little to do with why I watch films at all. Slumdog Millionaire

On the surface itâs Oliver Twist and Great Expectations revolving around the TV show âWho Wants to be a Millionaireâ (fortunately without Regis Philbin).  No one can understand how Jamal Malik (a kid from the slums) could possibly know the answers to rather difficult questions of the show.  After all heâs no Good Will Hunting, or Rain Man, or even Forrest Gump.  So how does he do it?  Itâs simple, he goes into total recall mode and the answers drop into his lap. 

Unlike the rest of us, Jamal completely knows the meaning of his life.  Jamal must suffer through life so he can answer the questions, and without the questions, he canât get the girl, and if he doesnât get the girl, he canât find happiness.  Jamal gets the money but we, the viewer, receive the answer to the age-old question of why bad things happen to good people.  

I do have to warn you that this film doesnât hold anything back on how rough life can be, and it will make you flinch at some of the scenes.  But with that said, go watch this, it should win best foreign film.    

Favorite Line:
Policeman: How does he know how to answer the questions?
Jamal: Because I know what the answers are.

A very different way of telling a story - as Jamal tries to explain to the police that he didn't cheat, the movie switches between the questions being asked in a quiz show, and the explanations of why a simple slumdog knows the answers to those precise questions.

Underdog stories are a dime a dozen, and that's the reason why it's so difficult to come up with above-average movies that follow said type of storyline yet don't feel like recycled material.  So, how DID director Danny Boyle manage to create such a good underdog story with [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i]?
   
   [b]A.[/b] His film has the best soundtrack of the year
   [b]B.[/b] Though set in India, his film has a universal quality to it that will make it appealing to all moviegoers
   [b]C.[/b] The main character is one of the most likable underdogs we've ever seen in this type of movie
   [b]D.[/b] All of the above
   
   18-year-old Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) was raised in the slums of Mumbai, India, and now works at a telephone company's call center, not as an actual phone operator, but as a [i]chaiwalla[/i] (tea server).  So, when he becomes a contestant on India's version of the popular game show [i]Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? [/i]no one expects him to do well at all.  He manages to answer the penultimate question correctly for 10 million rupees, and time runs out before he can be asked the final question for 20 million rupees, so he'll have to come back the following day for the next episode.  As soon as he leaves the set, police take him away to interrogate him, believing he must have cheated his way through the questions.  This marks the start of the narration of Jamal's story, which gradually reveals how the answers to the specific questions he was asked were all things he came across at some point in his life as a slumdog.
   
   I'm sure it wasn't hard to figure it out, but the answer to the question was indeed [b]D.[/b] All of the above.  [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]is blessed with an energy-filled soundtrack that fits every scene very well and makes the scenes have a vibrancy that they'd lack if they didn't have such great music as their background.  Another noteworthy aspect here is that the awesome theme music for the show [i]Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?[/i] is used to great effect here, particularly during the final scenes that involve Jamal's participation on the show.  It's no coincidence that the filmmakers chose this particular TV show as a piece of the plot, as it makes it recognizable to everyone; while the film is about an underdog in India, the fact that he's trying to win the grand prize on a show like this one will make it easy for people around the world to root for him.  Speaking of that, rooting for Jamal turns out to be extremely easy to do, as Dev Patel is note-perfect.  He doesn't fall into the trap that most actors and actresses playing underdogs would fall into of overplaying the nervousness.  While on the "hot seat," he infuses a lot into what could've easily been dull blank stares if anyone else had been playing the role, and the random moments in which he says something funny to break the tension are great.
   
   One of the reservations some may have with [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]is something that I had figured would probably be a problem before I watched the film, while reading the synopsis; obviously, it's awfully convenient that Jamal happened to run into situations throughout his childhood in which the answer to a question he'd be asked years later on a game show was somehow exposed to him, and that he'd always manage to remember it.  However, I think this is forgivable because you just NEED that contrivance for the movie to be able to move forward.  Similarly, some may not like that the film has a standard-order happy ending, but that, too, is okay because, when it comes down to it, despite great things like the soundtrack and Patel's performance that elevate this movie above average fare, this still is a conventional underdog story, and there's no avoiding that.  However, there are certain flaws that can't exactly be overlooked.  While the predictable happy ending is to be expected, the film overplays the destiny card ("it is written") in order to justify said happy ending; it's fine to have destiny be an element that contributes to navigating the plot, but it's not fine to make an exaggerated amount of references to it, almost as if it were necessary to do so to explain why any other type of conclusion would be impossible.  Also, most of the flashback scenes depicting Jamal's childhood work pretty well, though some don't ring as true and aren't as engaging - basically, even though it's obviously the same character, I definitely cared more about older Jamal than about younger Jamal.  The romantic element of the plot is helped immensely by a resonant, sublime score (again, all of the music-related elements are perfect), yet the story itself isn't the most interesting on-screen romance we've ever seen; we root much more for Jamal to answer that final question correctly than we do for him and the girl he loves to stay together.
   
   All in all, though, there are plenty of things that make this far better than your standard rags-to-riches story.  The folks over at Awards Circuit are referring to [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] as the current front-runner in the Best Picture race, and while I admit that I disagree with that and could name several other films released this year that have been superior to it, it's hard to ignore what a wonderfully colorful and euphonious piece of cinema this is.  Oh, and if you go see it, do NOT stand up right when the movie has [i]seemingly[/i] ended and the screen fades to black, because the film's last scene is followed by an amazingly well-choreographed Bollywood dance sequence that you simply can't miss.  It's better than any musical number we've witnessed in film this year (and puts to shame the crap that tried to pass as dance sequences in [i]Mamma Mia![/i]), and it's a worthy conclusion to this delightful movie-watching experience.

[b]Danny Boyle[/b]'s [i][url="http://www.foxsearchlight.com/slumdogmillionaire/"]Slumdog Millionaire[/url]  [/i]is the critic's darling of 2008. [b]MadProfessah[/b] has been a  big fan of Boyle's previous films, especially [i][url="http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0289043/"]28 Days Later...[/url][/i]  and[url="http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0448134/"][i]Sunshine[/i][/url](see [url="http://buckmire.blogspot.com/2007/08/review-sunshine.html"]my  review[/url]) although the director is probably best known for [i][url="http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0117951/"]Trainspotting[/url][/i].  


 Boyle's lastest film is a heart-racing look at India from the viewpoint of  two children who are forced to survive on their own from a very young age. It  depicts heart-breaking poverty and a stunning disregard for human life in a  country with a population well over one billion. The plot device used is of a  [i]chai[/i] [i]walla [/i](a guy who serves chai tea to telephone help desk  operators) going on the Indian version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" not  to win the money, but to "win" the girl.

 

 The amazing life story of the guy (played by a winningly handsome  18-year-old [b]Dev Patel[/b]) is told in flashback starting from about  the age of 8 or so to about the moment in time in which the film  begins.
 

 Having been to Indian within the last two years, including visits to Mumbai  and Agra the two main cities depicted in the film, gave the film an extra  emotional impact for me. The beauty of the Taj Mahal can simply never be  over-estimated, although what gives the film it's real wallop is its incredible  pacing. It literally starts with a bang and never stops. Although it's told in  flahback, we're really never quite sure how (or if) our young protagonists are  going to escape the predicaments they are placed in.

 
 But at the heart of [i][url="http://www.foxsearchlight.com/slumdogmillionaire/"]Slumdog  Millionaire[/url][/i] is two love stories: one between Jamaal and Latika, as well  as between brothers, Jamaal and Salim. How these stories get resolved in Simon  Beaufoy's screenplay adaptation of Vikas Swarup's novel cobined with the  technical expertise of Boyle's direction along with the absolutely incredible  score featuring the music of M.I.A. among others catapults the film to the very  top of all cinematic releases in 2008.


 [b]OVERALL GRADE: A. 

ACTING: A-. 
IMAGERY: A+. 
PLOT: A.  
IMPACT: A[/b].

Not only is this a riveting true story, it is also a wonderfully constructed film. The idea of traveling into a person's past to explain how they know the answers to questions on a game show is a brilliant one. It has been said many times that it is easy when you know the answers and Slumdog Millionaire shows this in powerful reality. The fact that it is Who Wants To Be A Millionaire makes it a relateable story to anybody who watches it. Patel really provides some acting chops that take him past his TV acting credentials. This is a real underdog story, that shows how intelligence is all relative. The only distraction for me was the final question. I knew the answer so a lot of the tension was destroyed. This is a fine film that deserves the attention it is gathering.

Like the India that it so vividly depicts, Slumdog Millionaire is an old-fashioned, unabashed romanticist of a film that holds the earmarks of modern filmmaking at its finest. The film's base levels of love, place, and destiny are familiar, but their representations are so refreshingly executed that the film is taken to an entirely new level.

The life of our on screen everyman hero is a soaring reflection of life and its many colours, and Boyle's deliverance of the many themes witnessed from our young slumdog are balanced with the utmost care. We are always questioning intent, hoping for a moral high ground, and pondering the ideals of fate in a world where there are so many controlling forces seemingly out of our grasp. 

Slumdog Millionaire is a winner.

In the theatre, I asked out-loud: "Okay, when the hell did this suddenly turn into an 80's school romance movie for TWEENS?!"  Luckily, I was the only one in the theatre. I know this movie is already bordering on being overhyped so I hesitate to give it five stars and tell everyone how much I LOVED this movie.  However,  it is really so good I can't help but spread the word.  Slumdog Millionaire is an almost perfect combination of comedy, gritty realism and fanciful romance.  The movie is directed by Danny Boyle who is most well known for his movies Trainspotting and 28 Days Later.  I think Slumdog Millionaire is actually closer to his lesser know film, Millions.  Like Millions, what really makes this movie is the terrific acting done by all of the child actors.  Slumdog follows three kids, brothers Salim and Jamal as well as orphan Latika, through their lives on the streets of Mumbai.    The story is uniquely shown as a series of flashbacks told by Jamal who is being interrogated for cheating on the Hindi version of Who Wants to be a MIllionaire?  To prove he is not lying he must explain how he knew the answers to each question asked on the show. In an unusual career step, Danny Boyle (Trainspotting, 28 Days Later) helms this eclectic Anglo-Indian fusion, the fictional tale of Jamil Malik, an uneducated product of Mumbai's vast shanties. At the start of the story, Jamil is interrogated by police after improbably edging to the final question on India's "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" With his impoverished background, Jamil must naturally have cheated. He is forced to recount his troubled journey and the incredible coincidences that led him to answer correctly each time to this final point.

Boyle's genre-leaping tastes between films manifest in "Slumdog". I was reminded not unpleasantly of "City of God" as we stared down the barrel of brother Salim's Colt revolver. Yet, Jamil's unyielding pursuit of his childhood sweetheart Latika is the bread and butter of all romantic fairytales, especially in Bollywood. Include the mainstay quiz show "Millionaire" and you have a product that should jar and nauseate if not for Boyle's energetic and gripping direction. He successfully blends the more timeless sense of poverty in India with its newly blossoming economy and the criminal elements that inevitably accompany it.

The viciousness of Mumbai's underworld (especially with the horrific exploitation of children) constantly bubbles beneath, as does the constant battle to survive against adversity, serving as a strange mirror to Jamil's appearance on the well-known quiz show. A young Jamil is willing to escape a locked public lavatory by swimming through a mire of sewage to capture the autograph of his Bollywood hero. It is an effective allegory for the movie as a whole.

The best thing about "Slumdog" is the relentlessly good cinematography that brings grandiose Western film making to the Indian genre. One memorable shot sweeps from the teaming fissures of the claustrophobic Mumbai slums to a birds eye view of the corrugated tin roofs packed tightly together. Such shots paint the slums in such a convincing way to make Jamil's ascension all the more authentic and charming.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is easily one of the best films to come out this year. It is a rare marriage of style and content which would please both: those seeking pure entertainment and those seeking aesthetic satisfaction. Easily Danny Boyle's best work in a long time (if not ever), "Slumdog Millionaire" is a million different things wrapped into one. It is a story of survival against all odds. It shows the trials and tribulations of brothers. It is a gritty depiction of the poverty of India and particularly, the city of Mumbai. At the same time, it is a celebration of life and all things that are beautiful about it. Ultimately, at its core, it is a tale of undying and true love. You will laugh and cry; feel heartbreak and an adrenaline rush almost simultaneously and leave the theatre with a broad smile on your face. "Slumdog Millionaire" is not just another movie. It is an experience that is rare and refined.

The story is of Jamal, the slumdog who wins Rs. 20 million at the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?"  How did he do it? Did he cheat? Is he a genius? Or was it his destiny? In finding an answer to this question, we take a journey that starts in the slums of Mumbai ends at the CST station there. In the middle, we are shown a side of India rarely ever seen in mainstream international cinema. 

The film works at several levels. The backbone of the film is the script of Simon Beaufouy which actually is a vast improvement of Vikas Swarup's disappointing novel. It is solid, effective and weaves a complex narrative almost effortlessly without making it too taxing on the viewer. He compensates for the far-fetched nature of the story by providing extremely interesting and wholesome characters. Danny Boyle, the director, takes over from there and tells the story with such passion and panache that one is left speechless. 

Technically, Slumdog Millionaire would satisfy even the harshest of critics. The cinematography is breathtaking and the impact of a number of sequences is heightened considerable because of the powerful visuals that are served up with it. It is slick and superb. The city of Mumbai where the principle photography has taken place is captured beautifully on celluloid! Danny Boyle always knew how to do this as can be seen in movies like Tainspotting and Sunshine. However, the visuals are used well to supplement the script and story rather than substitute it. An example of the same is the scene in the brothel. Next in line is the background score of A.R. Rahman that is racy, innovative and the complimentary to the tone of the movie throughout. 

Last, but not least are the performances. Dev Patel is a revelation. At 18, he delivers a knockout performance as Jamal and displays an potential to grow greatly in skill and stature given the right roles. Anil Kapoor, Irrfan Khan and Saurabh Shukla are also well cast in their respective roles. Freida Pinto has little to do but still leaves an impact. However, the true stars of the film are its child actors, Ayush, Azharuddin (young Javed and Salim), Tanay (also seen in Taare Zameen Par) and Ashutosh (middle Javed and Salim) who capture the transition of the characters' transition to a position of innocence and ignorance to one of street smart survivors  with a rare maturity. Their sequences often reminded my of Fernando Mereilles' City of God where similar such sequences and performances were seen by child actors. 

Overall, "Slumdog Millionaire" is superlative in almost every category. Come awards time, here is one movie which should emerge as a dark horse. This is a movie to be owned and honoured with multiple viewings! Super Solid Recommendation!

But the authorities assume he is cheating somehow and ask him how he knew the answer to each question. He tells them and in doing so, we see life in India through his eyes. 

We learn he was a poor kid from Mumbai who grows up an orphan after his mother is killed in ethnic-based attacks. He and his brother figure out ways to earn money giving unauthorized tours at the Taj Mahal,  peddling fruits on a train or just plain pickpocketing.

There is a Forrest Gump quality to this movie, although that is not quite accurate. There is a rags-to-riches theme, but that is not quite accurate either. I suppose it is mostly a love story showing the lengths someone will go to for the one he loves.

So I'd heard the rave reviews, I'd heard so many 
people saying they loved it. I've heard all the hype and 
I've seen some of the trailers. So of course I say to 
myself: what is all this about? I finally watch it today 
and I am somewhat, satisfied. Does this film amount to 
all the hype and adoration? Hell no. Is it still more than 
watchable? Yes, indeed it is. [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is an 
inspiriational tale, and although it occasionally lags it is 
egged on by the silently charismatic lead of the newbie 
Dev Patel that has you rooting for him the whole time.
 
What really got me interested in this movie was the 
premise. Young Jamal Malik plays on the Indian version of 
[i]Who Wants to be a Millionaire [/i]to gain riches and to catch 
the attention of his long lost lover. That just tickled my 
fancy, something that sounded so...unconventional. But 
when the premise is fresh and interesting the movie normally 
goes up in flames. Fortunately, not so for the [i]Slumdog[/i].
 
Well, it starts off very slowly. The plot lagged slightly, 
having very few interesting scenes only being held up by Patel's 
quiet yet powerful portrayal of Jamal and the beautiful imagery 
of Indian slums. As the movie sped up, as does your interest. 
Jamal's quest for greatness begins to pick up, and as I said before, 
you're rooting for him the entire time. You [i]want [/i]him to succeed. 
This role will surely give Patel an opening, as a fan favourite at 
the very least, and maybe a few accolades (dare I say, an Oscar?).
 
[img]http://img2.timeinc.net/ew/dynamic/imgs/081204/slumdog-millionaire_l.jpg[/img]
[font=Arial Narrow][i]"And he gets the girl too, YIPEE!"[/i][/font]
 
 
The film successfully tackles the theme of destiny, 
represented in Jamals struggle to become something better 
than his "destined" street rat. This idea is so rooted into the 
plot that you'll stand up and cheer when he breaks away 
from that ideal. Whether it's winning money very unbefitting 
of a slumdog or getting the girl everyone said he couldn't have, 
the movie uplifts and inspires you to believe that anything is 
possible. That greatness can come from anywhere. However 
what it lacks to fully "knock you out" with this optimistic 
little ideal is intensity. The film is a bit too light on it's feet
for my tastes, making it unable to fully leave you content 
with it. However, it's nice to see a film step back from this 
dreariness which has taken over the industry. Everyone needs
a good heartwarmer every so often, and this movie is perfect 
for that.
 
So to give you a basic breakdown:
 
[b]Strong Points: Unique, interesting premise, held together[/b]
[b]by Dev Patel's solid lovable lead, excellent directing [/b]
[b]and pretty visuals.[/b]
 
[b]Weak Points: Slow starter, movie doesn't get interesting [/b]
[b]until about 30-40 minutes after it starts. Lacks the intensity [/b]
[b]that would let it live up to it's hype.[/b]
 
Yeah it doesn't live up to it's hype. And I'm still not quite so
sure why it's being as lauded as much as it is. However I 
understand why it's a crowd pleaser. The [i]Millionaire [/i]can 
swoon you out of your seat and have you leap for joy! 
Definetly one of the best feel good movies of the year, and 
if you need a break from all the other depressing films out 
there, [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]is more than perfect for you.

[font=Palatino Linotype][size=3]One of the things the cinema has to offer is its ability to transport viewers to the places they've never been to and make them believe in everything even if highly improbable. That's its unquestionable magic. Danny Boyle's latest movie [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] seems so ridiculous in its premise that you will laugh hard, well, until you actually see the movie. [/size][/font][size=3]
 
[/size][font=Palatino Linotype][size=3]For most of his life, Indian street kid ("slumdog") Jamal Malik has been running from persecution, from pain and from povery that was about to swallow him whole. While appearing on the Hindi version of [i]Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?,[/i] Jamal is arrested by the police and charged with cheating. He is only one question away from the victory. After a quite brutal interrogation, the cops discover some interesting facts about the boy. Born in the slums of Mumbai, he recalls his life proving that he knows the answer to every question asked. [/size][/font][size=3]
 
[/size][font=Palatino Linotype][size=3]As versatile as he has proven to be in the course of time, Boyle applies numerous tonal shifts and experiments with approach. The first scenes are the funniest presenting a bunch of endearing child actors. Then, the movie gets dramatic showing the crime world in India. Some images even bring the close resemblance to Meirelles' masterwork [i]City of God[/i]. Furthermore, the movie transforms into personal story dealing with struggle for dignity and self-reliance. Lastly, the romantic aspect of the story becomes central. Boyle never stumbles making practically every scene (including narratively contrived romance) as magnetic and vivid as possible. It goes so far that the movie can be best described as a kinetic masterpiece abounding with energy that overwhelms, but more frequently stirs our imagination. [/size][/font][size=3]
 
[/size][font=Palatino Linotype][size=3]By dividing the story into pieces, Simon Beaufoy in his script examines the whole post-colonial India from overpopulated slums to the wealthy using slave-like labor. He slickly uses one very shrewd plot contrivance to present Jamal's life through flashbacks providing some exciting twists and moments of nail-biting tension superbly directed by Boyle. Besides, the movie is surprisingly coherent and its cast mostly comprised of newcomers occurs to be natural and always convincing. Especially, Dev Patel gives a breakthrough performance.[/size][/font][size=3]
 
[/size][font=Palatino Linotype][size=3]Overall, thanks to Boyle's genius, [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is undeniably great and multi-referential. From this moment, Indian cinema ceases to be one-note and uninteresting. It's time for the whole multicultural world to accept this foreign culture as it is. [b]10[/b]/10 ([b]A[/b])[/size][/font]

Director:Danny Boyle Released: 2008 Stars : Dev Patel, Irfan Khan, Anil Kapoor Genre: Drama/Romance Country: UK The story of the life of an impoverished Indian teen Jamal Malik, who becomes a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?", wins, and is then suspected of cheating. Slumdog Millionire has been heavily praised by critics both here in the UK and in the United States. Mainly due to its unique storyline and beautiful cinematography. Also heavily regarded as one of the best films of 2008. I really have to agree with that and more. Slumdog Millionire suprised me in many ways and is close to as perfect film as you can get. Director Danny Boyle, whose films I must confess I have not seen a lot of, has been heavily underated both here and around the world. Recently Oscar nominated for his superb direction, I'm 80% sure he'll take home the oscar. The direction in this film is just wonderful to see. Shots that aren't often seen in many American films and ones which really add to the setting of India and give us as an audience a real taste of life in the "slums". What I loved about the opening sequence, or about 50 minutes into the film was that beautiful sequence where the two Brothers are chased by the Police. Added with briliant cinematography and a wonderful soundtrack it was just stunning to watch. Slumdog Millionire, as I have just mentioned contains some absoulty stunning cinetography, and rightly socar nominated. It's just wonderful to watch a film that really gives us an insight into a world most western people just don't think about or know enough about. The shots of the town, Salim and Jamal lives in added with a touch of great lighting just looked great on the screen. Slumdog Millionire is definatly not as "feel good" as the film poster makes out. It contains a few gritty scenes, that you will see when you watch them. You don't expect it when you walk in as it has not been advertised that way. In a way that adds to your overall view of the film and perhaps that's why I enjoyed it. Again this is due to the social context within the film. Like I said before, you just don't expect that to happen and a few times in the film, you wonder is that what life is like over there? Well it certainly is. The realtionship between Jamal and Salim is a very close one throught the film. Althought there is some question as to what exactly does Salim get into. Both brothers are left orphans at a young age, and Boyle depicts to us as the audience that many children are like Jamal and Salim. This is evident in the many photos and shots of children in the slums, most of them are orphans and are working for themselves. There is also a little use of documentry like filming in this film, which really does work. The film tells 2 different stories; one- the story of jamal and the other Jamal and Latika. It's for the rags to riches sotry but also a sublot of romance. What was so engaging is that for many years Jamal was searching for Latika and didn't give up. Most likely a moral message delivered by Danny Boyle. Acting in this film was done by mainly unknown actors. I think 2 BAFTA nominations for the acting came. It's brilliant to see Dev Patel, known to UK audiences in Skins, suddenly become a huge star around the world. Played the part of Jamal so well and unexpecdily for me as I didn't think someone from Skins could produce such a great performance. Would love to see what he does in the future. Overall, Slumdog Milionire is every bit as good as everyone says it as and more. Close to a perfect film for me and one of the best film of 2008. Highly Recomended 9/10

This is more than just a take on a popular TV show, this is a love story in India... and all throughout we see the things which make up India, whether it be good or bad, black or white and any other divergenece of opinions, values, ethics, morality and life.  It can be bright, dark, spoltess white or shit-dirty brown... amazingly contrasted and alive with constant energy and backed up by great cinematography and a choice soundtrack. 

Having personally experienced India rom top to bottom, I was engaged and recognised most of the issues shown in the movie, and at times felt down that knowing the begging, the crime and the corruption shown is true... this is as close as it get to showing a real life account of what happens to the underprivleged, especially children. 

Then on the flip side, we have a few funny moments like the call centre gags (no wonder noone is at the other end of the line when the India vs Australia test is on) the idolisation of their movie stars to the point people would dive in their own shit (literally).

What Danny Boyle did here was create a love/life story surrounding Jamal Malik, an orphaned muslim from the slums of Mumbai, with his older brother Salim and the love of his life since childhood, Latika, and then, taking a popular quiz show as the format as the basis for building up the image of the life of a slumdog in India, where there is a vast bridge between culture, social status, religion and wealth.... and the fine line which connects surivial to crime. See the things which make "India" as a whole tick... the dystopic views of the poverty stricken to the wealth and the God-like status of its movie and sports stars, the blooming metropolis of Mumbai to the culutral icon and tourist spot of Agra, it is a contrast of colours, shades of grey, people... an entire nation. And really, one poor guy who so far in his young age has experienced and suffered more than anyone should, becomes an icon and a hero overnight to the massess, with criminals, corrupt executives and hardened police breathing down his neck, being betrayed by the only people he ever cared about, ridiculed and unnoticed, he becomes the man of the moment. and the fact that you can have the best education in the world and it will not mean anything to a person who grew up learning things the hard way... intelligence, will and determination is what makes a man, gives him character and what makes a real hero. 

And all this for what?? 

A woman. Love. As the story's ultimate tag line is, "It is destiny." And his destiny was foretold that day he met his girl.

Let me confirm that all the wonderful things you're hearing about this movie are true.  As I have said several times in my reviews, it is impressive when a movie can live up to high expectations, but a film that exceeds the highest expectations is a rarity and always earns my respect.  Slumdog Millionaire is one of those films.
 
At its heart, Slumdog is a love story.  Jamal Malik, played with heart wrenching aplomb by Dev Patel, is an Indian teen who appears on the Hindi version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire.  Jamal is not seeking riches in the form of Rupees, though, but in the form of reconnecting with a lost love that he knows is a fan of the show.  Through a series of flashbacks spurned by the questions Jamal faces on the show, we learn of his impoverished past and how he got to the 'hot seat' on Millionaire.
 
Slumdog is a truly original and moving film.  If you have had reservations about seeing it because you weren't buying the hype or even because of the name (this is actually the reason I have heard most for people's lack of interest in the film), I implore you to move past those things and just see the film.  It will speak for itself.

 "Slumdog Millionaire" -- An Excellent Movie 
Category: Movies, TV, Celebrities 

With all the good press, there is not much to add about this film, so briefly I will add that this movie is about two brothers and a homeless girl who grow up in the slums of Mumbai, India.  An actor from London, Dev Patel, plays the main character (oldest rendition) in Slumdog Millionaire.  His love interest, played by a new actress named Freida Pinto (again, oldest rendition), had been a model and a TV show host in India.  Each of these characters are played by three different actors to represent their respective ages (youngest at about age 10, teen-agers at about age 16, and then oldest at about age 20).  The casting for these parts was extremely well done.  The portrait of the slums and growth of Mumbai over a decade is also worth noting, and the music score provided by A. R. Rahman provides an energetic beat for this fast-paced film.

http://www.foxsearchlight.com/slumdogmillionaire/

This movie is done mostly (90%) in English, with sub-titles as needed, and it is rated "R" for violence. Salaam Bombay, like Slumdog Millionaire, used untrained actors in many of the key parts.  I recommend all three of these films.

"Slumdog Millionaire" revolves around a Hindi version of America's "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" and the contestant is Jamal Malik.  Your immediately put in the hot seat with Jamal one question away from winning 20 million rupees, but how did he manage to get this far?

Jamal is accused of cheating on the show and is immediately interrogated by the police with gruesome force.  The authorities think Jamal is cheating his way through the show.  Jamal pleads that he is not guilty and claims he has a legitimate explanation for each of his answers.  For which he does have a liable explanation, he experienced the answers.

For each question Jamal has the answer, and let alone a personal experience.  Each experience takes place in a flash back filled with brilliant cinematography.  In which he grew up in Mumbai, India.  The environment in which Jamal, his brother Salim, and their friend Latika grew up in reminds me of "City Of God".  In the slums surviving on little in which they had.  Jamal progresses to that second to last question through the film, but you know he answers each question right.  Even with that loss of the element of suprise you can't help to be so closely on the edge of your seat just waiting to hear if he is correct or not.

The story revolves around Jamal, Salim, and Latika in relation to the questions Jamal is answering on the show.  The best comparison for the story is yet again "City Of God".  Which best relates to sibling rivalry and yet the unatainable love.  The further Jamal gets in the questions the older he gets in the flashback in relation to the answers.  Leading up until that final question.  Which you will have to see the result for yourself.  Just from my personal experience, I was about to uproot the chair I was sitting in the theater.

Final Sumation (pardon my gradualreport reference),  "Slumdog Millionaire" has an amazing enagaging story with characters you yourself get involoved with their lives, and will remember them when you walk out of the theater.  You will feel the extreme tension as Jamal answers that 20 million rupee question, and hopefully you won't destroy the chair your sitting in with his results.

Danny Boyle has really outdone himself here, with a remarkable story about the turbulent and fascinating life of an orphaned Indian teen, Jamal Malik, who becomes a successful contestant of the Hindi version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire, during which he is detained for suspicion of cheating. As far as the plot goes, it's very much a mixed bag of emotions, as it's both sad and fun at the same time. There's a nice touch of humor to it in some scenes, while tragedy looms in the background, as you're exposed to the harsh reality of life in the slums. Kind of like the movie City of God, only not as melancholic in its overall tone, and a little less violent. A shame though that the rest of Doyle's films aren't as good, because with movies like Sunshine and 28 Days Later on his merit, I still can't think of him as anything more then a hit-and-miss director. I'm just happy that this one didn't suffer his tendency to make lackluster conclusions. In fact, in spite of my fears, the ending here was very satisfying and furfilling. So maybe there's some truth to that old saying, that every dog has its day...or in this case, slumdog ;-)

He is held by police on the assumption that he is somehow cheating, and only by explaining the coincidences in his life that lead to his knowing the answers can he hope to escape.  Despite the sad nature of this boy's life, the movie plays out as a fairytale, so much so in fact, the subtitles appear onscreen as if they were written on the pages of a children's book.  The first half of the movie focuses on Jamal's flashbacks to his childhood, and his life with his brother, Salim.  The last half of the movie isn't quite as gripping as the first and seems a bit more cliched, but then, as I said, this IS a fairytale (so of course the three street children grow up to look like models).  Jamal is the Knight in Shining Armor, his older brother is the wayward son, and the female lead, Latika, is the damsel in distress (she's almost a literal fairytale princess held captive by a wicked king whom she's been forced to marry).  It's the wayward older brother whose story is least compelling, as he moves from street-smart urchin to wanna-be hiphop gangsta, his character enters very wornout/cliched territory (if ever a movie injected unwanted cool "style" points into it's character, this would be it).  But it's a minor quibble.  It's the pre-teen kids who steal the movie.  Flashbacks show a childhood that is simultaneously horrifying and exhilarating: death and danger lurk around every corner, but the vibrant city street life leaps forth in a celebration of life.  It's a story of the lowest rung on the bottom of society's ladder.  A story of children who must literally steal or die, children with no future and no place to turn for help.  That it's both heart-breaking and uplifting is a testament to the filmmaker.  Even if the 3rd act pushes a little too forcibly towards that fairytale ending, it's still an unforgettable journey.

Based on his previous work, you may have thought of Danny Boyle as an artist grounded by the simple acknowledgement of life's inherent darkness. Like me, you would have misread him. In this romantic fairytale, he discloses that he's never been interested in the darker side of things, except so long as they illuminate the brighter by contrast. This is all the more disappointing for its profligacy: he squanders brilliant child actors, gorgeous cinematography, and shattering social revelations in the service of a lame flashback-driven plot about destined lovers, ultimately undoing all of the expose-style work he began.

The film opens with a Guantanamo-sytle interrogation scene (it's disconcerting that we're becoming accustomed to these) of a skinny boy by a fat man and uniformed officer Irrfan Khan. Twenty minutes later, the same officer is serving the boy chai and listening to him spin a reticent yarn: the introduction to flashback scenes that explain how such a boy (an uneducated orphan of the slums who, now in his early 20s, makes his living serving chai at a mobile phone call center) could win Rs. 20,000,000 on a quiz show; mystically, each question related to a dramaticâusually traumaticâexperience from his childhood and adolescence.

These flashbacks allow cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle, working in perfect concert with a team of astonishing child actors, to reveal the sordid slums of Mumbaiâa cross between a Hooverville and a trash heapâas little more than the children's playground: a playground where marauding terrorists light your home on fire and kill your mother, a playground where you are lured by a frosty Coca-Cola into the arms of a Dickensian villain who will burn your eyes out with hot oil (blind singers, and otherwise damaged beggars, earn more than the bodily able), and a playground where the girl you've befriended will be groomed carefully for the whorehouse. This is enough to make a movie; Americans don't like to see things like this happening, and when art shows it to them in a meaningful way, they do something about it.

They won't do anything about it, though, because halfway into the film, Boyle derails and decides to develop a romantic relationship between groomed-to-be-a-whore Latika and about-to-be-millionaire Jamal. When they finally kiss at the end (for the very first time), they are in their early twenties, and have spent a total of less than five hours together as adults. And yet, we expect them to live happily ever after, because "it is written." Audiences are so excited that Jamal has not only become a millionaire, but has also won the girl, they have forgotten all about the real orphans in India who do live on trash heaps (I know; I saw them) and who won't become millionaires or fall in love with a partner marked from before time. Worse, by giving his protagonist the two-for-one special, Boyle does not address the ugly reality that, had Jamal not won mad rupees, Latika (who is living with an abusive gangster twice her age when Jamal comes into his wealth) would not have run away with him.

This is a story set in the slums of Mumbai, about two orphaned brothers who grow up on the streets. Like "City of God" (set in the slums of Rio De Janeiro), one of the boys is good (Jamal) and one is bad (Salim). They both love the same woman (Latika). Each brother watches out for each other as they grow up, but it's clear that Salim is a ruthlessly violent character. This is an excellent movie. While it is clearly an Indian cast and setting, the language is English. It's a very clever fusion of Hollywood & Bollywood. The cinematography was stunning, the music was great, the characters very engaging, the plot was excellent, with an ending that tied up everything beautifully. The acting is sublime. The child actors perform naturally and are outstanding, particularly those who play the youngest versions of Jamal, Salim and Latika. Dev Patel is brilliant and confident and holds his own against the more experienced actors. The same goes for Freida Pinto. It's hard to define 'Slumdog Millionaire'. Is it a rags to riches story? Perhaps, but becoming rich was never the protagonist's goal. Is it a story of survival? Yes. A Story of love? Yes, the search of a lost love. A Comedy? Yes. Intense drama? Yes. Thriller? Yes...but forget about finding the answer to such questions because 'Slumdog Millionaire' is much more than one could describe in a paragraph. Watch for yourself and see. Many seem to label it as this year's 'Juno' (though I personally find 'Juno' overrated) and compare it to other great examples of cinema. However, I found it to be very much its own film.

I am in essence a fairly pessimistic person. A piece of literature, a song, or a film that can instill in me hope is a rare thing. Slumdog Millionaire is one of these rare masterpieces that is an intimate and personal film experience for me. Luck and fate have recently been on my mind a lot and are all prominent themes of this film. It's true that we can affect our destiny through our decisions and actions but there is always that mysterious element that determines the final conclusion. Danny Boyle's opus explores this idea. Almost everything about Slumdog Millionaire works. Great casting highlighted by the film's lead role portrayed with skill by British actor Dev Patel (Skins). A powerful screenplay that moved me to a full array of emotions. Slumdog is tragic, humorous, exciting and refreshing and cannot be likened to any other film. Slumdog is a truly unique film from it's historical relevance that may be something new to audiences to it's philosophical ideas. One of the years best soundtracks featuring M.I.A. and composer A.R. Rahman has already earned the film a Golden Globe nomination. When director Danny Boyle's film Trainspotting was first released it was quickly acclaimed but I never understood the hype. As Boyle's body of work expanded over the years two of his films; 28 Days Later and Millions, both impressed me with their originality. With Slumdog Millionaire I am now convinced that Boyle is one of Britian's finest directors. Perhaps upon detailed dissection one may find some minor flaws but the film's ultimate theme proves to be the solution to all of these qualms. I cannot describe to what extent I recommend this film and it's hopeful vision. See it and be sure to catch the Bollywood style musical number during the film's end credits.

Danny Boyle has directed better movies (I'm thinking of "Millions"), and he has certainly directed from better scripts (I'm still thinking of "Millions"), but it's rare to see such a fantastically great movie made out of such a mediocre script. There are a lot of problems with "Slumdog Millionaire" (some sloppy, and even silly, structuring, a lack of focus, some regrettable lines of dialogue, and a sort of immature and contradictory and sensational moralizing) but this is glorious, soaring, enthralling cinema, a fusion of Indian gangster picture on amphetamine, music video (including that awesome Bollywood dance number during the credits), game show, and old-fashioned celebration of true love. It's crazy, it's messy, and it's sappy, but it's one of the most exciting, refreshing, and genuinely innovative movies I've seen in quite some time. Not everything works, by any means, but it is a labor of love, a movie about love made with love, and I love it. Go Team Boyle.

Slumdog Millionaire is just what people need in this economy, an old-fashioned rags-to-riches tale of a "po' boy done good." It's effective, and the audience I was with cheered at film's end. So why was I unable to completely surrender to this picture the way some people have? Is it the one-contrivance-too-many nature of the script? Is it the film's occasional inability to keep tone? Or is it the nasty aftertaste this film left in my mouth thanks to Danny Boyle reveling in the misfortune of his characters, treating them like one of us one minute, and like distant Others the next? Despite the bang up editing job, the film's parts are better than the sum of them. As the time goes one it becomes clear that Jamal loves Latika but something always seems to get in the way of their being together. You will leave the movie feeling uplifted, and yet the reality of the sadness that is the daily lives of all these masses of people of the slums still knaws at you.

Can an uneducated orphan from the Mumbai slums really win "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" without cheating? Despite most of us not really caring about such a question, Slumdog Millionaire is a movie that answers this question. And there's lost love. Oh, lost love.
The story line is set up within minutes into the movie: after winning 10 million rupees on Millionaire, the protagonist, Jamal, is accused of cheating. But audience need not get wrapped up in the possibility of inappropriate conduct. Our little exposure to Jamal has already shown him to be uncomplicated: earnest, honest. We can now sit back and watch the flashback scenes of Jamal's troubled life - events which correspond remarkably with the questions he answered correctly on the game show.
We begin with Jamal at age five, fighting to survive a hard life of poverty in the slums of Mumbai. He relies on his brother, Salim, having lost their mother in an anti-Muslim attack on their neighbourhood. The boys are wonderfully resourceful, scrappy, and brave. Watching their escapades, filmed beautifully in crowded streets and dark corners, are the high point of this film. They are soon joined by a third "musketeer" (as they call themselves), Lakita, a little girl also similarly orphaned in the attack.
Despite the innocence of youth, Jamal's love for Lakita is true. After a tragic separation, he returns to Mumbai years later (they're both about 12 at this point), manages to find her and save her from unfortunate circumstances. But Jamal is soon betrayed by his brother, and he and Lakita are separated once again. We are then brought to the present tense, where they meet once again and Lakita rejects Jamal's love by refusing to run away with him.
Lakita has changed over the years. Most notably, her skin has gotten much whiter. And with that loss of melanin, she seems to have lost her power.No longer a tenacious little survivor, the adult version is passive and quite helpless.
Despite the rejection, Jamal persists (why give up now?) and enters as a contestant on Millionaire to prove his love--he knows that Lakita is a fan of the show. Maybe because he is not corrupted by greed, all of the trivia questions line up with events in his tragic life. But  rather than make him more lovable, his one-tracked effort only makes him seem simple. He gets the girl in the end. We knew he would. But the romance is not exactly... romantic. 
Finally, the closing credits are accompanied by a bollywood-style dance number that looked suspiciously like a Janet Jackson video circa Rhythm Nation. Was this supposed to be an ironic commentary on Indian film? A parody of the real stuff that I occasionally catch on TV on Sunday afternoons? I didn't get it.
