How odd.  I went to a movie about the church entitled [url="http://www.crimecritics.com/2008/12/doubt-2008-movie-review/"]Doubt[/url] and had my atheism confirmed.  The next day I checked out a film about a gameshow and had a religious experience.  My lines of communication with the gods must be crossed. [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is without a doubt the best film of 2008.  Danny Boyle is proving to be the rare talent that can make a film in any genre, with any cast, and hit a home run.  [i]Trainspotting[/i], [i]28 Days Later[/i], [i]Sunshine[/i], and now [i]Slumdog[/i] create a run as incredible for its diversity as for its excellence.  Of these, [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] stands out as a timeless piece of cultural art and not just as another of his above-average films.

 The India in [i]Slumdog [/i]is the same gritty one found in Aravind Adigas [i]White Tiger [/i]([url="http://www.crimecritics.com/2008/12/the-white-tiger-by-aravind-adiga/"]our review[/url]).  Orbiting the impoverished side of Indian life, it is a depressing view of the transitional stage that developing countries seem to suffer on their way to increased affluence.  Poverty is painful enough, but extra dismal when highrise buildings are popping up on the horizon and the occasional shiny car makes its way into the slums.  In this India of class envy and economic disparity, the American gameshow Who Wants to be a Millionaire is an oasis of hope.  A cultural phenomenon for those who are lacking.  A way out.

 Most of the movie takes place during a police interrogation of Jamal Malik, one of the Indian slumdogs lucky enough to get a chance to break free.  After an unprecedented run on the gameshow, a suspicious producer turns Jamal over to the police, who are trying to figure out how an ignorant street urchin has the breadth of knowledge to do what doctors and lawyers have not.

 The flashbacks are used to explain Jamals answers, but this crazy conceits real goal is to tell an amazing love story.  And this is what Slumdog is really about: Love and Ethics.  The ethical tale is told through the bond that Jamal has with his older, morally-challenged brother, Salim.  The love story revolves around another orphaned street urchin, the sweet and lovely Latika.  Both bonds are tested, broken, mended and broken again.  The flashbacks allow Boyle to cover many years and stages of their lives, developing a bond with the audience that is simply heartbreaking.

 Oddly enough, I thoroughly enjoyed the religious aspects of [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i].  There is a line at the end of the film, God is Great, that really hit my atheistic heart.  It didnt make me believe in a god, but it was one of the rare descriptions of a deity that made me, even for a brief moment, WISH that I did.  The god in [i]Slumdog[/i]s India is a god I can applaud, which is why I contrast this film with the movie [i]Doubt[/i].  I realized, as soon as the line was uttered, that Great didnt mean big, or better-than-good, it meant something that combines and exceeds these terms.  The god of Slumdog is beyond our ken.  Larger than our understanding.  This god has a plan for us all, and Slumdog gives us enough of a glimpse to see that it is just.

 The phrase It is Written is used constantly in the film as an expression of divine fate.  Normally I wretch at the concept of predestination, but again, Boyles brilliance is to suck me into his world so completely that I embrace normally distasteful concepts.  It is Written is made a beautiful slogan.  A reminder that, while the characters had free will and controlled their actions, all of these events were laid down before time and had to have transpired just as they did.  Not because a god deemed it, but because god created a fair mechanism that was always going to reward the moral man and punish the wicked.  In a rollercoaster ride of abject misery, I felt the comforting presence of the lapguard of faith that the religious hold so dear.  The result was a greater understanding of the addictive nature of this constant reassurance.  It isnt something that I want or need, but I can see that a miserable enough life would provide quite the demand.

 A third lesson, equally powerful, is that love is more important than money.  It is a trite cliche, but done so well in [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] that you believe it.  At the end of the film the viewer will feel the same apathy towards the 20 million rupees that Jamal does.  The only thing that matters is that he and Latika are together.  I could not help but think of my wife, and our simple, perfect existence, and weep during the closing scenes.  It felt like a movie that was made for my personal edification, and I enjoyed it immensely.  It made me think.  It made me feel.  It forced empathy on me for foreign circumstances.  I loved every single second of it.

 I urge everyone to find this movie and watch it.  It merits our attention and I look forward to discussing it further.  The perfect rating is easily earned.

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is a perfectly paced, loving, beautiful, stirring masterpiece, Danny Boyle has crafted a work of art for the screen and I am blessed to have seen it. The film is about a man who goes on India's Who wants to be a Millionaire and is arrested because it is believed he is cheating because there is no way an assistant at a telemarketing company that grew up in a Muslim slum could ever know these answers. Well it turns out his life on the streets has brought him the answers to the questions proving it was written. Boyle creates a film filled with brilliant camera shots and some of the most beautiful visuals of the year, it is amazing how the two most beautiful films I have seen this year have involved a lot of trash (WALL-E being the other). The story is fascinating and even though I knew what was going to happen at the end (because I knew the answer to the last question) but I was still cutting off circulation to my friends hand (and she was doing the same to mine). The movie just grabbed me and never let go, this is a movie comprised of individual parts that are brilliant and amazing and they actually add up to something of value and importance, it is truly something to behold.
So what of those parts, the score is breathtaking, and what happens before the end credits is truly awesome, the cinematography is also breathtaking, the images that are presented are something to be behold. The acting is wonderful and completely believable, and with a story like this the acting has to be believable or it loses all of its power over the audience. The script is the reason it grabs you, using just enough Hindi that it seems real but not enough to distract from the images the Boyle presents.
This is and WALL-E are the closest this year has come to having a perfect film, everything works so perfectly that even if you do not like the movie you have to sit back in awe at what is happening on screen. I have applaud three times this year, WALL-E because it was emotionally gripping and brilliant, Milk because it spoke to me a personal level, and now Slumdog because I see the work and I see the brilliance and I felt the power it has.

OK, I've changed my vote for Best Picture of 2008. "Slumdog Millionaire" wins hands-down. This triumph in storytelling is an exotic mix of brutal reality and heartwarming romance set in modern India. It is the story of Jamal (Dev Patel), a boy raised in the slums of Mumbai amid religious violence, child exploitation and cruel poverty. Orphaned and with little schooling, Jamal and his brother, Salim (Madhur Mittal), eke out an existence by begging in the streets, riding on top of trains and giving bogus tours of the Taj Mahal to clueless tourists. Amid this chaos, Jamal learns a few seemingly trivial things about his world---from who starred in India's biggest movies to who is pictured on an American $100 bill. These facts come in handy when Jamal, at age 20, ends up as an unlikely contestant on India's version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." He competes not to become rich but to find Latika (Freida Pinto), the girl he has loved since he was a boy. Through flashbacks, we learn how this kid at the bottom of society learned the answers (was it just coincidence?) to a game that changes his life forever. The film is not always fun to watch (it's rated R for some disturbing violence) but the moving climax will have you cheering. "Slumdog Millionaire" offers an accurate picture of a changing India---and it will move your heart with compassion for exploited children everywhere.

The genre known as "Indie" has become a favorite of mine. I was "head over heels" for Little Miss Sunshine, Juno was absolutely adorable with its quirky one-liners and top notch acting by Ellen Page, MIcheal Cera, and Jennifer Garner. The "Indie" has swept me away again, and this time it comes from Transpoiting director Danny Boyle.
  I had the privelege of seeing an adavnced screening of the best film of the year, Slumdog Millionaire. Slumdog Millionaire  is the most impressive, clever, and sharp pieces of filmmaking in the last decade. It tells the fictional story of Jamal Malik, an Indian boy born in the rough slums of Mumbai who gets the opportunity of his lifetime by "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" in India. 
As he prepares to answer the 20 million dollar rupee question; Danny Boyle quickly flashbacks to show Jamal getting interrogated and abused by two men who are convinced he has cheated his way to the top. Little do they know; his answers lie within his past. Jamal is played by the onscreen gem Dev Patel, and he is an interesting character study. As he begins to tell the evil men his past, we discover hardships, triumphs, and an array of chracters who add that extra zing to the film. Jamal and his brother were often attacked by Muslim attackers when they were young, and during one fatal attack he witnessed the death of his mother. He and his brother Salim were together through thick and thin after their loss, and they had to come up with ways to find shelter, food, and money. Their relationship becomes tested when Jamal meets the beautiful Matika. He and Matika share moments that are sincere and honest, for instance when they talk to each other about their future goals, their loss of their mother, laugh about random jokes, and their future together. However, like the classic films Casablanca, and Titanic there is always an obstacle standing in the way. In Jamal's case "obstacles"; During one night at a supposed harmless camp, Jamal and Salim find themselves in a unprecedented situation involving Muslim attackers. They want to cut open an eye, and put hot oil in their sockets, and after Salim quickly learns he uses his insight to trick the Muslim attacker, and he and his brother are off to the races. As they approach the train we see Salim's true colors, as the young Matika runs behind them and catches up,  slightly brushes against Salim's fingertips, and he pulls away without Jamal ever knowing. After Matika is out of the picture, Danny Boyle displays an exotic montage of the two brothers finding money, shelter, and food leading up to them finally getting caught, and then it ends; it is simply brilliant. Jamal may be unaware of what happened that night, but he still keeps focus, and tries to find her. His journey should become easier right? Afraid not, because during Salim's ways of finding money he becomes involved in some risky territory involving prostitution rings, gun toting, and drug kingpins. With his power he neglects Jamal's pleas for help of finding Matika by threatening him, and adding Matika in his web of madness. We truly feel sympathetic for Jamal after his hardships, and hope he finds the beautiful Matika. He then tells how he got the opportunity of a lifetime, when he sees Matika at one of the drug kingpins house he sees "Who wants to be a Millionaire" playing on the TV, and after she tells him "Jamal, I'm sorry but it will never work out, It's not meant to be". He says "If you ever change your mind "I'll always be waiting for you at the 5:00 train". Truly a heartbreaking moment in the film that "tugs at your emotions", and if you don't feel any sympathy "You're just cruel". He goes on "Who wants to be a Millionaire", and wants to win the money to leave his dead end job, and build a strong foundation with he and Matika. After the interrogation ends, they let him finish his feat, and answer the 20 million dollar rupee question. His past led him to the answers, but will his future lead him to Matika(*no spoilers here), Will Salim change his wicked ways; these answers lie within you paying 9.25 to see the best film of 2008. The casting is simply remarkable despite its lack of American actors, because they all shine as impressively as any other cast I've seen this year. Dav Petal should receive the young actor award at the Critics Choice Awards indefinitely, because he had a heart of acting full of sincerity, honesty, inspiration, and dynamics. Danny Boyle may be a unfamilar director, but after this film he is sure to be remembered. The tracking on the train is simply irresistible, he was able to capture so much activity as Jamal and Salim jumped from one train to the next on their journey as "young bucks". I truly felt as if I was I right in the mix of things. The way Boyle shifts from past and present works wonders, because never once is it jerky and unbalanced, it is organized and looks sharp on the screen. He is sure to get a nomination come Oscar time. The cinematography can't be silent, because every shot of Mumbai is elegant wheter it be the rough slums, or the newly designed parts of Mumbai when Jamal is older. I always feel as if I'm walking by the Taj-Mahal, the prostitution ring to find Matika, and the home of the drug lord holding Matika captive. The film is always entertaining, I never wanted to leave, the sharp storytelling kept me interested and alert. Not to often do I mention a soundtrack in a review, but WOW the music always related to each transition in Jamal's life, for instance the intense scene with Salim loading his gun to go do his daily work; the song that plays during this is called "Liquid Dance", and it is perfect for the situation. Not to mention, the very popular American version of Paper Planes during a montage of Jamal and Salim fending for themselves until they reach their teen years; heck they even have a hindu version. Even the end of the film despite everything Jamal went through A.R Harman's "Jai-Ho" is upbeat, and fresh and keeps the audience laughing and smiling as they watch the actors dance during the credits. I love this film, and with a year that was average compared to last year; this is trhe best film of 2008 HANDS DOWN. Every year there is a film that captivates, impresses, entertains, and satisfies you more than the rest; and this year my friend that film is "Slumdog Millionaire".

This is the best movie of the year. Slumdog was a clear and unambiguous cut above everything else in what I consider to be a good year for movies. How do I determine that it was a good year? I saw more movies that I loved or really liked this year as compared to any recent year (for example, Frost-Nixon, The Wrestler, Gran Torino, Rachel Getting Married, Milk, Let the Right One In, I've Loved You So Long, Happy-Go-Lucky, Dark Knight, and more).
 
At first I was put off by the pacing that I thought was a bit slow with the movie shifting from present to past. But patience paid off as I gradually got in synch with the pacing and structure of the film. And, it was a big payoff that provided me with an intimate view of an orphaned child's harrowing journey to meet his destiny. The nine actors that played the three key characters during childhood, preadolescence and young adulthood were excellent and believable. They were perfectly cast and played their parts wonderfully. 
 
Interestingly, when I saw the trailer weeks before, I thought that Slumdog was an Indian comedy about a poor kid who wins the game show I Want to Be a Millionaire. I immediately had an association to My Big Fat Greek Wedding. And, although I loved that movie, Slumdog is a sprawling epic compared to the hilarious sit-com-Greek-Wedding. Slumdog is much more than I expected. A young man, played flawlessly by Dev Patel, is trying his hand at the Indian version of the game show I Want to be a Millionaire. His motives are fuzzy at first. He is not a typical contestant. We learn that it was his destiny that brought him to compete. 
 
We discover how he came to know the answers to the questions (did he cheat?, is he a genius? or, did fate have a hand in his knowledge?). We learn about how close bonds and loyalty among three childhood friends are stretched to painful extremes over time despite dramatically different means that each must use to adapt to the cruel circumstances that they must overcome to survive. Slumdog is a hopeful movie, that underscores the value of resilience, and highlights the many faces and means of loyalty, against the overwhelming odds of poverty and evil; this movie deserves to be honored for its remarkable achievement.

This year's "Shawshank Redemption" - a fantasy that the filmmakers want us to treat as real; an exercise in wish fulfillment.  I guess that one should just accept the fact of the existence of such films; there are so many of them that, verily, they comprise their own genre.

Since I believe in a generic approach to fillmaking (no film is either beneath or above its genre, and films should be rated according to how good they are for their genre), the question becomes: how good is this film for the type of film it is?

Pretty good, but, as one critic noted, with apologies to John McEnroe, This is an interesting, inventively told, look at life in India, but Oscar-quality?  You cannot be serious."

The film offers a grab-bag of stylistic tricks, giving us just enough story to earn the label "weighty," just enough showpiece scenes in which genuine emotion flows to be called "powerful," and just enough visual elegance (i.e. the camera staying in place long enough for us to realize that the images of the film are not constantly calling attention to themselves) to be considered a "serious," "accomplished" film. 

Yet the coin (or rupee, as it were in this case) has a flip side: a little bit of everything can sometimes add up to a whole lot of less-than overwhelming effect.  The film certainly entertains and is well-acted.  But unfortunately, "Slumdog" wants to do more.  It wants to "tell" us something; ostensibly, that knowledge comes from having lived life (and that life is great, God is great, poverty is terrible - but glamorous as well, as it will ultimately make you rich, as this film would have us believe), and we must never give up on living life, because if we do, we will learn so much less.  In other words, life is great because life is great.  This is a simple, patronizing message whose whimpering little thud cannot be blunted, no matter how much hyperkinetic stylistic excess (of camera movement, of music, of editing) , or even great acting, is displayed in its service.  No wonder the film is such a crowd-pleaser - it tells us what we want to believe, even as we know (or should know, but do not, because filmmakers of the West continue to treat Eastern ideas and countries as test-tubes for the manufacture of insta-limousine-liberal guilt) otherwise.

Jamal Malik, a Muslim former street child from Mumbai,leads us through the history of his short but full life . Dany Boyle besides paying tribute to Bollywood and Mumbai, brought to the screen the spirit of the wonderful people of India not without showing some negative aspects. The use of temporal continuity was very skillful.  By jumping around in time, the film allowed one to see clear connections between sporadic early events in Jamal's life and his later (current) situation.

The use of the strobe effect was very cool.

Tying in a love story to the movie's overall story arch is an effective way to keep the audience yearning for one goal throughout the film: Jamal reuniting with Latika.  Auidences love watching two people 'destined to be together' struggle to meet this end.

The film combined a modern sense of style with the harsh realism of third world conditions.  The color and music made for an aesthetically pleasing but viciously aggressive image.  Sound and framing were also used to communicate a high sense of tension and violence throughout the film.  Silences interrupted by harsh explosions of sound, calm images colliding with close, fast movements..

The film does not shy away from displaying the harsh poverty that so many live in.  It is rare to see such a mainstream film that can be a social commentary at the same time.

Updated style and tenor don't really do much to save Slumdog in the end. Boyle's emphasis on the colors and sounds of Mumbai, use of frantic camera work, and pop music forays work well at first in conveying the energy of the slums, and in depicting a believable childhood gaze. However, the sugar rush eventually subsides and we're then forced to suffer through some Hollywood pitfalls that are primarily the fault of the script. The uber updated style and tenor of Slumdog also poses a problem when considering the social critique involved. Should the slums of Mumbai look like as if the characters are all about to slide off the screen because of it being too slick? Giving it the old Hollywood gloss sure will please the masses, but I'm sure if the citizens of Mumbai were to watch Slumdog they may have a problem with their homes being made to look like a centerfold shot of a magazine. In no way did I ever get the feeling of true filth and grit within these slums. Going back to the pitfalls. To be honest, I had a real problem with the use Who Wants to Be a Millionaire all together.  The strength of this film lies within the sequences that take place within the slums. Although the style may pose problems at times, there are some genuine moments of social insight and clarity. One such instance involves the two brothers first seeing the palace and the camera taking us on a tour via swoops, close-ups, and pans to depict the wonder and excitement of a child being enveloped in an upper-class social environment. These kind of subtlety's are sadly few and far between. I guess the only way an American audience can relate to Mumbai is through  a game show! and some crappy love story. 
	When the film transitions into present day it suffers from cliched characters,(One note villains and dirty cops) bad dialogue, and an underdeveloped love interest. In the end, nothing feels earned. The moments on the game show lack suspense due to the fact that the audience is given the knowledge of our protagonist's accomplishments when the film first begins. Boyle knows this, and by the end, tries to make up for it  by creating forced suspense involving the smarmy game show host feeding Jamal a wrong answer. Gee, maybe Jamal won't succeed after all! Oh Boyle, what a trickster.The film is trying to establish a destiny/meant-to-be type of story telling, and I get that, but the film strings the audience along the entire time with no sense of anticipation, and expects us to be rewarded by two individuals finally sharing a kiss that isn't earned. "The money doesn't matter." All that matters is that he finally found that girl who he kind of knows, and if he kisses her scar it may make it seem as if they actually share a deep love. As the credits roll, there is the sweet sound of some kind of Bollywood dance igniting the screen seconds after the death of a MAJOR character. "The dirty hoodlum did his good deed now light his ass up! It will be a great way to tack on some last second sympathy." Talk about one of the most overrated films in some time.

I'm something of an eternal pessimist and as such, films about fate and destiny and all that jazz tend to leave me cringing in my seat as I struggle to buy into the whole idea of it. I say 'tend to' though, because there are some exceptions, of which Slumdog Millionaire is one. 

Slumdog tells the story of Jamal Malik, an orphan from the slums of Mumbai who finds himself on the verge of winning Rs. 20 mn on India's version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?. The film tells the story of how Jamal came to know the answers to all of the questions he was asked and is told through a series of flashbacks, intercutting between Jamal's past experience, the game show itself, and the police interrogating him on the belief that he cheated.

As I said, I tend to dislike films with a strong undercurrent of destiny, and full credit goes to Danny Boyle for preventing this one from being another one for the scrapheap. The story is told with amazing energy and vibrancy. Boyle's attention to detail and seeming understanding of the Mumbai slum world shines through in every single frame - and is probably the biggest strength of the film. 

There are so many layers to this film and so much going on, and it all synchronises so seamlessly that you don't even realise how deep it goes until you're reflecting on it afterwards. The film is able to track India and Mumbai's own development from the 1980s to present day through Jamal's life and is able to paint an accurate picture of modern day Mumbai. The scene at the construction site, of Jamal and his brother Salim looking down on the slums being surrounded by high-rises, epitomises this perfectly, with the reflection in Salim's sunglasses (intended or not) insightfully showing where they have always aspired to get to.

If I had any complaints they are few and far between - and minor. One is Dev Patel's off-course Indian accent. He was pretty good most of the time with it, but I could still pick out the Brit in it - without needing to try. Only other thing is really that in creating the hectic and energetic film Boyle created, he inter-cut one too many times - the part of the climax regarding Salim almost seemed like it was meant to be a parody as a result. 

Bottom line: Slumdog is a thrilling, uplifting emotional rollercoaster of a crowd-pleaser - if you don't see it, you're missing out!

9/10

This modern fairy tale from the creative hands of Danny Boyle is life affirming, uplifting and totally engrossing from start to finish.  By now most people know the basic story of Jamal (Dev Patel) who wins big on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire.  How he gets there and his life experiences (which provide him with the knowledge to answer the questions) living on the street are what provides the compelling arc to the story.  Each question on the show precedes a flashback in Jamal's life that explains how he knew the answer to the question.  

Even though the film ends on an upbeat note some of the things that transpire in the two hour running time as Jamal makes his way through the streets are harsh and unsettling.  In one scene a boy is deliberately blinded so that he can sing on the streets for money.  This is because blind boys bring three times as much .   

The main driving force that keeps Jamal going is the search for his childhood love Latika(Freida Pinto), who was separated from him during an escape from a child exploiting gangster.  He spends the rest of the film trying to track her down and eventually he succeeds in finding her in a brothel, dancing for money.

Again, they are separated.  Again, Jamal does not give up hope.  

To say more would spoil the fun of watching this film unfold.  

Somehow Danny Boyle manages to pull the feel good movie of the year out of the slums of India.

So on Saturday my husband and I decided to go to a movie. We originally went to the theatre to see Revolutionary Road but at the last minute I decided that Slumdog Millionaire would be a better choice to see with him and that I could see the RR next time when I go alone. I must admit â I had done a stellar job at avoiding trailers and interviews for Slumdog. I had no clue what it was about. None. And like I usually suggest â try to do this as often as possible. The less you know about a movie going in â the better. In saying that, if you have not seen the movie, I actually suggest you do not read more of what I write about it. Let the film be seen through fresh eyes.

Slumdog Millionaire, directed by Danny Boyle, is one of the best underdog type movies I have seen. But because of that, donât think it is a straight forward or as common as those we are used to popping up in Cineplexâs across the country.  I actually think of this movie as a cross between Hoosiers, The Usual Suspects and Red Dawn. Except...it is nothing like any of those movies. So figure that one out!!

SM takes place in Mumbai, India. The main character, Jamal played by British actor, Dev Patel, is a contestant on Indiaâs most popular television show, âWho Wants to be a Millionaireâ. In India, this show is much more popular than it ever was in the US and the host is considered an idol. Jamal shocks the audience, crew and police by answering every question correctly. When they break for the day, just before the 20 million rupee question, Jamal is taken into custody on the grounds of suspected cheating. Believing that a âslumdogâ such as Jamal could know so much was impossible for those in charge.

After an entire night of questioning and what most of us would consider torture, Jamal goes on to explain what circumstances throughout his life brought to him the answers he needed to win the millions. Throughout the flashbacks, as he tells his story, the viewer delves deeper and deeper in to the lives of these gorgeous Indian children whom were orphaned in the slums of Mumbai. As they grew and faced obstacles the majority of the world could not even imagine we are given storylines which are very fresh and original to the typical American audience. 

Within this movie there is the magic of rooting for the unlikely, for true love, for justice and for mere survival. I wanted to see Revolutionary Road that day because I was feeling pretty somber and actually needed a good cry. Turns out what I needed indeed was a good cry, but through a smile. 

While I am usually reeled in by characters and dialogue when it comes to my favorites â with Slumdog, I was drawn in by the remarkable cinematography, film editing and soundtrack.  The camera work is artistic without being obnoxious. At the beginning of the movie there is a series of aerial shots of the aluminum roofs which cover the slum homes. It was a marvelous view of the massive poverty in which we were about to witness. The direction was just flawless. This is an all around beautifully made film with a beautiful story about beautiful children. So I guess I give it two beautiful thumbs up ;-)

Another thing that provides a masterful touch is the music used and its placement. This manages to illustrate different snapshots of Indian society into a feel good film while also provoking thought and emotion through some pretty disturbing scenes.

Slumdog Millionaire is the story of Jamal Malik (Patel), an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who is about to experience the biggest day of his life. With the whole nation watching, he is just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India¹s "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?"

But when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a street kid know so much? Desperate to prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika (Pinto), the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of his story reveals the key to the answer to one of the game show¹s questions.

Each chapter of Jamal¹s increasingly layered story reveals where he learned the answers to the show¹s seemingly impossible quizzes. But one question remains a mystery: what is this young man with no apparent desire for riches really doing on the game show?

When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out.

Essentially a Dickensian story in the Oliver Twist mold: plucky youth grows up under oppressive conditions and falls in with innumerable rouges, but after several family dilemmas and unlikely meetings with figures from his past, finds a way to make good. Within that very predictable and manipulative framework, I found the movie thoroughly watchable and even engaging. I certainly cared about the characters and was interested in seeing what would happen to them next, and there were individual scenes and performances that were well done. Still, the fact remains that Danny Boyle shows us images of astonishing poverty and exploitation and than asks us to forget about them as he moves towards a formulaic, uplifting conclusion. This is somewhat tasteless and insensitive on Boyle's part, and seriously hinders the effectiveness of the movie. And of course, his love of MTV style editing and Bollywood-inspired decadence (especially that ridiculous final dance number over the credits) is also insufferable. Hopefully, the fact that Boyle made any attempt to confront poverty in India will send clueless American audiences away with a little bit of food for thought (to be fair, I think the horrifying moment where a young boy is blinded is at least as memorable as the feel-good finale). At any rate, this is basically a trifling piece of commercial filmmaking that has no business competing for major awards, and the fact that it is demonstrates the true poverty of imagination facing Hollywood today.

This movie was creative and genius in many respects, except the final dance sequence; while I enjoyed it, I thought it was unnecessary. Based on the excellently written novel, Q & A, by Vikas Swarup (an Indian diplomat), the story chronicles the events that lead to an uneducated slum kid being on the threshold of history: to win the Indian Millionaire contest. The host of the contest, who incidentally was also a slum kid that rose to critical acclaim (according to him) by winning a similar contest, was reluctant to believe that this uneducated slum dog could be able to achieve such a feat. In come the corrupt police who were left astounded by the story retold by the young lad (he had to be a genius to really concoct such a believable story). However, the underlining message of this excellently directed movie is a social commentary on humanity that can tolerate such opulence existing side by side with such extreme poverty. India, a land of many extremes, and Mumbai, a city of extremes provided an excellent backdrop to this storey. The sound tract was cutting edge and Allah Rakkha Rahman masterful composition elegantly compliments the movie. A must seeâ¦.

Directed by Danny Boyle (Trainspotting, 28 Days Later, A Life Less Ordinary), Slumdog Millionaire is the story of Jamal Malik. The film depicts his life up until the point he appears on a who wants to be a millionaire like show. 

The movie is brilliantly shot and the images are both haunting and beautiful. The acting, when done by the adults is powerful. 

The movie opens with Jamal being accused of cheating on the game show. We then learn how he knows all of the answers. 

As a youth Jamal and his brother live with their mother in Bombay. (It's still Bombay then) Because they are Muslims they are persecuted and quickly become orphans. They then meet a young girl, Latika. As orphans they undergo horrific conditions and a terrible situation. 

We see the children in different situations as they become young adults and ultimately adults. The main theme of the movie is the love that Jamal has for Latika.

I don't want to give too much of the movie away, but ultimately it is brilliant.

The reason that I dropped the star is two fold. One is tone. The movie at times is haunting and tragic. But the whole who wants to be a millionaire plot point is almost unnecessary and is distracting from the maturation of Jamal. During the credits there is a further break of tone that really didn't need to be there. 

The second flaw is that the movie is a bit predictable. The final question is obvious from the beginning. 

Overall the movie just looks wonderful. You become invested in the characters. You want them to succeed. It is an excellent film.

Though set entirely in India, 'Slumdog Millionaire' is definitely not the usual Bollywood offering, even if there is the requisite love story and an element of destiny.  I have not read the book ('Q & A' by Vikas Swarup) on which it is based, but director Danny Boyle has crafted a story that is both gritty and charming.  Having traveled to India twice, I can attest to the existence and appearance of the slums in which much of this movie takes place. Granted, Mumbai's slums do not comprise the whole (or even a significant part) of the city, but they are visually and sociopolitically gripping when you see them. Mind-numbing poverty is part and parcel of the multifaceted land of India. This story happens to take place almost extensively among the poorest of the poor - that does not mean it represents all of India.  (I've heard some criticism of the movie as not being 'representative' of the real India.)  As for the story line, of course it requires a bit of the old disbelief suspension, but in many ways the circumstances in which Jamal finds himself are presented believably. The absolute strength and beauty of this film (in spite of its flaws) are the performances by - not the seasoned professionals (Anil Kapoor, Irfan Khan) - but by Dev Patel and the six children who play Jamal, Salim and Latika as very young children and slightly older children. A quick check of imdb.com shows that only one of them (middle Jamal) has a couple of small prior acting credits; the other five have none. These children are absolutely amazing and carry the weight of most of the movie. They are beautifully open and inquisitive, showing ranges of emotion in their small faces and jet eyes that many adult actors cannot find. I don't know how a director (or his assistants or whomever) coaxed such compelling performances from these young actors, but those performances are the backbone of the chaos swirling around them.  Likewise, Dev Patel's previous credits are limited, yet he deftly handles his role as the teen-aged Jamal quickly growing into manhood.  Freida Pinto as the older Latika is beautiful and capable, and Madhur Mittal is fine as the older Salim.  'Slumdog Millionaire' shows some of the very real warmth and beauty of India and reflects her colors and sensual richness, even in the midst of the poverty and ADD-inducing bustle of a city that simply has too many people.  That much it does well.  I could personally live without a lot of the MTV-like editing that makes scene transitions jarring and jerky, but it's a small criticism of an otherwise beautifully filmed movie. Of course it doesn't represent everything realistically - very few fictional outings can claim documentary-like realism. Call it poetic license. But the story is interesting, the acting i s uniformly good, and the score is a perfect accompaniment. This movie deserves its R rating for some hard-to-watch depictions of things the children endure in their hard-scrabble young lives, along with violence and language. It's not necessarily a feel-good movie (nor is it a feel-bad movie), but it's a compelling watch and offers a view of India that Bollywood would probably prefer not to showcase.  You won't find actors breaking into song and dance in 'Slumdog Millionaire' (unless you count the closing credits), but you will see much of what makes India so vibrant and unique.

The majority of professional critics are taking too strong a liking to Slumdog Millionaire, but as a mass appeal inspirational film, its dark side (which became darker after the film's location of Mumbai was under attack in November of 2008), its stunning cinematography comparable to Cidade de Deus, and its direction from Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tandan help the film survive. What hurts the film most is the blatant foreshadowing. For example, when the children ponder if the man that discovered them hiding in a landfill, took them in, and feeds them is a "saint," we already know by his Don Johnson looks that Fagin-like corruption lies ahead. Same goes for the used car salesman appearance of Anil Kapoor's "Millionaire" host - he constantly slings negativity toward his underdog contestant (Dev Patel, in a terrific film debut) on and off the air, so the mysterious punch of a scene he has later with Jamal in the restroom has quite an expected result after a little thought. There are several other instances too; in fact, the coincidental final question of the game show could be the ultimate tolerance-deciding factor for this film that is meant to celebrate knowledge but does so too mildly. However, considering the jaw-dropping showcase of landscape shots of Mumbai and the Taj Mahal (especially the overhead ones like Jamal's gangster brother's construction hideout), almost all is forgiven from me. Slumdog Millionaire is highly addictive to watch, not for its smitten-all-along love story (Well, okay, it helps a little...), but because of its enlightening flow of framing both economic sides of the country of India. The dusty luminous tint is of course not the only similarity it shares with Cidade de Deus - there are also kids with guns (the brother is the lovechild of both Benny and Li'l Ze) surviving their given difficult society with one exceptional boy choosing a different methodical path, but rather than resembling a knockoff based in another country, the vision is still welcome, making Slumdog feel like a popular younger brother. Perhaps not Best Picture-worthy, but especially with such a loyal and fun final credits sequence, it's still a distinguished sit-through.

[left]I've been of the opinion that as of late the hero losing it all or risking it all and dying has become way too common among "oscar" films. While I understand, and in many respects, share the viewpoint that those films that have such a profound end leave a powerful taste; I've always felt the right film and combination of risking it all and overcoming the greatest of odds and I firmly believe Slumdog Millionaire is that film. Now I don't want to go out and say it's perfect, it isn't, it has plenty of flaws and I don't want people going in with expectations that stretch beyond immagination (as it seems too many people have already done this year for other films). The best thing about Slumdog Millionaire is that its core, it's a tale of love, lost love, and the struggles of destiny to bring this love to existence.

Dev Patel is great as our central character, Jamal Malik, a young orphan who, along with his brother Salim, and friend Latika, go through many of life's struggles including poverty, slavery, theft, and ultimately the show that will change all their lifes. Danny Boyle, along with Loveleen Tandan, create a high paced, visual thrill, with a great blend of style, music, and power. Imagine in a sense City of God meets Trainspotting, as odd of a combo as that might seem. The movie does lag a bit towards the middle, but the intensity and overall desire to hope for a better life for our main characters carry's the film through quite nicely. The film serves not only as staple to the belief in destiny, but should serve as a guide to filmmakers on how to make a true underdog film. It would be too easy to throw the film's story under the bus for being cliche, but I feel with any other ending this film would simply be another depressing tale, dangling meat out on a hook for oscar voters begging for a vote because like all the other films of its nature it's "different," when by most acconts it would merely be the same.

Slumdog Millionaire (2008) by Danny Boyle
starring Dev Patel
 
[img]http://i226.photobucket.com/albums/dd114/besh1/poster1-1.jpg[/img]
 
In a nutshell: Tantalizingly close to a classic. Great filmmaking almost covers minor plot holes :fresh: :fresh:
 
Quick synopsis: Jamal Malik, an uneducated Indian boy from the slums of Bombay is suspected of cheating in order to reach the final question on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire
 
Content: I will get off to a bad start, pissing people off by saying that I thought this film was overrated. But that is mostly a result of the unbelievably high expectations I had based on what I had heard. Slumdog Millionaire is a great film although I disagree with those that assert it was the best film of 2008.
 
Danny Boyle directed the film. Further expanding his already diverse catalogue that includes Trainspotting, 28 Days Later and Sunshine among others. He is truly a storyteller that will maximize any script you give him. I didn't love all of the editing which at times seemed a little cheap, but Danny has earned my complete trust when he is behind the camera.
 
I LOVE the premise of the film. So original. I can see why some have been skeptical of a film that centers around an episode of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, but Boyle doesn't place too much emphasis on the show. The show itself is merely an incredibly creative way to connect the scenarios of one young man's life. I also loved its three timeline structure. 1) the past 2) the game show 3) the interrogation. We are not limited to just the show and the past which gives an edge to the story because we know where the game show leads. The three lines are balanced and woven together expertly by Boyle's team.
 
The actors are almost universally great and unknown to US fans. The only actor I did not care for was the oldest version of brother Salim. I especially liked the guy that played the host of the TV show. He had the slick yet sleazy charm of a car salesman that you aren't sure whether to trust. The trust issue is ultimately put to a test in a huge way in my favorite scene in the entire film. The showdown between Jamal (the contestant) and the host is the opposite of the showdown in A Few Good Men. While Tom Cruise and Jack Nicholson went at each other loud enough for the entire military base to hear, Jamal and the host are having a private battle of wits behind the professional facade that the camera adds.
 
The few things that let me down involve the ending. First, the big emotional moment where love conquers all was rendered slightly less impactful because this truest of loves hadn't been proven to me. I hadn't seen the characters falls in love and was just expected to accept that they had, I guess during their years apart. Second, I wanted a stronger reason for Jamal to pick his final answer. Just randomly picking proved one point (that he didn't care about the money) but left me without the ultimate moment of payoff that makes my very favorite films the best in my book. The build-up to the climactic moment was done extremely well but from the moment the phone hangs up, the rest of the film did nearly nothing for me. And there was one huge gap in what I wanted to see. How did Jamal get on the show?!?! Are we supposed to believe that he simply knew the right moment to call as he has explained earlier? I would have liked to see the moment when he made his fateful call, although I figure there's a good chance that will turn up as a deleted scene.
 
But I don't want to focus too much on what I did not like in what I think is one of the best films I saw during last year. I loved the setting in India. It gave me a taste of a culture I have never experienced, from the slums to the Taj Mahal. I loved Jamal's eternally naive, but feisty personality. He overcame so many hardships and could have easily fallen through the cracks so many times. He is truly a man to root for. I loved the intro multiple choice question that Boyle gives to his viewers that sets up all of the things that would unfold as Jamal plays the game. And I loved the Bollywood style dance number during some really fantastic closing credits.
 
I wonder whether the strength of the film will diminish as the game show itself becomes more dated. The film actually requires somewhat of an understanding of the lifeline structure in order to fully appreciate how things come together. But regardless, they certainly do come together beautifully even if the final 5 minutes let me down. I think it's a very very good movie but not quite a timeless classic as I feel the two best films of last year, No Country and There Will Be Blood, will be remembered as. The ending just wasn't quite strong enough for that. But with a more impactful conclusion, it could have been up there.

There is little to object to in a film, that's sole purpose is to sweep its grateful audience away. It need not make grandiose statements nor attempt to subvert the fabric of cinema. All which is incumbent upon it, is to entertain, to captivate.  But for this, certain things must be in place; Character, Narrative. It is with a heavy heart that I confess, that after a  second viewing, this film is sadly lacking in both. 
It is in no way an awful picture, Its sheer scope and the ingenuity of its central conceit is enough to bowl one over, but the lasting impact is ephemeral and hollow. Danny Boyle is a director of great vision, however in this instance, his bombastic style comes at the cost of emotional engagement. He is so beguiled by the frenzied environment, which he admirably  portrays without condescension, that he has forgotten about the characters. 
The writing is at once fresh and frustratingly derivative. The "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?"  artifice is unique and an intelligent device for exposing backstory. The first act is indelibly  charming but as the plot progresses, one's interest wanes. It is too formulaic; take 1 part 'City of God', two parts 'Cinema Paradiso' and two parts 'Oliver Twist' and you have an idea. Consequently on first inspection it is easy to be seduced by Boyle's latest offering but, ultimately, it is too superficial and too facile to last.

The story itself is pretty preposterous and, as for Danny Boyle, he should have slowed it down a bit. The editing is so bullet-speed (to manufacture so-called tension and exictement) in many parts making it difficult to contemplate what's exactly happening. Having said all this, you should still see it for yourself and I'm sure you'll fall for it, like nearly everyone else has. Or you may just want to wait for the far superiror "Rachel Getting Married" or "Milk".

Once in a while you see a movie that's really special. You leave the theater wondering, is this one of the best movies of the last ten years? Will it be a personal favorite of mine in ten years? Or am I just buzzing from post-theater glow?

I can say this, Slumdog is my favorite movie of 2008, without a doubt. Whether it will last in time, I can't say for certain, but I do know it has given me a piece of its soul.

Not all movies have souls. Only with a turn of luck, where all elements work and something magical transcends the screen, can a movie become a walking, talking, living thing. And for me, Slumdog Millionaire is as real as the UPS man I see every morning.

I don't want to give away too much. The basic synopsis sounds ludicrous and almost too manufactured, even to Danny Boyle who spoke after the screening I attended. Somehow it works- this boy who lived in some of the worst conditions around the world, by chance, happens to know all the answers to the questions on the Indian version of 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire'. To defend his position with the show, while interrogated for cheating, he retells the story of his young life as it relates to these questions.

Its an adventure, its a drama, its a love story, an all in one movie that has the ability to transport you to Bombay, India. Boyle used three different cameras, but depended on a smaller, hand held camera that connected to the laptop on the cameraman's back. With this approach, he was able to capture the feeling of running through the slums of Bombay, living in piles of trash, walking out of your car to join the thousands of people on the road tuned into a game show's grand finale. I feel like I was there. 

The movie-going experience has been stored as a memory of Bombay, not a memory of watching a movie.

Not only do I feel like I could smell the trash, sleep on the train, enjoy the white walls of a new hotel room, and surrender to that first kiss but I also felt like I now carry around a piece of this person's life (fictional or not) he is now under my skin and inside of me. He has touched me in a way I hope I never forget.

In recent years, "feel good" has never really been an appropriate adjective for end-of-the-year Oscar bait. Long gone are the days when films like "Star Wars" and "Raiders of the Lost Ark" were even CONSIDERED for Oscar nominations. Nowadays, in order for your film to be respected by the Academy, it has to be dark, and depressing, and downright gloomy ("There Will Be Blood", "No Country for Old Men", and "Capote" come to mind). How happy I was, then, when I finished watching "Slumdog Millionaire", by far one of the most inspiring and, yes, feel-good films in recent memory. Superbly directed by British filmmaker Danny Boyle ("28 Days Later" and "Trainspotting") and following a marvelous script by Simon Beaufoy, this film will go down as one  of the most uplifting masterpieces of cinema in history. A rags-to-riches story set in Mumbai, India, we follow the life of illiterate, poor Jamal Malik (Dev Patel in a beautifully understated performance), as he's one question away from winning 20 million rupees on India's version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire". Accused of cheating, Jamal must defend himself by reliving his life, one of pain, misery, and tribulation. Orphaned as a child and forced on the run with his older brother Salim, Jamal scrapes his way through life, forced into child slavery, begging, and thievery. While his brother grows up to embrace the criminal lifestyle, the innocent Jamal exists for only one reason: to find the lost love of his life, Latika (played as an adult by the beautiful Freida Pinto). A tender, heartfelt work of art, and wonderfully shot by cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle, "Slumdog" celebrates the very essence of the human spirit. Though at times depressing and downright heartbreaking, "Slumdog" rises above its dark brethren and ends on one of the highest notes possible. A glorious, spirited, life-affirming love letter to both India and the wonders of the movies.

A weird "love story" where not much time is spent on the love story but, instead is spent all over India from the slums to the corporate city of Mumbai and on the most overdone, overproduced show ever made: "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire". 

I thought that show's popularity had run its course but...okay.

In any case, the movie wildly shifts between drama to child torture porn to mafia flick with a little underdog and romance story sprinkled, randomly, throughout. 

The movie has so much going for it that there's probably 4 or 5 different movies here...unfortunately, it feels as if Danny Boyle has taken about 30 minutes from each movie, taped it together and pushed it into a reel to go into the projector. Heck, he even tosses in a Bollywood number during the credits for good measure because it wouldn't fit in the film. Perhaps, maybe, Danny...you shoulda just left it out and re-edited your movie.

All in all, this style of filmmaking is both refreshing and frustrating. The movie never spends too long on something (well, unless it's people in a weird child hostel burning kid's eyes out of their skulls - "uncomfortable scene" is putting it mildly) which keeps things moving but it's also kinda jarring at the same time. It's like going on a rollercoaster where the hydraulics are bad and the ride is rough because of lack of maintenance and you end up with whiplash. 

Danny Boyle's innovative digital-camera-style "you-are-there" approach worked in movies like "28 Days Later" where the up-close-and-personal feeling added to the feeling of unease and grimness. It also added humanity and excitement and color to "Sunshine" but, here, it's just more-of-the-same, making me wish that Boyle would branch out stylistically. 

The acting is good. That's the saving grace of this movie. The children seem better at showing emotion than the adults but that's all right. Dev Patel looks somewhere between constipated and confused while being shocked by a cattle prod, even when he's winning. Freida Pinto stands there and looks pretty...she really has no real acting talent. It's like watching Jessica Alba, the Indian Version. Madhur Mittal is the only one who shows any fire and he's just angry. So, there you go: you have zombie, pretty, and on fire. No depth.

Then there's the whole "Millionaire" angle. Annoyances with that dated POS show aside (what's next - wringing suspense from a Swahili version of "Deal or No Deal"?!?), we're also supposed to buy Jamal knowing the answers to every single question because every question asked has something to do with his past...uh-huh. What LUCK! Every single question has to do with something he experienced in life.

Right.

I mean, I thought it was silly that he was actually arrested and tortured (yes, if you're caught CHEATING ON A GAME SHOW IN INDIA, they string you up by your arms and zap you with electrodes and beat the holy shit out of you - the police don't have bigger priorities in Mumbai?) and I let that slide...but one would think that if Jamal has this kind of luck, he should play the lottery.

Who knows? The ticket could have been created by some ancient family member who made sure that Jamal would walk into the right convenience store at the right time.

It's not unrealistic.

Not in THIS movie.

I mean, it's no "August Rush" or anything (that movie gives the word "contrived" a whole new meaning) but it's a little beyond ridiculous.

I mentioned the editing and scene selection before. It's jarring. Especially the conclusion of the film which mixes sad and bloody violence with an ending that's gonna be happy (it's okay...the many "pick-us-please-please-please Oscar trailers on television already blew the ending ten times over). I mean, why would anyone show a happy ending, then cut to something terrible, then go back to the happy scene again? That's like showing "The Little Mermaid", then editing in 30 seconds of "Hostel", then going back to "Mermaid" again.

For all the accolades, this Danny Boyle masterpiece was richly awarded and heavily deserved. It is a heavy weight, but I struggle to confine it to one single genre - that is where the beauty lies however and where its magical affect, generated. 

Who wants to be a Millionaire is a Hollywood cliche - or so you thought. Whomever conjured up the notion of setting this within the Mumbai slums however was definitely onto something. The way Boyle weaves intricately a web of snapshots of one boys life is the best kind of storytelling. Through the answering of questions, an autobiographical tale is created, inviting you to experience the slum perspective of a boy, an Orphan, a worker and then a national icon. 

Trite and embarrassingly predictable are criticisms thrown at Slumdog but which completely miss the mark. For all the hype and electricity exhumed over this film, I finally felt a film was truly deserved of all the praise, warmth and generosity of the Academy. The cinematography, the visual effects, the plot and the acting all merged together to make the complete jigsaw. And a stunning one at that. 

Alas, it our great opinion as an audience that matters most however, not merely those present on the board at the Academy. The fact the film is still regularly being screened (at a cinema near YOU) with a massive audience presence cannot merely attributed to its eight Oscar wins, nor the rave reviews it has received. Lest we not forget the powerful "word of mouth" wave that can sweep you up in its grasp and transport you to  cinematic heaven. 

Like Jamal, I was transported to heaven - Boyle's heaven, with a little Bollywood thrown into the mix for good measure - where for 2 hours and 30 minutes, I felt like a Millionaire having won the *Best Two Hours and 30 minutes of my life* lottery. 

Thank you for the gift Boyle. You truly deserve yours - an audience who recognizes, appreciates and praises fully, your ability to make a damn good film.

Sublime, layered, and beautfiully shot, Slumdog is unapologetic in it's feelgood, without being manipulative. As much a celebration and love letter to the city of Mumbai as it is to this story of 3 enduring young souls, who for all their seeming poverty, find more than enough reasons to hope and strive, some of them noble, some selfish. Boyle piles on the emotional content, and if he does get you to cheer and indeed "feelgood" , it's only because as a filmaker he's unafraid to put these young actors (3 apiece playing each of the leads at different ages) into harms way, and really show you the reality of what it takes to survive on these unforgiving streets. 

At the same time within the 3 act flashback narrative, cleverly married into the answering of questions on the Millionaire game show is a real sense of energy, of hustle, Boyle never indulges and rarely lingers for any dallying camera shots, the city is breathtaking simply because it is, and there's a wonderful honesty to Slumdog for all it's Frank Capra hat tips because of that.

The young actors playing across the growing up of the children are uniformly superb, and rounding the cast off with accomplished superstars of the bollywood scene is a masterstroke. Finally emphasising the theme of fusion, growth, and evolution is a blinding soundtrack from A R Rahman, a man who's work based purely on the strength of this film I'll be seeking out more of. 

Slumdog Millionaire, is a delicious fusion in itself, the result of a superb, small but perfectly formed western crew and the unmitigated hospitality and support of the local Bollywood artists, it's like the city itself, it has some pretty dark, terrifying corners, but it's full of life, and is about the people living that life, striving, succeeding,hoping. For me personally this is where Danny Boyle exceeded Trainspotting, and stands head and shoulders next to worlds best filmakers. If I had to choose between this and "the Wrestler" for best movie this year, at this point I don't think I could.

I have not seen a better film all year.  I went to the preview screening for the movie and convinced every one of my friends to see it. Far beyond hunger and make-shift housing, the constant threat of use, abuse, unfair treatment, even bigotry are key factors in shaping the lives of the three main characters as each one forges past their circumstance to finding a life more abundant.  I can not recommend this movie highly enough.

Slumdog Millionaire deserves its Golden Globe sweep (Best Motion Picture - Drama, Best Director, Best Original Score, Best Screenplay). The surprise hit will jolt you out of your ennui from all sides.  

Simon Beaufoy based the screenplay on Vikas Swarup's bestselling novel 'Q and A', about Jamal Malik, a poor orphan from the slums who wins the US$410,000 jackpot on "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?" to attract the attention of the woman he loves. He is accused of cheating, however, and to explain how he managed to answer each question, he recounts the fascinating tale that is his life.
  
Director Danny Boyle (Sunshine, 28 Days Later, The Beach) and director for India Loveleen Tandan produced a frenetic film that still manages to be riveting enough to focus on equal parts colorful Indian landscape and gritty human reality, allowing you to experience a wide range of emotions. The original score by A.R. Rahman complements the visual assault with a fluid infusion of Indian-flavored electronic beats.

The film is brilliantly cast, with Dev Patel as the older Jamal, Madhur Mittal as Jamal's older brother Salim, and Freida Pinto as the older Latika, Jamal's childhood friend and ultimate love interest. The three main characters' stories unravel from their past lives, and the actors who play them in their early teens and childhood all contributed marvelously (Boyle was reportedly crushed to learn of some of child actors' real poverty-stricken lives, and ensured them of their education and trust funds).

Slumdog Millionaire is a socially-relevant drama that's also funny and heartwarming, modern without being cold. Consistent with Boyle's style, despite tackling dark themes, it still has room for positive vibes, daring you to see the beauty in despair. It may not be a Bollywood flick but it ends in traditional Bollywood style: a grand production number!

Slumdog Millionaire is a strange film in execution and reception. It's a Bollywood/Hollywood magic dust fable: a weird mixture of Fernando Mereilles and Frank Capra. The reviews for this picture, directed by Danny Boyle, are inexplicably through the roof. Many are calling it a masterpiece and it looks to be a sure thing for Academy Award consideration. I don't dispute that the movie, which is about a young Indian trying to win it all on the Indian version "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?", is a good one. It is. I found it be warm of spirit and entertaining. I do dispute that it's a great or important picture. Other movies this year like Darren Aronofsky's masterpiece The Wrestler confront us with economic downturn and a man trying to triumph against the odds. I found both its depiction of the man and his condition to be far more convincing and lingering. Slumdog Millionaire is ultimately a cute, but gimmicky picture that takes half an hour too long to find its feet and offers a rather pat, palatable portrayal of poverty. Bottom line: you will be entertained by this well directed, well acted, well meaning film. Your life won't be changed and there are still better movies out there. That's my final answer.

The character which really stole the show of course, was India itself, which is displayed in all its wonderful vibrance, beauty, poverty and decadence. As with Trainspotting, the music is almost central to this film and really sets the tone. In all, the first hour and a half of this film is refreshing and original, certainly amongst Danny Boyle's best. Then, as the last act set in, the story settles down and became predictable and cliche, loose ends are tied up, the camera work becomes straight-forward and we are left with an average, overly sentimental melodrama for the remaining 30 minutes. Up until this point I had been watching a 10/10 masterpiece. The ending doesn't ruin it, and it mostly makes up for it with a fun Bollywood dance routine over the end credits, but does drag my rating down to a 9/10. 

Still a great movie though, every film fan should check it out.

For millions like me raised on a staple-diet of commercial Hindi cinema, there's nothing particularly novel about its plot: the relatively lukewarm response it has gotten from Indian filmgoers compared to the rapturous applause elsewhere is proof of this. Its rags-to-riches tale, adapted from a novel penned by a diplomat, could well be a cinematic-metaphor for India's own rise during the period in which it unfolds. In so many ways, it is the story of India as well as those of us who have lived here through the tumultuous past two decades. 

Its phenomenal 'rules-breaking success'- to paraphrase the longtime film-critic, Roger Ebert- therefore owes equally if not more to the disenchanted times the world suddenly finds itself thrust into as it does to the movie's delightful intrinsic-charms (of which there are several): after all, what better medicine than a good healthy dose of unbridled Hope wrapped in wondrously uplifting Jai-hos to cure the globe of its seemingly insurmountable Recession-blues? 

All the other films nominated for Best Picture at this year's Oscars reflect the Gloom around- but also, within- us; none with the solitary exception of this film offers a way-out: even- or, especially- if the way-out is an implausibly exhilaratingly happy ending. And that is precisely what makes it work.

I leave you with this particular mise-en-scene: as Jamal weaves his way through Mumbai's reptilian traffic to answer that one last remaining two million-rupee question, a wrinkly old beggar knocks at his car-window. Thinking she has come to ask for money he ignores her at first only to be confronted with the realization that she doesn't want his money at all; on the contrary, she wants him to win it all. 'Beta,' she beams to Jamal as he is driven away, 'jeet ke aana.' (Son, win & come.) His victory, after all, would be hers as well. Much as Slumdog Millionaire's victory on Oscar Night would be India's- and of Underdogs everywhere.

On the initial point. I'll succeed. On the latter, you may have to put up with my mind vomit.

Slumdog Millionaire follows the story of Dev Patel's "Jamal Malik" a kid from the slums of Mumbai who is one question away from winning India's Who Wants to be a Millionaire. Trouble is, how did he get that far? He's just a kid from the slum?

The opening scene actively dispels any sense that this is going to be 120 mins of cheese, as Jamal is 'questioned' by authorities on how he has gotten so far. Surely he must be cheating?

What follows are a series of stories, as opposed to simple flashbacks, that link Jamal's past to his current situation and his path to the final question. They are perhaps terribly obvious and coincidental - but then sometimes life has that quality - and if it doesnt, this is a film after all. Through it all there is brutal, and dark, then immediately humour and light-heartedness. 

Friendship, love, brotherhood, betrayal and most of all survival. For it is through the latter of these, the film seems to say, that we truly learn and indeed literally live. 

The acting from everyone is spot-on. Patel does a solid job of holding the story together, and being able to retain a balanced level of contempt and yet acceptance and understanding of what he has been accused of. As his true motives, his love for the stunning Freida Pinto, imbue him with a great deal of sadness. 

The children who play the young Jamal and brother Salim are fantastic and deserve special praise. 

The camera is typically quirky and angled, as Boyle likes. The score is perfect. The jumping from English to Hindi never phases you, i find the way the subtitles are used on screen enjoyable as much as in the moments where subtitles are deliberately left out. But perhaps the most subtle yet important thing is the use of Mumbai as a character as we watch it grow along with the boy and his story. 

Perhaps it is not a true reflection of the true India. But then it is not meant to judge the country and is at the least, an outsiders view. The more pompous critics out there will tell you that it is too coincidental. But then is life not that way sometimes? They will perhaps tell you that its momentary touch on the clash between Hindu and Muslim culture (that Jamal is Muslim does not really return in the movie) is not enough. But in truth the film is not about these things. It is about Jamal's story and as such we can only see what has touched his life, and to the extent that it has touched his life through his words.To elaborate more would have turned it into something it is not and risked devaluing the movie as a whole.

What Slumdog IS is a breathtaking and thrilling rollercoaster of comedy and romance and drama. It is certainly a must see.

For every clever flashback that foretold what was happening in the present, there was a hackneyed piece of dialogue that I could see coming a mile away.   

There was only one character - the game show host - whose personality was unexpected.  You could predict Jamal lashing out everytime his beloved was besmirched.  You knew Salim was capable of being cruel to achieve his goals.  You were guaranteed Latika would reunite with her protector in the end.  

The lackluster character development and three or four cringe-worthy lines kept me from LOVING this movie.  Nevertheless, I can't say enough about the brilliant direction, scoring, even the choreography that makes this movie so distinguished.

More often than not, when a film is overly praised, normally it fails to click with me and/or I find it disappointingly overrated. The story was truly uniquely told and mind-boggling entertaining. I mean, who would have thought a film surrounding the television game show "Who Wants To Be a Millionaire?" would make for one compelling film. The main character trio, no matter which age version, were wonderful- Dev Patel and Freida Pinto had undeniable on-screen chemistry, Madhur Mittal (the last "Salim") was an interesting villain and he played his character pretty well. The kids were equally superb too, but I really got a kick from watching Irrfan Khan, who played the police inspector. He is such a talented actor but not a household name, but may remember him from his bit part in "Spiderman" and "Life of Pi" (which was also another awesome film with a unique way of storytelling).  Overall, this film was really good and the only complaint I have is all the circumstances were just too convenient. I mean, what are the odds Jamal would continuously run into Latika in his lifetime, especially in a country as hugely populous as India. But, if you can't suspend disbelief with films, when can you?
If you only see one film this year, make sure to pick "Slumdog Millionaire." It has all the elements of movies: romance, humor, action, thrills and drama.

This is easily one of the best films of the year and a lead contender for Best Picture. Jamal (Dev Patel) is a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" and has been answering all the questions right. In another plot thread, Jamal has been taken by the police and is accused of cheating. With no education and no money, the police think there is no way he could possibly know any of the answers. In trying to find out, the cops replay the show and we're taken on a journey through Jamal's childhood, including his early years where the movie is subtitled in Hindi. For once, the subtitles don't prove to be a distraction. The movie is essentially a Hollywood fable. It takes you to a new place and gives you a multi-layered story to get lost in. Director Danny Boyle fills the movie with insane visuals and camera techniques; it's brilliantly done. Dev Patel gives a great performance as Jamal because he is not an American 20-something pretending to be a teen. In fact, he is 18 in real life. Freida Pinto is equally strong as Latika, Jamal's childhood friend. In all my years of going to the movies, this has been the only movie where I was literally on the edge of my seat, especially in the last 15 minutes. It will make you laugh and cry. By the end, I was cheering for Jamal. A must-see!

Brit director Danny Boyle, famous for movies such as Trainspotting, The Beach and 28 Days Later, sets his latest film in the hot slums of India.

Slumdog Millionaire revolves around the life of teenager Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), who is one question away from the jackpot answer on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire.  However, due to him growing up in the slums, he is accused of cheating and is arrested. During interrogation, the story flashbacks to moments in Jamal's troubled childhood in Mumbai as he explains how he came to know the answers to the questions on the show, and how he spent his youth searching for his one true love, Latika (Freida Pinto).

There has been serious Oscar buzz revolving around this film, with serious hopes for Best Picture. But, personally, I don't think it's worthy of the accolade. It is an OK film at best, but it uses a number of soppy, cheap cliches along the way that make it predictable at times. It tries to 'emotionally rape' the viewer, and made me quite annoyed with it.

Boyle does a decent job in telling the story of living life in poverty stricken slums, but when it manifests into the cliched love story it starts to go sour and feels like every other romance out there.

The Academy seems to like this kind of thing (Such as Crash in 2006, which I found terrible). It shouldn't win the Oscar in my opinion. It's a bit too pretentious at times and seems like it's trying to earn awards, there have been better films over the past year.

However, due to the constant barrage of MTV-style editing and kooky camera angles, the film as a whole seems more like an edited-down mini series than a film and could have done with a few scenes of repose to consolidate the emotional message rather than sacrifice the tragedies suffered by the main protagonists in the name of entertainment. That said, SM is a testament to the human spirit and its episodic nature (using each question to highlight the hero's path to true love and riches) works well. Didn't have me punching the air like the huge cast of extras but a worthwhile experience nonetheless. Extra stars for the cast and cinematography.

Now, why would the host try to demean his guest who is a "chai-wala"? And even if he wanted, would he actually do it so blatantly in this age of TRPs? Okay, I am not being critical just for the heck of it... as I said, it is because of so much I had expected from the movie that I couldn't help pointing few glitches!

With this said, the film is a good watch! The narrative en faced each question is really done in style... And the music tracks are really good. The Ringa-ringa remix by Rehman is reverberating still now in my ears. The paper-plane by MIA and the ending Jai-ho are too good! Especially Jai-ho song makes the film end in a happy bollywood style. The film in spite of its slum milieu is a happy film and it doesn't make you feel heavy at the end.

I will recommend this movie... just that I thought there was a little hype about it!

Slumdog Millionaire bursts with life, delighting, shocking and constantly engaging through lively visuals and the rags-to-maybe-riches adventures of a young man who travels from the slums to the hot seat of the Indian Who Wants To Be a Millionaire. 
Like Jamal, Slumdog Millionaire succeeds against all odds and in ways that you think are impossible. In our cynical, contemporary times, it delivers a romantic fable that's as rich, complex, and beautiful as the city it comes from. 
Director Danny Boyle presents a world where garbage dumps serve as playgrounds, and criminality and cruelty are a matter of course. But its also a place where ingenuity can pay off and where hope, once sprung, can survive. 
This beautifully rendered and energetic tale celebrates resilience, the power of love, and the vitality of the human experience. Compelling and moving, bitter sweet and haunting, it is, above all, unforgettable.
