While certainly entertaining at times, I'm a bit baffled as to why this was so highly regarded.   (Here's yet another reason why the Academy Awards are about as relevant to my cinematic tastes as the Grammy awards are to my taste in music.)

Pros: Dev Patel's peformance; surprisingly good child actor performances, particularly by the 2nd Salim;  direction (the Oscar for this was well deserved at least)

Cons: MTV stylizing of cuts and sequences;  game show integration into this was overly embedded and became strange and distracting (seemed like one giant product placement); the soundtrack didn't particularly appeal to me, given its prominence (came off too much like a music video at times)

I'm not really sure what this film was trying to say, if anything.  It seemed more of a fantastical tale with no particular moral to the story.  I'd say, if you're looking for some sensory stimulation for sensory stimulation's sake (the sights and sounds of India -- the hustle and bustle), then watch this film.  But if you're looking for a bit more substance along these same lines, and a more realistic portrayal of things, see City of God instead (which is a far better film).

The centerpiece of this movie -- the love story -- is completely hokey and fabricated one (kind of like a Bollywood version of the Forrest Gump love story). Next, the story of brothers has been done much better in other films.   And the rags-to-riches thing has been done as well, but in far more realistic terms.  Finally, for a movie that touches on the ethnic-religious tensions of the country, especially as the cause for the dissolution of the family unit -- the separation of the kids from their mother and her implied death -- only to forget about it immediately afterward without so much as a word, seems like such an unforgivable exploitative device.  Jamal seemed more shaken after Salim sold his autographed picture of the movie star.

Overall, this odd hodgepodge of stuff makes for an unsatisfying "best picture".

The movie is mostly told in flashbacks, the main character is appearing on Indiaâs version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, and as each question is asked, he flashes back to an event in his life that led to him appearing on the show. These events trace his life from becoming an orphan, to working with other children begging, to becoming a criminal on his own before growing up and working for a cell phone company and appearing on the show.

slum

The story is great, itâs exciting and touching.  How each event ties into the questions asked on the show are all interesting, and the present-day story taking place in a police station keeps everything moving.  Along with the audience, two police officers are learning more about the main character Jamal and how he went from the slums to television.  Itâs pretty long, but I hardly noticed because the story stayed interesting the whole time.

The acting from the three young children that play the leads when they are small are all amazing.  Whether hanging from trains, singing for food, or running through the slums, they are all sweet and sincere, they are all three great at portraying the children.  I wasnât as impressed with the actors that played them at the medium age.  The actor playing Jamal was great, but his brother wasnât as good.  He seemed very stiff and I thought it was a little distracting whenever he was on the screen.   Again at the oldest age the actors do a great job.  Jamal especially is played by a great actor that does a wonderful job of telling the whole story.  When heâs thinking of the answers for the show, and interacting with the policeman and the showâs host,  he funny and very sincere.

Two last things that I donât usually notice in movies.  The music and the closing credits.  Both are excellent, the music fits each scene extremely well, itâs a good mixture of pop Indian and traditional music.  The closing credits are a combination of a Bollywood dance and cool graphics that were good enough too keep us there until they ended.

Slumdog Millionaire is a really well produced film with great acting and a captivating storyline, but I did have a few issues with the some of the overarching themes.  Suspending the critical lens, it's a great movie -- I can't complain about the flow, the editing, the acting, or anything like that.  There were a few odd directorial choices (money in the bathtub -- why?), but nothing that really detracted from the film.  I do have issues with the construction of 'poverty' type messages in the film -- after watching it a second time (and knowing how it would end), I think the film really oversimplifies the poverty/class issue.  I realize it's supposed to be the remarkable story of one boy, but I don't think it really did enough justice to the complex intersections of culture and class in India.  Postcolonial considerations aside, it is one of the best films of 2009.

Every once in a while a film comes along that picks you up, shakes every emotion out of your body and drops you only to do it all over again. Slumdog Millionaire is one such film. Released among the Oscar contenders and acting giants of Streep, Winslet and Mickey Rourke, this is a feast for all the senses, and quite possibly the most romantic movie I have ever seen.

Not wanting to give too much away, the film is told in flashback, as we follow a teenage Indian boy who has become a contestant on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire and has got further than anyone before him, to the horror or host Anil Kapoor, and we see him being brutally interrogated by the police, explaining how he managed to get the answers right, all the while thinking about his one true love, the stunning Freida Pinto.

Danny Boyle's film is a masterpiece of capturing the essence of a city. He is excited by it, from the colour and vibrancy to the darker side, the violence and brutality, and it is this city that is just as important as the other main characters. Dev Patel, who was last seen in Channel 4's Skins, is a revelation, giving a performance of such maturity that you forget he is acting. 

This isn't an easy journey, the film is littered with some quite shocking scenes, but by the end you are so full of joy and happiness. But it is a journey that is well worth taking and one that will stay for a very long time after. Sublime!

I was actually planning on viewing this film when it was still in theaters, but waited until it came out on DVD, instead. The film was a little confusing at times, and sadly, the film never really grabbed me. Yes, there were some emotional moments, and some intense and exciting moments, but alright. It was a little hard for me to reflect on this film. It was also hard for me to see myself in their footsteps. It seems to me the film revolved around a game show where a contestant seem to know all of the answers because all of the questions that were thrown at him were, well, simply life questions that had occurred sometime during his life. I had no problem with that, but I have to agree with some of the reviewers, some of the flashback scenes were a little too much. I know that the film had to touch base with the current time throughout the film, but it jumped around a little too much for me. Though, I think the better moments of the film occurred during the second half when the main characters were all grown up. The plot and story got more complex, and it was targeted more toward the older audiences. And of course, less flashbacks. Though there were some moments during the first half that young kids should not be exposed to, ie: the scene when one of the child became blind. But overall, the film was insightful in that I did learned a lot about the depressing treatment of poor and Muslim individuals in India, but unlike most of the reviews, I don't think I will be jumping and raving about this film. The film might be different than what we are usually exposed to, and I will probably tuned into other "Bollywood-style" films, but again, the film was just alright with me.

Danny Boyle's deeply implausible film is a beautiful feel-good experience. Young Jamal, a 'slumdog' from the streets of Mumbai is contestant on India's Who Wants to be a Millionaire. He's having a suspiciously good run and is in on the verge of winning the top prize. Suspecting him of fraud, the police interview him and the film explains in flashback how he knows the answer to each question through his own life experiences - playing as a child, surviving a riot, begging and stealing, escaping brutal gangsters and falling in love. The latter being the only reason he went on the show. Its a contrived but fascinating plot structure. Heaping 'real life' tension on top of the suspense that already exists in that particular game show. Its colourful, fast-paced, and romantic. It fully deserves the awards won so far and will get more.

Often when I'm discussing films with people, I'll state that Danny Boyle is a director of great range, only to have some git come back with "Yeah, but he's never directed a love story set in India where the lead character goes on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire and seems to know all of the answers has he?" 

Well, ha!

Now while this film is very much about hope and love, Danny Boyle hasn't forgotten his roots and isn't afraid to show a tough bleak side to this story - as harsh as Trainspotting in places. But what he's done is entwine that beautifully with this story about a boy who is driven only by his love for a girl, and it's a masterpiece from the start. It's very well acted by nobody that most Western audiences will recognise (including me), has a brilliant soundtrack, and is shot with a terrific energy as we witness India itself growing economically alongside the characters. There's little else I can say: it deserves all the hype, it took me through a myriad of emotions and is one of only three films that have ever bought me to tears (Shawshank and Big Fish - in case you were wondering), and I recommend it to everybody. I really hope cinema 2009 continues like this.

A great, gripping, epic drama that is brutally frank about the gap between rich and poor in India and the sometimes shocking behaviour of people at both ends of the social scale. There's action, comedy, a classic tale of love against the odds and some sharp social commentary: the effects of globalization are central to the plot, with its often hilarious call centre  scenes and the internationally familiar game show at the heart of the story. The main flaws for me centre on plausibility; the manner in which the answers to the quiz questions matched episodes in the hero's life in chronological order seemed less plausible to me that it apparently did to the policeman interrogating him. There is an unevenness of tone in the film that is sometimes disconcerting; after lots of harsh realism, it veers oddly into Bollywood territory towards its end. Slumdog Millionaire defies easy genre labelling and, having seen it, I find some of the ways in which it's been described elsewhere downright bizarre. It's been widely tagged as a 'feelgood' film and as a comedy, and certainly it does have an uplifting tale of love, resilience and courage to tell as well as some very funny moments. But be warned: there's also real horror here, including one particularly distressing scene of non-sexual child abuse that I fear will haunt me for a long time. Still, this is a bold and innovative piece of storytelling that really should be seen.

Slumdog Millionaire is one of the best movies to have been produced over the past decade, and it is a work of the highest caliber of cinematic prowess. Danny Boyle's direction on this film is a revelation. He brings his characteristically frenetic, fast-paced style and adapts it to an astounding screenplay penned by Simon Beaufoy (who did a stellar job adapting the novel on which the film is based to the big screen). I can safely say that upon seeing this film for the first time, I was awestruck by the beauty of the film as a whole. It has the stereotypical Hollywood ending everyone is accustomed to, but done in with such refinement that it breaches the boundaries between conventional film making and art. The ensemble cast is remarkable, and lends a great deal of leverage to the overall success of the film. The child actors Boyle selected for the film  shine just as brightly as the adults, if not moreso, and the fact that they were plucked from the slums and featured in the film, only serves to enhance the sense of gritty realism amidst a Hollywood fairytale. Dev Patel was criminally overlooked by the Academy for his performance as the protagonist, Jamal Malik. He deserved at the very least, a nomination for his outstanding turn. All in all, this is one of those rare films that can inspire, and evoke a variety of emotions, without resorting to melancholic theatrics. It will be remembered as Danny Boyle's magnum opus, a work of art that will be very difficult for him to top.

There are movies and there are movies. Some entertain while some are cinematically brilliant but lack mass appeal. And then there are some like âSlumdog Millionaireâ that transcend all barriers and manage to do both.

At its very core âSlumdog Millionaireâ is a magnificent love story, which seems like a fairytale, yet it is so damn realistic and believable. We have all dreamt of the perfect romance, the kind which blossoms and gets better over time like wine. Slumdog Millionaire is living that dream on celluloid for two hours. Itâs about the perseverance of the protagonist, a Mumbai slum kid named Jamal portrayed brilliantly by the two child actors and Dev Patel, to unite with the love of his life â Latika, whom he met, fell in love and was separated from in the direst of circumstances.

Filmed entirely in India, it captures the life, the spirit, the greatness and the follies of the nation and its people in a way, which perhaps no other foreign film has been able to. In fact the excellent production values achieved by this US-UK and Indian joint venture is something that will put many popular Indian film-makers to shame. Of course, it goes without saying that this venture would not shine without the A Grade effort of the Indian crew right from the assistant director to the lower level technicians. The soundtrack composed by A.R. Rehman is a major highlight of the movie. His brilliance in this foreign venture stands out proving that Indian artists can match the best of the best in the business. Each of Rahmanâs composition has the effect of cocaine injected into your blood stream.

The British director, Danny Boyle is clearly the captain of the ship. Slumdog has some clear and refined shades of his other highly acclaimed movie â Trainspotting. But here Boyle outdoes that effort by perfectly understanding the essence of this Indian story, bringing out its soul, thereby brilliantly executing it. In fact, Indian film maker Madhur Bhandarkar would do well to learn a lesson or two on how not to stereo-type and play the same record again and again.

Coming back to the film, the game show, 'Who Wants To Be a Millionaire' hosted by Anil Kapoor is the pivot around which the story revolves. Jamal, a chaiwala in a call center is on the verge of winning the grand prize in this popular show. But how could a chaiwala, a slum boy possibly do that? His euphoria is short lived as he is arrested on suspicion of cheating and interrogated by the police inspector played by Irrfan Khan. The story goes back and forth, with Jamaal revealing his adventurous journey with his elder brother Salim and Latika, the love of his life. The riveting tale starts from the slums of Mumbai. With a glib charm it gives us an engrossing depiction of their turbulent lives which take unanticipated turns time and again. It is commendable how brilliantly plots like the massacre of Muslims and the organized child- begging business are woven into the story. As is often the case to gain audience's sympathy for the characters, the film-makers do not resort to any emotional manipulation even in the most intense scenes. Instead, they establish a strong and resilient central character of Jamal backed up by equally powerful characters of Salim and Latika. Whenever they are in a spot of bother the viewer is rooting for them with all his heart just like in a football match when one supports a minnow against the league champion.

Slumdog millionaire will uplift you to a feel good pedestal where you are less cynical and in a more positive life state. That there is a thing called DESTINY will force even the cynic to think about once he watches this. Of course, destiny always doesnât have to be as over the top as shown in Slumdog but it does exist in everybodyâs life and that the elements of the universe conspire for you to achieve your's.

Maybe in that envelope for the 2009 OSCARS there is a card where it is written : BEST MOTION PICTURE â Slumdog Millionaire.

The best film that I have seen in 2008, "Slumdog Millionaire" runs just like Fernando Meirelles' masterpiece "City of God", both dealing with poverty and life in the slums, but other than that, there is no accurate comparison for the both film whatsoever. The story was character-driven, as the film only have a thin plot. The Indian actors are good, especially the lead, Dev Patel, who played his character very naturally. The "game show", for me, is not a literal one, but it is indeed very symbolic, because the "game" itself is an allegory of the character's life. The use of neorealism is perfect, capturing the slums of Bombay as realistic as possible, showing us the raw features of an impoverished nation. Danny Boyle's directorial transition was amazing, coming from a film about substance abuse(Trainspotting), and a futuristic horror film(28 days later) into a great picture about a romance trapped in the clutches of the slums. And again, ladies and gentlemen, I spotted yet another great use of irony in the film: (BIG SPOILERS AHEAD) the scene where Jamal won the 20 million rupees, it is juxtaposed with his brother Salim being shot and killed by gangsters, while the triumphant music still plays, an image of triumph and tragedy," one stands high, the other falls. It's a shame that due to the occasional use of subtitles and the cultural setting that many people will not watch this incredible film. For the record, the subtitles are easily absorbed and presented in an interesting way. And anyone who passes up the chance to see this side of India is a fool. This may not be where or how I live, but this is my earth and I want to experience all of it that I can. Danny Boyle takes us places and captures them with such honesty that I could help but feel richer for the experience. If not for the fact that someone close to me had visited India  recently and shared their experiences with me I would never have known how accurate the film is. It made the experience much more visceral and concentrated for me.  
The poverty presented in the first chapter of this story is suffocating. It made me very uncomfortable, but I had to keep watching. The cinematography was so unique and engaging that even the outrageous decay and filth that is commonplace in these locations would at times seem beautiful. 
The young actors working in this film are every bit (If not better in my opinion) than the adults portraying the same roles. The kids are incredible. 
The camera work is really fascinating due to the new hardware that Boyle was using. It made it possible for the camera to be closer to the players yet remain hidden so as not to disturb the natural and at times almost "documentary-style" action. And the colour correction is amazing. Incredibly rich Jewel-tones enhance this real world setting and almost make it seem "super-natural". 
The message IS a little syrupy for my tastes, but I buy it. The devices used to explain his success on the quiz show are also dangerously convenient, but I believed it. In the end this IS a fairy tale and I think Boyle handled everything perfectly. 
I don't think that Dev Patel is outstanding enough to garner some of the praise he's getting and believe his younger counterparts actually do more heavy-lifting in the performance department, but he's very good. 
It's simply a very unique and beautifully crafted piece that transports the viewer from a place of little hope to a suspense-filled and heart-swelling climax. It should keep all but the coldest hearts engaged and invested every second along the way. 
(The Bollywood dance number at the end was great fun too)

Hey look! It's an Academy Award Best Picture on my list. You dont see a whole lotta those. Actually, I think we've only encountered one before (and there's another 2 coming). I dont often enjoy the same films as the Academy, but this is one that I was just completely blown away by. It was also one of the Academy Awards I was most excited about because this film was leading the pack and I fully supported it. I cheered for every award it won, and not just because it meant I got another one right for my bragging rights Oscar pool.

When the movie was first released, it generated a lot of buzz. But really, all I needed was the one line summary: Kid is one question away from winning India's version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. How did he do it?. I really had no clue if he was a genius kid, or a cheater, or what, but I was so intrigued. I love movies that revolve around games (non-sports games at least). 

Needless to say, I was absolutely enthralled by the film. I love how the built in suspense of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire was used in the film. When he gave his final "final answer" I remember sitting on the edge of my seat, hand up to my mouth, heart pounding my throat. 

I read the book a few weeks later. The bare bones plot is the same, but so much of it was different. Definitely one of the most Hollywood-ized adaptations, but one of the most successfully done. Yes, it hit on so many cliches, but cliches exist for a reason. They work if dont right, like with Slumdog. Some comparisons to illustrate:
-In the movie, the backstory is magically chronological with the order of questions. They're more random in the book.
-In the book, if I remember right, Latika doesnt actually exist, but there are a couple of girls in his life. One of whom he finds a couple times.
-The book is a lot darker
-The book has a made up game show, whereas the movie uses the iconic Who Wants to Be a Millionaire
-The questions and backstory are pretty much all different, but some of them have the same general theme. On subsequent viewings of the film, the questions/backstory line up actually bothered me because they weren't very clear. (ie, the sequence in the orphanage never gives the poet for the song). They're much more explicit in the book.

The film also made me fall in love with Indian culture. I've never been one who wanted to travel the world, but I would've hopped a plane to India the next day if I had the opportunity. Even with all the underbelly it showed, there is such beauty in the movie. 

There's so many little elements I love too. This one sounds stupid, but I love the way the subtitles are displayed: with colored backgrounds on various parts of the screen. It adds some playful movie magic. The music is fantastic, both the original work by A. R. Rahman and the songs from M.I.A. The cast of unknowns was great. Dev Patel's charm is an arrow right thru my heart. 

Oh we're right at the end now, where she's running for hte phone. My heart is still pounding as much as it was that first time. 

Which now brings us to the final part of the movie, which, as a dancer and choreographer, is obviously my favorite part, the gratuitous Bollywood dance number, Jai Ho. Its inclusion is so cheesey, but you're so swept up in the rest of the film that you dont notice. This dance also made me wanna go and take a bangra class. I did steal a few moves from it when I choroegraphed Bat Boy for the MIT Musical Theatre Guild. I think I've talked about this, but in case I haven't, my concept for the opening number was as much blatant choreo theft as possible to kinda set alot of the tongue-in-cheek comedic tone of the show. So in between combos from "Single Ladies" "Backstreet's Back" "Thriller" and "Bye Bye Bye" were a few Jai Ho moves. When the show was over, one of my cast members actually came and hugged me and thanked me for including the Jai Ho combo.

And with that, it's time to go get dinner

It is easy defending your criticising of a film - mankind has an innate ability to pick out flaws and emphasise them or use them as an excuse for dislike. On the other hand, it can be very difficult defending a film you love.

Slumdog Millionaire is one of those films for me.

I was probably in the same boat as everyone else watching the trailer, jumping to conclusions about the film's look - until I saw Danny Boyle's name. That was when I immediately knew I had to see this film, for Danny Boyle was one of my favourite directors. Now I can safely say he is my favourite director. He is a flawed genius - he can make any film he wants, leave elements of his work in it yet remain under the general public radar. His films are never perfect, but it is almost as if Boyle leaves that slight crease in his films on purpose. I'll never know, but he could just fall short at the final hurdle like he did in Sunshine.

But whereas in Sunshine Boyle took us off on a tangent about two thirds into the film, in Slumdog Millionaire Boyle takes us off on a journey into a much undiscovered country for much of the film-going Western world - India. The word journey there lacks an adjective as you could easily string a hundred words together and still fall short of how much this journey connects with you. It really is a magical and engrossing story that will open your eyes for the entire length.

So starting with the plot - Jamal is one question away from the biggest prize on the Hindi version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire. He is being interrogated by the police, who want to know how a slumdog like himself knows the answers to the questions. It is in answering these questions we are drawn into Jamal's past, starting as a child in the slums. The police inspector and Jamal go through the questions one by one, each one with an engaging story with continuity that thankfully isn't obvious. We see Jamal, his brother Salim and their friend Latika grow up from extreme poverty through adolescence and into their young adulthood.

It is this excellent progression through their lives that drive the film. We grow up with the characters, sympathise with them, laugh with them, and feel each emotion expressed so delicately yet effectively upon every actor's face. We see the rare joys of being in the slums, the pain of loss, the horror of crime, the love of those around you.

But it isn't just the aforementioned that make the film so spectacular. The music helps the film along so well and you actually notice it. Interestingly enough, this film is not about dogs or any other kind of pet you may com across as you walk along the elegant streets of Bombay's up and coming slum district. So I was surprised at first; I was expecting a film inspired by such classic books as Bulgakov's Herat of a Dog or cinematic tales of human/dog bonding (aka mandogding) Old Yeller,  Lady and the Tramp or Lassie. However, it turns out the film combines Dickens's Great Expectations with a bit of Forrest Gump, a dash of Romeo & Juliet and Cinderella to create a wonderful fairy tale, one that adults and children alike can enjoy. I think the fairy tale is the main point of the film; the social commentary on the social conditions in the slums the occasional bursts of ethnic violence and vitality are secondary aspects needed to tell the tale, which gives the film an ultimately optimistic feeling. It is in fact a far different film than City of God, Gomorrah or the best film to explore the slums of Bombay: "salaam Bombay". So if social commentary os what you are after see those; if you want to escape for a few hours in a moern day fairy tale see Slumdog.

This is an amazing movie. In the midst of all the cynic mud of the start of this century (did the century really start?! Or did we simply get stuck somewhere?!), supposedly filled with danger, credit crunches, with disasters around every corner and even the pure event of chance is put in a destructive day light (I'm thinking of "Burn after reading"), Danny Boyle comes with this bomb of a "feel good" movie against the backdrop of a "not so feel good" world, bringing together all facets of today's life that holds grip of today's world (weekend millionaires and cricket) and turns it cunningly into a story that will instantaneously take grip of you within a visually stunning world of color, audio enslavement, Indian curry and not let go of you until the movie ends in a spectacular display of the east meets west mixture style of the end-scores. This is to say that the movie is brilliant from beginning to end.

A brilliant plot, simple in the first instance, but in realz infinitely complex. It tells us the story of two brothers that grow up together in the slums of India. How shocking this world may be, nevertheless, despite all its harshness, does not leave you with a negative expression. In fact, it shows us a micro cosmos of activity where labor equals life, and life being discriminately judgmental and indiscriminately unfair. It also shows us thievery and trickery on all levels as an integral part of the people populating this world, young to old, small joke to big kill. And in the midst of all these deplorable people is our hero - "a guy that always seems to answer the question truthfully" (WOW!). As the two brothers mature their lives become really complicated when money and women come into their lives (One gets obsessed with money, the other with love). From that moment on their fates twists and turns, hopelessly intertwined and influencing one another in all sorts of heart tearing ways (basically all crucial moments of their lives intersect in one way or the other). Along a bit of chance, fortune and misfortune, their relationship reaches a level of epic-ness in its own way, ending fatally for one brother and ending fortunately for the other. The latter getting both the girl and the money, although the money here is not really the point. 

Don't get me wrong, but this movie is really the best movie since Darjeeling limited (coincidentally also shot in India - I'm not one of those India lovers, I never even been to India, and suspect I wouldn't even like the place, but this aside). The movie is well crafted, brilliant in style, but was already a winner in its plot. Simple but complex at the same time; an epic tale of two brothers with an equally epic love story, that will simply never cease to fascinate you in so many ways.

The story of how impoverished Indian teen Jamal Malik became a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?" -- an endeavor made without prize money in mind, rather, an effort to...( read more   ) prove his love for his friend Latika, who is an ardent fan of the show. 

Slumdog Millionaire is the story of Jamal Malik (Patel), an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who is about to experience the biggest day of his life. With the whole nation watching, he is just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India¹s "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?"

But when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a street kid know so much? Desperate to prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika (Pinto), the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of his story reveals the key to the answer to one of the game show¹s questions.

Each chapter of Jamal¹s increasingly layered story reveals where he learned the answers to the show¹s seemingly impossible quizzes. But one question remains a mystery: what is this young man with no apparent desire for riches really doing on the game show?

When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out.

Visually arresting and fully human, Slumdog brought the cinematic goods where it counted. While I'm not sure the extensive word-of-mouth wonderment is entirely deserved, I do believe this is a solid, well-written, and tight piece of film. The three parallel narratives lined up perfectly and eventually coalesced into a satisfying conclusion. Tragedy was overcome, and destined love eventually won out in romantic, poetic form.
      ...However, I believe in part this is where I got a bit lost. While the romance at the heart of this story felt developed, I also thought it was a bit inconsistent from point to point, and that, in the end it relied too heavily on the "It Is Written" mechanic. Apart from that quibble, some questionable casting led to a couple unfortunate breaks in my immersion (Salim as a teenager and Salim as an adult are completely different looking individuals) which distracted me too much from the rich story. In addition, I'm afraid that the clever Bollywood credits send-up took me too soon out of the true weightiness of this movie, tossing me into a jolting and cheesy finale that I felt was incompatible with my movie experience.
     However, these complaints are mostly overwhelmed by the sheer cinematic virtuosity that is Slumdog Millionaire. Camera angles, elaborate real-world settings, a thrilling soundtrack, wonderful acting, and a multi-layered set of characters make this Slumdog well worth getting to know.

Danny Boyle must be God. He must be. There is no other explanation I can come up with. Time and time again he tackles genre after genre and just nails it every time.

This was utterly exceptional. I'm still in awe, truly. 

I'll be honest, I'm not especially cultured, and my knowledge of the history of Mumbai is somewhat limited - I've never gone out of my way to learn of its culture and society, and I know of it and its struggles only from the media.... Boyle obviously knew this would be the case when presenting this issue to a largely Western audience, and it proved interesting to learn of his take on the issues.

Boyle's direction (as always) is utterly flawless here. The cuts from past to present, back to the past are seemless, and the narrative flows in this fashion for a good 2 hours.

I got so wrapped up in Jamal's story, that I ended up crying for no real reason half way through other than I did that thing that all directors strive to do - touch an audience and make an impression. And I, for one, was VERY impressed.

Visually, this was outstanding. I've always had something of a fascination with Indian culture, and the journey of Jamal, Salim and Latika moved through their lives and how as they grewup they encountred different aspects of their own society. Often the darker, sinister side. This was paralled accordingly with the sinsiter aspects of TV gam shows, and you couldn't help but feel that Jamal was a fish out of water in the life style he was playing to be a part of.

My hat goes off to the actors. Especially the children. Seriously, I've not been so impressed in a very long time.

I watched an intervew with Boyle last night where he was telling how Bollywood directors in particular see their jobs as 'Dream Makers' and that the films they make are their 'dreams' - he told how 'Slumdog' was his own personal take on the Indian 'dream' - an you have to remember that ultimately, although the film is incredibly hard hitting, this is actually a feel good film. And my god, do you feel good at the end! It's so high spirited! The dancing in the credits has received a fair amount of criticism, but people are clearly missing this point.

Absolutely loved this film, and it deserves as much praise as it is sure to receive. My only concern is that it does seem to be a tad long.... and due to the nature of such a story, I don't think I could find myself sitting thgh it any time soon.... such stories are always excellent, but this was very hard-hitting.... so I'll give it a few months!

Initial Score: 9.4
 
 -It's as much of the ultimate romance film showing the lengths of what 2 people destined to be with each other will go to as it is the ultimate rags to riches story depicting the harsh reality that is living in the slums of India.
         
         -Simon Beaufoy deserves much praise for creating such a well woven script that blends lots of things together nicely while Danny Boyle deserves equal credit for so elegantly guiding the audience with his signature cinematic flair. What immediately struck me as brilliant was how the flashbacks were used as the anchor for most of the movie while also being a bridge between Jamal's harsh life as a slumdog and his present day situation. I appreciated how the movie shifted focus several times but only when necessary in accordance to Jamal's account and the journey never felt rushed nor dragged for even a single second, everything was perfectly paced.
         
         -Still probably in his teen years just so much is captured throughout the films running time Jamal and company experience so much and if ever a film can make you laugh, gasp, and cheer for the protagonist this is it. Boyle does a hell of a job capturing the brutality of living in India and how life just shits on you constantly but never did any part of the film begin to approach being preachy or too heavy handed. 
         
         -The cast is just as colorful and talented as the scenes Boyle chooses to showcase the beauty of India with. Dev Patal really stole it for me he was the Heath Ledger of slumdog, Madhur Mittal did a great evil yet ultimately compassionate brother, Frieda Pinto balanced out Jamal nicely, Anil Kapoor was so entertaining for every minute of his screen time. Irrfan Khan played an overly harsh but well intentioned police inspector, even Saraubh Shukla was a damn good bumbling idiot sidekick archetype.
         
         -the finale is everything a finale should be; a stunning culmination of everything the film was building up towards that provided a supremely satisfying ending following a great twist.
        
        -Favorite scenes: Salim witnessing the blinding of his peer and not wishing it on his brother, the bathroom conversation between Jamal and game show host, Latika's race to get her cellphone, and Salim giving Latika the keys whispering "have a good life".
      
      -The soundtrack was phenomenal it helped modernize the film, added a good punch to many scenes, and you have to be deaf and dead to not enjoy such a mix of homage and originality.
         
         -The emotional response and enjoyment the experience of this film prompts from me is exactly the reason I have such a passion for film in the first place, this is an honest and soul satisfying experience without any true flaw to mar the after taste whatsoever. In the face of so much tragedy and unforgiving reality slumdog perfectly captures the jostling energy of India leaving me in a pleasantly upbeat mood as I'm sure was Boyle's intention.

An incredible film from director Danny Boyle who, let's face it, hasn't made an engaging film since the 1996 sensation that was Trainspotting. Slumdog is an entirely different looking film, as you would expect given the subject matter, but is directed with such grace and ingenuity that it surprised me that a British director could achieve such a visionary look to a motion picture. The leads are sensational and every minute of the 2 hour run time is gripping whether it's in its emotional intensity (Jamal's desperate search for Latika) or indeed for the visceral nature of the slums themselves and the painfully real sequence in which the young boy is blinded by authority. Back that up with the simplicity of using the now world famous Who wants to be a millionaire backdrop for the story and the edge of your seat moments in the final act of the film and you've got a film that ticks all the artistic boxes. To say this is already one of the films of the year is no hyperbole. It's only January in 2009 but with this and Benjamin Button coming to our screens soon it looks like we've got some amazing films to look forward to this year. Oscar bound and highly recommended. i went to see this with a few friends, so it wasn't so much a movie i wanted to see as it was a movie i didn't object to seeing, and went to see more for the social element, heh.  not bad, but highly overrated- i really don't get what all the hype/fuss is about on this one.

i'm not sure if it's because india is on people's minds with the recent mumbai terror attacks or if it's the depiction of poverty and abject squalor , combined with themes of redemption and destiny, that drew people to this one.

my objections to the movie are several fold- i don't think this particularly ruins anything, but it will colour your perceptions if you read this before watching the movie, so keep that in mind.

firstly, much of the tension comes from the gameshow that the main character is participating in- and i feel this sort of "cheapens" the effect as it feels very contrived.  the flashback/explanation of question-answering as a narrative vehicle doesn't really work for me.  i just don't feel at all like i'm dying to know the story behind each successive question.

secondly, the characters start off as street-savvy beggars and urchins but eventually seem to become less and less street-smart.  certainly, the main character seems to become increasingly obsessed with the object of his chase to the point that he just looks doe-eyed and stupid- not the crafty tough slumdog he's supposed to be.  this is partly the fault of the actors' performances and partly the fault of the story.

the actual story is very "fairy-tale"y and ordinary, and so if the narrative gimmick doesn't work for you, you're left with little else.  the whole black-and-whiteness of the two brothers and the "evil" brother's eventual salvation was not at all unexpected.

anyway, it's not a "bad" movie per se, but it's not the greatest thing ever, and by far not the most original or "honest" or whatnot.  perhaps it's because it is able to strike a balance between mild cleverness in its storytelling and emotional heart-tugging elements that it has achieved such broad appeal.

(60/100) Summary Judgment: The plot and panache of a great 80s video but lengthened 6000%. Fernando Meirelles in Mumbai=CITY OF GODS. Fairy tale in modern dress.
On paper I should like this movie: CITY OF GOD is one of my favorite movies (but I can also enjoy less glossy presentations of squalor, e.g., CHOP SHOP);  I enjoyed Danny Boyle's first two movies; I can't take my eyes off Bollywood musicals when they are on in the background (though I can't imagine ever sitting down to one), which probably explains why the credits are almost my favorite scene. The movie is energetic, colorful, and novel in compositional content. I even like the idea of the framing device, though it probably drains momentum.
And yet...and yet this movie literally bored me to tears (and put my wife to sleep). The overall plot is so obvious I felt like I was watching it for the third time on my first time through and this made for a very long two hours--the movie felt like it was three hours to me. The details of the plot are so ridiculously contrived it made FORREST GUMP seem like cinema verite. But that is not necessarily a problem if the segments were enjoyable, unfortunately they only rarely are. It seems like about 50% of this movie is literally kids running away from something. (I find that a boring substitute for something actually happening so maybe that's why I don't like his zombie movies either.) The backdrop of modern India is very interesting and the true draw of the film, unfortunately this movie is no more about modern India than Ian McKellen's RICHARD III is about Nazi Germany--this is an ancient fairy tale in modern dress. Like MAN ON WIRE, this movie seemed to obscure what I actually found most interesting with the parts I was interested in the least.

"Slumdog Millionaire" restores my faith in the invigorating power of movies. It is a kinetic, frenzied thriller with a central love story as affecting and romantic as any that has come out of Hollywood. Danny Boyle's lightning fast directing and the spliced together editing--even the grittiness of the images--combine for a cumulative explosion of invention, joy, and uplift. This is why we go to the movies. As Jamal Malik, a poor Indian teenager who captures his nation's attention when he has an astonishing stroke of luck of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire," handsome Dev Patel gives an honest, earnest performance. The whereabouts of his love, Latika, played by the striking Freida Pinto, are unknown. Is she alive? If so, is she safe? The film intercuts scenes of Jamal on "Millionaire" with the exhilarating events of his life, and those final minutes as we anticipate whether his final lifeline--a telephone call--will be answered are agonizing and thrilling. Boyle crafts a one-of-a-kind spectacle here, and has been rewarded copiously for it. The awards and accolades are justified. This is the year's best movie.

Slumdog millionaire  - Warning Spoiler Alerts 
On hearing about how Slumdog millionaire was getting rave reviews in the west , I was damn excited and ran helter skelter to check out the movie .  My main thoughts was that the movie is based in Mumbai  and directed by somebody like Danny Boyle so it would be really an awesome experience.  
Also seeing some promos and  I loved the fact that the movie looked âIndianâ from the colors and people and the shots . 
So you can imagine my disappointment on finally seeing the movie !!! 
Let me explain
Some question for Mr. Boyle 
Why is it that Irfan Khan and Saurabh shukla speak exactly how an Indian would speak English  and our very own Slumdog  Patel bhai speaks English in a pure Brit accent ? 
Why is it that the cops, brother , goondas  can mouth M@#$%#od  every 2nd minute and our pure bred Slumdog doesnât even utter the word even once!  Even his brother speaks like how an Indian would speak english .     I understand that the movie is in English and characters will speak English  but then let everybody be equal , why to effect a pseudo realism by differentiating the characters by their accents ? 
The younger versions of the protagonists speak proper Mumbai hindi and suddenly everything changes ?   If Danny wanted he could have taken ,  instead of Dev,  a proper Mumbai born and bred actor, just like he allowed Loveleen Tandon to cast the younger versions , but he didnât . 
Coming to the aspects of stereotyping â the movie was replete with the Indian stereotype. 
Do Indians consider the Taj Mahal as a monument which they look up to or pray at  times of severe duress?  I donât think so , then why shots of Taj were used so extensively during the critical juncture of the movie ( the final question at KBC). 
The Amitabh Bacchan fixation â Again !!!  but I will let it pass as it was shown very nicely and the young guy really made it believable . 
The stark reality of Mumbai life coupled with the vibrant colour depicted , I read , was one of the most liked aspect of the movie  - but I ask havenât we seen this  all in our homegrown movies like Satya , Ek challis ki last local, Mumbai Meri Jaan  etc  the stereo type of the  stodgy disgusting policewallah, the  brothel sequences, the menacing underworld don, the unrepenting gun-shots , brother kill brother sequences , money=power sequences , rape etc  all these have been shown and shown better in some of our  movies already .  In fact if this style of filmmaking was released in India in the pre Satya days then it would have been a landmark cinema - no denying it . But in 2008 , for a viewer like me who sees almost every movie released , it is not something he hasnât seen already. 
Finally , why did they have to put the Bollywoodish dance sequence during the end credit !!!   at that point I felt that the director is trying to make fun of Indian Cinema as it felt so out of place and forcefitted. 
You may say that I am nitpicking, but I would say NO â nitpicking would be when I comment on things like we all know that KBC was never a live event and always prerecorded then why was it shown like being live ? anyways that was required for the flow and I understand that some cinematic liberty is ok. 
Anyways now letâs come to the things which really stand out in the movie . 
The first thing is that  the director credits the audience with some degree of intelligence in simple shots like , when the protagonists see each other  or speak to each after a long time they recognize each other immediately .  This is very unlike normal Indian movies where brothers / couples/father and son donât recognize each other if they are separated for couple of years!    Lots of things are left for the audience to assume  which I feel is a very nice touch.  Small things like this make the movie stand out.  
Most important -  The music ..wow .. Rahmanâs mark is all over the movie in every shot . In fact I think it is the background score which generates suitable excitement and tension at the right places . It is the music which stitches the narrative together . 

Having said that , the movie overall didnât appeal to me for the mere sake that it didnât feel different .  Which I really expected it to be .   But I am sure that the western audiences will be lapping it up as it gives them a completely different was of story telling , vibrant colours and a cinema which is pretty exotic for them.   
As for me , I just hope that Indian media doesnât overdo the hype once Slumdog wins awards as if it is an Indian Achievement .    
The only award which they should hold dear would be if Rahman wins  which would truly Indian achievement and very well deserved , rest of the awards will be the achievement of the West only for a movie which has only used an Indian theme for the western audience . "You don't have to be a genius."

Slumdog Millionaire
Director: Danny Boyle
Actors: Dev Patel, Freida Pinto

Slumdog Millionaire tells the humble tale of Jamal Malik, a seemingly ordinary chai-wallah, who is boosted to stardom in IndiaÃ¢s take on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire.  This story, reminiscent of the poor and aspiring youth Aladdin, describes the importance of fate and destiny - two idealized concepts which usually make for soppy romances and predictable storylines.  Thankfully, Danny Boyle masterfully breaks this rampant cliche in delivering one of 2008's classics.

The story begins in a rather horrifying setting, stapling a expression of shock and surprise on the faces of seemingly 'storyline-informed' viewers.  Boyle masterfully uses his iconic style to set the scenes of a film that is vigorous, fast on its feet and spiritedly beautiful. The cinematography is strangely imperceptible.  The rapid, hand-held effect captures the essence of the slums in India - an environment which is chaotic in its density and livelihood.  The spirit of these slums is further enhanced by A.R. Rahman's magical soundtrack. The pace of those electrifying percussive/hip-hop Indian songs creates one of cinema's most perfectly integrated OSTs.

The plot is something amazing. The original source of Vikus SwarupÃ¢s novel 'Q & A' must have been breathtaking to allow for the creation of Ã¢Slumdog MillionaireÃ¢.  The constant shift between past and present, between memories and answers creates one of the most original and compelling dynamics. 
The film is blessed with some heart-warming performances from the children playing Jamal and Salim. Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, the adorable, cheeky-faced (pooh-covered) version of Jamal, gives one of the films greatest performances. For such a young talent to upstage the rest of the cast is astounding.  However, that does not mean the rest of the cast act with lesser brilliance. Collectively the performances are amazing. The chemistry between the fated lovebirds, Jamal and Latika, throughout the film and throughout their lives is captivating. Their performance further justifies JamalÃ¢s seemingly naive search for his one true love.

Boyle could not help but give the film its final jolt - a Bollywood routine. After all, an Indian hit smashing through the American box office and most coveted awards needs to exude what is loved about Indian cinema the most!

Slumdog Millionaire is an highly entertaining, emotionally resonant love story where friendship and hope triumph over corruption and poverty. Its plot is utterly contrived, but because its focus is fate, it works. 
Oscar winning director Danny Boyle strikes the perfect balance between style and nuance, and with great cinematography and editing, a talented cast of varying ages, and a fantastic soundtrack, creates a high-energy ride that's most of all, a whole lot of fun. What's striking is how much humanity is celebrated despite the film's characters being subject to so much violence and depravation. It's a Dickensian story, with an orphan protagonist who comes to riches and love through a series of serendipitous events. It's a romance, and action flick, and a redemption tale, and much heart and humour punctuate it throughout. Really, people of all ages will enjoy Slumdog, and that wide appeal landed it the Oscar for Best Picture.

Although you wouldn't typecast Danny Boyle in a particular genre of film you wouldn't expect him make a feel good movie set in India.  Slumdog Millionaire uses flashbacks in a simple but clever way.  Jamal is a young man who grew up in the slums of Mumbai, he finds himself one question away from wining the Jackpot on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?"  As the program finishes for the evening Jamal is arrested and questioned as the host suspects him of cheating.  What unfolds as he is questioned is incidents in his life that gave him the knowledge to answer the questions to get to this point.  The scenarios are dramatic, tragic and comic and all add to the flavour of the film and the depth of the characters.  What also develops in the flashbacks is the relationship between Jamal, his brother Salim and Latika a young girl they befriend and Jamal's reason for being on the program.   The three main characters are played by three different actors each allowing for different ages.  All do a really good job in what for most of them is their first film.  The photography is stunning making full use of the locations.  The editing and direction are sharp and fast keeping the viewer interested and emotionally involved with the characters.  This is a film that most people will enjoy.

This movie proves that even a cynical pessimist such as myself can enjoy an uplifting story, properly told. There's never any real doubt as to the outcome, but it is still fun to root for Jamal to overcome all obstacles. Highly recommended.

The whole idea of a kid being a "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" champ/following his life story in poor India is intriguing, and it works on several levels, but not all. Once I got that idea in my head, things started to work a bit better, but there were still problems. The main characters as little kids/preteens were great, but as adults the acting was a little stiff. The main guy acted well when on the millionaire show or being interrogated because he seemed nervous, but it didn't translate as well when he was just in normal situations. The cinematography, while colorful and fun, got a little overbearing at times with some tilted dutch angles, but it never got on my nerves. Other than that, the film is a good time. Not perfect. Not even great. But I knew that I would at least like it from word go. It's a good mix of cuteness and grittiness, and it's definitely the best date movie of the year. When the unlikely Jamal (Patel) gets through round-upon-round of India's Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?, he is arrested for cheating. During the interrogation, as he tells his tragic life story, it seems fate may be calling the shots...

Danny Boyle somewhat broke the mould with his now iconic film "Trainspotting" where his own unique talent for bringing music and film to life were demonstrated loud and clear.

So here we have a film which, at first glance, may not sound completely inspiring- a story of a kid who wins the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? Yet here we have a film so vibrant and celebratory of life's ups and downs, that it's almost a rollercoaster of emotions set against the backdrop of the Indian slums- and Boyle does this to perfection.

It's a film cleverly balanced between the light-hearted tension of the Millionaire rounds, and the essential essence of the film- Jamal's life-affirming moments in his pretty harsh life. It's a film which uses music brilliantly, a film that is always on the move and always full of shocks and surprises.

With nods both to Boyle's previous efforts (the Indian call-centre training session of the latest Eastenders episode is particularly amusing) and even the superb "City of God", "Slumdog Millionaire" is an astounding achievement and a film which has that rare gift of being both poignant and uplifting.

Easily Boyle's best effort since the landmark "Trainspotting".

There is a difference between clever film-making and great film-making. Make no mistake, Danny Boyle is immensely clever. Slumdog Millionaire is made as an out-and-out crowd-pleaser through proper audience-targetting which is done in the same careful way the Chopras target the lovey-dovey high school/college crowd and the Anil Sharmas target the uber-patriots.

This crowd-pleasing is done through punching together as many stereotypes that Westerners have about India as is humanly possible. People live in garbage heaps.  A character jumps into a huge heap of human excreta and without batting an eyelid comes running out covered in brown slime, as if its the most natural thing in India, to get an autograph of a star.  The hero, a Muslim, sees his family slaughtered by Hindu rioters and sees along with it a rioting kid (presumably) dressed as Lord Rama, in blue paint and with a bow and arrow in hand, standing as a sentinel of doom, an image whose indelibility in the characters mind becomes a principal plot point.

A character is booked on the flimsiest of charges and then he is beaten black and blue in a police station and given volts of electricity.

What else? Lets see.

Child prostitution. Check.

Forced begging. Check.

Blindings of innocent children. Check.

Rape. Check.

Human filth. Bahoot hain sahab.

Call centers. Oh yes most certainly.

Destiny. Of course
 
Well yes these things do happen in India. However the problem is when you show every hellish thing possible all happening to the same person. Then it stretches reason and believability and just looks like you are packing in every negative thing that Westerners perceive about India for the sake of crowd pleasing. Because audiences and jury members feel good when their pre-conceived notions are confirmed. On the flip side, nothing disquiets a viewer as much as when his/her prejudices are challenged. So Boyle does the safe thing.

Lets say I made a movie about the US where an African-American boy born in the hood, has his mother sell him to a pedophile pop icon, after which he gets molested by a priest from his church, following which he gets tied up to the back of a truck and dragged on the road by KKK clansmen. Then he is arrested and sodomized by a policeman with a rod, after which he is attacked by a gang of illegal immigrants, and then uses these life experiences to win Beauty and Geek.

A highly enjoyable and rewarding rags to riches tale featuring a strong cast, impressive cinematography and an inventive and gripping story.

After successful attempts at working with the horror and sci-fi genres with 28 Days Later and Sunshine, Danny Boyle returns with this charming, rags to riches tale and using the energy and inventiveness of Trainspotting that has only briefly been seen in his later films.  Slumdog Millionaire, based on the novel Q&A, is the tale of Jamal, a boy who grew up in the slums of Mumbai and whose life-experiences seem destined to provide him with the all the answers to achieving riches he couldnât imagine by winning Indiaâs version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire?  Of course, the show runnerâs cannot accept that a boy like Jamal could possibly have all the answers without cheating; he is taken by police and interrogated.  It is here that the story begins as, through extended flashbacks, Jamal tells the tale of his life and how each major incident provided him with the answers he needed to win.  

While the plot might seem somewhat contrived, every question asked of Jamal on the show seemingly relating to a significant life experience, the execution of the story by Boyle, the performances of its cast and its hyper-kinetic cinematography make Slumdog Millionaire such a joy to watch that any concerns over the overwhelming coincidences you are asked to accept are accepted and willingly so.  Living in the slums of Mumbai, with his life involving losing his mother, being taken in by a group of child slavers, living on the streets and always by his wits, Jamalâs story and that of his brother Salim and love-interest Latika, might feel like the kind of story that should be shocking and depressing and some scenes are shocking and heart-breaking to witness.  However, Slumdog Millionaire is also infused with hope and warmth.  

Jamal, played by three actors at different places in his life, all portray him as a character with optimism, with conviction that heâll find what heâs looking for and that involves a life with Latika, the young girl of which he is separated from and reunited with several times.  An early scene from his childhood speaks volumes about his character and the journey in which he is to embark upon when, locked in outdoor toilet in the slums of Mumbai (easily worse than âThe Worst Toilet in Scotlandâ scene from Trainspotting), he leaps into human waste as his only hope for escape and manages to get through a crowd of people gathered around his childhood hero, a famous actor, and secure an autograph with a cry of success.  Jamalâs success, despite the sacrifices he had to take to achieve it, and the happiness he feels regardless of the cost gives the audience a sense that no matter how tragic Jamalâs story might sometimes become, he is destined for success and happiness by the filmâs end.  Less hopeful is the role of Salim, Jamalâs older brother whose envy of Jamalâs attitude and rewards leads him down a darker path of crime but who is still to redeem himself for life and his treatment of Jamal and Latika.  In addition to the fine casting of the three child leads, Dev Patel in particular that plays the present day Jamal telling us his story, are also several adult roles.  Anil Kapoor plays a somewhat slimy role in Indiaâs answer to Chris Tarrant as his TV presenter is one whose motives remain murky yet hides them in public with a smile and a cheer.  Also interesting is the role of the police inspector played by Irrfan Khan, who despite engaging in unpleasant methods to get answers from Jamal in early scenes manages to present his character as someone who is also reasonable and open to hearing Jamalâs tale.

As well as the strong acting performances and a gripping script, Danny Boyleâs direction of the events is impressive.  With the aid of a pulse-pounding score by A. R. Rahman, Boyleâs directing style here is his most inventive and hyper-kinetic since Trainspotting.  Inter-cutting moments between present day events, Jamalâs story and brief glimpses back and forth of other glimpses like brief, fleeting memories mixed into recollections and with the use of whip-pan camera moves with handheld, in the midst of the action feel, Slumdog Millionaire also keeps you as much on your toes with its camera work and beautiful scenery, capturing the growth of a country as well as the growth of a boy, as it does with its story.

Overall, Slumdog Millionaire is highly entertaining.  Great to look at with story, mood and characters that both grip and warm you, the film deserves is hype as a feel-good film and also marks Boyleâs most impressive work since Trainspotting hailed him as the future of British filmmaking in 1996.  A must see film.

I really didn't know anything about this movie since the trailer left basically everything to the imagination. All I knew is that it was going to be good, obviously. 

The story was so emotional. It had tons and tons of layers on all different aspects of life, so much that it was overwhelming at times and hard to comprehend. In most movies you can sort of relate or put yourself in the characters shoes, but when you see such a truthful, blunt story like this it's nearly impossible. Yet at the same time the overall message of just never giving up no matter how many times you're knocked back was easy to relate to. 

I think the most amazing part of this story is the fact that they're trying to tell people that life experiences matter. Relationships matter. The things that make you what you are matter. Not going to college, or even being educated, or having a great career. It's about who you are and what you stand for. 

I loved that nothing was glazed over or taken down a notch. The violent, difficult, gruesome story was told and shown to its full extent. It was like the things that haunted the characters lives would also haunt you as you watched. 

The cinematography was wonderful, the bright colors against the browns. The way they worked in slow motion and especially the flashbacks, those were the most powerful. 

My favorite part of this is the very end. It's so emotionally overwhelming and everything that happened is sort of thrown in your face. 

And I must say the original songs and the soundtrack in general was absolutely perfect. 

I could go on and on, but everyone already knows it's amazing. A must see, of course.

Danny Boyle attempts an interesting exercise: take a Bollywood movie, but tell it straight. There's all the elements of a great Bollywood flick in this one: the tragedy, comedy, hope, rags-to-riches storyline, the villains, hero, the girl, even the over-the-top side character. But in telling it straight, this becomes highly moving and affecting, even as bits of it slide into cheap stereotype. As much as Benjamin Button was an elegy on death and mutability, Slumdog Millionaire is a stark ray of hope despite the despair. Shot almost entirely in Mumbai, that sense of hope is brutally ironic, yet somehow also uplifting. I loved it! Glad to see it won as many Gloden Globes as it did, and I certainly hope it will do well at the Oscars. It deserves to!

A full throttle blast of cinematic joy.  On paper, a story about an Indian lower class young man who winds up on their country's version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" doesn't exactly sound like your typical Best Picture material.  However, credit both screenwriter and director here.  Credit the entire cast and crew, for that matter.  This is a collaboration in which almost everything works, from the amazing, hyperkinetic tracking shots through the streets of Mumbai to the pulse-pounding soundtrack to the colorful palette painting every frame of this film.  Even so, its really something that Danny Boyle pulls this off so effortlessly.  Let's be honest -- this is a farfetched fairy tale through-and-through, a film you'd expect Baz Luhrmann to tackle.  Yet Boyle sells you on everything he needs you to buy, and by the time the final question is asked of Jamal, its hard to believe many viewers won't be at the edge of their seat with a lot invested.

When i first heard about this film i wasn't interested at all. Then came all the Awards buzz and i'll admit i felt compelled to see it and i was suprised that i really did enjoy it. What i thought was great about the film was that paced wise it was excellent and it was clear that the story had been very very well planned.

There were three timelines going on at the same time in parts of the film and it didn't get mis-judged or anything and the audience were always clear of what was going on where. I thought the idea of a game show would be awful, but infact it was used very well as a narrative device to show certain parts of the backstory of the main character. I thought that was very clever and original.

However there were some elements of the narrative that i wasn't fond of. I didn't like how it just jumped between the main love romance, being together, then apart, then together, then apart. Also the secondary character kept flirting with being nice and then evil, then nice again, then evil. Quite a bit of repetition. 

The way it was shot was very nice, utilizing the close surroundings to make it feel more intimate using the shaky camera i think worked very well for the scenes and tone of the film. 

Acting wise, i don't think Dev Patel was the best choice for the film. Many people have been positive about him but i cannot see it. He seemed very wooden. The younger actor playing the child version i think showed him up in the acting department. 

Overall it's a nice suprise of a film which i think catches everyone  off guard. It's very clever and well planned out with a good solid story basis. However being touted as the "Feel Good Film Of The Decade" is just a lie. It's not THAT good.

I've been hearing nothing but great things about "Slumdog Millionaire" since last summer, and now having seen it, I can truly attest to its greatness. Not since "City of God" have I seen a film as electrifying and mesmerizing as this. A simple rags-to-riches tale crafted and told beautifully on screen, with gorgeous cinematography, great acting and an awesome soundtrack (which is now playing on my iPod). Most of the year's film's have centered on depressing themes and endings that make us question the state of our humanity, but "Slumdog" does the exact opposite by reminding us that even in the poorest parts of the world, hope and love can overcome all obstacles. Like the film's hero Jamal, you'd never believe that the film would amount to much from the premise (being set in India's poorest slums and centered around "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire"), but it succeeds on so many levels. It will have you laughing and crying throughout, and will leave you with a feeling of joy inside once it ends. Easily deserves the title of best film of the year if not best film of all time! Everyone... GO SEE THIS AS SOON AS POSSIBLE. You will not be let down!

Damn straight! A romance movie in the third world; instead of the couple facing stupidly simple obstacles such as "the parents don't like him" or "she's engaged to be married," Jamal and Latika face truly insurmountable obstacles in their romance (child prostitution, child slavery, death of the parents at an early age, etc.,) However, it is always completely certain that Jamal and Latika will get together at the end. Such a melodramatically predictable ending would be a silver bullet for any other film, but in Slumdog it works; the viewer is constantly reminded that even when things might seem impossible for our heroes, everything will eventually work out OK. As the film suggests during its opening "trailer," Jamal's eventual success in both his participation in Who wants to be a Millionaire and his love of Latika "is written" into the very fabric of Jamal's life.  In most films the idea of "fate" is vilified, an barrier that must be destroyed but in SLumdog it is a comforting, driving force behind all of Jamal's life. Slumdog Millionaire is unique and wonderful film, undoubtably the best of the year. A masterpiece from one of my personal favorite directors, Danny Boyle (go see Sunshine and 28 days later!)

I had heard some grumbling about this movie being overrated, and unrealistic, but until about halfway through the movie, despite enjoying myself, I was willing to give it maybe 9 stars out of 10. But then it became more than the story of a couple of kids from the slums - it became a great retelling of two ancient stories: the kid from humble beginnings who makes history, and the boy who gets the girl, loses the girl, and...well, let's not spoil it, shall we? The second half, as we see the protagonists mature, combined with the climactic finale of the game show, is easily one of the best pieces of film I have ever seen in my life.

Yes, Slumdog Millionaire is incredibly unrealistic. Let's be frank, even giving generous leeway for coincidence, there is no way this could have happened. The women featured in the movie are nearly always perfectly pretty; the prominent usage of perfect English is extremely unrealistic; there is just no way Jamal's life could have worked out in such a way that he would know the right answers.

But if you think this is a criticism of the film, all I can say is that I'm really quite sorry for how seriously you take yourself. Great stories are not about the real world; great stories tell us about a world that could be, and make it seem almost as real to us as the world we live in. Slumdog Millionaire is a fairy tale for the ages, and for all its unrealism, is an uplifting and inspiring story of determination, love, and destiny. While I would say that I am often too eager to cut films some slack and give them 10 out of 10 just because I enjoyed myself thoroughly watching them, I have no qualms about giving Slumdog Millionaire a perfect 10. I would give it 11 if I could. This is a movie that deserves it.

It's one thing to have a fairy tale. It's something completely different to have a fairy tale [b]done right[/b]. Slumdog Millionaire is that completely different something.
 
Slumdog Millionaire is about an Indian boy named Jamal Malik, an uneducated street kid who finds himself one question away from winning the final prize (20 million rupees) on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." However, he gets thrown in jail because they think he cheated. There's no way some punk kid could've known all of those answers...right?
 
This is where the incredible storytelling comes in. To prove he's innocent, he tells the story of his life, from witnessing the death of his mother to adventures with his brother Salim. He's able to describe in detail how he knew the answer to each "Millionaire" question through the various events he's been through in his life. The answers are so subtly presented within the story, and feel so minor in comparison to the situations he finds himself in. The visuals are stunning enough to leave you tense with anticipation.
 
They could've overdone it with the romance, but they didn't. Jamal meets Latika after the death of their families. They keep getting separated throughout the movie, going for years without seeing each other, yet they never forget each other. Other than when they're young, there's no emphasis on developing their relationship. The rest of the way it's driven purely by his idea of her; his desire to be with her. It's Jamal's quest to not let anything stand in the way of him reuniting with Latika, and the movie isn't cheesy about it. 
 
Using flashbacks to tell the story of this kid from the slums is smoother than I have ever seen. The fusion of real time, flashbacks from the game and flashbacks to Jamal's childhood is seamlessly brilliant. There's never a dull moment, and it's one of those rare films that evokes the entire range of emotions. It also captures and engages you in a culture completely different from America's. I couldn't help but think about Benjamin Button while writing this because of its great flashback element. However, Slumdog seemed to do the same thing, but did it better and in a shorter amount of time. Slumdog Awesomeness.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is rich with so many magnificent qualities: It is a vibrant, inspiring, and audacious film. And it just might be the apex of cinematic releases for the film year 2008. "Slumdog Millionaire" is the story of impoverished Indian teen Jamal Malik's Dickens-like life adventure during his childhood and juvenile years; from his turbulent childhood in India's slums to his destined juvenile experience of being a game show contestant of India's version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" Director Danny Boyle does a divine job of orchestrating on how Jamal is able to answer Millionaire questions correctly by Jamal's adventurous "lifeline" childhood & youthful slum experiences; the two interrelated juxtaposed narrative structures is the storytelling nature of "Slumdog Millionaire". Jamal and his older brother Salim together go through many childhood slum trials & tribulations and evade seizure & mortality in the most unique ways. Salim as he grows older eventually ventures into the bad seed of living a thug life, while genuine Jamal turns the other cheek and is just focused on living a love life. You see Jamal's foremost drive is to reunite with the love of his life Lakita, which he befriended as a child but were separated in a slum escape from some horrific opportunistic criminals. Jamal as a young man does eventually find the beautiful Lakita and is aware that she is an avid fan of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" Therefore, that is what leads our main slumdog Jamal to the game show experience. India's law enforcement is dubious on how a slumdog like Jamal can answers questions correctly on the game show, so they shake up Jamal a bit. Jamal then has no other choice but to tell his life story to them and fortunately for our cinematic delight to us viewers also. Dev Patel as Jamal was no slum in his motion picture acting debut with his brilliant performance. Anil Kapoor was captivating as Millionaire host Prem Kumar; and the steady veteran Indian actor Irrfan Khan did contribute yet another admirable performance to his underrated acting resume. The drop dead gorgeous Freida Pinto not only paints a pretty picture as an Indian sex symbol but she was also ready as Freddy, I mean Freida, with her thespian contribution to Slumdog. Simon Beaufoy's electric screenplay was one of the year's elite and Simon says "you best believe that it is a lock for a Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar nomination." The wondrous cinematography, production design, and editing of "Slumdog Millionaire" should also bark up more Oscar nominations on the Slumdoghouse. The celebratory theme song of Slumdog is entitled "Jai Ho" which means "Victory" in Indian. The rousing "Jai Ho" is also worthy of an Oscar jai ho as Best Song. The true hero of "Slumdog Millionaire" is Director Danny Boyle for his precise composition of this gem of a film; thank you Danny Boy! How do you say "Best Director Oscar" in Indian? Will there be many Jai Ho's for "Slumdog Millionaire" come Oscar night? I believe so and that is my final answer! ***** Excellent
