Who Wants to be a Millionaire??  Lotâs of people do it seems, judging by the fact that this famous question has been transformed into a hugely popular international game show franchise since its 1st airing in September 1998 in the UK.  Its bright lights; pressure-cooker atmosphere and questions to challenge the intellect put the pressure on even the most unflappable of contestants.  Add a novel by Vikas Swarup. Then change this format into a Hindi version and place it into the colourful; contrasting metropolis of Mumbai with sprawling slums and tall towers in equal measure. Into the middle of that put a enthusiastic & resourceful young orphan & you have the settings of this exhilarating; intoxicating and heartbreaking rags to riches; love story.
                                                                                                                           The boy in question is 19 year old Jamel Malik (played as a teenager by Dev Patel of âSkinsâ fame) and heâs getting a brutal beating and interrogation by the local police when we meet him 1st in the opening scene.  They and the game showâs producers are convinced heâs cheating after he getâs a series of challenging questions right.  After all, how can a street urchin; a âslum dogâ and worse still a Muslim be smart enough to know all the right answers on his 1st appearance on the show?  Itâs a common prejudice, but one which does Jamel, whoâs got to the 2nd last question of âWho Wants to be a Millionaireâ, no favours.  The slimy presenter of the show Prem Kuman (Anil Kapoor) made sure of that by calling in the police.  
                                                                                              Jamel proceeds to explain to the police captain how he came to know the answers to each of the questions.  Each answer not only unveils more information on how he knew the answers but opens up ours and the captainâs eyes to another part of the boyâs remarkably eventful and tough life.   It tells us how he was born into dire poverty in the Mumbai slums of the 1980âs and with his older brother Salim (Madhur Mittal) had to fight for survival from the get go.  When they witness the awful sight of their motherâs murder in a terrifying sectarian attack, they are forced to become street orphans and become friends with a girl called Latika (the older version played by Freida Pinto) in the process.  
                                                                                                                          They are soon taken under the wings of a seemingly kindly man running an orphanage. However when Jamal is about to get blinded by him to improve his begging potential, they go on the run.  Unfortunately they end up losing Latika when boarding the train and they keep on running right into their teenage years, surviving on pure graft; cunning and petty crime.  However, when the more aggressive Salim getâs involved with a prominent gangster, the 2 of them fall out and once again heâs separated. Approaching the day that will change his life Jamel rediscovers Latika whoâs now the property of Salimâs crime boss.
                                                    Danny Boyle (director of Shallow Grave; Trainspotting; 28 Days Later & Sunshine) has once again succeeded in creating an all out assault on the senses.  He along with screenwriter Simon Beaufoy an eye opening insight into the divergent cultures and social backgrounds that co-exist in the heaving democratic metropolis that is India, full of poverty; deep-rooted prejudices and simmering religious tensions. This is all set to a pulsating Hindu/hip-hop soundtrack; brilliant cinematography and brought to life by some superb acting performances by the lead characters.  Patel makes you really feel and root for Jamel; Pinto is enchanting as the older Latika and the veteran Indian thespian Kapoor does a great turn as the devious game-show host.  However, itâs the young actors who play the early parts of Jamelâs; Salimâs and Latikaâs life that steal their way to survive but steal the show and youâre heart aswell.

Filming in India about India is by no means an easy task. Do you go the Bollywood way and portray everything as larger than life? Or do you make it incredibly realistic? Now, India is a country that is striving for acceptance and recognition in the world. Do you then give the film the so called 'India is Shining' treatment or do you then arouse sympathy by portraying the country in a more negative light? These are the questions that Danny Boyle and co-director Loveleen Tandan must have asked themselves before shooting the film. 

Slumdog Millionaire's biggest achievement is that it is at heart an Indian film capturing the essence and pulse of India. No film has done this better in recent times and it is a testament to the hard work and research both Boyle and Tandan have done into this complicated and mystifying land. 

Jamal Malik is just one question away from winning 20 million rupees in the popular 'Who Wants to Be A Millionaire'. He is accused by the police authorities of cheating and arrested and tortured, as they simply cannot believe that a person serving tea in a call centre can do better than more 'qualified' people. Through the interrogation it is revealed that Jamal knew the answers out of the circumstances he was brought up in as well as the fact that he entered the show for the sake of love.

This film draws upon so many features of Indian life; the extreme poverty, child labor, the worship of stars (Amitabh Bachan) and TV shows, the caste system which pulls people down (as portrayed by Anil Kapoor, the millionaire host), the craze for cricket etc in a relative span of 2 hours. What could have been a tragic story with excess melodrama has been fused with optimism and vibrancy and energy. The lifestyles of the 'slumdogs' actually are not as depressing as we might think. Survival skills are also explored. The film's 2 biggest messages are how money cannot be a curse as well as the power of the human spirit with which even the impossible can be achieved.

Danny Boyle does a fantastic job, keeping us glued to the screen with the relentless tension and unpredictability of the plot-which seamlessly intergrates the flashbacks with the game show questions. But it is the emotional core of the film through which we root for Jamal that is his biggest achievement. Loveleen Tandon has clearly helped film the essence of modern India and this is accompanied by sweeping and dramatic cinematography and a pulsating score by AR Rahman which is used sparingly yet effectively in the film, as is MIA's Paper Planes remix. Simon Beaufoy helps to create an unusual love story through his adapted screenplay. All of the actors have done full justice to their roles, Dev Patel in particular along with the gorgeous Freida Pinto and the charismatic yet cunning Anil Kapoor and the understated portrayal by Irfan Khan. 

Slumdog Millionaire is a powerful and entertaining film which deserves repeat viewings.

A beautiful, heart-felt fairy tale. It features all of the drama, humor, inter-personal conflicts and epic romance one would want from such a love story, and it executes it in a visceral way.

The scenes depicting the life of the lower class in India are very intense in a pull-no-punches way, to the point that some people dismiss it as too upbeat and inauthentic considering the magnitude of the horrors actually experienced. 

In counter-point, it is precisely the presence of such ugliness that allows the movie to truly shine. It embodies the meaning of Browning's "In the darkest hour, Hope Springs Eternal." 

Additionally, it actually makes powerful statements regarding the human condition. These include the interplay between nature and nurture (faced with the same terrible situations, Salim chooses power and Jamal chooses Love), the overarching meaning of every situation in our lives (i.e. fate/chance, which is fairly obvious considering the whole premise of the movie is built around it), and the power of religion as a destructive and redemptive force, among others. 

It handles these themes in an vivacious and captivating way, that may pass off as cliche to some but offers a clear contrast to much of the darker and more understated movies that have won critical acclaim recently. In a cinematic era where stories are afraid to be inspiring lest they be classified as "hokey", Slumdog Millionaire is a visual feast, a well crafted story, and an interesting look into the various facets of a culture that is not well-known in the western world.

Unsparing as it is in its portrayal of violence, torture, and deprivation, "Slumdog Millionaire" is equally generous in its euphoric conclusion.  Ingeniously structured and well paced, this is an extremely satisfying film.  Despite some of its inventiveness, the story is rather traditional--something of a fairy-tale, in my opinion.  It is difficult to accept that Jamal wouldn't be more embittered and hardened by his life, but perhaps he is shielded from that by his older brother who suffers that fate.  By killing a criminal and exploiter of children, he protects Jamal and Latika but it sets his own life on a different trajectory (although he perhaps seeks a measure of redemption at the end.)

When Jamal Malik, a "chaiwalla" as the game show host unfailingly keeps taunting on every occasion, goes on to win 20 Million Rupees, he makes history. Throngs of Indians gather in front of televisions, regardless of whether in the comfort of their own homes or hanging around electronic stores, to witness a rags-to-riches story unfolding in real time. That, among many little things, is something that the writers have skillfully woven in their narrative - some of the nitty idiosyncratic details of urban India. I certainly remember the "Crorepati" (the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire) mania when it first debuted about 8-9 years ago, and we get glimpses of that in the movie. In true Boyle fashion, the movie is brilliantly styled. The photography is nothing short of spectacular and probably deserves awards simply for that. The dirty amber hue, the frequent blowing of dust, the congested density of crowds, all highlight the grittiness In the second half, when we are greeted with shots of piles of garbage and derelict slums right alongside multi-million highrises, we know the cameraman has understood the soul of Mumbai. In fact, so sensitive are the lens used to capture the movie that at no point did I feel that this was yet another westerner's ethnocentric view of India; the crew seemed absolutely immersed in the culture and have shot it from within that culture. It even seemed similar to a bollywood movie in parts! Another technical department the movie excelled in was the music. A.R. Rahman gives a fitting score that goes from the mellow love themes to the hip hop background for the gangster portions to the bawdy Ringa Ring to the triumphant Jai Ho for the end. The director does seem to have taken the route of the movie carrying the plot rather than the other way round. Stylistic elements, such as flashbacks associating with Jamal's answers, and the visuals do compensate for the lack of a plot. Again adding those little quirks and issues in Indian life - from the two boys conning the tourists to the Hindu-Muslim riots to the crime underbelly in these slums - do help to some extent. But one wishes that the storylines had been etched out with a little more focus, particularly the development of the "the one true love" story. Jamal's motivation to go on the show was also not exactly clear, nor was the reason as to why he kept guessing on questions that he didn't know (when he should have walked away). Dialogues were horribly cheesy, and the director should have opted for Hindi spoken dialogues. The dialogues came across like a direct translation from typical Hindi words, and in portions where that was not the case, it sounded extremely strange coming from the mouths of slum dwellers. The kids played the young versions of Jamal and Salim better than their adult counterparts did. Dev Patel has a one-note expression the whole movie, and I expected a little more... I dunno... reaction towards Anil Kapoor's character. Freida Pinto is quite confident. Among the "veterans" in the movie, Irrfan Khan is the best. Anil Kapoor comes across a little too smarmy, though that's probably the way his character is written, which is another issue. I doubt someone like him, who would take to insulting the contestants, could ever be a host. The guy acting as Mamman was really good. Mahesh Manjrekar is quite fitting in that role...heh.

Danny Boyle has a flair for filmmaking. No matter that this skill has waned since the back to back success of Shallow Grave and Trainspotting. This flair is the ability to make each movie he directs seem as if it's been made by a first timer. A film school graduate. A young gun who isn't going to take any shit from the money men. A maverick. An outsider. And when Boyle makes movies about mavericks and outsiders, society's outcasts, particularly those looking for a way out, he is at his best. There has always been that spark waiting to ignite in each film he's made since his Scottish highlights.

Astounding.   What The Kite Runner did for Afghanistan, illuminating a dark and desolate environment and its impact on children, Slumdog Millionaire does for India.  It also shares the former film's theme of fraternal betrayal and reconciliation.  However, Slumdog Millionaire is totally unique and utterly compelling.  Part love story, part rags to raja, part game show, the story captivated me every step of the way.   What a brilliant premise:  a poor young man is on India's version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire and does so well, he is interrogated and tortured because they believe him to be a cheat.  As his backstory unfolds we see in brutal clarity how he came to know a little something about Hindu gods, American currency and Indian poets.  As a bit of a trivia buff myself, this catchy structure appealed to me, but the depth of emotion in Jamal's story took the film beyond a mere gimmick and made it one of the best films of the year.  The editing was mesmerizing, the scenery sometimes gorgeous, sometimes gut-wrenching and Dev and Freida were wondeful.  I sincerely hope Slumdog wins best picture at the Academy Awards, in keeping with its success at the Golden Globes. Slumdog Millionaire is the story of Jamal Malik (Patel), an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who is about to experience the biggest day of his life. With the whole nation watching, he is just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India¹s "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?"

But when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a street kid know so much? Desperate to prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika (Pinto), the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of his story reveals the key to the answer to one of the game show¹s questions.

Each chapter of Jamal¹s increasingly layered story reveals where he learned the answers to the show¹s seemingly impossible quizzes. But one question remains a mystery: what is this young man with no apparent desire for riches really doing on the game show?

When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out.

I'm a big fan of Danny Boyle. I love that he refuses to repeat himself, hopping from one genre to another, mixing up the styles. I think many directors could learn from his decision to do this, and we, the punters, could benefit tremendously. I have, however, often wondered if he'd ever again scale the lofty heights of his sophomore effort, the mighty Trainspotting. Well, he's just, very empatically, answered YES! with this awesome movie. From the opening shots of Mumbai's slums to the faux-Bollywood closing credits, Boyle never puts a foot wrong. Sure, it's a feel-good movie at heart, but it's one with a harsh realism behind it not found in lesser, more cliched fare. It's a movie unafraid to shine a light into some uncomfortably dark corners, and yet it doesn't dwell on the darkness therein, rather choosing to show us hope, and fighting spirit. The brilliant camerawork and editing highlights the beauty in even the poorest areas and the stunning soundtrack punctuates the images perfectly. It's been a while since I've been so blown away by a visit to the cinema, and I tell you, this one's a repeat-viewer. Quite frankly, if you see this and don't come away inspired, with an enormous shit-eating grin, then it's probably time to donate your eyes and ears to medical science, they ain't doin' you no good.

The first half of the film is gritty, urban and reminiscent to realism in aesthetics. The rundown lived in qualities of India are rich and very human. I enjoyed them in Salaam Bombay and I liked them here. It's very pleasant to see India's culture unadulterated. India is beautiful and beautifully shot. I expect this film will get many props for Cinematography. The soundtrack is also very good, with many catchy easy-to-groove-to songs. The performances are all top notch. It's a sweet little journey Jamal and his big brother Salim (Madhur Mittal) are on. They commit all sorts of trickery and get into much hi-jinx to survive.

It's the main contrivance of the plot (the catch) that is irritating, and leads to the pulpy fluff of the second half. Nearly EVERY question asked on the show pertains to this young man's life in some key way? He didn't study at all? I just have to roll my eyes, and did several times. Many of the questions are also dead easy in addition to corresponding far too easily with Jamal's past. It's less a tale of a poor man making it to fame and riches with his own abilities than being carried there by the movie gods.

In the end, we have a rather good movie that should not be held up to the hype surrounding it. This happened for me with Babel a few years ago. It's a shame we have awards and award campaigning to cloud our judgments on films. This will probably be held up as better than it is by people looking for hope in our current depression. Slumdog Millionaire comes out of nowhere and it could very well be his best film and one of the best films of the decade. Visually like Boyles previous work it's stunning, Apocalypse Now and City of God come to mind and there are dutch angles galore. The raw style mixed with the amazing locations make this film one of the most cinematic experiences you'll ever see. The Sound is perfect, I haven't heard audio like this in a while, this film needs a Sound Oscar nomination it sounds that good. I went into seeing this knowing very little about it and the person I took with me didn't know anything about it, so I'll just say it's about a young man that goes on Indias Who Wants to be a Millionaire, it's a very unconventional film where they tell the story of his life in flashbacks while he plays the game. It's funny, sad, thrilling, basically a very enjoyable film that deserves numerous Oscar nominations. Also the lead actress is one of the most beautiful women I've ever seen, if she isn't a huge star after this I'd be extremely surprised. If the academy doesn't honor this film with numerous nominations it will be a shame but this film will be studied in 20 years and whoever sees this will love it, so even if it doesn't get a single nomination it won't matter. Don't miss this film, it's perfect!

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i], strangely enough, reminded me of [i]Pan's Labyrinth[/i].  Not in its story, execution, or anything like that.  Obviously, they're incredibly different movies.  I'm referring to my experience.  For both films, my anticipation grew as more and more praise was heaped upon them, but I had to wait a long time to actually make it to the theater.  During the waiting game, I came up with expectations not only for the quality of the anticipated film, but for the style and content (hard not to after hearing so many descriptors and such over and over again).  And in both cases, the movies proved to be quite different from what I expected, but neither lacked at all in the quality department.  They were just as brilliant as I wanted, but the brilliance was achieved in a way I didn't expect.

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is one of the best movies of the year.  It's utterly beautiful and inspirational, both as a romance and as a celebration of a hero for the common people, from the common people.  The simple premise unfolds to show a compellingly complex, detailed story that is brought to life by Danny Boyle's wonderful vision and Simon Beaufoy's epic yet personal screenplay.  It's all about reclaiming lost love, but the series of events that allows the finale to occur as it does (no spoilers, even though it's not hard to guess) is fantastic and beautifully chronicled in the movie's final, moving moments.

Dev Patel and Freida Pinto, both new talents, are fantastic in their breakout roles.  Patel particularly has a lot of tough scenes to play, and he handles all the emotions extremely well.  Just as impressive are the children taken from the actual slums of Mumbai to play the younger versions of the characters.  It's incredible to see how natural these kids are in front of the camera, and some of the movie's best scenes (uncluding my personal, smelly favorite) feature these talented youngsters, who were appropriately paid for their work by being rescued from the slums and put into better circumstances.

I also loved how the subtitles are presented, largely during the scenes featuring the younger characters.  Because this movie was created mainly for an English-speaking audience, the subtitles aren't relegated to the basic yellow or white words along the bottom of the screen.  Instead, they appear in colored rectangles superimposed over the scene.  It's a cool presentation that adds to the movie's unique, colorful flair.

That identity is further reinforced by some truly outstanding music.  The original score is one of the year's best, and the use of songs by M.I.A. is appropriate and genius.  I also loved the final Bollywood dance number, but I wish it hadn't been chopped up by the credits.  I'm looking forward to the extended version that will inevitably pop up on the DVD release.

[i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]is really one of those movies where everything comes together.  You have a brilliant cast, a skilled director, a beautiful screenplay, inspired cinematography, and fantastic music.  It's one of the year's best films, and a movie that you can really cheer for (as someone in our theater did).

First, let me say that I think Danny Boyle is capable of crafting stories that absorb and thrill the viewer.  Trainspotting was an undeniable masterpiece and throughout it's running time gripped and held a viewer's attention.

Slumdog Millionaire is a triumph.  The film succeeds in being gritty, hard, joyous, uplifting, worrying, and shocking in just short of 120 minutes.  While Danny Boyle has taken great pains during interviews to say that this film is a fairy tale, you can't help wishing that the story it tells of rags and hardship to riches and love is true.  Dev Patel and Freida Pinto make an exciting screen couple to watch, and the interaction Dev has with the rather malicious Anil Kapoor during the Millionaire scenes is a wonderful thing to watch.  There is little of the verbal jouster or fighter in Jamal, just a plain and simple truth that if he's asked a question, he will answer it.

The real heart and soul of the film is the manner in which Boyle tells the stories of how Jamal comes to know the answers to each question through the bizarre turnings of his life and the hardship he endured in the slums of Bombay, and his discovery and relocation of Latika.  The children playing the roles of the young Latika, Jamal and Salim (Jamal's brother) are a real find bearing resemblances to their older counterparts in sufficient detail that you don't question whether they are indeed the same character - and you accept that this film has been shot over about 15 years of history.

Danny Boyle succeeded in making an audience recoil in horror, groan in disgust, and sit through the first half of a credit sequence, which proves how absorbing this film really is.  It's a well crafted, and well told story shot with Boyle's varied style that makes this a truly awe inspiring film.

Unlike a lot of 'slum' films, there wasn't a brutalist subtext - the only way to survive wasn't to become hard - nor was there (much) over-glorification of the poor as pure/happy/simple. In fact, I found the most interesting element of it the character study of Jamal (Dev Patel).  Simple honest is an amazingly difficult thing to portray, and I felt came across masterfully in the film.

My disappointment is deep and unrelenting.  It is the kind of disappointment that is comparable to having a blind date with what at a glance appears to be a beautiful woman, but at closer inspection is a toothless tranny.  With a 94% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and Golden Globes forking over the top prize of Best Drama this film had to be watched if anything out of principal.  Of course, some instincts are better repressed.  The plot revolves around the decrepit and worn Who Wants to be a Millionaire franchise, and a contestant whose life in the slums of India led him coincidentally to know all the right answers.  Sure, it sounds ridiculous and contrived, and it is, but I expected the execution of the film to be the reason why this travesty would rise beyond the premise. 

  The film opens with a wonderful torture scene, which is a mere foreshadowing of the unnecessary and inexplicable gruesomeness to come.  It is difficult to understand how someone who is merely suspected of cheating on a game show with no actual money on hand would undergo extensive interrogation and electrocution in modern India.  Additional unbefitting gore includes purposeful, grizzly, and illogical blinding of a child, and the inexplicable and irrational disfiguring of a beautiful girl.  Personally, I am hardly squeamish, and enjoy a good blood fest such as Kill Bill volume 1 and Sin City, but here the use of violence exists for the sole purpose of extracting an unnatural emotion such as pity, concern, and disgust.  Since the film miserably fails at evoking natural emotions that come with intricate character development and creative plot points, violence is the only tool this film uses effectively. 

  The characters of this cinematic diarrhea are completely uninteresting and one-dimensional.   It is very difficult to pinpoint a single discernable characteristic any of the three main characters has that makes them interesting or at the very least transcend a cardboard cutout.  With this in mind, the romantic subplot is just confusing.  Aside from the obvious attractiveness of the romantic interest, there is no reason for the lead character to maintain such an undying interest in her, but what is more mystifying is why this interest would be mutual.

  Although only two hours long, the film feels agonizingly long perhaps since the premise of the film is worn thin less than half way through.  In the end of course the guy undeservingly gets the girl and wins the money by answering a predictable, overly simple final question.  This overwhelming disappointment is concluded with a strangely inappropriate dance number, and why not?
It was extremely interesting.  It makes you wonder how all the nuggets of knowledge one gains can end up more useful than ever imagined.

this film breaks the shell of call center caricature, and reveals a brutally sobering sense of reality deep within the slums. the screenplay magnificently articulates a story that grips you from the first frame, and the eclectic yet unified score accompanies the film's dialogue, actions, and emotions, consequently guiding your heartbeat as well. the grotesque and almost appalling bathroom comedy of jamal's childhood makes you burst and empty all the laughter our of your system; the film then fills that empty space with darkness, which ultimately gets saturated with the final resolution: love. the film ends into a somewhat transcendental realization of destiny, and then as if to soften its earlier blows, the actors break into a defining dance production, remiinding you that this film hails from the spirit of baliwood.

It doesn't seem like a stretch to suggest that America might now be ready to embrace films in the style of India's Bollywood films. While "Slumdog Millionaire" is far from a Bollywood tragic love story filled with singing and dancing, the way director Danny Boyle will rivet audiences with his film that is authentic to Indian culture while using a distinctly Western style of film-making might be enough proof that there is a profit to be made here.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is a drama exposing the tragic effects of poverty in gigantic Indian cities like Mumbai that is also fused with a modern day Indian fairytale. Jamal Malik is a young man on India's "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire" and is a question away from the piunultimate question when he's arrested on suspicion of cheating. Because Jamal is from the slums of India and has no educational background, it seems entirely improbable if not impossible that Jamal could make it this far, but each question is connected with distinct and sometimes painful memories for Jamal. It's as if he is destined to win, even though he only went on the show to impress a girl he has loved his whole life, Latika.

Danny Boyle ("28 Days Later," "Sunshine") takes us from memory to memory as Jamal advances question by question toward the million dollars. These memories offer vivid insight into poverty in India as well as the lives of Jamal, Latika and Jamal's older brother Salim. As children they are left parentless and taught how to swindle tourists, leading to lives of little fulfillment or even corruption. Despite being separated, Jamal and Latika are reunited several times and in fact Jamal's only motivation in life is his love for her.

While the young, unknown, Indian actors are absolutely amazing in this film, the biggest kudos go to director Boyle, who creates an astonishing film. For Boyle to go from science fiction and zombie thrillers to taking on a project as daring and unusual as "Slumdog Millionaire" proves that he's not only a brave director, but a versatile one. His great success with making this film intense, eye-opening and full of heart all at the same time prove that he's also an incredible one. "Slumdog" is just the beginning for Boyle who might be one of the most progressive and talented directors working today.

It's hard to be completely blown away by a film whose core message is about destiny and leans on the fact that Jamal is simply fated to do this well in explaining what has unfolded, but like any good film ought to, Boyle makes you a fan of the characters and not care as much about the logistics as you might normally do. The fact that this film starts out so dramatic and real makes it hard to embrace the fairytale it blossoms into, but it's the great visual storytelling along the way that makes it so enjoyable. 

This is a brilliant start to the new film year and I urge you to see this stunning film on the big screen.
While the movie was good, I think it has been drastically overrated. Danny Boyle should receive Best Director but should not even be nominated for Best Picture.

Slumdog Millionaire has a strange concept; young Indian man from the slums of Mumbai goes on Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire and is within an inch of taking the lot.

Of course there's more to it than that. First he is savagely beaten within the confines of the local police who believe that he is cheating purely for being from the slums. Of course with that comes a lack of education and a wariness towards the world which makes Jamal suspicious in himself. However, the film is carried well despite it, perhaps bizarre and almost ludicrous plotline, especially when you consider that it's been talked about by critics since it's initial showings, even being classed as one of the best feel good films of the last decade.

Danny Boyle's blue-print is all over it, the lighting, the camera angles, the way he links light humour and appropriate culture into serious moments, and Slumdog has plenty of those. Ultimately Slumdog... is a fighting adversity film for the world cinema crew.

Despite it's distinctly Indian feel (Boyle does a great job of emulating this) Slumdog... has it's share of faults. The acting at times is below par, one or two of the reasons for him knowing answers (such as how he knew who invented the revolver), and the ending is, poignant, but feeling a little tacked on.

However, you feel that Slumdog... was never meant to wow those who already were greatly cultured in film from around the world, especially with it's ending and it's patchy at times plot and despite it's sometimes effective, sometimes not flashbacks, City Of God it definatly isn't. However, Slumdog... is likeable and ultimately that's the point.

Slumdog... will certainly be more than a couple of people's introduction to world cinema as an art-form, and is definately a good starting point, and that's by no means a bad thing. it has just enough of a Hollywood touch but the storyline is highly unlikely, a problem from the very start, but Slumdog... has enough charm to keep it above water, despite the holes that pull it down.

So definitely a good movie, but by no means the best movie of 2008. The entire movie was carried by the very good plot device of seeing how he knew the answers. Danny Boyle went to India for his 8th film, and he returned with one of his best works. A film that is heartwarming, funny, poignant and exciting, it's beautifully shot and brings out the best of the city of Mumbai. It has street kid Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) finding himself on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? During a break, he is arrested, and is questioned on how he could possibly know the answers to the questions. He tells his life, and explains how his eventful life has a connection with the questions asked, and how it is all part of the destiny of life. It's a triumph for director Danny Boyle, who captures the vividness and tenacity of the slums of Mumbai, but it all looks beautiful. Even the cast knock out top notch performances, and it will have you on the edge of your seat and cheering along by the end of the film. It's a Bollywood film for those who have never seen a Bollywood film, but it is a very passionate film in which it's visuals are breathtaking and majestic. It'll be good tourism for India as well!! :D

Widely praised, Slumdog Millionaire is the tale of a young man from a shanty town who ends up on the Indian version of "Who wants to be a millionaire?". The film is told through two layers of flashbacks. The film starts in a police station, and looks back at the show itself and at the memories of his younger likfe that it triggered.

Aesthetically, the film is reminiscent of City of God, with its grainy digicam right-in-the-middle-ness. The fast editing and booming soundtrack sledgehammer emotions into the audience with more success than these techniques usually have. 

There is no doubt that the acting is good, the cinematography and editing and music competent, and the overall film quite clever. Unfortunately, all of that sits inside a film that really isn't a particularly enjoyable experience. The story - young poor kid with a heart of gold and a brother with a mean streak finds his way to power through sheer luck and TV-fame - strikes many vaguely familiar notes. It features a damsel, primarily there to be in distress and show us the impotence of the hero until he becomes a millionaire. (Moral of the story: fame and money are the only path to empowerment). Much of the film hits similar emotional tones to Grave of the Fireflies (without needing to firebomb any cities). 

In the end, the film was not the life-affirming tale that others describe. I left the cinema feeling empty and hollow inside, having just watched 2 hours of "luck is the only way out of dire poverty, and eventually luck favours people with a good heart". The film felt like a con. Putting a big lie at the heart of a film that uses cinematography and certain plot elements to seem authentic is painfully disloyal to its own aspirations. This is not a masterpiece. It is the film Walt Disney studios would have made if they had (for some bizarre reason) decided to blend Grave of the Fireflies with City of God and set it in India.

I'll keep this simple: Cancel whatever you're doing tonight and go see "Slumdog Millionaire" instead. Yes, you, the girl obsessed with "Twilight" and the guy still hung up on "The Dark Knight." Take the grandparents, too, and the teenagers. Everyone can play. 

What I found most amazing about this movie is how conventional the plot is. There is nothing particularly special about the story nor about the linear fashion in which it plays out. In that sense it is not a great film. However, despite the standard romantic drama tropes danced out onto the screen in that linear fashion it is a great film. Why is it a great film? Well, there is a subjective question. There is no easy way to explain this. For one there is a great energy and explosiveness to the tale, it is in constant motion. There is the emotionally charged relationship of the central characters, and the beauty of fantasy as fate plays out on the screen. 

You've never heard of the actors. A third of the film is in Hindi. Much of it takes place in the most fetid, poverty-ridden corners of the Indian subcontinent, and most of it isn't nice. Yet this sprawling, madly romantic fairy-tale epic is the kind of deep-dish audience-rouser we've long given up hoping for from Hollywood. "Slumdog" is a soaring return to form for director Danny Boyle ("Trainspotting"), but mostly it's just a miracle of mainstream pop movie making - the sort of thing modern filmmakers aren't supposed to make anymore. Except they just did.

Uniquely original fable with charm to spare. The tale of a young Muslim man from the slums of Mumbai who wins 20m rupees on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire - and the story of how and why he knew the answers. Told mostly in flashback we are shown the young Jamal and his elder brother Salim, and how they seek to escape their poverty-stricken existence after the brutal killing of their mother at the hands of religious extremists. At the beginning of the film as Jamal is being tortured by the police ,who believe he cheated on the show, we are asked how does a "slumdog" from Mumbai know all the answers? Slowly we are shown. For all those people who believe that India is a charming, mystical place full of awe and wonder, need to watch a film like this. Mumbai is shown to be the polluted, disgusting, corrupt-ridden sinkhole it is and the treatment of the street children is heartbreaking, even to a cynical sod like me. Many of the films best scenes are in the flashback sequences as Jamal, Salim and their young female companion, Latika, struggle to survive on the streets. The performances from the young actors who portray the main characters younger selves is astonishing and one forgets that we are watching actors (as its supposed to be in movies but often isn't). If Charles Dickens were alive today he would probably be writing something like this as many of the issues that were close to Dickens' heart (poverty, street crime, family, honour) are to be found here - there is even a Fagin character as well as the gang from Oliver Twist. It also has a Bollywood-style mass dance number as the icing on the cake. A must-see film. Note to Hollywood - please don't remake this.

"Slumdog" shows us the most intense game of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" ever played, and strangely it is an intriguing tale.  It's a satire at its heart, an elaborate sort of dark romantic comedy about how a regular old slumdog, who grew up with nothing but experience, used his knowledge of experience to gain it all, including the girl he loves.  It is such a unique concept in that it intercuts a game show with a person's - Jamal Malik's - entire life drama.  Boyle's style is sometimes annoying but it serves a purpose to what he's telling in his story unlike other stylistic directors.  This is just a genuinely satisfying, heart-warming (and heart-pounding!), fascinating tale unlike any film I've seen before.  There's a little bit of everything: comedy, adventure, action, drama, violence, and romance.

The most important element is that unlike so many underdog stories, it rewards its character through experience.  Jamal isn't playing a good game because he is a prodigy, or because he accessed information, but because he has genuinely earned the knowledge.  He deserves to win.

His first film since 2007 's criminally overlooked sci-fi horror Sunshine, Danny Boyle yet again shows us his wondrous tenacity at shifting between genres with comparative ease. Slumdog Millionaire is the story of one boy's survival in the harsh and often unforgiving enviroment of streetlife Mumbai. It is within the depths of Boyle's representation of this world, to neither romanticise nor demonize, and the strength between the leading characters that the film really succeeds. There maybe some who (SPOILER ALERT!) will wince at the overtly sentimental ending, but at heart this is a love story, and come Oscar time one which will truly earn its millions.

Danny Boyle's "Slumdog Millionaire" is a film that really resonated with the viewer after the credits have finished rolling. It is the story of love, loss, and life. It helps us understand a bit about what we are doing here and the greatest adventure in life, which is love. The finding of love. The pursuit of love. The happiness in love.

"Slumdog" tells the story of a young Indian teen named Jamal Malik, who has lived his life on the streets doing anything possible to make a little money and to get some food in his belly. It is in the life of the main character where we get this truly original story and how it is unfolded on screen before us is nothing short of a marvel.

Jamal is the latest contestant on India's hit adaptation of the game show smash "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire?" He is on the verge of becoming filthy rich. But how? How did this uneducated slumdog manage to make his way through the slew of questions only to find himself on the other side staring at a new life? This is where we get our story. In the how.

Boyle ("Trainspotting", "Millions", "28 Days Later") puts forth his best effort yet as director moving this film along at a breakneck speed while not passing by any of the core messages and key plot points along the way. It isn't hard to follow at all. And in this seemless storytelling do we find our hearts wide open and our minds in tune with the unbelievable story that is unfolding before us. 

I loved every single second of this film and every aspect of it. I haven't been simply floored by a film in quite some time. "Slumdog Millionaire" did just that. I felt vulnerable. I felt inspired. I felt as though all the problems I was, and am, currently facing in life were simply trivial compared to the hardships and heartache that these young children faced. It makes you think, not just of the characters in the movie, but of those who actually live in these circumstances. Those people who deal with this on a daily basis. Those people who live in a world without basic luxuries like indoor plumbing and a roof over your head that actually keeps the elements out. Everyone has problems in the world. Everyone. It is a simple fact. But sometimes in order to function as better human beings we need to take a step back and assess our problems and really ask ourselves; Is this the worst thing that could happen? Odds are it, probably, isn't and there are people dealing with things that we may never even fathom. When a film can really strike me like that I feel as though there isn't much more a movie can do. It's job is complete. Go check it out. We'll discuss over drinks later.

Danny Boyle's latest film, "Slumdog Millionaire", is hardly an obvious candidate for mainstream success. It is set in the slums of Mumbai, has scenes of torture and violence and is in Hindi for a third of the film. However, it has been nominated for a mountain of awards, is riding high in internet rankings and is doing well at the box office. When one takes a closer look, it isn't surprising that this film is doing as well as it is. It is a gripping, entertaining and ultimately wonderful piece of cinema.

The story, which is about a young man who goes on "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?", is utterly simple. He has, unbelievably, reached the final question. He is arrested between broadcasts on suspicion of cheating his way to the top. However, the fact of the matter is that he just happens to know every answer. As he explains why, his tough and unforgiving past opens up, raising questions about why he's on the show in the first place.

This film works because of the flashbacks which tell the story of a boy, his brother and a girl. It is not always an easy watch but moments of nastiness are rare, necessary and short-lived. As the story develops, Boyle's brilliance as a filmmaker pours off the screen. The raw, kinetic energy that he used to the maximum effect in "Trainspotting" is always apparent. The numerous sequences set in the slums are mesmerising to watch, accompanied by a magnificent score by A.R. Rahman, and vibrant photography from Anthony Dod Mantle.

Boyle also makes sure that this film is more than a "nuts-and-bolts" feel good story. The central romance is beautifully done and all of his characters are brilliantly sketched and excellently well performed. Dev Patel (in the lead) is a magnificent screen presence and really impresses in his film debut, whilst the supporting performances of Anil Kapoor as the host of the show and Irrfan Khan as the sceptical police inspector are superb. Boyle has also managed to find some brilliant child actors who inject the film with yet more energy.

Boyle also has a lot going on underneath. Like many great films, the location lives and breathes in the film. Mumbai, mirroring our characters, transforms through the film (for the better and for the worse). There is also a great deal about truth and integrity, neatly summed up in one of the answers. What is India's national motto? The truth alone triumphs.

Although there is a slight drop in pace in the film about an hour in, this is really gripping, really entertaining and thoroughly enjoyable cinema. Despite the darker moments, this is a feel good movie which, in the present climate, will be taken to people's hearts. The real joy is that this good natured and excellent film deserves every piece of success it receives.

There's no doubt that Slumdog Millionaire has had an interest ride this year. It struggled to even find its way into theaters before managing to be the sort of unlikely breakaway megahit that nobody can predict or recreate, and then enjoyed about 48 hours of hyperbolic celebration before the inevitable backlash matched intensities for a weird OK-vs.-amazing debate that will buzz around the movie's head right up through Oscar night. Any way you look at it, it's a big-ass movie that's selling out shows and getting people talking. This is strange to me because, for one thing, I found it to be sort of a universally "good" movie that doesn't really merit extreme opinions one way or the other, and also because it's so clearly not the crowd-pandering award-bait it looks like from a distance. Danny Boyle did a fascinating interview with the Onion AV Club recently where he talks about never making a movie if it's not a risk (which makes a hell of a lot of sense when you look through his weird-ass career path). Slumdog, on one hand, is surprisingly innocuous for a violent, brutal expose on Indian class relations, but it's also kind of nuts. Adopting the all-inclusive Bollywood style of filmmaking where pitch-black melodrama and quick-paced slapstick can travel the same circles, Boyle and his co-director Loveleen Tandan just completely go for broke in the quest for high-reaching mega-entertainment. The film's fantastical central gimmick - a particularly Fates-approved round of an exported take on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? - is the sort of odd, appealingly ridiculous concept usually reserved for short films and wacky comedies, but here it's played straight, used both as a clever framing device and a way to bridge the film's quirky syntheticism with its unflinching, frequently disturbing realism. The furious mish-mash of styles most closely resembles the quick, kinetic social rug-pulling of City of God, but it's admittedly much broader and friendlier towards the "aw shucks, ain't that cute?" crowd. But the mess from all the ideas being flipped around seems to be by design, and it's a strange, addictive experience to be jerked from scenes of tear-jerking cruelty into Ferris Bueller-esque hijinx with no breathing room in between. It's an exciting piece of gentle filmic anarchy that, combined with the absence of an American A-lister, really spells out "low-profile crowd-pleaser" rather than box office glory or critical acclaim, and should really be enjoyed as such, so it's kind of a shame that it's being presented as a potential Oscar winner instead. The performances are generally good, and it's an attractive and well-put-together film, but it's really more skilled at stirring up energy and emotions than it is at developing layered characters and complex storylines. Above all, it's a movie that boldly promises true love, riches, and dance sequences to anyone willing to persevere through the most fucked-up hard times imaginable, to which I responded with a resounding :).[/font]

Every year, I wait patiently for a movie to kick me in the ass with such aesthetic and emotional force that I won't easily forget it. In 2006, Pan's Labyrinth and Children of Men did it for me. Last year, it was No Country for Old Men and There Will Be Blood (among quite a few others, in fact. 2007 was a killer year for film). I had yet to experience that this year. Some that came close were The Dark Knight, but that effect died down on me over time; Wall-E, but that was a Pixar film, and Pixar films always do something like that for me; and The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, but it got a little too Gump-y at times. Slumdog Millionaire just hit that sweet spot, not quite as heavily as the ones I mentioned from previous years, but it certainly did the trick for now.

I loved everything about this movie. The story was well-calculated and struck the right emotional tones at the right times, the acting was absolutely excellent, the music was deliciously infectious and perfect for the mood, and the directing...oh Lord, that directing. Danny Boyle just keeps on directing up a storm with each movie he makes. What impresses me the most is his understanding of what each wildly different film in his repertoire calls for. From drug-addict dramedy (Trainspotting) to horror (28 Days Later) to unpretentious children's film (Millions) to heady sci-fi (Sunshine), he knows exactly what to do, and this is no exception. He goes all-out, channeling City of God by way of Wong Kar-Wai, and if anybody even knows what I'm talking about, they'll agree with me that that's a damn awesome combination. 

But the most prominent reason I love this movie is because of what it stands for as a whole. It's life-affirming, fist-pumping storytelling at its finest, and it reminded me why we watch movies to being with: to be entertained and get our money's worth of emotional manipulation. This makes you laugh and cry and ultimately want to cheer. It represents the best of what films have to offer, and as a result one of the best of the year, if not THE best.

Every once in a while there is a film that comes along that is as timely and relevant as Slumdog Millionaire.  It is allegorical but still has a fairytale quality.  A lot of people have compared it to "City of God" which I agree it has that kind of look and edge. I'd even say it reminds me of an earlier Brazil film called "Pixote" with a little bit of Los Olvidados. I think in a way it is also a neo-realist film, they used a lot of non-actors with the exception of khan and Kapoor two big named actors in India as well as references to Amitbah.   Many might know Danny Boyle's other films like Trainspotting from the late 1990s, which is now a cult classic, and 28 Days Later. I think certain sequences really remind me of Trainspotting, but the overall look of the film is gritty and raw, in the same way that it shows the beauty of a city like Mumbai, in the midst of all the tragedies experienced in the film, and recently in the city.  The story is told through flashbacks, as Jamal's memory is triggered by questions he's being asked during the hindi version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire".  The flashbacks feature these amazing orphans who were picked from the street in Mumbai.  Few filmmakers take that risk. Within a short amoutn of time you watch these kids as they grow up and you see what they see during the attacks. Then as Jamal gets older you are also seeing how Mumbai is changing because of technology, the internet.  The fact that a call centre has a significant role in the film is no accident.  The film is more about the city than it really is about Jamal, Latika, etc. But the fact that it is so timely with the recent Mumbai attacks, it is truly amazing to see a film like this get such a good reception and I think it will open a lot of people's eyes into what they thought they knew about India much like the tourists in the film who think they know India from things they read in a book. All in all an amazing film I know most wont get to see it, but if you have a chance make the time and deifnately stay for the credits!

I'm going to be honest....all the people who absolutely LOVE this movie will probably think i'm just trying to be that one negative critic who somehow manages to downplay everything...but i really feel that the hype has gotten to us on this one. Granted, Danny Boyle's abilities cannot be understated and neither can this great movie either. It brings to mind the more sweeping elements of Meirelles' "City of God" to mind. Combine that with a drama of stoicism and destiny and "Slumdog" comes pretty close. All things said though, i cannot agree with the overflowing praise of the movie however since it does in fact lack a great deal of emotional complexity and can get a tad predictable. And while some nags might consider the ending to be too commercial or the message as eminently too simple, it is in fact refreshing to see a movie introduced to mainstream audiences that isn't completely white-washed. It is also wonderfully visual and manages to capture the scope of poverty and slum society without devolving into an utterly depressing "look-how-bad-they-have-it" message. In either of those regards, "Slumdog" manages to smack the ball right out of the park. For those of you who enjoy the inspirational kick of rags-to-riches, then i implore you to at least sample this one!

Director Danny Boyle has not delivered a bad film to date. Admittedly he has had a couple of average ones in the form of The Beach and A Life Less Ordinary, but with a back-catalogue that contains films such as Trainspotting, Shallow Grave, Sunshine, 28 Days Later, and Millions, a couple of averages isn't too bad. With Slumdog Millionire he hits the jackpot once more, delivering a gritty drama, with some feelgood touches. 

The rags-to-riches tale has been done many times before, so what makes this film stand out is firstly the setting, and secondly the method of telling the story. Set in India, the film shows the grimier side of life in the slums that the Bollywood industry skirt around (indeed, some negativity has arisen in India as the film shows a side to the nation that they are not too happy with). The lead role is a humble tea-boy (Jamal) from a call center, who spent his childhood on the streets. When he enters, and begins to win big, on Who Wants To Be A Millionire, suspicion is raised as to how this slumdog with no education can know the answers to the questions set. 

The film begins with him being interrogated at the police station, as the authorities try to determine how he cheated the show. The film then flips back to each question on the show being asked, and then farther back to show the part of Jamal's life in which he discovered the answer to the question. We see the relationships he had with his elder brother, Salim, and a stray girl, Latika, as their lives thrust them in seperate directions. 

Boyle manages to grab great performances from all involved, from the young cast portraying the early lives of Jamal et al, to the adult cast. The drama from each flashback is complemented well by the tension of the Millionire TV show segments. Light smatterings of humour save the film from feeling too bleak at times, and by the end the audience find themselves wanting to cheer on Jamal. 

This is one of the first quality films of 2009, and a must-see movie.

the problem with western-made movies about other cultures has always been an unfailing squeamishness about actually centering the story on a character from the culture itself (e.g. "the last king of scotland" and its fictitious white doctor). the rationale being that american audiences relate better to "american" characters. the hidden meaning being that "american" means "white." interestingly, in an article i'd read on the topic of the small number of working female directors, the rationale was that action movies were more likely to get picked up because it was the overseas sales in illiterate countries that made a lot of movies profitable.

this movie dodges the white lead cliche, though it was pointed out that it's centered around an american gameshow. so the anglo-ness is narrowed to an abstraction. progress.

however, laudable casting, and a clever plot structure do not an entertaining movie make. the heavy foreshadowing required to frame the flashbacks muffled their suspense; meaning that the gist of the plot is gathered quickly, and watching the movie becomes an exercise in patiently waiting for the largely formulaic elements to play out.

This is a real gem. A film like how 'film' was 'meant' to be. No big explosions; no unwarranted scantily-clad females; no marketing/advertising tie-ins; no big-name Hollywood stars. Just proper filmmaking. You'd be hard-pressed to find an artistic achievement/vision like this again, maybe for a long time. Beautifully shot with terrific cinematography, and an amazing ray of music to back it up, Danny Boyle has shown he has grown as director, this effort even surpassing his pinnacle 'Trainspotting'. Funny, touching, dramatic, and at times ultimately romantic and meaningful, it has all the hallmarks of a melodramatic Bollywood film, but encased in the wit and irony of a British production. Boyle's connection to the author Alex Garland, in particular the way the narrative-pattern flows, is evident, but it's the message that the human spirit, no matter how many terrible things are thrown against it, will forever burn brightly that sees Slumdog achieve heights films haven't done in a long time. This beautifully told, well-acted Dickensian tale of an orphan who makes good and wins the girl he loves will hold special appeal for American audiences, who just really go for that sort of thing. Boyle uses an effective and universally recognized plot device--the ubiquitous pop culture hit "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire"--to tell the life history of an enterprising trio of modern day Mumbai musketeers, as the eponymous slumdog millionaire reveals how he knew the answers to each of the show's questions. I laughed, I cried, I left feeling better for the ride.

The poverty that tha characters live in is depicted unflinchingly and will come as a shock to many people who live far from the horrors of the world we live in. I do have a problem with that depiction though. Shanty towns and poverty in general are not naturally occuring phoenomena. Shanty towns in particular are probably not much older than a century or so. These things have causes. But none of this is even hinted at by the film. We have no inkling as to why in one of the worlds fastest growing economies so many people live in such dire poverty.  Secondly, a bit more unusually the character escapes poverty because it's fate. In most tradional rags to riches tales I'm familiar with the poor underpriviliged hero uses their street smarts or other talents gained from being trash to rise up and be successful. The very things their upper class peers dispse them for turn out to be what propels them to riches. Here however it's just a load of random stuff he hapens to remember. It's just luck. Or as the film suggests "it is written". 
 Why is it written for our hero and not the rest of the characters? Well it would seem it's because he's a nice guy and the rest of India are corrupt and treachorous villains. Be it the police who torture him, the gameshow host that tries to trick him, the evil fellows who want to blind him, the the gangsters who keep his one true love from him or his generally untrustworthy brother. No only our wide eyed innocent gets the girl and the cash. Thi sugest to me that all of those millions and millions of people who don't have clean drinking water probably deserve what they get because if they didn't fate would have selected them to get all the questions right on a Chris Tarrant divised quiz show.
 That's right. Who needs a political system that provides housing, education and helath care for ever one when you have TV game shows. I have heard it argued that it'sjust a movie. That I shouldn't read too much into it etc. But it wants the audience to question things. It wants us to be horrified by the poverty, to be shocked that a woman can be beaten to death while doing her laundry because of sher religious beliefs. As it should. But then it loses it's nerve. Instead of asking hard questions it like so many of us turns on the TV and forgets about it.#
 More generaly I believe all stories have a moral, a point of view, something to say. What this film has to say I find dishonest, unsavory and more than a little cowardly. Some of the music was great though!

Jamal Malik (adult version played by Dev Patel) has had a difficult life, having grown up with his brother Salim (Madhur Mittal) in the slums of Mumbai, India, struggling to survive in a harsh and dangerous world after being orphaned at an early age. The two brothers, who call themselves Athos and Porthos, two of the musketeers from the book The Three Musketeers, which they read during their brief time spent in school, befriend another lost youth, a girl by the name of Latika (Freida Pinto). Latika becomes their third musketeer (whose name they don't remember), and is with them when they are plucked from a garbage dump by the seemingly benevolent Maman (Ankur Vikal).

Later, though, they discover that Maman is not the savior they were hoping for, and the boys manage to escape but, unfortunately, are forced to abandon Latika in the process. During the course of the next several years, Jamal, who has developed a love for Latika, tracks her down only to lose her again while Jamal and Salim turn against one another, each taking drastically different paths in life thereafter. Salim gets involved in organized crime while Jamal takes a considerably safer path by becoming a "chai-wallah", or tea server, at a call center.

Meanwhile, men and women across the country are following the popular television game show Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? (or, more specifically, its Indian counterpart, Kaun Banega Crorepati). When Jamal lands a spot on the show, and proceeds to answer every question correctly, those running the show soon become highly suspicious of him. How could a chai-wallah, a former slumdog, go so much farther in the game than the professors and other more learned men that had been on the show before?

Clearly, they decide, he is cheating. Right before the final question, the question that would award Jamal with a staggering 20 million rupees, the show breaks, and Jamal is soon after taken into police custody where he is savagely interrogated by a police inspector (Irrfan Khan). After a brutal torture session, Jamal lays out the story of his life for the inspector, how he was able to answer each of the game's questions, and his reason for going on the show in the first place.

Slumdog Millionaire has been enjoying considerable acclaim since it's been out, having already won Golden Globes for best drama and best director among several other awards. Critics and the movie-going public alike have lavished great praise on the film, yet, while I think Slumdog Millionaire is a decent film, I honestly don't see what all the fuss is about. The film is essentially a tale of love and destiny as well as a window into the life of poverty-stricken youth in India. It is told largely via flashback as the film shifts back and forth between Jamal's appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? and important events in his life from his childhood through the present. The film does indeed offer an interesting story, but the execution leaves a bit to be desired in my opinion.

My main problem I have with the film is that, on the whole, it feels somewhat clunky. The time shifts in the story are a little jarring, and the revelation of key pieces of data that end up helping Jamal on the game show seem out of place at times, especially during those times when these little snippets of information come out through dialogue. There's just a random quality to some of these moments in the film that thrust me out of the story, and this, along with the sometimes huge temporal jumps in the film, kept Slumdog from flowing as well as it could.

I also didn't care for the character of the sleazy game show host Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor). I found him to be irritating and pointlessly antagonistic to Jamal. The film does offer up somewhat of an explanation as to why Kumar acts the way he does towards Jamal, but I found the explanation to be a bit weak and unconvincing. Besides, the film already had its share of bad guys. One more wasn't necessary, especially one as disposable as Kumar was.

I will say, though, that the first half of the film, involving Jamal as a young boy, works quite well, and it is only until later, when Jamal becomes a teenager, that the quality starts to dip a little. The story of young Jamal and Salim and the trials and tribulations they face growing up in the slums of India and vulnerable to those who would harm and exploit them for monetary gain, is compelling and, at times, shocking in its portrayal. These scenes are my favorite parts of the film, painting a bleak picture of a world that no child should ever have to live in while delivering cinematography that is often awe-inspiring.

Once the film makes the leap to Jamal's teenage and adult life, though, and shifts its focus more towards the love story between Jamal and Latika, I lost a little of my interest. Nonetheless, Slumdog does manage to build toward an emotionally powerful ending that closes the film on a high note (as well as an enjoyable little dance number, an obvious nod to Bollywood, that kicks off the beginning of the credits). All in all, I thought Slumdog Millionaire was a film that had a lot of great elements, but also a fair amount of stuff that drug it down somewhat. It's worth a look, but I definitely didn't think it was nearly as good as many make it out to be.

Slumdog Millionaire is a 2008 British drama film directed by Danny Boyle, co-directed by Loveleen Tandan (who began as the film's casting director) and written by Simon Beaufoy. It is based on the novel Q and A by Indian author and diplomat Vikas Swarup.
Set and filmed in India, Slumdog Millionaire tells the story of a young man from the slums of Mumbai who appears on a game show and exceeds people's expectations, arousing the suspicions of the game show host and of law enforcement officials.
Eighteen year old Jamal Malik is having an amazing answering streak on the Indian version of the television game show, "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire". He's only one correct question away from the big prize. However, some, including those associated with the game show, question how someone like Jamal, a self confessed non-genius who grew up in the slums of Mumbai, can be doing so well on the show when others who are brighter, more educated and wealthier than him have failed. Is Jamal cheating? Is it purely luck that they have asked him the questions to which he knows the answers? Seeing Jamal's life journey to this point ultimately answers these questions. His life journey includes being orphaned at an early age; growing up with an older brother, Salim, who was both his guardian/protector and antagonist; and having a relationship since childhood with another orphaned child, a girl named Latika. His motivation for being on the show also may provide some answers to his success. Perhaps it was all just meant to be an ALL TIME BLOCK BUSTER.

Jamal Malik, an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, is just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India?s ?Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?? But when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a street kid know so much? Desperate to prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika, the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of his story reveals the key to the answer to one of the game show?s questions. Intrigued by Jamal?s story, the jaded Police Inspector begins to wonder what a young man with no apparent desire for riches is really doing on this game show? When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out. My comment adn review for this movie is so much cause I liked it so much..: Slumdog Millionaire" is a drama exposing the tragic effects of poverty in gigantic Indian cities like Mumbai that is also fused with a modern day Indian fairytale. Jamal Malik is a young man on India's "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire" and is a question away from one million dollars when he's arrested on suspicion of cheating. Because Jamal is from the slums of India and has no educational background, it seems entirely improbable if not impossible that Jamal could make it this far, but each question is connected with distinct and sometimes painful memories for Jamal. It's as if he is destined to win, even though he only went on the show to impress a girl he has loved his whole life, Latika. Danny Boyle ("28 Days Later," "Sunshine") takes us from memory to memory as Jamal advances question by question toward the million dollars. These memories offer vivid insight into poverty in India as well as the lives of Jamal, Latika and Jamal's older brother Salim. As children they are left parentless and taught how to swindle tourists, leading to lives of little fulfillment or even corruption. Despite being separated, Jamal and Latika are reunited several times and in fact Jamal's only motivation in life is his love for her. While the young, unknown, Indian actors are absolutely amazing in this film, the biggest applause go to director Boyle, who creates an astonishing film. For Boyle to go from science fiction and zombie thrillers to taking on a project as daring and unusual as "Slumdog Millionaire" proves that he's not only a brave director, but a versatile one. His great success with making this film intense, eye-opening and full of heart all at the same time prove that he's also an incredible one. "Slumdog" is just the beginning for Boyle who might be one of the most progressive and talented directors working today. The Golden Globe Award was on its place for Boyle. Best Director.....Marvelous It's hard to be completely blown away by a film whose core message is about destiny and leans on the fact that Jamal is simply fated to do this well in explaining what has unfolded, but like any good film ought to, Boyle makes you a fan of the characters and not care as much about the logistics as you might normally do. The fact that this film starts out so dramatic and real makes it hard to embrace the fairytale it blossoms into, but it's the great visual storytelling along the way that makes it so enjoyable. I really recommend this film, highly... Its really Rocks...

I had somewhat high expectations when I began to watch this film. After hearing so much positive word of mouth and seeing the numerous Golden Globes the film won, should I have expected any less?

Unfortunately, the film was merely average. I found nothing about this movie to be exceptional; nothing screamed out that it was worthy of so much praise and good reviews.

Which doesn't mean it wasn't a bad film, it was simply just a little contrived. To me it felt like it was trying too hard to be this warming, positive story about a poor boy trying to make his way out of the slums and reunite with his romantic love interest. In the end, it becomes just another sappy, easily predictable and horribly dull film. 

I'm not sure where the excellent praise is coming from...is the acclaim steming from outside effects surrounding the film, or is it from the actual film itself? Sometimes it seems to me like some care more about the fact that the film incorporates the Indian and Bollywood culture so freely, or the fact that it was filmed entirely in Mumbai and generate big amounts of income for the impoverished area.

Honestly, I don't give a shit, and neither should you when it comes to reviewing this film. One should only be looking at the film itself and that's it. Do not judge it's worth based on outside factors.

Look at the film, and only the film for what it really is. A typical, extremely Americanized tale of rising up from the gutters and finally connecting with your true love.

This film didn't need to be filmed in Mumbai; it didn't need to have Middle Eastern actors. It could've worked in any country, with any type of racial group.
