[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Slumdog Millionaire[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Scamming the Audience[/size][/font]
[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Reviewed by Dan Lieberman[/size][/font]
[font=Times New Roman][size=3][email="dlieb10@gmail.com"]dlieb10@gmail.com[/email][/size][/font]
[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Heard about financial scams, medical scams, sport scams, government foreign policy scams? How about a cinema scam?[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Every once in awhile a seemingly ordinary film entrances an audience beyond its expectations. The film [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]appealed to Americans with its "rags to riches" story of a deprived youth from the slums of Mumbai, India, who used pluck, luck and an astonishing memory of incidents in his life to win 20 million rupees in a quiz program. The unusual coincidence of the film's arrival in U.S. theaters at the same time as the terrorist action in Mumbai provided an added kicker to the film's box office success. A fascination with the provocative news reports spilled over to a fascination with Mumbai. However, those interested in the attacks by Islamic extremists on mainly Hindus in Mumbai must have been surprised to witness a film that contains Hindu attacks on Muslims.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Slumdog Millionaire's plot is simple, enchanting and unique.[/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]An adolescent orphan, whose family had been killed in a religious pogrom that targeted Muslims in the slums of Mumbai, manages to become a contestant on an American look-alike television program: So you want to be a millionaire?  [/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]From the questions, the story unfolds.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Each question, by a coincidence, has played a part in the youth's life. Experiences have given him the answers.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Who was the Indian actor in a certain film during the 1970's? [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Oh, that actor landed one day by helicopter in a field close to where the youth was living. He raced to the helicopter and met the actor.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]And so on.

[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]However, the film, which reveals the oppression, prejudices and economic exploitation within Indian life, evolves into an insensible fairy tale love story. In their menacing voyage through the corruption and degradation of India's underclass, the boy and his brother bring a neighborhood girl into their lives, with whom the hero has no intimate contact but ardently admires. The plot shifts abruptly in later years when the grown brother becomes an assassin for a local gangster and the grown girl become the gangster's 'girl friend.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]In the finale, after a tense pause and nail biting correct answer to the final question, everything is conveniently resolved. The gangster and the brother are killed in a shootout. The girl is free, and the new millionaire can be finally united with his lost love. In a Sleepless in Seattle style, a film plot made several times, where the lovers are finally reunited at either the Empire State building, the Athens' acropolis or the Giza Sphinx, these lovers wander and search for each other until seeing one another across a platform at the immense Mumbai railroad station.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]That's the film we see.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Is that the film that is being shown?[/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]The plot is too simple; a fairy tale story that doesn't match the power of the cinematic expression. Characters are too cardboard, too stereotype, almost comic book, especially the gangsters. The love story is too insensible and contrived. The ending has no relation to what proceeded.  [/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]If the youth had sought the quiz program as a vehicle to ransom his love from the clutches of criminals and succeeded, the audience would have been involved and rooted for him. But the woman escapes because his brother kills all the criminals. What did all that have to do with the plot of an impoverished youth, who without education and experience to make a life, takes a strange journey in which unique circumstances of his deprivation leads him to riches?[/size]  [/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]The experiences that supposedly enable answers to the questions are undoubtedly true and pound the audience senses with revelation of the inattention to the downtrodden in India's impoverished neighborhoods. Nevertheless, they all have a slightly exaggerated quality, an almost surreal aspect that indicates the substance is true but the youth has embellished the presentation. The slum dweller has obviously added components to his experiences in order to establish reasons for his knowledge that will satisfy the inquisitive police chief, who after not being able to gain a confession by torture, is willing to accept the dubious answers.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]So, what is the explanation for the film's ethereal quality?[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Is there a plot explanation that could make the compelling film into a memorable film?[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]One explanation is that the adolescent contestant has scammed the quiz program and the film scams the audience. An alert audience should recognize the scam and think - well, what has actually happened?[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]We observe the film through the voice of the youth until the end. The cardboard characters of criminals and his long sought lover are as he wants us to believe them. The relationship between the characters are too movie like, unlike the naturalistic description of his childhood battles with deprivation and despair. The imagined criminals are undoubtedly associates in the scam. Most probably, the contestant is wired with a receiver (under the skin, similar to a pacemaker?) and is receiving broadcasted information from his collaborators, who watch the program, find the answers on the Internet and transmit the answers to the ultimate millionaire The transmission only needs one, two, three or four vibrations to provide either the A, B, C, or D response to the question.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]Perhaps this analysis of Slumdog Millionaire sounds absurd and conspiratorial. That's a valid response. But without the explanation, the film is a betrayal and disaster, only another fairy tale Sleepless in Seattle story? Isn't there something more that is underlying the words and actions of the characters? Isn't the movie more meaningful and dramatic if the audience can figure out the scam and not be scammed? The scam gives the film a moral: The difference between those who are poor and those who are rich is only a scam and underdogs can beat the odds if they adopt the practices of those who control their destiny.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3] [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]By a clever use of subtext, Slumdog Millionaire becomes a work of art.[/size][/font]

Have you ever watched some of those TV game shows and go "I know the answer to that!" no matter how supposedly difficult it's suppose to be? Well "Slumdog Millionaire" plays on that concept by having Jamal Malik go for the big win in India's version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire." The movie follows Jamal's life from when he was a child, to his young teenage years, to present time, showing us that his experiences in India have provided him the knowledge to answer the questions. "Slumdog" is a story about overcoming adversity, the sibling dynamics, the different paths life can take you, and the love of a girl that can overcome obstacles. This movie is also great as a peak on how life is in India, from the point of view of people who aren't as well off as others, including some incredible cinematography. Based on the novel "Q&A" by Vikas Swarup, screenplay writer Simon Beaufoy, director Danny Boyle, and co-director Loveleen Tandan has made a very memorable, adventurous, and dramatic film in "Slumdog Millionaire" despite some moments that does require some suspension of disbelief. I suppose I should also mention that a good portion of the movie is subtitled.

Refreshing, original, emotionally and visually strong, entertaining, gripping Slumdog millionaire is a great film. Danny Boyle has mastered his endeavour.

The film has a very clever narrative structure that builds up piece by piece like a puzzle with greater tension as the film progresses. 

Danny Boyle takes the spectator on a journey with a very Eastern philosophy by giving away the end at the beginning: the journey is more important than the end goal, that is our journey and the journey of the main characters. This gives Boyle time to develop the characters through impressionistic touches and leads us to focus on discovering characters who should be very uninteresting at first glance. Who would care about a few children of the slum among millions? The emotional bond to the characters Boyle succeeds in creating is very strong and we care more and more about what happens to them.

The actors play their role perfectly. As a bonus, the role of Latika is interpreted by the beautiful Freida Pinto.

The photography is vibrant and colourful. The saturated colours of India are admirably rendered on film and add texture to the film. The camera work is also very original and carefully planned and gives energy and rhythm to the film.

In addition to being a brilliant fiction, the film also achieves a tour de force of capturing the reality of various aspects of urban India with the precision of a documentary.

The story is of a young Indian man who is arrested because he is under suspicion of cheating in a well-known TV game show "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" (the Hindi version). As the interrogation comes along, he explains why he knows the answers to the questions asked during the show and revelations about his childhood unfolds. Ultimately, the true purpose of his participating in the show slowly unveils itself. The movie reminds me of "City of God" due to the theme, the tone, and the cinematography. Along the way, elements of Hollywood fairy tale-ness were infused. The movie has an excellent soundtrack as well. Worthy of the Golden Globes it won. It really did an excellent job in perfectly mixing reality with a healthy dose of fairy tale elements. Go see this movie, highly recommended.

Having finally seen what all the hype has been about, I can honestly say that I respect this film more than I like it.  SM is imaginatively directed by Boyle, and it's his style that pushes an often VERY predictable film into an original work.  For example, Boyle's clever use of subtitles, often appearing near a character as opposed to the bottom of the screen, allows our consciousness to stay with the action of the film rather than being distracted by having to go "back and forth"; as is, we don't miss a beat, and I'd like to see this technique employed in other films (if it hasn't already).  Also, the performances are quite good all around, featuring great child performances and a US star-making turn for Patel and Pitino.  

There is a major problem in the film, one that affects my ability to like most movies, and that is relative pacing.  SM, at two hours, feels like a three-hour film.  The cause of this is primarily the flashback framing device; since we know from the outset that Jamal has reached the penultimate question (from which one can deduce the climax), then the viewer constantly wants to get to that point.  During the first hour, the movie share's the viewer's anxiousness, and the scenes flow well.  During the second hour, as Jamal reaches adulthood, the scenes lose a lot of energy (save for the last fifteen minutes, where the pace picks up again).  SPOILER: For example, when Jamal visits Latika at the gangster's abode, tension is missing, and we get one too many shots of Jamal staring at the gangster, staring at Latika, etc.[/spoiler]  In addition to pacing, SM has a major plot hole (SPOILER): if the game show host has both the influence to start the police investigation, and the corruption to attempt to give Jamal a wrong answer...then why does he let him win the 20 million, or even allow him to compete for the question?  If there is a "change of heart"...i.e., Jamal has captured the heart and minds of India, so we HAVE to let him go for the final question...isn't that important enough to display?

Overall, SM is a bold, beautiful film with a lot to be admired.  There's a lot here to fascinate and endear the viewer, which is why, I think, it has had the reception that it has.  The last half of the film is problematic and nearly a dealbreaker for me, but this is still quite an accomplishment, and Boyle and Co. should hold their heads high.  Is it the Best Picture of 2008?  No...it's not even best among the nominees...but it's definitely deserves a look.

Boyle was probably trying to ask the audience the same question that Jamal asks Latika in the middle of the film whilst 'Who wants to be a Millionaire' is in the background: 'why do people watch this show (films) anyway?' Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) is a street kid (or "slumdog") who has landed an appearance on India's version of the hit TV game show WHO WANTS TO BE A MILLIONAIRE? Jamal exceeds expectations on the show, and the producers alert the police after they become suspicious of his methods. The young contestant is subsequently arrested and is interrogated at the hands of a nameless police inspector (played by Bollywood star Irfan Khan). As the interrogation proceeds, Boyle tells Jamal's story through harrowing flashbacks that both show the terrible poverty of Mumbai and help explain how he knew the answers to the MILLIONAIRE questions.
 
It's fairly clear that director Danny Boyle intends this film to be a fairy tale, with the love story providing the film its heart. But much of the film is nasty and unpleasant, reveling in every distasteful detail about Jamal's childhood. Within the first 20 minutes of the film, we've seen Jamal tortured with electricity, Jamal jumping into a vile pit of human excrement in order to get an autograph from his favorite Bollywood star (this scene is played for laughs, because isn't someone covered in sh*t always good for a laugh?) and we see his mother bludgeoned to death by anti-Muslim extremists right before Jamal's and his brother's eyes. Later, we see small children getting their eyes burned out with hot spoons in order to make them more effective beggars. Everyone in the movie but Jamal and Latika, who remain blank slates as characters, is hateful and repellent. Boyle heaps calamity on top of calamity for so much of the film that its facile, simplistic conclusion wrings impossibly false. You can't have it both ways. You can't have your film be both a gritty, slice-of-life indictment and a frothy romantic soufflé. The end product is like "City of God" meets "Moulin Rouge!" 
 
With crisp mature perfomances from Patel and company, Danny Boyle's vivid colourful film is a wondrous thing to behold. Whilst missing practicality, it becomes predicatable at times; a dangerous thing for a film to be if it wants to be big commercially. The ambition is there of course; there is a lot of heart In SM, though the plot could have been fleshed out a little more.
 
The execution falls very flat because of two basic flaws: The language barrier, and a wishy washy Bollywood story line. Read on. Its old Bollywood cliches are trotted out, and its superficial undertones are impossible to ignore. Taking advantage of India's sweeping beauty, and the Indian language (a little too much judging by the extensive use of subtitles) creates something truly special that you can't ignore.
 
Maybe the makers -- and half the world, apparently -- believe they have married Bollywood escapism with Western sensibilities, but it is not a match made in cinema heaven. It is more along the lines of 1970s Bollywood tear-jerker, the kind where the hero transforms from street urchin to gang lord in one running shot and where long-lost brothers are reunited by tattoos. While viewing Slumdog Millionaire, I found myself watching what could have been your average ordinary coming of a age family film. But make no mistake, it is so much more than that. Nothing like it, if that. But walking out of that movie theater for a second time I knew that I had just experienced a remarkable tale, something I hadn't seen all year. I was living an experience. Now that was special. 
 
Although essentially a love story and a film that strongly believes in its themes of fate, the film doesn't concentrate on any particular aspect too much or too little thus creating a mystical aura as all these emotions and events and so forth flash by, dragging you through each of them but always giving you a chance to absorb what's being presented. The liberties to do with the questions being presented to him in the chronological order of his life anyway did not bother me, nor did the fact they paused for a commercial break during a live question. Slumdog Millionaire is effective dramatically and touching at the other times it needs to be; tapping into hope and the errors of people's ways when labelling a certain 'type' of individual. It is certainly worth a look.

I'm not really sure what this film was trying to be. I guess it was "feel good" because all the voiceovers keep telling me so, but it didn't really leave me with any kind of emotion at all. It was good; there were definitely some really good parts to it, but then there were some parts which just left you stunned by how generic it all was - especially considering the enormous hype around it.

The story was pretty much bullet-pointed to perfection - all they had to do was make a good story out of it (the fact that the questions matched the exact chronology of his life is best forgotten). And for the most part they did that, exploring the city slums, violence, poverty, exploitism and with a very solid love story at the centre. I liked how the relationship between the two brothers developed, too. The shots and the music were also brilliant throughout the film (I quickly made my exit from the cinema when the ill fitting Bollywood number came on at the end) and Danny Boyle captured a real authentic blast of India.

But things bugged me. The "D: it is written" declaration. Because he was lucky - he guessed the right answer. It would have been better for Latika to have told him the answer over the phone - because then it would have made sense: through knowing her, and staying loyal to her, he would have won. Instead it made the phone call really pointless. I suspect he would have waited at the train station every day at 5pm regardless. And his brother dying at the exact same moment he becomes a mill-a-nare? UGH! What a tacky bit of filmmaking that was! I did like the very ending sequence though where they are reunited, and it does a clever reverse shot of the moment they see each other before she's bundled into a car. That was really well put in.

The case for this film is that it's original, but it isn't extraordinary. It doesn't deserve to win Best Picture at the Oscars, (BAFTA is a shoe-in), but with the other contenders around it as unremarkable as this, then the "feel good" factor that it supposadly has, and all panels love, will probably mean that it unjustifiably does so. I kind of wish everyone had just left it alone, so it could blossom on its own in a quiet, underground way!

Cineaste prolifique, Danny Boyle est decrit comme un brillant metteur en scene mais dont les oeuvres souffrent de nombreuses imperfections scenaristiques.
Selon moi, cette reputation n'est que partiellement justifiee ( c'est vrai avec un film comme la Plage) au vu de chefs d'oeuvres comme Trainspotting, 28 jours plus tard ou encore  le recent Sunshine.
Pour moi,  Danny Boyle est un grand est Slumdog Millionnaire ne fait que confirmer cette evidence.

Veritable triomphe critique , Slumdog Millionnaire a ete encense notamment a cause de son scenario qui n'est pas si surprenant que Ã§a au vu de la filmographie de son auteur.
En effet, on y retrouve un de ses themes de predilection: l'argent qui sert ici de catalyseur au recit des aventures de Jamal Malik.

L'histoire du film s'articule autour du jeu qui au centre de l'intrigue tout en racontant la vie du personnage principal et cela sur seulement 2 heures a travers une narration brillante qui n'est jamais bordelique !
Le scenario est ecrit comme une sorte de fable moderne mais une fable qui ne renie pas une realite parfois brutale.

Ainsi, si il y a indeniablement quelque chose de magique dans l'histoire de Jamal, le film n'elude pas le contexte social tres dur des bidonvilles indiens a travers quelques sequences difficiles notamment celles qui evoquent l'exploitation sordide des petits mendiants par des mafieux.
Toutefois, Boyle evite  le miserabilisme et  les cliches sur le tiers-monde notamment en ayant recours a une certaine forme d'humour.
Au final, les seules faiblesses scenaristiques du metrages se trouvent a la fin lorsque sont traites l'age adulte de Jamal et le denouement de l'intrigue.
Cela est du notamment a l'histoire d'amour entre Jamal et Latika ( Freida Pinto: une des plus belles femmes que j'ai vu...) que j'ai trouve touchante mais particulierement clichee et meme si cette naivete se trouve justifiee par la volonte bienvenue du realisateur de rendre hommage au cinema bollywoodien, je n'ai pas adhere.
De plus, le niveau de l'interpretation baisse lorsque les personnages deviennent adultes (Dev Patel sympathique mais pas transcendant , Freida Pinto canon mais fade) les gamins s'en sortant bien mieux.

Enfin, au dela de son histoire marquante, Slumdog Millionaire demontre encore le genie de Boyle en matiere de mise en scene et ce dernier trouve avec l'Inde un formidable decor pour l'expression de sa virtuosite.
Slumdog Milionnaire est donc une claque visuelle et sonore qui reussit parfaitement a retranscrire l'emotion de son recit et surtout la vitalite des bidonvilles en particulier et de l'Inde en general et cela sans tomber dans l'exotisme bon marche: respect !

Bref, si je n'avais pas des reserves sur la love story et sur la qualite de l'interpretation (geniale chez les gosses mais seulement correcte chez les adultes) je dirais que Slumdog Millionaire est un chef d'oeuvre !
Ce film prouve la formidable capacite de renouvellement de son realisateur.
Quant aux detracteurs de ce dernier je leur demanderais de me citer un cineaste occidental qui est parti tourne dans un pays qu'il ne connait pas, avec des acteurs inconnus et uniquement parce qu'il a ete seduit par la force d'un recit.
Les exemples sont rares n'est-ce pas ? D'ou la necessite de partir voir le film de Boyle pour tous les cinephiles qui se respectent !

Danny Boyle has been one of my favorite film directors for a while now.  He finally got his due with the magnificent "Slumdog Millionaire", winning the Best Director and Best Picture Oscars.  It is interesting that Boyle has either worked with  noted original screenwriters or made films adapted from novels - he has never served as his own screenwriter or dreamed up his own story ideas.  For Slumdog Millionaire, screenwriter Simon Beaufoy (who also won the Oscar) adapted the novel "Q & A" by Vikas Swarup.  From a plot synopsis of the book, I can tell that some of the characters and their relationships with each other were re-written for the film, but the main plot device is the same: the title character Jamal (Dev Patel), an 18 year old tea-server at a customer support call center, is suspected of cheating at the Indian version of the game show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" when he makes it to the final question.  The story is told in flashbacks as he tells his police interrogators the events in his life that taught him the answer to each question on the show (supposively to be continued the next night).  We are shown how Jamal and his brother Samil became orphans as small children, made friends with Latika who would become Jamal's love interest, and got mixed up with gangsters and criminal opportunists who exploit children and women essentially as slaves.  

So it's not really a feel-good film through and through as some of the movie posters might have us believe.  It does get a little violent and gritty at times, and because there are gaps between the flashbacks, I still wonder how Jamal was able to make it out of the slums even to have a modest honest employment as a tea-server.    It was because of his genuine, naive and honest nature that he didn't turn to a life of crime, like another key character did.  And it was just luck, I suppose, that he didn't end up dead for opposing and escaping the gangsters and criminals.  

I can definitely agree with Slumdog Millionaire's selection as Best Picture of 2008, though it must have been difficult to choose, considering the crowded field for that year.  In addition to the great story, superb on a technical level, which is amazing considering all the hoops Boyle had to jump through to get the movie made in India.  Also, you can't get through the movie without noticing the music.  There are some pretty cool Indian dance pop songs used to great effect.   

The film reminded me a lot of "City of God" (2002) except that it is less violent and more uplifting.  Depending on what one wants out of a movie like this that could be a good thing or a bad thing.  I don't think one is worse than the other- they are really just two different filmmakers takes on the same theme: survival and growing up in the slums of crowded poverty-ridden non-white countries.  One could easily write a long essay comparing "Slumdog Millionaire" to "City of God".  

I think Slumdog Millionaire fits in nicely among Danny Boyle's films, especially his recent ones.  Boyle has been noted for his broad range- jumping from genre to genre and one extreme to another.  The stories he directs still have a connecting similarity.  Though the story may be tumultuous,  tragic, or stressful  things somehow end up on a positive note for the main characters or for humanity.  There is always room for hope.  I think that is a awesome unifying message.

The movie begins with rhetorical forethought almost with a lust for sensationalizing the plot and a self-indulgence that only a potent visual medium like cinema can afford - the movie begins with this question

Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 Million rupees. How did he do it?
A: He cheated
B: Heâs lucky
C: Heâs genius
D: It is written

And then you receive the answer... through an experience called Slumdog Millionaire

I guess seldom you see the world celebrating Indian spirit in a way like this, seldom you see the Indian cinematic creativity being acknowledged on a global forum and without parody and seldom you see the world taking Indian cinema seriously and getting curious to know 'Who is that composer?' / 'Who is that actor?'. 

Such a celebration was done at the Golden Globe with a handful ambassadors of Indian Cinema. It was expected from Lagaan and it was expected from Devdaas. But it took a mix of desi and firangi crew to pull this off, may be hinting that India, by herself, is not ready enough to craft such a masterpiece. 

Well, any which way, the Indian Cinema finally arrived with Slumdog Millioaire... and arrived after decades....

It was a majestic sight Rahman mentioning India, SRK presenting Slumdog .. to GG and Anil Kapur , dressed in a tuxedo, springing on his feet like a kid, at the sight of Boyle holding the trophy.

Slumdog...  is a cinematic experience whose ingenuity renders you speechless and you ought to be fumbling for words other than the one that comes instantly - sheer 'genius'. Danny Boyle weaves together a cinema that is Indian in theme but certainly not in execution. That may not be great but certainly is clever. Smile. So now you know it, the reason it has hit the map is the very reason it has drawn the flak.

Story of Jamal and Latika , and many associated characters , this film is indeed a take on Mumbai's slums - rather a life from amongst slums. But one should be clear - It is NOT about Slums and it goes way beyond a mere narrative to become a string of episodes that baffle the audience when an undereducated call center chai wallah manages to unflinchingly answer all the questions in a variant of KBC. 

 I will not dive into the plot and I strongly recommend you dont do it either till you see the movie, because it is hard to believe now that after the global endorsement, you will not! Lol

Ups:

Script and execution - The way the scripts embeds a gameshow into the life of an ordinary boy both enchants and enthralls. This, in essence, is the crux of this beautiful cinema. Had it been done any other way, it would have risked a disastrous comedy of sorts by the sheer vulnerability towards incredulity
Actors - Lets first state that the movie is not about the actors, not about their lines and certainly not character driven - it is plot driven. Yet the cast of Dev Patel et al do too well to ignore. So does, Anil Kapoor!
Cinematography and Direction - Boyle did his homework well on India and made Anthony Dod Mantle (Cinematographer) do the exact same thing - They captured a wide glossary of Indian landscape so much so that few elite now accuse West of being fed on the lust for voyeuristic poverty in India. Well, so much for a piece of cinema and so much for a legacy in the making.
Mozart from Madras - Yes, the magician has waved his wand and created a score will be remembered for generation by east and west alike. His score in this movie lends a precious life to visuals. He has sealed his legacy in time when the entire world stood up and took notice of his music. Lets face it he has carved his name in immortal stones for generations to come and his music just keeps getting better. Jai Ho...
Downs:
Agreed that the same script that we extol has few logical fallacies that may give you more than a few chances to dismiss the movie as an imperialist's impression - the language of English spoken by Beggars in the movie, knowledge about Benjamin Franklin's to a slumdog and many more such possible loopholes ... but if you ever came across a word called creative license - this is the time to use it :) These are nothing but ways to relate to much wider audiences - Benjamin Franklin could well be Mahatma Gandhi and English could well be Hindi - Conceded with grace !
120 mins slightly too long :) As Alfred Hitchcock said - "The length of the movie should not exceed the strength of my bladder" . Lols
Caution: Please go and watch it with an open and unbiased mind - It is NOT an epic saga, It is NOT based on true story, and it is NOT meant to shake your inner soul and preach you a thing or two about the life in MUMBAI - It is an undemanding cinema which also turns out to be an effective entertainer, whether or not it garners any Oscar nominations as we speak!

Do not listen to people. Reams have been written about it and reams will be written about it in the days to come. Go and watch it and feel comfortable with the idea for not coming to like it. :) Not a shame, after all, the beauty of this cinema lies in the eyes of the beholder....

    The buzz around Danny Boyle's [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] has been incredibly huge during the past couple of months. This is a movie that has been on my radar for a while, but I just never got around to checking it out on the big-screen. So, with the astounding 10 Oscar®-nominations it received earlier today... I had to see finally see how special this movie actually is.
    
    [img]http://img516.imageshack.us/img516/7408/hrslumdogmillionaire282gl8.jpg[/img]
    [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]is the story of Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who is about to experience the biggest day of his life. With the whole nation watching, he is just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India's "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" But when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a street kid know so much? Desperate to prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother (Madhur Mittal) grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika (Freida Pinto), the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of his story reveals the key to the answer to one of the game show's questions. Intrigued by Jamal's story, the jaded Police Inspector (Irrfan Khan) begins to wonder what a young man with no apparent desire for riches is really doing on this game show? When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out... --© Fox Searchlight Pictures
    
    [img]http://img297.imageshack.us/img297/4374/photo04hires88647658870hz8.jpg[/img]
    All in all, [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is director Danny Boyle's best work to date. It's a truly breathtaking experience from start to finish with an ending that's so powerful and emotional. Everything from the story (based on the Boeke Prize winning novel [i]Q and A[/i] by Indian author and diplomat Vikas Swarup), the visuals, the performances, and the music is truly outstanding. Newcomers Dev Patel, Freida Pinto, and Madhur Mittal all make their feature film debuts here. And they head a very stellar, yet very unknown cast of Indian actors. Patel's breakout performance is not only an incredible feature film debut, but is easily one of the best of 2008. He has a very bright future ahead of him if he continues his acting career. Pinto is not only an incredibly breathtaking young woman, but her performance is outstanding as well. I really look forward to seeing what Pinto has in store for herself in Hollywood. The chemistry between Patel and Pinto is fantastic and these two should definitely hook up on the big-screen again. Mittal's performance is outstanding as well. Mittal also has a very bright future if he continues his acting career. As for the rest of the cast, it's great and the young actors that portray Patel, Pinto, and Mittal are all outstanding. Irrfan Khan ([i]The Namesake [/i]and [i]A Mighty Heart[/i]) puts on a great performance as the Police Inspector.  And Bollywood favorite Anil Kapoor plays the role of the game show host extremely well.
    
    [img]http://img294.imageshack.us/img294/828/hrslumdogmillionaire386zc7.jpg[/img]
    So overall, [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is not only one of the best movies of 2008, but it's another unexpected masterpiece from 2008. With that said, this is one of the best movies of the past 5 years or so. The 10 Oscar®-nominations it received are very deserving. Danny Boyle has really outdone himself here. Like I said earlier... everything about this movie including the performances, the visuals, the music, and of course the direction is incredible. This is not only a must-see for fans of Danny Boyle, but a must-see for everyone looking for a fantastic movie to check out. Anyways, I really look forward to checking this one out for many years to come. :D

Plenty of movies are released every year to the general public in movie theaters, DVD's, and broadcasts through television. Movies are fun to see with friends, or alone, on nearly any and every occasion. They appeal to a wide array of the populace who seek out escapes from everyday endeavors.

That last paragraph has just about nothing to do with Slumdog Millionaire, because director Danny Boyle hasn't created a movie, he's created an experience. Slumdog is the simple story of a rather poor kid named Jamal (Dev Patel) who gets every question correct on the Indian version of the popular game show "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?" After reaching the second to last question, the show ends on time limit, and Jamal is arrested on the accusation that he cheated. Jamal is forced to tell the police the truth, and he ends up having to explain how he knew the answer to each question one-by-one.


What this particular cinematic masterpiece lacks is a sense of being a movie. From beginning to end, Boyle completely entrances the audience into an almost surreal experience which follows a single character through all his hardships and achievements. From the beginning close-ups and adrenaline-pumped chase scenes to the suspensful ending, you, as the viewer, feel as though you're placed directly into the action.

The writing is spot-on, with clever, witty dialogue and expertly arc'd characters. Each person on-screen has so much potential lying within them than just their exterior motives and apparent inhibitions. Although adapted from a novel, the story is still engrossing and visualized perfectly from its source material (Q&A by Vikas Swarup). The music is intense when it needs to be, flowing when it wants to be, and beautiful where it fits, as well as the precision editing used to achieve maximum inclusion into this movie roller coaster. 

Jamal is a character that you may not initially empathize with, but you will certainly sympathize and end up nearly falling in love with his chivalrous tenacity and warrior-like perseverance. Beautifully scripted, directed, and composed, Slumdog Millionaire easily stands as one of the best cinematic achievements of the decade, and certainly the best film of 2008.

I noticed that there were no oblique shots of the "Who Wants to be a MIllionaire" set except for the shots of the cameras. All shots on that set that actually focused on talent were shot nonobliquely. Very little was focused on when the camera or talents were in motion. I also appreciated the strobe-effect shots using the train. 
 
 I liked the music. I knew, of course, Paper Planes, and possibly one other. I especially liked the remixes of normal "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" music used in other portions, such as the flashbacks. 
 
 Several shots at first glance seemed unnecessary to the plot, but after a time I realized that they lent to the believeability of the story. They showed people just being, whether they were directly involved or not - and they were all involved.

The phone call from the TV show is over-dramatic and not logical - Jamal could've called the brother for their location instead of going on TV (shouldn't be hard as he easily cons his way into a house). Slumdog is a vivid and entertaining film of a local Indian boy, Jamal (Dev Patel), who's a contestant on India's "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire" gets interrogated by Indian police as he recalls how he knows the answers to the questions based on his life. Jamal grows fond of Latika as they grow up, their relationship blossoms to romance in their teens while Salim becomes a gangster for an Indian mobster and separates them. Then as a young man, Jamal tries to locate Latika while working for the 'Millionaire' show's contestant audition agency, he reunites with Salim to reaquaint with Latika as he advances to the final question for 20 million Rupees.

Due to the harsh reality of India's impoverished slums, Slumdog Millionaire is a fascinating modern-day spin from "The Arabian Knights" and "Prince and the Pauper" that will leave you wondering what your final answer is to the Question; How did Jamal know the answers to the questions?

Danny Boyle's "Slumdog Millionaire" is a lot of things, but above all it's one of the liveliest films to become a critical darling in recent memory. Look at its fellow Best Picture nominees and you'll find ponderous, staid Prestige Pictures of the type that the Academy can never seem to resist (with the arguable exception of "Milk"). As conventional as "Slumdog" is at the basic levels of narrative, character, and themes, its furious sun-baked energy and the Orientalist alterity of its setting makes it seem much less predictable and generic than it really is...

"Slumdog" trades on the common narrative tropes of the "rags to raja" drama in undeniably obvious ways: overcoming obstacles, forbidden love and youthful yearning. It owes roughly coequivalent debts to both pull-up-your-bootstraps crowd-pleasers like "Rocky" and vibrant quick-cut portrayals of the Third (Under)World like "City of God". The look, sound, feel, and style of the film are its truest joy. Boyle deserves credit, but his team of collaborators aid him greatly. Anthony Dod Mantle's cinematography drinks in India like a fine tea, all multichromatic clutter and bright, sweaty vivaciousness. Chris Dickens' mastefully kinetic editing is a practical Oscar shoo-in. And A.R. Rahman will win an Oscar or two for his blood-pumping score and pitch-perfect contributions from M.I.A. (the "Paper Planes"-scored train sequence trumps the "Pineapple Express" trailer for the aptest visual companion to Maya's new modern classic track). The cinematic skill with which these elements are applied and the deep, abiding delight they continually produce overcomes every bit of the script's generic predictability. The plot and characters are a mere skeleton for the lovely skin of this film, a hanger for Boyle's robe of many colours that has a gutsy poetry all its own...

And anyway, "Slumdog Millionaire" is more a meta-commentary on the narrative conventions it is using than a mere parroting of them. The genius of screenwriter Simon Beaufoy's employment of the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" as the main thread of the plot is located precisely in its superficial predictability. "Millionaire"'s huge popularity is now a thing of the past in North America, but the kernel of its hit status was its simplicity, indeed its very contrivance: it is simultaneously entirely predictable and inherently dramatic and suspenseful...

In "Slumdog Millionaire", it serves as a common touchstone, a paradigm of the endlessly repeatable and yet viscerally engaging game-show tension that all of the genre's great success rely upon. Boyle and Beaufoy seem to recognize that a game show like "Millionaire" has shifted the axis of the rags-to-riches narrative in the popular consciousness; what's so compelling about an inspiring story of working from nothing to everything in "real" life when it can be done on primetime television in the space of an hour? Beyond its jump-cut editing and globalized soundtrack, the dialogue between the film's narrative conventions and those of the game show (which Jamal's "destined" knowledge of the trivial answers and his unflappable approach to the format's cliches upends, as when he asks Anil Kapoor's slimy host if HE is nervous) is what truly makes it a post-modern meta-commentary on genre. Despite misguided accusations of neo-colonialism and stereotyping in the film's use of the Indian setting, this absorption and adaptation of Western culture is what makes "Slumdog" such a prescient and timely film. It is not a film about India as much as it is a film about what the rise of India means to the world (read: the Western world), and how that rise incorporates Western culture and recasts it and views it through an Indian kaleidoscope. The presence of the "Millionaire" show at the heart of the film is a complex metaphor for this process, and it's simply too bad that so many critics of the film seem to have missed it...

Standing ovation goes to Vikas Swarup for his unforgettable tale, on which this movie is based, Q&A...and more ovation goes for Simon Beaufoy for his change in that baseline story to make it much more happening...The character, Latika is nowhere in the book...it was all Simon's doing. Through her, he created a heart for the movie, for us to melt into. The greatest asset for the movie, is in arguably the direction. Danny Boyle, is already a critic favorite and he doesnt disappoint with this one. He has done his homework about India well and has shown things exactly as it is. Maybe many a scenes might give us a bad outlook on Indian life per say, but hey, thats how we have come to being a great place. Indian directors should watch and learn this kind of movie making...we have all the scenes here, right in our own country...they should learn to exploit that beauty, instead of making stuttering actors and wannabe kings and size zero good for nothings change the future of Indian Cinema for the bad. A R Rahman is as refreshing as ever, the songs are good, the score is even better. It correctly points us in the direction of the kind of music Indian heart is based on. The technical staff on SDM has done a wonderful job with the editing, the cinematography and the sound. They are never dull, never boring and always a welcome change scene after scene. Watch it for a good time. It might not affect you like Revolutionary Road or Curious Case of Benjamin Button did...but it will surely put a smile on your face.

Here's a good crowd-pleaser that explores the development of India over the last couple of decades.

We find Jamal is one question away from winning the Millionaire grand prize (r20 million), but the police question his eligibility.  Turns out, Jamal knows all of the questions based on personal experience.  As the police review each question with Jamal, he explains how he knew it, and we flashback to his life (which, for the most part, just so happens to be in chronological order).  But Jamal's not done.  He has yet to win the prize.  Will the police believe him.  And if so, where will he find inspiration for the final question?

The screenplay, stripped bare, is actually pretty formulaic.  That's what makes this such a crowd pleaser.  But the movie is not predictable.  That distinguishes the movie.  If it were both formulaic and predictable, I'd be writing a bad review.  It is a movie that causes the audience to think and focus, but not as much as some Oscar contenders (remember it is a crowd pleaser--and today's crowd doesn't really like to think.  That's why summer blockbusters make so much money).

But the screenplay is not a bare piece of material.  It is put into the hands of Danny Boyle.  I'm sure Boyle knew he had an interesting screenplay on his hands when he got it, but what he did with it is extraordinary.  Boyle puts the focus on the country of India and the culture and how it influences the life of this so-called slumdog.  The country of India is put at the forefront yet it never distracts or becomes a documentary.  Instead, it just enhances the film so much.  And it takes a great director to get that.

From the beginning you know that this will be an exciting, fast-paced movie.  You're interested by the first frame.  As we're introduced to Jamal and his situation, we become hooked.  And then, at the first flashback, Boyle grabs the entire audience, swooshes (yes, swooshes) them into India a few decades ago, and A.R. Rahman's score comes in with "Oh...Saya" (nominated for Best Song) which introduces pounding drums and now those hooked before are now INVESTED.  I was literally bouncing in my seat with a smile on my face.  And the only thing that's going on is two young Indian boys rushing through the slums of India.  But it's such sensory entertainment.  You can't help but be invested.  With investment comes risk.  And you're never let down.  From beginning to end, your investment pays off and it makes the movie more enjoyable.

AND ON TOP OF ALL OF THAT, the story progresses.  The focus and the goal of the story and the characters suddenly becomes aware to the audience.  We were deceived.  You think he got on Millionaire to win the big prize and finally get out of his slum caste?  Wrong.  Why is he doing it?  You'll have to see it to find out.

This movie isn't necessarily about the actors.  There's great acting but the story wasn't written for the actors. Jamal is played by, I think, 4 actors (to represent different ages).  So one character is not on screen for a long period of time.

When (yes, when) you go to see this movie, please take note of the choices that Boyle uses as a director and how that may enhance/hurt the story in your opinion.  Some examples include his camera angles.  His photography in certain scenes.  Subtitles is a major choice that could divide audiences.  Pay attention to the subtitles when they show up.

Rahman's score deserves the Oscar since the Dark Knight score (its only true competition) was deemed ineligible.
The screenplay has some tough competition but could win if Slumdog is on a roll come Oscar night.
Right now, Slumdog is the front-runner to win Best Picture.  Button has the most nominations but most of them are in the techincal categories.  And Button had a $150mil budget.  Slumdog was made for only $15mil (keep that in mind when you go to see it--almost all of the exterior, and some interior, India shots were filmed on location.).  Slumdog is strong in the major categories so look for sweeps while Button will receive acknowledgment in the tech. categories.  Millionaire should win best picture.
The biggest lock, however, has to be for Danny Boyle for director.  There's no reason to give the award to anyone else, unless you're trying to give just one award to a deserving movie.  But Boyle is what makes this movie.  You can't use director as a throwaway.  Boyle will get the win.  And rightfully so.

Who would have thought that Danny Boyle would create one of the finest
films this year already, and probably one of the best I have watched.
Over the years we have seen the different types of brilliant genre
picture's that Boyle has directed, e.g. Shallow Grave (Thriller),
Trainspotting (Drug-Taking Drama), 28 Days Later (Horror), and Sunshine
(Sci-Fi). But then Boyle went out and decided to look for something
completely different, and found (bizzarely) a British/Indian Romantic
Gameshow picture. 

As always, it is another 'rags to riches' story of a young boy named
Jamal who lives and survives on the streets of Mumbai, and somehow
manages to become a contestant on the Indian's 'Who Wants To Be A
Millionaire' game-show. Jamal (played brilliantly by Skins-Dev Patel),
a young child who grows into his teens along with his elder brother
Samil, and which depicts the main part of the story towards the love of
his life, as Jamal says in the film, "The most beautiful girl in the
world." Freida Pinto, stars as Letika, and all three (Jamal, Samil,
Letika) encounter difficult stages of their life's, and some that
change drastically.

The film whilst showing the love story unfold between Jamal and Letika,
the other part is obviously focused on the game show that Jamal is one
question away from becoming a multi-millionaire, until being arrested
and accused by the game-show host Prem Kumar (played sneeringly by Anil
Kapoor) of cheating. Therefore, Jamal is then put through torture to
explain his actions (beware, this film although shares discomfort as
well as joy) and admit his wrong-doing, but instead confesses to the
Police, how he simply knew the answers to the questions with vivid
flashbacks from his childhood past, which is a brilliant piece of film
making by Boyle.

The films last's just under 2 hours, but it was so riveting and
exhilarating, I could never take my eyes of it, as I thoroughly enjoyed
every second of it. The score as well by A. R. Rahman is also one of
the best I've heard and was perfectly set in tone for the film
throughout, which also gives you a great insight into India's culture
and lifestyle, with some of the most gorgeous camera scenes you'll see
this year.

All of the characters in the film are brilliant, and with a bit more

So, I kinda went to see this on a whim. I was supposed to meet up with some friends to go see "The Wrestler". But, since Bradford Sargent loves to ruin joy, it didn't really happen. So, while I'm at the theater, I decide to go see "Slumdog Millionaire". I'd heard it's great, and the story sounded really interesting. So I saw it.

And I loved it. I adored it. It absolutely captured my heart. The story could've been awful if it hadn't been carefully and meaningfully constructed. Jamal, our hero, (and my new hero), ends up on an Indian version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire". Against expectations, Jamal answers nearly every question right, raising the hope of everyone watching, but raising the suspicions of the show. He's turned over to police, accused of cheating. He then tells of how every question he was asked relates to the events of his life leading up to him being on this show.

What follows is a well-crafted, well-acted, well-directed, creatively-shot, beautifully-scored piece of art, telling a tale filled with repeated tragedies but enduring hope, captivating you and leaving you giving your heart to the trials and aspirations of young Jamal. 

Besides the undeniable quality of this film, it's got that kind of protagonist that I just love: the innocent, pure-of-heart underdog, always getting dumped on, but always hoping against hope and carrying on. Particularly effective is his continued pursuit of Latika, the girl whom he's always fought for and had a pure love for, but who always gets taken away from him. 

This film has inspiring moments, many of which arise from its tragedies. Thus tying into an overall theme of the film...that this boy Jamal, and everyone around him have a destiny. Even though some awful things happen, and some of the characters turn some dark corners...they all meaningfully serve the overall destiny.

You watch this film go on, wanting more and more for Jamal to succeed, and no matter what happens, this film has your heart. In its direction, music, wonderful tone and pacing, and its fantastic acting. I am soooo glad this movie is nominated for an Oscar for Best Picture. I can't really say at this point whether or not it should get it, since I haven't seen any of the other nominees (although someone sitting behind me said it's better than Benjamin Button...). I can only think of one thing that bothered me about it, regarding something that happens in the story. I won't say what, but I initially questioned whether it would have been better if that plot turn had gone the other way. But even that I'm quite unsure about, and actually like it more and more as I reflect on it further.

I cannot recommend this film highly enough. It's one of those movies that is more than the sum of its parts. Upon just seeing it, I will say that it is one of the most beautiful and inspiring films I've ever seen. I'm curious to see if that enthusiasm will wear off and build up as time goes on. But for now, that's what I say about it.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is a most pleasant surprise. It is not what you think. I confess that I had small expectations for this film; I expected an indie drama weighed down by Indian accents and slow, boring pacing with maybe a flashy sequence in the middle somewhere (an excuse to paint the movie poster with all the colors of the rainbow). What I got, however, was quite the opposite.

In terms of the year's superlatives, where "The Dark Knight" is the coolest, "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" is the most unique, "Milk" is the most political, "Wall-E" is the cutest, and "Gran Torino" is the most Clint-Eastwoodest, "Slumdog Millionaire" is the most, and I mean the most, pleasant and inspiring. Pleasantry and inspiration, of course, do not draw crowds like they should, but the few who are willing to take a chance on a film that looks boring will be overwhelmingly satisfied.

Unfortunately, I can't help the film by talking about its details, because I would spoil it prematurely. Therefore, I am limited to simply strongly recommending it. I will, however, point out some of my concerns about it. My biggest concern is its stance on fate and destiny; theologically, the Christian elements are few, by-products of a western film production; morally, it is pretty good for the most part. Objecting to children stealing out of hunger is hard to condemn, but when I speak of morals I refer more to its pure depiction of love, for the most part. Yes, it is a love story, and it is a finer one than "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" simply because of the absence of sexual material. But I say too much.

See it. Enjoy it. Be inspired. Be content. Be diligent.

Slumdog Millionaire opens the rotten face of India, does it? Does it show the so called âdirty underbellyâ of India? Slumdog word is racist as alleged by a chap from Bihar. But really?? If I had one word to describe these comments it would have been a *beep*!!

By no means this movie is aimed at showing the chronic poverty of our nation. Many reviewers have criticized this movie for showing only the dirty reality of the country instead of displaying all those swanky buildings, glittering malls etc.

Slumdog Millionaire narrates a story of 2 siblings & a girl, who rise from the dirty slum life and move into different directions of life. The older brother (âSalimâ-played by Madhur Mittal) ends up working for a gangster, the girl (âLatikaâ-played by Frieda Pinto) ends up as a show girl with the same gangsters and the hero of the movie the younger brother (âJamalâ-played by Dev Patel) ends up living a rather straight life as a tea server in a call center. Jamal reaches the âhot seatâ of Kaun Banega Crorepati hosted by an arrogant quizmaster Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor) who donât want him to win the game. He calls the police to get Jamal Malik arrested on the charges of fraud at the end of day 1 of the show. At the police station Jamal is tortured first by the sound thrashing from Constable Srinivas (Saurabh Shukla) and then he is subjected to electric shock, all to make him speak about how a tea serving slumdweller can give the correct answers.

The movie revolves around the dingy slums of Dharavi. The heaps and heaps of garbage, dogs with flees, young Jamal jumping in a pit full of *beep* (*sic*), hindu-muslim riots, pimps, gangsters, rough language is some of the few characteristics of the film which together with the superb cinematography by Anthony Dod Mantle makes it an ultra realistic movie. Kudos to the director Danny Boyle and co-director Loveleen Tandon for the impressive direction and superb camera takes which shows the minutest of the details of the dirty slum life. The screenplay was outstanding.

Acting:If I had to rate the performance of the characters I would surely give a high five to the children artists of the movie. Almost half of the movie shows them and their acting was very natural and realistic. Dev Patel was fine too. Frieda Pinto didnât had too much of the screen time but delivered good performance. Anil Kapoor was cool. Irrfan Khan as the deadly cop together with Saurabh Shukla gave the top performances together with the child artists. Mahesh Manjrekar was looking a real gangster. He was rough, bad and whatever you may call a gangster. Madhur Mittal as the older brother Salim was quite good.

Sound/Music: Well the music has so many nominations for the Oscars what more can I write!!??!!
The sound effects were superb. The background score was creepy good. âJai Hoâ track comes at the end of the movie. The song is classic but I doubt whether it would take away the oscar. Letâs hope for the best. A.R Rahman proves that he is the best in this field!

The movie has been given an âAâ certificate and rightly so. It has some good amount of strong language, violence in the form of riots, torture, a child being blinded with hot syrup (something), murder and other such things happening in the slums. These violent scenes are quite chilling and tense.

Overall I would recommend this movie to every person who has a tag âIndianâ attached to him/her. A detailed insight into the murky life of slumdwellers. Slumdog Millionaire is one of those movies which has a happy ending. And out of the 10 oscar nominations it would bag atleast three i.e in âcinematographyâ, âeditingâ & for the song âJai Hoâ. I see that a majority of the people who ride this movie's nuts are really focused on the fact that Slumdog is a straight forward love story. Well that's true but what's even bigger and more important was the social commentary on class prejudice. The assumption that  everyone is 'uneducated' because they are poor. The simple story is also well developed through creative flashbacks and I love that a British film maker decided to make a movie based in India starring a mostly Indian cast. And I would have given a higher rating if the hand held camera work and editing weren't so modern. Too much shakiness and dumb confusing skewed angles and I have no idea how many times I've said that when it comes new movies. Even sequences which had the most potential for great photography are undoubtedly ruined by said camera work especially the part where Jamal and his brother make a living riding on top of trains and begging for money. Lastly the soundtrack is dumb and distracts from the dramatic effect of the film. It might have fit but it wasn't appropriate and I wonder why they just didn't consistently use the original score which was really good. So there's no real reason to ride this movie's nuts. Slumdog Millionaire opens the rotten face of India, does it? Does it show the so called dirty underbelly of India? Slumdog word is racist as alleged by a chap from Bihar. But really?? If I had one word to describe these comments it would have been a *beep*!!

By no means this movie is aimed at showing the chronic poverty of our nation. Many reviewers have criticized this movie for showing only the dirty reality of the country instead of displaying all those swanky buildings, glittering malls etc.

Slumdog Millionaire narrates a story of 2 siblings & a girl, who rise from the dirty slum life and move into different directions of life. The older brother (Salim-played by Madhur Mittal) ends up working for a gangster, the girl (Latika-played by Frieda Pinto) ends up as a show girl with the same gangsters and the hero of the movie the younger brother (Jamal-played by Dev Patel) ends up living a rather straight life as a tea server in a call center. Jamal reaches the hot seat of Kaun Banega Crorepati hosted by an arrogant quizmaster Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor) who dont want him to win the game. He calls the police to get Jamal Malik arrested on the charges of fraud at the end of day 1 of the show. At the police station Jamal is tortured first by the sound thrashing from Constable Srinivas (Saurabh Shukla) and then he is subjected to electric shock, all to make him speak about how a tea serving slumdweller can give the correct answers.

The movie revolves around the dingy slums of Dharavi. The heaps and heaps of garbage, dogs with flees, young Jamal jumping in a pit full of shit (*sic*), hindu-muslim riots, pimps, gangsters, rough language is some of the few characteristics of the film which together with the superb cinematography by Anthony Dod Mantle makes it an ultra realistic movie. Kudos to the director Danny Boyle and co-director Loveleen Tandon for the impressive direction and superb camera takes which shows the minutest of the details of the dirty slum life. The screenplay was outstanding.

Acting:If I had to rate the performance of the characters I would surely give a high five to the children artists of the movie. Almost half of the movie shows them and their acting was very natural and realistic. Dev Patel was fine too. Frieda Pinto didnt had too much of the screen time but delivered good performance. Anil Kapoor was cool. Irrfan Khan as the deadly cop together with Saurabh Shukla gave the top performances together with the child artists. Mahesh Manjrekar was looking a real gangster. He was rough, bad and whatever you may call a gangster. Madhur Mittal as the older brother Salim was quite good.

Sound/Music: Well the music has so many nominations for the Oscars what more can I write!!??!!
The sound effects were superb. The background score was creepy good. Jai Ho track comes at the end of the movie. The song is classic but I doubt whether it would take away the oscar. Lets hope for the best. A.R Rahman proves that he is the best in this field!

The movie has been given an A certificate and rightly so. It has some good amount of strong language, violence in the form of riots, torture, a child being blinded with hot syrup (something), murder and other such things happening in the slums. These violent scenes are quite chilling and tense.

Overall I would recommend this movie to every person who has a tag Indian attached to him/her. A detailed insight into the murky life of slumdwellers. Slumdog Millionaire is one of those movies which has a happy ending. And out of the 10 oscar nominations it would bag atleast three i.e in cinematography, editing & for the song Jai Ho. It is a perfect edge of the seat thriller wrapped in the ghostly realities of slums.
Hightly recommended.

Kudos to the director/writer for making the characters accessible this way. Proving that some themes e.g. young love are universal. plus points; they stuck to realism (the slum) even if the camera angles and music took any grittiness away (escapism has always sold at the cinema in india at least), the thing about learning from the bumps (euphemism i know) from the ghetto i know to be very true, from personal experience, it was a delight to see that on the silver screen, the love story was finely interweaved and so was the brother sub-plot (even though it could have been darker).

overall a great story, albeit rare, but one that is life affirming and realistic in some parts (no one helps you on your way out of the slums - presenter/cops) and it's an indian story, it could have been more polished, more gritty, and more realistic, the destiny bit was the weakest point i felt, and in that sense could have been left out, but i look around at the other fare, especially indian-set, and nothing as great as this has been achieved and for that reason together with my own personal resonance i give this top marks-

Really well produced movie. Everything technical is excellent. Capturing the essence of the characters is also done brilliantly.

However.

Metaphysically it is a Destiny movie. The background is poverty and rising out of it - which traditionally is a Hollywood presentation of the American Dream, only it is India. The povery is worse, growing up in slums without parents, surviving without any hope of meeting a rational world, and rational people.

Therefore, when the only way out of this wretchedness, is a such an incredible string of luck, that if taken seriously - means the presence of the Devine. Although this is not at all suggested by the movie itself, but a very appealing idea to may Americans as well as Indians.

So if this is meant to inspire the audience, by showing how to get out of the slums - it should fail, because nobody could repeat the string of luck that Jamal Malik had. Unless you realize that it was his commitment to the love of his life, that brought him to the game show, and won her back, you would think that it was the gameshow the movie was about.

Jamal is a moral character that deserve to win his love from the clutches of evil, and this is presented in the contrast between Jamal and his "brother." And so this is a proper love story, and it does have a plot, it has drama, and it is worth seeing. 

Well done, Mr. Boyle.

This isn't Danny Boyle's best, but it is great. As usual, he finds romance in some of the darkest places, and India is here presented as among the worst. The miraculous improbability of every question on the show having a specific reference point in Jamal's life sustains just enough hope to keep you watching through the horrendous story of his upbringing. India is at once beautiful and terrifying in this film, and while in the Western world we can all say "wouldn't it be nice to be a millionaire", that the million dollar prize converts to 20,000,000 rupees should tell us the that the drama of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire is completely false. Relatively speaking, we are all millionaires already. Boyle exploits the structure to tell a truly dramatic story, and the result is a film that has something for everyone. Great movie, as deserving of best picture as anything else made in 2008 - with better child acting than Gran Torino too!

For films such as Slumdog Millionaire, it can oft be hard to distinguish just what the director behind the project was intending to provoke from their audience. On the one hand, Slumdog tells a compelling and mostly interesting rags-to-riches story topped off with a sugar coated ending with extra sprinkles that- while notably hammy- doesnt cross over into absurdity. Yet it also tries to tell another tale alongside it, this time revolving around a romance that never quite takes off in the way that director Danny Boyle wishes it to. Boyle, who up to this point is known for his sensually driven works, surprisingly hasnt touched upon romance at least in the quantity and focus as to which Slumdog Millionaire implies; unfortunately, this lack of experience on his part shows throughout. So although the majority of the feature remains as a somewhat uplifting and compelling drama on base level, a distinct lack of focus in characterisation and chemistry stops the movie from ever going beyond its ostensible ideas and generic façade. In the end I found myself moved more by what Slumdog wanted to say rather than what it did say.

Taking place largely in flashback mode, Slumdog Millionaire tells the story of Jamal Malik (Dev Patel, Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, Tanay Chheda), a- well- slumdog. Born in the slums and raised for the most part as an orphan, Jamal is a quiet, well-intentioned boy with a big heart and even bigger eyes for opportunity and beauty. It isnt long before he spots Latika (Freida Pinto, Rubiana Ali, Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar) and from here on in it would seem the story writes itself. From here the script moves in and out of telling a mystery thriller seeped in slow paced drama, and diverging upon a romance which feels forced and laboured. 

A much more compelling element within Slumdogs narrative however lies in the way in which the story is framed within a retelling of the protagonists chance of lifetime on game show Who Wants to be a Millionaire?. This otherwise gauche framing device serves as a surprisingly effective way in which to chop up Jamals childhood and teenage life into its most digestible pieces without seeming too contrived, whilst also paving way for the movies big finale which makes the most out of the slow building momentum of the first two acts. The result of this clashing between engaging drama and forgettable romance is jarring however; there are times when Slumdog soars and times when it gets downright irksome.

One thing that usually remains as something to look forward to within a Danny Boyle feature however lies within its aesthetics. Taking place entirely within the impoverished areas of India, the movie establishes strong images and motifs throughout which in turn further the films emotional and psychological connections with the viewer. From the patched, duct-taped, second-hand nature of everything, the world of Slumdog Millionaire entices ideas of existentialism not just through its protagonists story but through the environment in which he exists. This, coupled with a magnificent score and soundtrack which more often than not gives the movie its biggest and most memorable sequences, provide a sensual experience that one now comes to expect when greeted by the name Danny Boyle.

I couldnt help but wish that such ideas and care were taken with the remainder of the feature however; especially concerning the romance played out by the lead performers. Boyle, who is inexperienced to some degree in handling such dynamics, doesnt do much to provide any interest in the protagonists love interest- its clear that youthful, whimsical love is certainly implied within the constructs of this average romance and yet it is never truly shown. This generic approach to storytelling inevitably hurts Slumdog to the point that many of its sequences which draw heavily upon this much needed chemistry fall on their face. The actors themselves are fine and able- and provide excellent performances in all other respects- but as a pair, there just isnt enough to invest in. 

This in turn brings me to my final conclusion on what is essentially a mixed bag of engaging drama and tepid fairytale; Slumdog Millionaire is a fine picture- it provides a heart-warming story with all its intentions in the right places, and yet it doesnt ever convince in its ability to connect with the viewer. What results is a lukewarm, temporal pleaser, but certainly not one to be cherished for years to come.

A really sweet and amazing film and one of the most thrilling, entertaining, and gorgeous movies of the year. Slumdog tells the story of Jamal Malik, a 20 year old boy in India who comes from complete poverty and how he progresses through a game Who Wants to be a Millionaire? using only his life experiences. The cast is all great and filled with most unknowns which helps give the flashback scenes more sense of reality though this is not a documentary by any means. It's much like the sweet moving Hollywood Golden Era epics but with the filmmaking styles and techniques very much taken from the indie & international circuit of recent years. The whole score and soundtrack for the film is always completely fantastic with lots of very interesting electronic and instrumental hip-hop music. The movie is visually stunning, Danny Boyle always has had a fantastic visual palette which he showed off to great degree with last year's "Sunshine" but here it's put to even more astonishing use showing the slums of India and some famous locales. This is easily one of the best movies I've seen this year being completely endearing, heartfelt, and at times heartbreaking, hilarious, and completely thrilling. Danny Boyle has really just continued to stun me with all of his work and ambition even if in the past sometimes his ambition has succeeded the film itself, this time he fully meets it and keep a lookout for Dev Patel and Freida Pinto, as I'm sure we're going to see alot more of them in Western Cinema in coming years.

We're ramping up for Oscarpalooza!  Nominations, as you may know, came out the other day, and I'll be spending about the next month or so desperately trying to see as many of the nominees as possible.  (Well--I'm not going to bother with [i]Bolt[/i] or [i]Kung-Fu Panda[/i], but it doesn't matter, because [i]Wall-E[/i] is going to win.)  Miriah called today and asked if I wanted to go see [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i], and I thought, well, why not?  I'm still not really in the mood for [i]Benjamin Button[/i], thirteen nominations or no, [i]Milk[/i] is out of the theatre, and I can wait a little longer on [i]Frost/Nixon[/i].  Maybe I'll see it with Heather or Moses later in the week.  We'll see, right?  So [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] it is.

Jamal Malik (as a small child, Ayush Mahesh Khedekar; as a teenager, Tanay Chheda; as an adult, Dev Patel) has gone on the Indian version of [i]Who Wants to Be a Millionaire[/i], playing for 20 million rupees (some $425 thousand in US dollars).  However, since he is from the slums, he is assumed to be cheating somehow.  He is taken to the police station, where they interrogate him as to how he could possibly have known the answers to all those questions when he missed an easy one early on.  To explain this, Jamal tells the police inspector (Irrfan Khan) the story of his life and how he interacts with his older brother, Salim (as a small child, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail; as a teenager, Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala; as an adult, Madhur Mittal), and their friend, Latika (as a small child, Rubiana Ali; as a teenager, Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar; as an adult, Freida Pinto).  Each answer, save the one he missed, ties in somehow to the life events shared with the other two.  

This is a delightful film.  It's dark and unpleasant in places--at least the children in [i]Born Into Brothels[/i] actually had homes--and things do not reliably go well for Jamal, Salim, and Latika.  You know that Jamal must survive to tell the story, but there are no such guarantees about the other two, but Jamal must reach that studio on that day in order to end up in that police station.  I will confess that I did not know the answer to most of the questions myself, because most of the questions are about Indian culture and tradition--and one is about cricket--but I think the suspense of some of the final moments of the film is rather spoiled for me, because that's one of the ones where I knew the answer myself.  I seemed to be practically alone in the theatre that way, however--the people next to me, for example, guessed wrong.

Jamal and Salim travel all across India, it seems, going through Mumbai, Calcutta, Agra.  Everywhere they go, the boys have some scam or another.  They save Latika's life.  Salim saves Jamal from a horrible fate.  And through it all, Jamal really believes in them both.  We do not find out until almost the end why he went on the show in the first place, but when we do, the whole thing makes more sense than what you would probably expect it to be.  There are at least three major betrayals, and there are a couple of incredible sacrifices.  Jamal cannot know the answers, they say, because he's just a slumdog, a child of the streets.  But every answer is there in the story, waiting to be uncovered and explained.  

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is up in Cinematography, Directing, Editing, Original Score, Sound Editing, Sound Mixing, Adapted Screenplay, Picture, and twice for Original Song.  There are several categories where I'm torn--it's up against [i]The Dark Knight[/i] in several places, for one--but I have to say, I was far more impressed with the music here than I was in [i]Wall-E[/i], probably its main competitor--in Original Song, its only competitor.  To be scrupulously fair, I do not actually know which of the plentiful songs were actually the nominated ones.  I suspect the song at the end, but I don't know what any of them were called, so I guess we'll figure it out during the telecast.
