If you think that Danny Boyle has already topped himself with both Trainspotting or Sunshine, then you have no idea what's in store when you see Slumdog Millionaire, his newest movie, and might I add, the crown jewel in his already fine career. As the film begins, you have no idea what to expect, but by the time the film ends, you will be walking out of the theater thinking you have seen the second coming of Christ (forgive the pun). If you think The Dark Knight is the best film of the year, then I would suggest seeing this film because this film puts that film to shame.

As the film opens, Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) has made it onto the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, and he is only one question away from the top prize when he is accused of cheating. The film's structure makes clear that every answer to the questions is part of his past. There's also the object of his affections with a beautiful girl named Latika (Freida Pinto) that by his appearance on the show may get her attention.

I can't reveal anymore than that (and believe me, I do), but for the many surprises this film has to offer, you have to experience the film for yourself because the less you know going in, the more the film will touch you in a way that Boyle has never done before. The first thing that deserves mention is the structure of the film, which can be off-putting at first, but once the story really gets underway, it is a structure that is pulled off amazingly. It's also helped by using a different kind of subtitles as well (Yes, a 1/3 of the film is in the native Indian language) that are colored are are bigger than normal so us as an audience can actually read them. If you hate subtitles, leave your prejudices against them at the door and just let the film absorb you with all that it has to offer.

Speaking of aborbing, I haven't even mentioned that the performances are just as good as well. Dev Patel has been carving out a name for himself in Britain on the television show Skins (which can be seen here in this country on BBC America), but here he makes a star-making turn as the naive, but shy and quiet Jamal, a guy who knows what he wants, but doesn't have the strength, skill, or money to get them. Especially when he has to overcome his brother Salim (Madhur Mittel), who thanks to a bunch of Indian gangsters has been forbidden from the things he really wants in the World. The finale of the film, when his brother must make that choice, is one that is not only heartbreaking, but also somewhat rewarding.

And regarding moments like that, there are numerous occasions (especially within the last 30 minutes of the film) where we root for the characters to get what they want or to realize that they are in tension-filled situations where they might be the ones we're waiting on to make their move. There are two especially (which I can't give away, only because they give away big plot points) that will do this to you. As I watched the film the first time, I was fully invested on those later moments, but as I saw it again the other night (in a packed house, I might add), the whole film had me invested in those moments even more and they touched me even more than they did the first time. I won't say this is a film that gets better on repeat viewings (It is best to go into this film knowing as little as possible), but it has the effect to get even more powerful.

There are moments that might be quite brutal to watch (which partly result in the film's R rating), but they have a power and intensity that very few films these days have. I'm glad Boyle showed these moments, as they show India exactly for what it is. It might not be the most positive image you'll see of the country, but it is an accurate image, and that is what is more important. It also shows that Jamal has a lot to overcome in order to have a better life.

Every year, there is at least one underdog of a movie that comes out of nowhere and surprises at the Oscars. 2006 saw it with Little Miss Sunshine and 2007 saw it with Juno. Which leads me to believe that Slumdog Millionaire might have the chance to pull off the same feat and get a Best Picture nomination. I desperately hope it does. This is a film that will touch you and make you feel awesome as you walk out of the theater. Its ending sequence(s) will do that in spades. Danny Boyle has managed to pull out all of the stops to make what I consider to be the best film of the year. When it hits your area, you will do your duty and see this film. I tell you, you are going to love it, and hopefully as much as I did.

2008's little movie that could.  Watching it, however, reveals there's not much about it that is little. An inspirational tale of a poor kid who gets on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?  Sounds like an Oprah special, but this movie's got the goods, starting with the presentation.  This is without a doubt the most beautifully rendered environments of the past few years.  The color scheme combined with amazing music give total immersion.  Even those, though, do not hide some of the darker elements taking place in Mumbai.  The main character Jamal is sent to prison and brutally tortured simply because he isn't supposed to know the answers to the questions on the game show.  He doesn't answer questions with book-smarts though, but with street smarts.  He draws his answers from experiences in his life, and the way director Danny Boyle meshes the game show and the flashbacks together is masterful.  Some may say that the movie relies too much on the fate concept to get the point across.  To them I say, so what?  This is the movie business, get over it.  When a movie is this stunningly beautiful and entertaining, it is easy to get lost in its world.

I liked the movie. Eventhough the story is fiction, the elements that were used to tell the story are real. 

The first time I went to Mumbai what shocked me the most was the overpopulation...and driving by the slums. It's a very harsh reality. I always wondered about the individual stories of people who live there. Eventhough, it's extreme poverty, they don't actually seem miserable. The children laugh and play, the women are seen doing chores, etc. I hate to think what the people who live there have to go through during the monsoon season...I have also driven past some parts of the slums where you don't see people...just a huge part of land filled with shacks. Simply alarming.

I was told not to give anything to beggars (because they are collecting money for somebody else, who is doing business thru them). Hard and sad to believe. 

So when I saw the movie, I recognized many things that I already knew. I could even guess what some scenes smell like. I even understood several Hindi lines! I liked the fact that it's a love story and that it ends well, that there are no song/dances to interfere the story (like in the Bollywood pictures). I thought the dance number at the end of the movie was a nice touch, though :)


What I absolutely HATE is the fact that this movie reafirms the stereotype that India is all about poverty. This is the image that many people in the west have about India and I have noticed it ever since I said I was going to live in Mumbai (or whenever I say that I'm going to visit) because many people have said to me "You are very brave." 

I would just like to say that the reality shown in this movie is just ONE reality...not the only one that reflects India. It is a very rich country with huge potential. I wish everyone had the chance to see that as well.

Few movies in recent memory have been as thrilling and as uplifting as Slumdog Millionaire.  Like most of Danny Boyle's films there is a feeling of heart pounding immediacy lent to the proceedings thanks to the energetic camera work, fast paced editing and music.  What makes Slumdog a special film is the authenticity in every shot.  The film was shot on the go in India, many of the extras just everyday people who just happened to get in the shot.  The film reveals truly horrific elements that exist in the country, yet it never comes off as preachy, rather it's just part of the fabric that makes up the lives of these characters.  What makes Slumdog a great cinematic experience is that the film holds you in it's grip from the opening shot til the closing shot.  There is not a single dull moment that I would want to be taken out.  Slumdog Millionaire is a film that will keep you on the edge of your seat but send you out of the theater smiling. I love this film.

Fifteen years ago, a new director produced a low-budget thriller about three flatmates who turn against each other over a suitcase of cash and Keith Allen.
He then made a film about drug addicts, which soon became an iconic film for the 1990s.
All the while, he broke British cinema, then America and by the looks of it, he is about to crack Bollywood.
Danny Boyles newest film, Slumdog Millionaire is a different approach compared to his most renowned projects  putting a fairytale love story and moulding it into celluloid doesnt seem like a wise choice for a director, whos famous for blood, guts and misery.
This tale of Jamal  the lovestruck teen on the verge of becoming a millionaire only to be suspected of cheating by the police  is uplifting to say the least.
His back-story from the slums of Mumbai to the hot seat of Indias version of who wants to be a millionaire is touching, yet as the timeline approaches the present day, it is surprising that his personality remain humble and wise  not visibly driven by the corruption of money and power that overtakes everyone around him, including his asshole brother.
Dev Patel, who plays the older Jamal, is determined as he follows a path believed to be destiny.  His role as the dreamer provides so much optimism and hope that as the film climaxes, you have to stop yourself cheering for him in your seat.
As opposed to his realist older brother, whose early dream of being the Little Zé of Mumbai consumes him towards violence.
Boyle has been careful in his direction, concentrating on the smaller details in what has become a love story to Mumbai  as reminded in the film by our protagonist:
You wanted to see the real India?  This is it.
Yes, the landscape and backdrop is indeed rich and eye-catching, but gone are the masses of colourful saris and numerous dance numbers.  By bringing the realism back into Bollywood, Boyle has created something special.
Simon Beaufroys Oscar-nominated script compliments the humility of Jamals character as well as the feel-good quality expected of this film.
People who have already compared this to The Full Monty will expect the same triumph in Slumdog Millionaire, and they will not be disappointed.

Danny Boyle is something of an oddity to me.  The man can direct the hell out of pretty much anything.  Drug Addict Drama?  Sci-Fi Thriller?  Zombie Horror?  All directed amazingly well.  I had problems with all of these movies, but none of which I could really pin on Boyle, but instead on his choice of scripts.  So it is fantastic to see Boyle find a script truly worthy of his considerable directing skill.  Slumdog is a success on every level, and there are many different levels to it.  It is at moments heart-breaking, hilarious, disturbing, thrilling, and romantic.  The acting is all top-notch, especially from the large cast of children that showcase many of the films most memorable moments.  The story is told in an out of order style, as we switch back and forth between the tv show contest, the subsequent interrogation, and stories of our heroes childhood as a street urchin in the slums of India.  This is handled in an almost frenetic manner, which lends a lot of energy to a story that might have been slow in lesser hands.  And of course, Danny Boyle's direction is the greatest success of the film.  His energy and style make the film a dazzling array.  Boyle is great at matching music to moments in the film, and his use of primarily Indian music really resonates with the story.  The only reason this isn't five stars is because I felt the resolution to the story was starkly sweet in contrast to the grittiness of the rest of the film, but most people will probably enjoy the happy ending.

If the title "Slumdog Millionaire" was mentioned six months ago when discussing Oscar Nomination most people would not have heard of it. Yet Danny Boyle seems to have come from nowhere and won the hearts and minds of many movie goers with this visually stunning movie but do i think it is worthy of it's ten nominations or of winning the best picture Oscar?........... 

Today is the biggest day in Jamal Malik's life.

A penniless, eighteen year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, he's one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India's "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" But when the show breaks for the night, suddenly, he is arrested on suspicion of cheating. After all, how could an uneducated street kid possibly know so much? Determined to get to the bottom of Jamal's story, the jaded Police Inspector spends the night probing Jamal's incredible past, from his riveting tales of the slums where he and his brother Salim survived by their wits to his hair-raising encounters with local gangs to his heartbreak over Latika, the unforgettable girl he loved and lost.

Each chapter of Jamal's increasingly layered story reveals where he learned the answers to the shows seemingly impossible quizzes. But one question remains a mystery: what is this young man with no apparent desire for riches really doing on the game show?

When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out...

I am a bid fan of Danny Boyle . He is an unassuming , humble man that makes great movies with the minimal of fuss and sometimes with very little publicity.

Slumdog Millionaire didn't need much publicity because critics loved it and word of mouth has made this film the success it has become.

I have to admit , although i really enjoyed this movie i was ever so slightly disappointed with it too.

I felt an hour in that it was dragging slightly and that the film lost it's focus and direction a little.
I also felt the "Who wants to be a millionaire " presenter ,played by Anil Kapoor was way over the top. A little too bollywoodish ( i just made that word up!) for me. 

Thankfully it came together in the the last half hour and i must admit i had a tear in my eye at the end. 
There are some great scenes in the film. One where Jamal goes to extremes to get the autograph of his favourite movie star by jumping through the hole in the outside toilet into what lay beneath and then running through a crowd of people covered from head to toe in muck to confront his hero.

The other , altogether far more sinister , when Salim watches as the gang blinds his friend just so he can double his begging income. That scene really made me wince.

Strangely enough , despite ten Oscar nominations none are for the acting and i think that is because they characters are played by several different people because of the ageing process.

Dev Patel does deserve a mention for his performance as does the beautiful Freida Pinto and i really enjoyed the scenes at the railway station in the final credits but they were not quite at the standard to get a best actor or actress Oscar nomination . 

So we go back to the question " Is this worthy of winning the best picture Oscar" ?.
In my eyes no. But because of past greats such as "Trainspotting" , "Shallow Grave" and "Twenty Eight Weeks Later" , Danny Boyle might just be due one .

8 out of 10

One of the strongest movies to be released in 2008, Slumdog Millionaire has a rich, urban feel with standout performances by multiple actors playing the characters of Who Wants to be a Millonaire contestant Jamal Malik and the woman he loves and longs for, Latika. Most notably, Dev Patel adds a wide-eyed understated charm and Freida Pinto's impossibly beautiful yet vulnerable and the two have dynamic chemistry. This charming romance fuels the entire film, but its drama, stories and subtle visuals within the film, rich cinematography, and brilliant, diverse music stands out as key players as well.

I found this film to display the country of India in a rather negative, brutal fashion, with very little compassion or sympathy. I imagine there are much more authentic Bollywood movies that are just as good as Slumdog that are regularly passed on by modern American cinema, but for some reason Hollywood thinks this is the right time to embrace a foreign film like this. I can imagine Indians not exactly fawning over this portrayal, as Americans largely ignore their movies and finally pay attention to one about a few children from the slums, with one on a potentially crooked game show. Still, there are few other flaws, besides a minor gripe in its plausibility.

Overall, this movie does not let up throughout its entire length, with some pulse-pounding action, a thoroughly simplistic romance, very funny moments, and a flawless directing effort by Danny Boyle. I've heard some complain about the way the plot is set up, but it makes for a breezy length and doesn't detract from anything to me. Definitely worth a watch, this crowd pleaser is unsurprisingly a strong candidate for the coveted 2008 Picture of the Year Oscar. It deserved a nomination, but I'm not sure about the win since I have not seen all of the contenders quite yet.

Perhaps the most satisfying thing about Slumdog Millionaire is the fact that it is deserved of its hype and consequently is every bit as good or even better than your expectations. Danny Boyle has proved to be a great, versatile director, injecting his trademark tension, and exceptional soundtracks into every genre going. The camera relishes in the novelty of Mumbai, making use of every opportunity going. The cast do their job well, but in honesty they are not at the center of the films sucesses, its all to do with Boyle'e achievements as a director. The marketing of the film as a movie about a poor kid who wins Who Wants To Be A Millionaire is deceptive - the movie itself surprises you in being more about life in Mumbai than the gameshow -- and in that lies its sucess - a moving, heartfelt success story masked as a social commentary. The contrived nature of the plot does not detract from the truly joyous ending, a warm feeling that will stay with you long after you leave the multiplex.

Despite all the oscar hype, after the Golden Globe wins, Slumdog Millionaire is City of God. However, Slumdog's story and noble intentions have been done before, numerous times on large scale to small scale productions, what sets it aside and makes it so famous right now is Danny Boyle as the director. Being a huge Danny Boyle film and his artistic vision and spin to unique storytelling, is what makes this film stand out on it's own. Perhaps if I saw it when it wasn't so overhyped I might've thought differently about it, although I don't think that's true. This film really is City of God but done by Danny Boyle and throw in Who Wants to Be A Millionare and Bollywood musical at the end. It's a fantasy movie with reality grounding images and circumstances that are tough and emotionally hard to watch (mainly when they are children). Slumdog is basically Bable, only it doesn't suck. However it's not the best thing I've ever seen. The acting is only excels when they are children (surprise I'm amazed by child actors for once?), as Dev Patel, who is charming and believable, I often found myself annoyed with his dumbfounded look during the game show sections. That and the hearing WHO wantsto be  millionare, I really think is the part that while some may think it's connecting everyone because "everyone" knows that show, it made me mad that it was used. The show went to 12pm day time for a reason in the US. This film is favored to win the oscars and is predicted to, however, if it won it'd be for the wrong reasons, in that Hollywood is thinking that it's doing a favor to those in poverty. The film has issues of circumstance with it, but isn't about it because it's a love story. (And once they get past the part of knowing what's going to happen, then it becomes emotionally engaging when you don't know what's going to happen). This movie deserves an oscar for Directing and for it's Score. It could also pick up Editing as well, but anything more then that, frankly if it didn't win I would not be surprised. I think because it's an eye opener for people (which who the hell hasn't seen or knew poverty and things like this existed, nutshell anyone?) then it will win. Foreign Press runs Golden Globes, hence why it won, hence why Babel won. This is a good movie, but nothing amazing, with the exception of Danny Boyle's spin on it.

He swiftly responded by asking the officer whatâs the price of bhel puri? which kids stole the constableâs bicycle?  After receiving a confused look, he candidly states that these facts even â5 year olds knowâ in the slums.  His point was, and almost blatantly so, that he lives in a different world, and from that moment on, the audience is almost subtly forced to let go of their environment and enter the world of a slumdog.  Boyle set this up flawlessly.  
The movie itself is multi-faceted.  Perhaps thatâs why it has the appeal that it does.  Anyone can walk away from it with a different understanding of the film.  The movie is a love story, an adventure, a ârags to richesâ triumph, a story of brotherly love and sibling rivalry, about forgiveness, jealousy, purity, honesty, liesâ¦.. however for meâ¦it is about faith and destiny.  The film exemplified my belief that faith shapes us, and destiny guides us.  Every person weâve ever met, every experience weâve felt, every eye-contact, handshake, smile, dream, fight, crush, heartache, joy and sorrow we have ever experienced, ALL of itâ¦shapes us to be who we are.  Faith has caused you to become who you are... sitting in front of your screen, sharing my thoughts at this very moment.  Destinyâ¦.on the other hand,  is where our faith takes us.  As the tagline suggests â¦it is all writtenâ¦however nothing is concrete.  The brothers essentailly had similar faith (rise in thier own world, etc.) however had different paths to get their.   Itâs all guided by choice.  
In the film, both Sameer and Jamal were destined for the money.  However, Sameerâs choices of lies and deceit resulted in his downfall, whereas Jamalâs truthfulness resulted in his rewards.  They both were surrounded with money at the end of it, however Sameer was certain to die in it, whereas Jamal thrived in his winnings.    Every experience Jamal had; from his mother being killed to his dealings with child beggar operatives, resulted in his knowing the required answers when it came to the moment of karmic reward.  The point is that there are signs all around you  in life.  Didnât you ever have situations that seemed like coincidence where you knew what to say or knew the right fact, as a result of a minor experience in the past?  Well this film purports that itâs not coincidence, but rather the guiding hand of destiny.  It is your faith in this destiny that determines your outcome.  
The love story aspect of this movie was the true representative of the power of choice in my opinion.  People who tend to believe in faith/destiny risk the possibility of having a âhands off approachâ to life.  Theyâd use phrases like âitâs godâs willâ, âitâs easier to go with the flowâ  âI have no choiceâ or âit wasnât meant to beâ as an excuse to not make decisions or take responsibilities for their actions.  This lack of choice tends to move people with the current, as if life will take them where they need to go and they donât have to be accountable for it.  But thatâs the point of faithâ¦ had Jamal been without choice, then he would have never found his true love.  He faced obstacles after obstacles to get to her, and still persisted.  That persistence wasnât destiny, it was choice.  But it was his destiny to be with her as a result of those same choices.  So it begs the question that when we are all faced with challenging times in a relationship, career, school, family, etc. should one persist, or move on to something else? Never before have I been so emotionally affected by a film.

By the end of this heart-warming, fresh, under-dog fantasy tale I wanted nothing more than to get back in line, purchase another ticket, and experience it again. And I indeed would have, had I not had to work an hour after the film got out.

I spoke to my girlfriend on the phone shortly after ranting and raving about the film.

"But was it better than 'Benjamin Button'?" she asked. We both througholy enjoyed "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" to a great degree.

My reply went along the lines of something like this. That I didn't even think of the film as better or worse. I simply loved it and was filled to the brim with joy for having seen it. I told her that it may be my favorite film I have ever seen.

I've always loved to make that kind of distinction. the difference between your favorite film and what you think is the best film. For instance I would love to watch "Slumdog Millionaire" over and over again because of how it affected me and how it made me feel. "The Godfather", which indeed is one of my favorites as well as what I consider one of the best films ever made, could not stand up to this test. It's simply too exhausting. I have seen "The Godfather" countless times and know just about every word to the three hour long epic. However the reasons I would watch "The Godfather" are a bit different than what I would watch "Slumdog Millionaire" for. I would watch "Slumdog Millionaire" simply to make me happy.

Now this does not mean that "Slumdog" is not a technical masterpiece. In my eyes it is. The bright, beautiful cinematography is matched with hip, frenetic editing. The shots are all from exciting, interesting angles, that never cease to make this film a wonder to look at. And the music. My God the music pulses with life that keeps you entranced with everything that is going on in the screen.

All of this fantastic technical work would all go to waste if the film had lost grip on the one thing that gives it its heart. 

Its story.

The story is a fantasy tale with a romance wrapped in that gave me a yearning feeling in my heart throughout its entire duration. The actors embrace who they are with such heart that to not be able to feel for them is almost impossible. The story, to put it simply, made me look at everything with more love and more empathy. This film made me want to get out of my seat and cheer on a number of occasions.

One reviewer hit the nail on the head when he called the film a "buoyant hymn to life". Never have I heard a reviewer perfectly describe the movie in such few words. However to understand what these four words mean you must see this film. 

You must see this film!

"Slumdog Millionaire" deserves every award that it is nominated for. But if it doesn't win, I won't mind. The film has already done it's job to me and so many other viewers. I couldn't see anyone asking for more.

Maybe the detractors of the movie in India and beyond should be focussing on attracting visitors so something more positive can be put back into the country.

Brilliant. Beautiful. Fascinating. Honest. Startling. Downright Surprising. How can you take something as convoluted as Who Wants to Be a Millionaire and make anything more than a trivial piece of pseudomotivational cinema? They did it. Slumdog Millionaire is a beautiful love story. The millionaire show takes the backdrop. Great editing cuts through the life of Jamal, the main character, as he remembers times of his life that conveniently taught him the answers to the questions hes is faced with, as he is chased by the mob, accused of cheating, interrogated, etc. There is alot to keep straight here, but it is cut together perfectly, so that you not once arent aware of whats going on, unless it is intentionally so. Slumdog Millionaire is a masterpiece, and a brilliant landmark in storytelling. The gameshow is nothing more than a medium through which the story is told, and really has no other significance to the story other than the glue that makes the whole package a cohesive and fascinating story. I have yet to see Benjamin Button or Milk, but so far Slumdog is my definite pick for Best Picture.

Danny Boyle's film was a massive with audiences, critics, and the academy awards.  And it's easy to be swept up with the magic of Slumdog Millionaire.  It really is a wonderful story with and excellent plot and some really stunning scenes.  But the film could have been so much more than it was.  It could have been a masterpiece.  For me, the movie will have to settle with being just a great movie.  Mind you, I do very much recommend this film, as it is really compelling.  And it's a technical marvel, from the excellent cinematography, editing, and filming methods.  But the film's main (and only, really) drawback is the dialogue.  For the most part, the dialogue is very simplistic (and rather cliched in some crucial moments), but there are times when it is quite good.  Near the end of the film, there are important moments when I wanted the characters to say something original and not trite or unimaginative.  But instead they say something like "You must go" or "I love you."  It's just a drag that the film's good momentum falters a bit during the third act.  The game-show scenes are easily the best sequences, as they seamlessly blend the movie's plot with the excitement of actually watching a game-show.  Really good stuff.  The last scene (before the credits and the dancing) is technically beautiful both in concept and visuals, but it's really kinda of a lazy ending, and everything gets resolved way way too quickly and conveniently.  But enough of me ranting.  Slumdog Millionaire is mostly a great movie, and you should definitely see it.  I just did not see it as a masterpiece.

Crowd-pleasers rarely please me. Chalk it up to my leftfield, non-conformist, maverick status. Or an inability to be pleased by anything. Whichevers cooler.
 
Slumdog Millionaire is a crowd-pleaser through-and-through. It's also very much what others would call a "fable" (and what I would call a "pile of complete and utter nonsense"). Hence the fairy-tale sensibility and the ridiculous plot developments. Given the sort of film this is, it's basically a miracle that it's any good at all. As it happens, it's quite entertaining. I have neither the time nor the energy to detail the film's myriad of flaws, but I'll tell you the two things it's really got going for it.
 
Firstly, it's beautifully directed, with great energy, great colour and great style. So sit back and enjoy - nobody's asking you to follow the plot. Second, the music is, for the most part, surprisingly good. Very few films have good music in them. 
 
What with awards season upon us, we've suddenly been bombarded with films begging us to take them seriously. Slumdog Millionaire isn't one of them - or if it is, it's extremely badly judged - which might be why I've warmed to it so. It might also go some way towards explaining the otherwise baffling torrent of high praise and awards it has garnered.

Slumdog Millionaire is one of the best films of the year that seemed to have come out of nowhere. The Story of Slumdog Millionaire is certainly a story of rags to riches. The film started out being a direct to dvd release and now it's the Oscar favorite for Best Picture along with Benjamin Button. The thing that is so great about Slumdog Millionaire is the fact that the film has a certain quality to it that other films do not. I can usually tell when I'm watching a master-piece and this is no exception. The film goes back and forth between the story of Jamal's childhood and the story of Jamal's journey through the Hindi version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire. The ebb and flow of this film through the two stories is just fantastic and really works well. 

Danny Boyle did a fantastic job of telling this complex story and the film really is a masterpiece and one I think will be remebered for a very long time. [font=Times New Roman][size=3]Scenes of poverty and squalour may appear romantic to Westerners and to our snooty elite but for ordinary Indians they are an everyday reality. One wonders what sort of mind can find such images aesthetically pleasing. Party-hopping socialites (for example,  Shobhaa De after all her bombast of "enough is enough", went and watched a pirated copy!) who are distanced from such reality may find this film an "eye-opener" but for us it IS just poverty-porn. Leaving that aside, I have six other objections to the film.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]1) The director seems to RELISH showing violence. Some of it (like the police-torture) is quite needless. And why was the boy arrested in the first place? On what charge? Was it realistic? [/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]2) How can a boy growing up in slums speak such accented English? Even if one assumes that the language he actually uses to communicate with the game-show host and the police officer is Hindi (granting the director the creative license to use a language better suited for international audiences), there are 2 instances where it is stretched too far: (a) when the boy becomes a guide for foreign tourists at the Taj Mahal & (b) when he becomes a substitute-operator at the call-centre.[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]3) When the boy uses his lifeline during the game-show, his friend discovers that she has forgotten her mobile and has to run back for it. This is plain Bollywood masala! Did the director have to make it so melodramatic?[/size][/font]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]4) How did the boy know who invented the revolver just by watching his brother use it?[/size][/font]

[size=3][font=Times New Roman]5) [font=Arial]Darshan Do Ghanshyam is NOT written by Surdas. It is written by Gopal Singh Nepali for the movie Narsi Bhagat (1957). This song is also credited as traditional and originally written by 15th century poet Narsi Mehta, whose life that film is based on.[/font][/font][/size]

[font=Times New Roman][size=3]6) The greatest flaw in the storyline is that programmes like 'Kaun Banega Crorepati' and 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire' are NOT telecast live. As a result the entire structure of the film becomes unrealistic. For a film that boasts of being realistic such a flaw cannot be overlooked.[/size][/font]

Good things come to those who wait. the rags-to-riches story of a boy who is born and bred in the slums of Mumbai is a perfect feel-good story. Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) who triumphs in the face of adversity is everybody's hero. People want to see a bit of themselves in Jamal especially when he overcomes harsh circumstances and gets the just fruits of his labour in the end. It is why millions of people tuned in to watch KBC every week; we want to see people win money and be happy hoping someday it will be our turn. Director Danny Boyle has very successfully managed to gain an insight into the psyche of the common man from the slums of India and talk about his dreams and aspirations. Compared to Swarup's Q&A which inspired the screenplay, the movie is all about destiny rather than luck. The writing, direction and camera work are so taut and precise that they manage to keep the viewer engaged in every scene. The narrative is heavily influenced by 70's Bollywood movies and overall seems to be an ode to Mumbai and its intricacies. The vibrant sights, sounds and smells of the living, breathing metropolis are vividly captured in this film. The direction of the film is so unique that the performances of individual cast-members do not seem very striking on scrutiny but together, they manage to weave the rich tapestry of a colourful and characteristic ensemble cast. Special mention for the brilliant and bold kids from the real slums of Mumbai who have portrayed the early years of the characters' lives. Last but not least, the brilliant music provided by the genius A.R Rahman shines through. This movie is a triumph and although it has not been made by an Indian crew, will still manage to attract the world's attention towards Indian cinema. Jai ho!!

Although a definite departure for Danny Boyle, I much prefer all of his movies made before this one.

Jamal Malik is poor young man from the slums of Mumbai joins the TV game show "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" From that simple yet ingenious plot and setting, this most memorable film unfolds, detailing the events in this boy's miserable life which (very) coincidentally enables him to answer the trivia questions in the quiz show.

I like that the movie delved on the relationship of two brothers, Jamal and his elder brother Salim. While Salim goes the gangster/hitman route, Jamal strove to make a more decent life for himself as a call center gofer. While there is violence in their relationship, brotherly love still comes through in repeated occasions.

In addition, there is also a love story here. A slum girl named Latika had her life intertwined with the brothers during an ethnic massacre when they were kids. Jamal and Latika naturally become fond of other, but are separated two traumatic times, but can they find each other again at the end?

The story was told as flashbacks from their childhood, teenage years and their young adulthood. The child actors were most affecting in their portrayal, especially the boys. The child Jamal had that wide-eyed innocence, while the child Salim had that worldly-wise jadedness. Very effective! I do not know why the adult Jamal (Dev Patel) was acting in such a flat manner in several parts, but he is most effective in his scenes with Latika (Frieda Pinto).

Honestly, I really felt that 'Slumdog" had a big similarity with the Brazilian classic "City of God" when it came to the brutal and unforgiving depiction of the squalor and violence in the slums. The unmitigated violence in the treatment of the poor slum kids is most disturbing. The big difference of course is that "Slumdog" is more neatly tied up and positive in its final message when compared to "City".

Jamal is one question away from winning the top prize on the Indian version of 'Who wants to be a Millionaire?' He is a 'slumdog' and has spent his entire life in poverty, with very little 'education', so how has he come to know the answers to such a wide variety of questions? How does he keep getting them right? Quite simple really; It is his destiny.  'Slumdog Millionaire' is a phenomenally uplifting film that proves that the good, honest and genuine people in this world will suffer, but will ultimately triumph and reach happiness. I know how unbelievably cheesy and naïve that sounds, but after watching 'Slumdog' that's all I could think about. It re-enforced my hope in humanity. To watch the horrendous amounts of degradation, violence and cruelty that its characters are put through, and then to see them finally flourish and get everything they have ever deserved is just the ultimate cinema satisfaction.  Danny Boyle has done a tremendous job directing here. He never shy's away from the horrors of human nature, the abuse, neglect, murder and torture; it's all in here, and it's all handled so precisely that it provokes the emotions and really thumps into the nervous system. Simultaneously, Boyle is also brilliant at highlighting the beauty of life. The shot of Latika's face, Jamal's first and only love since childhood, at the train station as she looks up at him is quite simply beauty personified. Even when the young actors who play Jamal and Salim are sprinting through the slums away from a policeman, the thumping soundtrack and amazing use of colour and shot make something quite dangerous into something breath-takingly beautiful. Dev Patel is superb in his portrayal of Jamal. His reserved and under-stated style of acting fits the character profile perfectly. He has fully shaken his character 'Anwar' from TV Series 'Skins' and has become an established and talented young actor. Freida Pinto is also impressive as Latika. Not only is she stunningly beautiful, she's also a convincing actress. The young cast members are also fantastic. They're a genuine pleasure to watch. Also to be credited is the fantastic choice of score. It makes the film so much more involving and memorable, and deserved both Oscars at the 2009 Academy Awards. 'Slumdog Millionaire' is worth all the hype. Miss it, and you'll miss out.

For the preordained Oscar Titan of 2008, this comes up short in just about every imaginable aspect except for aesthetically. And with Danny Boyle at the helm, aesthetics were a given, so really this film is sort of a glossy disappointment. It has unmistakable energy, but little else.

First things first, though - what DID I like about the movie? The soundtrack is by far the standout here. When A.R. Rahman and MIA trot out that fat beat in the chase scene within the first fifteen minutes of the film, you're completely entranced. Frontloading the score with its strongest track is a fantastic way to make a positive first impression. I'm willing to believe that the sound is integral to this film's continued success, in that it is evocative of both mood and setting. In tandem with the generally strong visuals, Slumdog Millionaire is expertly crafted, which I think has given it a pass from many people for the underwhelming plot and acting. The clever narrative framing disguises the fact that absolutely nothing is going on underneath the surface of Slumdog Millionaire - no thematic depth, bland characters, stilted dramaturgical attempts at showing off the HORRORS OF THE SLUMS while at the same time force-feeding the audience this totally unbelievable love story. Filmic escapism is fine, but if you're going to attempt a massive suspension of disbelief by aligning 10 game show questions perfectly to its contestant's life (and in chronological order!), don't try to simultaneously anchor the movie into seriousness by depicting child torture and exploitation and crushing poverty. Danny Boyle is an expert at juggling tones but Slumdog Millionaire got away from him. 

Complaining about the acting seems kind of inconsequential since none of the performers have parts longer than forty minutes, but the actors' collective inability to put out good performances really show off the cracks in the characterizations. I like Irfan Khan but there's nothing interesting about the policeman he's playing here. Dev Patel and Freida Pinto are cute, vacant kids. The child actors are fine but not revelatory. Anil Kapoor, playing the host of the game show, is the one standout here. Apparently he's been acting like a big douchebag at awards ceremonies, which is hilarious. 

Anyway, the most I'm taking away from this film is the soundtrack. I'm bumping O Saya right now - can't wait to see it performed at the Oscars. I'll be significantly less thrilled when the movie picks up Best Picture, though...and it will. It has too much momentum as the year's "little movie that could" even though this is nowhere near as little as they want us to believe. At the end of the day I don't mind this film's success - maybe it'll liven up Hollywood's totally stultifying comic book fetish - but I'm just not on board with the hype.

I thought it was a movie with a lot of really memorable moments, but it struggled to find the right kind of tone. Danny Boyle seems to have put himself in a kind of perplexing situation, where he wanted to make a revelatory film that shows the true face of Mumbai and how it's changed (or in many ways failed to change adequately) with its embrace of globalization, but he also wanted to pay homage to modern Bollywood, a film industry that thrives on escapism and complete denial of its country's age-old inequalities, let alone the nuanced injustices of post-colonial india. So how do you make a socially conscious Bollywood film? Well, Danny Boyle's route was to show all the urban squalor, the exploitation, the corruption, and then show one person's triumphant escape from it because of some vague notion of destiny, and then have everyone dance. That's basically what this is, which is actually pretty cool and I think would be really satisfactory to a lot of viewers, but I can't help but feel a little more concerned with what the destiny of the Indian people is as a whole. 

Still, Boyle did a commendable job on the love story, had a pretty firm hold on a narrative that jumped around a lot, and did a lot of other stuff that showed he clearly knows his shit. Also, for a Westerner I think he dealt with a lot of the nuances of globalized India with sensitivity and tact, but I just can't seem to feel like it provides much insight into why all of this stuff is going on. What can people concerned with the international working class do to change these conditions in Mumbai, bring in more quiz shows? I'm being facetious, of course, but I guess what I'm getting at is that the film is sort of inadvertently structured to kinda reduce people's will to act... first we're exposed to all these images of poverty and injustice, but then we're left feeling like everything's alright and nothing really needs to be fixed because india is so modern now, so yayy lets dance. And honestly I had a good time watching them dance, don't get me wrong... I was happy to see the two loves reunited, just like I would be in any movie, but I felt kinda empty too.


There are many more films, many of which were not made by Westerners and some that were, that have addressed the struggles of the oppressed in India, dating back to Satyajit Ray's Apu Trilogy, The Bandit Queen (about Phoolan Devi), or even Salaam Bombay, and I'm sure there are a mess more but that's what I've seen. Somehow, though, most of these films fail to artfully provide some sort of glimpse into WHY people are suffering, and that is the case with a lot of films about Africa or Latin America too, but not as much. I think that this is the challenge that many filmmakers face... to make an accessible movie that challenges us to face the real reasons why this kinda stuff is going on and still isn't complete torture to watch. Pretty hard, huh? I don't think I'd be able to do it, but I hope someone does.

EDIT: After having visited India for a month and seeing many of the neighborhoods where this movie was filmed, taking in as much of the country as I possibly could, talking to a few mumbaikars about what they think about the movie, and then re-watching it on my flight back to los angeles, I feel completely differently about the film as a whole. It's actually a much more perfect summation of india as it is and as it was than I could have ever imagined it to be. I'm truly glad I took the time to watch it again, because it was much more rewarding to watch the second time around, even if it still does have some of the issues that I mentioned in my first review. and also, I'd like to add that the complaints that I've heard from others about the soundtrack "not fitting" seem kinda silly to me. I think AR Rahman and MIA are actually perfect choices, not only because they're talented and making music that both Indians and Westerners can enjoy, but because they're actually Indian (well, M.I.A. is Sri Lankan, but the Tamil people are still part of the fabric of India,), unlike a sizeable contingent of the people who worked on this film. From what I gathered based on the ridiculous stack of newspaper articles I read, Indians were more proud to see AR Rahman win the oscar for his musical contributions to Slumdog than they were to see the film win Best Picture. Just thought that might be an interesting thing to share.

[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]Danny Boyles new film [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]has won accolades in the Western worldright from the Critics Choice Awards to the four Golden Globe Awards, the L.A. Film Critics Award, and several more as I write, making it difficult to list them all. Promos for the film describe it as showing the real India and the adjective authentic has been used in its reviews. But, in fact, the film is quite inauthentic from the beginning to end. [/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]Indeed, [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is as inauthentic as the wannabe Bollywood dance number that it ends with. Let me start from the beginning: [/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]That wooden latrine [i]out in the open[/i] does not exist in Mumbai slums--does not exist anywhere in India. I dont know if it exists in the outback of Australia. But it does not exist anywhere through the length and breadth of India where this movie is supposed to be set. While it is true that latrines of the type where the refuse accumulates at the bottom exist in India, the wooden stalls in the middle of a wide open green space does not exist, and certainly not in a crowded city like Mumbai. In India, people go out in the open, by the railway track, or in closed brick or concrete built latrines that have a septic tank attached. In a big city, there are very likely to be other built structures near the latrines. I think the movie makers so much wanted the young Jamal to be immersed in poop that they had to invent a contraption like that. Quite unnecessarythey could have had the young Jamal wade through an open sewage pool (Mahim creek, for example). This scene simply illustrates how out of touch with reality the film is. And this, in spite of having an Indian co-director, Loveleen Tandon.[/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]Next, I don't think it is the practice that when a religious pogrom is launched, a child with blue make-up is sent in to look like the God, Rama. First of all, it would not be safe for the child; he would probably get killed or beaten by one side or the other. An Indian in Mumbai--even a Muslim--is very likely to see a picture of Rama holding a bow and arrow at a roadside "temple", a shop selling calendars, a notebook cover, in TV serials, or at the paan/bidi shop. The filmmakers did not need to have this contrived sceneof a young lad covered in blue paint in the middle of attacks by Hindu fanatics on Muslims. This was just not real.[/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]In addition, there are colonial overtones in this film. I now live in the U.S., and I cannot imagine seeing a movie at the local film theater with the following scene: [/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]A couple of rich Japanese tourists are in Harlem, NY; a young American kid gets beaten up; the Japanese are surprised; the kid says you wanted to see America, this is the real America; the Japanese couple then hand him a wad of cash and a digital camera and say "Son, we want to show you the real Japan." Would any American accept that as the real America and the behavior of the Japanese tourists as reflecting the real Japan?[/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]This is what [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] expects its audience to swallowand people who dont know India are willing to simply accept this version. And now you can see why the Western world feels good about this movieit is constantly being pandered to and stroked positively while juxtaposing its so-called sensibility with the inhumanity of Indians shown in the film. The shock and empathy the audience feels (as does the American couple visiting India) stands in contrast with the complete absence of shock or kindness on the part of any of the Indian characters in the movie. Other than the children and their mother, every Indian character in the film is scurrilous in one form or another--whether it is the orphanage keepers, the police inspector, the constable, the host of Who Wants to be a Millionaire, the audience of the show, or the driver of the American tourists. The employees at the phone company are sort of neutral--but none is even slightly kind or empathetic. Those sentiments are reserved for the Westerners (the tourists) and the putative audience of the film that then "feels good" and self-righteous for rooting for Jamal against the wicked system. [/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]Just because Jamal could sing that [i]bhajan[/i] and knew a blind kid who sang it does not mean he knew the name of the person who wrote it. Actually, I know that song too, and I did not know who wrote it. In fact, even after seeing the movie, there is some controversy over who wrote this [i]bhajan[/i] ([i]darshan do ghanshyam nath mori [/i])was it Surdas or someone else? I doubt singing beggars in India know the name of the poets who wrote the songs they sing. The film intends to show exactly how Jamal knew the answers to the questions--but in the case of the [i]bhajan[/i], it fails to do so. (For example, with the question on the gun, there is a reference to Colt, but with the song question, I am still left wondering how he knew who wrote it). Then again, just because the youg Jamal had got the autograph of Amitabh Bachhan does not lead to his knowing that "Amitabh Bachhan" was the right answer to another question. Perhaps he was just guessing. But if simply making the right guess is a possibility, that could explain the correct answers to other questions too. [/font][/color]
 
[font=Batang]The brilliance of the story concept rests on tying up the correct answers to actual incidents in the life of Jamal based on which he simply [i]knew[/i] the answers. If that is compromised with or made fuzzy, the plot loses some of its brilliance. [/font]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]My mind is open to coincidenceseven if they seem implausiblebeing an important part of the story line. But the coincidences have got to workat least the incidents should be authentic and neatly tie up with what Jamal would have known. Take [i]Forrest Gump[/i] -- this movie was full of improbable coincidences -but it all tied up and worked--for me at least. I was not left wondering how Elvis learned to dance like that; I knew he learned it from watching the young Forrest, of course :-) [/font][/color]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]I am not going to quibble with the characters speaking in English after the beginning of the filmthat is artistic license. I simply accept it as being a result of some of the actors not being fluent in Hindiand the film being aimed at an English-speaking audience. As a viewer, I can just interpret it as the characters speaking some local language. [/font][/color]
 
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]And finally, the completely inauthentic Bollywood dance at the end. Even as a wannabe Bollywood dance, it was insipid--lacked the gusto, verve, and vibrancy of real Bollywood. Even the young Jamal (as a seven-year old) who did a five-second dance before Latika earlier in the movie had greater authenticity and punch packed in those five seconds. [/font][/color]
 
 
[font=Batang]I have heard some Westerners rave about this dance at the end (performed by Dev Patel and Frieda Pinto). I see them as infants enjoying processed carrots from a Gerber bottle, and while I accept their enjoyment of this dance as quite valid, I wish they would some day eat a real carrot and see what that feels like. [/font]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]The story concept of [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is absolutely brilliant. A great story concept should bring plaudits to the author of the novel [i]Q&A[/i] (Vikas Swarup), not the makers of this movie. [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] has good cinematography and music, and the film makers have created a fast, bumpy pace. The performance of the child actors is very good; the recreation of the set of Who Wants to Be ... is dazzling. But these good features of the movie are marred by the deep flaws mentioned above--most of all, a lack of understanding of the real India. In spite of the poverty and injustices in India, it is a society kept together by the social glue of family ties, tradition, faith in God, and a deep humanity. You might never guess this from watching this film. [/font][/color]
 
 
[font=Batang]The appeal of a rags to riches story is just as compelling in India as it is anywhere else. Yet the film draws lines between its audience and the audience of the show "Who Wants to Be...". While "we" want a chaiwallah to win the millions, the Mumbai audience in the studio is seen as being derisive towards the chaiwallah. It is the poor Indians outside the studio that are shown rooting for Jamal, but a feeling is created that the well-heeled audience inside the studio might want to prevent Jamal from winning. There isn't any appreciation shown of the integrity of the police inspector in making the correct assessment that Jamal was honest. This film wanted to see Jamal win in spite of the system, not because of the system. But think about it, would such a story be possible in an unjust system? [/font]
 
[color=black][font=Times New Roman','serif]The film is also being promoted as a great love story. But even as a love story, it lacks integrity. One reviewer noted that "Every little victory--and the final prize, which is not the money--is the result of ingenuity meeting opportunity." But the final prize [i]was[/i] the money. In an earlier scene, Jamal asks Latika to run away with him, and she replies: "And live on what?" So a chaiwallah's income (and any income she might earn) is not enough for her to live---she needs the luxuries that the gangster is able to give her. In this sense, she was a deeply compromised character--she needed to live off some wealthy man or the other. Latika is not capable of facing hardships in order to do the right thing. The true love was only from Jamal's side, and not on her side. In many similar ways, the story lacked integrity and I could not celebrate for the reunion of Jamal and Latika seeing that she would not run away with him while he was still a chaiwalla. That one dialogue: And live on what? prevents this film from belonging to that elevated genre of Indian films on the theme of a true love from childhood that is pursued in the adult life of the characters ([i]Jeena Sirf Mere Liye[/i], [i]Aan[/i], and numerous other). A Western sensibility might overlook this detail, but not someone who is raised on a diet of authentic Indian films (alas, now called Bollywood) where true love has its high standards. [/font][/color]
[font=Batang][b]P.S.[/b] [/font][font=Comic Sans MS]I have recently read the novel "Q&A" on which this film is supposed to be based. None of the scenes that I have objected to above are there in the novel. [/font]
[font=Comic Sans MS]In fact, I did not find ONE thing in the novel that is at all objectionable! So it is clear that all the parts that I intensely disliked were added on by the filmmakers--screenplay writer Simon Beaufoy. The set of questions asked on "Who Wants to Be ...." in the novel are much more probable. In the movie, the questions were just not the types of questions that would be asked on the show in India--for example, the Rama and bow and arrow question--that is just too easy--every Indian simply knows that! Slumdog Millionaire (2008) is a very good movie with the astounding cinematography, virtuoso directing, and the heartbreaking yet optimistic story. The acting by three main characters especially by a newcomer, Dev Patel, is compelling. Patel plays a street kid Jamal Malik (Patel), an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who made it to the Indian version of the TV show Who wants to be a millionaire?" and keeps answering correctly every question. The secret is that every question represents a chapter of his own life, his growing up and surviving on the streets, his adventures and experiences often dramatic and even tragic. When he is just one question away from winning 20 million rupees (around $450,000), the time is up, and millions of TV-viewers who root for Jamal would have to wait for the following night to see him go for the big prize. Jamal is arrested by the police right after the game and he will spend the next day been rather brutally interrogated by police officers who want to find out how the street boy with no education can answer the difficult questions correctly. Fifteen years from the lives of Jamal, his older brother Salem and another orphan from the slums of Mumbai, "the third musketeer", the girl named Latika (Frieda Pinto), Jamal's true love since their childhood will reveal in flashbacks, and by the end of Jamal's story, it won't surprise us why he knows all answers. IMO, the only weak point in the story was the big 20 million rupees question. I won't reveal it but trust me, the whole reading or movie watching world knows the answer, and the question was too easy for such high stake BUT it fits the story very well, so I tend to be lenient.

The best part of the movie is IMO the look at India from within, the glorious views of India's beauty and horrifying captures of its unspeakable poverty, from the slums of Mumbai and the dizzyingly crowded streets of Bombay to the heavenly magnificent Taj Mahal.

Danny Boyle is one of the most versatile and eclectic directors working in cinema today.  Never happy working within one genre, he has so far tried his hand at everything, from dramas (Shallow Grave) to comedies (Life Less Ordinary) to science fiction (Sunshine) to horror (28 Days Later). His latest, Slumdog Millionaire, could well represent the peak of his career so far. Essentially it's about a boy and a quiz show, but in essence it's about so much more. Shooting on the bustling, sweltering, sweaty slums of Mumbai, India, Boyle invests the tale with his trademark kinetic visual style, creating such an energetic feel, while the audience is is put through an emotional gauntlet, feeling joy, sorrow, happiness, laughter, heartbreak, shock and jubilation. It takes a powerful film to make you feel like that, and Slumdog Millionaire is certainly that. The structure is superbly original, as flashbacks show how young Jamal Malik got to the final question on India's version of Who Want's to be a Millionaire. The acting is all superb, with the 3 main characters each being played by 3 different actors representing the 3 different stages of their life. A lot of the characters are played by Mumbai locals, and that coupled with the location shooting, gives the film a real sense of authenticity, the kind of authenticity that can't be faked. The film also features the best soundtrack i've heard in a while. Vibrant, energetic, powerful. Beautiful, emotional, original. Triumphant, incredible, stunning. Am I just listing a random bunch of adjectives? No, of course not. They are all adjectives that can describe Slumdog Millionaire. Come February 22nd, at the 81st Academy Awards Ceremony, we could be hearing those magic words; "And the Best Picture goes to.....Slumdog Millionaire!". I hope so.

Slumdog Millionaire is the little-film that could -- a movie I enjoyed and appreciated.  It is a simple-premised film pieced together to tell the story of two impoverished brothers and the girl who came between them over the course of ten to twelve years.  I am certainly oversimplifying it by saying that I enjoyed the uncommonly happy, uplifting ending of the movie for an Oscar nominated Best Picture nominee (the last one I remember being so uplifiting and happy was Ang Lee's Jane Austen adaptation of Sense & Sensibility starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet --a movie that honestly made me smile from ear to ear).  Slumdog Millionaire is a tribute to Mumbai and the difficult world so many of its citizens find themselves in.  While the main characters find themselves living in destitute situations, they never give up their dreams of a better life in which they are in charge of their own destinies.  While I know and acknowledge that Danny Boyle is an exceptionally gifted director (Trainspotting is probably his best work), I do think this film has been slightly overpraised. SM is rather messy at times and it feels as if the production was rushed in order for it to have an Oscar-qualifying theatrical run (which is impressive in itself since it was originally going to be a straight-to-DVD release come spring).  Slumdog is a flawed picture  (one too flawed in my opinion for the movie industry's top prize); but it is one that reaffirms the importance of joy, hope, love and dreams in our everyday life.  While Slumdog most definitely tugged at my heartstrings; I cannot allow that to cloud my critique of it.  The movie has numerous errors which don't keep me from admiting that I liked and enjoyed the movie greatly but they should keep the movie from claiming Oscar's biggest prize.  The cast of relatively unknowns have nothig to be ashamed of and I am certain this is the movie that will be remembered for introducing the world to both future-stars Dev Patel and Freida Pinto.

Danny Boyle is a talented filmmaker, but I have never been a huge fan of his. His film are always a great idea with style but he always sabotages himself with bad writing and horrible endings. The Beach, 28 Days Later, and Sunshine are great movies for the first hour or so and then they go Bat-Shit crazy and the 3rd act ruins the entire feature. Slumdog Millionaire is no exception.*SPOILERS* The story follows the life of a game show contestant named Jamal. Every question has something to do with Jamal's past, and we see in flashbacks Jamal, his brother Salim, and a girl named Latika grow up orphaned in the Slums of Mumbai. I like the idea that every question on the game show opens a portal to his past, it's a great new way to tell someones life story. Boyle also made a great looking film with some beautiful shots of India and the gritty look of the Slums. The lead actor Dev Patel, who plays a adult Jamal, does a really good job and you do care about what happens to him. The first problem is how every flashback deals with a tragedy and every person in his life is a bad person. It's always his mom dies, blind homeless crippled children, his brother rapes his girlfriend and many more. I felt like I was watching a Lars Von Trier film where it's never subtleties it's always extremes. I also had a problem with the Game Show Host who turns out to be evil. He gives Jamal the wrong answer in private, and when Jamal doesn't trust him and goes against him on national TV, he pretty much tells him "Are you sure it's not B? You Should Answer B." That is straight up cheating on a national broadcast. Regis would be fired and brought up on charges if he did that to a contestant. Thats not all, after the Game Show Host tries to wain Jamal into the wrong answer he has Jamal tortured by the police, claims to the Media that Jamal cheated, and less than 24 hours later everything is smoothed over and he is back on the show. That is a major and ridicules plot hole. I know India isn't America, but it's not Stalinist Russia either. I also had a problem with the love story. They had chemistry, but I just didn't care and was waiting for her to be hit by a train. Slumdog Millionaire is similar to City Of God(2002) which is far superior in every way and didn't get the accolades that Slumdog is. I may be a little harsh on this film because it is a front runner for Best Picture of the Year. It's not a bad film, but there are about 15 films this year alot better than this one.

Danny Boyle has got to be one of the most versatile directors working today.  The man tackles so many different genres with such a fresh and vibrant energy, it is hard not to get excited.  His latest, "Slumdog Millionaire" is probably his most commercial and feel-good film.  The locations that him and his team shoot are amazing to behold and powerful images in and of themselves.  But, throughout the film I couldn't help but feel that Boyle was being a bit to arty for his own good.  The locations speak for themselves well enough, we don't need oversaturated colors or unnecessary camera angles, and most importantly we don't need a thumping soundtrack to tell us exactly how to feel.  Let the audience decide for themselves what the tone is and how they feel about that.  But darn it if this film didn't put a smile on my face in the end and help me to see a little bit more into life in other parts of the world.

There's something extremely moving about a rags to riches story. Slumdog Millionaire tells the tale of a boy from the worst imaginable ghetto becoming highly successful and achieving the status of icon. A bit like Nat Lofthouse and Bolton ...

The tale of Jamal Malik is an extraordinary one. As the film opens, Jamal has successfully answered every question thrown at him on India's version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" and is just one correct answer away from scooping the top 20 million rupee jackpot. With the show on an overnight recess, the police have become involved, believing the boy to be cheating. It appears inconceivable to them that a boy from the poorest part of Mumbai - a "Slumdog" - can possibly know the answers without outside assistance.

Under first torture and then slightly kinder interrogation, Jamal begins to tell the story of his life, revealing how each answer that he has given has been ingrained into him by an event from his life. And what a remarkable life! It's fairly eay to say that it's been a terrible, tragic and yet heartwarming life. The critics scream that the movie is "the feelgood movie of the decade" and yet we are confronted with such issues as police brutality, torture, orphaning, rape, child cruelty, begging, molestation and the horribly violent death of Jamal's mother. And yet the movie is uplifting in the extreme.

Jamal is accompanied on his journey from terrible beginnings by his brother Salim. This impetuous child is at first a companion and accomplice, and later a rival for the affections of Latika, Jamal's true love. Salim then becomes an adversary, and a gangster. His own downfall is as spectacular as Jamal's rise to glory. The interplay between the two central characters is utterly remarkable, and it's the scenes played by the "young" child actors which are at once the most harrowing and also most heartwarming. I have rarely been so impressed by child actors - nor so shocked at what the director throws at them!

This is a film which will have you cowering behind your hands at one moment and laughing uproariously the next - often within the same scene. For example, the young Jamal is locked in an outside toilet (effectively a cesspit with a wooden border) and has to dive into the effluent in order to escape and run to meet an arriving film star - which he does covered from head to toe in, well, excrement! It's utterly repulsive and brilliant!

Anil Kapoor excels as the effervescent - and yet shady - host of Millionaire. He is one of his nation's biggest stars and at first spurs on Jamal with every answer - then, as he realises he might be upstaged, he feeds the kid a wrong answer and later hands him off to the police! It's a terrible set of circumstances, and yet completely believable.

Danny Boyle has had many great cinematic moments - some of the high (and low) points of Trainspotting are remarkable, and "Sunshine" was a superbly conceived - if slightly flawed - movie, yet he may never surpass this movie. It's mesmerising from start to finish. The cinematography is superb - an early scene where the camera jumps out from the shanty town is great, and some of the angles and techniques used to capture some of the key scenes are terrific. The Taj Mahal has never looked finer!

The interplay between all the lead characters is wonderful, and it's entirely fitting that this should already have receive so many awards and Oscar nominations. The idea to tie quiz question answers to life experiences is so simple, yet superbly done. Go and see this if you are in any way shape or form a movie fan - and if you're not, go see it anyway. It's genius.

Slumdog Millionaire tells the story of Jamal Malik, an orphan from the slums of Mumbai who somehow finds his way onto India's version of Who Wants To Be a Millionaire? with only one question standing between him and the top prize of 20 million rupees. But with the allotted time for the show at an end, Jamal must return the following day to try his luck at the final question. However, circumstances don't always go as we would hope, and as Jamal is leaving the studio, he his arrested, taken to police headquarters where he's tortured to reveal how he is cheating. Because someone from the slums could never know the answers to all those questions, getting farther in the game than doctors and lawyers ever had. As he sits in the police office, re-watching the game show from the beginning, Jamal relates the life experiences from growing up in the slums, surviving riots which killed his Mother, made his escape from a monster while leaving behind a young girl, Latika. And with each glimpse, Jamal also reveals his growing love for the young girl and his attempts to free her from her hard life.

The first 20 - 30 minutes of the film are difficult to watch, and I can understand why some people walked out of the theater (from what my Mother told me of friends who saw the film). Torture, electrocution, the violent riots -- not easy to stomach. But CM and I made it through that and were rewarded with a remarkable film about love surviving through difficult odds. I realized this with an "a-ha!" moment towards the end, when Jamal used his last life line for the final question and when he heard Latika's voice on the other end of the call, the relief on his face told the movie audience that the game show didn't matter. That it never did.

Great acting, a great story, great directing, and a remarkable view of Mumbai and India -- we both finally understood all the most deserved acclaim and awards following the film.

Highly entertaining, if highly contrived, story of a young man who gets to the final round of the Indian "Who Wants To Be a Millionaire" but is arrested under suspicion of fraud, as surely no-one from the slums could know all the answers. The film is ingeniously structured so that each question of the quiz show is contrasted with an event from Jamal's often brutal and traumatic past which corresponds with his knowledge of the answer. It's one of the many plot devices that you could pick apart but need to accept to enjoy the film for what it is. The strongest part of the film is following Jamal and his brother as children through the slums, embarking on various criminal enterprises in order to survive. The ending of the film enters a different, unashamedly romantic mode but there is a knowing wink from Boyle at the end with an outright Bollywood dance routine suggesting that sometimes one shouldn't look further than bright and brash escapism. Isn't that what movies are best at?

Whatâs amazing about it is how the story is told â how it used an old game show as a vehicle of a usual plot and a foreign setting and culture to make it look brand new. But the truth is, most of the time I donât care if the story is fresh. What matters to me is if it affected me. And it did.

This is a great film & deserving of some oscar success. It's a grim tale which follows the progress of two young brothers from the slums of Mumbai & how they try to get ahead in life. Running through the story is the love interest between Jamal & Latika, a girl he has known as a child when he let her in from the rain after losing her parents too. The scenes in Mumbai are stunning. We are thrust straight into the slums with a chase scene, reminiscent of Boyle's other epic 'Trainspotting'. Only this time we are not amongst the council estates of Edinburgh, but the industrious poverty of Mumbai. It pulls no punches; the child abuse & poverty are harrowing & at times make for uncomfortable viewing. However, despite the poverty, the abuse, the corruption & the gangsterism, there's an optimism that wins through. The third act of the film reveals Mumbai in all its glorious new progress. There's a wonderful city-scape shot from the heights of building, reminding us that there's a different India emerging from its growing pains. Above all, this film is about the triumph of love. Perhaps this pushes it a little too far into the realms of fantasy, but this provides something of an antidote to the brutal struggle that pervades the whole film. Definitely worth seeing!

Sorry to rain on peoples parade, but I think this film has been over-hyped. I found it hard to engage with a film that has so many flights of fancy and plot holes. For example, you have to buy into the notion that the host of "Who want's to be a Millionaire" knows what all the questions will be and the answers...I doubt any major TV company would allow this in reality, which alone blows the story out of the water. The film makes it look almost desirable to live in a slum "Oooh, look, they are so colourful"-another notion I found hard to swallow. I also found the film pretty predictable-you know that he's gonna ....well, I won't print a spoiler!

The fact that it takes place in India doesn't change the fact that Slumdog Millionaire is pure destiny-driven, hyperbolical movie-magic cheese.  But movies like this remind us of why we used to love just that sort of thing.  Fate certainly lines up in some pretty unreal ways for Jamal, but, my God, shouldn't it?  Could we be any happier when it does?

I could go on about direction, and settings, and characterization, and blah, blah, blah, but when it really comes down to it, Slumdog is so wonderful because it does something more intangible -- something you can't pin with criticism.  It makes you care.  And so it makes you excited.  And then it makes you happy.
