Slumdog Millionaire
2008, 120mins, 15
Director: Danny Boyle
Writer: Simon Beaufoy
Cast includes: Dav Patel, Anil Kapoor, Saurabh Shukla, Freida Pinto, Irrfan Khan
UK Release Date: 9th January 2009
 
It would be hard to dislike a film as charming and ultimately upbeat as [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] but when open to the vast amounts of awards buzz the picture is gaining it's would also be quite easy to be underwhelmed. The film is a fine piece of work and sits nicely in director Danny Boyle's rather high standard CV but by the same token it's not quite the modern day classic the media are making it out to be.
The film basically charts the life Of Jamal (Dav Patel) in flashback form as he takes part in a game of [i]Who Wants To Be A Millionaire. [/i]As each question is posed to Jamal we learn how he knows thew answer thanks to his colourful life, and how all these years he's been chasing after Latika (Freida Pinto) his childhood sweetheart. However as Jamal answers question after question the law becomes suspicious, after all how can this boy from the slums of India know all the answers?
The adult performances in the film are effective but not remarkable, Patel makes a solid and likeable lead whilst other mature actors play nicely with the script but in truth it's the child performers who really steal the show. Those portraying Jamal his brother Salim and Latika in their younger years are the true stars of [i]Slumdog Millionaire, [/i]the film depends on them as much as it does the more experienced actors and in many respects the youngsters performances are key in making the later year incarnations of the various characters work. As the grown up Latika Freida Pinto is pretty and sweet but easily the dullest version of the character, whilst Anil Kapoor has great fun playing the host of the gameshow.
Danny Boyle's direction is superb, if the picture is to win one Oscar it should be for his efforts behind the camera. Boyle has directed some really kinetic and visually interesting movies in the past but his work here might be among the very best we've seen from the British helmer. He captures the Slums of India wonderfully and uses his camera to such effect that the viewer might swear he was immersed in the very area depicted onscreen. He also paces the movie well and develops the characters at a rewarding pace, slowly drawing the audience in until they're fully invested in this story of a boy looking for the girl he loves. Another really high point is the music from A.R. Rahman, the composer much like the director really capturing the essence of the story in his art.
The screenplay by Simon Beaufoy is well written and exudes a charm and charisma that make it hard for the viewer not to warm to his vision. He rarely treads into saccharine waters and keeps the film on purely reality based tracks, not everything is feel good in [i]Slumdog Millionaire. [/i]The story is essentially an upbeat piece of cinema but it manages to insert in a few moments of sufficent grit to keep the picture from being irritatingly twee. In many ways Beaufoy deserves as many backslaps for the well worked character structure as the director or actors, he has after all written the basic arcs himself. Yet some of the writing and occurences in the story are a little forgettable, never unwatchable just not always memorable. I can't say any of these segments where bad but a few felt unneeded and a cut below the better moments in the feature.
I think the majority of people will find [i]Sumdog Millionaire [/i]a worthwhile watch, it's not perfect and maybe as sensational as you might have heard but it leaves you with a pleasent buzz when the credits roll. I can't see it scooping best picture but [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]works well within it's own ambitions.

Where does one begin to describe the beauty of Slumdog Millionaire? All aspects of the film, its colour, its poetry, its complexity, its irony, and all its clever nuances of symbolism and splendor make Slumdog Millionaire more than a movie, a flawless work of art.  It is all at once a dark and beautiful romance, a vivid exploration of life in the indian slums, a heart pounding tale of suspense and dramatic realism, and in all ways a resonating anthem for life and mankind. 
	Not only does the film itself impress so highly, but the fact that they did it with what little they had to work with is incredible as well. Many actors and extras were people pulled right off the slums of Mumbai for the movie. Seeing it go up against such huge budget, star studded films as The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, and winning is a testament to Slumdog Millionaire's greatness. Before watching this, I was wondering if an "Indian" movie requires the skills of a British director to make oscar standard material. After watching Danny Boyle's production, there's an emphatic nod of the head for this question.

Take away the feel-good impression you walk away with, and you're still left with the little details that make you stand up to this "bollywood" movie. I'm talking about the appropriate casting, the masterful background score, the lilting tunes, and most importantly, the excellent script.

This movie is based on a book (Q&A) by Vikas Swarup, a diplomat currently based in Durban as the Deputy High Commissioner of India to South Afria. But the manner in which the screenplay is written and picturised makes you feel closer as an observer in Jamal Malik's world.

I liked the fact that the scenes as small kid to big kid is not done in sepia tones. It really gels well with the reason Jamal knows what he knows.

This production is definitely not perfect, but then again, perfection is averse to the art of cinema.

From Rocky to Rudy, The Mighty Ducks to Ratatouille, 300 to The Pursuit of Happyness, Americans love a good underdog story. Americans believe in a world where anyone with enough guts, determination, and resolve can achieve whatever goal they set their mind to. And while it may not be true it certainly serves as the basis for many a great film. Now picture this: your underdog is a slumdog (a term for a guy from the slums. Not just the ghetto or the bad side of town but a world where trash serves as the grass for the ground, houses are stacked one on top of the other, and the toilets are simply wooden shacks over a river with a hole in the floor). Now that you get that picture, get this one: this slumdog is a contestant on the popular gameshow WHO WANTS TO BE A MILLIONAIRE? And heâs only on the show in hopes that the girl he loves will see him and they can be reunited or in reality finally united. This is the set up for Slumdog Millionaire and Slumdog Millionaire is what people go to the movies to see. But what is fantastic is that the movie isnât American at all. The film takes place far from the comforts of the land of opportunity in the third world, in what was formerly known as Bombay, India. 

Slumdog Millionaire can receive comparisons to underdog films and to a film like CITY OF GOD, the 2004 best foreign film which takes place in the city of RIO DE JAINEIRO and its underbelly of crime. What makes slumdog shine though is its dichotomy. Its ability to show the slums and the life of a poverty and hardship without pulling any punches in contrast to a gameshow which glorifies capitalismâs promise that anyone can be rich. It is this dichotomy that makes it special. However it is not the promise of money that makes the film so enthralling and inspiring to those who see it: it is a love that persists, fights through, and ultimately wins out against everything that tries to smother it. It is a promise of destiny, or meaning, and of purpose. It is an innocence maintained in a world of greed. It is the belief that good things come to those who wait and great things come to those who must overcome great struggles. It is more than the American dream, it calls upon a worldwide dream and hope that we can make it through life unblemished, all right, in one piece. But the film doesnât actually deliver this promise. There are scars, both physical and emotional that make their mark on the main characters as the grow up in a dangerous world, but what the film does promise is that redemption is possible and that it is never too late for destiny. 

Iâve seen the film twice, enough to confirm that it is my favorite film of the year and, I believe, the best. Not enough can be said for the quality at each level of filmmaking called upon to bring this story to the screen. Danny Boyle, behind the camera, leads this film through a chaotic world to tell a very simple story. The cast, which recently won best ensemble at the SAG awards, makes every scene worth watching. The editing, the cinematography all work to introduce many of us to the world of Mombai. The music breathes so much life into the film and might just receive an academy award for doing just that. Itâs a movie that we can believe in, that reminds us that weâre all the underdog sometimes, that we must never give up hope. In many ways it is one of the most simple movies of the year, its message is that LOVE conquers all even in the slums of India. But isnât that the kind of movie we need right now? In a world of economic recession, continued wars, the constant fear of terrorist attacks, and an uncertainty in the future not just of the country but of every man and woman, Slumdog Millionaire reminds us that there is something that shines through the mess, through the crap, that lasts in spite of every obstacle the besets it. Love may be the underdog right now, but Slumdog Millionaire reminds us that in the movies the underdog wins. 9.8 out of 10

Slumdog Millionaire...Let me cut straight to the chase and say, "If this is what the Oscars claim is worthy of 10 nominations, including that of the Best Picture over masterpieces such as The Dark Knight,then they just havn't gotten a taste of what cinemas are really about..."

     Slumdog can be summed up with just 2 words: "Mediocrity", and "Inconsistency". Though the idea of Jamal answering the questions due to a sequence of happenings in his life is a great idea, its execution is highly flawed...Though we are treated to a flashback related to the question,we are left clueless as to how he obtained the actual answer as such...for example, the question regarding the poet of the song...we are shown where Jamal has heard the song,but there was not a mention of the poet...so how did he know?or the question of who invented the revolver...And as for the scene in which the tourists car is stripped to its bare essence and Jamal says, "You wanted to see a bit of real India?" and the Tourists reply with their "Bit of real America"...that is simply the heights!!!

     The only time the movie makes even the slightest impact is towards the last 15 minutes or so, where we are drawn in towards what is an expected and standard, but all the same enjoyable "Underdog on top" ending...   

     If Slumdog had been any other movie that claims nothing but standard,mediocre entertainment fare, its many glaring flaws might be pardonable...but for a movie that claims to be a trendsetter and acquirer of countless laurels, it simply falls flat as not even an average movie.There have been a million movies (Indian ones especially) that have covered the "feel good, underdog movie" way better, and Slumdog cannot begin to compare with even the most average of them...The only guess I can fathom is that maybe most people haven't really watched any of the really good Indian movies, for then they would surely see what a below average fare Slumdog really is...
    Doesn't deserve a single nomination on any count,except maybe for the background score of "Oh Saiya" and "Jaya Ho"...A very average movie this...

Most would think of Regis' old game show as something out of date. It was out of date when Regis took it over: Millionaire was a British game show first. From the attacks on muslims, to gang control...to the dirty and darker side. The film also shows an aspect of true love. From the moment Jamal and Latika first meet as young kids, they develop a bond for each other. And, everytime Latika finds herself in trouble, Jamal is always there in some way to rescue her. Jamal's brother, Salim, finds himself in trouble most of the time, and gets involved with a gang circuit, shortly after Jamal, Salim and Latika escape from this camp type thing that seemed to train in Beggars. Of course, there is some tension between jamal and salim from that moment they escape, and don't talk for a few years. Anyways - on to the millionaire part. Jamal lands a spot on the indian version of who wants to be a millionaire - and, it comes out later that the only reason he wanted to be on the show was because Latika would probably be watching. Now, if growing up in the slums wasn't bad...Jamal finds himself in "trouble" from the police or something there, because they - and the host - seem to think he's cheating or has all the answers. So, the police take him away after masking his face and try and force it out of him that he was. They have the first day's episode taped, and as they're going through most of the questions on the show...the memories come back to how he remembered the answers to the questions. Needless to say, they let him go to finish his show. Now - we all know he does the first part ok...but, this is where they leave it open! They ask him the last question that he needs to get the 20 million in rupees. Does he miss it? Or, does he get it? That's all up to his last lifeline, and how much he's willing to bet on his gut. India back in the late 70s, early 80s and then on, it was just coming up from 3rd world status. Enter the Taj Mahal, and everything that makes it a tourist spot, not to mention job spot now. And, a kid, Jamal...who's got his chance to come up out of the slums, and make something for himself, and get out of his pointless job. Honestly guys, if you've thought twice about waiting to check out this movie - just do yourself a favour, and go....international for once. This film won't disappoint! Whats in a Name?
Slumdog Millionaire
By Jimmy So

I met a friend for a drink just after I came out of Slumdog Millionaire, and I outlined the plot to him without giving away the ending. Wait a sec. You mean to tell me that in the beginning you dont know whether hes won the million bucks? The titles not exactly keeping that a secret, he pointed out. I suppose in a literal interpretation, the inclusion of the word millionaire would mandate that the slumdog Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) ought to win the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire? But titles also come in the form of the vague, the ironic, the satiric, and even the outright absurd. We need not know to which category Slumdog Millionaire belongs except to recognize that it is a good title: the film is as peppy as a puppy and fantastical as a millionaire-dream.

Slumdog Millionaire opens with the misstep of Jamal being tortured by a police inspector (Irrfan Khan)frankly, Patel looks more stoned than mutilated, but apparently America is not the only country fond of enhanced interrogation techniques. The police accuse Jamal, an uneducated 18-year-old orphan who grew up in the slums, of cheating in Who Wants to be a Millionaire? He is one question away from 20 million rupees, but before that final multiple choice the show propitiously runs out of time and takes a one night recess, while a billion and a half hardly affluent Indians ironically and fervently wonder if the rich-poor gap can widen just enough for Jamal to squeeze through.

Jamal, of course, is busy getting tickled by electric shocks, but he doesnt have a confessionhe has flashbacks. He explains how he has come to know the answer to each of the question, and in the process serves up the ultimate rebuke to pedantrya rich and eventful life has provided him with esoterica that might just happen to appear on a bad but very lucrative quiz show. His first explanation is a giggle. Asked to pick out the name of a Bollywood star, Jamal recounts how, as a kid, he crawled through feces three feet deep just to get the autograph of the superstar.

Next he tells of how his mother is killed in the 1992-93 Hindu-Muslim riots (a rather incongruous explanation of another answer lies in this episode), and Jamal befriends a waif named Latikaon the other hand, Jamals brother, Salim, seems to have something against her. The three of them are trained by a sinister gang to beg for money, but they escape, only that Salim leaves Latika behind. Why does Jamal know that Benjamin Franklin is on the U.S. 100-dollar note? Because, looking for Latika, Jamal reunited with a fellow slumdog who was not so lucky as the Maliks and had by then become a blind beggar, and he asked Jamal to look at whos on the currency to confirm that it was a Benjamin. He knows the inventor of the revolver because Salim used a Colt pistol to help Jamal rescue Latika. You get the idea.

Surely you know the trajectory of this tried and true story, but the fact is that you dont know if Jamal gets the last question right until the end of the film, regardless of what the title suggests. There is ample suspense to captivate an audiencetwenty million rupees are clinging onto one of four possible answers to a multiple-choice question. The title sequence, itself tied to four answer choices, might give something away, but does it even matter?

The opening title card reads: Jamal is within one right answer of winning the game show, so how did he get here? The letter they want you to pick is D: It is written. Simon Beaufoy wrote the script, based on the novel Q and A by the Indian diplomat Vikas Swarup. I wager that the two men are familiar with Lawrence of Arabiathe writings in the sand, surely, in the life of T. E. Lawrence, a man so driven to defy everything before him he only makes sense of his actions later. In the famous desert scene so engulfing you can taste the granules in your mouth, Gasim, an Arab fighter, fell off his camel unnoticed during the night, and OTooles Lawrence seizes the opportunity like a serpent spotting Eve, and against the advice of the Bedouins, turns back to look for him in the endless Nefud Desert. Nothing is written! Lawrence snaps at them; he manages to rise above not only the Bedouins but the desert and destiny as well, saving Gasimbut the sand has the last word, and later Lawrence personally shoots Gasim to prevent a blood feud among his fighters. The plot twist suggests the decisive victory of fateafter all, where would mythmaking be without it? Nevertheless let us be reminded that Lawrence was not above little contrivances himself, and if anything is written he is likely to have written it, and made it all up if he can help it.

It is so contrived! is the complaint I hear most often about Slumdog Millionaire. But what do you expecta film executively produced by fate? Or will you settle for a movie contrived by standard human beings? Once upon a time, movies were manufactured products of entertainment filled with set pieces to be devoured and enjoyed. Flights of fancy werent always results of dream sequences or signs of magical realism. You took the cosmic amusement of yesteryear Hollywood in stride. They used to manufacture flights of fancy not with expensive CGI but the old fashioned way, by taking a cute but implausible turn in the plot. Not all films are miracles of realism in the natural rhythm of life. And if you rightly anticipate that I take the view that they dont make them like they used to, I am unabashed about my romanticism for the spirit of the Golden Age.

Who else shares my fondness for supple storytelling, of bending reality to ones liking? After a late-night layover in a Calcutta motel watching a Dharmendra (the Burt Lancaster of Bollywood) doubleheader with two Indian mates I consider brothers, and a subsequent in-flight entertainment featuring 2006s Om Shanti Om, (only one of the biggest grossing Hindi films in history, an Indian redux of Singin in the Rain and Phantom of the Opera) I can say that the subcontinent of South Asia still has a good appetite for unblushing cinematic thrills worthy of the exclamation Thats Entertainment! The Tinseltown of the1920s to 1950s has immigrated to Mumbai, studio system and formula and all. In making Slumdog Millionaire, the British director Danny Boyle not only pays homage to the sari and mehndi, but he takes on the very spirit of what a movie out of India might feel like.

Slumdog Millionaire has the look of neon worship, a love for the vibrant urban life found in the best Taiwan and Hong Kong films but absent in American cinema since the gentrification of the Big Apple. Megalopolises are both beautiful and dangerous. Heroes survive by running past colorful lights, getting lost in the downtown maze, and they are rewarded with the temporary relief of having been rescued by a city. The best part of "Slumdog Millionaire" is the lasta full Bollywood dance number on the platforms of a train station, involving almost the entire cast.  [i]
 (The aim and intention of my reviews is to critique and recommend while not revealing the whole story to enjoy the movie when seen. But minor details have been divulged for a proper review!)[/i]
 
 [b]âItâs a tale about the trial, tribulations and ultimately the triumph of the human spiritâ[/b]
 
 Slumdog millionaire takes you on a journey of brutal existence, poverty, religious divide, exploitation, hurdles, humbug, survival and crime, all juxtaposed and interspersed with cheering scenes, exciting moments, fantasies, tender emotions, dreams and exhilarating situations. You go through a gamut of emotions all in one brilliant movie.
 
 The story is about how an orphan from the slums of Mumbai rises from rags to riches remembering his memoirs of life as knowledge for winning a game show. Jamal Malik a spirited kid, orphaned at a young age goes through many hurdles and challenges in life, yet overcomes and triumphs. He is a beggar, a thief, an imposter, a guide at Taj Mahal, a waiter, has a brother in underworld, is a tea server at a call center and finally goes on a game show- who wants to be a millionaire/ Kaun Banega Crorepati not for the money but to reach out to his lost love.
 
 His life shown in flashbacks juxtaposed with the questions of the game show and the reason for his awareness of the answers is brilliantly depicted. The slumdog becomes the underdog and rooted by audiences across India to win, but the showâs host gets doubts about the authenticity of his answers and knowledge and get him interrogated by the cops, where he further relates his poignant adventures of life.
 
 The characters, all relatively new artists acted brilliantly. Dev Patel as a somber and subdued Jamal who shows sudden wit and cleverness did a great job for an upcoming teen British TV artist. Ayush Mahesh Khedekar who plays the younger Jamal was amazingly talented. He shows the sweet innocence, the emotions, the depth of pain, the loss of friendship, betrayal by his brother, the exuberance of seeing his favorite hero [url="http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amitabh_Bachchan"]Amitabh Bachchan[/url], going thru shit literally, all portrayed so well.
 
 All the characters that played Latika were good. But the characters that played Salim were again brilliant. The young character Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail starts to build the mean, bigheaded, selfish character which gets further negatively built by Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala and get graduated by Madhur Mittal into a power and money maniac involved in the underworld. 
 
 Anil Kapoor as the condescending host is good, but the reason his character was negative is not detailed. The only reason may be to develop sympathy factor to the contestant. Irrfan Khan is his usual best. The rest of the cast gave good performances and I guess the co-director and casting director Loveleen Tandon needs to be credited for such a talented cast.
 
 The music By A. R Rehman is excellent and uprising. The cinematography and screenplay is exceptional, the direction is excellent. Dan Boyle has to be applauded for such a well made movie.
 
 The rags to riches slumdog kind outstanding bollywood movies have been made earlier, like Amitabh Bachchans, â[url="http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0072860/"]Deewar[/url]â or â[url="http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0082644/"]Laawarisâ[/url] and more. But what makes this different is the real life like depiction and possible dreams through modern day game shows. The depiction of how similar circumstances bring out different personalities is also showcased well, contrasting the lives of the two brothers. In a bollywood masala movie the parallel would be too contrasting and surreal, where as in slumdog it is more realistic.
 
 The depictions of parts of India in a bad way, the slums and the poverty and the condescending characters have been not appreciated by some media in India. But one has to accept the reality of life, ignoring them doesnât make them disappear. Every country and city has alternate realities, and thatâs a fact for many big cities. Itâs unfortunate but life is like that! One has to get over that and appreciate the movie for its brilliance.
 
 The movie is exhilarating, narrative is crisp, editing is perfect, pace is quick, music is rousing, and the story is moving. Not many movies in the recent past have that simply perfect movie experience. This is going to get an Oscar.

Director Danny Boyle ("28 Days Later..." "Trainspotting") never set out to make a masterpiece. He did, however, set out to make a film that tells a relatively predictable story with a voice of fresh innovation and a teaming pulse.
"Slumdog Millionaire" opened quietly at the Toronto and Chicago film festivals earlier this year and won the Audience Award at both festivals. The film was catapulted to the spotlight after it swept the Golden Globe awards, taking home four of the top awards, including Best Picture. Now, it has received 10 Oscar nominations and may walk away with every single one. What is it, then, that makes "Slumdog Millionaire" so ostensibly brilliant?
The story is centered on a young man named Jamal (Dev Patel), who lives in the slums of Mumbai, India. Much like life, though, the movie does not follow a linear pattern in telling this story. We become acquainted with Jamal as he is being harshly interrogated by police who think he has cheated on the game show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" because he has successfully gotten up to 10 million Rupees. How could a teenager from the slums be so smart or even get on the show? The film backtracks on itself to tell us.
Jamal and his older brother, Salim, have had a tough childhood. Left as orphans after witnessing the murder of their mother, the boys lead a life of petty crime and thievery to make ends meet. Early on, there is a young girl named Latika who befriends the brothers and Jamal falls instantly in love with her. It is through this love story thread that the film is held connected and given a universal appeal. 
Told with vibrant colors, a rhythmically original score, and unique editing techniques, "Slumdog Millionaire" transcends the average movie simply by the way it is made. The genius of the film, though, lies solely in the story. Jamal endures struggle after struggle through his life but never ceases in pressing on. It is a story of courage and integrity that can hold truths for any movie-goer, in any situation. 
"Slumdog Millionaire" is a movie that is worthy of recognition from the Academy with cast of complete foreigners. Finally, an uplifting and inspiring movie that had nothing to do with football!

[i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is the telling of a story revolving around Mumbai teen Jamal Malik, a proverbial "slumdog," as he becomes a contestant on India's version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" When Jamal begins to surpass virtually all of the show's previous hopefuls with relative ease, he is arrested and interrogated on suspicion of cheating. As the interrogation drags painfully on for the now famous slumdog, Jamal recalls the life experiences that have provided the knowledge needed to answer each one of the show's questions. What ensues is essentially a mildly predictable rags-to-riches story with a mildly predictable, yet rewarding ending.

As far as the story's progression is concerned, it has a very coherent structure to it, what with the questions Jamal must answer at the beginning of the show directly corresponding with the earliest years of his life. Personally, I feel that this is one the film's most appealing elements, on the basis of how each one of these sequences gives us a closer look at Jamal's life and the amount of both pain and happiness he'd endured on the long road to the present. With that being said, the movie as a whole exhibits a relatively fair balance between said emotions, allowing us to sympathize with Jamal's character and the circumstances he and those closest to him must endure; all thanks to Danny Boyle's superb direction.

The casting choices are also very excellent indeed, what with the more or less "unknowns" adding to the authenticity of the film, more specifically in terms of its setting and how you feel as if you're watching a documentary as certain events begin to unfold. Needless to say, the performances themselves are quite impressive, a good example of which can be seen within Dev Patel's portrayal of present-day Jamal. Hell, I was even impressed with the child actors featured towards the start of the film, as they clearly set the groundwork for the type of person each character would become as the story progressed.

Last, but certainly not least, we have the dazzling visual quality of [i]Slumdog [/i]that has critics and viewers everywhere talking. To elaborate, the cinematography is simply stunning, and the various imagery present throughout the film's duration is what really helps the story achieve its full potential. It's with this that all of the aforementioned greatness of this film manages to tie itself together to make one of the better films of '08; quite possibly of the past decade. Further still, with 10 Oscar nominations, [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]seems to be getting the recognition it deserves, prompting you to see it as soon as possible if this review didn't quite do its job.

Slumdog Millionaire is a cinematic gem, a crowd-pleasing fantasy that will sweep you away! It is a hymn to perseverance, honesty and unswerving love. Set and filmed in India, the film tells the story of a young uneducated man from the fetid slums of Mumbai who appears on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. There is a catch. Our main hero, Jamal Malik, is not interested in money. He goes to the show because he thinks that the love of his life would be watching and as such he could reunite with her. Every question brings him closer to his one true love! Jamal answers questions on the TV show not from book knowledge but from his own life experiences. We follow him and his older brother Salim - well played by three sets of actors at various ages - through a series of incredibly colourful adventures, all of which adds to Jamal's store of knowledge. It is an incredible story which begins with a dive into a latrine pit to steal a glimpse of a movie star and continues with their stealing shoes at the Taj Mahal as the brothers fall in and out with various bands of criminals and each other. The third main character is Jamals girl, Latika. He pursues her tirelessly even after she has been sold off to become the bride of a gang boss. Gritty realism and vigorous storytelling, superb direction, dazzling cinematography, fast-paced editing, unforgettable performances and indelible images of the Indian subcontinent have rendered this film a very strong contender for the Best Picture Oscar, on February 22nd. This movie truly is a romantic, modern fairy-tale epic of Dickensian proportions that will speak directly to your heart!

The press has been comparing the unlikely rise of this film as an Oscar front-runner to the travails of its main character Jamal.  What irony then that, much like Jamal who faces allegation of cheating when he is about to win Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, this film also receives its fair share of backlash lately, such as the accusation of glamorizing poverty.

Such publicity helped the film's cause initially but may have obscured what it really is: a tribute to populist traditions in films and literature, including but not limited to Bollywood.  At heart it is the same story of star-crossed lovers that have been passed down through generations in different languages and cultures.  A familiar story told with a clever plot, dazzling visuals and an earnest cast may explain why it manages to connect with even the most jaded of movie-goers.  So despite some imperfections, this film deserves to be considered one of the best.

I'm tired so this will be sort of brief. But this weekend we caught Slumdog Millionaire as it is playing at our local movie theatre. I really knew nothing about this film going in and had no idea what to expect. I have to say I enjoyed quite a bit of this. The story was quite engrossing, I was very into it and into the characters. In some ways everyone's roles are maybe too simplified, too black and white, and the ending at the train station definitely felt sort of Disney-esque in a bad way. But I was really into so much of this movie, and the way they kept building up Jamal conquering crazy odds to attain little goals or happiness and then time and time again turn around and tear it all away and tear your guts out, man I was expecting everything to end in a really sad depressing note. When the conclusion of the game show happens it was a shock and for me the climax of the film, a more genuine moving moment than the forced train station bit following it. The way all the little victories being ripped away horribly time and time again built up to that big glorious moment was really effective, probably too simple an idea for sure, like a chord being palm muted and slowly played openly to build up to a big crash of a different chord and the whole band jumping in is in a rock song, but like the rock song it is effective even if an overused device. And folks, the music is catchy as heck in this movie! I don't care for dance music really at all but the music in this film is catchy and made me want to do a little dancing! Very entertaining film, some engrossing storylines, some poor execution in a few places, probably too simple in several ways, but effective and entertaining!

If you go to movies to be surprised, Slumdog Millionaire might not be for you.  It telegraphs the ending early on: the poor Indian slumdog Jamal Malik will win 20 million rupees and get the girl. You have a good idea where and how   they will meet up and even what the final question will be.  For the rest of us, though, this is a poignant and wildly entertaining film that is one part fairy tale and one part Dickens novel. The technique of having Jamal kidnapped to try to force him to reveal how a boy from the slums can answer these arcane questions isn't original,but terribly effective. It's the story of dreams, love and achieving what you always wanted. It's not that much about India OR poverty - you have to look at the heart and not at the face I would say.

A boy in slums emerges as a potential winner of 2 million RS; Slumdog Millionaire is a journey of that boy from being a slum-boy who is no where important to anyone to a person who is being watched by millions on the TV and being cheered of. However, the heart of the story is Jamal and Latika and how they meet each other in different stages of their lives and finally make it. 

Though Salim and Jamal have lived in slums and roads throughout their childhood - they both have a dream in their eyes. It's that dream which overshadows the entire backdrop of dirt and vulnerability of both these boys. Jamal - who always being dominated by his younger brother right from the time when they used to "trade" toilet. The only light in his life is Latika; his childhood friend with whom he gets separated while running away from the group of "Begger makers". Jamal goes through various places and finally comes back to place where Latika is a ready-to-sell virgin in red light area. Salim uses his gun-power to get everyone out of that gutter only ends up using Latika for his own "good". They finally meet up again when now a Call Centre Assistant Jamal finds out Salim who is now an active member of a criminal gang. Latika is a living with the gangster where Jamal tries to free her up. Then it starts a journey of getting into a game-show coz that's the only place where he can find Latika. 

Within this story - the life of Jamal, Salim and Latika has played an background part. It is how they uses good, bad and ugly ways to come up from the slums to achieve their dreams. The narration and story-telling is very detailed and up to the earth. We might have seen the Mumbai slum-life in other films but this one touches your heart to the very core. The pace of story is always right on time so as the screen-play. You never feel left alone or boring in the whole journey. Though few logics of answers may not be convincing enough - but you do have such a bonding script ahead, you can forgive them easily.

Dev Patel as Jamal is absoluotely picture perfect - so as his childhood actors. Salim is that typical bollywood gangster and Latika is lovable. All the actors has given justice to this roller coaster ride drama. Special mention of Anil Kapoor as host with gray shades. Even Sourabh Shukla and Irrfan Khan has played their cameos well. 

Very special mention to AR's music. He has show that if the talent is there - it has it's special place. Specially his last Jai Ho song celebrates the mood of story and whole hindi film industry. 

It's a celebration of dreams, life and love!!! Watch it if you have a heart!!!

Slumdog Millionaire is at heart much more of a Bollywood fable than it presents itself to be. Despite the cutting edge, innovative, if a little melodramatic, film form, with all its heavily stylised cinematography, quirky camera angles, snappy editing, and unusual plot presentation (in fragments, each relating to a question in 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire?'), in terms of story this differs very little to any given Bollywood feature. I result we get a movie which is quite unsure of what it wants to be.

To be fair, I do not understand all the critical lauding 'Slumdog Millionaire' is getting across the board. To me it's a very generic film packed in shiny paper. I do not take away it's credits, most of which lie in a striking presentation of poverty-stricken life in India, the country's sudden transformation, and pointing out how insensitive to violence and filth modern audiences have become (after all this is marketed as the 'feel-good movie of the year', rather than the 'movie where a kid is blinded, a girl is raped and a child swims through shit to get out of a toilet'). In addition, the kid actors, as opposed to the terrible adults, are a joy to watch. Finally, it is a true and impressive reconciliation of Hollywood and Bollywood, symbolised by the credits dance sequence. And yet, all of this is marginal, overwhelmed by the constantly presence of a plot which has little to tell us, and even less to teach us.

If 'Slumdog Millionaire' wouldn't have been burdained which such heavy expectations, it would constitute for a much more enjoyable experience. However, all the context and hype one unavoidably brings along to the cinema simply expose what a mediocre movie ''Slumdog Millionaire" really is.

But film of year? Please.  I don't feel it's ground-breaking and there were times when I just wanted to slap the dumb look off Dev Patel's face. I actually like the soundtrack more than anything else in this film. Now that I've seen this film I can move on.

Slumdog Millionaire is the feel-good film of late 2008 that is sweeping the awards season. The triumphant story of an uneducated man who manages through luck to win the Indian version of âWho wants to be a millionaire?â in his quest to win a girl, it is bland, apolitical, and uncontroversial. There is very little that would challenge our comfort levels or open our hearts to any cause short of nodding at the poverty of Mumbaiâs slums. In other words, it is everything that Milk and Wall-E are not: a happy story that can be taken at face value and makes almost no comment on the current state of the world. In a dark time for the economy and global warming and in the wake of a major setback for gay liberation in last yearâs elections, the film allows is sublimely neutral.
That said, there is not much else going for Slumdog millionaire. It is a fairly routine rags-to-riches story of tragedy and struggle. Director Danny Boyle is careful to show the audience pieces of violence and tragedy without the gruesome details that one would find in the Coen brothers version or the sex that almost any other director would include. There is also precious little intensity or character development.
Still, Slumdog Millionaire is better than almost anything out there and a fun albeit mild bit of entertainment for a Saturday night.

I  tried to see SM not just a mere film about India made by an UK filmmaker, but also a film heavily tipped to carry the Oscar statue this year. And when you say Oscar, even if you scan the last 15 years when the quality of movies went down quite a bit, you are still reminded of absolute marvel of movies like "A beautiful mind", "Million dollar baby", the Lord of the rings trilogy etc. SM falls far short of those movies. The only recent Oscar winner that stands closest to SM's method of direct, in-your-face delivery style was the movie "Crash" (won in 2005 I believe) . But even Crash has some level of subtlety somewhere. Unlike SM, when you saw Crash you didn't feel that the director's intention was to pound upon the sensitivity of the viewers and smash it to a pulp. At least the first half of SM defintely stands guilty of being excessively and needlessly gory and gruesome on details that didn't mean much. And meaning much is a very important aspect right? We all have heard about the phrase "Chekov's gun". Probably originated by Chekov, what it means is that if the director showed you a gun on the wall in the first act, then that gun will be fired sometime before the final act. Meaning that no detail is meaningless, you need to remember everything that the director is showing you in detail because it will have some significance some time later. Harry Potter books followed this method of construction. So did Hitchcock's thriller movies. Now will someone tell me - what was the significance of the scene showing beggar children being turned blind by pouring acid? Was that the one scene where Salim realizes his brotherly feelings? Was it to show that Salim is good at heart and will always ultimately make the right call? What follows in the movie doesn't support that, except the forced ending. In any case, I don't see any justification of that sequence other than pure torturing of audience's nerves. 
A movie can't be just a photographed theater. I have always used that phrase to differentiate a quality movie from the mockery of a quality movie. D W Griffith laid down the grammars and syntaxes of movie more than 100 years back in his "Intolerance" and "Birth of a nation". From that point onwards, great movie directors created their own language and projected it on celluloid.  About 2 minutes from the beginning of Satyajit Ray's Charulata, Madhabi hears the drum beat of monkey dance. She takes an opera glass and looks at it from the window. A minute later her husband passes by, absorbed in his newspaper, completely ignoring his young and beautiful wife, and quickly reaches the end of the corridor. Madhabi smiles and looks at him through her binocular. On one hand, it shows the jovial side of a young wife. On the other hand, it also describes the huge mental distance, not the physical distance, between the two characters and that's why a binocular is needed. This is the language of cinema at its best. These are what classical good movies are for. Camera placing, close ups and long shots, accompanied by proper music and dialog, creates a language of its own that can't be recreated in a book. SM, on the other hand, is merely a photographed theater. If enough props were used, you could recreate the whole thing in a theater hall without missing anything. That's why I can't call it a good movie. Finally, just from a logical standpoint, the incidences in the boy's life brings him closer to some of the questions but there is no explanation on how he got the precisely correct answer. One was about a Bhajan and the question was who wrote it. The beggar children were forced to sing the song but I don't think the word "Surdas" was ever mentioned. There is a cricket match, possibly a one-day match, on the TV that the characters watch, but I doubt if that match would ever talk about Jack Hobbs (played in 1920s) and how his record of 197 first class century still stands. Just holding a Colt revolver for a few minutes isn't going to impart the knowledge on you that Colt invented the revolver. The list goes on. The same problem exists in the book also, except the Surdas's Bhajan incident.  
But I should at least say that the original book, "Q & A", is , in my opinion, worse by far. The director significantly rewrote it and for good reasons.

I would occasionally turn to my friend after another foray into child abuse and whisper, "Is it EVER going to end?" Without giving anything away, there is a scene that involves spoons. During the interrogation, his personal journey is explored and all the painful flashbacks soon reveal that he'd risk it all for his lifeline. I'll also add that the soundtrack for this movie deserves high recognition since some tracks are celebratory of Indian culture and also incorporates other styles of music with energy, spirit and passion.

Hence: six out of ten.

A contender for movie of the year, that's for damn certain. Slumdog Millionaire is easily one of the most aurally arresting films I've seen in the past year. The intercutting between scenes of dialogue and music is amazing, regardless if it turns this movie into a music video of sorts. The characters are fairly engaging, as well, which just makes the entire package that much easier to enjoy. The story is a bit heavy on drama and some violence, bu considering the time period in which this film takes (around the late 1980's up until 2006), nothing is too surprising. Dev Patel gives a solid performance in the present time sequences, but his younger counterparts are all ample actors. Freida Pinto doesn't give enough screen time, but her character is strongly written. When she is finally able to speak, her role doesn't become a side story or some sniveling bitch like most movies of 2008 had with their female roles. The only major thing wrong with this movie is the ending. This being a love story, the ending is, of course, cliched as hell. What rectifies this is the credit sequence, which is utterly fascinating to watch. Still, with such a strong selection of songs and beautiful use of segues along with superb direction from Danny Boyle, this film is a winner. Check it out!

Como em todo filme muito alardeado e que é assistido um tempo considerável após o seu lançamento, "Slumdog Millionaire" me deixava bastante curioso, pois nunca consigo ter certeza se "confio" nas críticas que leio/ouço. Nesse caso em particular, a surpresa foi muito positiva, felizmente.

Após o hype inicial, criou-se uma onda de falar mal de "Slumdog". Ouvi que o filme era maniqueísta, romântico-abobado, que fazia da miséria alheia um espetáculo, que chupava a estética de "Cidade de Deus", que os diálogos eram risíveis, que era absurdo e inverossímil e por aí vai.

E, com honestidade, acho que a maior parte dessas críticas procede de uma certa forma. O problema delas - e talvez o maior problema de qualquer opinião sobre cinema - é justamente o extremismo.

A primeira coisa que ficou clara para mim desde o começo é que o filme é uma fábula. O fato de ter um lado realista, mostrando a pobreza indiana e o excesso de violência contra crianças não torna o filme menos "fabuloso". Ou será que esqueceram o elogiadíssimo "Labirinto do Fauno"?

Partindo dessa premissa, que, para mim, é óbvia e inegável, dá para encarar o filme na melhor forma possível: a saga de Jamal, um cara cujo destino é ficar ao lado de seu amor de infância e ter um final feliz, apesar de todas as adversidades que são colocadas em seu caminho. E, assim como em "Magnólia", o roteiro joga com essa dualidade destino/coincidência o tempo todo.

Ora, daí fica fácil compreender o misto de inocência e determinação que acompanha o protagonista na sua busca por seu grande amor. Nem mesmo os vacilos da sua namoradinha de infância - que tem o caráter mais dúbio que qualquer Capitu - conseguem tirar do espectador a torcida para que os dois terminem juntos.

A forma como a trama vai se desenvolvendo em flashbacks para explicar o sucesso de Jamal no programa que dá nome ao título em português, se não é inovadora - e quem é hoje em dia? -, funciona muito bem, dando o ritmo ágil que o roteiro precisa e que é corroborado pela estética "quente" e pela câmera ágil e modernosa.

Certamente não é o melhor filme entre as produções da última temporada (até porque, como se sabe, a Academia não gosta de premiar as melhores produções), mas certamente traz à Hollywood uma proposta inovadora em termos de fonte de referência e é, sem dúvidas, um filme muitíssimo bem acabado, que funciona perfeitamente do início ao fim.

Vale também destacar o excelente desempenho dos atores encarregados de retratar os protagonistas quando crianças.

A very good movie about a young man that goes on the Indian 'Who wants to be a Millionaire' to find his lost love. With one question left before he wins the jackpot he's arrested for cheating and recounts to the police how he knows the answers through experiences in his life. We have 3 actors therefore playing the same character from childhood up to current time. The first half of the movie is the best with the orphaned children living and working through the slums of Mumbai. The acting as well as the presentation here was fantastic. You really feel for the kids especially when they are taken to a camp for orphans that isn't what it seems. This continues into the more cheeky but brutal incarnations of their early to mid teenage years, then the final part becomes something very different.  The final half to third of the movie concerns Jamal's search and saving of his love since Chilhood, Malika. The movie here instead becomes less about living difficultly and turns into an emotional rollercoaster of a ride. Dev Patel is the worst actor out of the 3 Jamal's (still a great actor though) and if you have seen him act before you realise his british accent slips through occasionally. I was a little disappointed by the ending as well, but I won't give it away here. So a great movie with very few flaws in my opinion - it is subtitled slightly so be warned if you can't watch a movie with subtitles (I have no probs with it) but definitely a movie I'd highly recommend.

If there was any film I would without hesitation tell a friend to go see, that film would be ?Slumdog Millionaire?. Not only is it truly an original film, it has one of the most memorable sequence of scenes involving a young boy that has ever been captured on film. I won?t spoil this sequence of scenes, but I will say it involves this young boy named Jamal, an outdoor toilet, and movie star in a helicopter. Intrigued? The young stars of this film really do shine bright as do all who perform in this film.

The slums of Mumbai (formally known as Bombay) is the setting for this film a love story ?Slumdog Millionaire?. The pains and the sufferings in these crowded slums are the backdrop for the characters and their life choices. Hate, murder, religion, class warfare, squalor, prostitution, pedophilia, robbery go into the make up of this story, along with personal values and true love. 

A TV game show, Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? is the backbone of this film, written by Simon Beaufoy who?s credits include ?The Full Monty? and ?Miss Pettigrew Lives For A Day?. Jamal, nine, a street urchin from the Mumbai slums along with his brother Salim, eleven, form two thirds of the Three Musketeers and a young female urchin Latika, nine, becomes the third, after their parents are killed in an attack by Muslim haters; they are set unbound and are left to fend for themselves in a world trended by greed and abusers of children. The three, while setting up a new home life under a tent, rummaging through a garbage dump, are taken into an orphanage run by a Fagin (Oliver Twist) type character, who with far worse intentions than Fagin, intentions of such darkness it?s hard to grasp the ugliness of his and his cronies abuses on children. Their lives take another tumble here and Jamal is forever trying to bring the three back together to rekindle happier more memorable times, the way Scout, Jem, and Dill would lament their summers lost to autumn in To Kill A Mockingbird. 

We sit with Jamal in his contestants chair across from the emcee surrounded by a cheering audience on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, with an Indian accent, while he is being tortured by a corrupt police inspector wanting to know how he, Jamal, an illiterate Slumdog, would know the answers to difficult questions posed by the game shows producer. We watch his success in answering the questions one by one and we become more and more taken in to his plight to become a millionaire and we do this along with an Indian nation cheering each correct answer with smiles and well wishing. However his true intentions for being on the game show are revealed only at films end.

Through Jamal?s travails in growing up he has learned to read the people who would confront him with an uncanny ability to tell the truth while disarming his combatant. The games questions and Jamal?s answers are an allegory for his path toward love and peace and he must pass these tests one by one as presented, in order to arrive at his paradise.

This is a well told story, told by Director Danny Boyle who works with this cast brilliantly bringing out the absolute best in their performances? making ?Slumdog Millionaire? believable to a Western audience, all the while staying true to the Bollywood and Hindi style of film.

This film is a rollercoaster ride of stunning images, sounds and emotions. The uncompromising picture of the slums of Bombay/Mumbai may not be a conventional setting for a fairytale - but a fairytale it is. The idea of telling the story of how Jamal has accumulated the knowledge to answer questions on 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire', despite growing up in poverty and abuse  is a great one and says a lot about the nature of knowledge. The fact that he is assumed to have cheated because of his background is pretty ironic, seeing as it is specific events in that background that gave him the answers. This is an unexpected gem of a film and one that had a huge impact on me. I don't think the dance at the end was silly, I think it was a deliberate reference to the chasm between the view we have in the west of a romantic colourful, musical Bollywood and the actual reality of life for people like Jamaal - and a reminder that it is a fairytale with a happy ending. The film is a 15, but I think it should be put on the national curriculum and seen by all of the kids with comfortable lives who think it's cool to be 'ghetto' and who celebrate violence. There are many lessons to learn from the massacre that robs Jamaal and Salim of their mother and the desperate lives of the orphans who are trained to steal by men posing as their saviours, or worse taught to sing and then blinded. The relationship between the two brothers, torn apart by the need to survive and the sacrifice that Salim makes for his brother at the end was stunningly depicted.Despite these horrors, this isn't a depressing film. There is plenty of humour, particularly the lovely scene were a young Jamaal jumps into a toilet pit and ends up covered in sxxxt!! This film is the real deal and everyone should see it.

First off, congrats to Danny Boyle. He really showed what a versatile director he can be. His ability shines through here. Yes, we knew he had chops - unique shots, vivid storytelling, consistent vision, and his own style and flair - from his previous endeavors. But this film, in my view, really places him firmly in the upper echelon of talented directors for me.

Part of the film's charm comes from the virtually unknown cast (at least, to most of us Westerners), that provides a handful of fresh, and remarkably talented faces. The film's soundtrack also helps to create a unique atmosphere that helps sell an immersion effect.

As stories go, while the premise is incredibly simple, it provides great insight into modern day India, while telling the compelling tale of a poor teen on a quest for his true love. Thankfully, it doesn't succumb to any of the pitfalls of a typical Bollywood film, as I'm sure many might be apprehensive about upon seeing the preview. Part drama, part thriller, part romance, Boyle's talent for blending genres in unique settings shines through here.

Parts of the film, yes, are somewhat predictable, and one or two of the coincidences are a tad naive; perhaps that's why I didn't give it a higher rating. Neither of these facts detracted from my overall enjoyment of the film though, and I highly recommend it.

A sensationalistic movie in both the best and worst sense of the word.  The best in that it's never boring, always engaging, and lively.  While watching it, it's easy to be swept up in the melodramatic techniques.  

The worst in that it just never stops moving or telling you how you should be feeling.  With some distance the movie doesn't really hold up.  The direction is so relentless that it just moves from one violent scene to another rarely stopping to show anything beyond raw brutality.  For a movie that ultimately winds up being a love story I would have liked to feel as though the main couple had an actual connection that existed away from an editing room.  Instead the beautiful moments between them flicker by so fast (in lieu of yet another violent setpiece) that the big emotional finale ultimately feels artificial. 

The biggest plus is an incredible cast.  All of them bring tons of personality to their roles, especially the kids! 

 I'll have to see this one again in order to really get a handle on it.  I just wish it took some time to relax, breathe, and let the wonderful actors interact without the use of a musical montage.

This movie was above average.  It had an interesting story, the images were powerful enough to stick with you, and it showed things that you would be not likely to see in other widely distributed films.  But it was nothing more than that.  The narrative was gimmicky and generated an uneven pacing that undermined any drama that the film may have been able to create.  The cinematography was sufficient at best.  The acting was passable.  But at the end of the day you're left with a contrived and irrelevant story that Boyle turned into a cheap exploitation flick.  It's not even a rags to riches tale: it's not like the hero built himself up to anywhere, thus proving the "important" fact that people can do things with their lives.  He got lucky.  The film makes it perfectly clear that this kid doesn't know much more beyond the handful of questions that he was asked.  Those answers he knew because of some impossible collusion of events.  So the message of the film--if you tone down the schmaltz just a little bit--is that highly improbable things can happen.  Why not make a movie about a poor Indian kid who finds a briefcase full of cash? Looking back at his career, Boyle really is an exploitation director: Debauched druggies!! (Trainspotting) ZOMBIES!!! (28 Days Later) Poor colored people turning to violence to survive in an unsympathetic system!! (this film).  It's formulaic: take a story that has questionable, if any, merit, and pair it with some hot selling point. If you can direct it competently so that it isn't total trash you have a "classic."  It may make money, it may make people vomit, it may make people feel good, but it isn't cinema.  Cinema is an art form capable of broaching subject matter far less trivial than this blarney.  I hoped that the Academy felt this way as well.  Maybe Boyle should make an exploitation flick about the perverse minds of Academy voters.

Firstly I don't understand why people are calling  this a little movie that became big, is Danny Boyle a small time/ indie director??? Or just because the cast is unknown. Then where does that put 28 days later, Sunshine ?? Anyway, This is a good film, but over hyped. A story set in the slums of Mumbai, about two orphaned brothers who grow up on the streets. Like "City of God" (set in the slums of Rio De Janeiro), one of the boys is good (Jamal) and one is bad (Salim). Each brother watches out for each other as they grow up.The plot is brilliant, A slum kid rises above fate to win Kaun Banega Crorepati (Indian version of Millionaire) and the love of his life. He is helped by destiny, as each of the questions on the quiz show is linked to an event in his life. Technically the film is brilliant, its a Danny Boyle film after all. Ditto for the performances. But I wouldn't call this Boyle's best because of two major flaws, the script and the language barrier. Many people have compared this film to City of God because the film are actually similar in many ways. Yet City of God has something Slumdog Millionaire does not have which is depth and character motivations. Here are the glitches... 
- Salim despised Latika from the beginning. WHY? Had they bought that storyline later, where even he has a crush on her sounds more plausible, but as a kid?
-Salim character arc isn't quite explained.
- And then there is the stereotyped, half-baked, black and white characterization, almost bar none. For example, Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor ), the KBC host, is the typical villain who taunts the chai-wallah on his show; and the audience joins in with jeering laughter. Agreed, slum children get life's rawest deal, but not on live television. What is the director thinking ? It is also not explained just why Prem goes after Jamal with such malice, beyond a muttered 'It's my show'.
- The visually challenged have a way of identifying notes by touch, agreed, but how the hell does a blind street kid know of Benjamin Franklin. 
- Aren't such shows pre-recorded? Even if his arrest get all the media hype, so what, they decide to air it live on television for that evening? 
- A.R. Rahman's oscar nominated music?? seriously?? Paper Planes is'nt even his composition. The guy is a genius, yes, but if this deserves an oscar... then so does RDB, Jodha Akbar, Dil Se etc. which were far better scores. Trust me "Jai Ho" could have easily gone unnoticed in an average B grade flick.
- And finally, the language, either it should have been entirely in English, or to keep it stuck to "reality" just left to plain Hindi, ok you can ignore the transition from Hindi to English, when they pose as tour guides, but what is it with the flawless English. A few grammatical errors and mis pronunciations would have been easy to digest. Think about the scene where Jamal does puts up a Scottish accent? Stuff of Ranjikanth movies..

Anway, its a feel-good film...loved by many, nominated for Oscars and I could be wrong and know shit 'bout movies.

Indian Teen Jamal Malik, is one question away from becoming a millionaire..

Why?  

We really don't know.

Slumdog Millionaire is the type of movie that will have you on th edge of your seat, wondering what would happen next, how did they get to where they are?  This movie is fast paced, breathtaking and has a million cliche words I could use, but the fact remains, it's outstanding and worthy of the recognition bestowed upon it.

The movie is the story of Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), who is just ONE question away, from literally going from rags to riches on the Hindi version, of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire".  But there's no possible way, that this "slumdog" as he is called, could possibly know the answers to these questions.  I mean, doctors and lawyers don't get very far on the show?  So how did this poor kid?

We really get to see India's true gritty and downright nasty side in this film.  And it's as real and nasty as it can get.  We see, the story of this young man, who along with his older brother, who does look out for him, but also his knack for wanting to be a man, and making money, truly turns him into quite the unlikable figure. 

With there mother mudered at a young age, the only love that Jamal has ever really known is Latika, who is also orphaned.  We not only see the life through the years, but we also see how Jamal captures the knowledge that allowed him to be in the position he's in.  

The character of Jamal is a very likable, honest young man, who wants nothing more in life, to give love and be loved, something that has been missing his whole life.  Money is not the primary focus, but more the only girl he ever loved, and has ever loved him back.  

It's not a type of movie where we see Jamal trying to move on, or date other girls, but rather continue about his life, until he can find her again.  It's his drive to find her, that keeps him going in life.  

Director Danny Boyle's filming tactics are at an all time high, he gives us the brilliant suspense of the game show scenes, that are remeniscent of the high octane intensity of "City of God".  And also gives his lead character' the dimension and tragic heroism, much like he did in "Trainspotting".  

This movie just seems to give us something that is lacking in movie's today.  A story with interest, practically ZERO deadspots, with good acting from the three centeral characters at three different ages of there lives, and a wondeful quest for true love.

Some may often criticize that love can't be built on what was made during a childhood, but the connection between Jamal & Latika is made as kids, and it's just that type of connection they have, that lives on forever, no matter how long they've been apart.  I believe such a connection is possible to exist.  And that's one of the things about this movie, that will get you cheering.

It's not the feel good story of the year....but I felt good by the end of it.

This is one of the few Oscar movies I've seen that deserves the praise. Although best Actor is a bit much, considering the movie is more of an ensemble cast, the best director nods are hugely appropriate. Boyle does an absolutely magnificent job with the film, using camera cuts and angles brilliantly in order to accentuate Jamal's various situations. Although I am not familiar with the novel, the screenplay is fantastic: at the end, when Jamal kisses Latika's scar, the tenderness and symbolism of that moment (caught intelligently with a short expository scene) blew me away. I didn't like the answering of the initial question in the end, mainly because it represented a couple of other moments in the movie with the same problem: the meaning of the relevant scene/movie was spelled out in bold instead of simply lying there to be read by an emotionally receptive audience. However, seeing as how this is not some obscure artsy flick, this is only a small gripe. "Slumdog Millionaire" is an excellent epic.

Deep down, "Slumdog Millionaire" is your traditional rags-to-riches story that functions on the level of a fairy tale, but it's most definitely the film I would love to see walk away with the "Best Picture" Oscar because it does what all great films should do: leaves you with a feeling of pure exhilaration and an upbeat perspective on life in general long after its over. The character of Jamal Malik is probably the most likable, sympathetic protagonist you are likely to find in a film in 2008 and it's utterly impossible not to root for him. The portrayal of his early days in the slums are reminiscent of "City of God", but since the narrative is constantly cutting back and forth between the past and Jamal's present run on "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire", the darker material doesn't overshadow the basic feel-good nature of the story since you know Jamal will eventually find a way out of his predicament. The screenplay utilizes the flashback structure brilliantly by presenting a plausible explanation for each time this uneducated kid is able to answer a difficult question on the game show; the "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" scenes often have just as much tension and suspense as the thriller aspects of the story, making the conclusion and the build-up to it all the more special.

So I saw Slumbdog Millionaire yesterday at a cozy, quaint, conservative old-fashioned theatre in Orinda (i.e. the Orinda Theater) and enjoyed this movie very much.

The overall vibe of the movie is beautiful colors, fast blinking imagery, fresh, and with a lot of music.

The overall story is literally the description of the movie.  About a young, 18 year old Islamic Indian man named Jamal Malikwho grew up in the slums of Bombay/Mumbai the hard way but with two other orphaned kids who out of sheer luck has been put on the Indian Satellite show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire."

Because this kid from the slums made it up to the 10,000,000 rupee question, the bitter, undermining and slyly cynical TV Personality has the boy arrested on the suspicion of fraudulently getting the answers correctly.

The movie then becomes the police interrogation in terms of looking at each question that this young kid got correctly.

How could an Indian from the slums actually know who's face in on an American 100 bill????

The movie then rewinds to this young man's past to both introduce us to the harsh life he lived as a 'slumdog' and how "destiny" more or less provided him with the answer to those questions.

The movie is also of the romantic relationship between Malik and his love interest, played by the very beautiful Freida Pinto.

If Freida Pinto is nominated for best actress, she will only win it because of how beautiful she is.  Her dialogue in the majority of the movie is acting of a cliche "good Indian girl."  So as breathtaking as she is, she just a beautiful female as far as I'm concerned.  The music, lighting, and dreamy imagery of her is where the oscar she be redirected to.

This is definitely a feel good movie and I would be happy if this Oscar Nominated movie for best picture wins it all because it was eye candy from the beginning to the end.
