A glimpse into the 'other' real India, Boyle shows us a man-eat-man world of hardships and survival. However, the beauty of Slumdog Millionaire lies in the optimism of how those most unfortunate adapt to make the best of what they've got. The film streams with high energy from start to finish, while its back and forth editing to Jamal as child then back to adult gives it a slick and modern feel; this juxtaposes nicely with the backward conditions of Jamal's world. The soundtrack is equally energetic, brilliantly bringing the 'you'd-better-have-eyes-in-the-back-of-your-head' world even more to life. Sadly, however, the film loses some of its magic and honesty in the second half when Jamal wins the money AND gets the girl. This is too much like a fairy tale, as are the clichéd and one-dimensional villains, and, whereas one can understand Jamal's childhood obsession with Latika, it's a bit over the top to have them actually fall in love since, in reality, they barely know each other. Perhaps keeping a more open ending with a promise of 'who knows what's to come' would have better suited the more realistic nature of the film's first half. Still, this is a very well made movie and an exciting viewing experience. You truly care about young Jamal as you laugh, cry and sometimes cringe with him, all the while sitting at the edge of your seat.

[size=3][font=Calibri]If (or I should say when) [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]wins the Academy Award for Best Picture of 2008, it will mark the zenith of the Age of Obviousness in film storytelling. Weve been heading this way for a while now, what with the serviceable but overly somber [i]The Dark Knight [/i]being hailed for its supposed look at moral complexities this past summer. And cheap devices and character short-hands have been a part of cinema, and American cinema in particular, since the first guy with the bendy moustache tied a woman to a railroad track. But I cant remember the last time I saw a film that is being so widely hailed, and felt so depressed that modern audiences could be so duped by an effort this cynical and lazy. If it sounds elitist to be distancing myself from the mass response of this film, so be it...the line has to be drawn in the sand, and damned if Ill stand by and let [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]slip by as an enjoyable crowd-pleaser, or worse, be hailed as some sort of populist masterpiece, without asking: Is this really amongst the best that this medium has to offer? I mean...REALLY?[/font][/size]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]Taking shots at a film like this brings easy accusations of contrarianism, so before I delve into the film, a word about some of my own personal tastes. Unlike some film reviewers who work for alternative publications such as Reverse Shot, I very often surrender myself to a good old-fashioned crowd-pleaser, if I feel like the filmmakers are showing some wit and inventiveness in what they are doing. Two films that many smarter-than-thou critics have enjoyed dumping on in recent times are [i]Amelie [/i](a wonderfully inventive jaunty romp that was as fun to watch as it was shallow), and, going back further, [i]Forrest Gump[/i]. I mention [i]Gump [/i]because it is not entirely dissimilar from [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i], and many of the intelligentsia have made [i]Forrest Gump [/i]a poster-child for what they see as sentimental, anti-intelligent, conservative trends in crowd-pleasing movies. Well, critics be damned, I love [i]Forrest Gump[/i], and I think that its actually a far more subversive and beautifully-rounded comedy than its detractors give it credit for. Never once in [i]Gump [/i]does it feel as if the filmmakers are asking us to accept something inherently insulting to our intelligence or our heart. In [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i], meanwhile, they do nothing but.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]The overly-schematic setup of the film is this: Jamal (Dev Patel), a young man in his twenties who has lived a life of poverty, is now a supremely successful contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire. In fact, at the beginning of the film, he is one question away from winning twenty million rupees. Seeing that he is uneducated and poor, the police (at the behest of the shows host) decide that Jamal must be cheating, and so, in the first of a series of implausible scenes, they brutally torture him to discover how he knew all of the answers. The conceit of the story is that Jamal didnt learn the answers through anything conventional and boring like, say, reading or education (heaven forbid!). Rather, he simply happened to know them because these bits of trivia happened to coincide with, or be related to, particularly memorable moments in Jamals life.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]And so, in a series of flashbacks, Jamal recounts how he came to learn each particular answer, and we see the events that shaped his rather traumatic childhood and early life. The film began losing me quite early with a chase through the streets of Mumbai, which director Danny Boyle insisted on shooting in a blurry, off-kilter style that unfortunately permeates throughout the rest of the film. I dont have anything against shooting scenes in a less-than-conventional way (although truth be told, Boyles aesthetic has bothered me in previous films). The problem is that the style Boyle uses in this early chase scene continues, ad nauseum, throughout the rest of the film, until it becomes abundantly clear that this is Boyles only way of signifying energy.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]But it wasnt until the next sequence that [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]really began to turn my stomach. In it, a six year-old Jamal is trapped in a latrine at the very moment that his favourite movie star is arriving in town and handing out autographs. So what does Jamal do? He jumps into the toilet so that he can get out, covered in feces. When he triumphantly emerges and manages to get the movie stars autograph, its supposed to be a great moment of triumph, and I cant even begin to articulate just how mind-numbingly phony this scene, and the rest of the film that followed, felt to me. There are other scenes early in the film that are intended to squeeze laughs or isnt that cute? smiles of approval like the toilet scene, and instead I felt on the verge of vomiting at the artifice of it all. If this makes me sound like a curmudgeon, let me just say that I am always willing to surrender to a film, but if my bullshit detector starts flaring up, then I become less forgiving. [/size][/font]
 
 
 
[size=3][font=Calibri][i]Slumdog [/i]proceeds episodically at the same rhythm from one contrived setpiece to another. The through-line, if you will, is Jamals interest in and budding love for a girl named Latika, who he and his brother Salim save during an attack on Jamals village (glossed over, in typical fashion for the film, by the hilarious subtitled line Kill them! They are muslims!). While Salim demonstrates a penchant for bullying and cold-heartedness even as a child, Jamal is much more caring and compassionate, especially toward Latika. Unfortunately, the three children happen upon a man who has a herd of child beggars under his wing...and in a horrific scene, we see that the man is willing to cause harm to those children if he feels it will lead to them making more money.[/font][/size]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]But is that scene really horrific? In content, absolutely...but in execution, no. The truly terrible nature of the child-begging scenes, and other scenes of harm throughout the film, are offensively glossed-over and shot in the style of a Michael Bay or Marcus Nispel film. Not ten minutes after weve seen great and horrific harm come to an innocent child, M.I.A.s chart-topper Paper Planes is playing to a montage of Jamal and Salim riding atop a train, and I guess were supposed to go with the flow. But the use of M.I.A. is a tip-off to Boyles approach...every scene is merely a product, like a music video, that can be packaged together and scored to a techno-beat. Im not insisting that Boyle has to shoot the film as if he was Satyajit Ray, but some sense of [i]direction[/i] would have at least made [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]feel like less of a depressing mishmash.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]As the film drags on, it becomes more and more monotonous, as one trivia question after another provides the backdrop for scenes of phony clichés. Jamal grows up into a handsome if dorky young man, his brother Salim falls into a life of organized crime, and Latika grows into the beautiful Freida Pinto, but unfortunately her looks arent enough to keep her away from the clutches of a gangster kingpin. Like pawns on a chessboard, the characters keep staying true to their places in the story, and the film drags (to the point where I was really hoping the next question would be the 20-million one). With a series of coincidences that would shame Dickens, Jamal keeps falling into Latikas realm, constantly attempting to rescue her from the clutches of her evil boyfriend.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]Understand that in a fairytale like this, plausibility is not a concern of mine. Only the hardest of cynics would start nitpicking a story that is clearly meant to have some fantastic elements...itd be like whining that no one could ever have been around for as many historical milestones as Forrest Gump was. But the best fairytales have to have some human truth to them, or at least some scenes that keep us surprised or on edge, and [i]Slumdog[/i] has neither. No one in the film has any shades, the bad guys are evil from the first moment they arrive on screen, and then they demonstrate new ways in which they are evil (sample scene: Latikas gangster boyfriend shouts at her and demands she makes a sandwich, then shoos her away from in front of the television when she delivers said sandwich, before finally spitting it out and claiming that the sandwich is awful. Duh...I guess its supposed to show that he doesnt treat her very well, but its such a subtle scene, who knows). And the heroes of the film arent much to write home about either. Dev Patel has gotten some acclaim for his performance as Jamal, and although he seems charming enough, there are countless scenes in which he has a blank, stunned look on his face, so much so that the character emerges as something of a zombie. And what do we EVER learn about Latika, this wonderful girl that Jamal would cross heaven and Earth to rescue? Well, uhh, she looks pretty, and I guess thats enough. As for Salim, hes a bully from the get-go (and commits an act as a teenager thats pretty unforgiveable). His final scene is a laughably obvious, out-of-the-blue nonsensical gesture...one that I suppose is intended to show that Salim does have some good in him, but feels as hurried as any of the other character development in the movie.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]Defenders of the film have said that it tells a great story. But what is the point of that story, really? That we should just accept our suffering in life, because who knows, fate might have something in store for us, and all of the crap weve had to put up with might come back to benefit us in quiz show form? Or how about the storys view of love? That we should just blindly chase after a girl we liked when we were eight for fifteen years, and that girl should automatically love a man because he is constantly rescuing her (and, if you asked me, weirdly obsessed with her?) This may sound like Im a grinch who doesnt believe in true love...far from it, but when exactly does Latika fall in love with Jamal? When shes seven? Uhh...OK. The ending of the film left me feeling more bitter toward this cynical treatment of true love than any film Ive seen since [i]Pretty Woman[/i]. Like that film, the message of this one seems to be: true love can exist, provided you have millions of dollars to distance yourself from poverty. Jamal wins those millions through sheer coincidence (or, I guess you could argue, the goodness of his character being rewarded for keeping his mind sharp during all his years of suffering). The core value or message of [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i] is that he wins because it is written...in other words, who needs to bother to learn about the world when youre not going to succeed unless it is destiny. Its the same type of mindless surrender to belief that so many people blindly accept, and which polluted the equally reprehensible [i]The Polar Express[/i]. Apart from its complete devaluing of intelligence (as a side note, the final question is ridiculously easy...I knew it even before the multiple choices came up, and were supposed to believe this is the 20-million rupee question?), [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]accomplishes what the critics of [i]Forrest Gump[/i] mistakenly believed that film was doing: it says that whatever you happen to have lucked into learning is enough, you dont need to understand anything, just as long as you luck into questions that match up with your life experience.[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]Apart from all of the problems I have with the films storytelling style, I must confess a subjective dislike to its presentation as well. Danny Boyle is a filmmaker I have long resisted, from his (I feel) overrated [i]Trainspotting [/i]to the dreadful [i]The Beach [/i]to the at least watchable [i]28 Days Later[/i]. He directs a scene to the point of suffocation...there`s no space for us to think or discover for ourselves. The one exception that I have seen in Boyle`s career is the family-film [i]Millions[/i], a sublime example of a crowd-pleaser that works. In that film, the motion of the camera moved at the same speed as its eight year-old protagonist came up with ideas of how to make the world a better place. That film was, like [i]Slumdog Millionaire, [/i]somewhat one-dimensional and featured some stock bad guys, but it was genuinely heartwarming and charming, completely lacking the blatant artifice of [i]Slumdog[/i]. Some people mistake [i]Slumdog Millionaire[/i]`s A.D.D. style of filmmaking as wildly inventive and original. But really: what shots in the film are anything more than style for the sake of style? What shots are organically linked to the part of the story they`re trying to communicate? I can think of perhaps one (Jamal`s POV glimpse of Latika at a train station, in which she looks up at him and smiles, seems like the type of moment we remember about the people we love).[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]There`s one final element of [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]that gets under my skin, and this is the one that ventures the most into being overly politically-correct (something I usually avoid when watching films). Boyle, a British director, is presenting a story of third-world poverty and hardship that is overcome, and it has been lapped up by Western audiences. Nothing wrong with that, but my problem with the presentation of the hardships in [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]is that they`re all attributable to individual malice, and to me that seems like something of a copout for the developed world. So much easier to blame a child beggar being blinded on a creepy, perhaps pedophilic gangster than to delve into the realities of India that have led to the need for mass begging. In other words, [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]makes Jamal`s plight seem like an aberration, the result of a bunch of weirdos, bullies and evildoers, rather than a reality faced by hundreds of millions of people because of the economic imbalance of our world. But hey, who needs to think about all that when Jamal can rise from the ashes, win his millions, and get the girl, right? And just in case lingering thoughts of poverty and suffering were still giving us the old buzzkill, Boyle pulls out all the stops to ensure we leave with a smile on our face: he puts a Bollywood-style dance number over the end credits, featuring Jamal and Latika. I`m guessing most people are delighted by this condescending nod to Indian movies (Oh, isnt that cute...it`s ending just like an Indian movie would end! ), but somehow I doubt Steven Spielberg is kicking himself for rejecting the idea to end [i]Schindler`s List [/i]with a dance number from [i]Fiddler on the Roof[/i].[/size][/font]
 
 
 
[font=Calibri][size=3]By now it must be pretty clear that I hated this film...not just felt it was kinda overrated (as many an Oscar favourite have been), or not anything too special, or even a flawed film with some moments that I could see winning people over. No, I hated it, and frankly, unlike some other movies that I have personally disliked but could see being defended, the popularity of [i]Slumdog Millionaire [/i]genuinely baffles me, and as I mentioned before, leaves me more depressed about the state of modern movies than anything in recent memory. Films like this tend to get a free pass even by those who are underwhelmed by them, because theyre just out to tell a good story and make us feel better, so why should they be dumped on? Well, damn it, because in their little insinuations and the ways in which they shrink our perceptions about the world around us, movies like this (or [i]Pretty Woman, [/i]which I mentioned before) are far more damaging than the violent films like [i]Kill Bill[/i] that are often trotted out by moralists as examples of Hollywoods debauchery. The script is brilliantly crafted in every sense of the word, weaving a complex narrative that spans years and hundreds of miles to come together at one focal point, with brilliant dialog and incredible balance between heart and heartbreak.  It shows so many aspects of Indian culture both good and bad without being judgmental, allowing the story room to breath in its own reality.  While from a certain point of view the ending can be regarded as having a certain degree of cheesy cheer -- which might be ill-taken by some -- by that point in such a brilliantly executed story it actually makes sense and fits the style of the film.

There are certain brutal aspects of the film, which is typical of Danny Boyle.  But it is only a clear sign of his maturity as a filmmaker: he knows that there is no reality without pain and isn't afraid of showing it.  So, in that it is not a family film at all.  But, like other similarly developed films -- such as the Shawshank Redemption -- the sheer brutality of certain parts of the film only serve to illuminate the hope for a better tomorrow that is pervasive throughout the tale.  In that, Slumdog Millionaire easily ranks amongst the best intelligent, inspirational films of all time.  Whether you're a fan of film from the technical or simply the narrative side, it is undeniably a must-see.

Slumdog Millionaire is, to put it simply, a film of beautiful, brilliant storytelling. Although the casting is awesome, the acting superb, and the dialogue candid, I, for one, think that this movie's genius is in how the story was told.

A scene with a young Indian man being forcefully interrogated opens the movie, promptly pitting the audience into puzzlement and curiosity, before launching them into the past, present, further into the past, and back again. The story pace goes from heart-pounding fast to agonizingly (yet deliciously) slow to just right. We are taken on a cultural tour of India without looking like a promotion made by the Department of Tourism. (For the record: I really don't know if they had anything to do with the movie. I doubt it.)

It's taking a mystery story, a romantic epic, and a slice of life film, and taking a wire whisk and blending them together to a seamless treat.

(Yeah, I know. There I go again with food analogies.)

On watching it in the movie theater
I first watched this at home with my family a couple of months ago before getting to watch it on the big screen last night. What's fun about watching it on the big screen is hearing the collective reactions of the theater (laughs, gasps, and synchronized exclamations of "ewwyuck!"). What's fun, however, with watching it on a home TV is... well... The game show "Who Wants to Be a Milllionaire" is a major key in the story, and that game show is mostly watched at home instead of in the theaters. So if asked which screening I liked better, I think I'm going with the home version. This movie deserves a spot in your video library.

And, by the way. Buy the original DVD. It'll definitely be worth it.

On it getting the Oscar for Best Film
I love the movie. But -- and I know I'm going to step on many toes here, but I'm going to say this, anyway -- I still don't think it should have won Best Picture. So sue me. To each his own, yeah?

Everything about the plot and title of this movie sounds cheesy, but this is an absolutely fantastic, and incredibly enjoyable movie to watch.  It has all the key elements that an entertaining film should have.  Heart, action, drama, comedy, a love story, and because the story takes place in a culture so different than our own it's like watching a completely different world where we're unsettled by the stories being presented as the movie unfolds.  I was unfamiliar with pretty much the entire cast, but it really didn't make a difference.  You really get enveloped by the characters and how their stories intertwine as they go through their lives, and as stupid as the basic storyline sounds...the simple idea of a average person answering the question on a trivia game show based on the experiences he's had throughout his tumultuous life is brilliant in this movie.  Now in any other movie, it may come across somewhat cheesy, but Danny Boyle does a great job of putting so much heart, suffering and joy in the story it makes for an amazing movie. The fact that it's ultimately a love story is so thinly vailed for the majority of the movie, makes it that much sweeter at the conclusion of the movie.  I'm not surprised this movie is raking in the awards.  It really is a unique movie, which hollywood has desperately needed lately.  This movie deserves all the praise it's been given.

I went into this film with an expectation of disappointment. I didn't like the premise, I've never been a Danny Boyle fan - and I've never really bothered with Skins. So there seemed to be no appeal whatsoever. How wrong can one person be? This film is captivating, well paced and has all the hallmarks of a great film. The writing and camera work are what make this film a cut above; the screenplay is beautifully crafted with lashings of foreshadowing, backstory and clever drops and rises in pace and tension. Combine the excellent writing with the auteur camera work of a director like Danny Boyle and you have the film of the year. The film takes you to India and drops you kicking and screaming into the heart of the slums, makes you live what they live and experience life the way they do. The relatively unknown cast all put in a fine performance but none of them stand out above the others, this film is a true ensemble piece, written by a genius and headed by a directorial master on top form.

Here's an answer to the question on everyone's mind : nope, Slumdog Millionaire is not the best film of the year, not by a long shot. But why spoil the fun? This extremely well-made inclusion into another cultural universe is just what Teh Movies needed by 2008. Bring on those awards.

Boyle has proved himself to be an extremely versatile director by now. Needless to say, when one's directorial projects include Scottish junkie existentialism, apocalyptic undead terror, sweet childlike fantasies and poetic outer space missions in a 12-year span, it's hard to deny that plenty has been covered. And yet, Boyle enters a completely different terrain despite some similarity in themes, capturing the essence of a life lived mostly in as a Muslim Indian 'slum' in fragments-- it's not a terribly original way to picture one's self-made journey towards freedom, love and bloss, but it is nevertheless brilliantly rendered here.

The english director's camera has never been so vibrant. Near the beginning of the film, when a group of children are chased through Mumbai streets, a succession of tight closeups, large panoramics and handheld camera moments (set to a superb soundtrack) results in one of the most exciting scenes I've seen all year. And it doesn't stop here. Although it takes a bit of time before we get to see something as grand again (Jamal Malik's dark, disturbing childhood takes a large portion of the screentime), there are plenty of wondrous compositions that go well-over being beautiful for the sake of being beautiful. Cut in-between moments where Jamal is interrogated by policemen who suspect him of cheating on the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire, an abrupt kaleidoscope of his life up to now progressively installed. Those vignettes vary in interest and energy, but every one of them adds to the story in their own way. I've rarely seen narratives so exhausting in concept ultimately turn so breezy in execution.

Those 120 minutes pass like 90. I swear. For a film so labyrinthic, not once did I feel like asking who's sitting with me what the hell was going on, or worse, the urge to check my watch. It's sleek, effective, and tight all at once, without losing an ounce of its epic gorgeousness. Most of all, it treats a harsh lifetime in an upbeat and inspiring way without committing the sin of making slum life seem pretty and easy. Also, this is not an easy feat to achieve : substantially increasing the sentimentalism in the third act without having it come across as phony or made-for-the-masses.

While there are some facilities in the writing that can be easily forgiven, they are indeed what handicap Slumdog Millionaire from being the very richest film of the year. A bit too anecdotic and sometimes flat-out contrived, the twists and turns of the story beg for a certain suspension of disbelief. The characters are not too developped beyond their reactions to what's happening, but I can't picture a two-hour film like this one working with awfully complex minds either. Of course, it helps a whole lot that these minds are portrayed by immensely charismatic performers, children, teenagers and young adults alike, with the instantly likeable Dev Patel as a lead. He is a strong presence that ties all of the film's floating episodes together, and he more than convincingly inhabits the different personas of himself shown previously in the story.

Capped with an exhilarating on-credits finale (which I'd rather not spoil) that renders Bollywoodian cinema great justice, it does not surprise that Slumdog Millionaire has a great chance of leaving most viewers in near-ecstasy once it is over. And while once looked back on, the story feels a bit shaky and somewhat plagued by shortcuts, there's no denying that Danny Boyle's latest is powerful, dazzling entertainment that's, all in all, truly necessary today for showing the worldwide public a triumphant Indian culture.

[font=Comic Sans MS][color=red]One thing is for sure, Slumdog Millionaire is no doubt a good movie. Is it 'the' best movie of 2008? Well... not meaning to knock it down or anything but after seeing it (finally) I think that's a very legitimate and debatable topic. [/color][/font]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS][color=red]Slumdog is a very nice, sweet love story that has 'feel good' written all over it. It's amazing images of the slums of India will stick with you far after leaving the theater. The performances by 'most' of the young actors are quite good (some were average). Yes, the movie will make most feel great... mission accomplished there for me as well. I really really enjoyed this movie.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS][color=red]However, I must confess for a movie given so much hype, I found it to have a 'few' glaring issues. Some of Slumdog's story seemed much too contrived... pushing the limits of credibility and realism. The cops who interrogate Jamal... seemed a bit over the top. I know crooked police exist but come on... the kid is simply on a game show and doing well... so you tie him up, beat the snot out him and shock him with a car battery to boot??? Slumdog or not... I didn't completely buy that. [/color][/font]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS][color=red]Also, I didn't entirely buy into the sleazy game show host. What were his reasons for wanting Jamal to fail??? Jealousy, is sort of what were made to believe to be the reason... but that didn't seem overly clear, nor did it make complete sense, high ratings (meaning more Rupees) for the game show is what Jamal's story was producing... and making money is the goal of every TV show.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS][color=red]So my point is... essentially Jamal's success was the game show hosts success as well... but instead... the host, with the whole Nation of India rooting this kid on and [u]tuning in[/u] to watch, has him bagged, beaten up and sent off to the police for torture the day before he goes for the big prize?  Simply because there is 'no way' a slumdog should or could be that smart? Really? Hmmmmm... just another area of the story I felt was a bit 'forced' and unrealistic.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS][color=red]Look, I really liked Slumdog... there is [u]no doubt[/u] it will end up on my favorite flicks of 2008 list here soon. But, after hearing all the Oscar hype and reading some of the perfect '10' reviews... I was a little surprised to find a 'not so perfect' movie. A really good... maybe even borderline great movie... but 'best' of 2008? There are several movies 'not' nominated for Best Picture that were better than Slumdog in my opinion. Oh well... still good stuff, not a 10 for me... but still a must see![/color][/font]

Let's be honest, the plot of Slumdog Millionaire is so far-fetched it borders on fantasy, but Danny Boyle does such a good job of grounding the movie in reality with his wonderfully vivid location photography, it's difficult not to be swept away by it. Even now, I am reluctant to start picking holes in the film because it's left me with such a pleasant afterglow. The one weakness I will mention is predictability; if you're plotting a movie by numbers, don't be surprised if your audience beats you over the finish line. For example, it really doesn't take a genius to figure out what that final question on Who Wants To Be a Millionaire? is going to be; fortunately, the pleasing sense of fate being accomplished more than compensates. Funny, shocking, exciting and moving, it may fall some distance short of being a masterpiece but I won't mind at all if Slumdog wins a hatful of Oscars.

This story reminds me of a documentary i once watched about the slums in india but the documentary focused more on kids who were brought up in brothels.

I need to review Slumdog Millionaire, now. As an [url="http://www.vjkrishna.com"]Indian blogger[/url] who has seen the movie, I dont want to be the only one yet to review this movie. Weve heard all the arguments for and against the movie. Before I get to that, let me make one thing clear. Its one hell of a movie. Superb screenplay, lovely cinematography and top class music. I just loved it. I enjoyed this movie so much that Ive watched it three times. As a movie, it is truly an enjoyable movie. Its a feel-good movie some elements of masala in it. Unless you have very strong sentiments against the movie, it is quite difficult not to like this movie. The movie is doing good worldwide because the very strong sentiments are all from some of Indian viewers. In the eyes of the global audience, it is a very entertaining, wholesome movie experience.

 To say that this is a Westerners portrayal of India is the worst you can do to this film. That also shows complete lack of understanding for movie as an art form. This movie would not have been as interesting if the hero Jamal (cut the protagonist crap, its hero in the Indian movies) had not had the slum beginnings. And I must appreciate Danny Boyles portrayal of slums. He did not show the slums so we can pity them. The focus was always on the characters and never on the slum by itself. With the slums as the background, lasting feelings or images could easily have been sorrow, pain, despair etc. Whereas the overwhelming feeling of the film was fun, adventure and joy. This is not because Jamal wins the prize and the girl. The sense of adventure and joy was spread throughout the time scale of the life of Jamal and his brother Salim. The guys are shown to have fun, be very enterprising and take on the life. If this was the Westerners portrayal of India - that no matter where they are, theyre mighty spirited people who never give up - thank you Danny!

 Like it always happens with movies, the value of positive and negative publicity is almost the same. All the controversies have certainly made the movie a bit more popular. I still dont understand why Indian slums should not be shown in a movie. Its more shameful to have them than to show them. Over the last 60 years, the slums in Mumbai have grown to be the largest in Asia, one of the few Asian records that China did not pip India. Remember, slums have only grown. Thats a harsh reality. The India of outsourced processes, internet reach and mobile market is still not the real truth. The last couple of decades of urban prosperity has not done much to our literacy rate and the poverty line. Thats the truth. Why get so defensive about it, especially when the movie is not at all about the negatives. Isnt it strange that politicians have not come out against the depiction of Indian slums in this movie? They wont because they had/have a responsibility to eradicate slums and theyre not doing much about it. If we had shown the energy that we show against such movie directors and pub-going women towards the politicians, we would have less reasons to complain. Tired of seeing people barking up the wrong tree.

 When Lagaan made it to the Oscars, I dont remember anyone making so much noise. In my eyes, Lagaan was more shameful because it showed the Indian bunch as some illiterate bodies in an obscure village, who acted stupid, silly and emotional. None of the villagers were keen about putting up a fight except one man who leads them to an unbelievable charge against the well-mannered, smart, disciplined English. Some of the villager characters existed in the movie just for comedic elements. All they did were stupid, funny things that youd not expect normal human beings to do. The movie completely undermined the Indians so that the hero can be a hero while youre having fun watching the movie. Lagaan was made for the Indian audience and when it made to the Oscars, it was so unfortunate that the whole world got to see how we projected our illiterate silly Indians against the learned British. SM has not done more damage to the image of India than Lagaan did. Isnt it hypocrisy of the highest order that Slumdog is being pilloried while Lagaan was not? If the same SM was directed by some RGV or Mani Ratnam, wed have gone bonkers. The pseudo-nationalists always need some reason to knock down anything thats not Indian.

 SM is not the perfect movie. It has its faults. It has its perceived plot holes and all that. Actually I dont mind that. The movie Life is beautiful was not the perfect movie, in terms of factual accuracy and hole-free plot. But no movie has ever moved me than Life is beautiful did. In just about 15 or 20 minutes into the movie SM, youd realise that looking for perfection would only spoil your movie experience. If you look at this movie very critically, I pity you because you missed the fun. Superb casting, great acting by the younger actors, Rahmans music, most lively camera work, smart direction, mementoesque screenplay with a bollywood-like ending. Its got it all.

 My favourite part of the movie is this. Jamal is on the final question for 2 crore rupees. He doesnt know the answer and he has the last life line that is phone-a-friend. He calls his brothers number and he is pleasantly surprised that Latika (Jamals love) picks up the call. Thats the first time he gets to speak to her after many months of forced separation. Upon the show hosts insistence, he asks the final question to Latika. She thinks hard but she doesnt appear to know the answer. Show host says just 15 seconds more for the call. Jamal, instead of asking if she knows the answer, asks her where are you and she replies Im safe. For me, that sums up the movie. You should watch to appreciate this fully.

 In another couple of weeks wed have known if SM gets the Oscars. I dont think that Oscars are the paramount, supreme awards that are given out in the film industry. Some of my favourite films which have been the best of that year, never went on to win the Oscar thereby substantiating my belief. Oscars are an American award given to American films and some foreign language films, all from the American standards of film making plus their understanding of world culture. But what Oscars can give you unbelievable publicity, reach and acceptance. For that reason, it helps to win the Oscars. I dont quite think that the movie would win the award, despite the Warner Bros connection. I really really hope that Rahman wins it. He deserves this award. To get nominated twice in a category that has three nominations means hes the odds-on favourite to win it.

 As many have noted, SM was not Rahmans best ever. And thats not to undermine his music in SM, but just to show the high standards he has maintained all through his career, right from his debut. At least 20 to 30 times in his career, I have thought that this is it, this is his best. Yesterday, I was listening to his Newyork nagaram song which still blows me away. The mans a genius and he deserves global recognition and acclaim.  His O Saya . . in Slumdog Millionaire is a very unique score. My bet is that it would win the Oscars.

 All these international awards do have some subtle business angle to them. All those Indian girls won the Miss World, Miss Universe, Miss Asia-Oceania and all that not just because they were stunningly beautiful but also that western cosmetic industry had to tap the Indian market. And boy, didnt they do well! An Oscar for Slumdog Millionaire would start a long season of foreign investment in Indian movie industry. With a humble budget of $15m (most of the hollywood actors get more than that per film) Slumdog Millionaire has amassed $130m. In the current economic conditions which other investment would give as much?

 Slumdog Millionaire is the new entrant in my list of my favourite films (I plan to review each of them here, over a period of time). You can say all you want, the one thing SM accomplishes is to remind us the magic of cinema. Roman Polanski said Cinema should make you forget you are sitting in a theater. I know some porns will achieve that, but as far as I know thats the most crisp definition of a good cinema. Slumdog Millionaire does just that.

My son and I suffered the ignominy of having been stopped by the security guards at the Cinema theater entrance that was screening Slumdog Millionaire. The problem was that my son was under aged according to the guards, and the film was rated Adults Only. After pleading with the guard for a full five minutes pulling out the ace defense of Father knows best what is good for son, not the censor board, we were allowed inside the theater.  My son and I secretly admired our audacity in the dark shadows of the cinema hall. After getting ourselves some nachos and not-so-fresh salsa, we settled into our seats and got ready to watch the much hyped oscar contender - Slumdog Millionaire.

Much later, on our exit from the hall after watching the movie, we secretly thought to ourselves and confessed to each other later, that we wished the guard had not allowed us in after all. 

I really feel that this was a left handed delivery of a western accolade meant to thank India for exposing its underbelly in all its glory.  Hairy private parts and all.

However, I am not here to rant but to understand.  So understand we will.  

SDM has a few tested strong threads that make the western movie creation a huge success. Here is a movie with an accepted Operating System, to use a PC paradigm. Who wants to be a Millionaire and its equivalent of KBC are game formats that the east and west agree upon. We know the anchor, participants, the nervousness, the lifelines, the stupid errors and the mind boggling success stories of the game show.

While India knows all too well some of the rogue runaway applications such as slums, children forced to beg, religious riots, gang warfare, the west on the other hand needs occasional confirmation to the ingrained accepted truths regarding an under developed country.

Such rogue runaway applications are hidden and unknowable, unless exposed by the glare of a western light and camera to a western audience.

Moving gracefully but rapidly between a known Operating System and its many unknowable rogue applications, the western audience is being helped in taking a flying leap from the known to the unknown and back, including a vicarious slow motion dip in a cesspool. The karmic rights of dipping in the Ganges to absolve us of our sins are definitely not real and oh soo yesterday.  The dip in the cesspool is the order of the day here in the Real India.

It happens to us everyday and we dont bat an eyelid before we take the plunge into the Real India. We are sometimes forced to bat an eyelid or two to stop getting shit in our eyes. But then again we were not the intended audience, were we? We were the intended characters, remember?

About twenty years ago, while I was roaming the western world, I happened to read a daily newspaper in a city called Milwaukee in Wisconsin USA. The Milwaukee Sentinel had dispatched a brave journalist to report happenings from India. There was no Iraq or Afganistan war or even the 9/11 attacks to write about or worry the safe American citizens back then.  It got to be boring reporting just a cyclical economic downturn. The brave journalist wrote about elephants and tigers that might leap out at you from the roadsides. He even wrote about a snake charmer climbing up a rope and vanishing into thin air. The small Indian student community was outraged at the false reporting of New India and I philosophized, much to myself, that such journalistic forays were meant to keep the western audience convinced that they live in a *known* world. Nothing has changed my western friends, said the journalist. The snakes, elephants and tigers are still roaming the streets of India.  You already know what I am confirming to you from out here.  Dont waste your breath with a trip.  Read the newspaper.

The western audience has come a long way and will not be fooled so easily by that. It will no longer fall for the Indian rope trick anymore. But hell, the dark secrets, the real truths are still there lurking in the slums of India irrespective of the glossy portrayal by Thomas Friedman of how Infosys has caught up to the ways of the hyper start-ups in the Silicon Valley.  The world may be flat Thomas, but sure as hell butt-ugly in spots.  Like the proverbial doubting Thomas poking his finger into a wound to ascertain the real resurrected master, a slow-mo dip in the slum to convince us that the underbelly is real and out there.

The western reaction to this movie is obvious.  Tell me the truth, show me the slums, and convince me that I live in a better world!  Give me a contrast, tell me life isnt so bad in the land of plenty.

Thanks Dave for the movie. Seems to me that an Oscar will be a token appreciation to a punchered step-knee tyre of a Bolywood steam-roller. Is there nobody to stand up and notice the Emperors clothes?  Maybe his bizarre underbelly, with hairy privates and all is leaving us dumb founded? 

Always remember, characters in a movie are not supposed to wash up and transform into sanitized audiences of a movie. I wish the security guards really barred you from doing that.

Now take a plunge, will ya?

Thrilling rags-to-riches story of Jamal (Dev Patel), a kid growing up in the slums of Mumbai with his older, more aggresive brother Salim (Madhur Mittal) and friend Latika (Freida Pinto), who Jamal loves. The film opens with Jamal on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, about to win 20 million rupees. Suspected of cheating, he is tortured and we hear his story: as children, they survive Muslim riots (where their mother is killed), child slavery, living on the streets. Jamal and Salim get separated from Latika; Jamal vows to find her. As they grow into their teens, Jamal becomes a tea server for a call centre, while Salim becomes a hood for a mob boss (Mahesh Manjrekar), who also has Latika under control. He will find her by appearing on the game show. Director Danny Boyle doesn't let up -- every shot is crammed with detail (the slums are very realistic), colour, sound and music, and though it has the happiest of endings, it is never predictable. Completely implausible, sure, but that's part of its charm -- the film truly sweeps you up in the energy of this "slumdog" and his "destiny." In this film, India is a chaotic whirlwind, where the most popular show is a Western game show, where high rises grow out of slums, where chance and fate decide your future. Technically dazzling in every department. Sure to win the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director this year. A feel-good film in the best sense of the word.

A: Good Plot
B: Brilliant cast

Instead, with sincere storyline, it is no doubt that even a simply done movie will be able to attract the attention of movie-goers worldwide.

The three main actors manage to give three dimensional portrayal of their characters, especially, the young but talented actor playing the youngest Jamal, captivating the audience with his endearing performance.

'Elk hoofdstuk in zijn verhaal is een wonderbaarlijke sleutel naar het antwoord op elk van de vragen'; een zin uit het plot en Boyle heeft dit tot in perfectie uitgewerkt. Het grootste deel van de film graven we in het verleden van Jamal, die precies laat zien hoe hij op een wonderbaarlijke manier aan al zijn antwoorden komt. Maar natuurlijk gaat het allemaal maar om Ã©Ã©n ding: zijn grote liefde Latika. Alle drie hoofdpersonages worden per verschillende tijdspanne vertolkt door een andere acteur en actrice.  Alle drie doen ze het prachtig. Het is gewoon hartverwarmend om te zien hoe de kleine kinderen je beetpakken en je niet meer los laten. Daarnaast is de chemie tussen Latika en Jamal in alle tijdsperioden geweldig, maar is het einde er Ã©Ã©n om nooit te vergeten.

Het camerawerk is in elke scÃ©ne subliem en de beelden die we te zien krijgen zijn een lust voor het oog. Daarnaast weten de drie kleintjes met de nodige, erg leuke humor hun avonturen een extra impuls te geven. Bij dit alles gooit Boyle er nog een festijn van prachtige kleuren op, die een eindresultaat leveren waar je mond regelmatig van open valt.

I still don't get the "Feelgood Film" thing - make your own mind up there - but I didn't think it was exactly "feelgood". You can only compare the 2 films. Slumdog Millionaire is my third favorite theatrical experience (behind Star Wars V: The Empire Strikes Back [from when I was 6] and Juno). There are about three huge parts of this movie that make it truly great.
One: the scope of India. I have never been to India, but after seeing this film, I want to go there. They make the country seem beautiful and, at the same time, brutal. Of course, just about any movie can seem brutal if you portray it in the right light. But the filmmakers completely took the look of India and made full advantage of it. It's beautiful, compelling scenery (backed by great camerawork). Even the slums are depicted with their own sense of beauty, though it's more of a horrifying beauty.
Two: the screenplay, which is just about as brilliant as any screenplay can get. The lines are written splendidly, but the story is constructed with an aesthetic grace that's so undeniably wonderful, it's impossible to bash. The screenplay and the story completely suck you in. You watch Jamal, Salim, and Latika fight their way out of the slums and the audience can't help but wonder if, were they in their shoes, they would be able to keep the will to keep going.
Three: the cheer. My God, does this movie get one hell of a cheer out of me. Just to watch all the people gathered around to root for Jamal in the end really brings up my mood. And yet, what you would think would get the biggest cheer from this movie isn't what does get the biggest cheer. It's the passion, the love story. One of my favorite movie passions is Slumdog Millionaire. It's one of those movies that you love every minute of the hero chase after his love.
Uplifting, beautiful, poignant, brutal, passionate, thrilling, aesthetic, brilliant, and profound, Slumdog Millionaire every bit deserves its award for Best Motion Picture.

Boy howdy, this wasn't just an awesome movie, it was an incredible feat. It's been some time where I walked away from a film marveling at not necessarily a performance or a scene, but how well constructed it all was and my hat is off to Danny Boyle for one of the best directing jobs I think I've ever seen. This movie is like a perfect stew or a well-assembled machine in the way it takes so many disparate moving parts and matches them up into a final product that just takes your breath away. I haven't seen much praise for any of the individual actors, but that's not because they're not good, it's because they give stellar but unselfish turns and allow themselves to be as much a part of the process as the music or the scenery, but without overwhelming it. The framing sequence and the use of flashbacks is so well thought-out and expertly managed by Boyle and his crew as well as the writers that my eyes never wandered from this remarkably compelling story being told to me both on an intimate human level and a larger scope of a people's plight. The drama, the comedy, the family story, the love story and the cerebral "how did it all work" aspects mesh perfectly. The child actors are phenomenal--among the best I've ever seen. The use of music to complement action sequences and create a mood is not something I usually take note of, but it's impossible not to here, as the score and song choice is top notch. The panoramic view of Mumbai takes your breath away. I have a great deal of difficulty putting my finger on the exact things that makes this movie so standout, but I know I walked away impressed beyond belief, and there's not much higher praise I can give than that. This truly felt like something special.

This critically acclaimed Hindi film which has won the hearts of millions is truly amazing to behold even though I must admit that I had some reservations prior to its viewing as I was somewhat jaundiced towards Hindi films in general. To say that I was completely floored and utterly impressed would be an understatement. It is quite simply put, brilliant. Although it is easy to dismiss it as a typical rags-to-riches love fable, and some may find certain elements of the tale a tad far-fetched, the plot is nevertheless sweet and affecting, depicting a love that transcends time and defies all odds. The story is set against a vibrant and exotic Mumbai backdrop, picturesque in its kaleidoscopic and iridescent glory, yet within it festers a nest of corruption, shady dealings and seedy establishments. Dev Patel gives a deft portrayal of the plucky and precocious protagonist, earnest and fierce in his quest to reach out to the love of his life by becoming a contestant of the household favourite gameshow. Freida Pinto is honest and vulnerable as the damsel in distress, trapped by circumstances of her ill fate. The characterisation is richly textured and layered, with the flesh-and-blood characters coming to life under the capable hands of director Danny Boyle. Apart from that, the superb cinematography sets off the flourish and mystique of Mumbai, capturing the splendor and resplendence of Taj Mahal as easily as it focuses on the unsavoury sights of the slums. This is a pulsatively moving and emotionally resonant melodrama that will sweep you off your feet, delivering the timeless message that love conquers all with sincerity and a touch of Bollywood.

My reservations have nothing to do with the style or direction, but more to do with the cookie-cutter story that is told.  I am not a fan of movies that deal with poverty in such a cavalier way, implying that destiny is a series of choices and events that lead to happy endings.  The love story was a little insulting as well.  There is no "Graduate" moment at the end of this movie.  I realize that it isn't the same movie and that Slumdog Millionaire is a fairy tale of sorts, but the resolution doesn't seem to be well earned--including the brother's redemption.  This makes it sound like I despised the movie, but that isn't the case.  I just found it a bit underwhelming.  It is the perfect Oscar-bait movie that appeals to an audience that likes to pat themselves on the back for rewarding a movie that is a bit exotic, a little bit arty and deals with big issues in a black and white way, but is ultimately safe and sanitized.

I've been on a roll recently with my trips to the cinema - First off I was lucky enough to catch The Wrestler and followed that masterpiece by watching Brad Pitt get younger and younger as Benjamin Button - but good luck has never come in threes for me and neither have good films.

Once again that proved to be the case. This wasn't a good film, it was astonishing, fantastic, pure dynamite.

Three storylines intertwine from the start of the film - we have flashbacks to the main character's past, his current situation and footage of his appearance on the Indian version of 'Who Wants To Be a Millionaire'. An ambitious plotline it may seem, but one which draws the viewer in so deep that you feel like you're part of the action at times.

I have to admit that I like the bad guys usually, I root for them to win. I'm not sure if that's because deep down we all like a baddie and maybe I'm just more in touch with that then most or if I'm just a horrible person at my core, but whatever it is I always feel more drawn to the villain(s) of the piece. Despite that I found my heart beating, hoping that it would all turn out well for the trio of main players in the story.

I would recommend that anyone go to watch this - the acting of the young children in the initial flashback scenes is world class and the efforts of everyone thereafter are also outstanding. Beautifully directed, funny enough in places to make you laugh out loud, but touching when it needs to be without becoming sugar coated, this is a must see film.

The acting from the children to the adults superb. The movie reminds me of another foreign slums to riches film from Brazil called City of God. But the weight of that film overshadows this one because of the crux of simple unrequited love, as ancient as it is to plot, it is the only note that defies plausibility here. And as with any love story, you are asked to overlook that in real life people move on after their hearts broken rather than return to the scene of the crime repeatedly. I haven't seen Milk yet, it's next on the list, but I have hard time believing any thing can touch this film for the best of 2008 but sometimes there is something hidden out there, a Gone Baby Gone, like there was in 2007 that escapes everyone's radar. Doubt it could top this though.

4 Golden Globes, 5 BAFTA awards and 50 other wins from various film festivals and academies around the world. Slumdog Millionaire is one of THE shows of the moment. But is it worthy of its 10 Oscar nominations?

1) Nominated: Best Sound Editing 
2) Nominated: Best Sound Mixing 

The above the technical categories; though Slumdog boosts a lively soundtrack, in general in the sound department, it was good, but not great. Barely justified nomination, unlikely for the win.

3), 4) Nominated: Best Original Song 

Two nominations for the songs in this show. Slumdog was infused with a dash of Bollywood style in its music choice, and many of the songs were very lively and catchy. But none was particularly left a deep impression. Were the twin nominations a case of novelty strikes? At most only one nomination was justified. Somehow I do not see a winner in this.

5) Nominated: Best Original Score 

As mentioned, a very lively score with fitted the entire presentation of the show very very nicely. A potential Oscar winner in this category, the score brought out the flavour of the show without turning it into a Bollywood production.

6) Nominated: Best Film Editing 

The success of a film depends largely on its editing. That is why for a long time, nominations for Best Picture have typically been following by nominations in film editing. The editing in Slumdog is sharp, concise and that is the very reason why the show is actually able to keep viewers glued for its full 2 hour running time. Definitely a contender for the win.

7) Nominated: Best Cinematography

All the scenes as part of the staged 'Who wants to be a millionaire" should be discounted, since it film pretty much similarly to the actual gameshow. The rest of the film, especially the front portion filmed in the slums, is simply stunning. From aerial shots of the slums, distance shots of the destruction after a racial riot and over the shoulder shots of a chase in the alleys, much of the film was close to perfect. Another stronger contender for the Oscar.

8) Nominated: Best Adapted Screenplay

Adapted from the novel Q&A, the plot is its entirely is not believable enough; however the screenplay and story telling was nicely interleaved between the present and the past. The story was kept smooth without confusing the audience excessively. A win is seriously largely deserving here.

9) Nominated: Best Director

Cinematography of a film is largely due to the vision of the director. I thought the cinematography was fantastic. That speaks a lot. A strong contender for the win.

10) Nominated: Best Picture

Overall, the film was a masterpiece in story telling. It helped that the premise revolved around the slums of Mumbai, a truely touching and engaging tale of survival, love and courage. Slumdog Millionaire might just miss out on this Oscar, but I really do hope it wins the big prize.

So here it is - the most critically acclaimed film of the year. Golden Globes and Baftas abound; Danny Boyle being hailed as a directorial genius; The actors not being able to believe their luck at being shot to stardom overnight; Cultural commentators propounding the bravery and honesty of the film to show the devastating reality of the conditions in the world's fastest emerging nation.
So does it stand up to the hype?
Strangely the journey of Slumdog Millionaire is much like that of it's protagonist, Jamal Malik. Shot on a low budget and with very little media interest, it almost disappeared into obscurity from very humble beginnings. Only after an extensive tour on the Festival circuit, and a large drive to find backing, did the film finally find a distributor willing to put it out to the masses. Thus, Slumdog was saved by the hands of fate and fortune, pulling on its own merits and experience to lift it from the mire of Hollywood hell, as others became interested in its story.
So, eventually, we get to follow Jamal as he attempts to win 20 million rupees and get his girl back. The frankly lazy set-up of using a game show to illicit our backstory takes us into the youth of modern India and allows for a rigid structure to the exposition - and soon we are caught up in the slums of Mumbai, running away from the bad guys, and unwittingly running towards our destiny.
As a Cinderella story, Slumdog hits all of the right notes. We feel for Jamal as he loses his family and finds himself betrayed by all those he trusts. However, this is not where the strength of the film lies. What really adds gravity and import to the story is the backdrop of the Mumbai slums. We get a short social history - including some riots, and then have to deal with the shocking reality of conditions for the lost generations of India's street urchins. Understandably the Indian tourist board have spoken out against the images in the film, as it does not paint a very pretty picture - but integrity and accuracy are preserved as we are consistently bombarded with the harrowing details of life for these children.
Slumdog does not really benefit form its 'Millionaire' status, feeling as it does like an amateur plot development tool. However, this status does add an investment of tension with which most audiences will already be familiar. The story too is not very original in its basic premise. We have seen the rags to riches story many times before; the battle against hardship and the struggle against all the odds to fulfil our own destiny. It's hard not to be critical of these elements. 
What saves Slumdog though, is it's heart. Danny Boyle and his co-directors have done an outstanding job in localising this story, whilst at the same time expanding on the themes which make it so completely universal. The acting talent too is phenomenal, mostly from the  Bollywood veterans, and they play an integral role in bringing this story to the audience. As you would expect though, the real stars are the locations themselves. Imbued with such history and importance - filled with heartache and hope - with devastation and beauty; they provide not only the context of the film, but mirror perfectly the feelings of the characters, as well as drawing a complete picture of what we are trying to understand about Indian society through Jamal and Latika's adventures.
What has been created here is a brilliant representation of the emerging society of the new world. It takes a very personal story and applies it to the world context, allowing everyone to become involved through its amazingly real scenarios. This is a story of hope, of tragedy, of crime and corruption, of love and friendship. It calls to everyone in some way to believe in the determinism of the human spirit and as such traverses many barriers to bring the world closer together. Slumdog teaches us what it is to be a part of an international community where we all feel similar things and share common moral beliefs - no matter where we were brought up. The influences on Slumdog are so global and the themes so universal that it brings the Cinderella story right up to date. It does so beautifully and with such belief that it becomes very hard to ignore. 
Forget the story, but believe in the characters. Immerse yourself in a new world and become part of a different community. Find out how the human sprit prevails over all difficulties - and discover yourself through the story of another. Slumdog can do all of that for you, if you let it. This is a true modern classic.

[color=white][font=Verdana]Though toted as Oscar worthy, [i][font=Verdana]Slumdog Millionaire[/font][/i] is yet again another overrated film from [/font][font=Verdana]Hollywood[/font][font=Verdana], falling in lines with Benjamin Button.  Though both films are solid and enjoyable, critics are vastly overrating their quality.  [i][font=Verdana]Slumdog Millionaire [/font][/i]follows the lives of underdog Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), who has grown up in the slums of [/font][font=Verdana]India[/font][font=Verdana].  The movie takes place just after Jamal has been a contestant on [i][font=Verdana]Who Wants to be a Millionaire? [/font][/i]and we learn about his past as he is tortured by police (who suspect him of cheating).[/font][/color]

[font=Verdana][color=white]The storyline is excellent, and the answers that Jamal gives on the program are cleverly tied to his past experiences.  However, the characters are painfully cliché and are either too boring or too unlikable for the audience to really care about them.  The main female character, played by Freida Pinto, is disappointingly shallow, having no real character of her own, and Jamal's brother Salim (Madhur Mittal), though more complex that the rest, is ultimately too nasty for us to care.  All the actors, both children and adults, are incredibly good, and make such hollow characters almost lifelike, but overall it is unconvincing.[/color][/font]

[font=Verdana][color=white]The beautiful cinematography is one of the films strongest points, but it is offset by the overbearing soundtrack with blasts away at the most inappropriate of moments (and did anyone else find a slow motion love run to the theme song of [i][font=Verdana]Who Wants to be a Millionaire?[/font][/i] a little off-putting?).  All in all, it's a solid film, but not the film critics are saying it is.[/color][/font]

People who love Slumdog Millionaire love it because it is fabulously well made, has a complex, intelligent construction (so you think its an arthouse film) and of course, a happy ending. I watched it happily and enjoyed it for these reasons.
 
Yet it also troubled me for a number of quite important flaws. Firstly, the plot was contrived and ridiculous. Too much suspension of disbelief was required of the viewer to accept that Jamal knew all of the answers because of his Slumdog upbringing. It was fate, as the character said througout. The last lines of the film were 'it is written.' This level of coincidence makes the storytelling primitive, not sophisticated. Wrapping it in sophistication does not make it sophisticated, but childish.
 
The characters are Dickensian grotesques. We have the saintly Jamal (I cannot tell a lie), his nearly completely evil brother, the Fagin character, the beautiful, flawless girl, the two faced TV host (best actor by far in this) and the corrupt cops who eventually buy Jamal's tale.
 
It is in the wit of the filmcraft that it manages to cloak the childishness and the creakiness of the story. The script has a sharpness to match the editing. But that is both the good and bad of it - Slumdog Millionaire is 'Reality Fantasy'. The reality is the setting and detail, the pace and the horror of Indian poverty, the fanatasy is everything else.
 
Great fun to watch, but upon reflection, totally unbelievable.

As a British born Indian, I wanted to see Boyle take on his version of a bollywood film with a good mix of his direction, all the charm that most of Indian films have. Result, a good directorial effort with an Indian version of City of God; far less brutal and replaces that sardonic hardship from City of God to the hopeful dreams of a young boy from the slums, very much a style common in Indian films today. 

I've been to India before and seen what this film shows. It doesn't make it less dreary by sugar coating; that's not Boyle's style, he will show what is there and this film depicts India's culture, beauty, depression, poverty, lustre, greed, vengeance, corruption and all the moralities. You might be mistaken into thinking I'm being patriotic but the fact is Boyle has made a very good film, with keeping the actual Indian viewers of this film in mind. He has given it a love story like most Indian films while providing the action and tension that so many Indian-film lovers sitting on corner streets in Mumbai and Delhi will want to see. 

I've lived in West London all my life and this is as close to showing India any European film has done in the last 20 years, that includes Bend it like Beckham, etc. 

West-Londoner-born, like myself, Dev Patel made his dÃ©but on SKINS, and excellent UK drama series involving the life of College/Sixformer teens. A good choice since learning an language and accent is easier, but also a familiar face to those who watch Skins. The main focus is on him becoming more than he is, a subtle underdog story that doesn't boast of its pious superiority. He just wants to find the girl, Latika, he met when he was a boy, save her from poverty, prostitution and give her a life she deserves. Along with that, Dev's character known as Jamal Malik has a older brother Salim Malik who cares for money and the high-life, anyway he can get it. It's the Romulus and Remus tale with loads of morality. There are 3 actors per character of Jamal, Salim & Latika, each depicting the 3 main characters at different ages who are excellently cast, cute and innocent from the younger ages; to the older actors who play them as time and chance have made them into what they are now, with their knowledge of the world changing their day-to-day perceptions. Dev's character gets the chance to play on "Who wants to be a Millionaire" in India (Indian Version) with familiar host and legendary Indian actor Anil Kapoor. What could a slum-dog know of the world, more than most. He's graduating from the university of life. 

Contrasting, political, brutal, and bitter-sweet. 8.5/10.

A film that went completely under Hollywood's radar, and has justifiably won almost everything in the award season. Slumdog Millionaire is a vibrant, gritty, dynamic and dark fairytale of an Indian orphan from the gutter who wins Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?. Whilst being interrogated by police, tipped off by the show's makers for suspicion of cheating, Salim tells of how he knew the answers which in turn tells his life story of survival, along with his elder brother, and the love of his life, Talika. This three way relationship is the heart of the movie; the tug of war between love and power, interspursed with the excitement of the gameshow.

From the very beginning, where Salim goes through great torture by police (why didn't the cheating Major and his coughing accomplice get that treatment?), to the great Bollywood ending, this movie brims with energy and gusto, and everyone in this fim, from Danny Boyle's superb direction, AR Rahman's thumping soundtrack, and a excellent ensemble cast, makes this one of the best feel good movies of recent times.

The major reason for this is that is doesn't shy away from the harsh, horrific way of life these children suffer; a couple of scenes are just heart breaking, especially where Salim meets a blind beggar he knew from a fake kindergarten. These scenes together with the love story heightens the colourful, if predictable ending. 

Where the major feel good movie of last year was fake, cringing and downright populist (Mamma Mia), this is the perfect antedote. A fantasic, emotional rollercoaster that deserves every praise it gets. Best film I've seen for quite a while.

Sadly, until just a few days ago, I had never seen [b]Pretty in Pink[/b]. But I caught up with it and loved it. Written by John Hughes ("Just Visiting") it features many of his 80s teen trademarks: Molly Ringwald ("Not Another Teen Movie"), the clash between rich and poor, and lots of angst. John Cryer ("Two and Half Men") does an excellent lip sync. This movie really is awesome.

From director Danny Boyle ("Sunshine"), [b]Slumdog Millionaire[/b] tells the story of a poor boy from Mumbai  who is accused of cheating on India's version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." As the police interrogate him, the film flashes back through his life to show the reasons he knows the answers to the questions. A love story hides amongst the tragedy and a lively soundtrack really makes the film pop. Definitely check this out.

Unfortunately named though it may be, [b]The Dark[/b] is really a tense little horror/thriller. Maria Bello ("The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor") brings her daughter, Sarah, to Wales to visit husband Sean Bean ("Far North"). On the creepy seaside, Sarah appears to drown, but while her parents search for her, another girl appears claiming to have returned from the dead to take Sarah's place. Very creepy and atmospheric, but not frightening. I got quite caught up in it.

Another 80's classic with which I finally caught up, [b]Working Girl[/b] puts Melanie Griffith ("Have Mercy") in the dog-eat-dog corporate world as a secretary determined to rise to the top. When her bitchy boss, a nice turn by Sigourney Weaver ("The Tale of Despereaux") steals her idea, Griffith fights back by pretending to have her boss' job. Then she falls for Harrison Ford ("Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull") and then things go awry. Sometimes funny, sometimes frustrating, but ultimately inspiring, this is a really good watch.

Most fairy tales have predictable plotlines, characters who are a little too good and a little too bad, brighter-than-life colors, bigger-than-life moments. Most fairy tales do not have religious persecution and murder, torture, sexual slavery and brutal poverty. That the worst of India's social ills are not only a part of the story, but the very setting of the story is impressive. That Danny Boyle managed to make one of the most uplifting movies I've ever seen out of it is astounding. Slumdog Millionaire is one of the most visually beautiful films I've seen, filled with color and motion. Its story is told in movement and image as much as it is in dialogue. It's not flawless, and it's faults can be (and have been) pointed out: the story is predictable, some of the characters are one-dimensional, etc. But these elements are not necessarily bad, and I smiled all the way through it. It's not literal, nor is it meant to represent reality. It's a fairy tale, told in large, loud, bold strokes. And as such, it's wonderful.

Not quite sure why this received so much hype but having finally watched it I can safely say it's completely overrated. Which is not to say it's a bad film, I just think that a film like City of God for example, of the same genre,  which is vastly superior, received half of the hype this one received and it's somewhat unfair. Visually Slumdog is great and the original idea is engaging but essentially, like Titanic or Shakespeare in Love, this is an average chick flick masquerading as something more meaningful. I just found that there was a lot of convenient plotpoints to buy in this film. First Jamal gets on the show, which is already near impossible, then he passes the first round (which we never see), and then every single question conveniently calls back to a specific thing which happened to him in the slums, then, to top it off, he claims to have gone on the show just because he knew the girl would be watching...Riiiiight. That's a lot to buy. Of course, the big explanation is that "it's destiny", "it's written", which is hardly original or relevant. The film's structure is also pretty repetitive: you get a a question, you get a flashback, you get another question, you get another flashback...And even though Dev Patel gives a fine performance, the Oscar nominations are mind-blowing. Overall, Slumdog Millionaire feels like a very good TV movie but ultimately it's overrated and is really not worth thinking too much about.

Danny Boyle soft-shoes it with Slumdog Millionaire, a strangely sentimental sleeper hit set deep in the ghettoes of Mumbai, and ends up with a contender for best movie of the year. Facially, the movie is about Jamal, a poverty-stricken young man who is chosen to be a contestant on India's version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire." As the story unfolds, we are introduced to several interlocking sub-layers. First, Jamal is accused of cheating when some of the game show producers think that an uneducated guttersnipe couldn't possibly be answering the questions correctly. Law officials question Jamal, which in turn leads to long vignettes of Jamal's childhood; some of these vignettes explain Jamal's unexpected knowledge, while others lead to more questions about Jamal's motives for wanting to be on the show in the first place.
 
The cast of Slumdog Millionaire is uniformly excellent, as is the direction, the cinematography, the script, and the soundtrack (which I'm going to buy, even though I already own some of it.) Like India itself, Boyle's film is a unique mixture of east meets west. We are presented with the familiarity of disposable television, and at the same time eastern influences yank the rug out from under us. Jamal is answering questions about cricket and Hinduism, not baseball and Christianity. Beneath the playful chitchat of the emcee rears the head of India's elitist caste system. Behind the spectacle of something as inocuous as a game show hides a level of poverty we cannot begin to fathom, a subculture whose roots we can't see, a religious war we don't try to appreciate. Still, the characters struggle with issues familiar to all of us...brute force, enduring love, and the desire to find happiness.
 
Despite Slumdog's seedy underbelly, its message is positive and hopeful, and it marks a trend; Boyle's early days of Shallow Grave and Trainspotting have morphed into something mellower, something less biting, something more universally palatable. In short, Boyle has gone commercial, and I would hazard to guess that most would consider the new Danny Boyle to be a step in the right direction.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is a breath of fresh air in a stagnated world of tired remakes, lame sequels and unoriginal films altogether. It is directed by Danny Boyle, director of the cult classics "Trainspotting" and "28 Days Later". He has always brought a distinct sense of style to his films, and "Slumdog" is no exception. Set in the heart of Mumbai, India, this film centers around the teenager Jamal Malik (played by Dev Patel). From a young age, he uses his wits and intelligence to survive amidst the poverty and crime in his neighbourhood. Through his adventures, he meets Latika, a girl whom he has fallen deeply in love with. Fate separates the two, and leads Jamal to become a contestant in a Hindi version of "Who wants to be a Millionaire?" where he hopes that not only he'll win, but he'll find Latika again. This powerful drama is beautifully shot, with strong performances, great music and an exciting "rags-to-riches" story. This is Danny Boyle's "magnum opus", a film that will stand the test of time. A must-see for film lovers, a masterpiece of modern cinema and well-deserving the Best Picture Oscar nod, I highly recommend "Slumdog Millionaire".

BTW stick around for the end credits. There's a musical number to the Oscar-nominated Filmi song "Jai Ho" (which is a brilliant homage to Indian musicals). Equally recommended!
