If you've seen Danny Boyle's finest film - Trainspotting, then you won't be surprised by the remarkable energy Slumdog has. This film bullets along with youthful energy that is seductive. In fact, I would argue that Boyle makes movies that are inherently aimed for younger audiences. This is clear when you realize that there isn't anything remotely profound about this silly fairy tale. Sure, it has a startling first half that doesn't shy away from the hardships and poverty of the slums of India. The children are engrossing to watch and the editing and score are first-rate. However, the film begins to fall apart with its contrived second half. The TV show is an awkward plot device and the love story is shallow and far-fetched. Why are they in love? In The Graduate, the young lovers are equally shallow but at least they symbolize rebellion against their parent's generation. What does Slumdog have to say? That Faith and Destiny are written and all we have to do is believe? The ending is atrocious. He gets the girl AND the money. Give me a break. Ultimately, this film is a shallow joy ride that tries to make subtitled movies hip, while preaching a fairy-tale conclusion. Take it for what it is, extremely well-made popcorn entertainment.

Without question the best part of this movie is the cinematography. There's an odd brightness to the vibrant colors in the shot against the more bland background, which really makes the actors stand out. India is shown in such a bitter sweet way, from the bitterness of the filthy slums to the vibrant shots of the Taj Mahal, the movie is a visual pleasure.
The plot isn't completely original but does take an interesting spin on the oldest of themes, whether our lives are driven by chance or by destiny. The only real problem for me came at the end. This fun story comes tumbling down in the last five minutes to become another generic love story, congratulations the boy gets the girl. There's nothing particularly wrong with the ending, it just doesn't meet the expectations of the rest of the film. Still, this is definitely one of my favorite movies of 2008 and should probably take the oscar for best film, though Milk is right on its heals.

When I read Vikas Swarup's novel 'Q & A' I thought it great fun - an uneducated poor young Indian who wins 'Who wants to be a Millionaire' (called Q and A in the fictional India-set version), who is suspected of cheating. A series of flashbacks of incidents from his life, explains how he knows these particular answers. I was hoping to enjoy seeing this story turned into a film.
Boyle's movie was indeed about a poor Indian who wins this quiz, is suspected of cheating and whose life story is told in flashbacks. It's just not the same story, nor about the same person. The exquisitely named Ram Mohammed Thomas (unnamed orphan brought up by a Christian priest influenced by the local all-religions committee - the Sikh member was off sick) is replaced by the more pedestrianly named Jamal Malik and a good joke disappears. I missed the story I wanted to see.
But Danny Boyle directed Shallow Grave and Trainspotting, and the script was by Simon Beaufoy, who wrote The Full Monty. This, in other words, is a classy film,  so forget the book, this is the film (the reprinted novel is now called Slumdog Millionaire, after the movie).
There are some really outstanding scenes that assault the senses (not least the shit-dipped child collecting a celebrity autograph as bystanders reel away). There is also misery and appalling cruelty. There is also a totally misguided coincidental ending as the hero's brother dies, shot, at the moment of triumph - sorry, but no, this was pretty poor.
But, ok, a lovely film. And the hero and heroine did dance as a finale, with loads of extras AND in a railway station, Hurrah! Yes, I did wipe away a tear before standing up.

I was FINALLY able to see this movie that caused such a stir last year, and I have to say that I was almost as impressed as a lot of people that I talked to about it.  "Slumdog Millionaire" is not a really fresh idea, but that's just fine - what makes this movie great is that it is a simple story told in a very elegant way, and it makes you care about its characters like family.  Have I mentioned yet that that is the absolute best thing that a movie can do?
Dev Patel has an absolutely star-making performance in this movie - in a film that features scenes of great poverty and striking human torture - he somehow manages to remain the focus of this film, and is the glue that holds it together.  You obviously won't find any big name actors (at least not in the States) in "Slumdog Millionaire," but everybody really invests their souls in this movie - no mail-ins or Nicholas Cage jobs here.
Overall, I just really enjoyed the story of "Slumdog Millionaire" - it's a very old school film, a story about human love and courage.  We need more movies like this.

What a feast, what a feast! Shortly after the movie opens, the audience is introduced to the "real India" (as quoted in the film) by a chase through the slums in Mumbai. The sights are unsettling, yet familiar to me. In essence a love story, of which the protagonist Jamal found love in Latika, his childhood friend and his journey to be with her. The questions from "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire" framed Jamal's life from young, although I found it a bit too convenient for the questions to flow perfectly with the sequence of events in Jamal's life. But remember, this is a fairy tale set in reality - harsh reality. Many scenes can be revolting and yet, enrapturing - such is the skill of the Boyle's direction. The chase through the slums, toilet scene (as in another Boyle's "Trainspotting"), the young Arvind's scene (very depressing), the meeting of teenage Arvind and Jamal, the train scene, the last lifeline scene, the last scene. Musical score is flawless. This could be A.Rahman's ticket to Hollywood. This is my favourite piece from the movie, unfortunately I couldn't find the last scene from the movie featuring this song. Boyle even take a dig at Bollywood with the ubiquitous song-and-dance routine. Cast wide, the child actors really capture my hearts. You can't single out any bad guys in the film, even the police inspector or Salim, Jamal's brother. If there is any gripes, it would be that the dialogue is in English instead of Hindi, which is kind of weird. By the end of the film, the audience is led to the answer of the first question. The answer is D, and that's my final answer.

The movie arouse many eye-brows between Indian people and i tell you why;

1. Mumbai looks scary! I've been there certain times and no it's not like what they show. Yes, I get it they are Slums children, and I gotta agree by certain scenes (Like, Stealing foods, Beggars, etc). But I still hope that they would show how Mumbai is like in the present days!

2. The language, yes I know that this is an English movie but the transformation between the younger Jamal to the elder one is hard to believe. His English accent sound westernize, and that makes certain people criticize! I'm not saying that Indian people isn't fluent in English, Heck I think that we are more fluent then certain countries (Again, No pun intended!), but they are Slums. But, my perception is different, Have you seen Memoirs of Geisha? Japanese people talk fluent English, so why not Indians?!

3. The questions. I was laughing very hard when Jamal was asked who the heroic figure in the 1000 Rupees note is? And he said 'I don't know'. Stop! when you spend your childhood stealing people's money, you would know it, I'm certain.

Once you passed this debate you would see that Danny Boyle's Slumdog version is only meant to be a feel-good movie and fiction, and he did an awesome job!
Though some scenes makes me cringe (specially the last line), And the scene where the younger Jamal jump into the crap pile is exaggerated! I was offended somehow.

Dev Patel is a great young actor, he balances his thick-British accent to the max, and his emotional expression is surely believable. Freida Pinto, though not as stunning as Aishwarya Rai, she is cute and act well for a supporting role. Other cast did good, specially Irfan Khan (The Namesake, A Mighty Heart) was a treat!

Background music is superb, it's about time that people recognize how talented Mr. A.R Rahman is (Check out his other score in Bollywood movies; Lagaan, Dil - Se, etc)

Still it's a hit and miss movie, some people will love it and some not. This is not the best Bollywood / English movie in my opinion (i still prefer Moonsoon Wedding) but it is one of the best movie of 2008.

I told myself that I've got to watch this film before the Oscar ceremony on Sunday, so I did. I'm so glad that I did because this is by far the most fun movie experience I've had the past year. It's light, it's fun and it's everything a great film should be. 

"Slumdog Millionaire" tells the story of a Mumbai slum kid, Jamal, who manages to "luck" his way through the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire. As he was about to take his last question to win it all, he was caught for questioning on the attempt of cheating as to how a slum kid could know all these impossibly hard questions one after another. Then the film moves along with a wave of energy and exuberance with all the flashbacks as to how he managed to know each answers â mostly in a funny and delightfully "awww" and "ooohh" moments. And of course there's a wonderful love story behind it all as well.

"Slumdog Millionaire" is that underdog film that many have come to love including me and is poised to make a big impact come Oscar time and I can definitely see why. Where "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" lacked in sincerity, heart and emotional attachment, this film clearly has them all in abundance. You will end up rooting for Jamal, the unconventional hero in the film, just like many of those who watched the game-show and rooted for him for the ultimate win. With no star-powers, well maybe except for Dev Patel who is better known for his role in the UK television cult show, "Skins", the rest of the cast was relatively unknown, this film moves along with grace and poise. Danny Boyle's overdue Oscar recognition should come sooner and with this film, he's guaranteed a golden man. The shaky hand-held camera works capturing the essence of the slums in India is what this film is all about. Compared to the beautifully stunning cinematography is many of these year's films, "Slumdog Millionaire" is gritty yet lively and gripping at the same time. The musical score is blasting for everyone to pay attention to and the songs "O Saya" by M.I.A and the final dance-off song "Jai Ho" is so addictive, I'm still humming these tunes while writing this. 

A great film for all to see. If you dismiss this as another India Bollywood film, then you'll miss out one of the best films of the year. And this is not even a Bollywood film with majority of them are UK-based director, producers, actors and etc. So WATCH THIS or regret. And I don't usually give a 5-star rating that often, easily, freely and this willingly. =)

In reality, I could go on all day about the standard features of a film production that 'Slumdog' excels at, be it the excellent pacing, stunning direction from Danny Boyle, the awesome and versatile score courtesy of longtime Bollywood composer A. R. Rahman, or the solid performances from Dev Patel, Freida Pinto, and Madhur Mittal, none of which were out of this world, but together formed a brilliant cast through their chemistry. I could do all that, but I won't. Instead, I will focus on what I believe made this film work on so many levels --- as a drama, a love story, and an inspirational philosophical journey.

Much has been made about the love story central to 'Slumdog's story, but I would like to point out and give credit to the union of the two brothers in the script, played by Dev Patel and Madhur Mittal. While they are relatively simple underdog characters on the surface, as one of my peers pointed out, they also each represent a different philosophy on how to live one's life. The protagonist, Jamal (Patel), embodies idealism in the sense that he strives to live his life in a true and pure way. He has clear set of morals and a code of conduct that he assigns to everyone, not just those close to him. His older brother, Salim (Mittal), is a metaphor for pragmatism, or realism. Salim is a survivor. He makes his way through life with the lone goal of self-promotion, only occasionally pausing to help those close to him. Morals are a guideline rather than a rulebook for him.

Throughout the story, 'Slumdog's' script never clearly chooses which path or philosophy is the correct one. It hints that both are needed to successfully navigate through life, but beyond that, remains silent as far as philosophical preaching goes.

'Slumdog Millionaire' is primarily a Cinderella story infused with philosophical contemplation of moral values. This mix of love story, underdog-against-the-odds tale, and examination of philosophy is what makes the movie work. I freely admit that multiple aspects of 'Slumdog' are cliched and overused in Bollywood, Hollywood, and elsewhere in cinema. However, it is the combination, chemistry, and delivery of all these various elements that make 'Slumdog Millionaire' great. The mastermind behind all that is writer, Simon Beaufoy.

Another section which I briefly alluded to earlier, mostly for those who pay special attention to the technical details of films (more so than the writing or character building moments), is the editing and the direction of this picture. Critics will certainly attempt to bully SM on its believability, but there is no way in hell anyone can chastise SM when it comes to the way it was shot, and how those shots were put together in postproduction. First off, multiple scenes stand out for there slick, inventive cinematography, such as the opening slum chase scene, the night train escape scene, and the climax's gangster shootout. Editing stands out in particular with the way the questionnaire MCTs and flashbacks are interwoven and whenever a major music ensemble forms. I could really go on all day about these two facets of filmmaking with regard to SM, however, so I'll stop there. You get the picture.

Lastly, for those people (probably mostly die-hard Bollywood fans) who watch this movie and cry foul at the less than flattering depiction of India and/or the so-called imitation of Bollywood cinema for Western audiences, you really need to get your head out of your ass. The criticism of nations in cinema is nothing new, and it's not going away anytime soon. Condemning a movie solely on these grounds is usually insufficient, unless the holier-than-thou attitude is truly excessive. Anyway, with all the criticism of other large, powerful nations like the United States, Great Britain, China, and Russia so frequent in the motion picture industry, I'm not sure what the big deal is with 'Slumdog.' I will also argue that this film does not take a low-brow, manipulative mode of self-righteousness the way films like James Cameron's 'Avatar' and Kevin Costner's 'Dances with Wolves' do. The dense, beautiful, and sometimes dangerous streets of Mumbai are the setting for this underdog epic, not the focus.

And finally, those who are Bollywood veterans and look at 'Slumdog Millionaire,' saying, "What's the big deal?" I have two responses: First, read the first 6 paragraphs of this review. This movie clearly separates from Bollywood with its gritty style and veteran direction. It may walk and talk like a Bollywood hit, but it is of a different breed entirely. My second response is this: Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, my friends. 'Slumdog Millionaire's success can only do good for Hindi films, acting as a bridge between Western and South Asian film audiences. That's what happened to me, anyway.

So, this picture is not really Hollywood's and Danny Boyle's take on Bollywood, rather, it is an experimentation of a variety of storytelling devices that chooses its home in India. It is NOT a ripoff of Hindi films. It has virtually nothing in common with them. Because of the aforementioned reasons, I argue that this is one of the few Academy Award dominations that deserved every Oscar it received.

Very loosely based on Vikas Swarup's first novel. Jamal is an uneducated Indian teen, competes on India's Who Wants to be a Millionaire so he might find the love of his life. He somehow knows all the answers and runs into fate along the way.

There are two ways to make a film from a novel. Copy the novel exactly, or take an idea from it and make your own film. Slumdog definitely does the latter and it pays off. Its very different from the novel, but it holds its own, with what I thought to be better ideas.

 Destiny and love are dominant here. Poor Jamal goes through so much in his life finds love, but they can't be together, but eventually do so through a game show. Rather ridiculous, but it all works.

The shots with middle-class Indians huddling around TVs to watch one of their own make it big time was the most powerful sequence of the film. Perhaps thats the Indian dream, having the chance.

[size=5][b]Slumdog Millionaire[/b][/size]
Directed by: Danny Boyle 

[img]http://www.mannythemovieguy.com/images/slumdog_millionaire_new_picture.jpg[/img]

This year's runaway breakout psudo-indie psudo-foreign film is undoubtedly an interesting blend of tones and styles, as well as the traditional and the innovative.  Yet, is it a great film?  I'm not sure.  It's certainly a good film.  Anybody telling you otherwise is either a cynical asshole or a contrarian for it's own sake.   Yet I'm not certain how the film will hold up to repeat viewings.

Anyhow, the concept sounds silly, a young man who grew up in extreme poverty who somehow gets to be on India's "Who Wants To Be A Millionare" is aceing all the questions in spite of a total lack of a formal education.  The show's security staff is sure he is cheating and goes about beating the answer out of him.  In response, he tells them how he came to know each answer, and tells his life story.

It sounds absurd and even a little annoying.  And I suppose it is absurd, but  it isn't ever annoying and it's realistic in it's portrayal of poverty in India and the classes and groups that fight for power and influence.  It reminds me a lot of "City of God" in that respect.  

It's also got a very Rockyesque feel to it.  The Rocky theme has been beaten to death, and most people don't really remember what the original Rocky was about and what it did.  This film did that, but it didn't feel dirivitive, it felt a lot more fresh.

The film is very enjoyable, alternatingly hreartbreaking and joyful, the novice cast is great, Boyle's direction is inventive and well done.  Yet I'm just not quite sure how much weight this film will carry in subsequent years.  It's a good film, but is it a truly memorable one?  I'm not yet convinced.  I guess the years will tell.

This movie was an unpleasant watch for a variety of reasons. My biggest problem with the movie was the constant depiction of cruelty - especially to children. It is one thing to understand how some cultures and the impoverished are subject to harsh lives, it is also important to use cruelty as key story elements but it is another thing for a story to pile upon pile vivid cruelty to advance a thin plot line and bang us over the head to force us to feel for the characters. And feeling for the main character and really getting inside the latter part of the story was impeded by the very limited acting ability of Dev Patel. If a film is going to present a Shakespearean tragedy of this magnitude, the filmmakers must give the audience a gifted actor so we may get inside the story but we were held at arms length by Dev's scene after scene of long blank stares, long pauses and out of nowhere and totally delayed reactions to the other actors. An audience only experiences a film story if the audience feels and sees the main actor truly thinking and feeling in a scene; blank stares do not equal an actor truly feeling and thinking in a scene. Reference Michelle Williams work in INCENDIARY as her character suffers and suffers and suffers- and you will see what I mean. The love story doesn't evolve at all; early on in the film (fault of direction or acting) the teenage Cherry doesn't seem to even respond to Jamal and later on the adult version of the character seems ambivalent to Jamal then at the end all of the sudden she loves him/goes to the train station- just doesn't work. The plot device of taking each Millionaire question and going into flashback made the film wonky and unbelievable; the film should have presented the story in chronological order and show the game show allowing the audience to piece how Jamal knows each answer. This film couldn't commit to tone; early scenes depict a cute child doing something funny to get an autograph but then follows a brutal massacre and then more brutality. The children at the "orphange" play a funny prank then next thing you know we are shown one of the most heinus acts I've ever seen in a film. This flip flopping of tone is jarring and makes this film derail and uneasy/confused. Speaking of confused- this film was layer upon layer of tragedy and then at the end there's a freakin' dance number with the characters all smiling and dancing????!!!! WTF? If you can"t tell by now, I do not recommend this movie at all. There were even rumors that this film was based on a true story- which it is not. I keep hearing rumors it's based on a true story yet VARIETY cleared that up:

Screenwriter Simon Beaufoy ("The Full Monty") took considerable liberties with the original novel, which is based on an apocryphal story about a teen from the slums of Mumbai who wins 20 million rupees (roughly $400,000) on "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire."

Trying to find out the truth of the tale in India was near impossible, Boyle found. "There's a billion people racing ahead in a 10% growth economy," he says, "enough to start up a decent-size planet from scratch. Did a slum kid go on the show? There are lots of stories. Educated people went on pretending to be rickshaw drivers. If the story isn't true, it should be."

This film does not cast India in a good light- rather it makes it look irresponsible for its poor, its children and a great divide of classes. The place seems rife with thugs, lawlessness where a game show host can order literal electrical torture of a unproven guilty citizen/contestant. Filmmaking was also inconsistent with lots of grainy dark scenes switching to bright stark scenes with grainy closeups intercut. Furthermore, last time I checked, outsourcing is pretty unpopular- especially to many Americans whos jobs have been outsourced to Countries like India and so what- it shows how OUTSOURCING is helping to revitalize Mumbai and telephone operators are lying to the people calling in for tech support and it just adds another layer of yuk to this film. And the contrived simultaneous climax of Jamal winning and his brother dying a valiant death in sacrifice for Jamal in a TUB OF MONEY - c'mon. (shaking head). I'd hope people have a better standard of films and I'm very surprised people think this movie is any good.

"Slumdog Millionaire" fails to rise above its contrived screenplay; despite covering every hackneyed cliche known to man, it fails to illuminate the lives of poor lower-caste Indian citizens and endlessly panders to Western convention. No wonder it won a slew of Oscars from a smug, overly politlcally conscious Academy. It's nothing if not this year's "Crash" dressed in a sari, using a familiar game show as a transparent plot device and too high on its own self-righteous fumes to become aware of its own ridiculousness. 

Or maybe that's the point. After all, every drop of suspense is killed at the very beginning, as we're informed of the climax and given cutesy "multiple choices" as to the main character's moral grounding. Is he Lucky, a Cheater, a Genius, or Is It Written? Of course it's the last choice, but does that refer to Fate Itself or does it refer to the formulaic, cringe-inducing screenplay dictating the fates of its paper-thin characters? 

Of course, most of the story is in English, except for the origin story of Jamal and Rashim, his sociopathic asshole of a brother. That's in Hindi with minimal subtitles. There could have been a lot more room to develop the characters and establish the atmosphere that could only have been achieved by shooting on location. Instead, the plot hurtles forward at a pace that would give Paul Greengrass an epileptic seizure.  By the third foot chase, we're exhausted and we've accepted that there will be no room to breathe, as the screenplay jerks us between THREE seperate time lines. The editing muddles up the chronology even more with countless unnecessary flashbacks, flash forwards, choppy slow motion, even playing some scenes in reverse for extra aggravation. Brutal interrogation scenes from pig-headed cop caricatures mesh with Anil Kapoor leading young Dev Patel in the most protracted game of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" of all time. Kapoor is a respected thespian in his native land, but all he has to work with is his Evil Beard. 

Patel's epic romance with Frieda Pinto is meant to be some character defining journey, but the character inspires nothing but scorn as he chases this sex object like some lanky computer-guided missile. They share only three scenes and talk about nothing save for their unrequited love and the usual prattle about Destiny. The love interest only exists to be persecuted and helpless. On the other hand, there are FIVE foot chases and so many other desperate attempts at creating suspense out of this simplistic premise. Most insultingly, the climax hinges on the game show being televised via live feed, which would be logistically impossible given all the post-production work required on "WWTBAM?" 

There is some stunning location photography and individual shots that shine through, when Danny Boyle isn't shoving things in front of the camera or cutting between crazy Dutch angles to the frenetic beat of some tribal music. I must confess a weakness for MIA's "Paper Planes" even though it's used during yet another Growing Up Montage. The story can't even slow down enough to tell us how Jamal learns English, he just magically ages in a disorienting jump cut. Awkward stabs at Hindu religion can't stack up to the condescension of the screenplay (written by a Brit). 

One scene involves a typical thuggish cop beating up on defenseless Jamal. An affluent, white couple comforts the kid, who snarls and says "You want to see the real India? Here it is!". The ersatz mother figure looks defiant, says "Well, here's the real America!" and hands the kid a large sum of cash. That illustrates the condescension of "Slumdog" better than any number of gleaming golden statues. All oppressed Indians are just waiting for an American cash injection, hence the necessity of learning English and the value of staying out of the employ of gangsters. And how the hell did Jamal get past the rigorous screening process of "WWTBAM?" I guess any of the plot mechanations can be explained by the handy catchall: "It is written".

When I used to watch "Who wants to be a millionaire?" with Regis Philbin as the host, I always found it very intense. The farther the contestant got, the more risks he had to take because there was always one question that would stump the contestant and they never had an easy way out. Slumdog Millionaire is very similar to this. Obviously because the main character Jamal is a young contestant on the Indian version and has a chance of winning 20 million rupees. Yet Jamal isn't all that interested in winning loads of cash, he is interested in a girl named Latika, whom he loves. The film is skillfully told, balancing the current storyline with vibrant and occasionally brutal flashbacks. The children who play the younger versions of Jamal, Latika and Salim are all truly delightful to watch. They are expected to do a lot. They act, sing and in some cases, dance. The rest of the cast is also fantastic as well. Their performances will keep you on the edge of your seat when you watch Jamal answer one question after the other. An intriguing note about this masterful film is it's final dance sequence to the award winning song: Jai Ho (which means may victory be yours). It is actually well choreographed and lots of fun to watch. I just watched this film win the Oscar for the best picture of the year last night and when you see this movie, you'll understand exactly why.

Okay, fine I admit it. This movie is awesome. It's very well directed (Boyle really surprised me, the only movie of his I was was The Beach and I didn't like it), and the storyline is original. Great idea to present Jamal's whole life as flashbacks he gets when it comes to answering the questions, it shows very effectively how much knowledge some one can get simply from living in the street. Having said that, I do not think it deserved the Oscar. At all. I think that in some ways, this movie is a cliche, and that all the fuzz was about the cute kids (they really were very cute) and Jamal's struggle in life. Yes, it did manage to tell a harsh story in quite an optimistic way, kudos for that, but it's still mostly a big drama about how awful life can be, specially in third world countries, and how mean people are. The apocalipsis will come when the Academy gives the Oscar to a magical, truly original and brilliant movie like Benjamin Button, which shows a different, more beautiful side of life. People say this movie reflects the reality of the world, but this is just as real as the beautiful side of it shown in movies like Big Fish, for example, which wasn't even nominated! I just wish the Academy realized Oscar worthy films can have happy endings and leave a special, magical feeling in the audience, a feeling I certainly didn't get when watching the last couple of Academy Award Winners.

Slumdog Millionaire is soap opera to the core, melodrama throughout, but a delight every bit of it, and grips the heart like epic poetry. 
In classic Dickensian tradition Slumdog tells the story of 3 children from the slums of Mumbai, all having lost what little they had in life to a senseless mob attack; one succumbing to human frailties, turning to a life of crime, finding redemption only in the end; two holding their ground against seemimgly overwhelming odds armed with nothing more than love for each other and an almost religious conviction.
Quite contrary to and beneath the superficial wretchedness, misery and cruelty, a thesis of hope runs through the movie-hope that life's sufferings and tribulations only serve to harden and prepare us, that they are but the darkness before sunrise, a precursor to a final triump. It is no coinceidence that every of Jamal's correct answers to the game's questions comes to him not from formal schooling, of which he has none, but from the experience of a traumatic episode of his life.
Danny Boyle takes an everyday slum tragic story, mixes it with his brand of quirky charm, infuses into it compassion and humanity, and conjures up a superb movie.

***written on 21 February 2009***

Sunday of Oscars means Friday of Oscar-nominated films coming finally to the theaters here in Mexico City certainly. Actually this last week has the first day of the FICCO (Festival Internacional de Cine Contemporaneo de la Ciudad de Mexico), certainly a chance to see very interesting films (The Wrestler, Maradona by Kusturica (which Im going to see this same night, for free, at the Zocalo for the first time on the big screen since I already saw it a couple of times on DVD), Waltz with Bashir, Bob Marley: Exodus 77, The Good, the Bad, the Weird are some of those that I dont want to miss), certainly Im glad it began and it began precisely with a film that the Academy nominated for Best Picture, it began with Milk. 

And I missed the chance to see Milk on the big screen before the big night (it will be released during the first days of March). Yesterday I had planned to see my first film of the FICCO yet Slumdog Millionaire came finally yesterday to Mexico City so is very very probable that tomorrow I will be watching the Oscars after seeing only two of the five pictures that are fighting for the big prize of the night (Benjamin Button being the other) yet after seeing what for most is going to be the winner of the night, certainly this one that was my fifth encounter with a Danny Boyle film and if not a perfect one sure it is a great film. 

Is a surprise to see a normal boy enduring a torture by some police men, certainly they want that the boy, who is our main character and who is played by Dev Patel, Tanay Chheda and Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, Jamal Malik talk but they will end saying something like hes a tough guy. So we go back to see that certainly Jamal during his childhood had no other chance but to fight for his life. This is absolutely my favourite part, when Ayush Mahesh Khedekar and Tanay Chheda are Jamal, the City of God. Realistic, we have who is apparently nothing but a hero, he sees street children and he comes with a tasty Coca-Cola for the heat, for them he must be good since he allow them to eat a little more, these are just children, many but certainly we known Jamal, Jamals elder brother Salim (played by Madhur Mitta, Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala and Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail) and Latika (played by Freida Pinto, Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar and Rubina Ali). 

Very early in the picture we see that of the two brothers one is more of a Zé Pequeno and the other is more of a Buscapé, and we see moments of happiness yet very tragic moments that become more tragic for the boys because they cant do anything, they are just there trying to get by day by day so when that mentioned hero comes their life has a little light, they dont have to worry for food, they have their minds in other stuff that is different from the stuff that is in the mind of the hero. So we now very well since the beginning both Jamal and Salim, we know that if it depend only on him Salim would have never return to Mumbai, after all they found something completely different, something more like the heaven of their heads, I guess seeing the Taj Mahal is more than impressive. 

But also we know that Jamals heart is only for one girl, this is a love story, a magical one, why Jamal was that tough? We have realistic answers, a realistic background, powerful part. Why Jamal knew all the answers when he was on the Indian TV show Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? if he never had a formal education, if he was just a slumdog? He certainly not cheated, for the police men was not too complicated to find that after Jamal talked about those moments of his past that came to his mind that night when he was on the TV show. Here the point, the most love moment: when Jamal, during the second night on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, is only one question away of the 20 million rupees he uses one of those lifelines, he doesnt know the answer, we know that when he says that on TV he is not lying, he marks the only telephone number he knows, his brothers, yet we know where is that cell phone, time to a dramatic little moment before he hear her voice, now the answer is not important, even if so she cant give it but he after all came to that show not for the money. So lets dance, why? it is writtenin the script.

Four months ago, it opened at the 35th Telluride Film Festival in Colorado.  It has since been on movie awards discussions all over the internet.  All of the hype allowed plenty of room for anticipation, and with it expectations, of the movie.

When I finally watched the movie, I knew the wait was well worth it.  This movie is high-powered entertainment that leaves no room for yawn.  Every scene is compelling, every material well-researched, every character charming.  You would expect no less from Danny Boyle, a director who never makes the same movie twice.

The movie is a testament to the filmmaker's scholarly knowledge of lighting and camera angles. It also showcases his powerful vision of the entirety of his story, choosing to display chronology of events in a narrative manner, and freezing dramatic moments at precise length and perfect timing. All of these combine to create a movie about the slums of India that is visually captivating and cinematically engaging.

It takes talent to capture beauty where beauty is everywhere.  But to depict beauty where ugliness resides, that's something else.

First of all, I'm sceptical about Slumdog Millionaire winning a full 8 Oscars. Seems slightly overrated. Fine if they won maybe one or two, but 8? At the end of the day, there really isn't anything all that special about it. It's a feel-good fairytale romance involving a "rag to riches tale". It was fun in parts, sad in others, and was certainly action-packed, but I have to admit, overall, it's a rehashed, outmoded Dickensian narrative that just happens to be set in Bombay. I swear, you could set that tale in London, America, Germany, France, Switzerland even, and no one will think twice about it. But soon as India's involved there seems to be this over-romanticised exotic appeal that completely glosses over any real issues. I know for one thing that the film originally struggled to gain any distribution rights. They nearly put it straight to DVD because they couldn't get it shown in theatres. Suddenly, Fox Searchlight Pictures (a multi-million $ corporation - one of the highest grossing entertainment conglomerates in the world!) decides to acquire it - hmmm, I wonder why? Well, considering the fact that India is fast becoming one of the world's richest economies (predicted to become 2nd only to China by mid-century) I don't think that Fox was thinking "Wow, this is one of the best films ever!" - more likely, "Wow, imagine how much money we can make by cashing in on the Bollywood scene!" 

Now, I'm not suggesting that companies are somehow "evil" because they're making profit, although lets not speculate too much on where the money earnt for that film will be going...to real people in the real slums? Don't bet on it. Hollywood isn't about social-realism or raising the consciousness of the masses now is it? Indeed, Bollywood can't be expected to care either - but as long as it draws crowds and makes heaps loads of money, who's going to think any different? Sorry, it gets me worked up, because there's so many geniuses out there working their ass off for their art, who get passed off as "a bunch of pretentious pricks". I bet there are tons of fantastic Indian filmmakers creating authentic pieces on their homeland that are completely unknown to most of the world. Yet, Danny Boyle sets foot in Bombay for the first time (or Mumbai as it is now known) and suddenly his film earns 8 Oscars? There's something fundamentally screwy about that.


What could have become a realistic representation of the many-faced India, excrementally failed, delivering at best, a half-attempt at a two-dimensional melodrama. Sure, it has an arresting attention to detail and stimulating cinematography, but its ?multicultural? posture (*cough* dare I say, colonial sucking-up) that this succeeds in capturing the paradoxical essence of Mumbai, is a bit much, considering that it only fulfils a nauseous and mediocre, formulaic love-story. Overall, the emotionally-charged social-realism it attests to becomes completely lost, drowned out by the naïve exuberance of a Bollywood R&B jingle. Ok, I'll calm down. I admit, the first time I watched it I thought it was fairly enjoyable. But I was still left feeling that romantic, gangster clichés and overdramatic farfetchedness distracted from its original potential. 

I sound like such a pompous old git!

Anyway, I'm sorry about my ranting. How are you?

This is a very good movie .  It's sort of an exercise in tragic serendipity, and is very, very violent from beginning to end.  I've talked to some Indian people about this and most say it's a fairly accurate portrayal of the life of the poor in India.  It's well-acted and well-scripted.  You really feel like cheering for the protagonist just because the guy is just so beaten down, both literally and figuratively, but never waivers from his focus in life.  You always get the sense that the situation is dire but never hopeless as the tragedies in his life align to facilitate the hope for happiness. He never loses himself or his faith in the future.  Is this the best movie of 2008?  No, but it's definitely top 5.  The big bollywood dance number is a nice touch for a movie that was for the most part very heavy.  If you don't like violence, you'll find this hard to sit through, but if you can stand it you'll be rewarded with a story of inescapable fate and unwavering love.

This would never have been my first choice for a movie, Poor people in slums I dont even like those bits on Comic Relief and usually the Oscar winning ones I fall asleep to, and I did shut my eyes a few times but not to go to sleep, I can admit when I am wrong its an amazing film, with comedic moments thrown in to break the tension, this was a sad story, sad because you see the way children are forced to grow up just because they were born in the wrong part of the world, you see the story through Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) who is on his way to winning the top prize on the Indian version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire", sadly for him he has been arrested and accused of cheating, he is tortured, beaten and even electricuted all to get him to confess how he cheated, because lets face it a boy from the slums knowing all the answers couldn't logically happen in their eyes, Jamal continues to claim he is innocent and as they go through the questions one by one, a story from his childhood, through to adult hood prove how he knew the answers.
The first answer in particular could have the strongest of stomachs gipping at what child Jamal does to meet his idol, after a cruel trick by his elder brother Salim locking him in a home made toilet cubicle, the other questions can be more harrowing as one leads to the death of his mother and others tell the story of Jamal befriending a girl called Latika after he allows her as a third musketeer to shelter from terrential rain when his brother says no, things seem to be looking up for them when a man arrives and gives them a drink, he then takes them to a camp where loads of other orphan children are and feeds them, he seems like a saint, he only asks them to sing for him to get a better life, only there is an underlining sinister plot that is very shocking, anyone who has child relatives or is a parent themselves will find a lot of this very disturbing, Salim has become boss of the kids in the camp but when it comes down to a choice of having his brothers eyes removed because blind kids earn more from begging, he soon shows where his loyalties lie and helps Jamal escape, along the way they lose Latika and Jamal makes it his mission to find her again, much to the annoyance of his brother.
They use ropes to climb on train tops to travel, people are not kind and they throw them off or hurt them if they are caught trying to get food, they often get slapped around by strangers for one reason or another and that was something else I found difficult to watch.
A very funny scene comes from the Taj Mahal where tourists are to take there shoes off before entering, Jamal and Salim soon find this very enterprising as they both get a nice pair of shoes themselves and sell the rest, at one time Jamal is mistaken for a tour guide and plays along for the money feeding the guilable tourists total rubbish.
The child actors really deserve Oscars of there own, they were very enjoyable to watch and portrayed the story amazingly. Then came the teen kids and as Jamal and Salim went back to find Latika the even seedier side of the slums were revealed as Latika was about to be sold to the highest bidder for prostitution, as Salim pulls out a gun and saves Latika he doesnt mind taking a few other lives in the process, showing that this is definately no longer an innocent child, salim becomes power crazy and eventually joins up with a gangster while leaving Jamal behind and taking Latika with him. Jamal is now on his own and working job after job, one where he is asked to recap the plot of Eastenders to the Indians who need to know the English for the call centre jobs they are given out there, its during the call centre job he applies for Millionaire and also manages to track down his brother Salim again leading to him once again finding Latika, she is now living with the gangster Salim works for and is obviously terrified for her life as his personal punch bag, a rescue attempt goes wrong and Salim steps in to take Latika back.
Also in the mix is the evil equivalent of Chris Tarrent, a game show host who is an absolute bastard, Jamal is bullied and laughed at on his show and he is the instigator, calling him Cha waller from the slums and telling him to take the money he has won and go, then calling him my friend whilst still plotting against him.
So as Jamal's story goes on Latika is missing as is Salim and his final hope is to be on the show as he knows she will be watching somewhere as he believes it is destiny for them to be together....Heartwrenching at times but a really good film.

This is certainly a good film and I enjoyed it, but I don't think it's quite worthy of the *huge* amount of hype it has now received. The fact that it has won 8 Oscars is just one of those freak happenings that occurs every now and then. Praise for the film just built up a head of steam that took it beyond what were arguably better films. I personally preferred Benjamin Button and would have given that the Best Picture Oscar. Danny Boyle is probably deserving of his Best Director Oscar because he has developed a style that is clearly recognisable as his own. Certain camera angles and quick shots along with the use of music to break up scenes and alter moods reminded me of several of his other films. Plenty of other directors use all of those devices but it's a unique skill for a director to put their own particular imprint on the processes, so for that he deserves some credit. And as his style benefits the breakneck speed of this particular story he was a great choice to helm the film. The story itself is a good idea well executed. Nice to see a movie not made in Hollywood and without a poor script. That doesn't necessarily translate into a great cinematographic experience however. It is more the surroundings of the plot, both physical and emotional, that are the true stars of this film. India (or more literally, Mumbai) is shown in both its impressive beauty and squallor. Danny Boyle takes the camera into the slums, not bollywood constructions, but the true thing, using slum children as two of the protagonists in their younger years. I could not help but wonder how their lives had changed from the experience, did those two slum kids turn out to be the real life Slumdog Millionaires? The film was engrossing up until the children turned to young adults when its grip lost me and it turned to melodrama. There is no other way the script could have gone really, as the unfolding of the story is predicted throughout the length of the film, it's just that I found it unsatisfying in terms of the characters and their relationships. Slumdog Millionaire is referred as the feel - good movie of 2008. But I wasn't feeling that good to see a small kid jumping into the crap hole just to see his favorite star at the beginning (No pun intended).

Slumdog is a good movie regardless, it shows the contrast of relationship (Salim and Jamal), love story (Jamal and Latika), and of course the haunting Mumbai city!

Danny Boyle love to mock certain culture and country, like what he did in Trainspotting (1996). He mocks the lifestyle of Scottish people yet at the end we still experience the 'feel - good' aura! (Love this guy!). In 2008 he did it again and now we see the exploitation of Indian people, mostly the central city, Mumbai.

The movie direction between the game show and Jamal's childhood flashback is quite enchanting. But it still left a silly plot hole.
You will feel the excitement and passion of Jamal's life story, the adventure he undergoes, the violent he witness and the love he finds is exhilarating.

The movie arouse many eye-brows between Indian people and i tell you why;

1. Mumbai looks scary! I've been there certain times and no it's not like what they show. Yes, I get it they are Slums children, and I gotta agree by certain scenes (Like, Stealing foods, Beggars, etc). But I still hope that they would show how Mumbai is like in the present days!

2. The language, yes I know that this is an English movie but the transformation between the younger Jamal to the elder one is hard to believe. His English accent sound westernize, and that makes certain people criticize! I'm not saying that Indian people isn't fluent in English, Heck I think that we are more fluent then certain countries (Again, No pun intended!), but they are Slums. But, my perception is different, Have you seen Memoirs of Geisha? Japanese people talk fluent English, so why not Indians?!

3. The questions. I was laughing very hard when Jamal was asked who the heroic figure in the 1000 Rupees note is? And he said 'I don't know'. Stop! when you spend your childhood stealing people's money, you would know it, I'm certain.

Once you passed this debate you would see that Danny Boyle's Slumdog version is only meant to be a feel-good movie and fiction, and he did an awesome job!
Though some scenes makes me cringe (specially the last line), And the scene where the younger Jamal jump into the crap pile is exaggerated! I was offended somehow.

Dev Patel is a great young actor, he balances his thick-British accent to the max, and his emotional expression is surely believable. Freida Pinto, though not as stunning as Aishwarya Rai, she is cute and act well for a supporting role. Other cast did good, specially Irfan Khan (The Namesake, A Mighty Heart) was a treat!

Background music is superb, it's about time that people recognize how talented Mr. A.R Rahman is (Check out his other score in Bollywood movies; Lagaan, Dil - Se, etc)

Still it's a hit and miss movie, some people will love it and some don't. This is not the best Bollywood / English movie in my opinion (i still prefer Moonsoon Wedding) but it is one of the best movie of 2008.

It is one of those miraculous entertainments that achieves its immediate goals and keeps climbing toward a higher summit. - Roger Ebert.

"Trainspotting" director Danny Boyle has pulled off the feel-good movie of the year with "Slumdog Millionaire."  Think of it as a modern day Charles Dickens novel where three kids from India who live in abject squalor pull off an existential coup and realize their greatest dreams of love and money.  Another way of looking at "Slumdog" is to compare it with those 1930s' Warner Brothers crime classics where one kid takes the wrong path while the other takes the right path.  The bad are punished in "Slumdog" and the good are rewarded.  Don't let its India-based storyline raise your native hackles.  The long-suffering hero Jamal Malik and his scummy brother Salim are artful dodgers in a society that hates anybody with a background in poverty.  Basically, the story focuses on Jamal becoming a contestant in the Hindi equivalent of the TV show "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire."  Jamal is poised to win more wealth that he can imagine when the question of questions comes around: Who was the third member of the Three Musketeers.  The lesson of "Slumdog" is savor good literature because it has its own rewards.  The drama of "Slumdog" is our hero is subjected to a night of torture by the police because he has been accused of cheating.  The chief police investigator, Irfan Khan, finds it difficult to believe that a kid from the slums could know so much.  The strategy of "Slumdog" is to alternate each question that our beleaguered hero must answer with an episode from his life when he learned the answer to that question.  The scene when Jamal plunges into an outdoors toilet, covering himself from head-to-toe with human fecal matter so he can get an autograph from his favorite movie dog is hilarious.  This scene is reminiscent of a similar scene from "Trainspotting."  During his youth, Jamal runs into some sleazy characters, especially one unsavory fellow who likes to 'rescue' children from the streets so that he can turn them into beggars.  Again, can we say Charles Dickens?  Anyway, this scoundrel like to blind small children and send them out to sing and beg. Jamal and Salim escape from this life, but in doing so, Jamal abandons--against his will--a girl named Latika who he has sworn undying love for.  Of course, the evil child exploiter sells her to men who want to see her dance.  Hmm, I wonder what the Indian Tourist Bureau things about this story.  Ten years ago, "Slumdog" would have taken place in Brazil.  Suffice to say that the hero and heroine are separated with little chance of being reuninted, but remember that "Slumdog" has a happy ending that will make you feel good, perhaps even great, depending on how much you treasure fairy tales.

On the suject of acting, I thought everyone from the kids who featured earlier in the movie, to the adult versions of the same characters (Salim, Jamal and Latika), were fantastic and really believable.  Another highlight for me was the performance of Anil Kapoor as the host of Millionaire - he was excellent.

I really enjoyed the score, especially "Jai Ho" - a certain purchase on the iTunes store.  The score seemed to match the movie perfectly.

As I stated, I can't fault this movie and I could not recommend this movie highly enough to others.  Just go see it and decide for yourself whether you believe it's worth the hype.  Personally, I believe it deserved all of the recognition it received recently at the Academy Awards.

Perhaps the most creative as well as the most ridiculous drama this year. Danny Boyle (director of 28 Days Later) brings us a visually stunning piece that is nothing short of a technical marvel. This film is so elegant in its production that it dulls your senses as to the actual validity of the story. Although the premise is certainly original and interesting (we are presented the main character's memories of his life with each subsequent question on the game show) the film's conclusion is both ridiculous and incredibly clumsy. Of course you don't actually realize this while your watching it because you've been visually and emotionally pulled into the movie by it's unabashed feel-good aura. But, once you've done listening to "Jai Ho" and sit for a few minutes to reflect, you will realize not just the absurdity of the ending but also the fact that there were several loose ends in the film that were simply never tied up.

Of course, seeing everyone else's reaction to Slumdog is almost as fun as watching the movie itself. The film is perhaps the most controversial film at the oscars this year because no one can really come to a consensus about whether or not this film downplays the poverty in Mumbai or not. As I see it, Slumdog is one of those movies that you could argue any point with because it never really focuses in on one obvious stance enough to really draw any meaningful conclusions from. I see the film simply as a modern day fairy-tale. I believe one critic said that Slumdog is a modern optimistic Charles Dickens story. This would certainly be the best assessment that I would agree with. The film is also big on fate. I have no problem with movies that explore the concept, but Slumdog has literally no subtlety on the matter which really cheapens any points that it is trying to make.

So anyway, if you're a sucker for EXTREMELY happy endings, to the point that you'll believe absolutely anything is possible, then you'll adore this film. But if you like a bit of grace in your storytelling, then Slumdog will ultimately fail you with its ending.

I think I always knew that Danny Boyle was a director worth keeping an eye on, and I think I feel justified in that statement with his latest film: Slumdog Millionaire.  I just got home from seeing this and I really loved it.  The cast is bar-none and everyone gives powerhouse performances.  All three versions of each of the principals all do strong work.  The frenetic frenzy and pace of the film is phenomenal, as is the cinematography, thanks to Chris Dickens.  The colors are rich and saturated, the textures are thick and loaded with detail and the lights and darks have a great contrast to each other.  In other words, everything is just wonderful to look at.  The story itself is very much original and holds your interest from the word go.  Most of the time tense and frenetic with a dash of black comedy, the thing just moves and doesn't let up until the end.  The score and music in the film are both refreshing and incredible.  Mostly driving beats and eastern influenced music, but it all works so well with the storyline, even in the quieter scenes.  On a more personal note, I find this movie somehow akin to Domino with its style because it kept popping up in mind during the film.  I do believe this was a worthy candidate for best picture this year, having not seen the others I can't say for sure whether it was the right choice or not.  This movie probably won't be for everyone due to a lot of its content, but the open-minded film fanantic, such as myself, will find it engaging and a feast for the senses.  A truly remarkable film from a remarkable director.

There's something to be said for the fact that I can't easily sum this film up. My musings on it take me many places, and I think that's a compliment to the movie. It certainly didn't blow me away or beg me to re-watch it. The story is told largely in a visual manner and is effective at conveying information without being dialog-heavy (which helps in appealing to multiple cultures). What dialog there is is pretty standard and the love story is shallow, even cheesy. The rest of the film on the other hand does not take the easy way out and goes to pains to show us the difficulty of life growing up in the slums. Those images and experiences do not fade by the end of the film and I believe we are to see the main character's achievements as bittersweet as we reflect on what we've seen.

Slumdog Millionaire is a masterwork of filmmaking craft.  It is an integrated mix of arthouse drama and uplifting, inspirational Hollywood tale set in a completely new and original setting (for most Americans).  Virtually everything about this film works, from sound and video editing, to directing, to the script, to music, to acting.  The movie tells a wonderful, utterly compelling story and you are guaranteed to leave the theater with a smile on your face, without later feeling like you've been manipulated, as is the case with many Hollywood films.  This is a film I would recommend to anyone.  My only real complaint is that this film takes place in a world completely foreign to most Americans, and much of the story is deeply rooted in Indian culture, yet the filmmakers make very few attempts to explain these cultural elements of the story to us, sometimes forcing us to play catch up.  There are only a few instances where this is a problem, however, and hardly detracts from the film at all.  See this movie as soon as you can!

Draft Two:

This is a strange film phenomenom.  Slumdog' pursues a double vein of reality that chews away at cognitive consonance and leaves something bigger in place of the cognitive dissonance it causes if a viewer will let it. But I don't want to let it, and I do not like that part of the film.

Here's why: take a moment stop what you are doing and  go to Google Maps or Google Earth. Key in the word "Mumbai". Zoom in. Scroll around. There you will see the ghettos of  extreme and abject poverty in India. The slums of Inda lying side by side with super-affluent development largely funded by the West. Realize if you will, that the images you see are NOT an abstraction. It is reality. In Real space, and  in real time YOU are experiencing the image of abject poverty right on your desktop in the comfort of your own home or office or library. 

And then think to yourself that it could be argued in a sadistic and schadenfruende kind of way that no one does poverty *better* than India. It's spectacularly heavy and outlandish and macabre relative to the West. The slums stand in sharp relief next to super-affluent developments. Driving through the streets, it's impossible to ignore the crush of impoverished yet vibrant and alive humanity. Rich and mostly poor, it's all there, mixing and swirling like a crazed Jackson Pollack painting that mesmerizes it's viewers with an onslaught of sound color, stench and sensory overload. 

That is one reason I thoroughly enjoyed this movie. While it's not without it's weak points it is a fantastic ride. The auteur's radically embraced the challange of inculcating some of Mumbai's swirling and dissonant layers of reality into one cohesive yet abstractive whole. The end result is a wonder to behold. While not real in any way the movie does in some sense, say that no matter how impoverished the poor do indeed have lives of meaning and value. If not to anyone else, at least to themselves or story writers and movie directors. 

The movie embraces is the idea of evil in an interesting fashion. Perhaps the Eastern world in general is more adept with a balanced understanding of evil or the dual nature of humankind. Indians perhaps would be quick to realize that the reason Hitler got into power was not because he presented the ugly underside, but rather Hitler was beautiful in a obtuse sort of way, as beautiful to some Germans as the two bottles of Coca-Cola from the hand of a person bent on evil were to 3 starving children in one of the most uncomfortable scenes of the movie. Those of you who have also seen the Coca-cola = happiness ads previewing the show in theaters may know exactly what I mean. 

While not realistic in any way.. (this IS a film mind you), the most sobering reality presented by the film (and one of the reasons the film works) is one that is not directly part of the film, or it's specific story line. The most sobering reality of the film is the ambient noise or humanistic architecture in which the film takes place.  That architecture is this:  super-affluent humans pretty much for the most part do not  care for the poor, rather it's the poor who care for themselves or miraculously survive in the face of overwhelming odds. Nor do the super affluent go out of their way to direcly inflict poverty upon the poor. Rather they will go out thier way to make sure the whims of their egos stay capitalized. This of course means that the needs of the impoverished stay perpetually under-capitalized so they cannot compete on an equal level in the marketplace. It's perhaps the poor that hurt each other directly, while systemically the cold shoulder of those who are super-affluent  is a far larger if not impersonal force. 

It's this impersonal architecture and backgroundof indifference that creates the setting for Jamal, the hero of the film who as an impoverished person  maintains a figment of human goodness, morality and steadfastness in the face of traumas that a life of abject poverty could bring to a person. What makes Jamal so attractive is that as a recent toddler he could not have set out on his journey with any kind of adult rationale.  Jamal's goodness is a mere by-product of the character.  The good things that happen to him are not things acquired by cleverness, deviousness or craftyness but rather through chance.

The most interesting thing about the film is that the climax focuses not on Jamal winning the money, but on Jamal inheriting something many may percieve as being of far greater value than money.  The happiness of his heart's longing being fufilled.

So go watch this movie.  Enjoy it's thematic myriad of color and sound.  Laugh at the some of the campy Bollywood moments such as the cheesy coreographed ending as the credits roll.  (Note: if you think of Napoleon Dynamite it's easier to swallow the campy moments)

Then go home and Google "Mumbai" again.  Scroll over their slums with the god-like ease of a mouse or touch-screen, and then ask yourself.  Is there anyting that may be done?

Better yet, check on the poor in your own village, city or province.  Chances are they may be just a few hundred yards away.  It could even be a friend.   But that would take more effort than sitting lazily with luddites in a church pew, listening to Limbaugh on the radio, or viewing a monitor, seeing a movie or clicking a mouse and keying words onto a screen now wouldn't it?

Overrated. I went with an open mind wanting to love it like the masses but left very unsatisfied.  I guess because we know Jamal will succeed (in multiple ways) there is little suspense in the ending.  And while that's no reason to dislike a movie, I found learning about Jamal's past to be mostly tedious. (While the individual vignettes are interesting they lack much subtlety, humor or drama).  But how we learn about his past, i.e., the plot device that frames the movie is the most ill-conceived part of all.  Torturing him because the host of Who Wants to Be an (Indian) Millionaire believes he cheated is unbelievably absurd.  We could have quite easily learned how Jamal knew the answers through flashbacks without the scenes of torture.  And while Boyle doesn't romanticize growing up in the slums, it does feel as if Boyle has in some (unexplainable) way exploited those living there.  Is this the Best Picture of 2008? Perhaps because it was a weak year for movies.  But is this destined to be a classic - I doubt.  Not as bad a Best Picture winner as Crash, A Beautiful Mind, Million Dollar Baby, to name just a few.

Slumdog Millionaire was a great Oscar winner, but it was also a movie with many controversy. It was an Indian movie made by a Westerner, on how a few kids who grew up in Mumbai slums grew up and one of them became a millionaire through a game show. While many Indians rejoiced at how an Indian film swept eight Oscars and gained world recognition, many Indians also condemned the show for how the West portrayed India's slum. The most notable condemnation came from old iconic Boolywood king, Amitabh Bachchan, who was ironically featured in the film as a superstar. He said in his blog, "If Slumdog Millionaire projects India as a third-world, dirty, underbelly developing nation and causes pain and disgust among nationalists and patriots, let it be known that a murky underbelly exists and thrives even in the most developed nations". I am a Chinese Asian, and neither Western nor Indian. As such, I am trying to speak from a non-bias view. I think it's alright to depict the horrors of Indian slums. They are there, and there is no denying that. While every first world countries have their "underbelly" slums, it is indeed a fact that India's slum is very extensive by proportion. The West is thus not making fun of India's poor. On the other hand, what disturbed me more in the show was the fact there not a single good person in the show. There corrupt and cruel policemen, ruthless and crazy gangsters, exploiters, rioters, thieves, killers, etc etc. Extreme cruelty like digging out kid's eye to make them better beggars. The game show presenter is slimy. The good buddy Salim betrayed his friend Jamal. Latika forsaked Jamal for Salim when he was in power. And even the hero Jamal was not in any way a hero or a model. He was simply living for his (selfish) dreams. There was a scene where young Jamal was kicked by an Indian adult for stealing, and he shouted "This is the real India" to a American couple to gain sympathy. The only one who show sympathy was the American couple, who replied "Let us show you the real America" and gave the kid some good money. In sense, I get a little depressed watching this movie as I couldn't find a Indian hero to identify with. Everyone is selfish. Everyone is for his own. Everyone couldn't care less about his fellow neighbour. But perhaps this is reality? In real life, a day after the boy Azharuddin returned from Oscar Hollywood, he was beaten by his dad for refusing to do a press interview because he was too tired from the jetlag. His day slapped and kicked him badly. The girl Rubina's return home was not good either. The child, who plays the younger version of Jamal's love interest, Latika, came back to a warring family with both her biological mother, Khushi, and her stepmother, Munni, claiming custody of her. These slum kids still live in the kind of slums that are home to half of Mumbai's population. I really wished for more love, compassion, and mercy in humanity. If everyone is only caring for his own, then we would be slumdogs even though we may be millionaires.

When walking into the cinema to see this low budget film I must admit I was the first to question whether it had what it takes to make it in this cut throat industry and in all honesty it proved me wrong. This rag to riches tale offered everything to the modern day film fan, and kept you on the edge of your seat throughout. The story centres on a young Slumdog from Mumbai who enters the Indian version of Who wants to be a millionaire? in order to find his long lost love. The structure of the film is truly innovative and offers the audience a fresh new incite in the ways of telling the story with each question in the show regaling part of Jamal Maliks (Dev Patel) life and indeed how he came to know the answer of that specific question he is answering in the game show. This, in my opinion was incredibly clever and allowed the film to flow and entertain its audience in a new and unique cinematic way.

This is another great film to add to Danny Boyles collection and can happily contend with other great films which he directed, such as Trainspotting,28 days later and  The Beach. I have been a fan of his for a long time now and have waited for a film to rival that of his earlier work particularly Trainspotting. Brilliantly, Slumdog Millionaire is that film and arguably Boyles best work as director bar none. With a staggeringly low budget this film made in India has taken the world by storm and has received high praise from most in this field, winning Golden Globes, Baftas and now of course eight Oscars. 

There has been a lot made of the success of the film but without the two leading stars, Dev Patel and Freida Pinto this film would not have become as successful as it has. Both making their silver screen debuts, they deliver Oscar winning performances and show that you dont always have to go for the big blockbuster Hollywood names in order to create a brilliant film. Both Dev and Freida create a wonderful onscreen chemistry and make the film what it is, they allow the audience in on this romance and you find yourself almost willing Jamal (Dev Patel) to find Latika (Freida Pinto). Indeed both deserve high praise but we mustnt forget the other young Indian actors who play the onscreen pair Jamal Malik and Latika growing up, they simply light up the screen and provide the audience with some great entertainment throughout the earlier parts of the film.

One integral part of this blockbuster was the music used within it, A. R. Rahman who was responsible for the soundtrack created a great backdrop for the film with music featuring several authentic types of Indian music and also featured Paper Planes by M.I.A, which again matched the film so very well. A great deal of credit must be given as the music provides the heartbeat for this film and gives it a fantastic atmosphere.

Slumdog Millionaire is one of the best of 2009 and this feel good factor film shows that even the lowest of film projects can be shot to success if the directing, acting and storytelling are right. I am sure that we have seen the birth of two great stars in Dev Patel and Freida Pinto, and for Danny Boyle he has got the acclaim he so deserves. This for me was a brilliant upbeat, clever and exciting film which has everything you could possibly want. Slumdog Millionaire a great feel good film for 2009.

Slumdog Millionaire, una película que tenía todo para pasar desapercibida, en circunstancias normales pudo haber sido otro drama mediocre; y es que al fin y al cabo la historia no es lo que mueve a esta, probablemente, la mejor película de 2008.

Jamal es un joven de barrio bajo en Mumbai, que entra a un concurso televisado con la esperanza de ser visto por Latika, la mujer que ha amado desde que era un niño y al fin poder estar con ella. Sin embargo y ante la sorpresa de todos, Jamal gana 10,000,000 de rupias contestando todas las preguntas correctamente, y como no es más que un "Slumdog" es detenido y torturado con tal de descubrir como fue que hizo trampa.
Es ahí que el liga sus respuestas, mediante flashbacks , con momentos importantes de su vida, momentos que lo llevaron directamente a ese momento.

El argumento puede parecer fantástico, incluso infantil; y sin embargo encierra un mensaje para tomarse en cuenta. El tema principal del filme es que algunas cosas "tienen que ser" y es cuando surge la pregunta, si es que estamos predestinados a ser felices ¿Cómo es que Salim, hermano de Jamal, termina muriendo de forma tan brutal? y si realmente todos fueramos predispuestos a la felicidad ¿Por qué la inmensa mayoría no lo consigue? ¿Qué hace que Jamal sea tan diferente?

El programa ¿Quién quiere ser millonario? representa para la gente de Mumbai la oportunidad de alcanzar la felicidad, siendo ricos y escapando del mundo que conocen; pero para Jamal la cosa es diferente, pues llega al programa impulsado por el amor que siente por Latika, que es lo que lo ha movido durante toda su vida.

El camino está ahí para los que saben como verlo, y para los que no le dan vueltas al asunto, Jamal amaba a Latika más que a nada, y eso lo guió de nuevo a su lado.

Slumdog Millionaire es una película ágil, en constante movimiento y que incorpora tanto drama, como romance, humor, crítica social, elementos de thriller... y los incorpora de forma extraordinaria bajo la gran dirección de Danny Boyle.

La fotografía es impecable, y retrata de manera impactante el movimiento de Mumbai; que además de todo no es retratada de forma denigrante como se llegó a decir, o tal vez ya olvidaron a la magistral Los Olvidados de Luis Buñuel, también criticada, y hasta prohibida, en su tiempo. El trabajo de cámara ayuda mucho para mantener el ritmo de la película, lo que aunado a la excelente banda sonora hacen díficil no disfrutar esta joya del cine moderno.

Slumdog Millionaire es bella por que es simple, no pretende ser algo profundo y sin embargo consigue tocar a la audiencia.
Una película altamente recomendable y un ejemplo de como hacer cine.

Slumdog Millionaire tells a story of love and compassion through clear ideas and inspiring stories-and yet I left dissatisfied.  Throughout the movie, Jamal expressed his love for Latika in an overly melodramatic fashion, which was almost unbelievable. 
	Also, every time a story of Jamal's knowledge was exposed, it ended as quick as it began like I was on a tour bus and was given 5 minutes for each sight.  Therefore, Slumdog Millionaire did not live up to my expectations.
	In Slumdog Millionaire, Jamal is constantly looking for Latika, while doing so, he constantly has a dumbfound look on his face.  Even when winning 20 million rupees he had the same look on his face as in every other scene.  The dumbfounded look became banal thus making him less believable.
	Though Jamal's stories were cleverly weaved into the game show, I still found no raw emotion from any of the characters through theses short stories.  I believe this is because the stories were so "rushed", as if I was on a tour bus. 
	Overall, Slumdog succeeded in telling and presenting an inspiring story in unique ways.  Yet it failed to show the inner essence of the characters.  On a final note, Slumdog gets my appreciation, despite that it failed to captivate me.

Danny Boyle?s Slumdog Millionaire is on one level a feelgood movie that in the finale wrenches out your heart, whilst on another level raises many difficult problems of a growing city.  The difficulty for this mix is the risk of serious debate being crushed by the romance.  The classic theme of a love story coupled with a lucky tale of success is juxtaposed with dark issues of religious violence, organised crime, slavery and police brutality, and it is the bollywood dancing at the end that ensures the romance that sticks in your memory.
The clever script writing blending in the history of the young boy Jamal?s turning into a young man providing the experience and in turn the knowledge that feeds the real time quiz show screening of ?Who wants to be a millionaire? keeps us transfixed to the end.  The need for the young man (Dev Patel) to guess each answer right limits the twists and turns to just one major diversion into a police station.  At this point we are taken back into Jamal?s poverty-stricken childhood.  Being a populist film the horror is not as gut wrenching as it could have been (see City of God).  Yes one of his friends is blinded and another sold into prostitution, but it lacks the realism to shock or spoil the romance.  Essentially, the director Danny Boyle keeps the film as a fantasy with just enough realism to be taken seriously as a modern fable.
But Dev Patel does not hog the performance - the show?s egotistical host (Anil Kapoor), who shamelessly dispatches the young man to the police, uses his huge personality and large eyebrows to amuse us.  As a device to hang the film together it works a treat.
The lively subject of the movie is equally matched by the colour and lighting that shows India for what it can be.  The plot of a young man, a chai wallah from the slums, somehow miraculously winning fame and fortune ? and getting his girl ? is nothing new and may feel tired for some.  It may also be too light to stay in people?s minds.  But it is a tale told with style, humour and powerful acting keep you gripped to the end.
