Trite Hollywood crap.  In a Western story, man struggles to create his destiny.  In an Eastern Story, man struggles to accept his destiny.  Slumdog Millionaire tried to create a story of predestination, where the protagonist Jamal cannot fail as if there's some preternatural force guiding him.  However, it's clear that Jamal is the most one dimensional character... all he wants from the beginning to the end of the movie is to be with Latika, and there's no character development, interesting choices, consequences, or any sense of loss.  Life just absurdly hands him everything on a platter.  The two stars for this rating are for the story of Salim, which is wonderfully steeped in karma.  He makes harsh choices for survival, is rewarded when acting for good, and is punished when acting upon his ego.  His story was the only one worth following, but sadly ended in a terrible ending.  Overall, I think this movie would have been equally well suited with African American Actors and Spike Lee directing.  Just take For the Benjamins and New Jack City, and you pretty much have Slumdog Millionaire.

Who wants to be a millionaire? The movie begins with Jamal Malik being questioned by a police officer, the scene switches to falling money bills. The scene switches again to the popular show "Who Want's To Be A Millionaire" where Jamal is the contestant. During these scenes this question flashes: "Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million rupees. How did he do it? A) He cheated, B) He's lucky, C) He's a genius, D) It is written.". The answer to that one is revealed at the end of the movie. The movie jumps from present time, when Jamal is being questioned because he is "suspected of cheating" in the game show, how someone can get arrested for that is beyond me but. Through the movie it flashes back to the game show and the questions Jamal is asked. But before he answeres said questions we flash back to his childhood. The answers to the questions are things he learned as a little boy in the slum in India. The movie is rather chaotic and jumps from scene to scene in true Danny Boyle style. His style is one I love, he has directed two of my favourite movies ever; Trainspotting and A Life Less Ordinary. The movie itself was actually pretty good. The first parts had me blown away but the ending was abit dissapointing actually. Because it had this, I don't know, twist that I didnt really like. But all in all it was a good movie. Defenitly oscar worthy, don't know about 8 though... It's got pretty much everything a good movie needs. An interesting plot and good characters that both captivates you and fit together. Even if it is a chaotic movie, I atleast didn't get confused. Mr Boyle is a master when it comes to that and well...one of his best in my opinion.

I was lucky enough to have the time to attend an all-day movie marathon at the theaters. It was pretty amazing: $25 for five Oscar nominated movies with bottom-less soda and popcorn. Life couldn't get any better.

After getting settled I had to watch three movies before I got to the coup de gras. First it was "Milk", then "Reader, "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button", and then "Slumdog Millionaire." ("Frost/Nixon" followed and it was a great movie too).

I never heard a thing about this movie. In fact, with the exception of "Benjamin Button" I had trouble remembering if I even heard about the others. So, I went with my friend and his family not knowing what to expect. When it finally came to "Slumdog Millionaire" I was constantly on the edge of my seat. 

I think to fully appreciate the movie, the viewer must have been outside the U.S. at least once. I lived for some time in the Philippines toward the Negros Occidental region so I can say with authority that this movie was very realistic. The filth that is prevailant in third world countries brought back memories, along with the people who are happy regardless of where they are. The myriad of colors and the crowded and busy life of the city was what I experienced whenever I had to resupply in a big city. The setting is very realistic and is every bit what you would see in a third world country.

The characters are likable and complex. The children echo third world children who face perils everyday but are somehow enlivened by it. The activities they did in the movie where what I watched some children do in a run-down basketball court.

But enough about my memories. Let's talk about the actual movie and story a bit. I really enjoyed the setup. It left me wondering where the story was going to go. Also, it was a great way to show how our character grew up and how his relationships with all his friends and family changed over the years. I don't think there was any moment within the movie where I had to tap my foot impatiently and beg the movie to continue. The movie was quick and to the point, rapidly bringing us up to date as to why the character is in his peculiar situation. It is simple at first glace, but then we are slowly exposed to the love interest who seems to take precedence over everything that involves the young protaganist. (Including his jealous, yet caring older brother). I've already written too much. Just go see it. It's worth it. I promise.

 Slumdog Millionaire is a 2008 British film directed by Danny Boyle, written by Simon Beaufoy, and co-directed in India by Loveleen Tandan.It is an adaptation of the Boeke Prize-winning and Commonwealth Writers' Prize-nominated novel Q & A (2005) by Indian author and diplomat Vikas Swarup.

After screenings at the Telluride Film Festival and the Toronto International Film Festival, Slumdog Millionaire initially had a limited North American release on 12 November 2008 by Fox Searchlight Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, to critical acclaim and awards success. It later had a nationwide release in the United Kingdom on 9 January 2009 and in the United States on 23 January 2009.It premiered in Mumbai on 22 January 2009.The DVD is set to be released on 31 March 2009.

Slumdog Millionaire was nominated for ten Academy Awards in 2009 and won eight, the most for any film of 2008, including Best Picture and Best Director. It also won five Critics' Choice Awards, four Golden Globes, and seven BAFTA Awards, including Best Film. Despite the film's success, it is the subject of controversy concerning its portrayals of Indians and Hinduism as well as the welfare of its child actors.

This lavishly gritty latecomer from 2008 (limited release in November) got the nod for Best Picture because they forgot about the others when Oscar time came around and critics and judges have only had short-term memories. Even so, Danny Boyle's flashback heavy saga of a young Indian man on a game show about to win the big 20 million rupies (like dollars) prize is at times epic. Based on the novel, 'Q and A' which was more like the Price is Right than Who Wants to be a Millionaire. The game show is an odd parody of Millionaire in the film, with a corrupt host who has the contestant 'slum dog turned telemarketer' arrested for cheating (so he will quit or something) where he is brutalized and tortured in a police station most of the night. It turns out that the young man isn't cheating but does know the answers from his life on the streets, through sometimes nasty trials and narrow escapes. (One of them is a dive into an outhouse and another an escape from a psycho gang of adults who torture kids to make them blind peddlers). India's slum lifestyle is portrayed raw and uncensored. Mockery of 'millionaire' is sometimes fun though, especially the host who can't seem to say the word, and says, 'milonare' or what sounds like it with such glee. The contestant?s gangland brother and his lost and found love play into the story and flashbacks, and it has 'a Bollywood dance number' which just throws the mood completely. Rated R for a reason, even a hared R and is not recommended for children.

So, After MULTIPLE viewing, the more and more i watched it, the more i enjoyed it, i have decided that Slumdog Millionaire is truly THE best film of the year! (To u-know-who:P I know I said TDK is the best, but nope it's SM).

The film is energetic and buoyant. Truly Powerful. And it has a huge heart which will move you and have u routing for the main character.

It opens with Jamal Malik- an uneducated boy from the slums- being tortured; beaten etc. to get an answer out of him; how was he able to know all of the answers. One question away from 20 million RBS,he begins explaining to the officer that every moment in his life was a clue to the answers.

But the plot doesn't stop here; IT EXPLODES with narrative force in a way i've never seen in any film except in the Pixar films. The questions are simply a way to navigate through his life and discover all he has been through and the reason he participated; to save his long lost love from a terrible fate.

Simon Beaufoy's screenplay is brilliant! It explodes with narrative force, giving the film reason. I wasn't expecting it to be that good! Boyle here shines. He mixes Western with Bollywood. He is able to mix fun with intensity and edge of ur seat moments. He shines in scene like; the train etc. But the best scene is when Jamal and his brother go to a brothel, Boyle rox! the way he mixes the score withthe editing and the cinemetography is genius; the scene is provocative yet not offensive, but in some way delicious! (not in a pervertive way:P.)

The performances r brilliant especially Dev and the host of the dhow.The score is unique! the cinematography is weird and the editing is energetic! It deserves 6 oscars out of the 8 it won (song; Wall-e, sound; Tdk/wall-e)

Slumdog is a must see piece of film-making.

Why does it have to be shot in such an obtrusive style?
The photography is grainy, and has been digitally manipulated to give a contrasty look throughout, there are lots of strange angles, and of course the shaky, fast-cut style that is so common now.

Of course a director is free to choose his style, but I just wonder whether this adds to the film or detracts from it.

I suppose that's down to the viewer.

For me:

1. It's distracting, obtrusive and annoying.
2. I suppose it was meant to give a sort of gritty, real, basic feeling. Well... I'd have thought that might have been perfectly achieved by the characters and locations. 
3. It's not new or very clever any more. In fact it feels just like so many other shaky cam films ever since Blair Witch.
4. I think it's cynical. I have a feeling that the filmmakers were a bit scared of their material. They've basically got an old-fashioned rags-to-riches story, complete with baddies, romance etc. I wonder if Danny Boyle was worried that the film would be too old-fashioned, too sentimental. It's as if he desperately wanted to make it a bit more 'street' - a bit more 'relevant', so he wobbled the camera around in a contemporary fashion.
5. I suspect and hope to God that this pseudo-camcorder-gonzo style of camerawork will run its course and then look a bit dated - a bit like the overuse of the zoom lens in 70s films. 
6. I urge anyone to watch some of the early films of Zhang Yimou, particularly 'The Road Home' and "Not One Less". Of course you can't qualitatively compare directors' styles, but there is a director who allows the power of his characters and stories to dominate, and his directing style always complements and never distracts.

Yes, I'm late to this party. All the hype kinda put me off on this. Good news; it's justified.

A mad Oliver Twist on steroids tale with touches of The Usual Suspects and Scarface. Director Danny Boyle keeps the audience on its toes by not casting known entities and by virtue of the action happening in a foriegn land. A land that, despite its importance in the global marketplace, many still don't know enough about. It's an established director going the independent route with a better budget. (Still not astronomical, but that's part of the charm.)

There's no comfort and while the film carries forward to conclussions you hope will come about; there's no guarantee.

Boyle uses harrowing situations to show how characters grow and develop, so that even when we make moral judgements about them, there's an understanding of how they got that way and how it could happen to us if placed there. (Rare qualities in a script and fiinished product.)

There's many harrowing scenes involving children that are difficult to get through. (Fun fact about me: I've long become inured to man's inhumanity to man in film and real life. Not so much when it comes to children or animals.) However, I urge you to tough it out, as this is a part of a journey. It speaks to all of the films characters and what it does to them.

Unlike many, I don't confuse portions of this film with a documentary. I believe there are things that may have been taken from a life, but interpreted and extrapolated. It forces you to engage it. The film does let you keep it at an emotional safe distance. (If you're able to, then I think you must be dead inside.) 

Still, for its manipulation, it's still more naturalistic than others who've tried this tact. I can see why it garnered the awards it did and why the messages it sends to the audience are so willingly embraced in our new dark times. 

Love (although most of us do not have the fortune of having a paramour so achingly beautiful as Frieda Pinto.) and prosperity while keeping a moral center. That's worth suffering and enduring for. That's worth sacrificing for. That's worth waiting for.

"Slumdog Millionaire" tells the story of  Jamal Malik (Dev Patel), an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who works at a call centre as a chaiwalla. We meet him as the whole nation is watching him being just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India's "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" But, when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a slumdog know so much? 

To prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika (Freida Pinto), the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of Jamal's increasingly layered story reveals where he learned the answers to the show's seemingly impossible quizzes. But one question remains a mystery: what is this young man with no apparent desire for money really doing on the game show? 

I bow my head for Danny Boyle whom I have admired as a director from the day I saw "Trainspotting" in 1996. He deserves recognition for his ways of creating cinematic experiences that just grasps you. "Slumdog Millionaire" is a well made, well structured, well shot and partly gripping and dramatic film. However, it is not Boyles best work if you ask me. [b]"Slumdog Millionaire"[/b] is a classic rags-to-riches story about a young poy named Jamal who lived in the slums of India. His mother was killed, he met a girl and his brother got involved with gangs. He loses the girl because of his brother's greediness. For Jamal, life was harsh.
 
That all changes when Jamal get's on an Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" It is like his entire life has been leading up to this moment: he knows all the answers based off his life experiances, (And maybe a bit of it has nothing to do with the answers.) He is one question away from winning 20 million rupees when he is suspected of cheating and taken away by the police.
 
While it may be a classic idea, [b]"Slumdog Millionaire"[/b] is a lot more complex than it appears at first glance. First off, it examines a lot of global problems far to often overlooked in today's culture. A lot of the things you see in the movie are real life problems. Secondly, Jamal was never even interested in the money. He used the show as his decoy for something much more important to him.
 
[b]'Slumdog Millioanire"[/b] is not to be missed.

The first 15 minutes consists of one of those visual and aural assaults that directors seem to feel are necessary to get the audience's attention now.  I checked my ears for bleeding.  After that, it settled down into a corny, contrived, Horatio Alger story.  I suppose all fledgling capitalist societies need those to give them false hope, and it is weirdly appropriate for America to tip it's hat to that kind of naive propaganda.  

The actors are all terrific, but the ones that play the same characters at different ages look nothing alike, which is weird.  The main character almost comes off as retarded when he reaches adulthood, he is so simple-minded in his pursuit of his lost love.  I didn't really dig him until the credits, when he revealed some serious dance moves.  I wished the rest of the movie had had that much imagination.

I am astounded that the producers of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire" haven't sued the pants off the moviemakers.  The host of the show is portrayed as a slimy bigot, who tries to manipulate the hero into giving a losing answer.  He even has him arrested for suspected cheating - and tortured!  I'm not in a position to say whether this is remotely plausible in India, but it is certainly grounds for slander.

So, overall, had this movie gone straight to video, as it nearly did, I would probably have recommended it to my friends as something of an overlooked charmer.  But again..."Best Picture?"  Hard to believe.

Its funny how this movie's plot parallel's its path to distribution. You see, they both came from obscurity. Dev Patel plays the titular Slumdog Millionaire, and while the titles gives away the outcome, its really all the back stories that really make this movie's story that much more powerful. 

Dev plays Jamal Malik, a young boy who grows up with a heart of gold in the slums of Mumbai, however, must actively play beggarwith his brother Salim for a syndicate of thieves in order to simply stay alive. Basically, his entire life experience culminates with all the necessary answers to write the rest of his life on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, as he not only does it to get the love of his life, but unite a nation enchanted with potential "slumdog millionaire".

And much like the lead, this movie was a product of its own irony. Initially unwanted for theatrical distribution and at one point was headed straight to DVD, Slumdog Millionaire began its captivating comeback story at last year's TIFF and hasn't looked back. Ever since the Oscar nominations, this movie has lit up the box office, climbing steadily like its titular hero did towards the 20 million rupee question in the final act! Last week, the movie finally became the number one grossing movie in North America, and it is unlikely to repeat this weekend due to Watchmen debuting, its still a remarkable thing to witness a once touted "straight to DVD" clunker, all the way to winning the statue at the Oscars!!

Anyways, without spoiling anymore story, its quite the incredible journey through the childhood of a young Indian boy on the streets of Mumbai, especially with the gravity surrounding the terrorist attack that happened late last year. The two leads, Dev and Freida, have such magnetic charm and even the younger versions of themselves were well acted too!

It's a no-brainer really. Danny Boyle makes good movies. From Trainspotting, to 28 Days Later and now Slumdog Millionaire, this is a movie that everyone should watch. Everything is awesome: the soundtrack, cinematography, editing, acting and so on all are just great. Go now!!

"Slumdog" is directed by Danny Boyle who is mostly known for "Trainspotting" and "Shallow Grave". "Slumdog" is every bit as good as those films and should give Boyle another chance at the career he deserves. 

The film is about Jamal (played as an adult by Dev Patel) and Latika's (played as an adult by Freida Pinto) journey to their destinies. Patel and Pinto have been getting a lot of press for their performances in the film. Both actors are very good but they each (Pinto, in particular) have a small amount of screen time. The majority of the film is carried by the child actors that play these characters in their youth. Jamal's brother, Salim plays a vital role in the whole journey and this character also spends most of his screen time as a child. 

The child actors were plucked out of the slums, with no prior acting experience. Considering this, the performances they give are quite remarkable. Anil Kapoor gives an interesting performance as the host of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire". 

I've heard this film described as a "feel good movie" and while this is basically true, this is not a Disney film. The characters all have terrible things happen to them and some of the hardship of their lives is brought out for all to see. 

This won the Academy Award for best picture. At this point, the only other nominated film I've seen is "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button". I think this film has broader audience appeal because of its story line. The length of "Button" has also put some people off. I look forward to seeing the rest of the nominated films. While this is a very good film, I'm not convinced that it is the best of last year.

There is little to object to in a film, that's sole purpose is to sweep its grateful audience away. It need not make grandiose statements nor attempt to subvert the fabric of cinema. All which is incumbent upon it, is to entertain, to captivate. But for this, certain things must be in place; Character, Narrative. It is with a heavy heart that I confess, that after a second viewing, this film is sadly lacking in both. 
It is in no way an awful picture, Its sheer scope and the ingenuity of its central conceit is enough to bowl one over, but the lasting impact is ephemeral and hollow. Danny Boyle is a director of great vision, however in this instance, his bombastic style comes at the cost of emotional engagement. He is so beguiled by the frenzied environment, which he admirably portrays without condescension, that he has forgotten about the characters. 
The writing is at once fresh and frustratingly derivative. The "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" artifice is unique and an intelligent device for exposing backstory. The first act is indelibly charming but as the plot progresses, one's interest wanes. It is too formulaic; take 1 part 'City of God', two parts 'Cinema Paradiso' and two parts 'Oliver Twist' and you have an idea. Consequently on first inspection it is easy to be seduced by Boyle's latest offering but, ultimately, it is too superficial and too facile to last.

And yes, it doesn't flinch, and that's a good thing.

But at the end of the day it's a feel-good fairy tale, and the boy wins the girl, and there is dancing in the streets.  Or in the train station, anyway.  Good for Danny Boyle for making an immensely likable fabric out of pretty thin thread.  The performers are terrific.  And there's some great stuff in here - it belongs on anyone's should-see list.  

But Best Picture?  Mickey Rourke was robbed.

This is an absolutely superb film. It is rare that a film triumphs on levels of both believable story telling and entertainment. The story is a romantic one, but it never fails to provide a glimpse into Indian lifestyle. The story of how Jamal wins Who Want's To Be A Millionaire, is convincingly explained through his life's adversities and his heroic battles as a child. The script has been written and captured in images in a such way, that each scene falls into the next, and the audience is transported into the slums of India. This film did not once make me feel as if I should be somewhere else, as so many films tend do these days. I was completely entranced.  

This movie is more relevant than ever, now that the world is facing an economic recession. What is the value of money when love is at stake? Who are the winners and losers of Western economic wealth? But all these questions merely came about through a wonderful engagement with the film. They were never starkly presented, nor was the film in any way didactic or depressing, as some films can be.  The film ends as both a Greek tragedy and a happy ever after fairytale. The Bollywood clip at the end was neither out of place nor unexpected. This film will go down as a classic in years to come....But more importantly its a film that is so very good for the soul........

Beautifully shot.  No Doubt. Danny Boyle uses bright colors and the sounds of India's busy city streets to immerse you into life in India.  Its cramped, its alive, and it can be an extremely dangerous place to be in.  
  
  Most of the performances come from young children and teenagers that have never acted before.  But, they do more than justice to their roles and especially the younger boys.  They get you involved enough into the movie in the first place and pull you through the story until they get older.  
  
  I liked the cinematography.  I liked the editing.  I liked the idea of the story.  I liked the acting.  And, even the ending made me smile.  But, for some reason, I did not really care about this movie.  And, I saw the movie 3 times.  I tried to make myself like the movie because everyone else is raving about it being the best movie of the year by far. Well, I could name at least five that made me leave the theater feeling more involved, more entertained, and more satisfied overall with my 2 hour or so investment.  
  
  On paper this movie has all the right elements. But, I just felt that the story was a little contrived.  Once you figured out the basic plot, if you don't invest some emotional interest into the two boys, especially the soon to be Slumdog Milionaire, then you don't really stand a chance to love the movie.  You will like it, as i do, but not love it.  So, its a question on whether you care about these kids or not.  I am definitely recommending this movie, but only with that afermentioned warning.

India's coming out party!  Hurrah!  India's newfound success, according to this movie, HAS BEEN WRITTEN, and is celebrated in this delightful romp into poverty and violence.

It must have been difficult for them to create such a nice mood of joy from all of the really horrible realities of Mumbai slums--and the plot itself is as hole-riddled as a bargain basement rickshaw--but the acting and infectious mood of the movie prevails to make this one of the better movies I've seen this year.  Perhaps in part because it is such a refreshing departure from plodding studio behemoths like Benjamin Button, this movie stood out and was able to capture an audience wider than was probably expected.  If you want some magic realism on your butter chicken instead of currying the favour of actual realism, have some fast food Indian feel-good cinema.  After all, you can't blame Bollywood for putting together something that's unrealistic--it's kind of their thing.  Definitely worth the watch.

A clumsily written but skillfully directed piece of drama.

Danny Boyle can do almost no wrong in my eyes. With the startling exception of The Beach (let's all just forget that one) he's a director that makes all the right decisions, goes for all the right angles, gets the most from his cast - he even made it look like Chris Evans could act, if only for a short while - and Slumdog Millionaire is a great example of him continuing his trend for making what would otherwise be average films good.

Everything in this film would work, would fit together perfectly; all the flashbacks, all the incredible events, all the coincidence and chance; if only there wasn't this bizarre device of having him on Who Wants to be a Millionaire to link it all together. It doen't make sense, it isn't explained and it's very clearly JUST a plot device to spur on all these flashbacks. Not only that but Jamal, the lead character, seems to have a total personality transfer at the exact point before he goes on the quiz show.
There's no denying the flashbacks themselves are tense, exciting, funny, even romantic and for the duration of them you are totally taken in by the story. But then we cut back to the present. Often rediculously easy questions for staggering sums of money puntuate the forced tension of the quiz show setting before the Jamal of the present; a sweaty, nervous, quiet adult; remembers his outgoing, charismatic, witty childhood.
It just doesn't fit together well enough.
It's a strange thing to say but aside from the bad writing Slumdog Millionaire is a great film. All the other ingredients are right: the casting is amazing, particularly the child actors; the camera work is what I suppose you could now call textbook Danny Boyle; not to mention the soundtrack, which I just did becasue it's fantastic. Even the funny Bollywood number at the end works surprisingly well.
So in short: Director good, writer bad.

This is a story set in the slums of Mumbai, about two orphaned brothers who grow up on the streets. Like "City of God" (set in the slums of Rio De Janeiro), one of the boys is good (Jamal) and one is bad (Salim). They both love the same woman (Latika). Each brother watches out for each other as they grow up, but it's clear that Salim is a ruthlessly violent character.

The story begins with Jamal playing for the top prize on an Indian version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire". Before he can play for the top prize, the show ends & he is asked to return the following day to finish the game. However, the game show host suspects the boy is cheating & has the police take him away for questioning. The police brutally interrogate Jamal, but he does not break down & confess, but re-counts his upbringing on the Mumbai streets to show how he was able to gather the knowledge to correctly answer the questions on the show. In the process, the story of his life unfolds.

This is an excellent movie. While it is clearly an Indian cast and setting, the language is English. The cinematography was good, the music was great, the characters very engaging, the plot was excellent, with an ending that tied up everything beautifully.

The film has had countless positive reviews and the posters sell it as the most uplifting film of the year so with an imdb score of 8.6 I had to check it out.  WARNING - Spoilers ahead.

It's a good film and I'd probably give it 7.9/10. My first impression after watching was that it wasn't really THAT uplifting.  Sure it has the happy ending where Jamal gets the 10 Million rupee, wins over his childhood love and his brother becomes a reformed man. But his brother is dead, I can't shake the feeling that Latika chooses him purely because he's just the better of 2 options, and I never really felt depressed about Jamal's situation. WHAT? Ok. Maybe I have a stone heart but that's what slum life is like and Jamal isn't truly affected by it because he's never really known better.

Don't get me wrong, Jamal has led a harsh life; being orphaned and having to beg and steal for a living, conning tourists and searching for his childhood love only to be betrayed by his older brother - the only guy that he's ever trusted and relied on. All of this is beautifully depicted as Jamal is interrogated under suspicion of cheating his way through the game. You get a real portrayal of what the slum life is, making you feel for the characters and possibly overlook some of the morally grey areas in the film.

Danny Boyle, de regisseur van âTrainspottingâ, â28 days laterâ, âShallow Graveâ, âSunshineâ en âThe Beachâ, gooit het nog maar eens over een andere boeg. Na zijn uitstapjes in het horrorgenre en de science fiction, waagt hij zich nu aan een liefdesverhaal van epische proporties. Van een veelzijdig regisseur gesproken. Hij is niet alleen veelzijdig, maar ook goed. Want bijna alles wat hij tot nu toe gemaakt heeft, was goed tot zeer goed. Zo ook dit. Maar deze film is meer dan goed. Deze film is fantastisch, dit is voor mij een meesterwerkje met, het moet gezegd, een heel inventief scenario. En een schitterende soundtrack en hele goeie (voor ons dan toch) onbekende acteurs.
De film begint explosief. Jamal (een jongen uit de sloppenwijken) neemt deel aan een quiz op televisie en staat op het punt 20.000 roepie binnen te rijven. Hij wordt gefolterd en ondervraagd door de politie, omdat iedereen ervan overtuigd is dat hij een bedrieger is. En zo komen we aan de hand van flashbacks te weten hoe hij het antwoord weet op al die vragen. We beginnen bij Jamal als kind (wat een schattig jongetje dat deze rol op zich neemt). Ze zijn aan het voetballen op verboden terrein en worden achterna gezeten door de politie. Dit levert een schitterende openingssequentie op met een hele snelle montage van de kinderen die zich als gladde aaltjes reppen doorheen de sloppenwijken van Mumbai, gestuwd door fantastische percussiemuziek. Wow ! En zo ontwikkelt zich het hele verhaal en volgen we de avonturen van de broertjes Jamal en Salim met hun vriendinnetje Latika (waar Jamal hopeloos verliefd op wordt).
Weinig negatiefs te vertellen over deze film, behalve dan dat de gimmick van de quizvragen naar het einde toe wat uitgewerkt lijkt, maar de film stopt net op tijd zodat je de tijd niet krijgt om je hieraan te ergeren. Hele mooie film met een leuke soundtrack, een originele montage, schitterende kleuren en goeie acteurs. Een adrenalinestoot van jewelste. Wat wil een mens nog meer ?

Props to Danny Boyle for creating a very slick, fast-paced movie about slumlife (thank God it's not about the Philippines!). But is the hype worth the watch?

I beg to disagree with the most critics.

Slumdog Millionaire's rags-to-riches storyline with Bollywood dance moves lacks emotional connection. I have seen other poverty-centered movies (local at that) with characters that linger with you long after the credits roll. Western first world countries may find such themes novelty due to their lack of first-hand experience with such. Or maybe it's just India's time to shine...just like what happened with Taiwan years back with Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon. 

But there are merits to the movie. The film editing is flawless, the cinematography of slum life very realistic. The acting is all-around consistently good. Not much overacting abounds. The actor who plays Jamal might actually appeal to the tweens due to his kind demeanor and lean physique. The film depicts Mumbai is filled with corruption and chaos -- it's a good thing Indians don't find this portrayal insulting.

This movie might have won the Oscar for best picture, but I still like City of God better.

[font=Franklin Gothic Medium][size=3]Wow. So I just saw this movie for the second time last week and have officially decided that it's pretty much perfect. A solid 10/10. Not that I didn't love it the first time I saw it, but seeing it again just sealed the deal.

Dev Patel is so awesome it's crazy. It will take quite a few mistakes on his part for me to stop going to see a movie just because he's in it, and I'm sure he'll be in plenty now that he was in the "Best Movie of the Year" (Oscars 2008). Freida Pinto is also excellent as grown up Latika. And the children did a pretty great job, knowing hardly any English, but conveying complex emotions that anyone watching could totally understand just from a look or gesture. There were moments when I found myself wondering if children in their situation wouldn't behave even more hysterically (during raids, chase sequences, etc), but then I realized that their lives are plagued by those things all the time and the differences you can discern in these kids from American kids really goes to show you exactly what the material is intending for you to gather.

Seeing the three kids - Jamal, Salim, and Latika - grow up, you get a really well rounded idea of everyone's personalities and relationships through their past in flashbacks. Even though flashbacks are sometimes overdone and often cheesy ways to force the audience to understand something, in this film, they are necessary and a perfect way of telling a very unique and intriguing tale.

Now let's talk about the editing. Chris Dickens is who I believe is responsible for some of the best editing... ever. Together with cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle, they create perfect visual transitions, shots, and cuts that create one of the most well put together films I have seen in a long time.

Danny Boyle, as usual, crafts a story into a classic. It's part fantasy in a way, which is probably my favorite thing about it. It's got this surreal element that really makes you smile when everything starts to head towards the wonderful conclusion. And the actors do a fantastic job (Dev Patel especially) of really making you feel what they feel.

There isn't an area I can complain about with this film because every job was clearly done right. I'm excited to show friends who haven't seen the film. I haven't run into anyone yet who hasn't at least liked it, and I expect there are still some people on my friends list who haven't seen it and will absolutely love it. The DVD is already scheduled for March 31. Can't wait.[/size][/font]

Danny Boyle has been making really good films for a while now and Slumdog Millionaire caps off what has been an impressive run, with what is Boyle's best film since Trainspotting.

The movie is about two young brothers or 'musketeers' who take very different paths. Both Salim and Jamal struggle at a young age to make ends meet after the death of their mother, and have to keep finding ways to hustle to keep themselves sheltered and fed. However, the inclusion of a third, Latika,  brings jealousy between the two brothers. While Salim chooses to live by the power of the gun, his younger love struck brother chooses to live by his mind and heart, and pursues his beloved Latika across Mumbai and across the years.

Slumdog is filmed with aesthetic joy, edited with bliss and scored with the sheer genius. Bollywood's own A. R. Rahman created most of the soundtrack numbers including the haunting melody entitled 'Latika's Theme.' Though its formula is transparent, the film does will you to want the conclusion it comes towards, thus making it one of the most uplifting and enjoyable films of the 2008.

I saw this film because of all the hype.  I hadn't seen many clips but I broadly knew the plot - man wins a gameshow and then has flashbacks to explain how he knows all the answers.  But the actual film is more than that.  *SPOILER ALERT*  It's actually incredibly brutal and graphic.  Okay, not much blood, but enough was in it to make you think you might have nightmares.  Boy's mother beaten to death in front of him.  Implied scenes of rape, and quite a graphic scene of a boy being mutilated to make him a better beggar.  And at the start, main character hung up and buzzed with electricity.  I was watching this with my mother-in-law thinking "What the..." and the BBFC had given it a 15 rating???  What is going on in the minds of the BBFC?  They do know what their job entails don't they?  Or do films pass the censors just if they don't show actual blood spurting, and sex and violence?  I think all the implied stuff in this film was enough to be very disturbing.  The baddies were very bad, almost cartoonish and one-dimensional, and the main character's great love of his life stays with a man just because she's an oppressed gangster's moll.... well it would have been nice if her motivation was explained a bit better.  Was she nothing but a poor victim or was she actually just a soulless money-driven bimbo who would put up with any amount of domestic violence just for the sake of the nice saris and jewellery the baddie bought her???  And she rejected the advances of the poor but honest Jamal (main character) and rejects his offer to "live on love".  This, to me, made her seem quite a heartless money-grubber and so she wasn't the great prize he ought to chase after.  I hate the fact that the writer of this made up the word "Slumdog" and now the media have picked up on it like it's not a new word but has been a valid word for slum-dwellers for years.  I heard the Indians hate this word and campaigned against the film because they don't like their slum dwellers being called dogs.  I can't blame them, talk about adding insult to injury!  I loved the cinematography and the happy big-number dance at the ending.  I can see why it won loads of Oscars, it's an Oscar-friendly flick, but .... I think the characters were too one-dimensional for me to really empathise with the plot.  And as I said I resented watching a 15 film that was so graphic.  "15" rating ought to *mean* something.  The acting was great, and Dev Patel ought to go far.  But I think given other choices I would rather have done something else with two hours of my life.

Finally got to see this film at the Island 16 after work - nice BIG screens! And after having missed out on the matinee a few times locally, it was worth waiting for it tonight. There isn't enough in the synopsis or any of the previews and commercials on this film to give the full affect of what this picture has to offer, WOW. Spectacular, riveting performances by the children in this movie - don't be mistaken, this is not a 'milk the children for a hollywood dollar'' film, these kids work in incredibly dramatic moments in the story, they are actors and actresses that put a lot of work in the film AND they were so believable! It's impressive alone that the casting crew found similar looking kids to play the leads in the chronology but to be so fantastic, is the truly incredible feat. Director Danny Boyle and the cast and crew, keep your attention throughout the film, even for part of the closing credits.  Freda Pinto gets a lot of attention for her beauty and she was good. But Dey Patel and Madhur Mittal and their younger versions of the brothers were remarkable. The actors playing the gangsters were so seedy you feel like you are getting to know real criminals ! Irfan Khan was so good, he had me believing he was a policeman in India at one time (maybe he was, perhaps, in a previous life?). After seeing this movie, I can see why it won the Oscar for Best Picture. The music is great, the cinematography is fantastic LOVE the camera work - especially the chase sequence with the kids running through the slums. The ending goes a little MTV and Holly er Bollywood but after that fantastic ride, they earned the few minutes of it. There's some things I do not want to mention that would give away some incredible moments in this film. It looks like it's winding down in the theaters so catch it now.

Regardless of the angle you choose to view this world-acclaimed movie (2009 Oscar's best motion picture, among other awards), you have to agree that the juxtaposition of a game show that happened one night ago and the childhood that was more than 10 years in the making prior to that night is indeed an unique way of telling a story of a slumdog waiting to go on to answer one more question in the "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire" game show and take home the grandest prize, and on the way, get reunited with his love.
 
We got taken back to see the way Jamal and his broter grew up in poverty, the chance meeting with his "destiny" and how life led them to separate pathways. Now Jamal sat on a chair in the centre of the very popular TV show, realizing that he knows the answers to all the questions and potentially a good and rich life (well, answers to all apart from two questions to be exact) because of what life was giving him so far. He knew who the movie star is because he jumped into a pool of faeces to get that movie star's autograph; he knew the inventor of a revolver because his brother pointed one at him; he knew who is on a US$100 note because he gave one away...When he phoned a friend to ask for help for the very last question, his "destiny", who he had repeatedly lost again and again, answered the phone.
 
I think money, or winning money, isn't that important at the end. As the audience (on set or around a TV set anywhere in Mumbai) erupted into a group euphoria watching Jamal wins, it did create a great but somehow unnecesary backdrop for the eventual romantic reunion of Jamal and his "destiny"; it was very romantic, enough to make me sit through the credit rolling, to which the background music is a musical performed by the two leads and extras. It would have been great if we were to be taken straight from the time he realised that knowing the answer to the final question did not matter now that he found "her" again, right to the time Jamal sat at a corner on the train station platform, looking downcast, looking like a slumdog, and met the girl again by chance.
 
But, Hollywood. I guess we need to see him becoming a hero, by winning a Western TV show ... Moreover, it's also the night his only relative, the brother who joined the gang, got murdered, the night poverty still straggle the slum, the night where all the injustice will be repeated...

I guess I am the ONLY person in the entire world who did not like Slumdog Millionaire...aside from the people who live where the film was shot, they hate it, saying it made a mockery of them and their home country of India.

But people, critics and movie buffs alike, seem to like it SO much, they attack me for NOT liking it, saying things like I don't appreciate independent movie making or that I don't like Danny Boyle, which is complete bullshit because 28 Days Later and Sunshine are two of my favorite films, like, EVER.

But the thing is this. It is supposed to be this great inspirational underdog story about coming up against all odds. It tells the story in flashbacks as a young man named Jamal is being tortured by the police because they believe he cheated on a game show (Indias version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire), because he is one question away from winning 20 million rupees, which is about $400,000. 

Anyways these cops are electrocuting this kid and slapping him around and dunking his head in water and all that good torture what not trying to figure out how he cheated when in fact all the questions have something in common with major events in his life(for example, who designed a certain handgun, the answer being Samuel Colt, and he knows the answer because his brother held him at gunpoint stating "im the one holding the colt .45, things like that), and the whole reason he is on the show is because he believes the girl of his dreams, Latika, would be watching it, and he believes their destinies lie together.

It's amazingly romantic, and an interesting story, but the pacing is so damn slow that it becomes boring until the last 20 minutes when the police let him go and he gets to play for the final question and the 20 million rupees.

Jamals story goes back to when he was a child, showing religious killings, how he met a famous movie star, his kidnapping in a child work ring , his adventures on a train jacking passengers wallets and food with his brother, and ultimately his searching for the girl of his dreams, who can make him complete.

Slumdog Millionaire, a film about the life of an Indian teen who grew up in as the title suggests, in the slums of India.  It is a very well constructed film as we go through it learning about the not so glorious up-bringing that this character had experience. The film shows the tragic death of his mother, them escaping from child slavery, to becoming a tourist guide, involvement with crime, as well with dealing with his crush on a girl that he met years before and now. As the title suggest, it also about his appearance on a game show (India version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire") where he selected as the contestant as he answers each question correctly. For each question, the films portrays scenes from his life of where he learn the answers from. He is force to unveil why he been able to answer all these questions properly to the legal authorities,  as there a growing suspicion  that he is cheating. The films acting was phenomenal as each scene was portray really well. The choice of music in this film was perfectly chosen. I also give credit to the film editor of this feature (Chris Dickens) as he really did a fabulous job of using unique creative editing. Director Danny Boyle did masterful film making as he did a great job of storytelling. My only criticism is not really regarding this movie, but the academy choice of top 5 movies for 2008. The Dark Knight should of got the recognizing it deserves by being nominated as best picture and very likely would of won. This would of been the second best film of this year. Anyhow, I really do recommend seeing this movie as it is all around well done film.

Coming in the same year as The Curious Case of Benjamin Button makes for a strange theme developing in 2008. The theme running throughout Slumdog is the age old question: who controls our lives? Do our decisions mater, or is it all up to fate? Has it, in fact, all been written? Finally came around to review Slumdog!! I had to see it twice to really make sure that I had such a positive opinion because of what the film really was, and not only on the basis of anticipation. NOTE I went to see it knowing as little about it as possible and having read as few reviews as I could. Luckily, Slumdog made me feel everything I hoped to feel, which constituted my only expectation. I'll get through with the story first: Jamal's entire life adds up to the moment in which he is about to win 20 million rupees on the Indian edition of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?. Thus far, his experiences have been difficult. He grew up in the slums of Bombay, where he lost his mother to an attack by Hindu fanatics against Muslims. From that moment on, he is forced to survive, along with his older brother Salim, the oddest, most terrifying situations that two small children could encounter. In the meantime, he is in constant pursue of his childhood sweetheart, another orphan, Latika. Jamal, Salim, and Latika are often caught up in the violence of Bombay, separated, and then divided again, for over ten years. The 20 million rupee prize is all the adolescent Jamal can hope for to fix his life and reunite with the love of his life, and yet it really means nothing at all. So the premise is interesting, even though the story of an unlikely hero that battles and triumphs above the jungle of urban adversity is not new. Fast narration and flashbacks are not new either. Fernando Meirelles put them to majestic use in City of God, a film to which Slumdog unavoidably remits? Some may argue this has all been done and been done better. BUT Slumdog has such an engaging optimism; it simply exudes such vitality, and happiness, even though the scenarios are hardly easy to take, that it stands out. OK some people may be upset that it isn't raw enough, that it's toned down, etc. And some expected a tko for City of God. Those people find Slumdog Millionaire disappointing, but I couldn't disagree more. First off, Slumdog is technically a fantasy. The prospect of any of this actually happening may seem laughable. Fate plays a very important role in the film, but India is often characterized by an acceptance of destiny anyways; SM just takes it one step forward. What if destiny meant for all of this to take place? Is it rationally impossible? The answer is no. It's "bizarrely plausible". We are asked to stop being so close-minded an accept a difficult scenery to believe, but if we do, we are rewarded. Slumdog is very human. It's compassionate, and I'm not sure that's only to the book's credit. Danny Boyle had a very tasteful and beautiful way of filming children and grown people distraught -with everything in the world to be hopeless about- with incredible music and amazing style. Is that escapism? No! There's one thing that characterizes and unites most "Third World" countries across the globe, and that is hope, cheer, positivity. Music and color are a fundamental part of their existence because they are lifesavers that even the most extreme poverty cannot take away. That sometimes other, more grave subjects are ignored or misunderstood is an entire different issue, and I don't feel it concerns Slumdog Millionaire. The actors that play Jamal and Salim as children and preteens are beyond amazing. They perform in a natural way and with a boldness that I hadn't seen since Los Olvidados. They're supposed to be wounded, tough, and earthy, and they are, but they don't neglect humor and brightness. For some reason, these wise children comprehended that those were not mutually exclusive things. Above all, they manage to transmit Jamal and Salim's incredibly tranquility regarding the future. They go with the flow. They understand things will fall into place eventually. I think theirs are the best performances of the film. Dev Patel was quite perfect for the role of the focused, stubborn, and lovesick Jamal. As usual, the well written role of Jamal is largely responsible for the quality of the acting, but I have to confess I thought that his understated performance was actually strong enough to carry the film. His is a strong character that appears to be helplessly weak. I watched the scenes of his childhood with fascination, but I wanted to go back to the "present time", to his exhausted face, and try to read into it. Especially after having caught a glimpse of his personality on TV interviews, etc, I admire his performance even more. His empathy for Jamal is captivating. I didn't want the film to end. THEN there's the visual genius of Danny Boyle. The cinematography is simply awesome, and the way Boyle captures every move, every word, is inspiring. He has and has always had an eye for movement. Slumdog Millionaire never stops to take a breath, it's dynamic, constantly jumping and running. Most importantly, his dynamism isn't violent like it may have been on other occasions; on the contrary, it just wishes to imitate and exalt life. Slumdog Millionaire is escapist and its fanciness may border on the bizarre, but it's more understanding of humanity -as far as I'm concerned- than most films I've ever seen. It hates money and it is critical of poverty and only gives value to character and principle. It's a beautiful, inspiring story, and a piece of admirable filmmaking. There's no waste in it. To me, it was one of those experiences in which you leave the theater wanting to take action, to change something, to do something. I can't recommend it enough. PS. The Rahman score is a must! I was a fan of his Bollywood scores long before Slumdog and I'm so happy his genius is better known now. His catalogue has something for everyone. He's a very versatile artist and his creativity is boundless. The songs in Slumdog are all pop hits, and they give the film an incredible power.

Perhaps I'm jaded, but I want to be astounded when I watch a film that won eight Oscars.

Let's start with the good.  I really admired the cinematography.  Slumdog Millionaire is shot incredibly well, and it keeps you watching because of it.  It's also edited well.  Although it uses the tired old method of starting near the end of the story and using flashbacks, it's done well and effectively.  I have no problem with this device when it works.

Unfortunately, this is about all the praise I have for the film.  It's mediocre to competently acted, depending on which child actor the audience is watching.  Some lines are delivered downright poorly.  The plot is simplistic.  I get the whole fairytale nature of it, the improbable coincidences, the love story that is fated, etc., but it's been done before.  It's not a particularly special or engaging script.  And, perhaps the biggest flaw from a plot perspective is that it failed to emotionally engage me.  Jamal, Salim and Latika are poorly written characters.  I did end up loathing Salim though, so it succeeded at that.  But of course, his change of heart scene arrives so suddenly that it's hard to see why, and consequently hard to care.  In fact, all the character motivations are hazy.  The millionaire host is jealous, but only as a plot point.  The cops are needlessly cruel, just for the hell of it really, to make us sympathize with Jamal.  Was it even a legitimate crime, one worthy of torture?  Is it a condemnation of the police system in that region?  I get that he's supposed to go through hardship before his dreams come true, but let's be a little more subtle about it.

And this brings me to my biggest problem with the whole thing: there's an impersonal sweet coat over everything.  You never really feel that Jamal is headed for anything else than a happy ending.  You never really catch the horror that Latika goes through.  You never really feel the gritty realism many claim that this film has.  No wonder people ate it up.  It's about as inoffensive as it can be while claiming to deal with issues of poverty, death, child prostitution, police brutality, and human nature in general.  Just add some music and bright colors and BAM, utter abject poverty and human misery looks fucking adorable and exotic.

Finally, like many other films released recently, the soundtrack is mastered far louder than the dialogue, making for jarring scene transitions when the score kicks in.  More than any other trend, I wish this would die in modern films, because it is incredibly irritating.

I'm hesitant in recommending Slumdog Millionaire for even a single watch.  It panders like it's trying to win an award for doing so, it's sleek and calculated, and an overall bore.  To be this critically and publicly acclaimed, I expected, I don't know, more?  At least not something so abysmally castrated by its agenda.  It may not be as rage-inducing as Crash or The Hurt Locker, but it's not up to the standards that a movie with this much praise should display.

Let me explain why. Firstly it's a typical monotonous bollywood drama, inpetly adapted from a good book "Q & A" by Vikas Swaroop, with several glitches in the final screenplay. The film striking a chord with the western audiences can perhaps be explained by the fact that they have never seen this kind of a  prosaic story before. Secondly, the picturization of the slums, perhaps not a blatant exaggeration, is none the less a cliche. 

Then, the music. Its not even close in standards to any of  Rahman's best works (compare the music with the scores in Lagaan or Swades!). Damn!, what the hell was the academy thinking?

Danny Boyle's a lucky dog, having got away after saying in his oscar speech that he didn't know squad about India when he was making the movie. 

I was really shocked to see Slumdog win the oscar beating the other movies nominated in the category like "Frost/Nixon" or "Benjamin Button".

Had this movie not win the Best Picture, I would have enjoyed this  movie more. But after seeing 'Milk' and "The Curious Case.."it's a little unsettling to see how this movie beat them out for best picture. The storyline was great but there were no strong or memorable acting performances. I understand that this movie is weighed more by the "whole", rather than the "parts" but good character development is something I look for in a best picture, so this movie should be no different. The characters are typically boy meets girl, so there was really nothing special about them. Often times they were trying to be too cute, which got old fast. One thing that I encourage why others should watch this movie is its authentic and eye opening appreciation for the Indian culture. The setting takes place from the slums to the bustling markets of Mumbai, taking the audience into its very depths. Other than the movie's strong commitment to global awareness, I think there were too many sympathy votes and a moral agenda to make this movie best picture this year. In fact, when this movie stands next to other best pictures in the past like schindler's list, forrest gump and braveheart, it's shocking.

How is it that a young "slumdog," as they call our main character, "Jamal," could possibly know all of the answers to questions that Doctors and Lawyers did not?
He has lived.  He has truly lived a life and through the vehicle chosen to tell his story we effectively and sometimes vicariously live that life alongside and through Jamal and his companions.
This movie touches the viewer on so many levels.  It grabs you from the first moment and never lets you go.  You are tied to the characters and all that they go through.  You will delight in the triumphs as well as dwell in the pains.
This is India from many angles.  This is not only the Calcutta one thinks of if you have been there or maybe seen "Born Into Brothels."  This is not only the India one might recall if you have seen "Monsoon Wedding."  It combines elements of all that you know of the 'real' India and much that we never will and brings us up from the slums to the studio where we live each moment in a question born of circumstance and randomness...much like life.
The pacing reaches for "City of God" though falls a little short in that it is too refined to touch the raw that "City of God" achieved.   Still, it is swift and will sweep you up in a whirlwind of trials and tribulations, recollections and memories perhaps better left untouched all bound together by that thing we all need most...Love.  
What else?
It is written.

Slumdog Millionaire


                                               
                                        An Unfortunate Fairy Tale




Once upon a reality, there was a need for fantasy.  Through a shared pursuance of redemption, human beings have created ingenious methods for enduring suffering.  Whether it is through performing physical activity, or turning to more creative outlets such as the human intellect, we as a species are consistently looking outside of our realities in order to enhance the quality of our everyday experiences.  This tool for survival could very well have been the same source that helped spark the storytelling genres of fantasy/science fiction, as well as the ageless legends and fairy tales that have been passed down from generation to generation.

There is, of course, a potential danger in using such survival techniques; dangers, which tend to spawn from the inevitable rebound effect of denying one's own personal reality.  In real life, this all-too common scenario can harvest tragic consequences.  This same situation constructed within the confines of cinema, however, tends to yield itself towards a more offensive exploitation.  It is within this precise consequence of romantic flair, where "Slumdog Millionaire" wrecks its own train of heart.

"Slumdog" tells the story of a young Indian man who is living in Mumbai and finds himself in an inquisition of sorts, as he attempts to justify the legitimacy of his recent success on India's version of the popular TV show "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?"  The movie begins with our protagonist (Jamal K. Malik, performed with an earnest sense of yearning by Dev Patel) having long surpassed the expected benchmark of achievement for the show's contestants.  For the Indian authorities however, this accomplishment by Jamal is all the more astonishing, given the nature of Jamal's background while growing up.  It is known that Jamal lived the majority of his young life growing up in some of the poorest, most violent and most diseased ridden areas in all of India.  As such, it is this reality of Jamal's upbringing that gives the authorities the 'justification' for their thorough inquiry.

Here we find ourselves back in the reality of customizing human suffering.  Yet once more we find ourselves within the clutches of pure Hollywood fantasy.  For this is yet another movie in a long line of factory like productions, where the depraved realities of horrific living conditions take a subordinate step backwards, in order to let in the stench of implausible delusions.  Remarkably, each prominent experience of suffering that Jamal endured as a child/teenager had within it a real life scenario that reflected the correct answers needed for "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?"  So as Jamal sifts through his own past in order to find the correct answers for the TV show, we the audience are supposed to buy in to the absurdity of this implausible plot.
Yes it is true, that director Danny Boyle was not afraid to reveal the harrowing conditions found underneath the rapid development of India's middle to upper class.  Still, it is the unfortunate path which Boyle and screenwriter Simon Beaufoy take, that only leads to the complete negation of "Slumdog"'s theme and message.  Let's face it: the combination of some of the world's most robust economies hitting a low point not seen since The Great Depression, and the continuance of countless wars and lands ravaged by famine, would seem to lend itself well to a movie like "Slumdog Millionaire".  With its story of rags to riches contained within a boundless sense of epic proportions, this movie would seem to be a panacea.

It is all very well to learn the lifelong art form of embracing the light in the ugliest of experiences, but to make an attempt of this sort through such an improbable dream that is "Slumdog Millionaire" is not only counter-productive, but futile.  Being able to acquire a sense of wisdom and profundity through one's own suffering, has been a courageous achievement witnessed time and again throughout human history.  Yet if we are to believe in the possibility of translating our moments of suffering into the correct answers for world issues/history on a hit TV game show like "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?",  then we might as well stop believing in the possibility of redemption altogether.  One of the biggest stretches of credulity for the audience is that Jamal's quest of being on this television show is based on his dreams of reconnecting with his childhood love.  He actually believes that she will be watching the telecast, but the plot is not convincing enough to give these dreams any real hope of becoming successful.  Since most of us go to the movies in order to escape (thus enhance) our everyday lives, one must ask what the point is of making such a movie as "Slumdog Millionaire"?  This film clearly does not work on a literal level yet it remains equally pointless on any metaphorical scale. It may have its endearing moments from time to time, but it ends up being no more substantial than the ridiculous Bollywood music video, found in the end credits.

And now for the million-dollar question:  How could I possibly write such a polarizing commentary on a movie that recently won 8 Oscars, including Best Picture and Best Director? 

Answer:  A) I am far from being an Academy Awards scholar.
               B) I copy and pasted Roger Ebert's review of "Slumdog
                   Millionaire".
               C) I've never even seen the movie "Slumdog Millionaire".
                    I took just one look at its title, and began writing.
               
   

                                         D) "It was destiny."

I have to say, after hearing all the Oscar buzz and having all my friends recommend it and say how great it is, I was... seriously underwhelmed.  It's good, don't get me wrong, but I think it goes over my head as to why it's so amazing.
I've dealt with this cinematographer before.  I really, really hate Anthony Dod Mantle and how he seems to think it's classy to throw in every kind of filter possible and change the framerate all the time at points where it's not artistic, it's just confusing.  Some were good, but some were thrown in, as if he said, "I haven't used this effect yet.  I need to push that in.  I am painfully aware he won an Oscar for this.  This is my opinion.

The acting was great, that I must say.  Nothing more and nothing less, they're all unknowns and from my understanding most of them are actual Hindi actors, which I DO SINCERELY APPLAUD Danny Boyle for doing.  Something about that adds an authenticity to it, and the fact they keep switching from Hindi to English throughout the movie.

The plot was... okay.  Here's where I'm confused.  I've seen dozens of shows or movies with plotlines similar to this.  I'm not sure why I wasn't impressed by it, but I guessed most of the plot twists before they happened and I was kind of disappointed by the ending.  I almost would have been more impressed if they had gone the other way, but.  C'est la vie.

One thing I must say, that may be the reason so many reviewers and critics are captivated by this movie, is the setting.  Indian culture and movie about such is something we rarely ever see over here and it's really fascinating to watch.  The sets (which are actually in the areas they are set i during the movie) are amazing.  One scene in particular where it showed people running around in the dirt, picking up whatever garbage they can salvage from tons and tons of it was especially impressive.  Despite all these points going for it, though, something about the experience of this movie made me tilt my head and say, "That's IT?"

Interesting feel-good movie, I'll give you that. It's not much more. Danny Boyle shows us how to shake his hand-held camera to give that "realistic" feel, but the technique is so overused it looks more overblown than anything else, just like his non-straight camera angles, as if his tripod had one leg too short or something. He also shows how he likes putting random pop music at any scene that doesn't have dialogueThat went well with Trainspotting's urban setting, but here it just looks awkward. The acting is decent, nothing more (those kids are adorable, I have to say). The story varies very nicely from comedy to drama, and it has some suspense even though the story's end is basically given away at the start. Unfortunately the love story and most of the characters are uninteresting. What happens to them is, but they don't have much depth to them, and the whole bad-gangster-brother-saves-the-day was stupid. How this film got 8 oscars whereas There Will Be Blood only got 2 is quite unnerving (at the same 2007 also had No Country For Old men, but still). The wink at Bollywood at the end was vey funny though. A well-made, well-written, sometimes funny, and fairly enchanting film, but on the whole nothing that special. People going on about how Boyle is a great director blablabla obviously haven't a clue of what direction is. A good film with good actors, good writing doesn't mean good direction, and this was probably the movie's fault (even though he got an oscar).

Finally came around to review Slumdog!! I had to see it twice to really make sure that I had such a positive opinion because of what the film really was, and not only on the basis of anticipation. NOTE I went to see it knowing as little about it as possible and having read as few reviews as I could. Luckily, Slumdog made me feel everything I hoped to feel, which constituted my only expectation. 

I'll get through with the story first: Jamal's entire life adds up to the moment in which he is about to win 20 million rupees on the Indian edition of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?. Thus far, his experiences have been difficult. He grew up in the slums of Bombay, where he lost his mother to an attack by Hindu fanatics against Muslims. From that moment on, he is forced to survive, along with his older brother Salim, the oddest, most terrifying situations that two small children could encounter. In the meantime, he is in constant pursue of his childhood sweetheart, another orphan, Latika. Jamal, Salim, and Latika are often caught up in the violence of Bombay, separated, and then divided again, for over ten years. The 20 million rupee prize is all the adolescent Jamal can hope for to fix his life and reunite with the love of his life, and yet it really means nothing at all. 

So the premise is interesting, even though the story of an unlikely hero that battles and triumphs above the jungle of urban adversity is not new. Fast narration and flashbacks are not new either. Fernando Meirelles put them to majestic use in City of God, a film to which Slumdog unavoidably remits? Some may argue this has all been done and been done better. BUT Slumdog has such an engaging optimism; it simply exudes such vitality, and happiness, even though the scenarios are hardly easy to take, that it stands out. OK some people may be upset that it isn't raw enough, that it's toned down, etc. And some expected a tko for City of God. Those people find Slumdog Millionaire disappointing, but I couldn't disagree more. 

First off, Slumdog is technically a fantasy. The prospect of any of this actually happening may seem laughable. Fate plays a very important role in the film, but India is often characterized by an acceptance of destiny anyways; SM just takes it one step forward. What if destiny meant for all of this to take place? Is it rationally impossible? The answer is no. It's "bizarrely plausible". We are asked to stop being so close-minded an accept a difficult scenery to believe, but if we do, we are rewarded. Slumdog is very human. It's compassionate, and I'm not sure that's only to the book's credit. Danny Boyle had a very tasteful and beautiful way of filming children and grown people distraught -with everything in the world to be hopeless about- with incredible music and amazing style. Is that escapism? No! There's one thing that characterizes and unites most "Third World" countries across the globe, and that is hope, cheer, positivity. Music and color are a fundamental part of their existence because they are lifesavers that even the most extreme poverty cannot take away. That sometimes other, more grave subjects are ignored or misunderstood is an entire different issue, and I don't feel it concerns Slumdog Millionaire. 

The actors that play Jamal and Salim as children and preteens are beyond amazing. They perform in a natural way and with a boldness that I hadn't seen since Los Olvidados. They're supposed to be wounded, tough, and earthy, and they are, but they don't neglect humor and brightness. For some reason, these wise children comprehended that those were not mutually exclusive things. Above all, they manage to transmit Jamal and Salim's incredibly tranquility regarding the future. They go with the flow. They understand things will fall into place eventually. I think theirs are the best performances of the film. 
Dev Patel was quite perfect for the role of the focused, stubborn, and lovesick Jamal. As usual, the well written role of Jamal is largely responsible for the quality of the acting, but I have to confess I thought that his understated performance was actually strong enough to carry the film. His is a strong character that appears to be helplessly weak. I watched the scenes of his childhood with fascination, but I wanted to go back to the "present time", to his exhausted face, and try to read into it. Especially after having caught a glimpse of his personality on TV interviews, etc, I admire his performance even more. His empathy for Jamal is captivating. I didn't want the film to end. 

THEN there's the visual genius of Danny Boyle. The cinematography is simply awesome, and the way Boyle captures every move, every word, is inspiring. He has and has always had an eye for movement. Slumdog Millionaire never stops to take a breath, it's dynamic, constantly jumping and running. Most importantly, his dynamism isn't violent like it may have been on other occasions; on the contrary, it just wishes to imitate and exalt life. 

Slumdog Millionaire is escapist and its fanciness may border on the bizarre, but it's more understanding of humanity -as far as I'm concerned- than most films I've ever seen. It hates money and it is critical of poverty and only gives value to character and principle. It's a beautiful, inspiring story, and a piece of admirable filmmaking. There's no waste in it. To me, it was one of those experiences in which you leave the theater wanting to take action, to change something, to do something. I can't recommend it enough.

The film, in my opinion, didn't live up to the hype.  The film captures the hurt, the hardship, and the depression of India's slums while mixing it with the glitz and glamor of the Who Wants to Be a Millionaire show and the love story of the main character Jamal and his friend Latika.  The film loses focus on the hardship of the Indian people and switches over to the obsessed desire of Jamal to do whatever it takes to profess his love for Latika and win her once and or all.  The questions on the show he must answer ironically (and hard to believe) all relate to key moments in his life mostly dealing with Latika and the final question can be predicted from the beginning of the film.  Happy, predictable and sadly overshadowing some of the real serious problems the Indian people have.  Still a technically sound film that is well shot, acted, edited and all together solid.  A worthy best picture considering the two best films of that year (The Dark Knight and Wall-E) weren't nominated.

Slumdog Millionaire is one of those movies that takes a different path from the rest of the pack in presenting an interesting, colorful human interest drama that should win the hearts of many viewers.
One of the best things that the movie has going for it is how the story manages to bring in culture to great effect - perhaps the effect on the viewer would be most pronounced on those who are not that familiar with traditional Indian culture and India society - much like how Kite Runner (another great movie) did with Afghan culture and history.
The plot in Slumdog too is varied in interesting. Though logically improbable - the story itself is a compilation of a whole series of improbabilites (or if you like to call it, as the movie does, "fate") - it's all very well done anyway and leaves you wondering how the protaganist manages to know the answers to the questions he is asked on the gameshow. And this the movie cleverly does through a series of flashbacks that not only answers how he knows them but also manages to develop the characters and backstory well.
Slumdog Millionaire is certainly one of the best movies of the year and is higly recommended for drama fans and most other viewers keen on an interesting rags-to-riches story with a twist. For a movie that doesn't need to resort to expensive gadgetry, effects and tricks, it comes off very well in presenting a movie that will be well-loved by many.

You are captivated by the questions and answers on the gameshow and keep watching to see how he came to know the answers from his journeys.  As great as the film is, the one problem I had with the film is the ending.  It all seems to wrap up all âcutesy Hollywoodâ with a giant ribbon at the end.
