Jamal est un jeune indien des bidonvilles de Mumbaï qui participe à la version locale de « qui veut gagner des millions ». A la surprise générale, il reste en jeu jusqu'à la dernière question. Comment peut-il connaître les réponses ? Alors que la police l'interroge, il explique que comment les réponses sont liées avec son vécu personnel. Avec cette fille qui revient sans cesse dans ses souvenirs... 
Oscar du meilleur film en 2009, je me suis enfin décidée à voir ce fameux Slumdog millionaire. L'ensemble est bien tourné, et l'idée de suivre les questions d'un jeu télévisé (inspirée d'un livre, au fait) pour raconter la vie de Jamal est bien trouvée. Un peu facile que cela suive parfaitement chronologiquement son histoire, mais bon, « it's written » comme précisé au début du film, laissons-nous persuader que le destin fait décidément bien les choses. Ce qui est sûr, c'est que la vision de l'Inde n'est pas limitée à la jolie version d'un guide touristique. On voit la crasse, la trahison, le meurtre, l'abus et la maltraitance. La lutte pour la survie de chacun. Et cette vie difficile qui amplifie le fait que l'on peut rester bon (version Jamal) ou devenir une vraie ordure (version Salim). Avec encore une fois la patte cinématographique si vive et particulière de Danny Boyle. 
Petits détails : il n'est jamais précisé comment ce serveur de thé a accédé au jeu télévisé. C'est suggéré quand il apprend le bon moment pour passer l'appel pour être sélectionné, mais ça m'a tout de même un peu frustrée. Aussi, la scène de danse finale est certes un hommage aux films de Bollywood, mais comme nous petits occidentaux n'y sommes pas habitués, je trouve que ça nous fait sortir un peu vite du récit en faisant une coupure aussi brusque.

A gritty and shocking portrayal of poverty and crime in India. This is the story of Jamal Malik (Dev Patel),  a street kid (or "slumdog") who has landed an appearance on India's version of the hit TV game show WHO WANTS TO BE A MILLIONAIRE? Jamal exceeds expectations on the show, and the producers alert the police after they become suspicious of his methods. The young contestant is arrested and is interrogated at the hands of a police inspector. As the interrogation proceeds,  Jamal tells his story through harrowing flashbacks that both show the terrible poverty of Mumbai and help explain how he knew the answers to the MILLIONAIRE questions.
I thought the director (Danny Boyle) did a great job of putting together Jamal's life experiences with his answers on the show and the film really does run the full gamut of emotions as we see him growing up, falling in love, coming close to death, and teetering on the brink of escaping from his terrible predicament. The dancing sequence at the end of the film was entertaining. Recommended!

This is an extraordinary film. From the original concept of the novel on which it is based (Q&A by Vikas Swarup), the screenplay by Simon Beaufoy (Full Monty) but especially the masterful creation and direction of the film by Danny Boyle. From the opening moments until the final scene, the audience was fully engaged. I was completely lost in the world that Danny Boyle created. This is not a story that has been told and retold, hashed and rehashed. It is fresh and engaging - all at once quickly moving, romantic, violent, culturally insightful, desperate and slightly fantastic. There are some comic elements to the film but to describe it as a "comedy" seems inappropriate. The film was shot on location in India, mostly in Mumbai. Slumdog Millionaire is yet another testament to depth and range of Boyle's artistic talent who has directed such diverse films as Shallow Grave, Trainspotting, 28 Days Later and Sunshine.

An about-face from Boyle's equally effective '28 Days Later,' 'Slumdog Millionaire' is a conglomerate of drama, humor, suspence, tragedy and sweetness. Containing surprisingly solid performances from young and relatively unknown actors, it is the story of how young love matures over time and is never forgotten and is told effectively using flashbacks that lead up to the present time. My only problem with the film is the use of the 'Millionaire' game show as the plot device that brings the story together...a bit too gimmicky for my taste and, really, not needed. I also would have liked to have seen a slightly different ending, but I won't ruin it for those who haven't seen it by saying anything more. Good film, great performances, and worthy of it's Oscar Nomination...but the award should have gone to 'The Wrestler.'

Slumdog millionaire Directed by Danny Boyle and starring a cast of Unknowns.  We follow the life of Jamal Malik(A wonderful performance by Dev Patel)  as he is attempting to get to  the 20 million rupee answer on the Indian version of who wants to be a millionaire. Through a series of flash backs we come to find out how a boy from the slums could know these answers.  We also follow the unwavering love Jamal has for Latika(Freida Pinto) starting out as a young child and going through to Adulthood. This is a film that is both shocking in its accurate depiction of the slums of Mumbai and how hard life can really be.  The cinematography is great and the film has an excellent soundtrack a trademark of Boyle?s films since Trainspotting. Jamal and his brother get mixed up with local Gangsters, Child Servitude and a series of tough situations. Throughout the game show Jamal?s recollection of how he came to know the answers are sometimes humorous but more often than not tragic and sad. It?s not a film that can be described in detail without  giving away to much.  Given the description of the film a lot of people might pass on this one but really should give it a shot it really has something for everyone. Torture, Gangsters, Poverty and a really sweet love story. A lot of people will think that the way he gets the answers is a little convenient but given a small suspension of disbelief the film is quite good. Finally if you ever had any interest in what bollywood movies are like stay through the closing credits.  Slumdog Millioniare has strong performances across the board and out of the movies that are nominated this is the movie that is going to win the Best Picture Award.

"Slumdog" is smart, enjoyable, even brilliant at times. Yet it's not what I would like to see as Best Picture of the Year. This movie seems to do everything in threes: Three main characters, three actors/actresses for each character, and associated with that, a trilogy structure to the story. Following the young children through a series of fable-like adventures, the first third of the movie sizzles with an astonishingly vibrant depicton of the Mumbai slums. As the children leap into early teens, the story takes a harsh turn into darker, occasionally extreme territories. The final segment lightens up considerably, eventually slipping into the sappy cliches of a Hollywood love story. The unfortunate effect is that after such a strong setup, the final conclusion comes off as a kind of let-down.

No se cómo empezar, han estado a punto de saltarme las lágrimas al final, pero no por el final en sí, sino por toda la emoción que me ha transmitido esta Película. Esto es cine, señores. Peliculón del año y Danny Boyle (director de la afamada Trainspotting) se ha superado y ha hecho para mí la mejor película de su carrera. 
La historia de este film se centra en un 'slumdog', un perro callejero, un chaval criado en los suburbios de Mumbay/Bombay y el cual no tiene estudios ni nada pero que participa en el programa ¿Quiere ser Millonario? (50×15, vamos) y contesta correctamente una tras otra las preguntas que se le proponen, por tanto, sin pruebas, deciden que es un tramposo y lo llevan a comisaría para que explique como lo ha hecho.

Así empiezan a poner un video del programa el cual vemos pregunta tras pregunta, mientras el explica como lo sabe recordando su niñez y adolescencia. Esto se hace de una manera muy bien empastada y también tengo que decir que en algunos momentos se me hizo un poco pesada (pero muy pocos que conste).

El tema social se trata con dureza y no dudo que realidad (no he estado en India para comprobarlo), y realmente es una patada en el estómago lo que viven estos niños y más alrededor del mundo. Pero no se cae en el recurso fácil de dar pena mostrando las miserias, sino todo lo que se muestra tiene un sentido en este guión magnífico.

Para terminar, pese a lo que pueda parecer por lo escrito anteriormente por mi, el tema central de la película es el Amor, y no ese amor edulcorado que nos venden muchas películas comedio-románticas de esas, no. Esto es AMOR y no diré más porque no quiero destripar la película pero si alguno la quiere ver pues ya verá porque lo digo.

At its very best, and with the right contestant, 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?' is an oddly compelling TV show, full of drama, suspense, social commentary and intrigue.

How then did the makers of this movie - in wanting to make a suspense filled drama infused with social commentary - get it so very, very wrong?

Firstly, they called it 'Slumdog Millionaire': this kinda telegraphs the ending, don't you think?

Secondly, they adopted a pretentious  time-shifting narrative that effectively removes any tension from the story. All along you know the protagonist is alive and kicking by the end, so the many life-threatening situations he recounts in flashback are dramatically void.

Thirdly, they cast Dev Patel in the lead. He spends most of the movie looking like he's suffering from painful flatulence and really doesn't have an effective dramatic range. He's outclassed by most of the actors in the flashback sequences, particularly Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, who plays the same character as a young boy, and Irrfan Khan as the police interrogator.

Finally, they chose to cap it all off with an incongruous and inept 'Bollywood' song and dance number!

Director Danny Boyle is responsible for making what I consider to be some of the most miserably inept films in the history of cinema, namely 'Shallow Grave', 'Trainspotting', 'The Beach' and 'Sunshine'. Slumdog Millionaire is a movie that doesn't have many strengths.  Its plot is continuously interesting and admittedly addictive and captivating, but also somewhat contrived and clichÃ©d, and of course ends in a typical and cheesy fairy-tale ending... not exactly brilliant stuff.  The whole police capture-and-torture thing was so stupid and contrived.  The main characters are only interesting in their childhood and adolescent stages, which is when they are played by competent actors.  While the children and adolescent actors did great, and Madhur Mittal did okay as the adult Salim, the two actors who are (inexplicably) the most hyped, Dev Patel and Freida Pinto, were lame and forgettable; Pinto being in the movie for perhaps a total of ten minutes, with few lines and doing little more than looking pretty, and Patel spending the majority of his on-screen time with a vacant stare, blank eyes wide open and mouth slightly ajar, as if being on a decade-old game show had rendered him catatonic.  Thankfully these two overhyped actors were not in consideration for Academy Awards for their acting, though I wouldn't have been surprised if they had been.

Besides the addictive (if cheesy and superficial) plot, the main strength of this movie comes from its overall look.  For what for many of us is the first time, we (as in, Western audiences) get to see the impoverished slums of Mumbai and the struggles that its denizens have to endure on a daily basis, and whether it's accurate or not (and it may very well not be) it is very compelling.  The Indian feel lends the movie considerable authenticity, and again, it may not be actually authentic, but it certainly FEELS that way.  Of course, much of this relies on our own ignorance of India (or most any non-European foreign country), but, for better or worse, it works.  Danny Boyle uses a fast-paced, edgy directing style (reminiscent of Infected attack scenes in 28 Days Later) to great effect and I do think he deserves his Academy Award for Best Director.  It's this intangible, indescribable look and feel that makes this movie so gripping, and the reason why I am (somewhat begrudgingly) giving this movie 4 stars.

For me, this movie had two strikes against it right from the start: directed by Danny Boyle, who has done nothing but shit since Shallow Grave (yes, that includes the insanely overrated, hopelessly dated, heroin-glorifying, totally-missing-the-fucking-point Trainspotting), and eight Oscars, awards that, for the most part, go to tripe that panders to the lowest common denominator.

Well, I can see why this movie won some of those Oscars - it's a feel-good hit that pushes all the right buttons, and, hey, it pushes them well, at least for the first half of the movie.

The cast is solid, especially the children - IMO, they turn in better performances than their adult counterparts. At about the "adulthood" part of the flashbacks, the film runs out of steam; I found myself just wanting it to end. The connections between the game show questions and the hero's life story are far too convenient, and the flip-flopping between game show and life story gets boring. And all the wonky Adam-West-Batman scene tilting gets extremely annoying.

Overall, however, if you've got nothing better to watch and you're in the mood for a good underdog story, it's worth a download. In fact, at times the cinematography made me wish I was watching this on the big screen.

Sporadic narrative, visceral cinematography and effortless direction are words that come to mind after viewing Danny Boyle's latest flick. Aside from the ridiculous nature of the plot (ie. knowing Latika as a young child for a week yet wasting much of the rest of your young life trying to find her again, and actually finding her???) this is a touching and heartwarming (If a little silly) drama that portrays India in a seemingly accurate way. Although it is generally the editing and score that holds your attention above the one dimensional performances, it is Anil Kapoor whose performance's exuberance, depth and gravity carries the film to it's suitably cheesy outcome. The 'destiny' idea also seems misplaced and totally pointless as it only add more cheese to the toaster. These problems seem hardly relevant when you consider that who wants to be a millionaire isn't broadcast live so the final scene really wouldn't have happened at all! But you walk out of the cinema with a big grin on your face wondering how they could have ever considered cutting the dance off at the end title sequence, which is a joy to watch. Even with it's good points I can't help wish that Milk should have won best picture, it's a better film on so many levels.

"It is written."  True, and not well written, I might add.  In Slumdog Millionaire, Danny Boyle has a bunch of cute kids and tosses them into an inane and corny fairy tale.  Note that I do not use "fairy tale" in a derogatory fashion.  I like fairy tales.  I like happy endings.  I do not not like slapdash writing. 

 Let me give you an example. . . the slumdog answers almost every question on his Who Wants to Be  Millionaire appearance  with information provided conveniently  by flashbacks.  Once I caught on to this, I disengaged from the story completely.  Did you ever have a class where the teacher made you answer questions about a movie while watching the movie?  This movie thinks that is a cool gimmick, but it's not.  It's a stupid stupid gimmick.  

The flashbacks of the first half of the film take place when our hero, Jamal, and his brother are slumdog kiddies.  They run a lot from bumbling adults and bumbling evil adults.  It's sort of a gritty slumdog version of Richie Rich.  Let's call it Slummy Slumdog.  

The second half has Slummy going after the girl he fell in love with as a youngster.  He fights gangsters and stuff*.  It's kind of sweet, but we keep cutting back to the stupid gimmick game show, diminishing the sweetness.  Our hero gets a moral test from the smarmy jackass show host (or what Slummy thinks is a moral test), and everyone thinks he is cheating.  Yada yada yada, this freaking movie was freaking voted the freaking best of freaking 2008!?

By the end, I was reminded of my final thoughts about the film, Spider-man 3.  It stinks and the dance scene is the best part.  I guess it doesn't technically count as a scene, but something should go in the film's favor besides the kids.

Slumdog Millionaire is an intense and brilliant drama about a young man (Dev Patel) that is one question away from being the first person to ever win the Hindi version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire. Thanks to an asshole host, Patel is thrown in jail and tortured for being a cheater. As the police grill him for answers, Patel goes in depth on how he knew the answers thanks to critical points in his life where he suffered love, loss, and many instances of inner and outer pain. Through the years, he is accompanied by his older brother, Salim (played by various stages of actors, along with Jamal), who digs further and further into the darker side of life as he gets older, and then there is Latika, the love of Jamal's life who keeps getting taken away from him. The events in Jamal's life lead him up to become a contestant on that show in order to find and be with Latika and to finally leave the life of a slumdog. Very powerful film with a wonderful cast of actors and actresses. This movie was indeed a very good film to watch. Also, what is a Bollywood film without a traditional dance number? Slumdog Millionaire is quite definitely NOT a perfect film by any means, but it has been a long while since anything came along that was this endearing, interesting, well-shot, well-acted, well-scripted, and beautiful to look at all at the same time while maintaining a relatively original plot idea, (though this movie is based of a book I hear).  I think it is enough to say that SM is a worthwhile film in every sense of the word and have the praise remain at that.  Besides, as far as drawing attention, it's always the negative criticism for films which garner wide positive acclaim that seems to be the most interesting.

Just picking the biggest flaw so as not to be nitpicky, I wonder if this film paints a bad picture of India as a whole.  While most reasonable people won't forget that "slumdog" is in the title and realize that this is the story about the poorest and most outcast of India's inhabitants, I think that the film seems to go out of its way to keep India as a whole appearing cramped, polluted, littered with trash, and altogether a third-world.

Furthermore, I couldn't help but feel that while the police may find Jamal's right-place-right-time story "bizarrely plausible," for a cynic, realist, and pessimist like myself, the script's overtones - ringing with words like "destiny" and "true love" - become more fairytale-like and surreal than the stark environments and darkly violent content warrant.  Of course, a film like this would be inconsistent (and ultimately unbalanced) with anything less than a "happily ever after" ending, but with it, I can't help but feel things getting contrived.

But realism aside, cinema is more about escapism I suppose, and SM never claims to be a documentary.  There is much pain and laughter here which work together over the oddest of structures (Who Wants to Be a Millionaire - India flavor) to create something that feels novel and proves endearing.  SM has its flaws, but is the first film in a long time that I've been wholeheartedly glad to have rented.

When I sat there watching Slumdog Millionaire I kept thinking about Charles Dickens. The story is so wrapped into Dicken's lore that it's hard not to fall into that trap. The film follows Jamal (Dev Patel), a slumdog in Mubai, as he becomes orphaned and goes through the hell of trying to stay alive in India with his brother Salim and a girl they stumble on named Latika (Frieda Pinto). As time goes by Jamal sees the slums ground into the earth by the new hotel developments and continues to carry the love he has for Latika, even though he is never in a position to do anything about it. He resorts to becoming a contestant on her favorite television show, the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, going further than anyone has gone before on the show and causing the producers to think that he's cheating somehow.

There are many things that jump out at you in Slumdog. The first is the amazing cinematography director Danny Boyle utilizes to show the scale of the slums and India as a whole. It's almost like a travel video from hell. There's also the performances of the two leads, Patel and Pinto. I've already heard about the numerous offers these two great young actors are getting. In Slumdog you know that Jamal loves her, but you can never really gauge her feelings toward him. Does she love him or not? That's the answer that you die to find out as he film progresses and Pinto plays it up, never letting her hand be seen until the time is just right. Going beyond the two leads there are a pair of performances that are even more amazing. The two children that play the young Jamael and Salim (Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail and Ayush Mahesh Khedekar) were outstanding. I was blown away by the performance they give us in this picture. I'm still in awe over these two kids that atced rings around most of todays adult Hollywood talent.

Slumdog Millionaire seems to have developed an either love it or hate it audience out there. People I talk to seem to be split 50/50 on whether this was as good a film as the Academy would have you believe. It's one of the gems of 2008, a real standout in a year that had its good and had its bad. Did it deserve the Oscar? You can't really answer that because does nay film ever deserve the Oscar. It does earn a place as one of the best films of last year.

The ending is equally as troublesome, reminding me of "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" in terms of how contrived and manipulative it all was. Also, did anyone notice that this movie was shot and edited like a music video? I love Bollywood films and this had no where near the same mystic and passion that it was trying to emulate. I'm also pissed that this movie be brought up in the same sentence, paragraph, yet alone page or essay as "City of God," which wrote the bible on how to shoot a gritty, dirty looking, stylish film such as this. I felt Danny Boyle was trying to prove to us how "cool and street" he really could be. Once again, Hollywood is trying to pull the veil over our eyes on the real tragedies taking place in India by presenting us with this piece of fluff, which has no bearing on the realities and horrors in the region. Another thing, pretty much all the main actors involved belong on soap operas on TV, NOT on the big screen. One more point, the Indian peoples have every right to be offended by the title of the film --I hope the term "slumdog," which I've never heard in my entire life, doesn't catch on as what to refer to the peoples in the slums. Make no mistake, this is a very well-shot film, painting the spice of Mumbai as vividly as possible. The soundtrack is excellent, and I didn't even cringe at the song-and-dance routine at the end (rather awkwardly tacked onto the end). A lot of love obviously went into shooting it. There are some wonderful segments with the children trying to make money through various schemes, and these little asides really do make you smile.

But not of that saves Slumdog from the fact that this is, in the end, yet another underdog competition story. The Who Wants to Be a Millionaire theme is just as grating in the film as it is in real life, and I became so frustrated by the romantic storyline that I wanted to scream. Getting the girl and then accidentally losing her again just makes me very angry. It's a lazy plot device, and I find that a big shame.

The police torture scenes seemed unnecessary, and the pliable nature of the interviewers (softening after the heart-string-tugging story) also made me cross. It all seemed unbearably contrived and wrong.

So... essentially, it's a very beautiful film with a rubbish plot. But what more can we expect in this day and age?!

"Slumdog Millionaire" is by no means whatsoever a perfect piece of filmmaking. What it is though, is a very solid, well written, beautifully shot film. While it might not be the best movie released last year, it is more than worthy of being mentioned in the same sentence. the films tells the story of a boy growing up in the slums of India, who ends up falling in love, then getting a shot at winning a million dollars on the television show "Who Wants to be a Millionaire." At heart this is a love story. The money itself ends up playing second fiddle to the lead - more of a means to an end than anything - and I like that. The performances are solid from top to bottom, and Danny Boyle's frantic camera style works wonderfully here. Despite being shot on a barely there budget, the film has a surprisingly epic feel to it to boot. For all of its good points, and there are a lot, "Slumdog Millionaire" is not problem free. There are a couple moments that Boyle misses the mark emotionally (one of the most noteable coming late in the film). Despite being sold and marketed as a multicultural masterpiece, a case of Bollywood finally meeting Hollywood on its own terms, "Slumdog Millionaire" is anything but. It relies on exploitation and manipulation, presenting "shocking" images and sequences without context or frame of reference and juxtaposing them with artificially cutesy, whimsical scenes of children having the time of their life. This is all edited, photographed and directed with a relentlessly "in your face" almost ADD style which gives the film an effect that is not unlike that of watching a tabloid journalism exposé as filtered through MTV.

The film takes place in India but it may as well take place anywhere as far as Danny Boyle is concerned. Not once does it genuinely feel steeped in a complex culture that can be as terrible as it can be beautiful. That the film is colorful and the actors are are locals means nothing when it is directed with such a dystinctly western sensibility and with such an emphasis on western values. Nothing that appears on the film, save for the architecture, represents hindi culture specifically. By simply changing the names of the characters and the film could well be set in Latin America, Subsaharan Africa, Eastern Europe or the rest of Asia.

The much praised first half of the film is particularly disappointing. The film moves fast and free from one tragedy to the next without considering the implications it is unwittingly raising. Children in slums are survivors. They either do what they have to in order to live or they die. Rather than showing, even momentarily, what a life under these circumstances would truly be like, the movie opts to move right along, focusing only on the great and unrealistic tragedies and the cute and unrealistic whimsies. Anything in between does not exist. A child stealing is represented as cute and amusing, not a trained act of survival. The film's tone, score and direction let us know we are supposed to giggle and smile. A beggar's camp is represented as the pinnacle of evil, with its leader, a pimp with an angelic face, framed in such a way so as to leave no doubt he is the antichrist. When his "secret" is revealed we the audience are expected to nod our heads in understanding and murmur "Yes, this is India." The film is so condescending, so patronizing that it becomes very uncomfortable to even sit through it at times.

The shame of it is this is a very well acted movie with an at times fantastic score. The framing device, while offensive (our lead will finaly achieve happiness, get the girl and the adoration of a nation if he can simply become a millionaire) could ostensibly have worked as a means to reflect back on a life in the slums. The movie took a fantastic opportunity to show the two sides of underdeveloped nations, the wealthy elite and the poverty stricken masses, which coexist not uneasily but comfortably and who are fully dependent on one another, and wasted it. This was never more obvious than during the next-to-last question on the titular game show.

*spoilers*

When Jamal is given the wrong answer to the question by our nefarious host, he ultimately chooses to defy him. The way this scene is handled is indicative of how shallow and manipulative the film is. Jamal, as a street kid, would have learned very early that most adults do not have his best interest at heart. His very survival would have relied heavily on his ability to discern between those who meant him harm and those who meant him well. He would have, instinctively, known to distrust the guy. The film, rather than show this and use this opportunity to shed some light on the cost of extreme poverty and the permanent scarring it would have caused our lead simply treats it as a throwaway moment, yet another in a series of attempts to manipulate the audience.

*end of spoilers*

By the time the inevitable ending comes, the film has revealed where its ambitions truly lie. A Bollywood film could not have ended on that specific shot for obvious reasons. One of the things I had most respected thus far is how it had not felt the need to rely on that particular show of affection. By including it, and as the very last shot of the movie no less, the director all but confirms his picture's disingenuous tone. Danny Boyle, smugly seems to be saying "Yes folks, Bollywood is fine and all that but here's what a REAL Bollywood film looks like, eh? Western style!". This makes the energetic and well choreographed dance sequence that takes place during the credits feel like less of a tribute and more of a condescending pat on the head.

Their is no denying the addictive, entertaining charm of this film. Although some of spoken of this film as being somewhat sensational and gimmicky, there are so many different elements and parts of this film that make this credible. I am inclined to think that part of what may seem sensational in this film is its choice to approach a heavy handed subject with a certain degree of hopefulness, fun and creativity. But I don't agree that the entertaining value causes Slumdog to lose sight of its heavy core. 

It is obvious from the get go that what makes this film stand apart is its notion to do something unique and different. And it certainly seems to succeed in making that accessible, because this film flies along leaving you impacted but entertained all at the same time. The film work alone is a great, oscar worthy achievement. 

What is most telling about this film is that it is not a success as a character drama. This is a film that celebrates all of tis different elements, and a film where the story, the cinematography, the soundtrack and its tone all share different moments on center stage. And that is a result of a film that has many different elements but yet a consistent vision that make it all come alive.

SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE (2008) dir. Danny Boyle cast. Dev Patel, Freida Pinto, Anil Kapoor

Lets be honest, last year was poor in terms of movies, though we had some surprising quality blockbusters like Iron Man, Wall-E and The Dark Knight. Besides those, very few movies seem to have left te audience wanting more but Slumdog Millionaire is one of them. When Danny Boyle makes a new film, nobody knows what to expect, cause the man never does the same thing twice. Here we have a feel-good movie slash hommage to Bollywood when an 18-year-old kid from the slums is a contender on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire ?.

Everything is perfect, the acting, the score, the cinematography and even the emotions are genuine. Everything is crafted in such a way no one can deny its beauty. As Jamal Malik, the main character, is being suspected of cheating, he tells his story and shows how his life seems to have brought him right there, learning the answers to the questions he would one day have to answer on the TV show since his childhood. Though his prescence might be more than just for the money.

Slumdog Millionaire's plot isnt what makes it such an interesting piece of cinema, its mostly the way the Indian culture is presented, the talent involved and the way it all comes down in the end. My only complaint, a ridiculous one I know, would be about the closing credits with all the dancing to pay tribute to Bollywood movies. Seems like it wasnt necessary, even though it might have been, but that doesnt hurt the film and its good for a laugh.

One of the only excessively well-regarded 2008 films I've seen that's lived up to the hype. Danny Boyle's previous film, Sunshine, was quite good despite the less than brilliant turns the film took in its last half hour. With Slumdog Millionaire, everything's turned up to 11 in the best sense possible.

It's heartbreaking watching the film's central characters grow up experiencing all the hardship that they do, and it's in the midst of that hardship and chaos where a love story as pure and simple as the film tells at its core best takes root and thrives, where in most cases, a story like that would falter under scrutiny. There's not a single bad performance in the entire cast.

The soundtrack is stellar, and expertly integrated to complement the story, as you'd expect from Boyle. The direction is strong throughout the film, with numerous stand-out camera and editing techniques used to keep the viewer both viscerally and emotionally invested in the film. And the cinematography and use of color are absolutely phenomenal. Slumdog Millionaire is, on not only the story/acting front, but the technical front as well an excellent example of how to make a fantastic, fresh film in this day and age.

Immediately after the show he is pulled in by the police and is tortured because they believe he has been cheating.  When the police officer shows him the replay tape there are various flashbacks of the mans life that reveal how he knows each answer to each of the questions.  It starts off with Jamal, his brother (Salim) and his other friend (Latika) becoming orphans.  As each question progresses in the millionaire show, Jamal's history also progresses as we learn what happens to him and his loved ones as they grow older. Danny Boyle couldn?t have timed his resurrection as a populist director much better than this. Half the planet is desperate to enjoy a feel-good hit that doesn?t involve Abba songs.

The other half will be astonished by his chutzpah. Slumdog Millionaire is exactly the kind of exotic, edgy thriller that the new generation of Academy voters on both sides of the Pond absolutely adores. The rags-to-riches story is set in the grubby backstreets of Mumbai. Half the script is delivered in Hindi. And the plot is impossibly shallow.

The film starts at the end. Dev Patel?s 18-year-old Jamal is just one correct answer away from winning ? or blowing ? a 20 million rupee (£280,000) fortune on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?

The handsome and terrified youth is an orphan from the gutters of Mumbai. Jamal?s unexpected success on the show over two intense days turns the stuttering youth into a national sensation.

When the programme breaks for the night before the all-important final question, Jamal is bundled through the back door of the television studio, whisked to the nearest police station, and beaten to a pulp by corrupt and jealous cops who want to know how he cheated. This is where the film actually begins.

?What the hell can a slum boy possibly know?? barks the irritated police chief (Irrfan Khan) as a plump minion clips a pair of electric cables to Jamal?s big toes. ?The answers,? spits out Patel?s bruised hero. The plucky martyr reveals how each loaded question asked by the slimy host of Millionaire unlocks a seminal childhood injury.

This being a Danny Boyle movie the precious answers are nailed to brutal scenes. They involve frantic sprints through Mumbai?s crowded markets and grisly flashbacks to medieval slums where the nine-year-old Jamal, and his slightly older psychotic brother, Salim (Madhur Mittal), spend most of their childhood fleeing the clutches of sinister pimps and hungry gangs. It?s terribly Dickensian.

The fairytale power of the film is the way Boyle manages to capture the evolution of the city through the eyes of a child. It?s visually astonishing. The film gets under the skin of the city on every imaginable level. The cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle is an insouciant genius with a camera. You could hang his lush stills of garbage heaps, frowning waifs and skeletal tower blocks in any respectable art gallery. By the same token the film must have been murder to edit.

Jamal?s shocks of growing up alone unfold like dreams: the death of his mother, murdered during a riot; a comic shaking of hands with a Bollywood legend, and then a long litany of ghastly wounds inflicted on fellow urchins by smiling pimps and lethal Fagins.

The rift between the sensitive Jamal and his increasingly domineering brother is the rip that hurts the most. The adolescent orphans barely understand the pain that they inflict on each other. Boyle uses this simmering tension to turn up the temperature at critical moments.

The director has never been shy of manipulating emotions and characters to crank out the maximum screen emotion. The scented backdrops and flavours of Mumbai dilute the crude liberties that Boyle occasionally inflicts on the melodrama.

The fact that these memories stack up into neat answers is spookily inconvenient if you?re a poisonous bastard such as Anil Kapoor?s deliciously smug television host. Or an emotionally detached viewer. Indeed Slumdog Millionaire is guilty of all sorts of implausible twists, not least a thundery long-distance romance between Jamal and a sultry captive beauty (Freida Pinto) forced into prostitution. It keeps pulling at your sleeve like a needy child.

Despite the wobbly structure, Slumdog is a far more sophisticated film than the plot suggests. There isn?t an inch of Merchant Ivory on view. And, like the best parables, Slumdog doesn?t simply plunder India?s troubled past and a boy?s bitter-sweet memories in order to look forward.

What?s great about the film is that it looks sideways as the past and future grind past each other like tectonic plates. It?s the kind of dynamic that Robert Lepage explores so brilliantly on stage. Here, Boyle takes on a bewildering mess of contradictions to make a surprisingly pure point.

Mumbai?s brand new skyscrapers sprout out of patches of mud; Jamal?s old-fashioned principles will forever be out of synch with the slick, nightclub world that his older brother Salim inhabits. And so it goes. The romance? Fear not. It?s fabulous icing.

Danny Boyle's Oscar winning Best Picture is extremely worthy of winning such a prestigious award. You see a problem I have with some films is that the narratives are told near the middle, or afterwards, so if the film is centered on "will this person live?", we already know, which really sucks for the narrative, though we may still be invested in the journey to where they are now. In this film, we start off knowing that the main character answered all of the questions on Who Wants to be a Millionaire? correctly, and is accused of cheating. Instead of focusing on the fact that he got these questions right during the retrospective, we focus on how he knows the answers to these questions, in a move that is written really cleverly, and is really gripping. Boyle's direction is fantastic, carrying a lot of big, great style, and mixes great story with modern elements that people know of. Boyle just really has a knack for crafting great modern stories, and remain relevant, because they do not rely on technology to a point where when proven obsolete, the film sort of seems silly. It's just a really cool story, told with great stylized writing, and it is a wonderful journey through the main character's personal history, and you grow to really care for the three characters throughout time, and it all ends in such a glorious way that one cannot help but feel both a bit sad and happy at the same time. Also, it pays a great homage to Bollywood cinema through it's ending sequence.

I thought it was an enjoyable movie, but I was disappointed. Given that it won so many Oscars (at the time I saw it, it was merely nominated) and the critical acclaim for how "original" the idea was, I had really high expectations coming into the theater. While the series of connecting incidences in his life are interesting, I would hardly call them original. You can find a similar story in "The Great Gatsby." Or really, in any Horatio Alger tale.

The ending was predictable, but I suppose that's to be expected for this rags to riches tale. Rather than what many critics have claimed, this is a film that extols the virtues of capitalism and working within the system. I've heard that it was a condemnation of the caste system, et cetera, but this is not true. Certainly, the major villains in this piece were authority figures (and obvious Snidely Whiplashes, every one of them), but the ultimate goal of the main character is to attain material wealth to attract a girl. And to top it all off, it has a cheesy Love Conquers All motif as garnishing. I'm not saying I don't enjoy a good romance. All the serendipity involved in this film, especially the romance, made it look more silly than sincere.

But enough negatives. Let's talk positives (after all, I did LIKE the movie). The best scene was near the beginning. The part where I thought "this could be a good movie:" the outhouse scene. I won't spoil it for anyone here, but everybody in the theater laughed at that one. I thought the characterizations of the two brothers were realistic and well done. The main character's love interest was the classic subservient woman who Needs a Man (which irked), but it seems to make sense in the context of the story and given her background.

If you should rent it, don't set your expectations too high. It's a good flick to have while eating some popcorn with family or a loved one, but it isn't the Greatest Film Ever, nor is it something that will make you think deeply, whatever pretentions the director may have had.

Slumdog Millionaire deserves a place among the masterpieces of world cinema. Praise is pouring in for this brilliant film, directed by Danny Boyle from a screenplay by Simon Beaufoy adapted from a novel by Vikas Swarup.

The settings move from the bleakest - the slums outside Mumbai, where our hero, Jamal Malik, lives as a child with his older brother Salim - to high rise vistas and no less than the Taj Mahal. The story ranges from the worst despair and heartbreak to the noblest sacrifice and most romantic love.

We are introduced in the opening moments to the young adult Jamal, played by Dev Patel. He is a contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire and has just answered the ten million rupee question prior to the end of the show. His next question will be worth twenty million rupees, an unimaginable fortune to the average Indian. The arrogant, primping star of the show, played with artificial charm concealing an oily narcissism by Anil Kapoor, cannot stand that young Jamal is stealing some of his spotlight, and believes that the young, uneducated "slumdog" is cheating. (One of the key sequences involves the host "proving" to himself that Jamal MUST be cheating.) Jamal has been handed over to the police, who torture him to make him confess his deception. This moment in Jamal's life frames the rest of the film, told in flashback, and explains the torturous road that allowed Jamal to answer even the most difficult questions.

We are not told about Jamal and Salim's father, but in an early sequence we see their mother murdered in a brutal religion riot as club-wielding Hindu's attack a Muslim slum. Orphaned, Jamal and Salim live in the trash dump at the edge of the slum. They befriend another orphan, the young girl Latika.

The remainder of the film fills in the gaps of the lives of Jamal and Salim and Latika, who call themselves the Three Musketeers, but only got far enough in school before the murder of their mother to learn the names Athos and Porthos. Along the way they encounter police brutality, orphanage directors who make Fagin and Bill Sykes look like Mother Teresa, as well as Indian gangsters and other people-traffickers. Several sequences show us that Salim is becoming hardened by their harsh life, although he retains a degree of love for Jamal. For his part Jamal makes the most of what life gives him. He only resorts to the criminal activities Salim sees as the only way to make it out of necessity. At two different times Jamal is heart-breakingly separated from Latika, and at one level the entire film is a love story about Jamal's single-minded dedication to reunite with the only girl he ever loved. (Nine astonishing performances are given of the "Three Musketeers" at three different ages of life, and it is appropriate to give credit to Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail and Rubiana Ali as the youngest Jamal, Salim and Latika as well as Tanay Chheda, Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala and Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar as the just-past-puberty versions. Dev Patel and the beautiful Freida Pinto may become international sensations as the adult star-crossed lovers. Madhur Mittal has less screen time as the adult Salim, but his character plays an important role.)

The faint-hearted should know that the language could appear on American television and that there is no nudity, but the violence, in particular two torture scenes, are flinch-inducing.

Slumdog is a piece of fiction - a fantasy - but it includes real emotions and believable human characters. I walked from the theater feeling a little better about being alive, and knowing that I had just viewed a stunning artistic achievement

To finish I must say, not many films really deserve the Oscar for best Picture and almost none really make you feel greateful with what you have in life, but this movie, deliver on both accounts . . . .

for someone, like me, who's tried dealing with the question of holistically representing the country, sdm provides the much awaited answer. instead of relying on a singular definition of India, it chooses to provide an unabashed episodic overview of contrary Indias that coexist - the perpetually expanding middle class india replete with its call centers and gameshows as well as  the india that is mostly poor; the india that religiously worships one Mr. Amitabh but which can be unscrupulously riotous over religion; where the beauty of the Taj somehow still manages to outshine the surrounding filth and squalor;  and where the hypocrisy of the classes rules the lives of the masses.

it cleverly compiles and strings together such episodes of an out and out Indian existence into a storyline that reveals itself in three places - on the game set, in the police station and in the slums. the from the first question onwards the game only intensifies as the life of jamaal- a muslim boy born into the slums of mumbai- is episodically laid bare.

The more-than-deserved Academy Awards Winner of 2008 is a must-see movie for everyone, whether You are a movie enthusiast or a movie illiterate. The underlying story of the movie is one of the purest signs of true love that was ever displayed in this world and it should serve as an inspiration to all the people who can take a wide array of lessons from the story about a boy, the so-called slumdog known by the name of Djamal who takes on unprecedented challenges and even risks his own life just to fulfill a very simple objective of his, to be reunited with his childhood love, the symbol of the true beauty and female exceptionality, Latika. This movie is a great motivational tool for anybody who has ever doubted that his or her chances of capturing or living that true love story, that so often appears to be elusive for the majority of population nowadays, are mere and even slimmer that it is not even worth trying to pursue such love story.
It is definitely worth it and Slumdog Millionaire serves as a clear proof of that. The Oscar winner takes place in the deep middle of 1980s India when the riots and poverty ravaged all over the country and it made the living in the villages, well slums really for they were not the typical villages as we know it nowadays with only a fairly limited supply of key commodities present. Those were needed to live a meaningful life and not be entrenched in the deep poverty at the same time, but people in India would not get to be as lucky as to get the supply of safe drinking water, healthy fresh food or proper medication to treat their wide-spreading illness and infections. As such they could easily grow out of the proportions and it is those conditions that made everyone who has survived living in those dreadful suburb slums realize how lucky they are to be healthy and most importantly still alive. The movie does a brilliant job of capturing the real-life situation and the unexpected that could arrive at the same time. Djamal would play with his brother Salim one day, when all of a sudden the raging Hindu neighbors would come racing at their Muslim shelters with deadly sharp tools that all too often proved to be the final undoing unless You have not managed to escape many of the deadly diseases that were present in those places everyday. It is exactly during one of these attacks that Djamal's life gets turned upside down and the incredible power of love takes its toll. Djamal's mother is killed during an outrageous attack on their community, but thankfully Djamal and Salim do a great job of escaping from the deadly attacks only to find themselves racing for a tiny little shelter on the hill nearby as the heavens open abruptly. They are little children, aged 6-8 at that time, and sadly they are not the only ones who have lost their families and happy settled passage of the childhood in that one moment of brutality unthinkable in the 21st century. A little girl is standing outside the shelter in the downpour and Djamal shows his first sign of kind heart when he addresses the girl and invites her to join him and his brother. And that's when the love story was ignited.
They live as a little family, stealing things and doing their best to survive in the dreadful conditions when all of a sudden they are discovered by a man who seems quite nice and willing to take care of them. In fact, he is only interested in turning his "possession" of children into real money and the children are forced to go out to streets and beg whole days. Eventually, in order to earn more, the mafias invite them for a late-night session of becoming professional. The objective is to have them recite the poems of the most famous Indian poet. Should they succeed, they should be blinded and turn into golden boys for the mafias. Djamal is close to becoming blinded but since his brother Salim is aware of what is going on, he saves his brother and they manage to escape their own certain death by catching the train leaving the station, Latika, however, does not make it and she is left behind. 
This moment never leaves Djamal's mind and years later he decides to go back for her, yet they are separated again, a dismal situation that repeats couple of times and makes Latika realize how true Djamal's love for her really is. She would certainly not let go the opportunity to escape the highly-dangerous live on the streets of Indian suburbs when Djamal finally becomes that Slumpdog Millionaire. 
The idea behind narrating the love story is brilliant and it is the decisive piece, in my opinion, of what made it the Oscar winner. At the beginning of the 21st century the TV competition "Do You want to become a millionaire?" gained a huge momentum all over the globe and even more so in India when answer 15 questions correctly often meant the only escape from the poverty-drained life. When Djamal meets Latika for the last time before becoming the millionaire, she, due to her pure beauty, the clear favorite of the bandits and wealthy mafiosos is watching the show in the kitchenette and tells Djamal that this is a way to escape the hopeless situation many people find themselves in. Djamal, being completely devoted to Latika, knows that the only way to capture her love and live in the wonderland is to enter the competition and win it. Incredibly, he knows how to get the call from the vast majority who apply to participate as he knows the technical system behind it from the colleague of his who has developed it. Then he is seated into the hot seat and gets question after question, knowing all the answers in the process as they are directly from his life and narration of the movie sequentially continues as each question is asked. 
The viewers, thus, have an unforgettable opportunity to learn about his life and story through his progress in the competition, which he is eventually on the brink of winning. Yet, it seems to be such miracle to the main producer that he does not believe Djamal has made it onto the final question for over 1 million US dollars on merit. But after being beaten and brainwashed by the local police, the investigators realize that "it is the destiny". And that is exactly the main theme of the movie, everything is destiny and now matter how impossible it may seem for anything to become the reality it will eventually. I certainly got a proof of that in my real life. ;)
The only answer Djamal Malik does not know is the one for the last question that poses an inquiry about the third name of the famous musqueteer trio. It is a lovely ending to the competition as it takes the audience back to the first meeting between Latika and Djamal. When she joined him and his brother, they called her the third musqueteer but not in the million years could they remember the exact name of the damned third musqueteer. Now the correct answer meant spending the rest of the life in paradise; or spending the rest of the life on the uncompromising streets of Mumbai. What this movie certainly does not miss is the appetite for the scenes full of actions, anxiety and heart-breaking moments. Djamal eventually decides to call a friend on the phone and to his surprise Latika picks up the phone. She does not help him to find the answer, but just hearing her sweet voice gives Djamal such encouragement that he risks everything on the answer A and... wins! The miracle becomes the reality just as the destiny wanted it and after being separated from Latika for many years, be it due to her just missing on the train, be it due to his brother who locks Latika in the hotel room and shies away his brother with a head of a gun pointing right on him or be it due to money and incredible power exhibited by the richest of casino mafiosos, Djamal's love for Latika has only grown stronger as did hers every time he would find her again and so the only plausible conclusion to Slumpdog Millionaire, the Oscar-winning movie is the meeting of Latika and Djamal on their favorite spot inside the train station when they can finally freely experience the true lovers' kiss for the first time...
In brief, it is a clear recommendation for everyone. The movie is so interesting as it has so many twists and turns that even during the course of this review; I was able to touch on the handful of them. Furthermore, it shows what the reality was like during the late 20th century in India and the cast is brilliant and Djamal (Dev Patel) and Latika (Freida Pinto) contemplate each other all so well and they are the match made in heaven. And last but not least, the movie really teaches us an important lesson, "no matter what You do, or how difficult it may seem to achieve what You really strive for, have a belief and confidence in Yourself and the determination that can best be ignited only by that real passionate love will take You there." Good luck all along the way! And don't forget to bring the whole set of handkerchiefs to the screenplay. ;)

The editing, digital cinematography and Danny Boyle's direction with co-director Loveleen Tandan create a fascinating aesthetic which is perfect for the material. Slumdog Millionaire is very tasteful in almost every respect. The romance scenes are either beautifully understated, most of the scenes with them as children/young teenagers and a couple after that or fantasy melodrama like much of the stuff near the end of the movie, although the actual final pre-credit shot itself is again, a tender and beautiful moment. Even the very realistic and brutally true-to-life scenes involving the raids of Muslim sections of the slums by Hindus and the luring of children to a life of begging on the streets (for gangsters and criminals) in exchange for accommodation and food are done in a manner that is both tastefully evocative of reality while fitting in tone with much of the rest of the movie, which has a more hopeful tone. It sounds improbable, but that's what the screenwriter and director(s) achieve here. The movie doesn't strive for 'gritty realism', but everything in the movie is perfectly evocative of reality. The trouble with 'gritty realism' is that it often is gritty and hopeless in a way life rarely is to most of us, and is actually laughable if done wrong. Like Juno, Slumdog Millionaire is by genre a comedic drama, but it becomes much more. The movie asks questions about fate, righteousness, greed, and even urban sprawl. Above all, however, it asks about love in the face of the most dire obstacles and if it can truly prosper. Jamal K. Malik's story is a tragic and unfortunate one, but as seen through his eyes, it is still beautiful. The vast colour palate of India overwhelm any negative feelings and Jamal K. Malik's hope of finding and being with Latika overwhelm despair. For Jamal K. Malik, 20m rupees isn't his prize. It would be nearly impossible for there to be a better picture this year.

"Slumdog Milionaire" is definitely a feel-good movie - from early on,young Jamal [Dev Patel] wins our hearts as he desperately tries to find his childhood sweetheart Latika [Freida Pinto] by entering the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" Incredulous and sceptical of Jamal's intelligence [after all, Jamal is a 'slumdog'], the show's host [Anil Kapoor] gets him carted off by the police for interrogation. Faced by the cynical inspector [Irfan Khan of "Namesake"], Jamal proceeds to convince the policeman of his innocence by recounting his childhood experiences till the present that accounts for his almost miraculous run of good luck on the show.

I loved the child actors in this show - the ones who played Jamal, his brother Salim and Latika as children were absolutely incredible and wholly credible as street children struggling to survive, falling prey to the most predatory and repugnant of criminals, those who maim children in order that the kids may 'convincingly' beg on the streets to fill the criminals coffers. One of the most horrifying scenes in this movie is the part where the criminal mastermind watches over the removal of a little boy's eyes.

So why only 3 stars you may ask - I liked this movie a lot but I did find that it didn't truly explore the plight of street children which it purportedly aims to portray on-screen. The coverage somehow seems shallow, using the story arc of the child maiming syndicate to shock audiences instead. Perhaps this is due to the fact that I've watched too many Indian movies that deal more convincingly with such themes - "Nayagan" [Tamil, starring Kamal Hasan, a renowned South Indian actor], Thalapathi [Tamil, stars Rajni Kanth], the incomparable Salaam Bombay [1988,Hindi by Mira Nair], and also City of Joy [1992, English, starring Patrick Swayze] all are more credible in showing the plight of street children.

"Slumdog Millionaire" on the other hand is a Bollywood fairytale with a predictably happy ending. It makes one feel good, and in a world filled with cruelty and depravity, most of us are happy to see the fulfillment of Jamal's dreams. But reality is very different, and the majority of street children in India will never experience even a fraction of the success that Jamal attains in this movie. Final verdict: excellent and visually stunning escapist fare.

Hollywood is afraid of movies like "Slumdog Millionaire."  Just take a look at it, and compare it to "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button," another contender for the Best Picture award this past year.  "Slumdog" is a film of shameless idealism, juxtaposing the horrific and the sublime to emphasize those two extremes - the result being a film of such sheer exuberance and beauty that its crystal clear message of hope cannot be overlooked or forgotten.  "Benjamin Button" is far more complex, featuring multiple levels of ambiguity and so many shades of grey that there is no longer a correct interpretation.  Because of this, it is a work of cinematic art, the kind of film Hollywood loves to endorse.  It is also utterly forgettable, because we have seen so many other films similar to it.  So the executives weren't sure what to do with "Slumdog."  They knew it was original and good, but would it draw an audience?  Would it generate any critical acclaim?  I wasn't sure myself how to rate it, at first.  The film is so simplistic, so uncomplicated, and yet so dynamic and emotionally charged.  I enjoyed every minute of it, but was the pure emotion it portrayed enough to justify the presentation of the countless awards it received?  My final answer: absolutely.  Hollywood is wrapped up in themes; it has largely forgotten how to move its audiences, something that "Slumdog Millionaire" excels at.  "Benjamin Button," although an excellent film on its own, celebrated life in roughly the same tone as a eulogy at a funeral.  It felt stiff and self-important, like it was purposefully bucking for nominations.  "Slumdog" throws caution to the wind; it is true and unconcerned with pandering to those determined to analyze it.  Because the immediate experience of watching it is so thrilling and joyful, I find all the arguments of those who find it overrated largely insignificant.  The acting is what it needs to be, and the plot, while episodic, works well and efficiently blends past and present to preserve momentum.  "Slumdog" is not a beautiful film dressed up to look artsy, or to be technically brilliant.  It is simply a beautiful film.  I wish there were more like it.

But occasionally the Best Picture Oscar winner will truly be the best picture of the year, and such is the case with "Slumdog Millionaire".

It is my hope that the film industry begins to allow filmmakers more creativity to present stories that move viewers in the way that "Slumdog Millionaire" has moved the world's population. We deserve better movies, we deserve high levels of excellence. There are great writers and great directors just waiting for that single opportunity to tell simple stories in basic terms. And I hope that Slumdog's example will open the doors for these artists. By doing so, we just may come to understand the global community that is currently sheltered from America. When that happens, we'll all be better for it.

Watching "Slumdog Millionaire" is like watching a familiar story being told in such dazzling way. Telling the story of an orphan from the slums of Mumbai who "luckily" enter "Who Wants to be a Millionaire", the movie fills with lots of "lucky" incident on why he able to answer the question. 

It also tells the "familiar" love story between Jamel and Lathika. Jamel first found her when they were children. Separated by a gangster, Jamel tried hard to be reunited with his girlfriend again. Knowing that Lathika loves to watch "Who wants to be a Millionaire", Jamel decide to enter it.

Although praised by its realistic depiction of slum life in India, some might feel "luckiness" factor in the movie too good to be true. While I agree that the movie feels too gimmicky at some point, but I believe that the luckiness factor is intentional as a tribute to Bollywood movie in general. 

Special notes I also want to give to the music. Don't get me wrong, I am fond of AR Rahman music. The music is able to live up the movie, especially during its first part. But praising AR Rahman with an Oscar for Best Original Score and Best Music for "Jai Ho" (which, based on what IMDB saying, is not a song that specially written specifically for the motion picture) is such a shame.

In the end, is it better than "The Dark Knight"? While it is one of the interesting movies to watch in 2008, I still feel "The Dark Knight" is better.

[i]Consider this a kind of time capsule project. The following is how I believe this year's Oscar winners and nominees will be remembered years from now:[/i]
 
[b]The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button[/b]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS]As far as general popularity goes, I don't think this film will be up there with some of David Fincher's other work, such as [u]Fight Club[/u] or [u]Se7en[/u]. I'm sure it will still be cited as one of Fincher's better films, but maybe not the one the Academy should have recognized. 2007's [u]Zodiac[/u] was a far tighter film and better than most of the other films released that year, No Country included. The person who will most benefit from this film will be Brad Pitt. Pitt has shed so much of that pretty boy image these past couple of years in films like [u]The Assination Of Jesse James By The Coward Robert Ford[/u] and [u]Babel[/u]. I think he will be taken far more seriously as an actor in the future.[/font]
 
[b]Frost/Nixon[/b]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS]The limited release of this film was unholy. It was such a good film and I think as time goes on, more people will see it and it will be recognized as an underappreciated masterpiece, probably Ron Howard's best film up to this point. Frank Langella's performance as Richard Nixon will cited right alongside Sir Anthony Hopkins' depiction in [u]Nixon[/u], probably to much greater acclaim. [/font]
 
[b]Milk[/b]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS]The timing of this film's release couldn't have been better, with the gays rights issues going in California. But, frankly, I feel that may be the biggest reason the film got all the attention and nominations that it got. This film may looked at in the same way as [u]Gandhi[/u]; the celebration was about the film's message rather than the actual film itself. Not to say [u]Milk[/u] wasn't a good film, but it was rather conventional, and if it was released, say, two years back, it may not have made much of a splash. [/font]
[font=Comic Sans MS] [/font]
[font=Comic Sans MS]There's been a lot of fuming over Sean Penn winning Best Actor over Mickey Rouke ([u]The Wrestler[/u]). If you read the polls as to who the public thought should win the award, most of the time, Rourke was the most popular choice. So, I think Penn's win may go down as a sort of Oscar upset, in every sense of the word.[/font]
 
[b]The Reader[/b]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS]When [u]The reader[/u] was announced as a Best Picture nominee, it was a WTF moment for a lot of people. After seeing the film, I think I understand why. It's a film that had good intentions, to try and create an emotional story, but the motivations of the characters are unbelievable and downright silly sometimes. I think the film, once released on DVD and more people can watch it, will have some kind of following. But, the critics and such will probably not look at this movie with much favor. [/font]
[font=Comic Sans MS] [/font]

[font=Comic Sans MS] [/font]
[b]Slumdog Millionaire[/b]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS]From long shot to front runner, [u]Slumdog Millionaire[/u] was the success story (onscreen and off) that Hollywood came to love. The look, the music, the acting, the drama; people (myself included) just loved this movie. It's interesting, however, now that it's won Best Picture and it's box office revenue has dramatically increased, I start hearing more criticism about the film. Most people say it's good, but great? Others have stated the plot is too unbelivable to make good drama. Yes, the plot is a little far-fetched (it's even acknowledged by a character in the movie), but I think the real story was about the main character's survival and reuniting with the woman he loves and the game show plot is used to keep the audience interested and move the story along in a unique way. Maybe they won't put it alongside the best Best Picture winners (it's far from the wrost, I assure you), but I know it will have it's own celebrated legacy.[/font]
 
[b]The Dark Knight[/b]
 
[font=Comic Sans MS]As long as Batman still has a following, as if he was in danger of not having one, the Batman films will continue to be seen and seen again. [u]The Dark Knight[/u] will continue to be recognized as probably the best Batman film made up until this point in time (we'll have to wait a few years to see if Chistopher Nolan can top himself again). Many years from now "Slumdog Millionaire" will be one of the treasures of modern cinema that will be enjoyed by generations for years to come.

Very good. I was very pleased with this film. After being disappointed by fellow Academy Award nominee and locally raved about film "The Wrestler," I'll admit I was a little on edge about watching this film, for fear of disappointment. However I was not let down and was thoroughly entertained (and thoroughly annoyed that I had to split up watching the film into to separate days).

This film IS the "feel good" film of the year as proclaimed on the DVD box, but not TOO "feel goody" to where it drags you down with happiness and positive morals. The story and adventure of Jamal is inspiring in it's own right. And at the end of the day, the film is about love and destiny. The story is great and moving; touching. (And the dance sequence at the end, while seemingly random, actual serves a greater purpose and is very interesting to watch and was creatively put together with it shifting from full-on dance number to what seem to be group "practices" in the empty train station with the "past," "middle," and "present" characters, shifting between the three. I consider it the alternative to a blooper reel.) My only gripe is that some of it was kinda predictable after a certain point - but with a feel good film, they all are somewhat the same - either the main character wins it all, or wins half and counts his blessings rather than his losses; the steps to get those points are pretty much the same across the board. 

The camera work is very good as well. The constant focus shifts are a bit hard on the eyes in close ups, but are otherwise very good and help emphasize things (as well as add a sense of independence to the film). One of my favorite shots is a low angle b-roll shot of a street and people walking on it. In this shot, Danny Boyle has his fourth wall broken as passing security guards tell the cameraman "no filming" (after which of course, the scene cuts to a different shot). This got quite a chuckle out of me (for both the incident itself and Danny's choice to put it in the film (after all it's not something you can go "oops missed that, didn't know he said that" nor is is something the audience will miss)).

All in all this is a great film and, while not on my personal favorites list, should still be watched soon as you can.

Slumdog is a movie that, above all else, is driven by the careful organization and deployment of plot; it is a movie about structure, and framework, rather than through development of characters. This is a modern example of magic realism, a genre that favors original and captivating storytelling and precise plotting over fully fleshed out characters, who are generally developed only enough to leave an impression. The story is about Jamal (Patel), a young man hailing from impoverished Mumbai who ends up on India's version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?; more accurately, the story is about how his life is structured in such a way that he is able to answer the game show's questions, and (or can he?). At the center of it all is a story of true love, perhaps a bit of a cliche but a cliche that is made fresh by Boyle's utterly engaging storytelling. With Freida Pinto and Anil Kapoor, having the time of his life as the game show host.

They did a good job setting the story up from facing the pressure of the game-show answers to his destitute past,but--- this was DEFINITELY NOT worthy of the 2009 Best Picture Oscar.Call me a disgruntled "Dark Knight" fan still seething at the "Little Critical Darling" taking the prestige prize from the "Generic Popular Movie",but the emotional tension feels forced,instead of natural.It may have an interesting story to it and a unique cast,but that certainly won't hold your interest during the entire film's run time.

Slumdog is a rare treat that almost never comes around in mainstream films. Boyle has created a multicutural fairytale unlike any before it, even when it has the cliches. 
   Slumdog Millionaire takes place in modern day India, Jamal, who is on an Indian game show "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" He is from the poverty ridden area and seems uneducated and many already foreshadow a quick loss, yet he keeps getting the answers right, but how? From this, the movie sidetracks with many background stories in his life and shows, friendship, love and respect even in the worst of conditions. Ultimatly, giving a powerful and fairytale-like ending. This movie themes not only a struggle with soicety but the protaganist himself in a classic, yet innovative way.

Boyle creates a complex, beautiful and well crafted film with massive exotic settings and vibrant colors of Indian culture. Slumdog Millionaire (seen it at last!) is an overall masterful achievement. From the novel (which I found out is "Q&A" by Vikas Swarup) to the screenplay by Simon Beaufoy (who wrote for Among Giants and the Full Monty) all the way to the on-screen command and direction by Danny Boyle.

After having seen "Sunshine" not too long ago, I came to the conclusion that Boyle gives privilege to aesthetic rather than plot. In Slumdog, however, he proved me wrong and successfully combines a good story with fascinating shots and character development as well as intelligent use of sound and music - all that at fantastic pace and avoiding the temptation of becoming a Bollywood movie (the danse at the end is basically a mocking message from Boyle about that).

Besides, Boyle and his crew manage to combine elements of drama, comedy, rags-to-riches and even Tele-reality. The way the cop questioning of Jamal on how he cheated reminded me of the scenes in Usual Suspects when Chazz Palminteri confronts Kevin Spacey. 

Slumdog is rich in emotion and a praise for courage and love in the ever-changing developing world. I am usually irritated with children in lead roles, but here I thought that they were very well cast and authentic.

I have never been to India and therefore Boyle's vision of poverty and slums as well as the modern Mumbai and the Taj Mahal seemed stunning and representative of the idea I have of the country. I wonder what people of Mumbai think.

I suspect Slumdog has two audiences - those who love the film and those who find it irritating for the reasons I have outlined above. 

Personally, I think Slumdog must be watched for the overall pleasure it provides and then one can decide whether it deserves all the hype and oscars. If I had to choose who deserved the oscar, I'd go for the Wrestler, which was also nominated. I enjoyed it but for totally different reasons than Slumdog.

Grabbed many Oscars as the best movie of the year. Unlike many other Oscar winners, this movie has a simple storyline and it requires no deep thoughts. It tells about how a slum Indian boy wins in the Indian version of "Who Wants To Be a Millionaire". The movie focused on how Jamal Malik answered most of the questions correctly from the contest, although some questions were based on his luck. Most of the right answers came from his real-life experience and his hard-time childhood memories as a slum. However, the purpose of joining the contest is not to get the prize, but to capture the attention of his beloved childhood sweetheart Latika, who is an ardent fan of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire". It was a good movie, however I don't think it's worth that many Oscars. Perhaps the featuring of Indian culture, slum and poverty appeals to the Western audience as it provides different view and culture compared to the usual Hollywood blockbusters. Personally, I still prefer the story and cast from "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button" which I think is worth more Oscars that what it actually got.

I waited way too long to see this movie.  Turns out all the hype was not hype at all, just well-deserved praise for one of the top 5 movies of my lifetime (that's 54 years to you & me, son!).

Slumdog has it all... rags to riches, love-conquers-all, the inhumanity of humanity, the kind of truthiness that laughs in the face of tortured interrogation merely because one knows one is right, if not in factual answer then (more importantly) in goodness of heart and purity of intention.

The third world of the slums of Bombay/Mumbai collides with first-world reality TV gone wild in the form of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?", the popularly syndicated international game show, as a backdrop to this timeless tale of triumph over adversity, brother seemingly against brother and then brother selflessly, finally, and when it counts most, making the ultimate sacrifice not only for the other brother, but for all that is good and right in the universe.

The scenes of this story run the gamut from the most heart-wrenching and violent loss of goodness and innocence, to the glee of playful childhood, to the purity of love in its truest form, to the desperation of poverty and the glory of murder for undreamed of sums of money.  All of these are captured beautifully on film, in a way that burns them onto one's heart with tentacles wrapped around one's soul.

If you've seen it, you know what I mean.  If you haven't, you really must.  And if this film doesn't tug at your heartstrings in the least, well... you better see a good cardiologist.
