Many believe that an unseen force controls the world. Since man came to be, we assumed that such an indefinable higher power existed that brought forth and manipulates us all, thus rendering coincidence non ? existent, making us conclude that everything, arguably, has been ?planned?. To get our heads around such an unfathomable theory, we have conveniently created ?gods? to define this seemingly cosmic energy which we believe rules our lives. But, whether how many more religions we may come up with to resolve our unexplainable existence, we forget that we already came up with one word that may very well explain all the innumerable occurrences of life. And that is destiny, the core of the beautiful story that is Slumdog Millionaire.

              To best stress this point, the film, once it began, opened with a question: ?"Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million rupees. How did he do it?? The viewer was presented with four possible answers to choose from. (A) He cheated, (B) He's lucky, (C) He's a genius and (D) It is written. 
          
      To understand and be able to answer this inquiry, you must first know who Jamal Malik is, how he arrived at the cusp of winning such a fortune and what took place that made it possible for him to nearly win it.
         
       Jamal Malik (played by recently unknown Indian actor Dev Patel) was the poor Indian boy fated for greatness whose life the film revolved around, along with his equally fated older brother Salim (played by also unknown Madhur Mittal) and the eternal love of Jamal?s life, Latika (played by the lovely Freida Pinto, who also happens to be an unknown Indian actress).
         
        Though jarring at first, the storyline of Slumdog Millionaire started at the edge of its climax where Jamal was shown being tortured by two police officers (played by Irrfan Khan and Saurabh Shuklah), forcing him to confess to  allegedly ?cheating? his way to nearly winning 20 million rupees in India?s top game show, Who Wants to be a Millionaire?
        
        Growing up as a ?slumdog? child who ended up becoming a lowly coffee attendant at a local call center; some, especially the host of Who Wants to be a Millionaire (played by Anil Kapoor), doubted that Jamal could ever know all the winning answers, so much so that the game show host himself had him hauled off for ?intense? interrogation so he?d fess up to the assumed crime.
      
         When they realized that ?conventional? torture wouldn?t work, the officers decided to question Jamal and make him explain how he knew the answers. From here, the real story of Slumdog Millionaire began.
      
          As simple yet bizarre as it may seem, Jamal told the officers plainly that it was through his life experiences that he got to know about the answers. Guiding them through every query he correctly responded to, Jamal recounted all the periods in his life from when he learned, heard, or read about all the answers; brought to life in vivid detail by Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tandan, the film?s directors.
    
          Jamal and his older brother Salim were typical Indian children who lived wretched lives in the slums of Bombay, India. As if life wasn?t hard enough for them, Jamal and Salim were suddenly made orphans when a mob of crazed Muslims attacked their village, killing many innocent people, including their mother. With no one else to turn to, Jamal and Salim were forced into the streets. It was when they became orphans that Jamal and Salim met the person who would singularly influence their fates: Latika, a village girl who also lost her parents when the Muslims razed their village. Together, they grew up as beggars living off garbage across Indian slums. 

         One day, a seemingly good man named Maman (played by Ankur Vikal) took them to his secluded compound to take care of them along with other orphans. At first, Jamal, Salim and Latika considered Maman a God send whose saintly virtue was the answer to their plight. But they soon found out that Maman was actually an evil child abuser who took orphans off the streets to make them work for him as a syndicate of street urchins.
     
           Once they discovered this, Salim, Jamal and Latika fled. Pursued by Maman and his henchmen, Salim and Jamal clambered onto a train to escape. The not so agile Latika tried to board the train as well, but was swatted away by Salim; clearly jealous of the budding love between Latika and Jamal.
    
          Free from Maman?s clutches, but left with no means to take care of themselves, Jamal and Salim were forced to work as illegal hawkers aboard trains and fake Taj Mahal tourist guides. 
    
         For a time, Jamal and Salim were able to fend for themselves. Enough so that Jamal was able to save enough money to return to Bombay, despite the refusal of Salim, to find Latika. Even with the years that went by, Jamal never forgot about her.
    
         Once he arrived in Bombay, Jamal discovered that Latika was alive and well, but was being pimped as a prostitute by Maman in a brothel at Pila Street, one of India?s red light districts. Jamal then stormed to the brothel, intending to save Latika. But, when he got there, a stand ? off ensued between him and Maman who held a grudge against him and Salim for managing to escape long ago. The stand ? off was broken when Salim suddenly appeared, brandishing a pistol and threatening to kill Maman and his men. Salim escaped with Jamal and Latika after he shot Maman in the head.
    
         Finally free of Maman, the trio hid in a decrepit hotel and spent the night. Envious of the openly affectionate Jamal and Latika, Salim left them for the evening, but returned the following morning and man handled Latika away from Jamal, furious with jealousy. He claimed Latika for himself and ordered Jamal to leave. Although refusing to at first, Jamal yielded when Latika told him to after Salim threatened him with the pistol he murdered Maman with the day before.
     
         Jamal never heard from Salim and Latika again in the many years that followed. But, as Fate would have it, he was able to contact them at the call center he worked at as a coffee server. Salim asked to meet with him, who was now a henchman of Javed (played by Mahesh Manjrekar), one of India?s crime lords. 
     
          Once they met, Jamal nearly beat Salim to death, never having forgotten about how he stole his beloved Latika away from him. But, despite being enraged towards him at first, Jamal ended up forgiving Salim and even accepted his offer to move in with him. While living with Salim, Jamal was overjoyed to discover where his Latika was. As it turned out, Latika now lived with Javed as his wife. 
     
          Salim went to Javed?s mansion and managed to get inside, pretending to be a newly hired dish washer, and finally met the beautiful, all grown up Latika. All the love between them was still ablaze. But, sadly, Latika forced Jamal to leave when Javed came, telling him that it was far too late for them to be together.
     
         Undaunted by this, Jamal continued to pursue Latika, telling her before he left that he?ll wait for her every, single day at the train station until she came. Eventually, she did. They could?ve almost left, scot free, if only Javed hadn?t discovered about their clandestine rendezvous. To curtail their departure, Javed sent Salim to capture and return Latika to him. Salim succeeded.
   
         Desperate, Jamal decided to play on the show Who Wants to be a Millionaire, hoping to win the top prize which will enable him to have Latika. 
    
        Against all odds, Jamal was able to answer all the questions right, all the way to win 10 million rupees. Correctly answer one question more and he would win the grand prize of 20 million rupees, if only people would believe he did know all the answers despite being poor and uneducated.
   
       After Jamal finally told his entire life story to the two police officers, they let him go, moved and convinced by his life?s tale, to have a chance at winning the 20 million rupee fortune.
   
        Unknown to Jamal, Salim was finally having a change of heart. Having realized just how much his younger brother loved Latika after seeing him on Who Wants to be a Millionaire, Salim decided to let her go and kill Javed, knowing that she and Jamal would never be left in peace as long as Javed was alive. He managed to achieve both, resulting in his death after a skirmish resulted between him, Javed and his men after they discovered that he had let Latika escape. 
    
          On the show, Jamal was stumped by the 20 million rupee question, ?what is the name of the 3rd musketeer?? He decided to use his remaining life line, call a friend, to contact his brother Salim, hoping he knew the answer. Much to his surprise, it was Latika who answered to whom Salim gave his cellphone to before letting her go. She told Jamal she was fine and that she didn?t know the answer either. Jamal finally submitted to chance and made a wild guess. Miraculously, Jamal chose the right answer and won the 20 million rupee prize.
   
           Once the show was over, Jamal went to the train station one last time where he met Latika. There, they finally fell into each other?s arms and sealed their destined love with a kiss.
    
          If you haven?t realized it by now, Slumdog Millionaire is a typical love story about star ? crossed lovers who go through many trials and tribulations in life

        Even though this type of tale has been told and retold countless of times through equally countless permutations, what?s so brilliantly captivating about this movie was how Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tandan made this eternal type of tale their own.
  
          Sure, Slumdog Millionaire was a love story. But such an epic, impeccably crafted, and well ? told love story it was; made even better when Boyle and Tandan juxtaposed the progression of the movie?s core love storyline between Jamal and Latika with the retelling of their tragic and poignant lives along with Salim?s as they grew together; framed by a panoramic and candid view into the lives of people in India which, in the movie, was always blighted with poverty and crime.
    
            On that note, I just loved the exhilarating and creative way Boyle and Tandan shot this film, employing fresh, dynamic and effective cinematography to evoke within the viewer the intended emotion in every scene.
    
           Yet, despite winning 8 Academy Awards, I still personally think that this movie wasn?t quite as perfect as many have lauded it to be.
   
            First and foremost, I didn?t really like the performances of the cast. Sure, I knew they weren?t exactly well ? known and seasoned actors and actresses. I?m not saying either that all of their performances were total trash. Given the quality and depth of this movie, I?m just saying that I expected more from all of the actors so as to at least give justice to how good the story was.
  
           Moreover, being that this film was obviously all about the story, I?ll have to say that the script was pretty bland. 
  
           Assessing the movie from a technical point of view, I?m not sure that the film?s soundtrack was the best choice for it and, as I?ve already mentioned before, the cinematography got pretty confusing a couple of times, despite how good it was.
   
            Lastly, though it was admittedly fun to watch, I?m not sure either that the surprising bollywood number was appropriate to accompany the ending credits. 
   
          Nonetheless, this film may very well be one of the best movies ever made.

          If you haven't seen this movie yet, please do yourself a favor and go watch it.

Iâm more or less prepared to drink the Kool-Aid on Slum Dog Millionaire.  Itâs a pretty compelling movie, though a very traditional one at heart.  It is essentially a love story (boy meets girl, overcomes tremendous obstacles to win girl); whatâs different here is the setting of India, and in particular the slums of Mumbai.  The portrayal of urban poverty, especially in the first half hour or so, is stunning.  Seen through the eyes of seven-year-olds, it is not so much a life of deprivation, but one of frantic, often exuberant, and inexplicable action.  The mother of the brothers Jamal and Salim, is cut down in an anti-Muslim riot while washing clothes (anti-Muslim sentiments are an undercurrent throughout.) and they become orphaned street children (no reference is ever made to their father).  Along with another little girl, Latika, they take under their wing, they soon are sucked into the cityâs criminal underworld, a world that Jamal embraces and Salim keeps at armâs length.  So, in addition to its traditional love story, it is Hollywood in the plot line in which one brother turns to evil and the other remains, if not pure, at least on the side of the angelsâ traditional even to the extent that the evil brother eventually sacrifices himself for the good.  (Didnât Cagney and Bogart do this gig?) By their early teens Jamal has killed one of their gangland oppressors; he takes Latika as his mistress, and rejects his brother.  Five years pass, and Salim has found honest work as a tea server and, after futile attempts to relocate Latika, he decides the only way to reconnect is for him to appear on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. That he is able to do so, and that the questions he gets happen to be answerable from his experiences as a âslum dog,â requires viewers to suspend their disbelief, but itâs worth it as the movie ends (who wouldâve guessed?), with the loversâ kissing, reunited at last.  The film is really dark and violent, not for the kiddies. Director Danny Boyle (Trainspotting) used real slum kids for the roles of the boys at seven, but actors for them at 13 and 18.  Iâm not fully sold on the actors in the final phase, and the lack of physical resemblance at the various ages is a bit disconcerting.  Itâs a feel-good movie, except for the poverty and violence, which makes for an odd mix.  Stick around for the credits; thereâs a fun dance sequence in the train station.

The films of Danny Boyle have always been a bit of a mixed bag for me.  I consider "Trainspotting" to be on my top ten film of all time, "The Beach" was a disappointing piece of flotsam and "28 Days Later" fell somewhere in the middle for me.  "Slumdog Millionaire" is certainly in the top tier of the British filmmaker's pantheon.  Despite all the media coverage, clips you might have caught just from "entertainment osmosis" and all the critical hype, this flick still managed to be consistently surprising.  Tonally, the film is borderline schizophrenic.  From Jamal's harrowing origins in the slums of Mumbai to nearly slapstick moments as he and his brother try to survive as thieves, from the tension of the game show scenes to the Bollywood dance extravaganza of the closing credits, the audience is pulled in a myriad of different directions emotionally.  The performances are a quirky and hypnotic match for the film visual verve.  Dev Patel and Freida Pinto make for a winning couple and it's borderline torture to watch them get separated by cruel circumstance over and over again.  Madhur Mittal, who plays Jamal's older brother Salim, has us guessing constantly with his changing loyalties and Anil Kapoor's smarmy game show host is note-perfect. The kids that play the main characters at earlier stages of their lives are also a tremendous asset to the film's appeal and one hopes that they won't be allowed to vanish back into anonymity.  Danny Boyle has always been a strong visual filmmaker and the color palette he has to work with in exotic India really plays to his strengths.  This certainly deserves it's rightful nod as one of the best films of 2008.  Tilt: up.

The visually varied and well acted "Slumdog Millionaire" might still be amongst the weakest films to ever win Best Picture.

Where to start?

Okay, first: It's difficult to believe this film is only two hours long. It felt like an easy three. The pacing, to put it mildly, is wildly uneven. The format of a question being asked to Jamal in the present day, followed by a flashback to how he happens to know the answer, got old quickly.

For that matter, I could not swallow how the questions ALWAYS coincided perfectly with a memorable event in his past. I have no problem suspending my disbelief in movies. Ever. However, this screenwriter took an approach so convoluted that it pushed me away from his movie instead of drawing me in. It reminded me of "Memento", and not in a good way.

The ending is hilariously contrived and predictable, and the attempt to make a villain out of the show host is awkward and never fully developed. Jamal's kidnapping and torture happens, and the film never makes anything of it nor gives a believable reason for it.

These examples highlight the central problem in "Slumdog" - poor writing. I have never disagreed with the Academy more. For all the frenetic direction by Boyle and the dynamic performances by some very young actors, it's not as inspiring as it wants to be because it deals in idiot plot contrivances as opposed to realistic behaviors, and cheap platitudes as opposed to real emotions.

Dialog example:

Jamal: Come away with me.
Latika: And live on what?
Jamal: Love.

That is all.

Also, do not get me started on "Jai Ho", the song which plays over the end credits in a scene which reminds me of the "Age of Aquarius" dance sequence at the end of "The 40 Year-Old Virgin".

Poorly paced, poorly written, and endlessly trite, "Slumdog Millionaire" deserved not a single one of its Oscars. I'm not one of those pretentious hipster-types who takes joy in ragging on everything popular, but this just isn't a great film. It's adequate, but it's one of the strangest success stories in Hollywood history.

Overrated in the extreme, and once people remove the stars from their eyes, I predict a major backlash on the level of what we saw when the hubbub over "Titanic" had subsided. Only with 'Slumdog', the backlash will actually be deserved.

I can't quite put my finger on why I don't like Danny Boyle's movies. I think it's because the storyline/plot, while usually interesting and ambitious, for me always seems to trump genuine character development. 
I thought the story was kind of unbelievable and that behind the scenes of a game show would be nothing like what was displayed on screen, but then again, what do I know, and what perspective do I have, especially about India. They make this huge deal about how Jamal is uneducated and how nobody can win the million because the questions are too hard, but jesus, the questions all seemed relatively easy to me. I mean seriously, they're torturing him because they think he's cheating? Is it that hard to imagine someone actually knowing the answers to these relatively easy questions, educated or not? And by what means could he even be possibly cheating? Jamal uses the ask the audience lifeline on the most BLATANTLY obvious one, that every single person around the world over the age of five would be able to use basic deductive reasoning to figure out. I mean, I don't think we should be able to have it both ways. I mean, is he bright, or braindead? If he was truly street smart, he'd be able to figure it out. That's just lazy screenwriting.
How could a relationship between brothers turn so sour? It just feels so forced, and puzzling. I mean, they had the same upbringing, so what gives? Why would you abandon your one true companion in a harsh, unforgiving life? And I thought the "love interest" had no personality and no purpose but to just be the love interest, but then again maybe that was the point, because she was being almost dehumanized. But I mean, there's no screen time whatsoever devoted to showing Jamal and her develop any sort of actual relationship or bond. It's like they're just doing their jobs to service the somewhat predictable end of the story.
Above all, I thought the movie was boring, and I just didn't really care. Sorry.

The story of Jamal Malik, an 18 year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai, who is about to experience the biggest day of his life. With the whole nation watching, he is just one question away from winning a staggering 20 million rupees on India's "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" But when the show breaks for the night, police arrest him on suspicion of cheating; how could a street kid know so much? Desperate to prove his innocence, Jamal tells the story of his life in the slum where he and his brother grew up, of their adventures together on the road, of vicious encounters with local gangs, and of Latika, the girl he loved and lost. Each chapter of his story reveals the key to the answer to one of the game show's questions. Each chapter of Jamal's increasingly layered story reveals where he learned the answers to the show's seemingly impossible quizzes. But one question remains a mystery: what is this young man with no apparent desire for riches really doing on the game show? When the new day dawns and Jamal returns to answer the final question, the Inspector and sixty million viewers are about to find out. At the heart of its storytelling lies the question of how anyone comes to know the things they know about life and love.

I did not want to give this movie five stars; maybe because of all the hype and positive criticism this film has received.  But if I didn't give this five stars, I would not be honest.  The movie was brilliantly crafted realism with shades of romanticism reminiscent of such literary works as The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and such movie masterpieces as Apocalypse Now.  To ignore the brilliance of this instant classic just because it received some awards would be a crime.

Where should I begin?  With the masterful character development?  The perfect soundtrack by A. R. Rahman and M.I.A.?  The parallelism between the main character Jamal's appearance on Millionaire and his life growing up?  The  lessons that one can learn from the film?  The beauty of the romantic subplot, one of the few romances that I have seen add to the value of the film overall?  The realistic dialogue?  The peerless acting?  The creative cinematography?

It is rare that I see all of the elements of a movie work in harmony as they do in Slumdog Millionaire.  Don't let the fact that some negative reviewers have found themselves carried away by a sense of jealously and misguided elitism deter you.  There is a reason that so many highly qualified critics have praised this film, and it is not because it is shallow or easy to watch.  Do yourself a favor and don't miss this one.

Jamal Malik has made it onto India's version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire, but how he got there is even more amazing than a 'slumdog' like him making it onto the show. We see Jamal's childhood, his ups and downs, everything from getting the autograph of an Indian action movie star to the murder of his mother at the hands of a mob. He's not alone, though. He has his brother Salim and over the years they go from being pan handlers working for a greedy criminal who uses children to lower class employees. Through it all Jamal carries a huge torch for a woman named Latika whom he grew up with and has been kept apart from either due to tragic circumstance or by others stopping him. The only reason he goes on the Millionaire show is because he knows she watches it and he believes that if she can just see him one more time, she will come to back to him. 

Wonderfully shot and spectacular acting, especially from the Indian children who play Jamal, Salim and Latika in their younger years. It's no mystery why this got so many accolades all over the world, though it's a different story for why our Hollywood went ga-ga over it. Every year they need some foreign film to focus on, making themselves look cultured and sophisticated. Most of the time they choose some foreign film that didn't get much attention outside of its home country, but when a world wide hit like Slumdog or The Lives of Others comes along, they have to choose it or else they will look like the pandering, arrogant bastards that they are. Don't see this because Hollyweird gave it a bunch of nominations and won 8 Oscars while that jackass Ryan Seacrest made fun of the Indian children from the movie who came all the way from India to be at the Oscar Awards. See it because this is a beautiful and moving film.

Slumdog Millionaire is certainly a triumph for Danny Boyle, and I am truly happy for all his success with the film. He found a reasonably mainstream story and added enough "Danny Boyle" to the film to keep it unique.

What keeps the film alive (at least for me) is everything other than the plot, which Boyle has always mastered. The colors jump right off the screen in such a natural fashion. The score is almost hypnotic. Slumdog has its own aura, just like Sunshine and Trainspotting before. Boyle never really hits you over the head with his artistic talent, he likes to sneak up on you like that fifth glass of Jack and Coke at the work party. 
 
Anyways, I enjoyed feeling the film more than watching the film if that makes any sense.

To end the year of 2008 is to review the Oscar winning Bollywood/British production, and adaptation from the novel: Slumdog Millionaire.
It is the story about an Indian kid who enters a quiz show and seemingly knows every single answer because of his past experiences. The prime achievement of Slumdog Millionaire is the direction and method that goes into innovatively adapting the amazing story from the book. It has been ignored for acting nominations but the heart of this film is Dev Patel, managing to give an outstanding and brave debut perfomance as well as the turn of tide generated to the audience from the constant turns of the relationship between Jamal and Salim, as the audiences half way through would want the two brothers to be together. When they are against each other's throats and the viewers feel sad, then that is the success of the film. Another thing about this clearly amazing feature is how it is edited as well as using the important issue of the Indian slum dwellers in Mumbai to provoke the mind as a background of the hero's journey. It is certainly well deserving of the best picture award and becomes the most emotionally captivating film of the year with particular credit going to A.R. Rahman for his dramatic and powerful music added for the film.

He grows to be a man committed to truth as well as living out his highest desire, which in this instance simply being with the person he loves the most. With a single focus he never seems to forget even over length time separations and a vast array of circumstances.

Me?  I didn't love Slumdog Millionaire.  I just couldn't, even upon a second viewing.  Why?  First and foremost I found the film to be incredibly manipulative.  Obviously it's not uncommon for film's to manipulate.  Strike an emotional chord early on to pull your viewers in.  It's nothing new.  But sometimes it becomes so blatantly obvious that nothing is really earned here.  Your expected to follow along because by doing so you will feel good at the end.  So we start with the harrowing backstory of young Jamal, Latika and Salim, orphaned due to the cruelty of their enivironment and forced to make it on their own.  We see the young Jamal seperated from the young Latika who he obviously knows is his "true love" or why else would the adult Jamal endure torture for being the smartest person ever to be on India's version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire".  Because it's all about love and this is the only way she can find him.  It's destiny!  Of course to insure we get the desired "feel good" ending we have to make bad guys REALLY bad, the conditions deplorable and the odds seemingly insurmountable.  Of course the entire plot's implausible but who cares, it's destiny!  No grey zone here.  I mean not only will you be leaving this film with a smile on your face, you will be dancing with a smile on your face thanks to the closing credits!  You've been programmed to feel good!  Hooray!
 
After seeing this a second time I liked it even less.  It reminds me of "Crash" which was probably the other most blatantly manipulative film I've seen the past 4-5 years.  And another that fares worse with each subsequent viewing.  Slumdog may not be an awful film afterall it looks and sounds great, but it's awfully smug in how it approaches it's audience.  I know I'm in the minority but I'm not buying the hype.  
 
[b]The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008) - 7.3/10[/b]
Director - David Fincher
Starring - Brad Pitt, Cate Blanchett, Taraji P. Henson, Tilda Swinton, Elias Koteas, Julia Ormand, Jason Flyming, Jared Harris.
 
I guess if I'm going to be so harsh on "Slumdog" I shouldn't go easy on "The Curious Case of Bejamin Button" either.  Except I liked it more.  
 
Implausible?  Yes, but what isn't.  Manipulative?  Well sure, especially the whole deathbed flashback storytelling.  But it still doesnt feel as "in your face" as Slumdog.  It's a melancholy film.  Benjamin (Brad Pitt) is born with the body of an old man, but the mind of child.  His body goes one way (younger) and his mind goes the other way.  He meets Daisy (Cate Blanchett) when she is a child and they eventually hook up as she gets older (and he gets younger).  There you go!
 
Essentially this is "Forrest Gump" in reverse, just not quite as good.  That film received quite a bit of critical backlash after the fact.  You know for being overly sentimental, being manipulative and for being a too much of a self-serving ode to the Boomer generation.  But it was pretty unique in it's day and had a character so simple, yet so charming, that it was easy to go along for the ride.  Benjamin Button, his "curious" condition aside, isn't nearly as memorable as Forrest.  And despite it covering a much longer period than Gump, it doesn't feel as nostalgic.   So for brief periods the film just felt gimmicky, reliant on a "curious condition" that allowed many visual effects, but not much else.  That changed however when Cate Blanchett (adult Daisy) enters the picture.  Ironically at this stage both characters are nearest their real ages and the picture relies less on visual effects and more on the chemistry between the two characters.  It's quite moving and easily the best part of the film.  Of course they know as we know that it can't last forever because Daisy is getting older while Benjamin is getting younger but it's touching to watch it play out.  
 
In the end it doesn't quite measure up to "Forrest Gump" but Fincher quietly guides this sentimental journey rather than hammering away like "Slumdog".  It doesn't end up as a classic, but it's a worthwhile journey nonetheless.
 
[b]Taken (2009) - 3.5/10[/b]
Director - Pierre Morel
Starring - Liam Neeson, Maggie Grace, Famke Janssen, Leland Orser, Katie Cassidy, Jon Gries.
 
Bryan Mills (Liam Neeson) is an ex-CIA operative who takes an early retirement so he can spend more time with his estranged 17 year old daughter Kim (Maggie Grace).  Of course his ex (Famke Janssen) hates him and she has married up since they split.  When Kim wants to travel to France with her 18 year old friend Amanda, Bryan is hesitant.  But not wanting to alienate his daughter he agrees to let her go where she's immediatly kidnapped by some meanies who intend to sell her and Amanda as sex slaves.  Bryan has 96 hours to find her and kill the bad guys!
 
One of the surprising early 09 box office hits, this film offers everything action junkies love.  A generic easy to follow storyline with a very quick set-up, a take no-names badass, and non-stop action.  It helps if you have a pair too.  Balls not boobs, because it's definitely one of those mindless testosterone popcorn flicks.  Hey I admit action isn't my favorite genre but I can appreciate an action film that has a shred of originality or doesn't use the same cookie-cutter characters, but there isn't anything original here so I can't help but laugh when adrenaline junkies get a hard-on for this film.  90% fresh according to RT users.  Really?  I mean when our hero (on foot) is chasing a speeding car that's true comedy!  Except it's suppose to be intense.  Suspenseful.  And who would you take in a fight, 20-30 crazed Albanians, or one middle-aged Liam Neeson?  I mean it's not even fair.  Those poor Albanians don't have a chance.  I've seen this film too many times.  You can change the actor, or the bad guys, but the same approach equals the same film.  Maybe I should grow a pair.  Not!

Slumdog Millionaire, winner of 8 Oscars including Best Picture in 2008. This low-budget, sleeper hit captivated audiences and critics alike. By the time I got around to viewing this film, its reputation preceded itself. Slumdog is an endearing film that centers around a poverty-stricken "slumdog" kid named Jamal who is a contestant on the Indian version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire." The narration is unique and effective because director Danny Boyle chooses flashbacks of his life to tell the story of how the uneducated Jamal is able to answer every question correctly. Danny Boyle is the best thing going for this film. His signature flare and effective use of bright colors is mesmerizing. The way he unfolds this brilliant and unique story is absolutely perfect. Slumdog is an inspiring love story that is both memorable and charming. It is also exceptional what Boyle had to go through to complete this film. It should also be noted that he has helped raise a lot of charitable donations for the slumdogs in Mumbai.

Despite all this, I believe Slumdog Millionaire is a bit more flawed than most people are willing to admit. It's easy to get caught up in the spectacle of such a great story... but the fact remains that the plot is inconceivable and a bit foolish at times. The acting was very sub par. Much has been said about Dev Patel and Freida Pinto, but I don't think their performances were anything special (hence Best Actor and Actress were just about the only 2 categories that didn't receive a nomination). The best actors in the whole movie were the young kids... and also Anil Kapoor as the talk show host.

My main problem with the plot is the reliance on something as lousy as "fate." I'm no psychologist, but I'm sure there is one out there that could prove that it would be impossible for a man to remember one small event 10+ years in the past without repeating the information at some point. For example, an uneducated Indian boy remembering that Benjamin Franklin was on the US $100 bill. It's inconceivable.

Boyle's Slumdog Millionaire is a good movie worthy of praise and multiple viewings, but it's not worthy of total Oscar domination. It happened to be the beneficiary of a weak year in film. It would place runner-up to both 2007 hits No Country for Old Men and There Will Be Blood. 10 years down the road after the heart-warming stories attached to this film have disappeared, all that's left is a good movie (not a GREAT one) with an exaggerated resume of glamorous awards that well exceeds its potential.

   Danny Boyle, conocido principalmente por su polémico y excelente film Trainspotting, nos trae este año una de sus mejores obras con Slumdog Millionaire. Ambientada en la sociedad hindú, se cuenta la historia  de Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) un adolescente pobre de Bombay que, tras participar en la versión de ese país del programa "¿Quiéres ser millonario? desata una historia cruda y sorprendente que  trasmite un halo de esperanza sin sacrificar el duro realismo.Se trata de una película conmovedora, realizada con pericia, que vale la pena no perderse.[/size][/font]
    [/left]
      [left] [font=arial,helvetica,sans-serif][size=2]Boyle, tiene en su haber una filmografía irregular pero sumamente interesante, con títulos como Shallow Grave (1995),su debut en pantalla grande, que es un canto al humor negro, luego en 1996 entregó la cinta ya de culto, "Traisnpotting", sobre el mundo de la heroína y  a los "outsiders". La intrigante "The Beach" (2000), 28 days Later en el 2002, un film bastante extravagante, Millions en el 2004 una cinta muy interesante, por solo citar las más resaltantes de su filmografía. Slumdog Millionaire es quizás la película más madura e integral que ha realizado hasta el momento.[/size][/font]

   A primera vista, este film, parece ser una historia de amor muy original, que se basa en la premisa que Jamal, es concursante de quien quiere ser millonario con la finalidad de hallar al amor de su infancia y de toda su vida. Las cosas se complican cuando Jamal gana el concurso y las autoridades lo detienen porque creen que ha hecho trampa. Parece inconcebible que un chico pobre de Bombay sea capaz de ganar el premio gordo. Durante el interrogatorio,  Boyle aprovecha para dar una doble narrativa al film, en base a los flahsbacks que el personaje de Jamal  introduce para explicar cómo obtuvo cada una de las respuestas del concurso. Esto nos remite a su infancia en Bombay, sumergido en la pobreza, en la violencia, en situaciones tan inverosímiles pero tan crudas que nos hielan los sentidos. Aquí percibimos, la dureza del contexto de la infancia de Jamal, en un país muy golpeado y subdesarrollado en extremo. El director hace uso de una fotografía exquisita sin caer en excesos de color y logra trasmitir con realismo la esencia de ese país.

   Excelentes encuadres de cámara, todos muy dinámicos lo que le da un ritmo  narrativo resaltante. Like The Dark Knight before it, Slumdog Millionaire is the kind of film which is so overhyped that you cannot now see it without having to deal in some way with that emotional and critical backage. Where Slumdog differs from The Dark Knight is in its tone, or more precisely, in the difference between the tone of the advertising and the tone of the film itself. Where The Dark Knight was always advertised as being dark, and hence its darkness came as no surprise, Slumdog Millionaire's advertising made it look light and superficial, at least comparatively. Critics praised it as "the feel-good film of the year", when in fact much of it is fairly dark.

The film overall could be described as 'feel-good', insofar as the rag-to-riches story at the centre of it has been done so many times before, and the ending is very sentimental. It could be said that, had this film been set in Britain rather than India, it would have been billed as a Richard Curtis film in all but name. However, there is more to it than just the feel-good factor at the end, and it is certainly not the case that the flashy visuals disguise the plot holes.

As far as the acting goes, generally the child actors outshine their adult counterparts. The early sequences of the film in which Dev Patel's character is trying to get an autograph from his favourite film star, is very charming without being overbearing. The scene in the toilet is also a nice, if rather disgusting, homage to Boyle's earlier work Trainspotting. When the action switches back to the game show, Patel spends much of the performance just gaping inanely, and often this adds nothing to the character he is playing. We already get the message that he is neither intelligent nor in this for the money, so why diminish him still further? As for his love interest, played by Freida Pinto, she's largely convincing, though there are odd moments where he falters, for instance on the phone call between her and Patel live on the show.

The main success of Slumdog Millionaire is not in its storyline, which is decent but not a masterstroke. It lies in the way that story is told, both in the narrative structure and the images of India it gives. The film manages to flip back and forth between the past and the present without resorting to a distant narrator fading in and out, as in The Princess Bride or, more recently, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button. And unlike Hideous Kinky, whose portrayal of Muslims was at best questionable and at best awfully stereotypical, Boyle gets right to the centre of what life in the slums is like, depicting love and hate equally with not a hint of judging or sanctimony.

Films with happy endings are always going to appeal to audiences more than those who endings are ambigious or pessimistic. Hence Slumdog Millionaire is always going to be revered in some way. Fortunately it deserves a great deal of this reverence, being a film which walks the tightrope between poignant and sentimental and makes it successfully to the other side. Its dark elements mean that it has staying power which its more sentimental counterparts - Benjamin Button included - may not have, and from a visual point of view it is easily Danny Boyle's best film. Thoroughly recommended.

Slumdog Millionaire hits the ground running. This is a breathless, exciting story, heartbreaking and exhilarating at the same time, about a Mumbai orphan who rises from rags to riches on the strength of his lively intelligence. The film's universal appeal will present the real India to millions of moviegoers for the first time. The film uses dazzling cinematography, breathless editing, driving music and headlong momentum to explode with narrative force, stirring in a romance at the same time. For Danny Boyle, it is a personal triumph. He combines the suspense of a game show with the vision and energy of City of God and never stops sprinting. When I saw Slumdog Millionaire, I was witnessing a phenomenon: dramatic proof that a movie is about how it tells itself. I walked out of the theater and flatly predicted it would win awards. Seven days later, it did, Best Picture at the Golden Globes with its director bagging the Best Director title. And that it could land a best picture Oscar nomination. We will see. It is one of those miraculous entertainments that achieves its immediate goals and keeps climbing toward a higher summit.

It's rare to see a movie this vibrantly, brilliantly alive. The story is a archetypal rags-to-riches story with most of the time spent in rags. The large ensemble cast all turn in believable performances, which really should not be that surprising, since many of them are probably playing characters not too distant from their own experiences. The film's perspective on poverty and crime in India is jarring and realistic, and reminded me strongly of Brazil's City of God, but with more joy than that film had. The Indian techno/hip hop soundtrack, while almost overpowering at times, is very cool and appropriate to the movie's mood. The film really shines in its expert editing, color-rich cinematography, and breakneck direction by Danny Boyle. This is a good example of very reliable substance being treated with great style. Given all the different technical and emotional levels on which this film succeeds, it is no surprise that it won the Oscar for Best Picture.

Much like "The Last Emperor" and "Titanic", I don't quite understand the almost universal acclaim of "Slumdog Millionaire".  The film itself is finely crafted when it comes to acting, directing, production design and the technical details such as lighting, etc.

Where this film falls apart for me is that's it is simply a paint by the numbers underdog movie with a girl he's trying to impress by gaining fame and fortune using the game show "Who Wants to be a Millionaire".

Speaking of theme's... Disney's "Aladdin" has all the same thematic elements, but is done much better and is still entertaining upon repeat viewings.  I don't believe "Slumdog" will hold up on repeat viewings and will go the way of "The Last Emperor" and "Titanic" where they will be barely remembered within the coming decade.

So this review sounds largely negative, but what's worth mentioning is this is a good, solid film and I do recommend it for a one time viewing.  It's just not the film it was hyped to be and it's a shame it won all the awards when "The Wrestler" was a much better experience and a far superior film.

Slumdog, which has done a pretty good job of living up to the hype IMHO is simply great.  Great story, great art direction and great acting.  We get a troubling glimpse into the horrifying conditions of Mumbai's slums, but not so much that it dominates the mood of the whole film.  We know it gets much worse than what is depicted, but we get enough to service the story without being distracted by it.  And what would a movie set in India be without a Bollywood-style dance number tacked on during the end credits?  Good stuff.

A real life Cinderella story came true on Oscar Night 2009 as a wild card entry ended up becoming the year's Best Picture, seemingly mirroring the film's own rags-to-riches story. Yet, for the apparently simple premise this is a much more complex movie; after all, it's directed by Danny Boyle.
From the get go you can tell Boyle has lost none of his hyper-active verve, with shards of film edited on top of each other in a frenzy of canted angles and whip-snap cuts. His intensely close-up style, adopted in recent years, also homes in on individual faces or parts of faces; and, of course, a storming soundtrack pulses vividly close to the surface of the whizzing images. At the beginning Boyle's highly-charged style feels like an exercise in just that, having the feast of visuals that is India to make for dazzling onscreen rainbow. Yet once the story takes centre stage and the more grim aspects of real life seep through all of the cinematic tricks seem to fade away to something much more emotional.
The beginner's guide to Indian cinema shows two distinct 'genres': the fable-like kitchen-sink dramas of Satyajit Ray and his contemporaries, and the modern song-and-dance marathons of Bollywood. 'Slumdog Millionaire' finds it's way across both, bridging this very large gap. The opening scenes of young children scurrying about the city slums recall the adventurous travels of 'Aparajito', though now there's a more explicit documentation of violence and a seedier nature to the poverty. This is far from the breezy romp one would think it is, showing uglier and more brutal details of a whole race swamped in poverty, and this atmosphere doesn't really ease off for most of the film. To balance this darker context we have Jamal's enduring spirit, constant and unshakeable in his goal to be with the one he loves, and it works, mostly when it's Dev Patel shouldering the role with an abundance of charm and likeability.
But it's far from the perfect measure of happiness it's been made out to be. Taking a leaf out of Bollywood's book the proceedings are pure melodrama, with the children leaping from impoverished 'hoods veering shockingly into 'City of God' territory to becoming the flunkies of the Mumbai equivalent of Harold Shand. Somehow it fails to convince this could really happen to characters who know each other intimately, given the fact that India contains one fifth of Earth's population. It might be dreamy fun for Indian audiences to image two lovers somehow finding their way back to each other in such a populous country, but to Western audiences it just seems impossible. 
That's mostly Beaufoy's fault, especially seeing as how his earlier drafts would include even more cliches. But the cast also have problems of their own. While most acting is competent, which is fine, sometimes they can slip in key scenes or fail to keep up a particular rhythm. It's understandable however, since the cast haven't exactly studied at RADA, and the major players are brilliant to watch. Dev Patel is a very capable performer, successfully combining all manner of emotions to fantastic effect. Madhur Mittal is great fun to see as an Indian wide boy, though handling the final betrayal with a mature conviction. Anil Kapoor as the smug Prem is an effortlessly greasy reflection of the original Chris Tarrant, while Irrfan Khan is solid but stiff as the police inspector. Minus points for Freida Pinto though, who does little other than look pretty in an unfortunately, frustratingly wooden performance.
Really, even the showcasing of grim destitution is glossed over with the gaudy colours and incredible sense of flavour, but all of this is overcome by the sheer emotional strength of the story. When Jamal wins the jackpot by pure luck, we somehow feel a little cheated, since we all know he only cares about getting the girl, and that should be prize enough for him and us. Yet when Jamal at last has Latika all to himself, the knowledge that their love can flourish is an unexpected sucker punch, married to a beautiful closing scene. The story's real power all of a sudden erupts into realisation and enormous satisfaction, and either of those purposes easily leaves a smile on your face.
So while there are some obvious flaws and faults, the overall effect is much greater than the sum of its parts. With some charismatic leads and a hugely effective pay-off this is a fantastically apt winner of the 'Best Picture' and is a newer, simpler kind of feel-good.

This is a captivating story of a street dweller who winds up on his country's version of "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?", and ends up winning the million, but not before he's accused of cheating and has to explain, question by question, how he knew the answers. Along the way, we see his neverending love of an attractive girl he somewhat grew up with. Talk about rags to riches! But what's up with her? Will he and she ever find each other? What will happen when they do? We get to see the characters both as children, teens, and young adults as this great story is told. It'll make you laugh, you'll feel suspense as you watch and wonder if the children will escape certain situations, you'll get angry at certain characters for what they do at times, and feel sorrow for others.

This colourfull fairytale is told through the eyes of an Indian teenager named Jamal,who after battling on to the final question of the Indian version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? is arrested on suspicion of cheating.During the interrogation Jamal is forced to reveal the events of his traumatic upbringing,which will explain just how he knows all the answers to the questions and tells of his love for a girl,which is his motivation for taking part.
Slumdogs huge success is due in large part to the fact its such a beautifully and perfectly constructed film.
The amazing soundtrack and complicated camera angle's blend so fantastically into the pacey montages,especially that breathtaking opening chase scene through the Mumbai slums (possibly the most stunning scene of the film).
Theres no disputing whether the films editor Chris Dickens deserved an Academy Award,he did a phenomenal job.As for Director Danny Boyle his Oscar was well overdue,although a degree of credit should go to Co-Director Loveleen Tandian for his valuable contribution.
Slumdog may have won critical acclaim,but its also had its share of bad comments,people who question  its credibility and predictability as a story and I can see points to both sides of the arguement.Slumdog does border on the lines of being ridiculous and far-fetched,all because the plot builds on the premise of fate and destiny.But then this is a fairytale love story,so I managed to suspend disbelief in the interest of what is actually a fantastically made,brilliantly acted,emotional and stylishly energetic tale of meant-to-be love.
I did find it laughable though that during an interval,while contemplating an answer to a question,Jamal was allowed to wander around backstage unsupervised free to speak to anyone in the production staff.Surely pretty stupid if they were that concerned he may be cheating.I'm sure that wouldn't be allowed to happen in real life.

Danny Boyle's Slumdog Millionaire is what type of film? A) an inspirational underdog story, B) a harrowing look at the life of a Mumbai street child, C) an epic romance punctuated by tragedy and victory, or D) an affecting crime drama centered upon bitter sibling rivalry.

Give up? Slumdog Millionaire is all of those things and more. It's the reason we go to the movies in the first place, and by the time it reaches its climax, you're likely to be yelling at the screen the same way that television viewers around the world did back when Who Wants to Be a Millionaire was at the peak of its popularity. Whether you go to the movies to be thrilled, terrified, elated, inspired, or simply entertained, Slumdog Millionaire does not disappoint. At this point in his career, Boyle has worked in a variety of genres, and here they all come together to create the perfect cinematic storm, an irresistible burst of big-screen optimism that will have the critics swooning and the cynics smiling. Of course, there are times when the waters can get pretty rough for India's most beloved dark-horse game-show contestant, but what are the best moments in life without the worst ones to make them all the more meaningful?

The first time we see Jamal, he's being tortured by the police. He's just come off the set of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, and the authorities are convinced that he's just cheated his way to the million-dollar question. But Jamal is no cheat, and as he recalls the life experiences that taught him the answers to the questions he was asked on the popular game show, we come to learn why street smarts are as essential to surviving in the slums of Mumbai as ruthless business savvy is to rising through the criminal ranks. Jamal and his older brother, Salim, were just young boys when their single mother was killed by rioters right before their eyes, and after being orphaned they lived in a garbage dump just to survive. In those dark days, the only thing that kept Jamal going was his love for the beautiful Latika. She, too, was an orphan, and upon joining the two brothers, she was forever bound by fate to both of them. Later, when Jamal and Salim were driven apart by lust and greed, Jamal and Latika were forced to go their separate ways. Now, years later, Jamal is determined to get his lady back, and reasoning that the best way to find her is to become a contestant on the nation's most popular game show, the lovelorn "chai boy" lands an appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? But Jamal never thought that he would even get close to winning the top prize, and when he does, the authorities want to know how a kid born in the ghetto could possibly know the answers to such difficult questions.

Thus begins a truly remarkable tale of hope, love, and profound adversity. As the detective reviews a videotape of Jamal's appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, the irrepressible "slumdog" tells the story of how he came to know the answer to each question in vivid detail. Each answer is a journey unto itself -- sometimes heartbreaking, sometimes humorous -- and the further we travel, the more we become invested in the characters. Through it all, we come to understand just what a decent person Jamal truly is, and why his romance with Latika seemed doomed from the moment they first met. This effect is owed largely to actor Dev Patel, who portrays the older Jamal with such terminal honesty that he gives us a constant place to project our optimism. We relate to him, and after experiencing his hardships, we want desperately to see him win the money and walk away with the girl. His innocence is infectious, and even as different actors take over the role throughout Jamal's journey to adulthood, that purity remains a compelling constant. It's a testament to the casting that we always know Jamal, Salim, and Latika the moment they appear onscreen, and in a movie as nonlinear as Slumdog Millionaire, it's essential that the viewer doesn't get distracted from the story by the struggle to pick out the main players. Fortunately, that never happens, leaving us free to lose ourselves in Simon Beaufoy's smartly structured screenplay, Anthony Dod Mantle's hyper-saturated, glowingly gritty photography, and Chris Dickens' crackerjack editing -- all of which are marvelously held together by veteran Bollywood composer A.R. Rahman's buoyant score, an invigorating fusion of Eastern and Western musical sensibilities. A great movie is something more than the sum total of all its parts, and here, the elements all come together to form a feature that speaks a universal form of optimism that isn't likely to get lost in translation, no matter where it screens, or who is watching.

Jika saya jadi Amitabh Bachchan, saya juga pasti tercengang-cengang dan loncat dari kursi ketika menonton Slumdog Millionaire (2008). Saya, eh, Amitabh punya alasan yang kuat untuk itu. Selama ini dalam film-film Bollywood ia begitu heroik dan selalu berperan sebagai jagoan, orang kaya yang tinggal di rumah mewah, dan menampilkan kehebatan-kehebatan negerinya, serta terkenal seantero dunia.

Namun, tiba-tiba pria asal Inggris itu (baca: Danny Boyle) membuat manuver tajam yang sama sekali tidak diduga banyak orang. Ia dengan vulgar menggambarkan kehidupan masyarakat paling bawah dalam masyarakat India; potret anak-anak jalanan ala Charles Dickens, yang hidup dalam lingkungan yang kumuh, penuh kekerasan dan minus pendidikan yang layak. Saya, jika jadi Amitabh, juga pasti emosi melihat anak-anak India, yang mengidolakan saya, dijadikan binatang dan diburu, dan dicaci maki karena nasib mereka. Dalam blog-nya, Amitabh mengatakan:

"If [Slumdog Millionaire] projects India as [a] Third World dirty underbelly developing nation and causes pain and disgust among nationalists and patriots, let it be known that a murky underbelly exists and thrives even in the most developed nations.
Sepanjang film kita disuguhi tur gratis kehidupan jelata orang India. Dan barangkali, yang paling membuat Amitabh geram, hal tersebut disaksikan jutaan orang di seluruh dunia. Itulah yang dibuat oleh Boyle dalam film yang membawa pulang delapan piala Oscar, yang di antaranya untuk Best Motion Picture ini.

The Power of Coincidence
Slumdog Millionaire diangkat dari novel best-selling India berjudul Q & A karya Vikash Swarup. Diadaptasi ke dalam skrip oleh Simon Beaufoy, film ini bercerita tentang seorang pelayan yang mendapat kesempatan untuk ikut kuis Who Wants to Be a Millionaire yang pernah begitu booming pada periode 2003  2006. 

Semua orang suka kuis Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. Boyle sendiri mengakui bahwa salah satu dasar pembuatan film ini adalah karena ia menggemari kuis tersebut. Nasib film ini sepenuhnya terletak di bahu Jamal (Dev Patel) yang sedang duduk di kursi panas berhadapan dengan Prem (Anil Kapoor), sang pembawa acara kuis. Selangkah lagi Jamal akan memecahkan rekor dengan memenangkan 20 juta Rupee. Namun sang pembawa acara dan polisi tidak percaya: bagaimana pula seorang yatim piatu, yang tidak bersekolah dan tinggal di daerah kumuh itu bisa menjawab seluruh pertanyaan dengan benar? Skeptisisme yang masuk akal dan wajar. Lalu, Boyle membawa kita ke tiap suspense, flash back, klimaks, dan detil kejadian yang memberikan jawaban untuk setiap pertanyaan kuis. Plot yang unik.

Tapi apakah semua itu bukan merupakan kebetulan belaka? Kebetulan saja setiap pertanyaan yang diajukan dalam kuis adalah representasi hidupnya. Kebetulan saja, misalnya, ketika Jamal diberitahu temannya bahwa foto dalam lembaran US$100 adalah Benjamin Franklin. Namun, cinta akan menemukan jalannya dan Boyle mengeksplorasi tema itu dalam setiap bingkai kilas balik kehidupan Jamal. Jika tidak percaya pada probabilitas dan peluang, silakan saja menganggap Slumdog Millionaire film yang mengada-ada.

Tapi seperti yang kita ketahui, tujuan Jamal bukanlah uang, tetapi cinta (huhuhu mulia sekali dia). Jamal benar-benar merepresentasikan lirik lagu Who Wants to Be a Millionaire (1956) yang dulu pernah dinyanyikan oleh Cole Porter: Who wants to be a millionaire? I dont, and I dont, cause all I want is you... Setiap detil kejadian dalam hidupnya, Jamal berusaha mencari Latika (Freida Pinto), teman masa kecilnya yang sangat ia rindukan. Walaupun pada akhirnya ia tahu bahwa Latika telah dijadikan gundik seorang kepala preman, ia tetap mencintai Latika. Dialah jawaban semua pertanyaan yang diajukan kepada Jamal. Jamal hanya ingin memenangkan Latika.

Anomali 2008
Menurut saya, Boyle sangat berani membuat film seperti Slumdog Millionaire. Padahal ia nantinya hanya akan punya dua hasil: gagal total atau sukses besar. Dan kita semua tahu bahwa pada akhirnya Boyle memperoleh yang kedua. Delapan piala Oscar bukanlah prestasi sembarangan (saya benci menjadikan Oscar sebagai parameter, tapi mau bagaimana lagi?). 

Namun, Amitabh yakin bahwa Slumdog Millionaire terkenal hanya karena dibuat, disutradarai dan ditonton dari perspektif Barat. Amitabh merasa nasionalisme-nya ditelanjangi (memang dalam beberapa adegan Boyle menunjukkan superioritas Barat, seperti ketika dua orang turis Amerika mengajari orang hitam India agar memperlakukan anak-anak dengan pantas. Dalam hal ini, Boyle gagal menghindari stereotip negatif yang mungkin muncul dari adegan tersebut). Salah seorang teman saya bergurau dengan mengatakan, Coba kalau pembawa acara kuis itu diperankan oleh bung Amitabh Bachchan, pasti reaksinya akan lain. Terlepas dari praduga teman saya, Amitabh punya poin sendiri yang dapat ia perdebatkan.

Namun bagi saya film ini tetaplah sebuah anomali pada tahun 2008; berbudjet rendah namun sangat menghibur, dibangun dengan tema sederhana bahwa uang tak dapat membeli cinta namun sangat dalam. Film ini juga diperkuat oleh tiga karakter (Jamal, Salim dan Latika) yang diperankan oleh sembilan orang dalam tiga fase. Semuanya begitu personal dan individualistik, sehingga kita tidak pernah salah mengetahui mana Jamal kecil, Salim remaja, atau Latika dewasa. Selain itu, Anil Kapoor yang memang merupakan superstar di India, juga memberikan karakter yang kuat kepada tokoh Prem, si Pembawa Acara kuis yang pongah itu. Sedangkan latar yang diambil begitu jujur dan nyata menggambarkan sisi lain kota Mumbai. Ditambah aransemen yang menggetarkan dari A.R. Rahman, Slumdog Millionaire rules! 

PS: Oh ya, jangan khawatir untuk mengajak anak-anak berumur 10 tahun untuk menonton film ini. Walaupun ada sedikit adegan kekerasan, namun tidak begitu ditonjolkan. Sepertiga film ini diisi oleh Jamal kecil, yang penuh perjuangan untuk bertahan hidup. Hal ini bisa jadi pelajaran bagus untuk anak-anak, bahwa di luar sana banyak yang bernasib sama sekali berbeda dengan mereka.

SLUMDOG MILLIONAIRE:Visually Dazzling, but shallow interior due to inferior acting...7.8/10
Well its all change, and here I am two months absent from a single review. Alas I am writing this from a college computer, and was shocked to discover RT's confusing new change. Slumdog combines a dazzling array of visuals with sumptuous Oscar winning music that is utterly captivating, exciting and generally pleasurable. Boyle deserved his best director oscar (Fincher was the only real competition, but his toned down aesthetic style was disappointing), as the talent on display here is outstanding and engaging. Boyle places us in the slums of Mumbai, and while the plots unravelling is slightly mundane and predictable he patches it up well, masking the films flaws with flawless taste and elaborate set pieces. Whlie Slumdog is a powerful display of 'rags to riches' the acting on view is often weak, flimsy and cardboard. Dev Patel's average performance along with Freida's overacting is distracts the viewer from the films plot and atmosphere often instantaneously jumping from irresistable to unbelievable. Apart from the 'Slum' chlidren no one is really worthy of note, hence only 8 Oscars and not 11 like most successes that at least take a single acting gong (though LOTR's always puzzled me with its lack of nominations ). I could  not help feel that the overhype had aroused a certain disdain from me really enjoying the film. The final 20 minutes are dressed up to reach the 'feel good factor' that dessimates the majority of credit from slum reality. Boyle went all out for a cinematic often overblown and overdramatised experience rather than a biographical outlook, which although means the film lacks some authenticity and a credible interior, its exterior is radiant and fresh and for that Boyle deserved a few accolades to his name, even i think that Fincher was robbed with his Button.

Now I understand what all the excitement's about: if Slumdog Millionaire doesn't move you, you should probably check yourself for a pulse.  This is an astonishing movie: brilliant acting, great music, incredible photography . . . but what impressed me most was the lack of narration and exposition: the story is told visually, with enormous impact.

At first I thought the producers glossed over the realities of slum life in a poverty-stricken nation: they give you little glimpses of the horrors these kids grow up with (if they live, that is), but quickly move on to happier interludes.  On second thought, I realize they knew that Westerners could not have handled a totally honest depiction of third world slum life; without the fairytale rags-to-riches plot moving the story along, audiences would simply have slit their wrists.

Well, thank God for the fairy tale, I say.  It turns the movie into an uplifting, inspiring experience . . . and there's nothing wrong with that!

Slumdog tell the story of two brothers, Jamal and Salim, who grow up in the slums of Mumbai. The real slum kids who play Salim and Jamal as children are so adorable! Here's more: the basic premise of the film is that Jamal falls in love with a girl when they are both children and because life is complicated and stuff happens, they get separated. In order to find her, he goes on a popular game show in India which she (along with twenty million other people) watch. In the end he gets the money AND the girl. Like I said, clichÃ©d. But somehow it works. Dev Patel plays the part of Jamal with an honesty that is endearing and Danny Boyle, the director manages to weave together a story that is both believable and entertaining. This film grabs you in the gut; from the early scene where a child is blinded so he can earn more money, to the scenes where Jamal and Prem the gameshow host are engaged in what appears to be a duel to the death (metaphorically speaking). Slumdog Millionaire is the story of an extraordinarily lucky boy who finds the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. A brilliant piece of work from British director Danny Boyle.

This movie is pretty damn excellent.  But I hate to say it, I thought The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button was the better movie.  That doesn't mean I disagree with the numerous "Best Movie" awards this movie won, it certainly is one of the best (3rd best in my book) movies of last year.  The problem I had with this movie was the "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" game show segments.  They weren't bad at all, in fact they were excellent since every question gave a lot of backstory to 3 main characters, since Jamal knew the answers because of the experiences he had as a child and teenager in the slums.  That's also the problem with the movie, Jamal knew every answer (with the exception of the last question) in those segments because of his life experiences in the slums.  I'm sorry but that's just a corny way to give us his backstory.  Every question, conviently enough, had a flashback to some experience in Jamal's life that led him to know the answer to the question.  I just thought it was very stupid and that's probably the worst part of the movie since by the end of the movie it just starts becoming a joke.  I wouldn't have minded if that was the case for a question or two, but every question in the damn thing, Jamal had experienced in one way or another.  I know it might be nitpicky, but I just didn't like that aspect of the movie very much.  But I DO have to say that the last question of the millionaire segments was actually very suspenseful and it was very well done.  Also, the dancing sequence during the credits was also really stupid and very Bollywood-ish of them to do.  For a movie that's based mostly on reality and how the 3 main characters grow up and mature, it was just a very silly thing to do.  And I don't really understand what the purpose was for the dancing sequence, that probably won't affect the score I give this movie since the dance sequence was after the movie ended.  If this had happened DURING the movie, man oh man, I would've been all over this like a motherfucker.  But other than that, the rest of this movie is really excellent.  I love how the 3 main characters are portrayed and how they're shown as little kids, teenagers, then as adults so I really felt attached to the characters since I saw them "grow" up in 2 hours.  The story is also very intriguing, not necessarily great but it's effective.  The acting is also very good.  Dev Patel, for a guy who's only been acting 3 years now, he was very good in his role and he had a presence about him.  He'll only get better as the years move on.  Freida Pinto, man is she pretty, she was good but she's also going to get better as she gets more acting roles.  The children were also very good and normally I'm never big on child actors, but I gotta say they were pretty damn good especially the child Jamal Malik.  Everyone other supporting actor played their part very well, but one minor nitpick, Anil Kapoor played the host of the millionaire game and every time he said rupees he just said it in a weird way, it kind of annoyed me a bit but it's nothing that really hurt the movie.  Danny Boyle did a great job directing this movie, and it's always good to see a very talented director get the recognition that Danny Boyle has gotten with this movie.  I always thought that Danny was one of the more underrated filmmakers out there but now hopefully he'll be given a place among the elite.  I don't really know what else I can say about this movie to be honest.  Outside of the fact that the Millionaire questions convienently recall a memory that Jamal experienced, this movie is just amazing and I think everybody needs to see it.

Edit:  Having seen the movie a second time today, I pretty much have come to the conclusion that I enjoyed this movie probably as much as I enjoyed The Curious Case Of Benjamin Button.  Everything in Slumdog Millionaire made much more sense the second time around.  I even thought the Millionaire segments made much more sense this time and the dance sequence wasn't as stupid as I said before.  Plus I just felt very pleased and happy with how the movie turned out.  I can't really pick which film is better though since both films are very different in style.  In my opinion they're equally as excellent for different reasons, if that makes any sense.  With that said as it stands right now, Slumdog and TCCOFBB are tied for second best movie of last year (The Dark Knight is still, by far, the best movie I saw last year, fanboyism aside).

Now that Ive seen this film, Im promised myself that from now on, Ill be seeing the Oscar-nominated films for best picture before the awards actually air. That way, I can have an honest opinion.

Now, I havent seen any of the other films yet, but from what I witnessed in Slumdog and what I read in reviews of the other films, I have a strong feeling that Boyles masterpiece will take home the final prize.

The first thing I noticed about this movie was the exquisite editing, and not just well-crafted editing, but intentional editing that exponentially added to the appeal of the film. When the scenes cut from the game show to the police station to the slums of Mumbai, formerly Bombay, the audience didnt get confused where the characters were. And all of the jump cuts were incredibly clean, and at the end when we saw exactly all the time sequences catch up with each other, it helped bring the story together without seeming too ostensible.

What else was also ostensible was the love story. The fact that Slumdog carries on across a lifetime, the love story between Latika (the oldest played by Freida Pinto) and Jamal (the oldest played by Dev Patel) was completely believable because you got to see how long their friendship went back  literally back to their childhood; whereas most love stories that say they started back in child just relies on the audience to infer about the long relationship. The young actors who played the various ages of Jamal and Salim did a wonderful job in playing such tragic and complex characters. And as their adult selves, Jamal and Salim were even more tragic. Jamal lived all by himself as a chaiwalah, or one that serves tea, and Salim was basically a hit man for one of Indias most prominent crime bosses.

What was tragic was also so beautiful. Jamal, in learning of Latikas life in danger, went on Indias Who Wants to be a Millionaire, because he knew shed be watching. And when he came upon those questions, he found that he knew all the answers. All of the horrific things that happened to him all led up to this one moment that hed been waiting for his entire life. Not for the money, but for Latika to hear him.

Quite enthralled by Patels portrayal of oldest Jamal, I went exploring online for further information on him, and his resume was remarkably short for such a promising young actor. Patels only substantial item on his acting resume is a character on Britains teen drama Skins, a series similar to Canadas Degrassi. For how young he is, the way he depicted Jamal was uncanny. There was so much baggage and terrible history in Jamals life, and Patels vulnerability was very advantageous in this instance.

A.R. Rahman also composed a superb soundtrack, taking help from M.I.A., who have now received an Oscar nomination of there own. The mixture of classic Bollywood and contemporary dance floor beats matched quite well with the non-sequential storyline. My personal favorite was OSaya. It gave a light fun beat to such a tense scene in the film.

With such a sad story came the purely entertainment-oriented addition of the game show. Anil Kapoor played a perfect snarky game show host, and the sequences in which Kapoor and Patel are on the television show, its a subtle break from Jamals heartbreaking story. And not until the end does the audience find out the full meaning of all the encounters preceding the game show.

I especially liked the sequence during the last question, where Jamal made the decision to phone a friend. I wont spoil it for you, because I strongly recommend the film to everyone. It kept me on the edge of my seat, not to sound clichéd, but it was a perfect ending to a perfect film.

It was a perfect, not cheesy, believable, and hopeful ending.

If you dont believe in destiny, Slumdog Millionaire will surely change your mind.

Jamal Malik sits back in his seat as the lights shine down upon him. The man across from him has asked a question, and now he is being watched by the man, by the studio audience, and by countless millions of people throughout India. If Jamal answers correctly he will be rich beyond fairy-tale lore, but if he is wrong he will be just another slumdog. Or will he?


Danny Boyles (Sunshine; Trainspotting) new film Slumdog Millionaire begins with suspense and never lets up. That the movie is a beautiful piece of art is unquestionable, and I will only venture to write that I found the scenery and rhythm of this film to be the best of the year, and so artistically breath-taking that words here cannot accurately describe what the eyes must see. The sweeping scenes of India and specifically the slums of Mumbai will leave a lasting impression on the viewer, especially if you have had little to no experience with such conditions.


With that said, this is a film that is a story within a story within a story, though all three are told fairly seamlessly and intertwined. The first story is that of Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) and his opportunity to win millions on a game show. The second story is Jamals desperate attempts to reunite with his lost love, Latika (Freida Pinto). And the final story is that of Jamal and his brother, Salim (Madhur Mittal) as we watch them grow from small children to young adults, each taking a distinctly different path to get there.


The three stories unfold with the game show acting as the glue, and by which we come to learn (through multiple actors playing the Malik brothers and Latika as they grow older) how it is that Jamal could possibly go from being just another slumdog to a multi-millionaire answering questions to which he should seemingly have no business knowing the answers.


Along this journey we are taken into the slums of India as children are forced and tortured into a Gypsy life-style. We also play witness to religious violence and the overtly stated caste system of India, in which children can live in the worst squalor next to men driving Mercedes and throwing cash away as if it is trash.


The screenplay, based on the book Q and A by Vikas Swarup, follows Jamal as he answers questions on a game show, and we are treated to flashback sequences of his life to see just how it is that a person from his background came to know answers to so many random questions. Throughout this process we are taken for a sibling roller coaster ride as Jamal and Salim take very different paths in their efforts to escape their birth conditions. 


Though the love story is the driving force behind this film, and it is the central hinge for which all of Jamals experiences are hanging, I found the part of Latika to be the Weakest Link (pun intended) in an otherwise brilliant display of character development. Ultimately, I just didnt believe or get or fully comprehend her love for Jamal in the way I understood his. There are also some very undeveloped roles of the goons and thugs of which I would have liked to see more, and just a few too many leaps of faith in the plot line. These are, however, to be taken as fairly minor points, and that still leaves me feeling that this film deserves a spot at or near the top of the best films of the year.
