This is such a brilliant movie because it contains every type of emotion.  It is sometimes sad, sometimes funny, sometimes serious, and sometimes exciting, with the ups and downs of the friendship/romance between Jamal and Latika running through the whole movie.  It's a brilliance you come to expect from a director as fantastic as Danny Boyle.

The frequent flashbacks to the childhood of Jamal and his friends, growing up in a very poor, unsanitary slum are extremely effective, and fit the plot perfectly.  The questions in the show all have some relevance to the young Jamal's life.

The love story between Jamal and Latika is never smooth, and is portrayed perfectly.  It really tugs at the heartstrings and makes you feel sympathy for the characters when they can not be together due to circumstances, though at least it is a happy (though corny) ending.

There are some very violent and gory parts of the movie, such as the scene in which a boy's eye is gouged out, and these moments make this a very gritty movie.

The cinematography in this movie is nothing short of excellent, especially the shots taken in the slums, with all the local people who took part as extras in the shooting of the movie.  Visually, this movie is brilliant.

The acting in this movie is fabulous, especially by all the 3 main characters as youngsters, by Dev Patel (the older Jamal), by Frieda Pinto (the older Latika), and by Anil Kapur (the quiz show host).

The movie boasts an excellent soundtrack, especially 'Jai Ho' by A.R.Rahman and The Pussycat Dolls.

Overall, there is one word which really sums up this movie, its plot, actors and director - genius.

For a film that won 8 Academy Awards, Slumdog Millionaire has very high expectations to live up to. How can a story involving answering questions on âWho Wants To Be A Millionaireâ â in another country â culminate into an adventure of trials and triumphs for two brothers and their friend that earned so many awards? Danny Boyle knows how, and boy does he show it well hereâ¦

Slumdog Millionaire tells the incredible story of a young man who goes onto the Indian version of âWho Wants To Be A Millionaireâ, gets to the last question, and then is interrogated by police on allegations of cheating. By telling his life in flashback, the explanations how he knew the answers are revealed via incredible key moments from the development of India, and in particular Mumbai, all the while trying to find out the fates of his older brother and female friend from years agoâ¦

The main strength with this film, and one that many other films completely miss the point of, is that it is just about as simple a concept as there can be, and yet it is done brilliantly. The rags-to-riches story makes you laugh as much as you are appalled at the treatment of the poor and sick, and it is this mix of two extremes that keep you constantly hooked. Through the despair there are moments of triumph, which also bring about new challenges for the main characters. For most people watching. It provides great insight into the rapid development of one of the busiest places in Eastern civilisation; Mumbai. To witness the development and impact of the changing face of Mumbai, especially how it affected all classes and people within its city, is a real eye-opener, and is easily as big a character within the film as the lead actors.

There is one warning - people expecting the feel good movie that was constantly advertised will be shocked at the honest brutality the film shows. To expect a film that will put a smile on your face through some truly shocking moments will horrify some people, but it is certainly a rewarding film to watch.

It may be a simple as 2 + 2, but Slumdog Millionaire is a highly entertaining and emotional adventure, that really stands out when it is flying along. The triangle of family and loved ones is involving, and it rightly highlights Mumbai as a beacon for the future development of the Eastern world. Plus Anil Kapoor is brilliant as the host of Indiaâs âMillionaireâ!

Jamal answers all of the questions right up until the ten million rupees mark (500,000 USD), and is then taken in for interrogation for the accusation of cheating. While Jamal is being interrogated, he explains that he knew the answers because the questions that he was asked were, at some point, a life experience he had. Jamal explains to the interrogators how he knew each of the answers to the questions. When Jamal explains how he knew the answer to each question, the movie flashes back to Jamal's past life experiences of why he knew the answers to each question. After going through each question and explaining how he knew it, the interrogators let him go back onto the show, to answer the million dollar question.

I have only the opinions of a few individuals of Indian descent, but it seems enough to make a statement. As an acquaintance of mine (let us call him Raj) said: 'So now we see how the poor live in India; but what about the rest of us? Is this really the only impression of India we want to give? But does it really detract from the appeal of the film? Not significantly; but it is something worth thinking about.

On a second negative note, this film really can?t seem to make up its mind what it wants to be. I see some typical 'Bollywoodness' (the dancing, the colours, the romance) and some 'Britishness' (everything else). 'Slumdog' is something between comedy, drama and a biopic. But not in a very appealing way. It's like pancake dough and batter balls; a welcome change in small quantities, but too many and you just get put off. Danny Boyle needs to up his stirring technique to reach my highest ranks.

That's about it from my side; otherwise a very good film and definitely worth your time. Feels like a lot less than 2 hours, although somehow I'm not tempted to invest in the DVD.

I have always felt that the best movies are the ones which tell the best stories, and in this case Slumdog Millionaire achieves this by telling a story about hope.  Throughout the entire film, Jamal never loses hope.  He hopes for a better life, he hopes to make himself better, he hopes that he will one day be united with Latika.  At the same time, his success in going from a "slumdog" to a national celebrity and millionaire through his appearance on Who Wants to be a Millionaire gives the entire country of India hope.  When you think about it, this movie seems to have the basic plot of "follow your dreams and they will come true" which we have seen in so many movies and stories.  However, this film adequately showed Jamal's beginnings in the slum and how millions of India's poor live, not in a fictional world, but in our actual world, which really drives home the message and reality of this movie.  On a global perspective, with the challenges and uncertainty that we face today in 2009, this movie rightfully is the best picture of 2008 because it shows that regardless of how bad things may be, there is, and there should always be hope.

In the world of Jamal Malik, "Millionaire" is the only way out of a hardscrabble existence scorched on the streets of Mumbai.

The story is told in reverse as Jamal is on the verge of winning a million dollars on India's version of Millionaire. The host of the show is convinced that Jamal is cheating and sets him up for a round' midnight interrogation the night before the big question is to be answered. While the entire country is championing Jamal, he must answer his accusers.

During the interrogation, Jamal is forced to explain to the police how it is that he knew each and every answer that he had given on the show. This is a brilliant vehicle for story telling and done here in four-star fashion.

The flash back interrogation allows Jamal to tell his grim tale of survival and sorrow. We learn that Jamal and Salim are survivors in the truest sense of the word. The two are bound by blood and have seen more devastation and loss by the age of sixteen than anyone should see in ten life times. From religious motivated attacks that leave he and his brother orphans, to falling into the clutches of a sadistic Fagan-type character, Jamal has only his brother and Latika (his one true love) to keep him company (and alive).

The colors used in this movie are spectacular as they somehow find a blance between the depressed existence in the slums of Mumbai marked by browns and grays and the bright yellows and greens of a dream world. India is seen at once as a place of great possibility and sweeping despair. The directing is done in quick shot fashion that could be described as MTV era but is too effective to be pigeon holed.

The magic of Slumdog is that, after all the trials and suffering Jamal endures to earn the right to answer the final question, it really doesn't matter whether he gets it right or not. His survival is his reward.

Slumdog reinforces the notion that what we go through is who we are and that our pasts cannot be forgotten. When the final scene plays out, Jamal hears a voice that he thought he would never hear again. It is a voice that is more important to Jamal than all the money and fame the world could offer. We should all be so rich.

Overall: A

J'ai ete tres decu par ce film multi-oscarise, son intrigue simpliste et guimauve qui recycle une fois de plus les schemas les plus ecules de l'industrie hollywodienne. "Slumdog Millionaire" est une enieme success story manicheenne avec des gentils tres gentils, des mechants tres mechants, beaucoup de pathos degoulinant et le "happy end" de rigueur. Je n'ai pas non plus aime la realisation racoleuse et tape-a-l'oeil. Pourtant, j'ai plutot adhere au depart a la facon dont Danny Boyle construit son recit imbriquant le jeu televise, l'interrogatoire muscle chez les flics qui soupconnent le heros de fraude et les souvenirs de son enfance malheureuse. Mais j'ai rapidement ete lasse par le montage epileptique, clipesque, et la musique quasi-incessante. Boyle multiplie les effets de style vains et creux. Pourquoi autant de plans decadres, moches et illisibles ? Il esthetise de maniere outranciere la misere exotique des bidonvilles indiens et la violence qui y sevit. La forme est tellement artificielle que je n'ai jamais vraiment reussi du coup a rentrer dans le film, a croire a cette histoire abracadabrantesque, a eprouver une quelconque empathie pour des personnages finalement tres peu travailles et developpes. Les scenes qui devraient emouvoir comme la mort de la mere, les retrouvailles avec l'amour d'enfance, le sacrifice du frere font totalement "pscchiiit". Boyle ne fait qu'effleurer superficiellement les choses : il evoque le developpement economique indien, les inegalites sociales, les conflits religieux, la mondialisation symbolise par le "call center" ou bosse le heros, mais absolument rien n'en ressort. La critique de la machine a reve televisuelle est a peine esquissee (on en reste la encore au stereotype du presentateur star megalo et cynique...).

Leaving the controversy surrounding payment and welfare of child actors aside, Slumdog Millionaire is a beautiful, entrancing and thoroughly colourful film, with a great cast and a touching plotline that doesn't feel contrived at all, despite being pretty atypical. Street child Jamal seeks the true love of his life, Latika, and because he knows she will be watching, he decides to become a contestant on the Indian version of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" Acting cannot be faulted, with every character, from the major to the most minor, being portrayed superbly. The cinematography and music in many areas is just brilliant, such as the subtle way the classic "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" music is woven into several key scenes, or how the young Jamal and his brother Salim fall from the roof of a train, and then emerge at the end of their fall as much older. In a way, it has some mild overlap with Danny Boyle's earlier film Millions, but this production has much greater scope and sense of style. I am not surprised this film won Best Director and Best Picture at the Oscars, because when a film looks, sounds and feels this good, it is impossible not to be drawn in by it.

"Slumdog Millionaire" depicts an authentic and modern rags-to-riches tale

By Lynne Carty

Set in Mumbai, India, Slumdog Millionaire follows the life story of an illiterate, impoverished boy who rises from the slums, lands a spot as a contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, and makes a run up to the million-dollar question. Who would have thought that a film with such a corny premise would have the makings to rack up 10 nominations for this year's Oscars? Surprising as it may be, Slumdog Millionaire delves into and unmercifully exposes the brutality present in India's slums, proving that it's anything but shallow. Though jam-packed with horror and disturbing realities, the fast-paced and energetic feel of Slumdog Millionaire will keep you hopeful and in high spirits as it flippantly bounces from one terror to the next.

  The movie opens to Jamal Malik (the game show contestant and protagonist played by Dev Patel) in the midst of being tortured by the police in their hopes of getting him to confess how he could have cheated his way up to the 20 million-rupee question. Since Jamal continues to insist that he simply knew the answers, the interrogators make him explain how, without being formally educated, he came across the answers before being on the show. As a result, Jamal is forced to relive all of the devastating yet opportunistic events of his childhood through various flashbacks. Each tragic story of Jamal's life involves some random fact that he learned from the experience and was later asked on the game show. Though somewhat clichéd, Jamal's limited source of answers aids director Danny Boyle and screenwriter Simon Beaufoy in proving that the most useful intelligence usually comes more from life experience than it does from textbooks.

  Jamal spends the majority of the movie attempting to reconnect with two people from his childhood: his corrupted older brother and former partner in crime Salim (played by Madhur Mittal) and his childhood sweetheart turned child prostitute turned gangster girlfriend Latika (played by Freida Pinto). As he retells his adventures with and searching for the two, Jamal also reveals the series of events by which he was able to acquire all sorts of facts. For example, he can answer a question about Indian actor Amitabh Bachchan because as a child he jumped into a puddle of fecal waste in order to get the performer's autograph. He knew that Ben Franklin's face lends itself to the U.S. hundred-dollar bill because a blind street singer made him ascertain the actual amount of money Jamal gave by reading who's name on the bill so he wouldn't be cheated out of money. In one of the darker anecdotes, Jamal explains that he knew the inventor of a gun because he heard it mentioned as his brother Salim shot a gun for the first time and killed a man.

  Not only does the film offer a moving storyline and compelling characters, but it's a visual treat for the eyes as well. Cinematographer Anthony Dod Mantle brings the streets of Mumbai alive by utilizing India's rich palette of colors and working off of Mumbai's explosive energy. The soundtrack also enriches the film and includes several songs by M.I.A. including the well-known hit, "Paper Planes." To capture the quick and stealthy feel of Slumdog Millionaire's action sequences, Mantle used compact digital cameras. The cameras were a wise choice because they allowed both Mantle and Boyle to add realism to the film while still playing up Mumbai's bright and vivid colors. 

  The film's setting may provide a gorgeous backdrop, but Boyle used the setting and culture of Mumbai in another way as well -- as a means for commenting on the real life horrors of India's suffering. Using India's culture, Boyle relentlessly exposes the poverty of India's slums and corruption by local gang leaders' overwhelming power.

  Slumdog Millionaire is both brutally honest and caustic about the problems going on in Mumbai today, but what makes it so uplifting and moving for audiences is that the passion within India is abundantly clear through all of Jamal's hopes and hurdles. Boyle's newest film is captivating, visually brilliant, and soul stirring. Although Slumdog Millionaire is only playing in selected theatres, the trip to Bellingham or Randolph is absolutely worth it because this is a film that everyone should experience on the big screen.

The structuring of this film was very well done. I loved the idea of an entire life story being told through a game of 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire'. The cutting between the three timelines- Jamal's childhood, Jamal being interrogated, and Jamal on the show - worked to beautifully tell Jamal's life story in the slums.

The issues of survival, violence and danger are presented with a heart. The audience is given a taste of Jamal's slumdog life, and not only do we empathise with him, but we feel a sense of guilt. How can we sit in a luxurious cinema and watch this film, when children in other parts of the world are surviving like this? This isn't the first film to evoke such a response, and nor will it be the last, yet every time I still feel as if I should be doing something.

On Novemeber 12, 2008, Slumdog Millionaire made its way to select theaters in the United States. Since then, it has won almost every award it was nominated for, even Best Picture at the Oscars. A glimpse into a whole nother look at the world.

Slumdog Millionaire begins with Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) being beaten up. His is asked constantly how he cheated on the answers. Minutes later, Jamal is in a chair in front of a episode of Who Wants to be a Millionaire? The previous night, he was on that episode going for one million dollars. Seconds into Slumdog Millionaire, everything just clicks. It perfectly sets you up for a magnificent story. Telling it in flashback form will make you grin from ear to ear at the end. I love foreign films. I feel this way because storytelling comes first. If explosions, skin or violence is required to accurately tell their stories, so be it. But the story is everything in films made outside the USA. When I think of great `story' based films, `The Usual Suspects' (USA), `Run Lola Run' (Germany), and `Roshomon' (Japan) come to mind. There is only one element to these films that is similar. They all involve a recounting or revisiting of events that lead up to the finale. `Slumdog Millionaire' belongs in this category as well.

This film has the courage to go almost two-hours. The `standard' for movies these days is 90 minutes. That's mainly because studios listen more to focus groups than directors. The same standard applied in the sixties with record releases. The cardinal rule: never go over three minutes in length. This `wisdom' was obliterated when FM radio and `album oriented rock' ushered in an era of unprecedented creativity. In 'Slumdog Millionaire', Writer, Simon Beaufoy, Editor, Chris Dickens, and Directors, Danny Boyle & Loveleen Tandan complimented each other in a magnificent display of ensemble work behind the scenes. The precious extra minutes were used unselfishly and gave the story room to breath, and ultimately triumph

Another aspect of risk (beautifully handled here) was in seaming together multiple time periods. Many potentially excellent films are ruined as the story gets lost in the time tunnels, and confusion ensues. In `Slumdog Millionaire', we have three characters, interpreted by nine actors. Six of them being children. Each part was brilliantly acted, and the continuity was allowed to develop clearly and naturally. Again, Directors, Danny Boyle & Loveleen Tandan were the reason it worked. They say you get what you give, and they must have been quite generous with the young cast.

I would be negligent not to mention a marvelous supporting cast. Not to be outshone, the people and settings throughout were spectacular. Cinematographer, Anthony Dod Mantle, made the most of capturing an amazing country. The film was shot entirely in India. A few months before viewing `Slumdog Millionaire' I was extremely fortunate to have seen the amazing documentary `Story of India' on public television. I am certain that it enhanced this film for me.

`Slumdog Millionaire' is funny, adventurous, cruel, dramatic and clever. Boyle and wove all of these elements into pure delight. A.R. Rahman's score set the tone for lively, dramatic and humorous sequences. At the end of the film, I felt a sigh of relief; having already known everyone mentioned in this piece was recognized for their excellence. I don't know why, but when I have experienced outstanding film making, I want everyone else to have the same chance as well. If this piece was truly headed straight to DVD, one wonders if it would have been seen at all.

Much speculation has occurred in Hollywood over the connection, particularly financial, with Bollywood. But here is yet another example of something originating from outside of Hollywood that is literally defines `world class' film making. I hope the global boundaries that are falling `flat' in the business world take root in movies as well. Here's hoping that we can do away with the preface and just call them `films'.

The leads Dev Patel and Freida Pinto do a commendable job with their respective characters and the supporting cast is great. Anil Kapoor shows various shades as the host of the show and Irfan Khan plays his role delicately. In the hands of a less talented actor it could've been easily overdone. In my opinion the real stars of the movie, which you probably won't see in any of the interviews are the kids portraying the younger Jamal, Latika and Salim. (Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, Rubina Ali, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail.)They carry the movie for nearly 90 minutes before the older Latika shows up. A great debut by Freida Pinto who after watching her on screen reminds me and probably a lot of other people of an Indian Keira Knightley. A girl certainly worth waiting and fighting for as our hero does. Her character ultimately galvanizes the film forward. The film is also a personal triumph for the versatile Danny Boyle. He has given us some uniquely wonderful films, from "Trainspotting" and "28 days later", to "The Beach" and "Sunshine". The latter being my favorite, if you haven't seen it, I highly recommend it. The soundtrack of this film is also a great one and matches the story's pace. It features. M.I.A, Shankar Ishaan Loy and the genius work of A.R. Rahman.

This film could've certainly been made by a Bollywood director, although would it have garnered so much attention and praise? I doubt it. It needs to be labeled a Hollywood movie because the word "Bollywood" comes with the stigmata; of movies having song and dance numbers and being over 3 hours long. "Lagaan" could've been a real contender back in 2002 for best picture if the songs were eliminated and it was about 40 minutes shorter with a Hollywood director attached. I love the songs in a lot of the movies but when it comes to gaining momentum overseas, they prove to be a handicap.

With that said "Slumdog Millionaire" is a film to celebrate not only because of its underdog story of "rags to raja" but it will invite even more interest to Bollywood cinema and maybe they have a chance of winning "Best Foreign Film" the next time around. Meanwhile, I would love to see this film at the Oscars. Boyle and his team have put together an amazing film. It's gritty, dirty and it's inspiring and uplifting. It captures the real India like never before. "Go Slumdog go"! The last ten minutes will definitely have you cheering and if you're aching for a dance number, stay for the credits!

Slumdog Millionaire is Danny Boyle's masterpiece. Thank god Boyle has finally recieved the recognition that he has long deserved. Slumdog Millionaire is an absolute triumph of cinema. It crafts love, pain, and destiny all into one uplifting and inspiring film. This movie is a true work of art.

Every performance in this film is fantastic. Boyle enlisted the aid of an extremely skilled set of actors. Since the film takes involves flashbacks to earlier parts of the protagonist's life, we see the characters at different ages. That is three different actors portraying each of the three lead characters. Ayush Mahesh Khedekar, Tanay Chheda, and Dev Patel give wonderful performances as Jamal Malik, the lead character of the story. As Salim, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail, Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala, and Madhur Mittal all do great playing the more troubled of the two brothers. Playing the Jamal's destined love are Rubina Ali, Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar, and Freida Pinto. They are everybit as good as should be expected. Anil Kapoor is great as the host of India's "Who Wants To Be A Millionaire?" All the actors bring their characters completely to life in the film.

Beneath all the darkness in Slumdog Millionaire is a love story. The film follows Jamal Malik (Petel) on his journey to be reunited with his lost love Latika (Pinto). Labeling this film as a romance wouldn't quite be right. Slumdog is a movie that can't be placed into any specific genre of film. There are moments you will be laughing out loud and then moments that will move you to tears. This is a feel good movie, even if sometimes it is the complete opposite.

Director Boyle displays an extreme sense of skill with this film. The visuals are breathtaking and display a real distinct style. The music in this film is inventive and unlike anything I've heard before. A.R. Rahman brings this movie to life with his outstanding score. 

Don't let the unusual title of this film keep you from seeing it. I promise that you will not be disappointed with Slumdog Millionaire.

Like The Dark Knight before it, Slumdog Millionaire is the kind of film which is so overhyped that you cannot now see it without having to deal in some way with that emotional and critical backage. Where Slumdog differs from The Dark Knight is in its tone, or more precisely, in the difference between the tone of the advertising and the tone of the film itself. Where The Dark Knight was always advertised as being dark, and hence its darkness came as no surprise, Slumdog Millionaires advertising made it look light and superficial, at least comparatively. Critics praised it as the feel-good film of the year", when in fact much of it is fairly dark.

The film overall could be described as feel-good, insofar as the rag-to-riches story at the centre of it has been done so many times before, and the ending is very sentimental. It could be said that, had this film been set in Britain rather than India, it would have been billed as a Richard Curtis film in all but name. However, there is more to it than just the feel-good factor at the end, and it is certainly not the case that the flashy visuals disguise the plot holes.

As far as the acting goes, generally the child actors outshine their adult counterparts. The early sequences of the film, in which Dev Patels character is trying to get an autograph from his favourite film star, is very charming without being overbearing. The scene in the toilet is also a nice, if rather disgusting, homage to Boyles earlier work, Trainspotting. When the action switches back to the game show, Patel spends much of the performance just gaping inanely, and often this adds nothing to the character he is playing. We already get the message that he is neither intelligent nor in this for the money, so why diminish him still further? As for his love interest, played by Freida Pinto, shes largely convincing, though there are odd moments where she falters, for instance on the phone call between her and Patel live on the show.

The main success of Slumdog Millionaire is not in its storyline, which is decent but not a masterstroke. It lies in the way that story is told, both in the narrative structure and the images of India it gives. The film manages to flip back and forth between the past and the present without resorting to a distant narrator fading in and out, as in The Princess Bride or, more recently, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button. And unlike Hideous Kinky, whose portrayal of Muslims was at best questionable and at worst awfully stereotypical, Boyle gets right to the centre of what life in the slums is like, depicting love and hate equally with not a hint of judging or sanctimony.

Films with happy endings are always going to appeal to audiences more than those who endings are ambiguous or pessimistic. Hence Slumdog Millionaire is always going to be revered in some way. Fortunately it deserves a great deal of this reverence, being a film which walks the tightrope between poignant and sentimental and makes it successfully to the other side. Its dark elements mean that it has staying power which its more sentimental counterparts  Benjamin Button included  may not have, and from a visual point of view it is easily Danny Boyles best film. Thoroughly recommended.

I saw this back in December after hearing a little bit about it on the net. I was so excited to see that it was playing at my local theater and I didn't hesitate to see it when it was released. There are a lot of people who are just asking why this film is so popular or loved, the reason why in my opinion is that it's just a happy film. We usually have a best picture winner that is depressing, but instead Slumdog Millionaire just lifts your spirits and makes you cry in joy. I couldn't believe how much I loved this film, after reading a summary on what it was about, I was just confused and wondering if this film was really going to be good. But we have these unknown young actors: Dev Peitel, Freida Pinto and Madhur Mittal who pull in heart wrenching performances and you can't help but love their characters and just keep rooting for them. All in all, this film is a love story. Most film lovers fear those words after Titanic because everyone thought it to be a predictable puppy love story, this love story however is made in strength and faith and you can't help but keep wanting Jamal and Latika to be together. Even though I saw the film a while back, I still remember it like I saw it yesterday.

A title card is presented: "Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million rupees. How did he do it? A) He cheated, B) He's lucky, C) He's a genius, D) It is written." Jamal is a contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? hosted by Prem Kumar in which he was on the show and won 20,000,000 rupees (about US$500,000). Jamal then explains that, while at least the question about Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan was very simple, he knew the answers of most questions by chance, because of things that happened in his life. This is conveyed in a series of flashbacks documenting the details of his childhood. This includes scenes of him obtaining Bachchan's autograph, the death of his mother during the Hindu anti-Muslim violence, rekindling the memory of the 1993 anti-Muslim attacks in Mumbai by Hindu nationalists in the slums, and how he and his brother Salim befriend Latika. The children are eventually discovered by Maman while they live in the trash heaps. Maman is a gangster who "collects" street children so that he can ultimately train them to beg for money. Salim is groomed to become a part of Maman's operation and is asked to bring Jamal to Maman in order to be blinded. Salim protects his brother, and the three children try to escape; but only Salim and Jamal are able to do so. Latika is re-captured by Maman's organization and raised as a culturally talented prostitute whose virginity will fetch a high price. The brothers eke out a living, traveling on top of trains, selling goods, pretending to be tour guides at the Taj Mahal, and picking pockets. Jamal eventually insists that they return to Mumbai since he wishes to locate Latika. When he finds her working as a dancer in a brothel, the brothers attempt to rescue her, but Maman intrudes, and in the resulting conflict Salim draws a gun and kills Maman. Salim then uses the fact that he killed Maman to obtain a job with Javed a rival crime lord. Salim claims Latika as his own and when Jamal protests, Salim threatens to kill him and Latika intervenes, accepting her fate with Salim. 

Years later, Jamal has a position at a call center. When he is asked to cover for a co-worker for a couple of minutes, he searches the database for Salim and Latika. He gets in touch with Salim, who has become a high-ranking lieutenant in Javed's organization. Jamal confronts a regretful Salim on tense terms. Salim invites Jamal to live with him and after following Salem, he sees Latika living there. He talks his way in as the new chef and tries to convince Latika to leave. She tries to discourage him, but on the first day that Jamal waits at the train station, Latika attempts to escape with him, but is recaptured by Salim and Javed's men. One of the men then slashes her cheek with a knife, scarring her as Salim drives off, leaving Jamal with the onlooking crowd. Jamal again loses contact with Latika when Javed moves to another house. In another attempt to find Latika, Jamal tries out for the popular game show because he knows that she will be watching.

I cannot wait for this movie to be released on DVD, it's a terrific uplifting movie that just captures your heart and makes you feel good. I couldn't believe that people were just complaining about the ending dance sequence, it was a TERRIFIC way to end it, to see everything that Jamal went through and that dance just makes you feel happy because you can tell the joy of him having his Latika in his arms. It was a beautiful ending and makes you extremely joyful. The story is brutal, funny, sad, original and beautiful. Danny Boyle, I knew that this director had something special when he made the horror film 28 Days Later, but who knew he could pull of such an uplifting beautifully made film? He picked the perfect actors, made the film wonderfully, and the whole crew seemed to enjoy making this together. Who wouldn't? It was a pleasure to watch on the screen and if you haven't seen this film in the theater, buy it when it comes on DVD, it's one of the most terrific experiences I've had watching a film. 

10/10

Slumdog Millionaire. You know what? I've been meaning to for a long time to sit down and actually review this film, but somehow, I never got the chance to. That said, I'm finally doing it in my recent 'review these films or it's death' kind of situations.

Here we have a film that has garnered a lot of success from the critics and it has so for good reason. This is a very inventive film which takes a typical fairy-tale love story and manages to apply it to real life, in this case, India. The story goes like this. Jamal Malik, a very poor dude, who's being tortured by the Indian police under suspicion about him cheating in a game show. While being interrogated about how Jamal knew the answers, Jamal truthfully talks about his life story. He talks about his childhood; the 1994 Hindu attacks on Muslims and how it cost him his mother's life, and then he met the love of his life: Latika. From there he talks about his separation from his brother to how he got reunited with both of them and then how he got on the show. When he's done, Inspector dude believes him and lets him go. So on, so forth.

Now the way the story is crafted, man was it great! Everything was right in its place; it never felt too dark or too light, it was funny at times, and it had a good consistancy and a great story to boot. The romance here was compelling, and the way the characters were developed was nigh extraordinary. That, and the fact that the movie itself was awesome. Story: 8.7/10.

As far as the acting goes, none of it was over the top. In fact, the performances were believable. Everyone hit the right spot; the lead actors were truly convincing and the characterization was astonishing. The emotion expressed by the actors really made me feel an attachment to them, and even though the ending was known to be typical, they really made me feel for the characters and made me want to see "love conquer all". Acting: 9.3/10.

Hell, as far as the score goes, A.R. Rahman did a great job. He balanced all the music to the particular scenes, and each tune, especially the romantic ones, are memorable. When the movie ended and treated me to Jai Ho!, I felt giddy and exhilarated. I even remember humming the tune out after I came out of the theatre. Hey, the dude got an Oscar for the music for a reason! Music: 10/10.

Overall, the film is great, and if you haven't seen it yet, for the love of God, SEE IT! It's really good, and worth all your while. If you liked this kind of film, also check out My Name Is Khan out too, it's awesome as well. All in all: 9.3/10.

Charming, light underdog comedy about an Indian teen (Dev Patel) who wins a million rupes on the Indian version of the game show "Who Wants to be A Millionaire?". As the movie opens Jamal is being interrogated by investigators who question how a boy from the slums could know all the answers. They suspect he cheated. Seen in flashbacks, Jamal recounts the events in his life that provided him with the answers to those questions. Writer Simon Beaufoy adapted the novel "Q&A" by Vikas Swarup into this clever premise which is filmed with a lot of style and vitality by director Danny Boyle. There is a lot of humor such as the scene when Jamal, Huck Finn-like, acts as a tour guide to American tourists at the Taj Mahal. The filmmakers show us the harsh conditions in the Indian slums contrasted with the influence of American pop culture there. A concluding music sequence is straight out of Bollywood. Some of the rough edges are smoothed over and the love story is conventional but we root for the hero to triumph. Anil Kapoor as the game show host is superb. He has a sharp wit and knows how to work the audience but is unexpectedly cunning. A surprising box office hit, the movie won eight Oscars for Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay, Cinematography, Editing, Sound, Score, Song.

Until I am forced to reconsider my opinion when I return from Iraq to the United States and someone tries to force this thing through my retinas again, I'll defer and respectfully guide you to the venomous argument of someone named jhildner, who posted comments responding to a couple of Christopher Orr's pieces at The New Republic's website: 

http://www.tnr.com/blog/the-plank/oscar-grouching

http://www.tnr.com/article/books-and-arts/the-orrscars-2008

jhildner wrote: 
***  Slumdog was more crappy than scrappy -- totally empty from the standpoint of character and theme -- and I've yet to hear anything approaching a convincing case for it along those dimensions.  ***
&
*** I make the case against Slumdog any chance I get -- so much so that my friends are now former friends.  In short, it has no genuine characters and no genuine point, though it sort of pretends to.  Cross-posted from Orr's "Orrscars":

Obviously, you [Chris] are not alone in effusively praising this allegedly "Dickensian" story about a kid from the slums of Mumbai who is knocked around in life until he finally, spoiler alert, achieves his destiny, which consists of getting both the money and the girl and leading a Bollywood-style dance number over the credits. Most seem to view this film as about life and love and the triumph of the human spirit. I had a different reaction. Slumdog is, on serious examination, about nothing and nobody, least of all the human spirit. It's a black hole -- the void that sucks you in. I tried to keep at a prudent distance and I think was able to escape with my wits about me as a result. The movie's one-note characters are objectively tedious. Jamal is not a person, but a mere vessel of cosmic, inhuman love. That love is directed exclusively at one Latika, who, in turn, is also not a person, but a mere manifestation of beauty and vulnerability -- just how we like 'em. When these forces collide, angels get toothaches. As for theme, the film helpfully identifies it in title form: "It is written." Or is it, love conquers all? Either way, the suggestion is insipid and false. Dickens's stories are not merely about the hard journeys of the ostensibly good-hearted and scrappy. His characters face internal conflicts as well as external struggles. His protagonists grow and make mistakes and are brought low. Jamal, by contrast, is just a lucky pinball. Well, maybe that's not fair. We're to understand his reward, I suppose, as karmic. The problem is that he has no demons, and so strength of character is made dull. He's a superficial goodness machine. Such things exist only in movies -- movies like this one. Slumdog is not, as Chris wrote in his review, a "fable." Fables have points. To be honest, there are some pointless movies -- movies about nothing and nobody -- that I have enjoyed. Speed is an example. Of course, I've always had a crush on Sandra Bullock, and I confess to a boyish giddiness in re vehicular peril. Maybe it comes down to what sort of emotional pornography is up your street. Then again, Speed didn't play in arthouses. Strip Slumdog of its pretensions, and all that's left are pretty pictures, unearned exuberance, and that yawning chasm.

I'll add that even Speed had more believable characters.  Can you picture this couple's life after the movie ends?  I can't.  Because their lives ended when the credits ended.  Their destiny was to find each other and dance about it.  That was their point -- to be soulless plot devices.  Not only is the movie superficial, but it seems to luxuriate in its superficiality.

Is that enough to put the ball in the defenders' court?  I've been trying to get responses.  What I usually get is one of the following:  "Hey, it's Bollywood!"  (Well, if this is Bollywood, then Bollywood's pretty vacuous.)  Or, "So, I guess you only like downers."  (Nope.  Just movies with the basic elements of decent story-telling, like character and thematic coherence.)  Or, "Lighten up!"  (Fine, but parading this around as a Great Film, as opposed to the irrelevancy it is, is annoying.)***

a good film, but oscar worthy - methinks not.  Compare this film with the Kite Runner - both about 3rd world scenes, culture clash, and street violence.  They are very similar, but Kite Runner, in my opinion, is the more grounded and fluid film.

Slumdog tends to run all over the map, piling disjointed scenes together to paint its picture; and while some of this is a brilliant cause and effect (showing how an impoverished petty thief knows the answers to Who Wants To Be A Millionaire questions), there is too much back and forth and questionable motivations; from the fat police sargent to the game show host.

Throw in some total implausabilities (the two brothers able to speak perfect english and con their way as guides at the Taj Mahal, to the simply lame questions on Millionaire - the million dollar question could be answered by any 15 year old who was paying attention in school - the name of the 3rd muskeeteer), and then add some overly modern camera shots and goofy quasi India/disco music and you end up with a mish mash that destroys what was otherwise a compelling film that, in spite of the aforementioned, does a good job of conveying the squaller and poverty of the Indian slums.

The last third of the film relies on the game show to carry it, as its counter story of love becomes increasingly ludicrous and implausable.  The hit man brother's ultimate sacrifice plays false - as he gives up and allows himself to be slaughtered - a shrewd "player" could have figured out a better way - as is the case with much that goes on with this film.  Sorry to say - Kite Runner again has many of the same elements, but does a better job of presenting it all.

Director Danny Boyle takes us to the slums of Mumbai, India to discover the lives in poverty and success. Winner of four Golden Globes including Best Director, Best Drama, Best Screenplay, and Best Original Score, Slumdog Millionaire continues to enlighten audience about life in ups to downs and vice versa.

Set in the slums of Mumbai, India, the story starts in a police station where Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) was being interrogated and tortured by special police agents. What did he do? He was accused of cheating in the famous quiz show "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire" Indian Version. He was winning 10,000,000 (ten million) rupees when the host of the show Prem Kumar (Anil Kapoor) accused him of such.

Jamal, an uneducated call center assistant was becoming the greatest hero of the slum people when he got into the quiz show. He got the support of most people when he exhibited his great knowledge in pop culture, entertainment, sports, etc. He was winning big time and the people loved it. Is he a genius or a cheater? That was the question. But what everybody did not know was Jamal was getting the answers to the questions from his childhood to the very moment he was sitting on the hot seat. Probably, he can read and he can write, but he wasn't fond of learning. He just got lucky that all the questions in the show he could vividly remember the answers. But searching for the answers was somewhat a bitter and painful experience for him. His flashing back took him by the time of his childhood, to the time when his mother died, up to the time he got his work, and up to him getting into the show.

It was drama, comedy, romance, gangster, action, adventure all in one. But it is not a movie experience of a lifetime. It tells us simple stories of under simple individuals but it gives us a lot of things to ponder. Can a slumdog really be a millionaire? Everything happens for a reason. It is written. But what we are right now is our choice.

Nonlinearity in films is of great use in today's cinema. But it must be given much attention to. Scenes are properly charted. The music and the action are well synchronized. Actors are amateurs. It is hard to watch a film with actors speaking with their second language and you can feel their struggle to utter a single phrase they could hardly understand. The music too pop for the scenes.

There are three stages in main characters' lives in this, childhood, puberty, and adulthood. There are also three main settings, in the police station, in the set of "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire", and Jamal's childhood.

One local film that I remembered first time I saw this film was 1975 Lino Brocka's "Maynila: Sa Mga Kuko ng Liwanag". The life of Jamal is merely similar to that of Bembol Roco's role in "Maynila". His search for the answers to his questions has led him to reminiscing the past in bitterness and pain. 
It was a team up of two of the Philippines' greatest film-makers Lino Brocka and Mike De Leon.

It is conspicuous in the film the use of unusual camera angles. Some photographs are shot tilted in some degrees, unlike most films that use conventional camera works. This maybe a product of modern cinematic techniques. Colors are of high contrast and there are a few of good applications of modernism in this. But those are not enough. A true great film should be natural in a manner, not second rate, trying hard, copycat (just like a local actress Cherie Gil once said).

Jamal meets Latika, in a sad time of his life, but immediately knows she is the one. From that time (they are both roughly 7) through them becoming 18/19 he never forgets her, and gets on the show because he knew she'd be watching. With the cops beating and electrocuting he maintains his innocence of cheating, and tells the truth as being questioned. With a nail-bating ending and the best of the best "I have had too much" type scenes in recent memory, everyone needs to see this grand ode to India and the strength of love.

Slumdog Millionaire is a movie that you will either connect with, or not. The movie has such a great spirit that endures through good and bad times like its main character.

The first initial connection I felt was to that very part of someone who sits at a trivia night with their friends and they ask you "how the hell did you know that?" and typically the story connected to it is something that is totally random. In the case of Slumdog Jamal does not only know answers due to previous occurrences in his life, but it seems like they were also defining moments that have led him to this moment on Who Wants to be a Millionaire. The very first question/answer, and more importantly, the story that connects Jamal to the answer is a great portrait of Jamal's character. He will do, and go through anything for something he wants or is passionate about........in this case a simple autograph. 

As I mentioned, these stories are not fleeting moments that come and go in a man's life, they are all linked to a moment that would be unforgettable in one's lifetime. These stories are not simply recollections for Jamal a lot of them are the opening of old wounds, almost to the point where you wonder if the show he is truly on is "Who Wants to Exercise Their Demons". 

The film moves at a good pace, and also develops the characters and their surroundings as well. Whilst we see the progression of Jamal and Salim as they grow up we also notice the transition of the city of Mumbai. It is a place of opportunity, and a lot changes around Jamal, as people he knows are trying to make good at a time when their poverty stricken town is on the rise. What was interesting was the difference between he and his brother and the choices they make in order to keep up with progress. They both are petty thieves and one embraces the outsourcing boom while the other simply escalates to higher level, and higher paying crime. The movie is also a classic endorsement for karma, especially when Jamal clearly believes that fate will take him to where he wants to go and the obtaining of dreams is a matter of destiny and nothing else.

Patel and Pinto are great leads and there is a bright future for both I think. I would have to say my favorite though was Anil Kapoor as Prem, the consummate host when the cameras are rolling, but a ruthless and corrupting personality, that wants to protect what he has, off the screen. I have no doubt he will be gracing our screens further, in fact I heard he will be appearing in the next season of 24........I can't wait to see how it turns out.

Boyle's direction is spot on, and he has made a great transition movie for those who have seen Hollywood movies, but not Bollywood. The film is a great combination of both. I think the driving force of this movie though is its story, Jamal's story, and it's a great one to sit through. It has been a few months since I've seen the movie, but I think I could answer all of the questions he is faced with, on account that the flashbacks leave as much an impression on the viewer as they do on Jamal..........ok, not quite as much, but there are plenty of moments in this movie that stay with you. The dancing at the end credits to Jai Ho was a nice touch, and while totally irrelevant in comparison to the movies themes it seems to fit in an odd way, and reminds you of the spirit that this movie has.

Great movie, and thoroughly deserving of every award, and praise that it got.

Slumdog Millionaire is a rare gem. It is a disappointment knowing Slumdog may never get the attention it deserves. This film is like a buried treasure chest: inside, it is full of rich material and delivers great reward, but, unfortunately, it is quite difficult to find. Boyle has such a simple storyline, but shapes it into an innovative picture that does not just glorify the game show we all love (or used to love), but also identifies with India's culture.
	The film, which is based upon Vikas Swarup's novel Q&A, is about a boy named Jamal, who is a boy from the slums of India; a Slumdog. He goes on the India version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire, hosted by Prem Kumar, played excellently by Anil Kapoor, well known as a villain in many Bollywood films. Here, Jamal makes it all the way to the twenty-million-rupee question, but the siren goes off! Backstage, the host takes him to a van, where Jamal is brought to government headquarters, not his two star hotel. The government accuses him of cheating, because they are perplexed as to how a boy from a slum could know the answers to such difficult questions. The story then transitions from Plot 'A' to 'B' to 'C' to 'D' like the game show. Although a disjointed tale told in fragments and flashbacks, it still works because the viewer is lost within the tense and unusual experiences that Jamal endures. 
	Boyle does go somewhat cliché, however, by telling Jamal's life in chronological order. It begins with Jamal as a young boy, when his mom is killed in a Muslim riot, and he and his brother, Salim, have to survive on their own. Of course, though, there is a love interest. Fortunately, Boyle goes beyond this cliché, and like his past films, such as 28 Days Later and Millions, you feel the experience first-hand, as if it is your own journey. Boyle's characteristic use of long shots and sway shots, during fast paced chases, make India's aura feel compact and hectic, as how one predicts it to be. But along with that, each shot is so colourful that it saturates the screen with its floridity. Boyle's crafty work in style, gives the film a set of lungs, breathing its expression out through the screen. 
	However, Boyle, to me, has always struggled with endings. His plot premise has one dilemma: do you end with Jamal losing the twenty million rupees or does he take home the cash? His choice works, but Boyle does play to the audience, and the film seems to float into a sea of caricatures. Like Changeling, both are great films, but they still suffer from melodrama's ailment: the contrived love story and the over-done Asian gangster scenario. Nevertheless, most of the film, primarily the beginning, is brilliant and moving. The adolescent Jamal struggles with heart-breaking and sometimes shocking situations, in slum town India. Therefore, there is enough originality in this film to state that Slumdog is one of the better films of 2008, and with such little hype that it is getting, it would be a crime to not use a phone-a-friend lifeline and get them to see this film.

Like most fairy tales, Slumdog Millionaire is predictable for the most part. If, as the movie unfolds, you believe that Malik will not win the 20 million rupees or get the girl, then you are probably either a wee bit of a cynic or else a contrarian. I think most of us know that this story will have a happy ending -- just from the title alone. If that had to be the title of this movie, then the only way not to tip us off would have been to put a question mark at the end of the title: Slumdog Millionaire? -- and trust me, a writer should never do that : )

So is it a problem for Boyle that the outcome of the story is predictable?

Yes, it is a problem for Boyle and for anyone else making a movie, telling a story. If the outcome is predictable, then you must have a way of making the story keep the audience interested. And here, Boyle does an excellent job. Malik's story is fascinating, a series of hardships that all add up to providing just the answers he needs to take home all the money.

That alone is fascinating. Imagine if each experience of our lives added up to a big payoff -- another sure sign of a fairy tale unfolding. Of course we all know this is unique; our lives usually add up to little more than our lives. There are no big payoffs, monetary or otherwise. This movie is a great example of a very predictable story told in a very unpredictable way.

I feel most for all the orphans whose fairy tale is cut short when they are disfigured by Maman and his ilk in order to make them more successful beggars, and for older brother Salim who makes the choice for his own fairy tale life based on the murder of Maman. A fairy tale life based on murder -- even though we all know that Maman deserves death and worse -- can almost never lead to a happy ending for that character.

Jamal, un ragazzo di Mumbai cresciuto nelle slum, sta partecipando al quiz Chi vuol essere milionario?. La tensione in studio è palpitante e davanti ad un pubblico incredulo il giovane sta per rispondere all'ultima e decisiva domanda, che potrebbe fargli vincere 20 milioni di rupie (poco più di 300.000 ?). Prem Kumar, conduttore dello show, prende in antipatia il ragazzo, lui stesso proviene dalla strada e non si capacita come un ragazzo di tale estrazione possa conoscere tutte le risposte. Prima di rispondere all'ultima domanda, Jamal viene arrestato ed interrogato dalla polizia con l'accusa di imbroglio.

La polizia gli fa vedere un video in cui gli mostrano la sua performance al quiz e gli chiedono come faceva a sapere quelle cose e, da quel momento, il ragazzo ripercorre le tappe della sua vita da quando era un bambino di strada: ogni risposta data corrisponde ad una fase della vita di Jamal. Da bambino perde la madre in un assalto di integralisti indù e insieme a una bambina di nome Latika e suo fratello scappano e vengono raccolti da uno sfruttatore che li costringe a fare l'elemosina facendo cantare i bambini più intonati per le strade e accecandoli per impietosire di più. Quando è il turno di Jamal, il fratello lo salva e i tre cercano di scappare dal rifugio dello sfruttatore. Durante la corsa, Salim lascia la mano di Latika per vendicarsi di uno scherzo che lei gli ha fatto: solo i due fratelli riescono a salire su un treno e a fuggire.

I due vivono vendendo di tutto sul treno: una volta cresciuti e diventati adolescenti si uniscono ad una banda di bambini che derubano i turisti. In seguito, per volere di Jamal che vuole ritovare Latika, ritornano a Mumbay. Lì effettivamente ritrovano Latika, che fa la ballerina. Stanno per scappare insieme quando arriva lo stesso sfruttatore che li aveva imprigionati prima e che vuole catturarli, ma Salim ha trovato una pistola e minaccia lo sfruttatore e i suoi complici di sparargli. Libera Jamal e Latika, prende i soldi, e quando stanno per andarsene uccide lo sfruttatore per non avere altri problemi in futuro. Mentre Jamal e Latika cercano un rifugio, il fratello va dal più grande mafioso di Bombay e gli propone di assumerlo come assassino, quindi ritorna da Jamal e per ordine del mafioso lo caccia e prende Latika.

Nel frattempo Jamal cresce e diventa adulto, e si ritrova a lavorare per un call center di Bombay. Lì, approfittando dell'assenza di un operatore, prova a cercare il fratello e Latika. Latika è un nome troppo diffuso, ma quando cerca il nome del fratello ne trova pochissimi e li chiama uno ad uno fino a quando non lo trova. Così i due fratelli si incontrano in un cantiere di Bombay dove discutono sul fatto che lui sia diventato un mafioso e che Latika sia stata data al suo capo.

Jamal prova a mettersi in contatto con lei andando a lavorare come cuoco dal mafioso e in effetti la incontra. Vede che lei segue molto Chi vuol essere milionario?, e dopo essere stato licenziato dal mafioso, dà un appuntamento a Latika. Il giorno dell'appuntamento si incontrano ma Salim, venuto a riprendersi Latika, con la forza impedisce a Jamal di parlarle. Jamal decide che per incontrarla deve partecipare al quiz in TV. Qui finisce la versione che Jamal racconta all'ispettore di polizia, che oramai gli crede e decide che Jamal deve andare a cercare di vincere i 20 milioni di rupie. Quando va lì tutta l'India lo segue e anche Latika cerca di seguire lo show in tv, ma il mafioso glielo impedisce. Nel frattempo Salim, pentito del suo operato, decide di farla finita e dà il suo cellulare a Latika, dicendole di scappare e di cercare di incontrare Jamal. Latika scappa mentre Jamal sta per rispondere all'ultima domanda. Nel frattempo il mafioso si accorge che Latika è scappata e capisce che è stato il fratello di Jamal a farla scappare.

Vuole ucciderlo, ma Salim si rifugia in bagno, comincia a riempire di soldi la vasca e prepara la pistola per sparare al mafioso. Nel frattempo Latika è rimasta imbottigliata nel traffico e guarda attraverso un negozio di televisioni Jamal che sta vincendo. Jamal non sa rispondere alla domanda e chiede l'aiuto a casa, ultimo aiuto rimasto. Il telefono squilla a lungo e il conduttore gli chiede chi ha chiamato. Jamal gli risponde che ha chiamato il fratello, dato che è l'unico numero che conosce. Latika si ricorda di avere il suo telefono e cerca disperatamente di raggiungere l'auto dove ha posato il cellulare, rispondendo proprio quando stanno per riattaccare.

Finalmente Latika e Jamal si possono parlare ma nessuno dei due sa la risposta alla domanda "Chi fra questi nomi è il terzo moschettiere?". Latika non sa la risposta, ma rassicura Jamal di essere, adesso, in salvo da tutto. Il tempo scade e si interrompe la telefonata. Nel frattempo i mafiosi irrompono nel bagno dove sta Salim. Il ragazzo spara al gangster, ma viene ucciso dai suoi scagnozzi. Alla fine Jamal dice di voler rispondere la A, ovvero Aramis, nonostante non conoscesse la risposta esatta. Jamal vince 20 milioni di rupie e all'uscita dalla trasmissione finalmente rincontra Latika e insieme si giurano amore eterno.

I've often called movies "Dickensian" when they take fairly disparate characters, events, places and ideas and tie them together in interesting and thought-provoking ways. It's a quality of storytelling and filmmaking that I really admire, and most movies that I would describe using that adjective tend to become favorites of mine. Slumdog Millionaire is not Dickensian...exactly. It doesn't quite have the feeling that one small character or occurrence near the beginning of the film suddenly becomes vitally important near that end, as many Dickensian films do. What it does have is a sense that EVERYTHING is connected, as each flashback Jamal experiences on the show is tied to a specific question he is asked, and thus provides him with each answer in a particularly unique way. That in itself is a pretty cool filmmaking scheme.

But where Slumdog Millionaire really stops being a good film and starts being a great one is when it takes a look at that pretty cool scheme and says "Okay, we're not going to use that all the time." Several of Jamal's answers he comes up with either by actual luck, by some basic deduction, or by purposefully doing what is not expected of him by the show's host--in other words, by being himself. This decision really showed that the film was about a person as a whole, not about a person who has had just the right experiences to beat a game show without cheating. The latter situation would merely be a film about coincidence. The former is a film about humanity. And as such, Slumdog Millionaire deserves every award it's gotten. 

Another thing I often give movies props for is doing great work with unknown actors. I can't say how well-known any of Slumdog's actors are in India, but just how well this movie did with American audiences is a testament to how awesome its unknown-in-America actors did. There didn't even need to be a token American, as many films decide is necessary to make their film marketable in the States, and I think the decision not to include one (if such a decision was even made, lol) actually made Slumdog MORE marketable here rather than less. Not to mention a hell of a lot more genuine. 

And while I'm talking about things I usually like about movies, I have to mention the fact that Slumdog had a happy ending. I know, I know, not EVERY film needs to have one of those, but when one builds up and builds up and builds up to a very expected ending, to torpedo that ending seems like an utter betrayal of the moviegoer by the filmmaker. (See also my reviews of Cube and 13: Game of Death.) There were a couple moments where I thought that Slumdog might go the same way, and my relief was immense when it did not. That's not to say that there were parts of Slumdog that were hard to watch, because there absolutely were. But the triumph that came out of that hardship and pain, no matter how cliche that triumph seemed, was well-earned, appropriate, and just plain felt amazing to watch. 

Simply put, an amazing movie on all counts.

The Academy awarded this garbage "Best Picture"?  This is the film which has inspired so much positive furor around the globe?  A bulbous conglomeration of Bollywood caterwauling, bleak violence, persistent human degradation, and shimmering fairytale cloy, Danny Boyle's little treasure trove of predictable twists and contrived turns left me yearning for the broken cynicism of Frank Capra.  If viewers yearn to see human degradation, I would encourage them to seek out Terry George's Hotel Rwanda; if one is salivating for beautifully depicted child abuse, seek out Siddiq Barmak's Osama or Terry Gilliam's Tideland.  If one desires a simple, poignant story of unexpected success, turn to Gary Ross's Seabiscuit.  If one wishes for all of these, seek out Fernando Meirelles's Cidade de Deus, a gloriously violent, intoxicatingly beautiful modern noir.  While many detractors of David Fincher's The Curious Case of Benjamin Button inexplicably wish to denigrate the work as a remake of the Tom Hanks vehicle Forrest Gump, I could not help myself from wondering why the same accusations were not made against Danny Boyle and screenwriter Simon Beaufoy's shameless pilfering through the screenplay of Cidade de Deus.  Nonetheless, it should be noted that Anil Kapoor, as the uber-sleazy Indian counterpart to Regis Philbin, and Irrfan Khan, as the surprisingly sympathetic police interrogator, give solid performances.  Dev Patel's titular performance is too humdrum to inspire much sympathy, and Freida Ponto, while visually stunning, is equally insipid.  The best performances in the film are actually those given by Ayush Mahesh Khedekar and Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail as the youngest manifestations of Jamal and Salim.  They are certainly the only part of the film infectious and compelling enough to warrant the cavalcade of positive criticism being bestowed upon this ilk.  A bathetic glorification of a genre in dire need of euthanasia: the Rocky-inspired underdog milieu.

Completely contrary to the expectations I had, given that I had assumed it was just about an everyday boy getting lucky on a game show, and then living in the lap of luxury. The fact of the matter is, is that the game show is just a sub story to the saddening tale of a young boy, his brother, and their female friend as they escape an attack on their family and head for a life of squalor making ends meat by any means possible. It is then the horrific events that we learn he has had to endure which ultimately help propel him to that million dollar question. Sounds like it's going to be a typically fairy tale ending but it's certainly anything but that as right before the very final live question, our hero Jamal is being quizzed by the police in the assumption that no 'slumdog' who has led a lowly life with next to no education could possibly answer a single question correct, never mind all of them. As we watch his struggle for innocence with the police, as well as his brother and friends battle with indian gang culture, it's gripping to the finish. It's a very poignant film that despite the rags to riches synopsis, has a much deeper meaning about Indian lifestyle and some people's struggles to get through life. The film does not dwell on the prize money, or what happens following the game show, but cleverly leaves us with the harsh Impact of reality that money cannot necessarily buy everyone's happiness. Admittedly, it's not necessarily a film one would want to watch again and again repeatedly, but most definitely a must watch film for all.

Rarely do I give a movie five stars. It is even rarer that I agree with what wins "Best Picture" in any given year. Dear readers, you are witnessing a rare moment on both counts. "Slumdog Millionaire" is deserving of every accolade that it received. 

Shortly before being presented with the final question in the Hindi version of "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire", Jamal Malik is detained due to allegations of possible cheating. Jamal grew up in an impoverished area and has no formal education, so the show's host doubts he actually knew the answers. As he is questioned, Malik flashes back through his remarkable life to each moment where he learned each answer. In the process, you find that Jamal is not on the show for the money at all ...

So well done. Rarely have I been this impressed with a movie, especially one that I went into with no expectations. I am let down by the "Best Picture" nearly annually and expected no different this time around. But this movie has it all. There is drama, action, intrigue, horrifying moments, touching moments, and ultimately a pretty solid love story. Most of all, the end game is always in doubt. Right up until the very end, you have no idea if Jamal is going to a. get a shot at that last question or b. get it right. 

If you haven't seen this movie, drop what you are doing and do so.

In my opinion, this was the best film of 2008, and that year had A LOT of great films (Wall-E, The Dark Knight, Iron Man, Frost/Nixon, etc.). WARNING: This review may contain spoilers! 

The Plot:

"How the hell is this damn kid doing so well?!" That was the thought going through the Indian authorities' minds as they witness the extraordinary performance of this mere, teenage boy from the slums, Jamal Malik, who is one question away (ONE question away, dammit!) from winning several million rupees in the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire." 

After we see the cops literally torture poor Jamal, the film explores his past. Over the course of the film, we learn how he and his brother, Salim K. Malik, became orphans, how he met the love of his life, Latika, and how he ends up on and knows most of the answers on "Who Wants to be a Millionaire." 

The Bad:

At heart, Slumdog Millionaire is a romance film, and more often then not, the endings for those types of films can be predicted easily. Also, Lakita, the love interest, did not have a lot of depth to her character. Though she did save Jamal's butt in one scene. 

Oh, and the scene where 5 year old Jamal ended up covered in feces was a little unnecessary.

Speaking of Jamal, one my friends who also saw the film mentioned that he was somewhat obsessive of Latika, and in a way, she's right. He was quite obsessive.  

The Good: 

Despite the last complaint my friend and I had made, Jamal had some decency towards others. At least he did not kidnap kids and treat them like tools, unlike some men in the film. 

There was a scene where preteen Jamal sees Latika coming out of shower and looks away. 

In a way, that scene showed that he had some respect for her. It almost reminded me of the scene in Forrest Gump where Jenny, alone in a room with Forrest, stripes down and he looks away. Ah, I'm getting off topic a little.

Going back to Slumdog Millionaire, with the authorities and even the host of the show against Jamal, you can't help but feel and cheer for he as he faces against though odds.  

Speaking of decent and not decent men, Jamal's brother, Salim, did some things that made me want to yell "What the hell is your problem?" However, what was so fascinating about the character was that deep down inside, he had a caring side to him. 

There was a pivotal scene in the middle of the film where Salim practically saves Jamal and his pretty black eyes (you'll know what I'm talking about if you saw the film).

Along with the awesome characters, the soundtrack was AMAZING! I could feel my heart pumping when I watched the scene where Jamal is in the limo and at least half the Indian population was crowding the streets, eager to watch if this boy from the slums could win this game. The techno music in the background added so much energy to that scene. 


Overall: 

In a year where the most of the critically acclaimed films end in a sad and depressing way (The Dark Knight, the Wrestler, and Benjamin Button to name a few), it's nice to have a film with and optimistic feel and end to it. I thoroughly enjoyed Slumdog Millionaire. It was a very memorable film indeed.

Slumdog Millionaire features a host of unlikely stars: the kids from Mumbai, an unfashionable director - most of all India, or to be more specific, Mumbai if you are a Hindu or Bombay if not. Director Danny Boyle captures the city: its crowds, the rainy season, the flimsy shanty towns; the trains that form the ever-moving spine of this sub-continent; its custard sun, hazy through the dusty mirage of deceptively opulent Mumbai. Most of all he shows us the division between rich and poor in this tale of a boy that escapes an Oliver Twist existence to stop the pulse of a nation as he plays Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? The film relies heavily on Dickensian coincidences. The series of questions faced by the Slumdog boy, Jamal, reflect a wretched life of poverty and exploitation, allowing him random access to the answers. Enter the clever use of the all-important sub-plot.
As with earlier Danny Boyle films, Slumdog is more dark than light. I question whether it would have been preferable had Jamal not answered the final question correctly, thus putting a greater emphasis on the real prize in his life - the girl he had always loved. Perhaps because its subject matter was so far removed from life in the West, well acted and directed as it was, I found it failed to grip. This will not concern those involved with a project that won eight Oscars including Best Picture, particularly the actors that rose from the carcass of Mumbai to become famous. The film's record speaks for itself; an individual revue, quite rightly, palls into insignificence. It is more a case of asking the audience.

Danny Boyle's adaptation of the book Q&A is very impressive. Winning 8 Academy Awards including Best Picture, Slumdog Millionaire will keep you entertained through the whole running time. SUMMARY:

Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) is a teenager who has just won $10,000,000 from "Who wants to be a millionaire?". He was raised in the slums, and is uneducated, so how was he able to win this much money? He is captured by police inspector Irrfan Khan who tries to get the answer out of the boy. Was he cheating, or did he actually know these answers? We follow his story, from when he was a child, til the present time, seeing how he was able to answer these questions. REVIEW:

The concept is actually very clever. Showing his life in this method is very engaging. We see nearly all the reasons why he was got all those questions right, but some of them weren't shown to us, and it felt a bit like a plot hole. Putting that aside, the different storylines are very well written, some of them intriguing and some were romantic. The characters are interesting, and the dialogue is decent. The acting is superb. Dev Patel is wonderful. Frieda Pinto is very talented, and she played Latika, Jamal's love. Madhur Mittal played Jamal's brother, and was good. Ayush Mahesh Khedekar was very cute, playing Jamal when he was younger. Are the visuals any good? Yah. They're beautiful, and it's a feast for the eys.. I liked some of the lighting in some scenes, and the camera angles worked well. They use the locations quite subtly, with the slums and the beautiful Taj Mahal. The ending was probably the most breathtaking moment of the film, right before the credits, The themes are actually quite dark. They're are many themes that have a lot to do with what happens around slums, gangsters, and the most important theme of the film - Destiny. These are all conveyed well, with the intriguing tone used on the darker themes, and a more joyful type for the romantic and lighter themes. I really liked the soundtrack in this. Each song in this was used so well, with "Paper Planes" by Mia, and a very beautiful song called "Dreams on Fire" by Suzanna. The music was fantastic, and we can't forget "Jai Ho" (not the PCD version, the original.). At the credits, we see a whole dancing sequence that can even be called awesome. The most engaging element of the film is it's method of storytelling. Boyle has done a great job of telling us the story of Jamal. They show us his life with each different question he was faced with on the TV show, and I think it works really well here. This is a remarkable film. The ending is so heart-warming. I loved every second of this, it's admirable, and it really is wonderful work of art. Slumdog Millionaire should be witnessed by everyone.

Sucking-up to an establishment has never been my strong point and it is a trait that generally extends into the Academy Award season. Given in particular my belief in the strength of 'The Dark Knight' and its underachievement regarding oscars, I felt determined to find to this film unworthy of its eight oscar haul. As a Westerner I am admittedly oblivious to the controversy surrounding the use of Hindi language and the exact details in the portrayal of India that are provoking such offense, however I certainly feel that there are very few films that would find it a disgrace to lose to 'Slumdog Millionaire' in the Best Picture category. 

'Slumdog Millionaire' is a blend of several genres working like a finely tuned hybrid as opposed to a 'Chelsea tractor' confusion. Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) is embroiled in the ultimate rags-to riches story as an apparently suspicious contestant on 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire'. Through police interrogation, Jamal's impressive knowledge garnered from his slumdog past comes to the fore in a series of beautifully constructed flashbacks featuring his elder brother Salim, who descends steadily into moral depravity. The anchor between past and present is Jamal's love for childhood sweetheart turned beauty Latika (Frieda Pinto) who is herself trapped amidst the gang politics running Mumbai.

The integration of past and present is acheived with such verve and brilliance that nary a single step is misplaced. Every character, however minor, is lovingly constructed with enough credibility to maintain the sense of reality vital to founding such an adaptable plot. More importantly, the child-actors and actresses are as strong and engaging as their more mature counterparts.

Visually as vibrant as any bird of paradise, Danny Boyle's direction draws upon the colourful optimism of Bollywood productions to reference India to the Western audience. However, the movie does not gloss over the extreme poverty and corruption of the Indian slums, resulting in the portrayal of a gritty realism that adds deep yet available emotional handholds for the audience to grasp onto the characters. 

Lightly humorous, visually and orally resplendent and eternally optimistic and uplifting, Boyle's adaptation of a film is delightfully entertaining and beautiful without losing any of the substance and grittiness that grounds it within the audience. A masterpiece of storytelling and film-making.
