Jamal grows up an orphan in the slums of India when destiny steps in and gives him a chance to become a millionaire on a popular TV show where the circumstances of his life, shown in flashbacks, gives him the answers to the quiz questions. The show represents everyone's desire to escape their situation and start over, but surprisingly for Jamal and his eternal fight for survival, it becomes the chance to play out history as it was written and capture the ultimate prize, true love. Slumdog Millionaire was one of my favorite films, until I saw Salaam Bombay!. Life is not a fairy tale as it seems to be in the Oscar winner for Best Picture. Hollywood embraced it's uplifting, unique story where happiness is not only found in love but as the film was made by a Westerner the story is depicted through the lens of American values, including capitalism. So it doesn't hurt that the "slumdog" won a ton of money either. This seems to be the icing on the cake in American cinema, if one can avoid the world of poverty they are considered to have a happy ending. Slumdog Millionaire's title of course is an oxymoron, which is not the only contradiction in the film's world of overwhelming paradox. The film was criticized by Indian audiences for depicting a too-true image of the realities of what it is like to be categorized as "street children" and Indian poverty. However, the real truth is that there is no reality in the story at all. Of course there is value in showing how street children survive, but the happiness in the ending is defined by Western objectives. Hollywood reciprocates the notion over and over again that in order to achieve happiness, love and money are all you need. The fact that the film won an Academy Award for Best Picture proves that when you mix a little bit of reality with the falseness of idealism, people begin to deceive themselves into thinking what they just saw was good because it was "real." If anyone walked out of Slumdog Millionaire (myself included) thinking that they just saw "what it's really like" or "how it is for 'them'," was deceived by the masterful paradox's of Slumdog Millionaire's Hollywood guise. Both films used real street kids as the actors, but something is to be said about the Westerner "using" the child under the lens of the camera as a microscope for his project in Slumdog Millionaire where after the project is completed, similar to neocolonial projects, the subject is abandoned.  Unlike in Salaam Bombay where the children were adopted by crew and helped set up centers around India for similar street kids after the project was complete.  Why is it that the poor are studied and subjected by the rich, why do the poor never have the opportunity to study the rich?  Salaam Bombay had children that were not under study or under a microscope, but they were in it together, along with the director who was also poor, in fact they all shared an empty flat and the director allowed them to sleep in it during filming.  If you were under the impression that when you saw Slumdog Millionaire you were seeing a foreign film (which I know people who have) you are gravely mistaken. If you want to see that foreign film with everything that you thought Slumdog Millionaire was supposed to bring you, or that you thought DID bring you, see Salaam Bombay!.

Though it's a phenomenal film I shouln't claim to be ignorant to the fact that I, myself am a Westerner and I value the entertainment in Western films more, not understanding many cultural references and themes presented in this film (I should make it clear that I still love Slumdog Millionare, but it will remain a PERFECT example of a Western filmmaker trying to depict a non-Western life and culture, or neo-colonialism at work).

The story of how Indian teen Jamal Malik became a contestant on the Hindi version of "Who Wants To Be a Millionaire?" An epic tale of love and destiny that captivates you with its brilliance. The most triumphant movie I have seen this year!

Rarely do I give a movie five stars. It is even rarer that I agree with what wins "Best Picture" in any given year. Dear readers, you are witnessing a rare moment on both counts. "Slumdog Millionaire" is deserving of every accolade that it received. 

Shortly before being presented with the final question in the Hindi version of "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire", Jamal Malik is detained due to allegations of possible cheating. Jamal grew up in an impoverished area and has no formal education, so the show's host doubts he actually knew the answers. As he is questioned, Malik flashes back through his remarkable life to each moment where he learned each answer. In the process, you find that Jamal is not on the show for the money at all ...

So well done. Rarely have I been this impressed with a movie, especially one that I went into with no expectations. I am let down by the "Best Picture" nearly annually and expected no different this time around. But this movie has it all. There is drama, action, intrigue, horrifying moments, touching moments, and ultimately a pretty solid love story. Most of all, the end game is always in doubt. Right up until the very end, you have no idea if Jamal is going to a. get a shot at that last question or b. get it right. 

If you haven't seen this movie, drop what you are doing and do so.

Meh. That's what I give this movie. A loud, obnoxious, tired meh. The story is that a "Slumdog" gets a chance to be on "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire", and somehow answers every answer correctly. We find out throughout the movie that through past experiences he had, he was able answer the questions. There is also a touching love story and a side story about him trying to meet up with his brother who joined the local mob. Danny Boyle is a very contemporary director who has found his place in the 21st century and has made some spectacular period pieces such as Millions and 28 Days Later, but I think that even though this movie could be described as his masterpiece, it's an oddity and I didn't care for it much.
   
Boyle finds a way to add his signature fast paced spontaneous-absurd acting and plot into this heartwarming script, and makes it lack the humanism that you might find in such a controversial movie. 
   
For those of you who don't know, this movie protests the corrupt and poverty stricken society of India, which is a current situation that does need attending to, but as you can see in the movie it is so chaotic that there's really no way to help. This message of the movie is the only thing that is going for it besides the use of catchy pop tunes (Paper Planes) which to be honest I didn't care for but I could understand how other people might enjoy them.
   
The acting was acceptable, not really worth mentioning, but I mean when there was tragedy, they were sad, when there is a moment of triumph, they are happy, and when there is a reminder of the past, you can tell that they are focusing on what is in the past and not what is currently in front of them. Actually, never mind, the kids in this movie did an exceptional job. That would be the highlight of the movie: the flashbacks to the main character's childhood.
   
Slumdog very accurately portrays the horrors of modern day India, wrapped up in a sweet romance that's injected with Danny Boyle's fast paced relentless unforgiving view of the world. There is gore, so not a good movie to see with children, but it might be most appreciated by people in their late teens.

The "Rocky" of game shows.  "Slumdog" precisely lived up to everything I heard about the film:  the concept is gimmicky (the life story of an Indian untouchable is told through a series of game show questions) but the execution is brilliant.  The first half of the two hour run-time is a tough sit as Jamal the protagonist faces the worst a brutal Indian society has to offer but in the meantime learns the answers which will eventually make him successful on the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?"  However, that emotional investment of watching slaughtered mothers and intentionally blinded children pays off in the second half as you become emotionally invested in Jamal continuing his dream run on the show and his continued pursuit of his oldest friend from the slums / love interest.  The very end of the movie veers into Disney Bollywood style (stay for the dance number) territory but up until that point any ground gained by Jamal is paid for in torture and betrayal. In short, the film's emotional resonance is hard-won by the audience and is well-worth the effort. By the way, the central conceit for the ending of the movie came from the first winner of the American version of the game show who used his "Phone-a-Friend" lifeline to get in touch with his father not to ask for help but to let him know he was about to win a million dollars.

Slumdog Millionaire is a British film based on the book "Q and A" , by Vikas Swarup. The film was released by Fox Searchlight and Warner Bros., and won eight Oscars, seven BAFTA's and four Golden Globes. It won the Oscar for best director, adapted screenplay, editing, original score, original song and sound mixing.
This film was one of the cheapest productions on the cinema, whose costs were estimated at just $ 15 million, but it raised more than $290.526.218  around the world.
    Slumdog Millionaire is much better than many people think, because it isn't a typical story. Normally, the films and books about India just show the positive things, such as Taj Mahal, palaces, the life of the rich or they show things about religion. Slumdog is different; you can't guess the ending of the film as you can do with the classics.
For us, who don't live in India, it is normally a bit difficult to understand the Indian accent in English, so I recommend watching the subtitled version of this film, not the dubbed one. 
   Those who have already been to India can realize that the story of this film really happens in real life. At the traffic light you can see a lot of small children asking for money and singing or doing something else. The shantytown is exactly that way and when you go to Taj Mahal you really need to take off your shoes to get there. Some images surprise us, such as the scene of the police torturing Jamal, and they make us think: "Is this real? Does This really happen?"
    Slumdog Millionaire mixes music, good drama and reality. The best film ever.

So I just sat down with Slumdog Millionaire for the first time. Even if I adore the cinematic medium, I avoid the Academy Awards like the plague, and when that time came I decided to watch this film instead which happens to have won in 2009's major categories. As the film came out, I was into the thick of travel, and moreover the film didn't seem to me like a good fit for Danny Boyle's style. No less, it is one of those films about foreign poverty, with a grand conscience, and those can turn out just awful. My perception is that, inevitably, people patronized (and then patronized) the film with work-righteous emotions fit for the occasion, and its distributors piled onto that package with the moniker that it was the "feel-good movie of the year." No thanks.

But I watched it anyway, because it was just remastered onto Blu-Ray and I became an admirer of Danny Boyle's wild directorial style from his science fiction masterpiece Sunshine, which ranks with Kubrick's 2001 and Tarkovsky's Solaris as perfected speculative fiction, lacking any mess of cowboys and indians in space with noises magically permeating vacuums.

Something surprised me about Slumdog Millionaire, though I ultimately found it flawed from its failure to resist utter sappiness with a hyper-romantic disregard of reality (too many perfect coincidences; it might as well have tried to be a Greek drama about gods and fates). The surprise for me was in its brash, stylistic disregard for the culture. Boyle shot the film with agitated camera movements, super-wide-angle lenses (practically fish-eyed), avant-garde compositions, skewed framings, and so forth -- in other words, idiomatic to Boyle's modernist style. (His cinematographer is the genius who shot Lars von Trier's brilliant prelude to Antichrist.) Yet, if the original vision were that of the typical Birkenstock-armored documentarian, all of these stylistic measures would be a violation. It is in fact only at the end of the film (train station dancing sequence) where the Hindi cultural sensibility of Bollywood bridges the gap, and it becomes a merged work of cinema.

And that is the whole point. A Westerner visiting India arrives a Westerner and leaves a Westerner -- show me exceptions and I'll show you a skeptic. The pretense of all filmmakers, composers, authors and visual artists who immerse themselves for the purpose of divining native art is perfectly inauthentic. (Notably, my favorite living composer, Philip Glass, "invented" the last major movement in serious contemporary music -- Minimalism -- under the guidance of Ravi Shankar when tasked with transcribing microtonal indigenous ragas into Western notation. Minimalism, and Glass's Minimalism, does not sound Indian, yet those Eastern fingerprints are all over the place.)

It only increased my otherwise simple affection for the film when I surfed around a bit only to find significant mass criticism against it for failing (in one fell swoop?) to "capture" the spirit and the desolation of Mumbai. I also find it comical as well as hypocritical that many are quite furious to know that the untrained child actors are still living amidst the depicted poverty. Surely they can only be prosperous and happy in comparison to Western standards of heavyweight wealth! And surely, snatching them from that "slumdog" environment will solve it all. Yet in truth, actors are merely work-for-hire, and only an organized labor force with the full faith and credit of an adoring pop culture (I'll say it: the Hollywood Establishment) could twist that vocation into something of hocus-pocus and when-you-wish-upon-a-star.

In short, this is a subversive film -- and on that level, I rather enjoyed it.

It may have brought him massive attention from Oscar, and it may not even be his best work, but Slumdog Millionaire is unmistakably the work of Mr Danny Boyle.
From the running scenes through the slums, evoking memories of Renton's run down Princes street in Trainspotting and the opening titles of Shallow Grave, this is a fast paced, fast edited movie and is combined with a great idea told in a wonderful fashion.
Dev Pattel is questioned when he is accused of cheating on the Indian version of Who Wants to be a Millionaire and his confessions as to how he knew the answers build the story of his life and search for the love of his life.  It's an amazingly simple idea but one which is so effective, you wonder why it's never been done before.  Combined with Boyle's amazing cinematography, this is something very good indeed.
As per usual, Boyle has assembled a great cast of mostly unknowns and they all perform brilliantly.  The film is free of Hollywood star pretension.
Slumdog Millionaire is a charming movie about the innocence of youth and the search for love and a tribute to how certain events can allow you to remember the most trivial of facts.  It's a film about memory and the wonderful things that it can do.  The film is moving and tragic and even the end credits being set to a Mamma Mia style dance routine cannot spoil it.  The only sticking point is some sloppy exposition in the beginning which robs it of full 5 star status.
Slumdog Millionaire will be a hard act to follow for Danny Boyle.  It could be argued that he'll never better his debut, Shallow Grave, but that shouldn't stop him trying if the results can be this good.

Another wonderful movie from Danny Boyle!
In many ways it tells a familar story, but there's nothing routine about the way it gets there. Laugh out loud moments follow dramatic highpoints to great effect....regardless of the fact we know where it's going.

All three of the actors who play Jamal are wonderful to watch and it's the appeal of this character, the sheer beauty Boyle finds in all the locations and situations (even the grim ones!) plus a first-rate script that elevate it considerably from the standard "feel good" fare served up by the big studios.

*** This review may contain spoilers ***

Slumdog Millionaire chronicles the odyssey of Jamal Malik from the slums of Bombay to now modern Mumbai. The film's framing device is Malik's attempt to win the Hindi version of "Who wants to be a Millionaire". He ends up answering each question correctly and a day before he attempts to answer the final question for the grand prize, he's whisked away by the police on suspicion of fraud. The police want to know how a kid from the slums could possibly answer all those questions correctly. As they question him (sometimes using torture at first), the viewer is treated to a series of flashbacks which explains how he's able to successfully answer each question.

The first half of the movie (the much better part) involves Malik first as a young child (of about five) and later at about the age of 10 (played by two different child actors). Malik's older brother, Salim, is the more aggressive of the two, in contrast to the sensitive younger brother. We see how they are orphaned at an early age when their mother is killed during a riot where Hindus attack Muslims. The children must fend for themselves in the slums of Bombay and there are many memorable and shocking scenes that chronicle their tactics of survival. One indelible scene involves Malik securing an autograph from a famous Indian singer who is on a publicity tour in the area. Malik extricates himself from inside a locked latrine and appears at the autograph signing covered head to toe in human excrement. Eventually Malik and Salim are lured by a gang of criminals who end up training them to become professional beggars. The gang goes so far as to increasing their profits by blinding certain children who have sweet singing voices. The blind children are used by the criminals to manipulate unsuspecting tourists who feel sorry for the now handicapped children. Salim alerts Malik to the gang's nefarious plan and they escape along with another child, Latika who Malik falls in love with.

At the midpoint of the film, with Salim now a young teenager, he takes revenge on head of the gang who almost blinded Malik by shooting him to death. But Salim incurs Malik's enmity by raping Latika. Flash forward to the present as we find Malik working at a menial job as a gopher at a large international customer service company. Malik eventually locates Salim who is now working for the boss of Mumbai's biggest crime syndicate. And he finds out that Latika is basically an indentured servant in the boss's mansion. In the film's climax, the police release Malik who goes on to answer the final question correctly and hooks back up with Latika who escapes the crime boss's lair (with the help of Salim, who, in a final act of contrition, sacrifices himself by murdering the crime boss and in turn is killed by the boss's bodyguards).

Slumdog Millionaire has a lot going for it. It's highly entertaining and features some great performances (especially by the child actors in the first half). Dev Patel as Malik is also excellent as the low-key hero who eventually gets the girl. The passionate conflict between the two brothers adds to the verisimilitude of the story.

Slumdog is really designed to be a gritty fairy tale. But even fairy tales must have some kind of internal logic. The weakest part of the story for me was the whole idea that the producer of the 'Millionaire' show was some kind of crook who wanted to fix things so Malik would lose. And was it at all believable, that Malik, who had become a national hero, would suddenly be brought in by the police and tortured merely because they could not believe a kid from the slums could answer such the tough questions on the show? In reality, the police would never have chanced abducting Malik while the show was going on and risk losing their jobs due to possible adverse press coverage. And why would the producer of the show want Malik to lose? If he wins, the producer's ratings go much higher and he makes more money.

Slumdog also stumbles by becoming a Bollywood production in the second half. The villain in the first half, the child exploiter is much more believable and menacing than the crime syndicate boss in the second half. And Latika is wholly an underdeveloped character?she has nothing much to do except being the love object of Malik.

I'm not sure if Slumdog Millionaire deserves to be nominated for an Academy best picture. But as a solid piece of entertainment, it will keep you riveted in your seat.

On a revisited look at Slumdog Millionare, the evidence that this is a great film 'is' evident. It's the type of thing Frank Capra would have loved watching. It's a rags to riches about people getting what they deserve. The movie is clever to point out that this story is one in a million. It shows the harsh life of an overpopulated caste systemized India and relies heavily on it's setting to work it's 'Capraesque' conclusion that the audience already figures out in the first few minutes. However director Danny Boyle (who was criminally neglected by the Academy for his work on 'Trainspotting') is not so interested on surprising us at the end as much as he is interested on holding our attention and surprising us throughout. Like any great flawed hero in a Capra film, it's about what leads up to the eventual redemption or downfall. This type of story play out more so for our narrators (Patel) brother than for the our narrator himself. However nonetheless a crucial story arc that influences most of the film. There are a great many themes in this film and the one it relies on most is fate. Patel is the driving force in the film because he leads us on this journey of flashbacks that tell us who he is rather than the answers to his questions. The Millionaire game show plot line is a clever device in relating to a story that is based on decisions. There is a scene in the film where our narrator is given the answer during commercial break to a question he does not know. It is done so by the host of the show (Kapoor) who relates to Patel's character, as being a poor boy from the slums who got on the show and changed his own life. This scene shows us what our narrator can become; the man sitting across from him, the one asking the questions and not having to answer any. They come back from commercial break and what happens next I won't say, however it really cements into our minds for the remained of the film, who this character is and why we care about him. My special consideration goes out to the child actors of the film who are all wonderful. Patel is stellar. Frieda Pinto is solid, not to mention stunningly gorgeous. The real credit to the film though is from Anil Kapoor, the game show host. He drives the movie in the few scenes that he is in, relatively most of the scenes shot in the present with his charisma. He's the mirror image to what our hero can become and it's so fitting that they have to stare at each other for most of the film. Of course last but not least, the creative, imaginative blend of Holly-Bollywood, intense sweeping shots that resemble portraits and direction that was long overdue on credit; Danny Boyle is a true artist. In all the film is sweet charming and most importantly, memorable. Even with my reservations about it being the wrong film to win Best Picture (The Wrestler which was not even nominated should have won) It was still the most feel good film of the year and definitely one of the best. That's my final answer.

Accused of cheating and desperate to prove his innocence, an eighteen-year-old orphan from the slums of Mumbai reflects back on his tumultuous life while competing to win 20 million rupees on India's Who Wants to Be a Millionaire in Danny Boyle's inspirational drama. Jamal Malik (Dev Patel) may not have a penny to his name, but that could all change in a matter of hours. He's one question away from taking the top prize on India's most popular television game show, but as with everything else in Jamal's life, it isn't going to be easy. Arrested by police under suspicion of cheating, Jamal is interrogated by the authorities. The police simply can't believe that a common "slumdog" could possibly possess the knowledge to get this far in the game, and in order to convince them of how he gained such knowledge, Jamal begins reflecting back on his childhood. As young boys, Jamal and his older brother, Salim, lived in squalor, and lost their mother in a mob attack on Muslims. Subsequently forced to rely on their own wits to survive, the desperate siblings fell back on petty crime, eventually befriending adorable yet feisty young Latika as they sought out food and shelter on the unforgiving streets of Mumbai. Though life on the streets was never easy, Jamal's experiences ultimately instilled in him the knowledge he needed to answer the tough questions posed to him on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. And though Jamal makes a convincing case for himself, one question still remains: why would a young man with no apparent desire for wealth or fame be so determined to win big on a national game show? Of course, it won't be long until everyone finds out the answer to this burning question, because as Jamal sits down to find out whether he will be rich beyond his wildest dreams, 60 million viewers remain transfixed to their televisions eager to see if he'll correctly answer the final question.

British director Danny Boyle, best known for "Trainspotting" and "The
Beach," has made the rags-to-riches feel-good film of the year with
"Slumdog Millionaire." Mind you, Indian co-director Loveleen Tandan,
who served as a second unit director on "Monsoon Wedding" (2001),
helped Boyle out. Set in contemporary India, this winsome tale about
three dirt-poor orphans who rise above abject squalor and poverty to
attain their most outlandish dreams of romance and riches qualifies as
modern day Charles Dickens morality play. Indeed, you could also
compare "Slumdog Millionaire" to those vintage 1930s' Warner Brothers
crime classics where one kid plunges down the wrong path while the
other takes the right path. Ultimately, the brothers here find
themselves at odds with each other on different sides of the law. The
bad people are punished in "Slumdog," while the good people are
rewarded. "Full Monty" scenarist Simon Beaufoy based his lively script
on diplomat-turned-novelist Vikas Swarup's first book, "Q & A," about
an Indian waiter who was arrested for cheating on a quiz show. 

Don't let the foreign oriented storyline discourage you from enjoying
this inspirational yarn. Boyle provides interesting, off-beat looking
subtitles for the Hindu dialogue, but the cast deliver most of the
lines in English. If you're looking for a change of pace, "Slumdog
Millionaire" is just the ticket. As upbeat and optimistic as "Slumdog"
is, prepare yourself for some scenes that may make you wince. "Slumdog"
deserved its R-rating as much as it deserved his Best Picture Oscar.
This movie is far more entertaining than the imaginative but
long-winded Brad Pitt epic "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button."
Basically, "Slumdog Millionaire" concerns the coincidences that land a
teenaged Muslim refugee from the Bombay slums, Jamal Malik (Dev Patel),
on the Indian equivalent of the ABC-TV show "Who Wants to be a
Millionaire." Since he is a product of the slums, our long-suffering
hero is regarded with considerable suspicion. Jamal keeps surprising
the slimy quiz show host Prem Kumar (veteran Bollywood actor Anil
Kupoor) with one correct answer after another and the jealous Kumar
turns him over to the authorities. Kumar is convinced that Jamal is a
cheater. Kumar is far from saintly himself and doesn't want Jamal to
steal his glory. It seems Kumar's meteoric rise in show business came
about as a result of giving the right answers on a game show. At the
outset, "Slumdog" creates suspense for audiences with the important
question: "Jamal Malik is one question away from winning 20 million
rupees. How did he do it? A. He cheated. B. He's lucky. C. He's a
genius. D. It is written." Indeed, Jamal is poised to win more wealth
that he can possibly imagine when the police subject him to a night of
torture. They beat him up and finally attach jumper cables to his toes
to make him confess. Our stubborn hero refuses to capitulate. The chief
police investigator, Irfan Khan (Irrfan Khan), finds it difficult to
believe that a kid from the slums could know so much.

Boyle's strategy in "Slumdog" is to alternate each unusual question
that our beleaguered hero answers with an episode from his traumatic
life that relates to each question. The scene when Jamal plunges into
an outdoors toilet, covering himself from head-to-toe in human feces,
so he can obtain an autograph from his favorite movie superstar is
hilarious. Actually, the fecal matter consisted of peanut butter and
chocolate. (This scene is reminiscent of a similar episode from
"Trainspotting" where an Edinburgh junkie dives into a toilet to
retrieve a narcotic suppository.) During his youth, Jamal and his
brother Salim (Madhur Mital) encounter some genuinely sleazy
characters, especially one unsavory fellow who likes to 'rescue'
orphans from the streets so that he can turn them into beggars. This
part of "Slumdog" may remind you of Charles Dickens's second novel
"Oliver Twist." Anyway, this scoundrel likes to blind small children
and send them out to beg and sing for money. Jamal and Salim escape
from this life, but in doing so, Jamal abandons--against his will--a
girl named Latika (Frieda Pinto) for whom he has sworn his undying
love. Of course, the evil child exploiter sells Latika to men who want
to see her dance. Hmm, I wonder what the Indian Tourist Bureau thinks
about this saga. Ten years ago, "Slumdog" would have taken place in
Brazil. Suffice to say that the hero and heroine are separated with
little chance of being reunited. Happily, however, "Slumdog" takes
several astonishing twists and turns before fade-out that will surprise
you, and ultimately make you feel good, perhaps even great, depending
on how much you love fairy tales.

Although it runs two hours in length, "Slumdog Millionaire" never
wastes a second. Boyle and Tandan turn this helter-skelter saga into a
roller-coaster. As a glimpse of India, "Slumdog" is enlightening as
well as horrifying. If nothing else, you'll learn to never shed your
shoes around the Taj Mahal. The casting of our heroes from adolescence
to teenagers is nothing short of brilliant. This is no Hollywood hokum
where the children look nothing like the adults. Jamal follows the
straight and narrow after Salim and he indulge in juvenile delinquency
that recalls the shenanigans of the Jewish kids in Sergio Leone's
gangster classic "Once Upon a Time in America." You won't forget
"Slumdog Millionaire." The irony of all this is "Slumdog," which
received 8 Oscars as well as two more Oscar nominations, almost wound
up going straight to DVD because nobody believed it could recoup its
$15 million budget. At this point, "Slumdog" has coined over $116

As a drama, it truly stirs the emotions, and even has moments of groundling humor. Small wonder why this film has such universal appeal.

Finally got around to seeing this. I have to say I was a little hesitant in getting around to it because I'm usually not big on the Oscar hype, especially when the winners (and as a result the losers) seem to be political more than anything. And this particular set of Oscar winners and losers seemed to display exactly that. You get the impression that Slumdog wins over Benjamin Button because it tries to throw you a message about poverty. That Sean Penn won best actor over Mickey Rourke because he played a gay guy, and the list goes on.

Nevertheless, a movie should not be judged until it has been watched, and I definitely don't regret watching Slumdog Millionaire.

Right off the bat, I had some inherent problems with the message this film tries to give us. At first it kind of seemed like it was that anyone can accomplish great things, even if they're a slumdog. I liked that, it seemed kind of like a modern day fairy tale. But as the film went on, it kind of seemed to turn into you can only accomplish these things if they are "written" for you.

It just struck me as a little pretentious. As well as a turn towards the unrealistic for a movie that seemed to gain a lot of its glory from the fact that it tried to be realistic in its portrayal of the slums of India. From a few posts that I've seen around here it seems like I'm not the only one who felt that way.

Still, I thought the film was gripping and very well told, regardless of some of the inherent flaws I found in the story. The score and sound was great, the visuals and cinematography were near perfect for the film and it was well cast and well directed. 

Does it deserve to be a film that won 8 awards, including best picture? Compared to the other 4 films it was up against I'm not sure, but on it's own, I definitely think it was Oscar material.

Gripping film that brings you into the story and makes you like the characters even if they might not be the most relateable in the world, and a movie that has everything from action to romance to drama and even a few bits of comedy for relief.

Anything I find wrong with the film, i always seem to come back to the good things, and that's where I think this film thrives. It's not a perfect film, and it doesn't try to be. But it makes up for its mistakes with all the good things in it. Inconsistent story or not, this is still a top film in my eyes.

Danny Boyle's new film Slumdog Millionaire is like watching blind people make love. Though it seems naturally instinctive, you know there's a whole lot of thought and preparation to make sure it's not just the pillow. It follows the life of a Chai waiter living in India who winds competing on the Indian version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?". Mixed into this simple description is a convoluted past filled with love inspired devastation, but mostly the film maintains a romantic theme which is anchored around a poor kid on a tacky game show. That description does contains a lot of prepositions, which is usually bad sign, especially for a film that I assumed would be full of high-pitched Indian princesses playing sitars and wearing way too much clothing. But I immediately caught interest in the film's high caliber, which caused me to ignore my ex-girlfriend's advances. Though I ended up sitting alone for the last hour, I felt I had made the right decision. Slumdog Millionaire, better than a brunette. 

Slumdog tells the story of Jamal (played by three separate actors Dev Patel, Tanay Chheda and Ayush Mahesh), a young man whose true love has been consistently separated from him throughout his short life. But unlike the typical lover in lament, Jamal grows up as a homeless child surviving the Dharavi slums of Mumbai by thieving and conning tourists. Alongside his older brother Salim (played by Madhur Mittal, Azharuddin Mohammed Ismail, and Ashutosh Lobo Gajiwala), Jamal spends his life living mostly carefree despite his constant adoration for Latika (Freida Pinto, Tanvi Ganesh Lonkar, and Rubiana Ali), an orphan girl whom Jamal falls in love with despite Salim's protests. Because of his feelings for Latika, Jamal ends up being sensitive to all things around him, while Salim turns wicked, holding strong resentment to what he sees as society's neglect for him. The two different brothers bring out their hidden intentions and polar opposite attitudes, which became incredible to watch all three sets of actors portray three different characters through three different times of their lives. 

But setting a new standard is typical of a Danny Boyle movie. There are quick shots amidst intense dialogue followed by cool montages with great music as a backdrop. I hadn't heard MIA's Paper Planes before watching Slumdog, because I'm massively uncool, and was shocked to find out that it wasn't written specifically for the movie though it is a separate remix. A constant wave of fresh music isn't a new concept to Danny Boyle, but the level of immersion with this soundtrack is incredible. Also similar to Boyle's early films Trainspotting (written by Irvine Welsh) and The Beach (written by Alex Garland), Slumdog is based on acclaimed author Vikas Swarup's novel Q and A, an international best seller and winner of the Commonwealth Writer's Prize, whatever that is. Swarup wrote a powerful novel that uses dark and brooding elements based around the epitome of glitter and glam Hollywood, the Game Show. 

By using the show to tell the story, Slumdog creates an obvious difference between the protagonist's humble beginnings and the media frenzy of Bollywood. Jamal's total lack of interest in the show, despite the pressing of the villainous and shady host (played surperbly by Ani Kapor), makes it impossible to not get the point and think it's making a positive statement about Regis Philbin's Ode to Trivia, as some genius reviewers have chose to insinuate. It's a constant reminder of all that Jamal stands against, and if you didn't get it, you shouldn't watch it. I heard Underworld 3 just came out. 

Though many American audiences will just label this one as another weird Foreign film, those that appreciate good cinema will be rewarded. It's difficult not to identify with some character in this film and you are forced to end up rooting for Jamal in the end. Slumdog Millionaire is easily one of the best films out since Guy Ritchie married Madonna and Tarantino grew up. Go to the theaters, but be wary of taking a date.

"The film's amazing emotional and enthralling ability to grab onto the viewer and not let go is what drives the fascinating tale of how Jamal Malik goes from rags to riches through the Indian Version of Who Wants To Be A Millionaire."

This movie, for me, is the best movie of the decade. Never have I seen a story told like this, and it deserves the praise, due to those 8 Academy Awards. Slumdog Millionaire is an Academy Award Winning film about a poor boy from India named Jamal, who becomes a contestant on the Indian version of Who Wants To Be a Millionaire. Jamal answers all of the questions right up until the ten million rupees mark (500,000 USD), and is then taken in for interrogation for the accusation of cheating. While Jamal is being interrogated, he explains that he knew the answers because the questions that he was asked were, at some point, a life experience he had. Jamal explains to the interrogators how he knew each of the answers to the questions. When Jamal explains how he knew the answer to each question, the movie flashes back to Jamal's past life experiences of why he knew the answers to each question. After going through each question and explaining how he knew it, the interrogators let him go back onto the show, to answer the million dollar question.
The breathtaking film is beautifully shot through the brutal slums of India, has an intelligently crafted story-line and features a music score that will urge you to just get up from where your sitting and joyously dance to the finely tuned music (especially the train-station scene at the end) 

A perfect film about an imperfect world of poverty and cruelty

Slumdog Millionaire (2008)
Written by Simon Beaufoy, Novel by Vikas Swarup
Directed by Danny Boyle and Loveleen Tandan
Starring Dev Patel (Jamal Malik), Freida Pinto (Latika)
Awards: Golden Globe for Best Director, Best Motion Picture-Drama, Best Original Score, and Best Screenplay

Movie reviews are supposed to offer an informed opinion of a film based on the elements that succeeded as well as those that failed. I can say, informed-ly (yes I made that word up and I will use it again) that I cannot pinpoint any elements that failed in "Slumdog Millionaire." Without considering individual taste preferences, it is a perfectly made film.

"Slumdog Millionaire" artistically chronicles the life of 18-year-old Jamal Malik, an orphan from the ghetto of Mumbai, who is arrested and accused of cheating his way to the final round of India's "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" Disguised as a suspense/romance/Indie film, this adventure memoir skillfully weaves through events of Malik's amazing life that provided the unlikely contestant with the previous nights' correct answers. With all of India sharing in his rags-to-riches tale, he must prove his innocence to the police in time to answer the 20 million-rupee question.

It's an extremely simple concept manifested into a sophisticated and complex story. And I wouldn't change a thing about it. Credit is due to everyone who worked on the film. To me, this film is like the perfect chocolate chip cookie. While you're eating it, you don't realize all of the things that went into making it the perfect cookie because when you make them at home, you just use the Break-and-Bake kind. But this particular baker, after years of cultivating his own recipe, used a pinch of orange, a smidgen of nutmeg, and a dash of cinnamon, things you'd never think to use in your recipe. And now his cookie is the one that you crave after work, can't walk past, and eat slower than you thought possible just because you want it to last. You don't care what he used to make it, just that it warms you all over and that you are ruined for the Break-and-Bake forever. But it's still just a chocolate chip cookie.

At the end of the day, "Slumdog Millionaire," isn't just another Cinderella story...it's the perfect Cinderella story that makes you warm all over and ruined to all other movies for life. And that's because every element -- directing, acting, writing, editing, cinematography, etc. -- is perfect within its own department. The most obvious genius would be Danny Boyle for wrangling such a giant project and turning it back into a chocolate chip cookie. The staggering performances by Pinto and Patel are also easy-to-recognize genius. But the unsung heroes here are the editors and the writers.

We often take for granted the screenplay. The audience can't always recognize the difference between Lucas-caliber writing and shitty acting. But we do know its bad. When a screenplay is wonderful, we often can't recognize it past the great performances. This is one of those cases. The perfect chocolate chip cookie takes a lot of thought and careful measuring even though the consumer can't taste the individual ingredients. And this film, despite being simple in concept, was meticulously measured. It is obvious that the plot was worked and reworked, and much intention and time was put into every line. The temporal weaving of the story is both precarious and impeccable. The timeline was so complicated that I was just waiting for it to stop making sense. But it didn't for one moment. The transitions were seamless and the pacing consistent. Credit for that is shared by the editors, who are rarely awarded, but should be.

This would normally be where I talk about the things I'd have tweaked, but, as I said before, I am completely stumped. The cinematography was creative and reflected the tonality of the subject matter perfectly. When we were in the slums, it was rough, bright, and dirty. When we were in the police station, it was sterile, grey, and simple. And the transitions between the two moods were appropriately jarring and important to the ease of the story-telling.

Even the costumes added to the story structure. They were ethereal and beautiful when the characters were in a hopeful, positive moment, and they were muted and unnoticeable when the focus was on the slum. I think the baker may have even mixed and melted his own chocolate chips.

Overall: One must always account for taste, so I will not tell you that this will be your favorite movie. Maybe you don't like chocolate chip cookies. But I can tell you that they don't come in a higher quality than "Slumdog Millionaire." It is as close to perfect as a movie can be.

Rating: Braveheart

The reason for this is the young man is from the slums, with no education at all. Throughout the course of the movies, the cops ask him how he knows the answers to these questions, and we get flashbacks of his life (in chronical order) explaining how he knows this. 

Over the films perdiod, the main character deals with his brother, growing up alone, all balanced with romance. The film also serves as a very good social commentary on the slums, being involved in different situations and how to deal with problems. The simplistic version: it's interesting. That's it, the whole time I was thinking ''How could they come up with that?''. It's original, and so entertaining. The one thing that kept this movie from being perfect is that I felt that it kind of had repetition with the romantic ordeals. Still, that's such a little thing.

We know this because he seems like a pretty calm man, but when meeting his brother for the first time in a while (because of something bad that happened), we see that the main character grabs him and throws himself and his brother off of a building because of this anger. The visuals are so awesome in this. The beautiful composition of each and every shot is astounding, and mind boggling. The use of in camera effects, lighting and cinematography are so great. Jamal (Dev Patel among other actors), a young boy from the slums of India and his brother Salim (Madhur Mittal among other actors) sadly lose their mother early to a violent death.  While most of the movie starts from when they are very young, the different scenes show them growing up and fending for themselves on the streets.

More of the plot however, centers around Jamal being on the show of India's version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire."  One question away from winning the grand prize, he is forced into police custody and tortured to see how he is winning (they believe he is cheating).  Instead, he tells them how he knows the answers and in doing so, gives them the story of his life.  Prominently featured in these stories is Latika (Freida Pinto among others) who is a young girl who joins them in their travails after their mother's death.

Each question a new part of Jamal's life is uncovered.  Most of it is very brutal; to be sure there are not many happy parts in this movie.  Now as a contestant on this show, his only thought is to get Latika back, which could prove very dangerous.

For warning, this movie is very graphic.  It features beatings, murders, and other acts of violence.  Definitely not a good movie for the younger crowd.  It is realistically done though so I could imagine things like this happening.

The characters were well played I thought.  Dev Patel especially as Jamal did great at portraying his worry over Latika and his quest to find her.  For some reason the actor who played his brother reminded me of Michael Jackson in his younger years, but it was only mildly distracting from the movie.  All the other characters seemed authentic enough as well.

The music in this movie was fantastic.  It was a mix of Indian/English so while a non-Indian dialect speaker might not be able to understand some of the lyrics, there were some that could be understood.  They had great rhythm and fit the flow of the story nicely.

Overall a great movie.  There was a lot of action but enough story to keep you engaged in the characters.  I truly cared about how the ending woudl turn out and was pleasantly surprised and equally as shocked at the results.  I can see why it won so many awards.

I fell in love with Slumdog Millionaire the first time I saw it, and indeed saw it three times in theaters with intent to see it more.  From the moment the film started, I was entranced by this world, and director Danny Boyle succeeded in weaving it perfectly and immersing me in it.

Telling the story of a young man explaining how his difficult life has taught him many uncommon things, Slumdog Millionaire proceeds to tell a story full of drama and pain.  Though there are plenty of laughs along the way, Jamal Malik's tale is constantly plagued by tragedy.  Forced from his home, losing a friend, always on the run - it seems like fate is out to get him.

Malik is deftly portrayed by Dev Patel, a young British actor who proved he has star potential with this role.  Patel imbues the character with a humble, softspoken air that carries the character well, yet also maintains the constant drive of the characters ambitions.

The direction of the film is top notch.  Boyle earns Academy cred by portraying India as is - a poverty stricken, over populated, crime ridden place.  This is part of the genius of the film: Before Slumdog Millionaire, most of the world didn't realize or didn't care about India's condition.  The film was eye-opening and has brought focus to the country's problems.

Combining the above factors with some excellent film editing, clever use of sub-titles, and a nearly flawless soundtrack by A.R. Rahman, Slumdog Millionaire instantly carved out a place for itself as a classic from the moment it opened.  This is my favorite movie because of the wonderful story telling, the honesty, and the love portrayed in this film.  An absolute must see.

First, this reviewer must indulge himself in a bit of fan worship for director Danny Boyle, whose frenetically masterful Trainspotting warranted countless visits to the cinema. With an almost religious devotion, viewings of Boyles Shallow Grave, 28 Days Later, and Sunshine would followall very different genres, but each beautifully realized. What amazes this reviewer  whether it be the battleship gray depression of Edinburgh or the discomforting isolation aboard a long space flight  is how expertly Boyle captures a setting and makes it a character in the film. Together with Loveleen Tandan, he accomplishes this feat again, capturing the kinetic verve of the city as thriving metropolis and overrun slum. This palette provides the perfect backdrop for a wonderfully rousing story with more energy and optimism than all of the other award contenders combined. 

In this R-rated drama, a Mumbai orphan (Patel) damns the odds and appears on a popular game show to win the heart of the girl of his dreams (Freida Pinto).

Though Patel and Pinto will doubtlessly have filmgoers wrapped up in their complicated love story, it is Ayush Mahesh Khedekar and Rubina Ali as their younger selves that truly captivate audiences. With such authentic performances, the rest becomes an easy sell. There is the rub, however: Slumdog Millionaire forgoes what should be its true ending and lets the action play out a little too long, pandering more to HWood fluff than heart by films end. Still, the overall feel-good sentimentality and toe-tapping Bollywood closing credits sequence earn the film high marks.

Bottom line: Feels like a million bucks.

Creo que puedo decir sin miedo que Danny Boyle alcanzó el cénit de su carrera con "Trainspotting".

¿Y qué tenemos aquí? Poca cosa: una historia de aires Dickensianos que juega poner en relieve la pobreza y degradación de la India mediante una historia de tintes mafiosos.

Pero lo que se cuenta es tramposo, poco creíble (el que crea que esto es "Ciudad de Dios 2" está equivocado) y bastante manido. Por mucho que lo disfrace de exotismo hindú, la historia es harto convencional: bien podría haber sucedido en otro país sin que hubiera supuesto una gran diferencia. 
Algunos temas clave que se discuten sobre esta película:

Verosimilitud: A mí, sinceramente, la falta de verosimilitud me la trae flojísima. Es que vamos, me da exactamente igual. Lo que sí me molesta es que los detalles del guión sean tontos, obvios, rutinarios.
Otro tema es que haya quien alaba su supuesta veracidad pero defiende su falta de verosimilitud, algo que no acabo de entender. Con todos los respetos, creo que es como decir que "Pulp Fiction" te gusta porque los gangsters de verdad son así. Pero eso nos lleva a que creo que si molesta esa falta de verosimilitud es precisamente porque juega al despiste: por una parte pretende ser una especie de cuento de hadas y por otra reflejar la realidad de un ambiente concreto. Lograr el equilibrio en algo así es complejo. Demasiada ambición para un cineasta tan limitado y preocupado por lo superficial.

Tópicos: Muy en la corriente de las modas actuales (como todo en la película), se busca el cliché partiendo de un envoltorio pretendidamente original. La originalidad resulta fresca cuando es espontánea, así logra sobrevivir a todos sus imitadores. Hoy en día, hay cineastas de los años 20 que siguen resultando frescos, porque sus aspectos más rompedores partían de la sinceridad, eran una consecuencia, no un fin. Ahora uno puede imaginarse a Boyle y el guionista pensando en cómo pueden hacer que su historia sea más original. Estamos tan obsesionados con ver algo diferente que hemos olvidado dos cosas: que la historia de siempre es buena si se cuenta bien, y que la verdadera frescura es espontánea, no buscada.

Por otro lado, Boyle sigue arrastrando los peores vicios que ya mostró en la endeble "Sunshine" y se deleita con una inacabable andanada de planos exageradamente cortos, desenfoques, reflejos en la lente, encuadres inclinados y una que son atronadoramente videoclipera selección musical que muchas veces parece no venir a cuento. Da la impresión de que el cineasta británico trate de gritarle al público en cada escena "¡EH, MIRADME! ¡ESTOY AQUÍ!", igual que un niño que se empeña en atraer la atención de una madre a la que cree no interesar lo suficiente. 

¿Mi conclusión?
No es una de las mejores películas del año NI POR ASOMO. 
Lo peor es que la jugada de Boyle ha funcionado, pues se llevo calientitos galardones diversos y las críticas no hacen más que loar su film.

So I just sat down with Slumdog Millionaire for the first time. Even if I adore the cinematic medium, I avoid the Academy Awards like the plague, and when that time came I decided to watch this film instead which happens to have won in 2009s major categories. As the film came out, I was into the thick of travel, and moreover the film didnt seem to me like a good fit for Danny Boyles style. No less, it is one of those films about foreign poverty, with a grand conscience, and those can turn out just awful. My perception is that, inevitably, people patronized (and then patronized) the film with work-righteous emotions fit for the occasion, and its distributors piled onto that package with the moniker that it was the feel-good movie of the year. No thanks.

But I watched it anyway, because it was just remastered onto Blu-Ray and I became an admirer of Danny Boyles wild directorial style from his science fiction masterpiece Sunshine, which ranks with Kubricks 2001 and Tarkovskys Solaris as perfected speculative fiction, lacking any mess of cowboys and indians in space with noises magically permeating vacuums.

Something surprised me about Slumdog Millionaire, though I ultimately found it flawed from its failure to resist utter sappiness with a hyper-romantic disregard of reality (too many perfect coincidences; it might as well have tried to be a Greek drama about gods and fates). The surprise for me was in its brash, stylistic disregard for the culture. Boyle shot the film with agitated camera movements, super-wide-angle lenses (practically fish-eyed), avant-garde compositions, skewed framings, and so forth  in other words, idiomatic to Boyles modernist style. (His cinematographer is the genius who shot Lars von Triers brilliant prelude to Antichrist.) Yet, if the original vision were that of the typical Birkenstock-armored documentarian, all of these stylistic measures would be a violation. It is in fact only at the end of the film (train station dancing sequence) where the Hindi cultural sensibility of Bollywood bridges the gap, and it becomes a merged work of cinema.

And that is the whole point. A Westerner visiting India arrives a Westerner and leaves a Westerner  show me exceptions and Ill show you a skeptic. The pretense of all filmmakers, composers, authors and visual artists who immerse themselves for the purpose of divining native art is perfectly inauthentic. (Notably, my favorite living composer, Philip Glass, invented the last major movement in serious contemporary music  Minimalism  under the guidance of Ravi Shankar when tasked with transcribing microtonal indigenous ragas into Western notation. Minimalism, and Glasss Minimalism, does not sound Indian, yet those Eastern fingerprints are all over the place.)

It only increased my otherwise simple affection for the film when I surfed around a bit only to find significant mass criticism against it for failing (in one fell swoop?) to capture the spirit and the desolation of Mumbai. I also find it comical as well as hypocritical that many are quite furious to know that the untrained child actors are still living amidst the depicted poverty. Surely they can only be prosperous and happy in comparison to Western standards of heavyweight wealth! And surely, snatching them from that slumdog environment will solve it all. Yet in truth, actors are merely work-for-hire, and it could only be an organized labor force with the full faith and credit of an adoring pop culture (Ill say it: the Hollywood Establishment) who could twist that vocation into something of hocus-pocus and when-you-wish-upon-a-star. One wonders whether, for example, any particular A-list actress complainant regularly follows up on the well-being of her immigrant gardener who, ahem, trims her bushes at her Malibu home.

In short, this is a subversive film  and on that level, I rather enjoyed it.

When the Academy Awards snubbed the Dark Knight for a best picture nomination back in 2009, I said whatever won better be a damn good film. And sure enough, I can see why they chose Slumdog Millionaire, as it's one of the best movies I've ever seen.

Slumdog Millionaire tells the story of Jamal Malik, a young man from the slums of Mumbai, India, who is one question away from winning the Indian version of Who Wants To Be a Millionaire. Considering that all kinds of doctors, scientists, and other geniuses have been previously stumped on the show, the producers and police think he cheated and interrogate him about how a nobody from the slums could possibly know the answers. In his defense, Jamal uses his past and childhood to tell how he knew the answers, and also reveal his motives in participating on the show.

Danny Boyle is another one of my favorite directors, and this movie in particular is the reason why. He directs the film beautifully and the cinematography is absolutely breathtaking. After watching the movie, I had a sudden desire to visit India.

The story is highly original, based off of a novel by some dude (sorry, too lazy to look it up). It's really a romance in disguise, but I won't say anything else about it to avoid spoilers. The way the story is told through flashback is highly intelligent. While many elements of the plot seem highly unlikely, it all ties into the film's theme of destiny.

The acting is pretty good, the standout performances being Dev Patel (by the way, The Last Airbender?!? WTF were you thinking?!?!), who plays the older Jamal, and the young boy who plays the younger version of Jamal. The woman who plays his love interest is also great. This movie also has one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in a film and it's used very effectively (Paper Planes, anyone?).

In summary, if you're still pissed about The Dark Knight not making the cut for the Oscars, don't be. While it's not as good as that film, Slumdog Millionaire is definitely a fantastic piece of cinema and a satisfying movie to watch. It's certainly one of the best movies I've ever seen.

Slumdog is a film that must be seen to be believed. It's a near-perfect masterpiece that totally deserves all the acclaim has received.

Set in 2006 India, the story revolved around Jamal Malik, a slum kid who managed to get on the Hindi version of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire?" and manages to get all the way to the final question. But, before he can answer the final question, he is arrested on suspicion of cheating. Then comes full force is basically his life story, and it's a powerful one that that. Interwoven with the questions, it tells how he knew the answers from his life experiences. Not only are the stories entertaining, they convey a powerful portrayal of how tough and unforgiving life was in India during the time period in which Jamal and his brother Salim were growing up.

The questions Jamal encounters on the show aren't entirely believable, which is a minor flaw, but the writing throughout the different sections of Jamal's life which coincide with each question is so superb (and some questions are just so hilariously coincidental) that this flaw can easily be overlooked along with the spots in which the pacing or script falters (which are few and very far between). Couple this with a terrific score, and taut direction from Danny Boyle (he was able to build the tension to the point of making my heart race by the end of the film) and you have an absolute winner.

Slumdog Millionaire is a brutally honest tale about a "slumdog" from India who was a contestant on "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" and won. He is accused of cheating because he is poor and uneducated. However, he claims "You don't have to be a genius to get the questions right" and most of the film is about him trying to prove this.

Although it is harsh and has a shocking truth about prejudices, it is very much a feel-good film. The soundtrack is incredibly upbeat and there's even some humor thrown into the mix.

What irked me though, was that its non-linear storyline was meant to be clever, but came off as formulaic and repetitive to me. The story can be summed up as: The slumdog is asked how he knew the question, he has a flashback to his childhood, which proves he knew it. Then they move on to the next question and it repeats in this manner about 8-10 times. This was only a minor issue for me though.

What amazed me the most though, was the cinematography. Every scene shines with dazzling, vivid colors and the lighting enhances them. Even the subtitles were enclosed in delightfully colored boxes, which is a bonus since the subtitles are used quite often. The immense beauty of Slumdog Millionaire really absorbed me into the film and is part of what made the movie memorable. 

Do I think it was deserving of its Best Picture win? Not really. However, it was still very entertaining and possibly one of the most visually stunning movies I've ever seen.

UPDATE: After a rewatch, I now believe it deserved its Oscar. :P

Slumdon millionaire is many things, it's a romance film in the vain of romeo and juliet, it's an underdog story in the vain of the Karate Kid, its a foreign film, an academy-award winning blockbuster, a tearjerker, and a feel-good film all rolled into one package, and also one of the best pictures of 2008.

I'm writing this review before I read all of the "I hated it so apparently I'm unique because I hate anything that's popular" threads, because every time I read those first I end up defending the movie and feel like I'm writing a personal message to those people instead of just saying why I did or did not like the movie. So here goes.

I loved Slumdog Millionaire. I am still somewhat baffled over the R rating. First of all as far as language goes I don't remember one single use of the F word although apparently it was used like twice. Which still shouldn't make it rated R because I've seen quite a few PG-13 movies that have used the F word twice or more. I do remember a couple of times hearing the S word. But hey its a movie. Lots of movies have the S word. Nudity/Sex: well you see a little kids bum and there's a scene where it is implied that a young girl is coerced into sleeping with a young boy. OK well, I see that on the news every time a kiddie porn ring is busted. They didn't show anything. They just imply that it happened. Blood/Violence: there is some violence and some pretty intense scenes but there is literally no blood or gore. You see people get shot and hit in the head with a crowbar and have acid poured into their eyes but you don't actually see any of the gore. Intense yes. Take a child to see it no. But I do remember watching an episode or 60 of 24 where Jack Bauer more than implies that he killed some dude by biting his jugular vein. I mean come on. Point = TV shows are more intense than this. Drugs/Alcohol etc. again TV is worse or equal to what was seen in this movie. I mean couldn't they have just put a Parental Discretion is advised instead of slapping an R rating on there just because it was made by Danny Boyle? Wow. OK rating rant over. The movie is a very charming story about two young brothers living in the slums of India who lose their mother and are forced to fend for themselves. It is also a love story about one of the brother's quest to reunite with a girl they meet who also has no parents. The way the story is told is interesting. We get to see the main character Jamal on the Indian version of the show Who Wants to Be a Millionaire answering all kinds of questions and at the same time he explaining how he knew the answers to the questions to a police chief who is trying to get him to confess to cheating. Each question leads to a flashback which is where the main story comes in. It is a very creative story and I thought very well crafted. While the actual elements are quite text book, (hero starts at home, goes on a quest, has adventures and whatnot, rescues the princess from the evil dragon, etc. whatever) but since when is that kind of a story not welcome? I like stories with happy endings. I don't think there is any hidden political agenda in the movie. I don't think Danny Boyle is naive or pompous or trying to talk down to anyone. I think he just wanted to tell an interesting engaging story about three very likable characters who are trying to deal with life, but in a very different setting than a lot of people are used to. Its kind of like Oliver Twist meets Homer's Odyssey meets -insert love story here- in India. I knew what the 20 million rupee question was going to be from the second he gets whacked over the head with the book in the beginning by the way, but the predictability of the movie doesn't take away from its enjoyment because it doesn't try to present itself as a movie that trying to keep you guessing or surprise you with intricate plot twists.

Great there I go. I haven't even read the hater's posts yet and I'm still defending the show based on what I'm sure they are all saying. Well whatever. I give the movie a 10. It deserved Best Picture of 2008.

Scenes of poverty and squalour may appear romantic to Westerners and to our snooty elite but for ordinary Indians they are nothing new. They are an everyday reality. However, one wonders what sort of mind can find such images aesthetically pleasing. Party-hopping socialites (for example, Shobhaa De after all her bombast of "enough is enough" after the Mumbai attack, went and watched a pirated copy!) who are distanced from such reality may find this film an "eye-opener" but for us it IS just poverty-porn. Leaving that aside, I have eight other objections to the film. 1) The director seems to RELISH showing violence. Some of it (like the police-torture) is quite needless. And why was the boy arrested in the first place? On what charge? Was it realistic? 2) How can a boy growing up in slums speak such accented English? Even if one assumes that the language he actually uses to communicate with the game-show host and the police officer is Hindi (granting the director the creative license to use a language better suited for international audiences), there are 2 instances where it is stretched too far: (a) when the boy becomes a 'guide' for foreign tourists at the Taj Mahal & (b) when he becomes a substitute-operator at the call-centre. 3) When the boy uses his 'lifeline' during the game-show, his friend discovers that she has forgotten her mobile and has to run back for it. This is plain Bollywood masala! Did the director HAVE to make it so melodramatic? 4) How did the boy know who invented the revolver just by watching his brother use it? How does his friend know about Benjamin Franklin? 5) "Darshan Do Ghanshyam" is NOT written by Surdas. It is written by Gopal Singh Nepali for the movie Narsi Bhagat (1957). This song is also credited as traditional and originally written by 15th century poet Narsi Mehta, whose life that film is based on. 6) After winning the game-show, the boy sits on the railway platform and nobody recognizes him! Considering the popularity of the show, is that realistic? 7) Two glaring omissions: To qualify for the show one has to answer several GK questions over phone or Internet. Even after making it to the show, a contestant can reach the hot-seat, only after "fastest finger first". All this is conveniently forgotten in the film. 8) And of course the greatest flaw in the storyline: programmes like 'Kaun Banega Crorepati' and 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire' are NOT telecast live. As a result the entire structure of the film becomes unrealistic. For a film that boasts of being realistic such a flaw cannot be overlooked.
Anyone else wants to say this is a g-r-e-a-t film despite all these flaws?

Rarely do I give a movie five stars. It is even rarer that I agree with what wins "Best Picture" in any given year. Dear readers, you are witnessing a rare moment on both counts. "Slumdog Millionaire" is deserving of every accolade that it received. 

Shortly before being presented with the final question in the Hindi version of "Who Wants to Be A Millionaire", Jamal Malik is detained due to allegations of possible cheating. Jamal grew up in an impoverished area and has no formal education, so the show's host doubts he actually knew the answers. As he is questioned, Malik flashes back through his remarkable life to each moment where he learned each answer. In the process, you find that Jamal is not on the show for the money at all ...

So well done. Rarely have I been this impressed with a movie, especially one that I went into with no expectations. I am let down by the "Best Picture" nearly annually and expected no different this time around. But this movie has it all. There is drama, action, intrigue, horrifying moments, touching moments, and ultimately a pretty solid love story. Most of all, the end game is always in doubt. Right up until the very end, you have no idea if Jamal is going to a. get a shot at that last question or b. get it right. 

If you haven't seen this movie, drop what you are doing and do so.
